141613.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
141613.value: 根據最近的研究發現，校園暴力及校園欺凌個案迅速上升，而在亞洲國家的情況更為嚴重 (Huang, Hong, & Espelage, 2012)。如何幫助及預防學童免受暴力傷害已經是教育和社會工作者一項迫切的任務。不幸的是，以往的研究發現，大部份防治校園欺凌計劃的效果欠佳 (Baldry & Farrington, 2004; Smith, Schneider, Smith, & Ananiadou, 2004)。而這些計劃都是由西方的國家發展出來，因此並不能完全適切地應用在本土華人的境況。以華人文化為中心，來發展一個有效防治學童暴力行為的介入方法，實在非常困難。但出乎意料地，過去三十年的研究卻發現日本及韓國的武術訓練，例如跆拳道、空手道及柔道，均能有效地減少學童的攻擊行為。但是，至今仍沒有實證為基礎的研究來評估中國武術（即功夫或國術）訓練作為介入方法去減少學童攻擊行為的成效。 此研究的目的是透過中國武術訓練計劃來重建小學學童的認知、情感及行為模式，藉以減低學童的攻擊行為。此舉既沒有標籤效應，亦可強身健體，而普遍華人家長都易於受落，視為其中一項的課外活動，傾向支持子女參加。 本研究不僅是首個以華人文化為中心思想，以武德提昇兒童的道德發展階段；並且，以嶄新的文獻作為基礎，來辨識兩類型的攻擊行為：反應型攻擊及操縱型攻擊行為 (Dodge & Coie, 1987; Fontaine, 2006; Cima & Raine, 2009; Fung, Raine, & Gao, 2009)，作為防治校園欺凌的創新介入策略。反應型攻擊者的特點是情緒暴躁、易於衝動和對週遭環境反應過敏，而攻擊行為是由憤怒驅使和情緒波動而產生的 (Raine et al., 2006)。相反，操縱型攻擊者則被視為有意圖和利益導向的欺凌者，他們對受害者欠缺同理心，被形容為冷血、透過攻擊行為來達到個人目的的欺凌者，是屬於精神病態的人際關係和情感中的範疇 (Brendgen et al., 2006)。 是次研究運用了縱向實驗及追蹤研究的設計，三種實驗的組別（武德訓練；武術訓練；武德和武術訓練）和兩種對照的組別（一般體育活動；沒有任何活動）於三個不同時段（基線、治療後及治療後十二個月）的結果作為比較。本研究假設反應型攻擊行為兒童衝動行為及憤怒情緒，會持續地減少；相反地，自我控制的能力會逐漸地提昇。而操控型攻擊行為兒童的自戀、缺乏情感等精神病態的特性會持續地減少；相反地，同理心的能力會逐漸地增強 (Lee, Vincent, Hart, & Corrado, 2003)。 總括而言，此研究旨在透過嚴謹的科學方法和數據，來驗證中國武德及武術訓練作為介入減少學童的反應型及操控型攻擊行為的成效。

141613.label: Realisation of objectives
141613.value: The project has been successfully implemented and completed on time. Open recruitment was through sending written invitations to all primary schools and children’s homes in Hong Kong. Responses from thirty-nine schools and three children’s homes were received. Eventually, twelve schools and one children’s home were randomly selected based on their geographical locations and academic bandings. Written consents from all schools and parents have been obtained before conducting the project. With this representative random sampling, a screening questionnaire was completed by 3,511 schoolchildren of Grade 2 to 5 from those twelve schools and one children’s home in Hong Kong. Through a rigorous experimental design and screening procedure, a high-risk clinical random sampling was well-identified. This is achieved by shortlisting those who scored z ≥ 1 on the total score of the Reactive-Proactive Aggression Questionnaire (21.09 out of 46) in their respective sites, resulting in total 298 schoolchildren (232 males and 66 females) out of 3,511 schoolchildren participating in the experiment. Since the mean of the total score of the Reactive-Proactive Aggression Questionnaire for general population was 5.28, all selectees are high-risk schoolchildren with the mean age of 8.53 (S.D. = 1.08). The selected 298 schoolchildren were randomly assigned into four conditions of groups: Skills-only, Philosophy-only, Skills-and-Philosophy, and Physical fitness (placebo). All participants, their parents/guardians, and the school personnel were blinded to the purpose of the four training packages. Each condition consisted of ten 90-minute weekly sessions (15 hours in total). All participants were assessed at baseline, post-training and 6 months after training. Each training session was administered according to the session plans written by four experienced martial arts instructors with at least 10 years of experience in Chinese martial arts practice, who were also the instructors of the program. The completed program was the first in the world to adopt the Essence of Chinese Martial Arts and Ethics (ECMA) to reduce reactive and proactive aggressive behaviour among schoolchildren. It resulted in the first piece of world-class scientific publication proving the significance of Chinese martial arts and ethics in improving mental health and externalizing problems. The publication generated from this study was a ground-breaking one even in the Chinese martial arts speciality. Having perhaps the longest history of all martial arts (over a thousand years), traditional Chinese martial arts training encompasses both skills (martial techniques or “wu gong”) and ethics (moral principles or “wu de”), under the directions of a highly respected instructor (“shi fu”) to his or her participants (disciples). Yet there was no literature and publication could be found in Chinese martial arts at all. On the other side, judo, taekwondo, aikido, karate, and boxing have been well proved and documented that it could effectively reduce children’s aggressive behaviour even in 70s and 80s. This study actually could make a distinctive contribution in Chinese martial arts field. The content of the ECMA program has been well documented and specifically addressed the characteristics of both reactive and proactive aggressors. In particular, the Skills-and-Philosophy Condition included both wu gong (skill-based martial techniques) and wu de (moral principles of martial arts). Teaching of wu gong involved the basic hand-forms and foot stances, che quan (dragging punch), defense skills, and dui chai (two-person combat sets). Teaching of wu de included a brief history of traditional Chinese martial arts, the fist salute, the martial idiom “xi quan xian xi de” (whoever wants to learn martial techniques must first acquire virtue), elucidation of wu jie (martial elite) versus wu zha (martial villain), an introduction to the wu jie ba tao (eight virtues of a martial elite: ren (benevolence), yi (justice), li (propriety), xin (trust), qin (diligence), jie (cleanliness), zhi (wisdom), and shi (timeliness), the principles of bu zhan er sheng (to beat the opponent without aggression) and bu zheng zhi zheng (non-violence and non-competition), elucidation of the martial motto “the least resourceful one is the most violent one,” and the idea that forbearance is no cowardice but strategic. Based on the social-information processing (SIP) model, we designed this original intervention to tackle different steps of cognitive distortions between reactive aggressors and proactive aggressors. It is known that reactive aggression is associated with cognitive distortion in the encoding and interpretation of social cues, which results in impulsive behaviour; whereas proactive aggression is related to distortion in evaluation of outcomes and aggression itself, which results in personal goal-oriented behaviour. The aims of the study were to redefine how aggressive children value and perceive aggressive behaviour, and to change their perception of power and control through Chinese martial arts training. Those aims have been well achieved. The intervention encouraged participants to handle their interpersonal conflicts in a nonviolent way through Choy Li Fut martial arts and moral philosophy training. Reactive aggression and proactive aggression were expected to be reduced through tackling proactive aggressors’ instrumental view of aggression (steps 3 to 5 in the SIP model) as well as reactive aggressors’ misinterpretation and hostile attributions toward neutral situations (steps 1 and 2 in the SIP model). The martial skills taught were Choy Li Fut defense rather than attack techniques, while the martial moral philosophy focused on changing participants’ beliefs toward aggression, enhancing empathy and encouraging prosocial behaviour to provide participants with alternative solutions to interpersonal conflicts. The intervention intended to help children with proactive aggression by developing other-centeredness and team cooperation. The intervention also intended to reduce proactively aggressive children’s overestimation of their competence, narcissism, and egocentricity, which are associated with proactive aggression. For reactive aggressors, the shi fu focused on teaching them how to perceive and assess others’ provocations in an objective way and provided alternatives to ease tension and conflicts among peers. This was expected to help reactive aggressors by expanding their ability to pick up cues in ambiguous situations. During classes, the shi fu observed the children’s anger arousal during provocative and conflictual situations, then strengthened their anger management and competence through breathing exercises and Chinese martial skills practice. The children also had to reflect and practice both in training and daily life, and regularly report any changes and difficulties they encountered to the shi fu. Results from linear mixed model indicated that the Time × Training interaction effects were significant for aggressive behaviour (reactive and proactive), delinquent behaviour, anxiety/depression, and attention problems. Although all measures declined in all conditions over time, only the Skills-and-philosophy condition showed a significant reduction at post-training and/or 6-month follow-up compared with the placebo condition. In short, these results showed that the Skills-and-Philosophy training was the most effective intervention among all conditions across the three checkpoints. Nonetheless, it was out of our expectation that no significant mediation effect was found between the group assignment and reduction of proactive/reactive aggression. One of the possibilities may be that there were a lot of variances among children as they were still in their developmental stages. An even larger sample size in future studies might help to solve this problem. To conclude, the project has achieved the main objective which traditional Chinese martial arts and philosophy training was proven to be superior to solely playing sports or merely teaching moral lessons in reducing aggressive behaviour.

141613.label: Major findings and research outcome
141613.value: This pioneering study produces wide impacts, both academic and social, locally and internationally. Being the first scientific study which aims at utilizing Chinese martial arts to reduce reactively and proactively aggressive behaviour among schoolchildren, this project has generated important implications to many stakeholders in the society, including schools, teachers, parents, social workers, counsellors, psychologists, and every individual who needs to deal with children and aggression. The results provided innovative and valuable social impacts to promoting “zero” violence and anti-aggressive cultures in communities. This single-blind, cluster randomized longitudinal study found that only the Skills-and-philosophy condition showed a significant reduction at post-training and/or 6-month follow-up compared with the placebo condition. In the past, the general public used to hold a negative view towards martial arts training, which may enhance childhood aggression, instead of reducing it; but the findings of this ECMA project suggested otherwise. In order to inform this finding to as many audiences as possible, the Principal Investigator and the Co-investigator organized a press conference "An evidence-based evaluation on the effectiveness of Traditional Chinese martial arts training in reducing schoolchildren aggression" on July 11, 2016, which attracted attendants including reporters from Ming Pao, Headline, am730, Metro Daily, Hong Kong Economic Times, Ta Kung Pao, Oriental Daily, Hong Kong Commercial Daily, Wen Wei Pao, etc. The press conference was a huge success and resulted in widespread news coverage which ensured successful transfer of the message to the public. Since then, the Principal Investigator and the Co-investigator were interviewed by numerous newspaper, TV, and radio programmes. For example, Dr Fung was invited by Radio Television Hong Kong (RTHK) to present the findings of the ECMA program in two radio programmes (教學有心人 and 我們不是怪獸) in September 2016 and April 2018 respectively. Internationally, the project led to publications in top international journals and presentations at worldwide conferences. This work was presented in two international conferences, one held in Switzerland (ICBTS 2016 International Social Sciences and Education Research Conference) and one as a Keynote Speaker held in Hong Kong (ICCAP 2016: 18th International Conference on Child and Adolescent Psychopathology). In 2017, this research was awarded with Excellence in Knowledge Transfer Award. In 2018, this research was published in a Q1 international journal, Journal of Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics (Impact Factor: 2.393).

141613.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
141613.value: In December 2017, OECD announced a worldwide survey on life satisfaction among 540,000 15-year-old middle school students. School bullying in Hong Kong was the worst among 72 countries and regions. 32.3% of HK students said they have suffered bullying in a month, which was 3 times higher than Taiwan (10.7%) and much higher than United States (18.9%). Despite this alarming situation, there was no intervention to date aiming to reduce aggressive behaviour among high-risk children. The result of this study proved that combined traditional Chinese martial arts skills and moral philosophy training is an effective way to reduce proactive and reactive aggressive behaviour. In fact, not only aggressive children could be benefitted from learning martial arts and philosophy, children without an aggressive tendency could also be benefitted. Martial arts training per se is an enjoyable exercise, which could benefit psychological well-being and enhance moral standard. Children with martial arts training were more confident in their physical and mental abilities, more disciplined, and more cooperative. Therefore, martial arts training should be considered to be included in school curriculum as a non-labelling way to reduce school violence as well as promoting physical and mental abilities of students.

141613.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
141613.value: Dr Fung’s “Essence of Chinese Martial Arts and Ethics” (ECMA) Program is the first scientific study aiming at utilizing Chinese martial arts to reduce reactively and proactively aggressive behaviour among schoolchildren. High-risk children were selected from 12 primary schools and 1 children’s home, and received one of the four kinds of 10-session intervention: Martial arts skills only; Martial arts ethics only; Combination of skills and ethics; or Physical fitness only. Results suggested that the combination of martial arts skills and ethics showed the greatest effectiveness in reducing aggressive behaviour compared with other interventions, the high-risk participants displayed 42%, 65%, 55% and 40% of reduction in their reactive aggression, proactive aggression, delinquent behaviour and attention problems respectively. This study also provides insights for school-based interventions that solely playing sports or merely teaching moral lessons may not be comprehensive enough for high-risk aggressive schoolchildren. This study supports that when sport involvement is combined with children’s improved moral reasoning, it could enhance the effectiveness in reducing aggression. In short, combined traditional Chinese martial arts skills and moral philosophy training should be considered for inclusion in school curriculum as a non-labelling way to reduce school violence and facilitate the creation of harmonious schools.

142013.label: Project Title(Chinese)
142013.value: 中国离婚法实践及两性不平等

142013.label: Co - Investigator(s)
142013.value: Dr Ng, Kwaihang Prof Peerenboom, Randall

142013.label: Project Objectives
142013.value: Different from previous studies that rely on court archive, legal regulations, sporadic interviews, published judgments, media reports, and anecdotal accounts to study divorce law practice in China, in this Project we will employ a new method – by directly examining the dynamics of the divorce case hearings. It will identify the genres and characteristics of discourse deployed by Chinese judges, which will form the basis to understand the developing norms and the operational patterns of Chinese courts. The Project will explore whether the discourse of judges may reinforce and perpetuate the patriarchal norms and values that render women the passive recipients of the consequences of marital breakdown. Specifically, by looking at how discourses are deployed in situ, we will explore whether judicial mediation as an institutional procedure reinforces the gender hierarchy, despite its formal commitment to promoting gender equality. Judicial mediation has long been hailed as a unique way of dispute resolution in China (Fu and Cullen 2011; Hand 2010). This Project explores whether judicial mediation may undermine the rights of these battered women in divorce cases. It will shed light on the hidden problems created by a system that values conciliation and quick resolution over adjudication and the delivery of justice. It thus raises important questions with regard to the policies on China’s family law procedures; in particular, it points to the inadequacies in safeguarding the human rights of women who suffer domestic violence. Policy recommendations will be generated for reforms to China’s civil procedure and social policies against gender inequality. Through examining the ways judges negotiate the contested meanings of divorce with litigants in China, this Project will provide a story on the relationship between courtroom discourse and gender inequality in China’s context. Exploring the social forces underneath the discourses, it will enrich the literature of comparative studies on law and language, which has most drawn from the experience of other countries (see Collier 1988; Fineman 1991; Ehrlich 1998; Hirsch 1998; Mir-Hosseini 2001).

Exploring the social forces underneath the discourses, it will enrich the literature of comparative studies on law and language, which has most drawn from the experience of other countries (see Collier 1988; Fineman 1991; Ehrlich 1998; Hirsch 1998; Mir-Hosseini 2001).

142013.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
142013.value: Divorce law practice is at the heart of realizing gender equality. The existing literature, until recently, has rarely addressed this relationship, despite the fact that gender inequality is a grave social problem in contemporary China. This Project expands our preliminary research on the interplay between courtroom discourse and gender inequality to four places with representative profiles of different levels of caseload, education level, economic development, and institutional development. Through empirically examining the dynamics of court hearings and paying particular attention to courtroom discourse, this Project will identify how judges and litigants understand and make use of the family law. This focus on actual family court practices further allows us to explore the underlying social and cultural forces shaping the rule of law in China today. The findings of this Project will contribute to the scholarship on both law and society and law and language, including how gender hierarchy is contested, reproduced, and perpetuated in court, how ordinary people view the law and justice, and how the patterns of divorce law practice affect the realization of basic human rights. It will also generate policy recommendations for legal reforms in China and provide evidence for broader theoretical debates. 基于实地调查和话语研究，本研究试图理解中国法院离婚法的实践与两性不平等的关系。它将揭示两性不平等是如何通过法庭调解完成和强化的。本项目将提升我们对中国法院运作的理解以及对社会平等的影响。

142013.label: Major findings and research outcome
142013.value: The approaches of the Chinese courts in handling divorce litigation have perpetuated gender inequality in China's society. It is most clearly seen in the mediation process. This is clear shown on the issues of divorce itself and domestic violence. fundamentally the reasons are the incentives created by the assessment criteria on the judges.

142013.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
142013.value: I am developing these findings into a book systematically examining the divorce litigation. I am now collecting more data on the issues of child custody, property division, and sex related injuries. Together they will offer a comprehensive picture on how divorce litigation is processed in China and the gendered consequences.

142013.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
142013.value: Based on observations of court trials and extensive interviews with judges, we explores how judicial mediation and other practices in China undermines the rights of women in divorce cases. We find that, for example, even if the judges are able to establish that domestic violence is committed, it is often erased in the stage of judicial mediation. This is because judicial mediation inevitably focuses on settlement arrangements. Lingering reference to domestic abuse would simply invite new denials or refutations from the abuser. It thus risks ruining the mediation efforts made by the judge. This tendency is also clear on the discourses' impact. Our findings raise important questions with regard to the compulsory practice of mediation in family cases in China. It also sheds light on the hidden problems created by judicial mediation or conciliation in general.

142513.label: Project Objectives

142513.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
142513.value: Today more and more people are interacting with genetic information outside of the context of the traditional medical system. One example of this is the proliferation of direct-to-consumer genetic testing services, which purport to provide customers with information about things like ancestry, disease risk, paternity, athletic ability and intelligence. Critics of such services insist that laypeople lack the requisite expertise to make sense of genetic test results, and that such tests may lead people to have a distorted understanding of their risk for contracting certain diseases or developing certain medical conditions. Proponents of direct-to-consumer genetic testing, on the other hand, insist that customers have the ‘right’ to access knowledge about their own genomes, and that, through interacting with their genetic information they can develop the knowledge they need to take control of their health and make better medical and lifestyle decisions. This project aims to understand how users of direct-to-consumer genetic testing services use online forums and social networking tools to share information and advice, engage in joint problem solving, and collaboratively construct knowledge about genetics. The project combines the expertise of a discourse analyst with that of a geneticist in order to determine the relationship between the ways participants in online discussions about genetics discursively construct ‘facts’ and negotiate claims of knowledge and expertise and the quality and accuracy of the information and advice that they exchange. The primary data will come from the interactions among participants in public discussion forums of commercial and non-commercial websites for personal genomics. Data will also include in-depth qualitative interviews with users of direct-to-consumer genetic testing services focusing on how practices of sharing information and engaging in online discussions about their genomes with other customers affect their health decisions and behavior. The project has direct applications to understanding and improving health communication related to genetic testing, as well broader implications for the study of how laypeople understand and make use of scientific knowledge. Results of the project will be used to design an undergraduate course in personal genomics for non-science majors using online collaborative knowledge building tools. They will also be used to formulate recommendations for doctors, nurses and genetic counselors for dealing with patients who have engaged in direct-to-consumer genetic testing, and for customers who need to develop useful strategies for interpreting their results and communicating about them with others. 現今，越來越多人在傳統的醫療體系之外接觸基因資訊。為顧客提供血緣、疾病風險、親子鑑定、運動天份及智力等資訊，直接面向消費者的基因檢測服務日漸普及，就是其中一個例子。有批評聲音指出，一般外行人欠缺必要的專門知識理解基因檢測結果，引致人們曲解對感染某些疾病或發展某種症狀的風險。另一方面，支持者則堅稱顧客有知道自己基因資訊的權利，透過接觸自己的基因資訊，顧客可認知如何掌握自己的健康及作出對自己醫療上及生活方式最好的決定。 本項目旨在理解此等基因檢測服務顧客，如何利用網上討論區及社交網絡工具 ，分享關於這方面的資訊及意見、參與排解疑難、及合作建構關於基因的知識。本項目結合篇章分析及遺傳學兩方面學者的專業知識，找出網上關於基因知識討論中，參與者推論得出的「事實」以及說服過程中提出的所謂專業知識，和他們交流資料及意見的質素以及準確性的關係。 主要分析數據來自商業及非商業個人基因網站上，公開討論區參與者的交流。其他分析數據亦包括與這些基因檢測服務用家的深入質性研究訪談，訪談集中了解資料分享與網上討論參與如何影響其他顧客對他們健康所作出的決定與習慣 本頂目對理解及改善關於基因測試的健康傳播有直接應用，亦可擴闊一般外行人如何明白及利用科學知識的研究。本項目的研究成果會用作設計一個給非主修理學學生，關於個人基因知識的本科生課程，課程運用網上合作知識建設工具建立。研究成果亦會用於幫助醫生、護士及基因顧問，作出應對這些顧客的建議，以及幫助這些顧客如何有用地理解測試結果，及跟別人表達這些資訊。

142813.label: Project Objectives
142813.value: To integrate positive psychology and elements of music therapy in designing a protocol for treating adolescents with suicidal ideation. To examine the effectiveness of the designed protocol in increasing a sense of hope, enhancing emotional competence and promoting problem-solving abilities, hence decreasing anxiety, depression and suicidal ideation in adolescents. To produce a soft copy (DVD) of the manual detailing the protocol, program materials and results of the study, which will be distributed to all secondary schools in Hong Kong.

To examine the effectiveness of the designed protocol in increasing a sense of hope, enhancing emotional competence and promoting problem-solving abilities, hence decreasing anxiety, depression and suicidal ideation in adolescents.
To produce a soft copy (DVD) of the manual detailing the protocol, program materials and results of the study, which will be distributed to all secondary schools in Hong Kong.

142813.label: Realisation of objectives
142813.value: Based on the theoretical framework of positive psychology and music therapy, a protocol on positive psychology (PP) and another protocol integrating positive psychology and elements of music therapy (PPMT) were developed with the assistance of a music therapist and our research team. Increase in emotional competence, hope, and problem solving abilities of people have been found to be associated with decrease in anxiety, depression and suicidal ideation. Music therapy has also been found to be related with the alleviation of mental health problems. With reference to the conceptual framework in enhancing emotional competence, promoting hope, and increasing problem solving abilities, the intervention program aimed to facilitate the adolescents to (1) increase sensitivity to and understanding of self-emotions, (2) develop appropriate ways to express emotions and enhance positive emotions, (3) develop goal-setting skills and increase a sense of agency, and (4) foster competence in problem solving and develop different pathways during the goal-pursuit process. The full protocol was published in Chinese in a standardized manual. Each protocol consists of 10 sessions, with different types of group-based programs such as mirror game, percussion variation, music hunt, emotion radio, collage art expression, music guided imagery, guided drawing, music and craftwork, music story, and lyrics sharing. The principals of nine secondary schools with different bandings from the three main geographical districts in Hong Kong were invited and consented to participate in this project. A total of 9 integrated PPMT groups (positive psychology and music therapy) were launched in 3 schools, while 9 positive psychology (PP) groups were launched in another 3 schools by three social workers with training in positive psychology and music therapy. The remaining 3 schools act as wait-list control schools. Supervision and monitoring were constantly conducted by the Principal Investigator and the music therapist to ensure intervention fidelity. Screening was done by Suicidal Ideation sub-scale and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) and grade 8 to grade 9 students with high score in both scales were invited to join either the PPMT or PP group. Each group has about 6 participants. Consent forms were signed by the participating students and their parents. A total of 10 sessions was carried out for each group and each session lasted for about one and a half hour. The groups were run in the schools after the normal school hour. Hence, objective 1 has been achieved. To evaluate the effectiveness of the programme, questionnaires incorporating measures of anxiety and depression, hope, social problem solving, emotional competence, and suicidal ideation were designed for screening, as well as conducting pre-test and post-test evaluation. The questionnaire was completed by all grade 8 and grade 9 students in 9 schools, while those with the highest scores in HADS and suicidal ideation sub-scale in the experimental schools were invited to participate in the PP and PPMT groups. A total of 18 groups, 9 on PP and 9 on PPMT, have been launched. Pre-test and post-test data (T1and T2) were collected from the participating schools. Qualitative feedback on the programs from the participants was also collected. Evaluation meetings were held with the school social workers and the teachers, and positive feedback was obtained from the schools and the students. A series of 2 (experimental vs. control) x 2 (pre vs. post) repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) showed that students in both the PPMT and PP experimental groups had significant increase in emotional competence and hope, and significant decrease in anxiety and depression when compared with those in the control groups after intervention. Students in PPMT groups also had significant decrease in depression when compared with the PP groups after intervention. Hence, the designed protocol was found to be effective in increasing hope and emotional competence, while decreasing anxiety and depression in adolescents. However, results did not show significant increase in problem solving abilities and significant decrease in suicidal ideation of the adolescents. So the designed protocol was not effective in increasing problem solving abilities and decreasing suicidal ideation. As the principals of the wait-list control schools could not spare time for us to collect T2 data, comparison of the experimental groups with the control schools could not be made. Efforts have been made to encourage the principals to help collect the questionnaires but in vain. Hence, the final control groups were students from the six schools that participated in the PPMT and PP programmes. As discussed in the journal paper, further mediation analyses showed that the PPMT intervention predicted significant increases in hope, while hope was significantly associated with reduced adolescent anxiety. The PPMT intervention also predicted significant increase in emotional competence, yet the path from increase in emotional competence to decrease in anxiety was not significant. Objective 2 has been achieved to a great extent. A press conference was held in Jan 2016 to disseminate the results. The conference was officiated by Prof. Linda Li, Associate Provost, City University of Hong Kong. About 100 participants, including social workers, teachers, educational and clinical psychologists, joined the conference. Immediately after the conference, a workshop was held to share our experiences in conducting PP and PPMT groups in the secondary schools. The event was reported by different newspapers and media. A total of 500 CDs, a manual comprising the protocol, program materials and results of the study were produced and distributed to the secondary schools and social welfare agencies in Hong Kong. The soft copy of the manual was also uploaded to the Positive Education Laboratory for downloading by people all over the world. There is constant request from the social workers and teachers to get a copy of the manual. The Principal Investigator has presented this study in four international conferences from 2015 to 2018, both in Hong Kong, Toronto, and Orlando. The presentations received positive feedback from both local and overseas participants. Hence, objective 3 has been achieved.

142813.label: Major findings and research outcome
142813.value: A total of 1402 Grade 8 to Grade 9 students from 9 secondary schools filled in the Chinese version of the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) and the Suicidal Ideation sub-scale. Nine integrated groups (both music therapy and positive psychology) were conducted in three of the schools. The mean age of the participants was 13.6. A total of 108 students with the highest scores in both scales were screened as potential participants. They were randomized into treatment groups (n=55) and control groups (n=53). The integrated program groups and control groups had matched demographic variables. Following the same procedure, participants of the nine positive psychology groups were recruited from the other three schools. There were 60 participants in the positive psychology groups and 59 in the control groups. The positive psychology groups and control groups had matched demographic variables. Participants of the integrated program showed greater increases in hope and emotional competence following the intervention, when compared with the control group. The Group × Time interaction for hope was statistically significant (F=9.583, p<.01). The Group × Time interaction for emotional competence was statistically significant (F=4.291, p<.05). Yet the integrated program might not impact the participants’ problem-solving abilities (F=.075, n.s.). Participants of the integrated program showed greater decreases in anxiety and depressive symptoms following the intervention, when compared with the control group. The Group × Time interaction for anxiety symptoms was statistically significant (F=10.001, p<.01). The Group × Time interaction for depressive symptoms was statistically significant (F=4.930, p<.05). Yet we failed to find evidence on the impact of the integrated program on change in suicidal ideation (F=.589, n.s.). Similarly, participants of the positive psychology group showed greater increases in hope (F=7.988, p<.01) and emotional competence (F=3.966, p<.05) as well as greater decreases in anxiety (F=7.563, p<.01) and depressive symptoms (F=17.357, p<.001) following the intervention, when compared with the control group. The increase in social problem solving abilities and decrease in suicidal ideation were not significant. Participants in PPMT groups showed significant decrease in depression when compared with those in PP groups. As discussed in the journal paper, further mediation analyses showed that the PPMT intervention predicted significant increase in hope, while hope was significantly associated with reduced adolescent anxiety. The PPMT intervention also predicted significant increase in emotional competence, yet the path from increase in emotional competence to decrease in anxiety was not significant

142813.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
142813.value: The programme can be tried in primary school students. The Principal Investigator has conducted a similar programme with eight groups of students (64 students) in 5 primary schools and the result showed that the programme was effective in decreasing students’ anxiety. In addition, with some modification in the level of difficulties and programme format, 2 groups (12 students) were run with primary school students with dyslexia. Positive result was obtained. As positive psychology and elements of music therapy are found to be effective in alleviating mental health problems, different components of positive psychology, e.g. gratitude, optimism, use of character strength, can be further incorporated into the programmes, integrated with different types of expressive arts therapy such as art therapy, music therapy, drama therapy, dance therapy, etc. The programmes can be tried in different target groups, such as students with special education needs and students with different types of mental health problems, such as autism and ADHD. Furthermore, programmes in enhancing emotional competence and social competence, integrating elements of music therapy, can be conducted with students with anxiety and depression. The number of participants can be increased and different evaluation methods, such as observation and case study, can be conducted.

142813.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
142813.value: Incorporating the theoretical framework of positive psychology and music therapy, the present study aims to examine the effectiveness of a designed protocol, integrating positive psychology and elements of music therapy, in increasing the sense of hope, enhancing emotional competence and promoting problem-solving abilities, hence decreasing anxiety, depression and suicidal ideation in adolescents. A total of 227 Grade 8 and Grade 9 students from nine secondary schools participated in the project, with 55 participated in 9 positive psychology and music therapy (PPMT) groups, 60 in 9 positive psychology (PP) groups, 112 in control groups. Results showed that both the PPMT and PP programs were effective in increasing hope, enhancing emotional competence, decreasing anxiety and depression in adolescents. PPMT program is more effective in decreasing depression than PP program. The integrated program can assist in early prevention and intervention for adolescents with mental health problems. This research provides evidence that integrating music therapy and positive psychology is effective in in increasing hope, enhancing emotional competence, decreasing anxiety and depression in adolescents. The soft copy of the manual detailing the protocol, program materials and result of the study is uploaded to the website and benefits social workers and psychologists all over the world.

143113.label: Project Objectives
143113.value: Examine and compare existential quantification in Mandarin and Cantonese. Examine and compare distributivity and universal quantification in Mandarin and Cantonese. Examine and compare counting and proportional quantifiers in Mandarin and Cantonese. Examine the syntax and semantics of multiple quantifications in Mandarin and Cantonese. 143113.label: Realisation of objectives
143113.value: The five objectives have been achieved, with results summarized as follows: Objective 1: Examine and compare existential quantification in Mandarin and Cantonese Our focus has been on Cantonese pre-predicate jau5 ‘have’, which has been argued to be (i) a preposed perfective marker, (cf. Cheung 1972/2007, Yue-Hashimoto 1993, etc.), or (ii) an emphatic adverb (cf. Cheung 1972/2007, Matthews & Yip 1994, etc.). We instead found that Cantonese pre-predicate jau5 is an assertive existential quantifier, operating in the domain of verbs and their event time, with its assertive meanings sensitive to (i) the lexical aspect of the verbal predicates, and (ii) the specificity of the event or situation denoted. The findings and analysis of jau5 ‘have’ have further deepened our understanding of existential quantification in Chinese, which reveals that Chinese does have a type of existential quantifier intertwined with assertion (cf. Huang 1981). The results lead to two theoretical implications on eventualities: (i) final endpoints or boundaries of telic situations should linguistically be differentiated between actualized ones and potential ones, following Dahl’s (1981) proposal; and (ii) stage-level statives form a natural class with Activities, Semelfactives, Accomplishments and Achievements, suggesting a remapping of stage-level statives to the event group rather than the state group. The above has been discussed in the paper titled “On the semantics of Cantonese pre-predicate jau5 “have” --- an existential quantifier of the assertive type” (under review, see Part C, (1)). Objective 2: Examine and compare distributivity and universal quantification in Mandarin and Cantonese The concepts of “distributivity”, “universal quantification” and domain restriction have not been made clear in previous studies. To give a clearer picture of these concepts, we have examined classifier reduplication in Mandarin and Cantonese. Classifier reduplication “CL + CL” in Chinese is said to convey two readings: (1) a universal/distributive reading and (2) a plural reading of “many”. Our study found that adnominal “CL + CL” cannot be a quantifier, which accounts for its natural co-occurrence with another distributive quantifier, with the distributive interpretation of the sentence coming from the distributive quantifier. Adnominal “CL + CL” is instead a modifier, and depending on whether a distributive operator (D-operator) is present or not, it has two interpretations: (a) licensed by the D-operator, “CL + CL” in “CL + CL…dou1/dou” does not serve as a quantifier but a modifier of which presence serves to regulate the quantification domain of dou1/dou; and (b) without the presence of any D-operator, “CL + CL” serves as a modifier to convey the “many” reading, which is ambiguous between the strong “proportional” reading and the weak “cardinal” reading. Our study of adnominal “CL+CL” implies that domain restriction in Chinese is overtly realized in grammatical form by means of the reduplicative classifier (when combined with a D-operator). Overt restriction is observed not only in adnominal reduplicative classifiers, but in the adverbial universal quantification of quan-dou ‘all-all’ as well. Both seem to suggest that Chinese may not be a covert strategy language. Moreover, the heterogeneity of the meanings of reduplicative classifiers also calls for a finer classification within the family of universal quantifying expressions, which will have impact of theories related to quantification in Chinese and natural language at large. The above has been discussed in the paper titled “Maximality and Classifier Reduplication in Cantonese” (under review, see Part C, (4)). Objective 3: Examine and compare counting and proportional quantifiers in Mandarin and Cantonese Cantonese proportional D-quantifiers and A-quantifiers are analogous to those in Mandarin Chiense, except that Cantonese D-quantifiers tend to be more readily to be modified and constitute morpho-syntactically more complex quantifiers. However, Cantonese has some distinct proportional or partitive quantifiers not found in Mandarin Chinese. Firstly, Cantonese can express proportional meaning through the verbal suffix –hoi1 ‘open’, defined as a generic quantifier, relating the set in the restrictor, which can be contributed by variables of any kind, to that in the matrix or the nuclear scope, giving a proportional reading. Secondly, Cantonese gam2 can be considered as a post-verbal particle indicating partitive quantification, as in V-gam2-quantified NP, with the presence of gam2 giving the quantified NPs a partitive reading out of a total which may be determined contextually. The above has been discussed in the paper titled “Quantification in Cantonese” (to appear, see Part C, (2)). The study proportional quantifiers has also been extended to the occurrence of Mandarin cai ‘only’ in complex sentences, which focuses on the licensing relation of cai in the main clause with the restrictive clause. The findings have been summarized in the paper titled “The semantics of Chinese adverb cai in complex sentences and the license of relevant constructions” (under review, see Part C, (3)). Objective 4: Examine the semantics of multiple quantifications in Mandarin and Cantonese Co-occurrence of multiple quantifiers generally renders ungrammaticality or unnaturalness if relevant sentences are literally translated into English. This is particularly productive in Cantonese, and despite the multiple occurrences of quantifiers, relevant sentences show no redundancy in meaning. However, no systematic account within semantic frameworks has been proposed to account for the natural co-occurrence in Cantonese. Our study of scope relations among multiple quantifiers reveals that word order is a parameter for determining scope relation in Mandarin and Cantonese, which further supports the linearity principle given in the Isomorphic Principle, as pointed out in S. F. Huang (1981). Cantonese may be a language with strict isomorphism or iconicity. Moreover, the relatively less productive co-occurrence in Mandarin makes it appeal more to syntactic structures and adverbs, with the latter accompanied by lexical stress to compensate its lack of post-verbal focus particles. Contrarily, Cantonese relies on post-verbal particles and their co-occurrence, governed by scope order and the linearity principle. The above has been discussed in the paper titled “Quantification in Cantonese” (to appear, see Part C, (2)) and the paper titled “Maximality and Classifier Reduplication in Cantonese” (under review, see Part C, (4)). Objective 5: Derive a landscape of quantifiers and predict possible and impossible patterns of quantification in Chinese Regarding this, we found that negation in Chinese reveals two possible types of negation in natural language: (1) negation solely determined by semantics, with semantics overriding any possible syntactic constraints; and (2) negation pre-determined by syntax, with semantics failing to override syntactic constraints. Based further on their relation with eventualities, a landscape of negation has been built up. This has been discussed in the paper titled “Non-uniformity of Chinese Negators mei(you) and bu towards Focus”, which has been published (see Part C, (5)) and the one titled “Focus, Negators and Event Quantification in Chinese --- How focus helps shape negation in our natural language” (accepted, see Part C, (6)). Secondly, based on results of the above objectives, we have further examined the overall quantificational pattern in Cantonese, and come up with an overall description of quantification in Cantonese. This has been presented in the paper titled “Quantification in Cantonese” (to appear, see Part C, (2)). Finally, we have also conducted a brief overview on the quantificational pattern in Naxi, a Tibeto-Burman language. Naxi is chosen due to its special syntax , which would therefore help predict possible and impossible quantificational patterns in the Chinese language family. The picture of quantification in Naxi has been presented in the paper titled “Quantification in Naxi” (to appear, see Part C, (7)).

143113.label: Major findings and research outcome
143113.value: Major findings and research outcome of the project: (i) Chinese has a type of existential quantifier intertwined with assertion --- assertive existential quantifier, which is realized by Cantonese pre-predicate jau5 ‘have’. (see (1), Part C) (ii) As an assertive existential quantifier operating in the domain of verbs and their event time, assertive meaning of jau5 is sensitive to (i) the lexical aspect of the verbal predicates, and (ii) the specificity of the even t or situation denoted. (see (1), Part C) (iii) Domain restriction in Chinese is overtly realized in grammatical form by means of the reduplicative classifier. (see (4), Part C) (iv) Reduplicative classifier in Chinese cannot be a quantifier, but a modifier serving the function of domain regulator. Counterparts can also be found in quan-dou ‘all-all’, with quan claimed to be a universal quantifier. A finer classification within the family of universal quantifying expressions is needed for Chinese. (see (4), Part C) (v) Although Cantonese proportional D-quantifiers and A-quantifiers may be similar to those in Mandarin Chinese, Cantonese is distinct in having verbal suffixes performing proportional or partitive quantification. (see (2) and (3), Part C) (vi) The co-occurrence of multiple forms of quantifiers is particularly rich in Cantonese, as compared with that in Mandarin. Cantonese may be a language with strict isomorphism or iconicity. (see (2) and (4), Part C) (vii) Regarding negation, it is found that negation performed by bu ‘not’, mei(-you) ‘not(-have)’ and bu(-shi) ‘not(-be)’ reveal a preliminary landscape of negation: (1) negation solely determined by semantics, with semantics overriding any possible syntactic constraints, as in bu; and (2) negation pre-determined by syntax, with semantics failing to override syntactic constraints, as in mei and bu-shi. (see (5) and (6), Part C) (viii) Regarding quantification in Cantonese, an overall quantificational pattern has been presented. The rich repertoire of post-verbal particles in Cantonese and its natural occurrence of multiple quantifiers are what make the quantificational pattern of Cantonese not completely the same as that of Mandarin. While Mandarin appeals more to syntactic structures and adverbs, with adverbs accompanied by lexical stress to compensate its lack of post-verbal focus particles, Cantonese relies on post-verbal particles and their co-occurrence. (see (2), Part C) (ix) A brief overview on the quantificational pattern in Naxi, a Tibeto-Burman language with special syntax, helps predict possible and impossible quantificational patterns in the Chinese language family. (see (7), Part C).

143113.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
143113.value: The research can be further developed in at least the following directions: (i) Further study can be conducted on negation to examine how the landscape of negators can be incorporated into the landscape of quantifiers. (ii) More cross-dialectal and cross-linguistic data can be included to enrich the landscape of quantifiers. (iii) More quantifiers which are claimed to be universal quantifiers can be further studied to verify the finding that Chinese may not be a covert strategy language in terms of domain restriction, which has gained support from our detailed study on reduplicative classifier and quan ‘all’. (iv) The study on Cantonese pre-predicate jau5 ‘have’ reveals how assertive existential quantification operates in the domain of verbs and their event time. Further study can be conducted on the issue of the extent to which semantic representations bear on event and individual quantifications. (v) The study of the co-occurrence of multiple quantifiers in Cantonese shows that Cantonese may be a language with strict isomorphism. Further study can be conducted on the extent to which syntactic difference bears on the semantics of counters in natural language.

143113.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
143113.value: Quantifiers are used to express quantity of things or amount of stuff in human language, and languages may differ with respect to strategies of quantification. Much cross-linguistic work on quantification covers a wide range of languages from different linguistic families, but barely touches on Chinese. This study makes special reference to Mandarin Chinese and Cantonese, and investigates the semantic aspect of existential, universal, distributive, counting and proportional quantifications. It focuses on the following issues: (a) examine and compare existential quantification in Mandarin Chinese and Cantonese; (b) examine and compare distributivity and universal quantification in Mandarin Chinese and Cantonese; (c) examine and compare counting and proportional quantifiers in Mandarin Chinese and Cantonese; (d) examine the semantics and syntax of multiple quantifications in Mandarin Chinese and Cantonese; and (e) derive a landscape of Chinese quantifiers, based on results obtained from (a) to (d), and predict possible and impossible quantificational patterns in Chinese. This study contributes to the current linguistic endeavor by refining existing theories on quantification in Chinese and in natural language at large. The description of quantificational features in Mandarin Chinese and Cantonese will also prove useful in any contrastive studies of the two.

143913.label: Project Title(Chinese)
143913.value: 中国文学中的疯癫与精神病形象: 作为跨文化医学人文的贡献

143913.label: Project Objectives
143913.value: Objective #7: To produce knowledge in the form of an article and a first book draft and a corpus of translations that addresses a multiple audience of literary, cultural and medical scholars, and to participate actively in the international academic community that does research in this field.
rows: Objective #7: To produce knowledge in the form of an article and a first book draft and a corpus of translations that addresses a multiple audience of literary, cultural and medical scholars, and to participate actively in the international academic community that does research in this field.

143913.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
143913.value: This research project investigates representations of madness in Chinese literature and puts the findings into the context of comparative literary studies and cross-cultural Medical Humanities. In the West, the theme has long been recognized as an essential inquiry into the human mind in conflict, and the medical and popular engagements with madness have continuously attracted diligent inquiry and artistic expression. New insights into and education about the nature of mental illnesses have intensified this nexus between literature and medicine, particularly with regard to narrative modes of cognitive and affective disorders. In China, too, there is a growing awareness of psychological conflict and mental disorders that find resonance in literature. Until now, no systematic research has been conducted on the theme of madness in the modern and contemporary Chinese context, and even less in the field of Medical Humanities. A key question this research seeks to address is how madness is expressed in fiction and poetry, and how these representations reflect back upon cultural and medical perceptions. While the Western traditions link madness to creative genius, religious guilt, trauma, romantic singularity, and psycholinguistics, Chinese literature predominantly represents madness as an articulation of historical and personal trauma. Representations of actual mental illness are still rare in Chinese literature, and many of the texts that are central to the theme have not been translated into English. Hence, the purpose of this study is twofold: to illustrate how madness functions as a literary symbol, and to demonstrate how such writing enhances our understanding of mental distress and illness experiences from a Chinese perspective. The inquiry draws on some existing scholarship (Messner 2000, Ng 1990, Schneider 1980, Chan 2001, Chen 2003, Meng and Xu 1993) to provide an overview over the historical concepts of madness and mental illness in China, and, thus contextualized, explores contemporary representations of madness within the critical context of trauma theory, psychoanalytical theories, narratological theories, and comparative literature. In addition, this study looks at literature as a potential source for an understanding of psychological distress, adding to the literary approach the perspective of the Medical Humanities. A second part of this project consists of translations of key texts from Chinese into English. Together, research and translations contribute new knowledge to the fields of Chinese literature and cross-cultural Medical Humanities. This project also facilitates collaboration with non-Chinese speakers in the field and adds important materials to courses taught on Madness and Literature. 本研究项目主要研究中国文学中出现的关乎疯狂的文章，并将研究结果应用于比较文学研究中的语境分析以及跨文化医学人文研究。一直以来，该主题被西方国家认为是研究人类思想矛盾的重要途径之一。各种针对疯狂所进行的医学研究和流行性研究继续吸引着众多研究者的注意力乃至艺术表现。关于精神疾病特性的教育所出现的新见解强化了文学和医学之间的联系，特别是在叙事模式的认知和情感障碍方面。在中国，也出现了越来越多的关于心理矛盾和精神错乱的文学作品。到目前为止，特别是医学人文领域，还没有出现任何以当代及近现代中国为背景的关于疯狂主题的系统性研究。本研究的核心目标是研究疯狂在小说和诗歌中的表达方式，以及其折射出的文化和医学理念。按照西方传统，疯狂往往与创造性天才、宗教内疚、创伤、浪漫奇异以及心理语言相关；而在中国文学中，疯狂主要是一种表达历史性或个人创伤的方式。中国文学中很少作品是关于真正的精神病患，而在这些重要的文章里，许多都还未被翻译成英文版本。因此，该研究有着双重目标：一方面阐释疯狂是如何作为文学符号来运作；另一方面解释这一类型的作品如何帮助我们更好地从中国人的角度来理解精神病痛以及患病经历。 基于现有的学识 (Messner 2000, Ng 1990, Schneider 1980, Chan 2001, Chen 2003, Meng and Xu 1993)，本研究对出现在中国的关于疯狂和精神病患的历史性观念进行了概述；并基于上下文研究，根据创伤理论、精神分析理论、叙事学理论和比较文学的重要语境，开拓了关于疯狂的近现代表达的新领域。另外，本研究把文学视为解密心理困扰的潜在资源，促进了以医学人文为视觉的文学方法。 本项目的第二部分包括对关键性文章的中英翻译。总体而言，本研究和翻译工作为中国文学和跨文化医学人文领域做出了全新的贡献。该项目同样也促进了与该领域的非中文使用者的合作，提供了关于疯狂和文学课程的重要资料。

143913.label: Realisation of objectives
143913.value: To date, all objectives have been achieved. Objective 1: I have done wide-ranging research on my topic throughout the past three years, gathered an extensive bibliography on madness in Chinese literature, and established myself as an expert in Chinese medical humanities through scholarly networks and conferences. I have also kept abreast with research in the medical humanities, in particular with the recent discussions surrounding the ‘critical medical humanities’ which call for a greater input from cross-cultural studies. In my anthology, The Madness of the Past Century: Stories and Poems from China, the objective is reflected in its structure: to reflect social and cultural change, I have grouped the stories and poems under five themes but have kept a chronological order within the themes. Because Chinese literature is often self-referential, I have included a pre-modern part that frames the writing of madness in modern and contemporary literature. I elaborate upon this approach in the Introduction, where I also introduce other prototypes of madness in Chinese culture. The five sections of the anthology are: “Beginnings” (pre-modern context), “This Culture Makes Me Sick” (cultural madness, alienation), “Trauma and Truth” (personal and historical trauma, voice of truth in madness), “Cognitive, Affective, Disordered” (writings on schizophrenia, depression, other), and “Mental Illness Poetics” (autobiographical poetry that addresses depression and schizophrenia). Objective 2: In addition to what is described for Objective 1, I have achieved Objective 2 by introducing Chinese materials at international conferences and by publications in journals not focused on Chinese studies (Journal of Medical Humanities, Literature and Medicine; The Northeastern Popular/American Culture Association, Inter-Disciplinary Net (UK), Madness and Literature Network (UK)). On the other hand, I have introduced a medical humanities approach at conferences and publications usually focused on Chinese studies (International Communication of Chinese Culture, Discourses of Disease: Writing Illness, the Mind and the Body in Modern China, Chinese Medical Humanities Review; International Convention of Asian Scholars (ICAS 8 & 9). Objective 3: I have addressed Objective 3 in the Introduction to my anthology and in a separate set of stories collected under the section “Trauma and Truth” in the anthology. My previously published 2011 paper “Trauma and Truth: Representations of Madness in Chinese Literature”, (Journal of Medical Humanities 32), was translated into Chinese and re-published in 2014 in the Chinese Medical Humanities Review (Beijing University Medical Press, 2014). Objective 4: I have addressed literary representations of mental illness in all sections of my anthology, but in detail in the section called “Cognitive, Affective, Disordered” and the Introduction. It is also addressed in both articles on the Chinese poets Wen Jie and Guo Lusheng (aka Indexfinger) (“Metaphors Unto Themselves”) which addresses issues of chronic depression and schizophrenia, and the article on Xu Xu “Psychic Threesomes: Madness and Psychotherapy in Xu Xu’s Novel Elegy of a Psychotic” which addresses psychosis, electroshock therapy, and life in an asylum. I also addressed these issues in several conference papers. Objective 5: Objective 5 has been addressed by including a pre-modern section (“Beginnings”) in the anthology and in the Introduction. It was also addressed in my talk in Oxford in 2014 (“This Culture Makes Me Sick: Madness as a Symbol of Eccentricity and Cultural Critique in China”) and my publication on Xu Xu’s novel Elegy of a Psychotic (Jingshenbing huanzhe de beige 精神病患者的悲歌) (“Psychic Threesomes”). Objective 6: I have addressed this objective in the anthology, in the two papers mentioned above (“Metaphors Unto Themselves” and “Psychic Threesomes”) and in the Brill book chapter. I also use the stories and poems by lesser known (or better, less translated) authors (Sun Lianggong, KS, Wang Luyan, Xu Qinwen, Wen Jie, Zhou Daxin) as readings in my GE course Madness and Literature. Once the anthology is published, I will be able to disseminate stories with commentaries in my scholarly networks. Objective 7: A draft of the completed project has been submitted to University of California Press. It includes 183 of 508 pages. In the proposal to the editor, I identified the readership as including general readers of literature, scholars and students of Chinese studies, comparative literature, medical and health humanities, critical medical humanities, cross-cultural studies, and cultural studies. In addition, I have published one article that addresses the newly developed critical approach of cross-cultural medical humanities (see article in Literature and Medicine) that introduces Chinese materials to the medical humanities readership, one book chapter that introduces the critical medical humanities approach to Chinese studies readers (see chapter in Brill), and one article that applies the medical humanities approach to the previously mentioned novel by Xu Xu (1900-1990) (see article in ICCC). Two of my articles related to this research have been solicited for translation and publication in China (“Trauma and Truth”, published in 2014 in the Chinese Medical Humanities Review, and “Metaphors Unto Themselves”, forthcoming in Contemporary Chinese Poetry and Poetics 教育部名栏: 现当代诗学研究).

To offer an interdisciplinary approach from the perspective of Medical Humanities that fills a critical void in cross-cultural Medical Humanities, and to open up venues that generate new and comprehensive interdisciplinary and cross-cultural research on a long-term basis.

To draw upon and analyze literary representations of clinical mental illness as an important source for the understanding of illness experiences, and to examine how these representations reflect and shape social and medical perceptions of mental illness in China.

143913.label: Major findings and research outcome
143913.value: The initial question that guided my research was why some cultures more than others are interested in the workings of the psyche. This was based on my early research that revealed that, compared to the Western tradition, there is a dearth of writing of madness in the Chinese tradition. However, over time, and during research periods in China, I discovered more and more stories and materials. I was especially surprised to find that in the 1920s and 1930s, almost every writer had written something on the topic, reflecting on and adding to Lu Xun’s inaugural story “Diary of a Madman”. At the same time, research on illness narratives, medical humanities, and cross-cultural studies rapidly developed in Western academia, and many scholars became interested in the Chinese literary and scholarly contribution to those fields. Perhaps one of the most lasting outcomes of this grant is the integration of the Chinese literary canon into some of the most rapidly growing disciplines in the humanities. The grant has allowed me to contribute from the start to the newest disciplinary development in the medical humanities: critical humanities (initiated by Durham University), which studies, among others, cross-cultural notions of madness and mental illness. The most important finding my grant research has to offer is the perspective that has grown out of the initial research question: rather than stating that Chinese culture reveals less interest in the workings of the human psyche, I would now say that this interest is simply expressed differently. This difference contributes a new perspective to the concerns of the medical humanities: while the Western tradition and practice focuses on soul searching, inner quests, guilt, and self-realization (so-called ‘soteriological quests’) that are representative of a true subjective inner self, Chinese writers describe madness as related to social and cultural contexts, which suggests that 1) the true self reveals itself in its social context rather than in soul searching, and 2) that this ‘lack’ of dwelling on inner processes of the mind or the heart results in a healthy acceptance of the givenness of life. That some Chinese writers do not pre-occupy themselves with questions of “why am I sick” or “why me” and instead focus on how to live is a valuable contribution to medical humanities that is addressed in my anthology and in the publications and presentations.

143913.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
143913.value: Because the theme of madness in literature and culture is both long-standing and continuing, there is a lot of potential for further research. There are some topics I have not covered, such as the mental asylum and women and madness, or the focus on specific pathologies, which is rapidly developing in Western scholarship (autism, dementia, bipolar disorder, and especially the field of “hearing voices”). It would also be important to cover other Chinese regions, such as Taiwan, Hong Kong, minority literatures, and overseas Chinese writing. This would add an interesting dimension to this theme. My next step with regard to my research is a monograph on this topic that brings together all my research, including analyses of narratological approaches to the writing of madness.

143913.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
143913.value: This project addresses the theme of madness and mental illness in Chinese literature and contributes a new Chinese perspective to the field of Chinese literature and medical humanities. It also introduces the medical humanities approach to Chinese studies. Medical humanities study the relationship between humanities disciplines and medical fields, in the case of this research, between literature and concepts of madness and mental illness. Because research in the field is limited yet there is a growing interest in it, I translated over 600 pages of Chinese short stories and poems into English and submitted it for publication as an anthology for general readers as well as scholars and students in Chinese literature, medical humanities, and cultural studies. In addition to the stories that are divided into five thematic topics, the Introduction to the anthology (The Madness of the Past Century: Stories and Poems from China) gives an overview over the historical and social developments that frame the writing on madness in Chinese literature. This is the first thematic anthology of Chinese literary madness. It serves as a resource for research and teaching, while my scholarly publications contribute a new Chinese perspective to cross-cultural medical humanities and Chinese studies.

144013.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
144013.value: The jury system in Hong Kong has been practiced for over one hundred and fifty years, first introduced when Hong Kong became a British colony. Since then, the jury system has been described as one of the most important features of the legal system, and its maintenance is stipulated in Article 86 of the Basic Law. However, despite its significance and highly praised values, access to jury trial is limited in Hong Kong. Trial by jury is not available to defendants tried in the District Courts. Defendants are tried by a single judge, who is empowered to pass a sentence of imprisonment of up to seven years. The uncommon sentencing power bestowed on District Court judges has led to calls for the extension of the jury system to the District Courts. However, the Secretary of Justice noted that any change at the present arrangements would require a lengthy, detailed and in-depth study. It is against this background that the research team empirically assesses the practicality and feasibility of the extension of the jury system to the District Courts in Hong Kong. Practicality and feasibility of the extension would be justified (1) if the general public favours the jury system, (2) if jurors are competently performing their roles as fact-finders and (3) if there are enough jurors to support the case load. Our preliminary research suggested that the problem of jury shortage can be resolved by lowering the minimum age requirement to 18 years. The encouraging results in our previous study motivated us to extend our research on jury decision making. Our previous study has left important questions unanswered. In the proposed study, we will focus on testing the first two claims supporting the feasibility and practicality of the extension of the jury system. We propose approaching the first issue through a more rigorous study recruiting a representative community sample instead of using a college sample as in our previous study. We will approach the second issue by asking participants to deliberate with others to come up with an agreed verdict as our previous research focused on individual juror decision making. Responses from the public will also be compared with those of legal professionals to assess the degree with which they converge. We believe that this research will give us a clear picture of the public attitudes towards the jury system and the fact-finding ability of potential jurors. 香港自成為英國殖民地以至現在，實行陪審團制度已一佰五十年，由那時開始，陪審團制度就被認為是一項極重要的法律制度，而且基本法86條中亦確認它的重要性。不過，雖然在本港這制度被受讚賞及重視，但接受過陪審團審訊的案件不多，在區域法院中審訊的案件是沒有陪審團審判的，被告是由一位法官判罪，區域法官最高可判犯人七年監禁。區域法官獨擁這樣重要的權力，引起了將陪審團制度延伸到區域法院的呼聲。律政司對這樣的改變，表示需要長時間仔細及深入的研究。這是本研究隊提出要將陪審團制度，在本港區域法院中實施的實用性及可行性作全面檢討的背境。延伸陪審團制度之實用性和可行性會是建基於三項要素:（1）社會大眾是否認受將這制度延伸至區域法院，（2）陪審員是否有足夠能力尋找案件中的事實真相，及（3）有否足夠陪審員以應付區域法院之需求。 我們做過的初步研究結果中，顯示有陪審員短缺的現象，在這方面的解決方法，可以是將陪審員的最低年齡降至18歲，這研究得到一些正面的意見，這些意見鼓勵我們要延續關於陪審團制度的研究。這研究亦讓我們發現有重要的問題尚未有答案，因此我們會集中研究上述的延伸陪審團制度之實用性和可行性的首兩項要素。關於第一要素，上次研究我們集中在搜集學院學生的意見，然這次研究我們會向有代表性的社區人士搜集意見。關於第二要素，我們會研究陪審團的意見，研究參與模擬陪審團的準陪審員對判決罪犯的過程，而不似上次研究，只訪問準陪審員的個人意見。此外，我們更會將公眾的意見與有法律背景人士的意見作出比較，看看有何相同或區別之處。 我們相信這研究讓我們清楚了解陪審團制度和準陪審員找尋事實真相的能力。

144013.label: Realisation of objectives
144013.value: One of the reviewers gave the following comment: "I am not keen about the suggestion of using incentive to secure eligible jurors' participation. I can understand and endorse it if the study is on consumer behaviour. But this is about public service and good citizen behaviour. It goes again the ideology." Based on this comment, the GRF panel requested the research team to cut the incentive of half of the respondents. In response to this comment, the research team adjusted the sample size and reduced the incentive to the samples (approved by the panel), as follows: (1) Sample for public attitude towards jury system through telephone opinion survey: original = 700 (paid); revised = 530 (unpaid) Since we did not give any incentive to this group, so reducing the original sample size from 700 to 530 was necessary. This sample is still an acceptable sample size in public opinion polls conducted by various universities in Hong Kong. (2) Sample for community participants: original = 126 (paid); revised = 198 (unpaid) One of the objectives of this project is to assess jury competence in Hong Kong. Jurors are considered competent fact finders if they appropriately base their decisions on legally relevant considerations and disregard legally irrelevant information. To conduct more indepth analysis, we enlarged the sample to enhance the statistical power but did not give any incentive to this group. (3) Sample for deliberation group: original = 126 (paid); revised = 70 (paid) The sample size of the deliberation group has been scaled down because of the reduction in budget, which affected the employment period of the RA. Since this involved more than two hours of work, we continued to give incentive to the participants. (4) Sample for respondents with legal background: original = 100 lawyers; revised 100 lawyers & final year law students. One of the objectives is to compare layperson’s verdicts to that of legal professionals to assess the degree with which they converge. However, in view of the difficulty in soliciting lawyers as our sample, we consider expanding the sample of the legal group to include both lawyers and final year law students as the sample. Objective 1: To assess the general public’s attitude towards jury trials and whether they support an extension of the jury system to the District Courts of Hong Kong. We had collected 531 questionnaires (target 530) through phone survey on the general public’s attitude towards jury trials and whether they support an extension of the jury system to the District Courts of Hong Kong. Our target population was the general public of Hong Kong. We generated around 60,000 random phone numbers starting with 2, 3, 5, and 9 using Microsoft Excel. Our final sample contained 531 respondents (7 respondents were excluded because they were below 21 years of age). All respondents were aged 21 years or above, with an even split of gender (50.2% female, 49.8% male). The majority of respondents were aged between 21 to 30 years (34.9%), followed by 41 to 50 years (18.5%) and 31 to 40 years (14.4%). Almost half of the sample completed college or university degrees (45.8%). Interviewees who obtained F.5 and primary school accounted for 23.5% and 13.6% respectively. The largest proportion of respondents (31.3%) reported earning monthly income above 40,000HKD, followed by those who reported earning monthly family income below 10,000HKD (12.6%) and between 10,000HKD to 15,000HKD (11.3%). All respondents verified that they 1) are citizens of Hong Kong and 2) are aged 21 or above. Our three-part questionnaire contains a total of 39 questions. Part 1 investigates interviewees’ perceptions on the following topics: justice in Hong Kong, jury’s and judge’s verdicts, police, democracy, national identity, the Umbrella Movement, triad society, and the extension of jury system to the District Court. Part 2 asks for interviewee’s demographic information, such as gender, education, etc. Part 3 asks whether interviewees have had past experiences of being victims of crime, have/had friends of relatives are/were police or working/worked in judiciary and whether they had unpleasant experiences with police and those who work in judiciary. Objective 2: To assess jury competence in Hong Kong. Jurors are considered competent fact-finders if they appropriately base their decisions on legally relevant considerations and disregard legally irrelevant information. Layperson’s verdicts will be compared to that of legal professionals to assess the degree with which they converge. We had collected 198 questionnaires (target 198) from occupied sites of Occupy Central and further collected 165 questionnaires (target 100) from final year law students so that we can compare layperson’s verdicts to that of respondents with legal knowledge. We visited the Occupy sites in Admiralty and in Mong Kok to recruit participants. Researchers took stacks of questionnaires and randomly approached participants in the Occupy sites. Researchers briefly introduced the purpose of the study and asked them whether participants met the jury eligibility criteria in Hong Kong. Participants had to verbally verify that they 1) are citizens of Hong Kong, 2) are 21 years or above, and 3) attained an education level of Secondary 7 or above. The three criteria corresponded to the jury eligibility criteria in Hong Kong. Researchers reassured participants that no identifying information was required on the questionnaire. Those who met the criteria and who agreed to complete the questionnaire were randomly given one of the six versions of the questionnaire. Participants were reminded to complete the questionnaire on their own. Around 30 minutes later, researchers came to collect the questionnaires. Upon completion of the study, participants were thanked for their time. No monetary compensation was given to participants. For the law student sample, we recruited them in the campus of City University of Hong Kong Objective 3: To assess the use of deliberation in jury’s search for truth. To assess the use of deliberation in jury’s search for truth, we conducted 10 deliberation groups with 7 mock jurors each. So, the target of 70 samples of deliberation group has been achieved. We had three recruitment strategies: (1) asked if our phone survey respondents were interested, (2) convenience sample (referral by friends and colleagues) and (3) snowball sample (focus group participants to refer their friends). All participants met the jury eligibility requirement in Hong Kong, i.e. have attained Form 7 or above, reside in Hong Kong for more than 7 years, and are 21 years old or above. Since the minimum and maximum age requirement of jurors in Hong Kong are 21 and 65, therefore, 9 different age groups are being sorted out, which are: 20-24, 25-29, 30-34, 35-39, 40-44, 45-49, 50-54, 55-59 and finally 60-64. Take the age group of 20-24 as an example, since people in this age group accounted for 5.9% of the whole population, therefore, through the calculation of 84 x 5.9 % / 68.4%, a result of 7.245 is generated. Therefore, 7 people will be included in this age group for our focus group. For the age group of 25-29, 30-34, 35-39, 40-44, 45-49, 50-54, 55-59 and 60-64, after the calculation, 9, 10, 9, 10, 10, 11, 10 and 8 people are needed. There are no specifications on gender in our deliberation groups.
