144013.label: Major findings and research outcome
144013.value: The present study aims to provide an empirical demonstration that a feasible solution to expand the jury pool to the District Court is to lower the minimum age requirement to include 18-year-olds. It compares the following three types of responses from a youth sample and from an adult sample: (a) the ratings of reliability of commonly seen evidence, (b) guilt judgments in a hypothetical rape trial, and (c) rationales for verdicts. Results showed that both youth and adult participants were capable of basing their judgments largely on legally relevant information. When guided by evidence, some youths in the present sample could reach similar guilt judgments to the adults. However, youths appeared to have a lower threshold for being satisfied beyond reasonable doubt when certain evidence was presented. In recent years, there is saying that jurors' fact finding ability has been affected by television drama such as CSI. Television is a powerful medium through which to convey information and messages to the public. The recent proliferation of forensic science and criminal justice information throughout all forms of media, coupled with raised expectations toward forensic evidence, has led some to suspect that a “CSI effect” (Crime Scene Investigation effect) is taking place among jurors so that their fact-finding ability may be affected. The present study contributes to the literature addressing the CSI effect in two ways. First, it examines whether the CSI effect exists in the Chinese population of Hong Kong. Second, using a mock-jury paradigm, it empirically examines a more integrative perspective of the CSI effect. It was found that, although the amount of media coverage involving forensic evidence does influence participants’ perception of legal evidence to some degree, such a perception does not affect participants’ legal decision making. Viewers of forensic dramas were not more likely to convict the defendant when forensic evidence was presented and not less likely to convict when only testimonial evidence was presented. The only significant predictor of the defendant’s culpability when scientific evidence was presented was participants’ ratings of the reliability of scientific evidence. Results from the present study lend no support to the existence of the CSI effect in Hong Kong.

144013.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
144013.value: Respondents in the present study were given a brief description of a criminal case in simple direct language and were asked to make a judgment. Although the materials used in the present study were adapted from published studies, future studies should be conducted on a set of materials that is more representative of the realities of actual court cases (e.g., more technical and complicated language, extensive descriptions of trial evidence and cross-examination testimony) to assess how participants react to the discrepancy between fictionalized accounts of criminal investigations presented on television and real investigations. Moreover, since we used mock jurors as the participants of the present study, who might not have the real experiences when compared with the real jurors, future research should aim at recruiting actual jurors who have first-hand experience and information on jury trial. Regarding CSI effect on potential jurors, apart from television crime scene and investigative drama, related resources and effects generated in the Internet or through online materials should also be assessed and investigated, taking into consideration the increasingly use and even addiction to the Internet.

144013.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
144013.value: The enormous impact of jury on the criminal justice system has begun to attract scientific interest in recent decades, and skepticism has been frequently raised. In recent decades, the police have increasingly used scientific methods, such as DNA and fingerprint analyses in their investigations. Scholars have frequently argued that the technical nature of the evidence increases the jurors’ difficulty in evaluating the evidence presented to them. When jurors are presented with complex testimony, they are more likely to have difficulties in reaching a judgement. Jury fact-finders are expected to make decisions only based on facts that are formally admitted as evidence during the course of a trial. However, the increasing use of scientific evidence makes it difficult for the jurors to decide on complicated cases. In particular, the amount of media coverage involving forensic evidence does influence mock jurors’ perception of legal evidence to some degree. Using mock jurors as research participants, this study attempts to assess jury competence in Hong Kong. Jurors are considered competent fact-finders if they appropriately base their decisions on legally relevant considerations and disregard legally irrelevant information.

144913.label: Project Objectives
144913.value: To explore intra-state responses to infectious diseases – both to chart how the state and (where relevant) subnational and social organisations implemented prophylactic measures as well as to understand the drivers behind the securitisation responses (or lack thereof). To analyse state-regional and international organisations’ policy engagement on infectious disease outbreaks so as to: (a) evaluate the extent of cooperation between the different levels, (b) identify where the securitisation catalyst originates, and (c) comprehend how engagement between these three levels shapes the securitisation response. To collect data from secondary sources on other Asian countries affected by these diseases. In addition, secondary source material will also be collected on international and regional civil society organisations as well as the role of the Asian Development Bank, APEC and the World Bank. We will compare these state-based cases based in part on their exposure to infectious disease outbreaks as well as (1) the nature of their economic and political systems and (2) their level of engagement with the global community. The organisational responses will be reviewed to see how other institutions and groups contribute to the resolution of health threats at the state level; and To develop results sufficiently robust that can act as a platform for a much larger study in the future.

144913.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
144913.value: 此研究項目之目的為了解傳染病爆發期間，各亞洲國家及鄰近地區與國際組織之間的合作關係。當某亞洲的國家出現傳染病，該病毒便很容易在其鄰近的城市以及國家之間漫延。另一方面，透過旅遊及貿易的渠道，亦使外來的病毒迅速在整個地區傳播。為了面對傳染病所帶來的威脅，了解亞洲城市及各機構間處理傳染病的方法將成為重要的一環。 愛滋病及近年爆發的H1N1新型流感便是兩個外源性疾病如何影響亞洲人口、經濟、國家安全及福祉的例子。而非典型肺炎和H5N1禽流感便是兩個內源性疾病對亞洲和世界其他地區造成存在性威脅的例子。 此研究項目將以系統性的探討來了解三層架構的管理，即國家、區域及國際之間的互動如何影響健康問題安全化的過程。此項目將基於普特南雙層理論和安全化理論下作研究 (附件一的圖表闡述我們如何分析過去二十五年以來四種最主要威脅亞洲及國際社會的傳染病問題 (愛滋病，非典型肺炎，H5N1禽流感，H1N1新型流感)。 透過研究上述之傳染病，我們將可明白三層架構的執行者在處理這些傳染病上有不同優次的原因。當明白以上的原因，我們將可以評估亞洲國家及其相關地區和國際組織在處理不同的傳染病問題上，會因著種種原因，例如政治或經濟上的考慮，從而影響執行者在健康問題安全化的投入程度。 我們將與不同國家的公共衞生人員、地區及國際性組織的代表，並國家本地和國際的非政府組織進行實地訪談。訪談的地點將位於東南亞和亞洲東北的國家，以及紐約和日內瓦。相關的文獻將會補充訪談所得的資料，並將與其他疾病爆發時的反應及處理進行比較。

144913.label: Realisation of objectives
144913.value: This has been a very good project. It was very large in scale and ambitious in scope but the combination of the three researchers was carefully chosen so that the mix of domestic and regional policy experience and knowledge of fieldwork sites would enable the project to be realized. Unfortunately, the Co-I left the project due to other commitments. This not only limited our capacity for fieldwork but also expanded the range of topics the other two project members had to cover. While our fieldwork was scaled back, careful preparation prior to fieldtrips as well as some instances of beneficial snowballing enable us to reach excellent primary sources (particularly in China, which had been a concern of the initial grant reviewers). We also gained excellent access at the Asian Development Bank, the World Bank, the World Health Organization, the Food and Agricultural Organization, as well as with the US Centers for Disease Control and various field operations sponsored by other governments. We were unable to secure interviews with either APEC or ASEAN. However, there is sufficient secondary literature to cover these gaps plus, as our field research uncovered, these two bodies are not as directly active in this area as the policy rhetoric would suggest. The absence of the third team member meant that it did take us much longer to research and write the additional chapters, which had a knock-on effect on our own respective work but, as noted below, the interpretive model we have developed has been applied to the MERS Co-V and Zika outbreaks. This has enabled us to extend the case studies included in this project. To a certain extent the first two objectives are intertwined but will be reported separately as far as possible. The first objective - to explore intra-state responses to infectious diseases - has a critical focus on developing a theoretical model to understand such responses as well as to explore the nature of the responses. Initially, we intended to use the securitization theory (Buzan, Waever, and de Wilde 1998) that is well established in the literature. However, once we could compare our field work results from several initial sites, we realized that the theory does not go far enough into unpacking the causal policy logic behind the primary decision to treat an infectious disease as a threat. What we have developed is a model that draws upon historical institutionalism and punctuated equilibrium theories to understand the dynamics of the decision making process. The unexpected finding from this approach (which we subsequently verified in discussions with representatives from international economic and health organizations) is that responses to infectious disease outbreaks (at least in Asia) are governed less by health considerations and more by political and economic negotiations for resources - as a result of the infectious disease response. This finding held true irrespective of the background of the interviewees (policy, medical, veterinary, scientific, commercial) with whom we discussed it. As a result, the second objective to chart how national governments, subnational units, and social organizations would implement prophylactic measures could not be fully realised. In this respect our model led us to two conclusions that were subsequently verified. First, the idea of a learning curve between infectious disease outbreaks is imperfectly realised (at best). States tend to only allocate resources when the primary communities (economic or political) are challenged. For example, in the case of H5N1 in Vietnam, large-scale responses are driven by economic challenges (impact on trade) than by disease eradication. As a result, humans become sentinels for assessing policy responses rather than implementing programs prophylactically. Where programs are introduced between outbreaks there are frequently additional political or economic logics in operation. Second, the competitive nature of resource allocation between different policy communities in the countries studied means that - even in authoritarian countries and even under the threat of disease outbreaks - subnational, market and/or social actors can seek to subvert national level responses for their own local agendas. Our resubmitted paper on AMR in China explores this in detail. At a theoretical level, our intention with this objective to uncover where the catalyst for action resides was realized; although we are still trying to fully understand the conditions by which a level of the model is the initiator of a response. For example, frequently the national authorities are the initiators of a disease response (eg SARS or H1N1). Occasionally, the initiating actor is outside the national level (such as in the case of H5N1 and Thailand). Yet, the international community can also act to push states to respond to a disease or other health threat - even when it is not a high priority health issue for that country (such as Zika or AMR). It is intended that this will be addressed with the co-authored book but a definitive conclusion on the problem is yet to be developed. The third objective was relatively straight-forward to realise as a lot of the bio-medical literature is in English; although, as we found in all the countries we visited, accessing local publications and other documents provided a wealth of knowledge that is otherwise unavailable. Importantly, we also managed to gain access to key officials and policy groups in the ADB, World Bank, WHO, FAO and other bodies. At all sites, we had very detailed discussions that were theoretically and empirically productive. One unexpected finding was that the political and economic pre-response negotiations between policy communities that we identified at the state level were also present at the international level. In many ways, these divisions and debates at the global level filter down and exacerbate divisions at the domestic level - even though there are attempts by the country offices of the international health bodies to develop cooperation. Hence the domestic public health communities almost exclusively interact with the WHO, while the animal health communities are similarly engaged with the FAO. The final objective was realized in the model we have developed. That said, we no longer have any intention to implement a larger scale project. This was already large enough. Going forward, this research could be usefully extended by comparing different threats where trade-offs are necessary (such as between health and environmental objectives or health and economic development considerations). This would not only be useful in deepening the model we have used by injecting a comparative element, it would also be more easily realizable with fewer resources.

144913.label: Major findings and research outcome
144913.value: In terms of major findings: (1) Our initial hypothesis of the political nature of disease responses was upheld. What was unexpected was that this politicization extended to negotiations between different policy communities that took place before the response was initiated. What this does is subordinate the healthcare aspect of the responses to political and (frequently) economic concerns. (2) The primary focus of our analysis was on governmental responses. Civil society, market actors, and the international community were originally considered to be of secondary importance. This approach was derived from both the literature on East Asian political systems as well as the realist nature of regional states' foreign policies. While we found that civil society indeed plays a secondary role, market actors were frequently found to act in their own economic interests first. Within the literature on regional authoritarian systems, market actors are either subsidiary to or co-opted by the state; our research suggests that a more complex relationship has emerged (largely enabled by the policy environment arising from the first finding). (3) A third major finding pertains to the relationship between the international policy community and their domestic counterparts; where the bureaucratic division between (for example) the WHO and the FAO was structurally reinforced into domestic policy responses. This has significant implications for regional states being able to implement whole-of-government responses to health threats. In terms of research outcomes, the approved grant proposed one co-authored book arising from the research. This is our benchmark for realizing the output success of the project. We published a sole authored book that later won the International Studies Association Global Health award (in 2015). Despite our commitment for the co-authored book, the mid-term review suggested that we should be publishing more. For that reason, the last two years have been devoted to getting articles out. We now have two articles out with leading journals in the field and a third resubmitted. We have also presented our findings at a wide range of conferences. The feedback from these meetings have been fed into the book, articles and co-authored chapter drafts. Our attention is now turned back to getting out the co-authored volume. The award winning book and the three articles already exceeds the committed output from the approved grant proposal; however, the book is well advanced and will submitted to a publisher (JHU Press) this coming year.

144913.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
144913.value: It is worth remembering that feedback by one reviewer on an early version of this project questioned whether the field of health security actually existed. The intervening period has seen not only our primary case studies become well known but a range of other threats (MERS Co-V, Zika, and AMR) emerge into global public and policy consciousness. The foundational issues (discussed below) that underpin responses to these new and re-emergent threats are the same ones that underpin our earlier research. This validation of our approach allows us to export our model into future studies. Going forward there are a number of plans. Research: a narrower project focused on subnational units with cases compared against other priorities (such as development or environment issues). Contribution: the PI is now the Global Health section co-chair for the European International Studies Association and will be convening a series of panels on theory and methodology in 2019 as a first step towards an international collaboration grant between scientists and social scientists on mapping the parameters of the global health discipline. Teaching: the research outcomes from this project have been fed into a new UGC course - Death and Disease - that will be launched in 2018-19.

144913.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
144913.value: There is an expectation that when an infectious disease or other health threat emerges that states an international organizations will act to stop the outbreak. That action takes place is inevitable but the reasons why it takes place is more complicated. Our research takes us behind the veil of decision making processes. It shows how the decision to respond to an EID or similar health threat is primarily based upon resource competition considerations that emerge for intra-policy community bargaining processes. These considerations and processes mean that the aim of the response is not necessarily to eradicate the health threat. Even when the threat is significant (such as with HIV/AIDS or HPAI H5N1 or AMR), these foundational issues can reduce the efficacy of responses so that sub-optimal strategies are chosen (optimal being the eradication of the health threat). This is important because it provides a benchmark for understanding why certain pathways are taken in responding to health threats. This research enables us to look beyond the political rhetoric to the substance of the policy response and to ascertain its value as a strategy.

145013.label: Project Title(Chinese)
145013.value: 在東南亞的民主及其不滿

145013.label: Project Objectives
145013.value: Inject vital new data from Southeast Asia’s political trajectories into mainstream debates over issues of authoritarian resilience, democratic instability, and scant democratic quality. In short, this project’s chief aim is to make a major conceptual advance in the literature on comparative democratization. Build and test an integrative model for investigating shortfalls in democratizing progress. Key insights from modernization, institutional, and crisis-based analysis will be incorporated into a broader, but tightly coherent model that centers structural forces and elite-level strategies of socio-political mobilization. Contribute to major debates in political sociology today over the conceptualization of, and interaction between structure and agency. This project aims to elaborate new measures and operationalize proxies that capture ethnic identification, class affiliations, and elite-level relations and strategies. Revitalize the notion of socio-economic class, enabling this project to bring distinctive data from contemporary Southeast Asia into new debates over the impact of stratification and disparities on democratic change and persistence. Additionally, a revitalized notion of class will permit advances in the understanding of populism and populist mobilization, essential to investigation tensions and elite-level strategizing in many Southeast Asian country cases today.

145013.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
145013.value: This project asks why, in comparison to most other parts of the world constructed as regions, democratization has been so limited in Southeast Asia. Notwithstanding the long-term exposure of many countries in the region to democratic procedures and their attainment of middle-income standings, they operate a variety of resilient authoritarian regimes and unstable or low-quality democracies. In addressing this major puzzle, this project will draw on the insights of modernization theory, institutional analysis, new crisis-based explanations, and other strands of democratization literature. But in recognizing the indeterminacy of each of these genres, we seek to build and test a broader, but tightly coherent model that gives prominence to social structures (understood in terms of ethnic identification and class affiliation), institutions (with a focus on party and electoral systems) and national elites (conceptualized as cohesive or fractious). The project’s guiding hypothesis, then, is that democratization may in varying measure be impeded by ambitious elites who, if they can instrumentalize social cleavages and seize institutional opportunities, issue communalist or populist appeals through which to mobilize social constituencies. In this way, they may constrain democratic change, with cohesive elites either colluding to perpetuate authoritarian controls or to block increases in democratic quality. Alternatively, fractious elites may compete so fiercely that they precipitate democratic breakdown. In striving to provide an in-depth account of contemporary events of key countries in Southeast Asia over the past decade and a half, this project features an innovative case study methodology and rigorous usage of process tracing techniques. But in aiming also to undertake comparative analysis, a first ‘tier’ of three country cases has been selected—Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia—in which hypotheses are proposed and tested over ethnic identification, class affiliation, electoral rules and political parties, elite-level mobilizing, and limited democratization. In cross-checking results, analysis will be extended to a ‘subsidiary’ set of correlative cases—Singapore, the Philippines, and Myanmar. Countries in Southeast Asia whose records feature no meaningful experience with democracy are excluded from this study. 在東南亞的民主及其不滿 馬道光 這項目使用東南亞不同政治體系去找出促進或破壞民主變革和合併的因素。從方法論，東南亞的偉大政治多樣性顯示民主'滾雪球'的免疫力發生在發展中世界的其他地方。因此得清除內源性因素的因果至上從而幫助控制民主。在這種多樣性下，我們發現了不同的民主模式改變，鼓勵了我們仔細比較分析。由於限制研究於東南亞國家，我們可以有效地通過民主的鏡頭檢視這些民主制度。在馬來西亞，我們發現“發育不良”的民主（有些競爭性選舉，但對公民自由有嚴格限制）, 在泰國有“間歇性的”民主（常年風險威權逆轉）, 在菲律賓民主“退化”（增量下降）, 和在印尼的民主選舉（穩定，但低“質量”）。 在過去的幾十年中的這項比較民主化的研究, 現代化理論，制度設計和變革的危機已經獲得青睞。這個項目將證明使用一個簡單的相反證據方法是不能用以上方法解釋東南亞的民主軌跡。但這樣做亦收部分見解：當納入一個創新的框架，便能集中解決複雜的社會結構之間的相互作用和精英級之間的關係。 簡單而言，這個項目推測在社會分工，如族群認同或類隸屬放棄調動的機會，雄心勃勃的精英試圖利用民眾。因此，在呼籲種族（在馬來西亞1960年代後期以來）或民粹主義的渴望（在泰國他信•西那瓦, 在較小程度上，在菲律賓約瑟夫•埃斯特拉達）。精英動員選民支持通過民主程序允許競選。但是，通過激活社會群體，並聲稱自己的至上, 叛逃者精英提示他們已經在不同程度上放棄了報復精英的滾動民主步伐。正是在這種背景下，在馬來西亞，泰國，菲律賓，民主已分別發育不良，出現間歇性和退化。因此只在印尼，本地仍可在社區和民粹主義動員, 但在國家級則不可，這引致自我消除的社會整體結構。民主選舉雖繼續，但只是有限的質量。

145013.label: Realisation of objectives
145013.value: In terms of objective one this project was very successful in injecting 'vital new data from Southeast Asia’s political trajectories into mainstream debates'. It also made a number of conceptual advances and developed an alternative theoretical framework (objective two). Key insights from modernization, institutional and other theories were critiqued in order to offer explanations which centered on class cleavages and elite-level strategies. To begin with the critique of existing explanations, publications 1, 3, 4 and 11 argued that existing explanations of democratic durability in developing countries are inadequate: beneficent historical legacies (particularly British democratic ‘tutelage’), favorable social structures (particularly relative ethnic homogeneity), medium to high levels of economic modernization (not dependent on fossil fuel production), and favorable institutional arrangements (particularly parliamentary over presidential rule). These factors would have suggested democratic persistence in Thailand, instability in the Philippines, and breakdown in Indonesia. The reality was nearly the opposite. A 2014 military coup ended democracy in Thailand after a decade of extreme polarization and political unrest despite the country’s relatively high per capita income levels and social homogeneity. Indonesia remains the only stable (if low quality) electoral democracy despite much lower per capita income and greater ethnic heterogeneity. Despite the British colonial legacy, Myanmar and Malaysia have only recently (and partially) begun to democratize (with Malaysia in addition being the second wealthiest country in the region per capita - the wealthiest country per capita not reliant on oil production is of course Singapore which remains an illiberal electoral authoritarian regime). In terms of the supposed perils of presidentialism vs. parliamentarism, in a special journal issue co-edited by the PI with a co-authored introduction and single authored article (publications 3 and 4), four cases of presidentialism in Southeast Asia were examined - East Timor, Indonesia, Myanmar, the Philippines - and compared to parliamentary Thailand. The Philippines appears to provide support to ‘the perils of presidentialism’ thesis given the collapse of democracy there several decades ago and periodic instability since then. But Indonesia, despite ostensibly having the additional institutional perils of multipartism, has proved stable and Thailand’s parliamentary democracy has faced similar crises to the Philippines. Among the hybrid cases of presidentialism, both Myanmar and Timor Leste have forged elite accommodation through creating presidential-style institutions, including one considered particularly unpromising for achieving political stability in the literature. Because presidentialism has been associated both with elite accommodation and stability as well as political conflict and instability, the Southeast Asia cases do not clearly demonstrate the dangers of presidentialism. Instead, they point to the relative lack of explanatory power of this institutional arrangement in understanding political stability. Aside from critiquing existing explanations the project put forward an alternative explanation of democratic 'discontent' in Southeast Asia that included both structural forces and elite mobilization strategies (objective two). The co-I, William Case (publication 1) argued that elite division due to the rise of populist politicians who mobilized a latent class cleavage and led to extreme political polarization in Thailand and, to a lesser extent, the Philippines, resulting in to long-term (Thailand) or at least temporary (the Philippines) democratic breakdown. Relative elite cohesion due to the lack of a populist challenge in Indonesia kept democracy stable but of a low quality. The PI, Mark Thompson argued (publications 6, 7, 17 and 18) along similar lines but pointed to the importance of a ‘pro-poor' narrative used by populists in the Philippines and Thailand who mobilized class divisions to overcome clientelist particularism thereby nationalizing a ‘moral economy of electoralism’ (publications 6 and 17) which led to extreme political polarization as it challenged the prevailing ‘liberal reformist’ narrative of royalist elites in Thailand and an alliance of big business and the Catholic church in the Philippines. This led to temporary or longer term democratic breakdown as traditional elites supported the military in repressing ‘outsider’ populists in both countries. Given the diverse political outcomes and limited democratization in Southeast Asia, additional case study analyses were offered: Case published a case study of Malaysia’s electoral authoritarianism (13) while Thompson analyzed the the current crisis of Philippine democracy (4, 5, 8, 9, 16 and 18). The project’s major contribution to debates about structural factors (objective three) involved an effort to show (publications 1, 5, 6, 7 and 11) that democratization has been impeded by the agency of ambitious elites who mobilized social cleavages and issued reformist or populist appeals. The argument was then further developed by the co-I in publications 1 and 11 to argue that cohesive elites either colluded to perpetuate authoritarian controls (Malaysia) or to block increases in democratic quality (Indonesia). Alternatively, fractious elites competed so fiercely that they precipitated democratic breakdown (Thailand) or created chronic instability (the Philippines). With the rise of ‘order-over-law’ populism in the Philippines since the election of Rodrigo Duterte as president in 2016, the PI argued (publications 4 and 5) that there are also cases where ‘outsider’ populist elites have directly challenged a prevailing democratic system, turning the country into an ‘illiberal democracy’. One difficulty arose in meeting this objective: the surprise victory of the opposition coalition in the May 2018 general election in Malaysia, the first time the ruling coalition has lost since independence, upending an electoral authoritarian regime. Rather than fueling instability through polarization, in the Malaysian case a divided Malay political elite was crucial to the opposition victory. This apparent contradiction to the argument of the co-I (1) will undoubtedly become a new focus of research of his research. The project also had considerable success in achieving the fourth objective of revitalizing the notion of socio-economic class in order to enhance understanding of populism and populist mobilization in the Southeast Asian cases. The major quantitative contribution was made by the co-I in publication 1. There he developed measures of 'ethnic fractualization' and social inequality, alongside per capita GDP and corruption rankings in his explanation of the differences in 'democracy's fate' in Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand (summarized in a table on p. 5). But these factors contributed only a limited amount to the actual explanation because aside from socio-economic inequality (higher levels of which did correlate with democratic instability), they served primarily to critique existing explanations. As discussed above, these factors would suggest Thai democracy would remain stable while Indonesia’s would be endangered while, at present, the opposite is the case. In fact, given that it is also has a presidential system, Indonesia belongs to those democracies many structurally minded scholars deem most likely to fail given its low per capita income, high levels of ethnic fractualization and corruption. The more important contribution of the project in regard to this objective was thus qualitative: putting social class and 'class conflict' at the center of the explanation. While many existing explanations of political instability in Thailand and the Philippines point to regional differences, clientelist politics, and ideological divides, this project suggested that at the heart of the disagreement between 'yellow' and 'red shirts' in Thailand or between 'cinematic' populists and their enemies in the Philippines was a class divide mobilized by populists (Thaksin in Thailand and Estrada in the Philippines) against a royalist establishment (in Thailand) or alliance of big business and the Catholic Church (in the Philippines), resulting in extreme political polarization and democratic breakdown.

145013.label: Major findings and research outcome
145013.value: This project offered an explanation for why in Southeast Asia, compared to most other world regions, democratization has been limited and the few electoral democracies there have been troubled (publications 1, 3, 7, 11, 14, 15 and 17). In addressing the limits of democratization and the instability of electoral democracies, modernization theory and institutional analysis, particularly on the supposed perils of presidentialism (publications 2 and 3), were critiqued. Pointing to their weak explanatory power in the Southeast Asian context, the project instead offered elite cohesiveness or fractiousness (publications 1 and 13), the mobilization of social cleavages (1, 6, and 7), and competing political discourses (5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 16 and 18) as major explanations. The project’s chief argument is that democratization has been impeded by ambitious elites who instrumentalized social cleavages and issued reformist or populist appeals to mobilize popular constituencies constraining democratic change, with cohesive elites either colluding to perpetuate authoritarian controls or blocking increases in democratic quality. Alternatively, fractious elites using competing popular discourses competed so fiercely that they precipitated democratic breakdown. Given the diverse political outcomes and limited democratization in Southeast Asia, both comparative and case study analyses were offered. Case (1) developed measures of 'ethnic fractualization' and social inequality in his explanation of the differences in 'democracy's fate' in Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand. As Thompson has shown, 'pro-poor' populists in the Philippines and Thailand, mobilizing class divisions to overcome clientelist particularism (7 and 17), nationalized a ‘moral economy of electoralism’ (6 and 17) which led to extreme political polarization and temporary or longer term democratic breakdown as traditional elites supported the military in repressing ‘outsider’ populists. Case published a case study of Malaysia’s electoral authoritarianism (13) while Thompson analyzed the post-Marcos period and the current crisis of Philippine democracy (4, 5, 8, 9, 16 and 18). In total, the PI (Thompson) and co-I (Case) published 18 research outputs: two special journal issues with lengthy introductions (3 and 4), eight journal articles, several in top ranked journals (2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. 15 and 18), one short monograph (1), the "Routledge Handbook on Southeast Asian Democratization" (10) with a comparative introductory chapter (11) and an additional chapter (12) by the co-I as well as another chapter contributed by the PI (14) as well as three further book chapters, often in edited volumes published in top presses (13, 16 and, 17).

145013.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
145013.value: The further development of research focuses on case studies of the Philippines and Malaysia. With GRF grant 9042600, Thompson is analyzing Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte's 'violent populism' which has turned a flawed liberal into an illiberal democracy within two years. While drawing on insights of the earlier GRF project given strong elite backing for Duterte despite his contempt for liberal norms, it moves beyond it by developing a 'bottom up' perspective given the strong popular support he enjoys across class lines despite the targeting of the poor in the bloody 'war on drugs' and continued high levels of inequality. Case, who retired from CityU in 2017 and has been appointed head of the School of Politics, History and International Relations at the University of Nottingham, Malaysia, continues to analyse Malaysian politics. A major explanatory challenge is the surprise victory of the opposition coalition in the May 2018 general election, the first time the ruling coalition has lost since independence upending the electoral authoritarian regime. A divided Malay political elite was crucial in the opposition victory, apparently running contrary to the earlier thesis of elite factionalism inhibiting democratic change which will undoubtedly become a new focus of his research.

145013.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
145013.value: Why has democratization in Southeast Asia been quite limited and the few electoral democracies so troubled? Notwithstanding long democratic traditions in several countries and the attainment of middle-income standing in many, most countries in the region are 'fully' or partially authoritarian with the two remaining electoral democracies suffering from low-quality with growing threats against liberal institutions (Indonesia and, particularly, the Philippines). In addressing this question, it was shown the level of economic development or the difference between presidential and parliamentary systems does not explain democracy's discontents in Southeast Asia. Rather it was argued that democratization/democratic consolidation has been impeded by ambitious elites who instrumentalize class or ethnic divisions and issue populist or reformist appeals to mobilize constituencies. In this way, cohesive elites have constrained democratic change, either colluding to perpetuate authoritarian controls or blocking increases in democratic quality. Alternatively, fractious elites have competed so fiercely with competing popular narratives that they have precipitated democratic breakdown. Comparative analysis for the project was aided by the fact that the diversity of regime forms makes Southeast Asia a 'natural laboratory,' leading to conclusions which raise questions about some of the conventional explanations of democratic crises and which offer an alternative approach.

145113.label: Project Title(Chinese)
145113.value: 建造城市模範村：中國公營住宅起源研究(1920-1940年代)

145113.label: Project Objectives
145113.value: To provide a comprehensive history of early public housing development in China. To identify the national policy on public housing provision in Nationalist China from 1928 to 1949. To compare the design and planning of early public housing projects in eight Chinese cities: Nanjing, Guangzhou, Shanghai, Beijing, Wuhan, Hangzhou, Qingdao, and Shantou. To identify the precedents and references for the design and planning of public housing in Nationalist China.
rows: To provide a comprehensive history of early public housing development in China.
To identify the national policy on public housing provision in Nationalist China from 1928 to 1949.
To compare the design and planning of early public housing projects in eight Chinese cities: Nanjing, Guangzhou, Shanghai, Beijing, Wuhan, Hangzhou, Qingdao, and Shantou.
To identify the precedents and references for the design and planning of public housing in Nationalist China.

145113.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
145113.value: Although public housing was one of the most important components of China’s socialist urbanism, its creation predated 1949. Curiously, compared to the vast amount of studies on the Socialist era, the development of public housing before the Communist occupation remains a gap in current housing scholarship. In fact, the provision of collective housing to China’s working poor dated to the 1920s, first as a community service of philanthropic organizations and later as a Nationalist state-sponsored program. If housing was regarded as an individual problem everywhere, then why and how did the provision of housing and the removal of substandard dwellings become state responsibilities during the Nationalist era? What form did early public housing take? What were the design references for Nationalist architects and planners at the time? This research project traces the origins of public housing in China to the Nationalist era and examines the state’s efforts to make housing into a domain of the government. During the studied period, living in the city became an increasingly popular choice for Chinese people and posed a new governmental problem for China regarding how to regulate urban spaces and the urban population. The Nationalists embraced extraordinarily radical changes in both attitudes and public policies toward urban living. Prioritizing rational life, sanitary cities, and a moral community, they problematized slums, which emerged extensively in Chinese cities as a result of increasing industrialization and urbanization, as detrimental to hygiene, sanitation, safety, and social morality. These changing biopolitics led to the belief that the removal of private problems was intrinsic to the modernization of China. This research project portrays the built environment of the early public housing as the product of a dynamic process shaped by changing biopolitics, the National reform ideology, and the early urbanization of China. It argues that the Nationalist architects and planners adopted an environmental determinism, believing that the design of the physical environment could shape the behavior of the people. As such, they worked not only toward providing accommodations for the poor but also toward creating a “model village” that represented a sanitary and moral urban environment in the new republic. Their design ideas, such as regular neighborhood planning, uniform building design, sharing of communal facilities, and the integration of the social reform program, remained major features of public housing not only in the Socialist era but also in present-day China.

145113.label: Realisation of objectives
145113.value: Objective 1: To Provide a comprehensive history of early public housing development in China The research team carried out extensive historical research on the development of public housing in Nationalist China to understand, first, the Nationalist state’s attempts at placing housing, a traditionally private matter, in the government’s domain and, second, the development of public housing in every city. The historical research involved the study of government publications, historical newspapers, and magazines published during the studied period. The research team initially believed that public housing had been developed in eight major cities in China, but the historical research yielded an exciting result: various kinds of government-initiated housing projects were developed in at least 30 cities during the studied period. These cities included: Nanjing, Qingdao, Shanghai, Chongqing, Shantou, Beijing, Guangzhou, Wuhan, Tianjin, Changsha, Hangzhou, Zhenjiang, Guilin, Chengdu, Xian, Zhengzhou, Wuhu, Xuzhou, Ningbo, Taiyuan, Shaoguan, Suzhou, Jiangyin, Kunshan, Lanzhou, Nanchang, Baoding, Datong, Ganzhou, and Wuxi. The public housing projects in these 30 cities employed various names, such as “commoners’ village,” “workers’ village,” “poor people’s village,” “model village,” and “urban residents’ village.” Based on the information from the historical publications, the research team selected cities with the largest proportions of public housing development: Nanjing, Qingdao, Shanghai, Shantou, Beijing, Guangzhou, and Wuhan. The research team visited the historical archives and libraries in all seven cities. The archival research provided valuable primary sources, such as government reports and records, correspondences between departments, and architectural drawings. Nevertheless, the research team also encountered some difficulties during the research process, as some archival records were not available to the public. Building on the historical research, the research team created a timeline for the development of public housing in Nationalist China. The research team also summarized the scope and scale of public housing development in each city. Objective 2: To identify the national policy on public housing provision in Nationalist China from 1928 to 1949 A major goal of the research team was to explore whether the construction of public housing was an initiative by individual cities or a top-down instruction from the Nationalist government. Through the archival research, the research team discovered that the provision of housing for the urban poor was first initiated in 1928 by the municipal governments in Nanjing, Shanghai, and Shantou, respectively. It would soon become a national policy when the Ministry of Interior of the Nationalist government issued a directive in October of the same year, requiring all municipal cities to build “commoners’ villages” for the impoverished working class. Appended to this directive were two village plans, one circular and one rectangular in configuration, suggested by the Ministry of the Interior. The research team was fortunate to have found these two plans from the Shantou Municipal Archives. Later in 1930, the Ministry of Industry, Commerce, and Labor made a detailed proposal for the construction of a “workers’ village” in China. The proposal and the suggested village plan, which was subsequently published in various popular magazines at the time, were prepared by Thomas Tchou, the former executive secretary of the Industrial Department of the Young Men’s Christian Association (YMCA) in China. Objective 3: To compare the design and planning of early public housing projects in eight Chinese cities: Nanjing, Guangzhou, Shanghai, Beijing, Wuhan, Hangzhou, Qingdao, and Shantou. An important goal of the archival research was to understand the design and planning of the public housing projects. The research team was able to copy some old architectural drawings from local archives. The design and planning of public housing projects in Nanjing, Qingdao, and Shanghai were particularly well documented. Based on the collected drawings, the research team conducted a design analysis and reached the following conclusions. Almost all the public housing projects were developed in the form of an urban village. The planning of the village usually fell into two categories. The first included the two hypothetical plans made by the Ministry of Interior and the Ministry of Industry, Commerce, and Labor, respectively. The proposed plans emphasized the provision of community facilities (such as a community center, school-cum-library, playground, etc.) in the center of the village. Surrounding these community facilities were the village houses. The research team found only one case in Nanjing that went according to the ministry’s plan. The second type, which was built primarily by local governments in China, employed a regular plan that followed a simple grid. Sometimes, community facilities, such as schools and playgrounds, were also provided in the village. The design of the village house took one of three forms. The first and most common was a simple house with a long, rectangular plan, which allowed it to be subdivided into several small units for individual families. The second, which targeted more affluent families, was a semi-detached house containing two residential units, each comprising two to three bedrooms, a living room, and a kitchen. The last one, one of its kind and founded only in Guangzhou, was a multi-story apartment. Objective 4: To identify the precedents and references for the design and planning of public housing in Nationalist China To explore the origins of the idea of public housing provision in China, the research team analyzed the writings published during the Nationalist period to understand the various housing theories proposed by technocrats and scholars at the time. The research team found that the provision of public housing in China was influenced by three important references. The first was the “New Village Movement (Atarashiki-mura)” suggested by the Japanese novelist, Saneatsu Mushanokōji. The second was the “Model Dwelling Movement” developed in the United Kingdom and the United States after the Industrial Revolution. The final and most important of the three references was the “model workers’ village” built by the YMCA in 1926 for workers in Pudong, Shanghai. The YMCA’s “model workers’ village” proposed by Thomas Tchou, the executive secretary of the YMCA’s Industrial Department, was the first welfare housing project built for the urban working poor in modern China. To learn more about this project, the principal investigator (PI) conducted an archival search at the Kautz Family YMCA Archives in Minneapolis, the United States. The research team also studied almost all the writings published by Thomas Tchou during the studied period. The research team believes that the YMCA’s model village served as an important welfare housing precedent for the Nationalist leaders for several reasons. First, Nationalist leaders such as Chiang Kai-shek and Kung Hsiang-hsi had been invited by the YMCA to visit the model village. They were so impressed with the village that they agreed to personally patronize the project. Second, shortly after the completion of the model village, Thomas Tchou, the YMCA secretary in charge of the project, was recruited by Kung Hsiang-hsi to join the Ministry of Industry, Commerce, and Labor. He was responsible for the development of the hypothetical “workers’ village” plan on behalf of the ministry.

145113.label: Major findings and research outcome
145113.value: In 1926, the China Branch of the Young Men's Christian Association (YMCA) developed a “model workers’ village” for factory workers in the Pudong section of Shanghai. This was the first welfare housing project built in modern China, and it served as an important precedent for the Nationalist government. The Principal Investigator (PI) presented the research findings in the Eighth Biennial Conference of the Urban History Association in 2016. The PI’s article about the ways the YMCA model village influenced public housing’s development in the Nationalist period is under review by the Journal of Urban History. Nationalist leaders were impressed with the YMCA’s model village. Not only did they back the YMCA’s projects financially, but they also carried the model village’s ideas to the Nationalist government. The year 1928 saw the emergence of public housing in the form of small urban villages in Nanjing, Shanghai, and Shantou. It was also in 1928 that the Nationalist government made public housing a national policy. In October, the Ministry of Interior required all municipal city governments to build public housing for impoverished working people. Since then, public housing has been developed in at least 30 Chinese cities. Nanjing, Qingdao, Shanghai, and Chongqing are among the cities with the largest-scale public housing developments, with thousands of residential units. China’s government-initiated housing projects employed various names, such as “commoners’ village,” “workers’ village,” “poor people’s village,” “model village,” and “urban residents’ village.” Albeit having different names, almost all the public housing projects employed a regular village plan to create a tidy environment. All village houses, which employed a uniform design, were planned in an orderly fashion following a simple grid. Some community facilities, such as schools and playgrounds, were also provided in the village. The design of the village house took one of three forms. The first and most common was a simple house with a long, rectangular plan, which allowed it to be subdivided into several small units for individual families. The second, which targeted more affluent families, was a semi-detached house containing two residential units, each comprising two to three bedrooms, a living room, and a kitchen. The last one, one of its kind and founded only in Guangzhou, was a multi-story apartment. The PI plans to publish a monograph on the origins, development, and design of public housing in Nationalist China and is in the process of preparing the manuscript.

145113.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
145113.value: This research has the potential for further development into two future studies. The first concerns the various types of welfare housing and shelters for the emerging urban poor. In the early 20th century, China experienced rapid industrialization and urbanization, which led to a serious housing shortage in the cities. Public housing was only one of the many housing efforts developed in this period of tremendous social changes. A comprehensive study should be conducted to investigate the various building programs developed by the government, charity organizations, and individual philanthropists to accommodate the poor. These included the almshouse, workers’ dormitories, homeless shelters, and so forth. The second study concerns the planning of new housing districts in Nationalist China. Alongside the development of public housing for the poor, some municipal governments actively planned luxury housing districts, often employing the name “model housing areas” or “new housing areas.” Unlike the public housing projects’ regular planning, new housing districts often featured a neighborhood design with curvilinear roads, Western-style detached houses, and plenty of greenery. A study on these new housing districts could provide a better understanding about the planning of city and the production of housing in Nationalist China.

145113.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
145113.value: This research project seeks to correct a common misconception that suggests that public housing in China was invented by the Communists after 1949. In fact, the provision of welfare housing to China’s working poor dates to the 1920s, first as a community service of philanthropic organizations and later as a Nationalist state-sponsored program. Between 1928 and 1949, the Nationalist government launched an ambitious program to modernize Chinese cities and to eradicate urban slums. It was also at this time that the Nationalist government began to develop public housing to accommodate an increasing urban population. By tracing the origins and design of public housing, this research project examines the state’s effort to make housing, traditionally a private matter, into the government’s domain. It contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of China’s urban housing history, theory, and design. It also argues that the Nationalist architects and planners adopted environmental determinism, believing that the design of the physical environment could shape the people’s behavior. As such, they worked not only to provide accommodations for the poor but also to create “model villages” that represented a sanitary and moral urban environment for the new republic.

145213.label: Project Objectives
145213.value: To investigate how cultural heritage is embedded in places and objects. To explore the role that objects and domestic spaces play in encounters between peoples. To understand, and interpret, the lived experience of residents from Tai Ping Street, Tai O fishing village, Hong Kong and to make cultures in their various local strangenesses available to one another or (semi)translatable via the production of a fine-grained simulation of a series of houses from Tai Ping Street, Tai O. To produce a high fidelity 3D visualisations of 12-17 dwellings from Tai Ping Street, Tai and to gather oral history and evidence of intangible culture via extensive interviews with residents. To create a content-rich, interactive cultural heritage exhibit that combines the 3D visualisations with the oral histories. To create numerous meta-data tags so that social science scholars and other interested parties can access additional layers of information and details about the houses and objects visualised. To display the exhibit in Tai O and at The Creative Media Centre, City University and to conduct evaluative research into the effectiveness of virtual representations in cultural heritage conservation by interviewing visitors to the exhibit.

145213.label: Realisation of objectives
145213.value: The project followed the original application's objectives and schedule in most parts. Between April 2015 and March 2016 I worked on the project with 6 Research Assistants. We together took thousands of photos, built hundreds of 3D models and finished several virtual house interiors. I also made the interactive programming and designed the installation to show the finished project for the people. I also presented different versions of the project in several exhibitions and festivals. In these exhibitions and festivals the project's name was "Homes", because the official title of the GRF project would have been too long. The exhibitions of "Homes" are: 2013, Goethe Institut Hong Kong; 2013 CMC Summer Festival, City University, Hong Kong; 2015, Lumenvisum Gallery, JCCAC, Hong Kong; 2016 ISEA2016 International Symposium of Electronic Arts, The Hong Kong Polytechnic, Hong Kong; 2016, "Age of experience" exhibition at the "Angewandte Innovation Lab" of the University of Applied Arts in Vienna, Austria. During the development I realized we cannot produce the originally planned number of dwellings from Tai Ping Street. We were able to produce about 8 of them. The reasons are: 1. My project received less RGC funds than the project required (I asked for HK$ 545,750 and was awarded HK$ 377,750, about the 69% of the required budget). Therefore between November 2013 and September 2014 I was able to hire only one Research Assistant and we could produce much less than planned. Then I won a donation of of HK$ 226,800 from the Drs Richard Charles & Esther Yewpick Lee Charitable Foundation which helped me to hire more RAs, but still we could not produce as many dwellings as I originally planned. 2. The available technology is not as fast as I expected. With the use of the modern photogrammetry software I hoped I can automatize the 3D object building process, but the result produced by the software was not appropriate for interactive, real-time presentation. It contained too many polygons, it was not precise enough and the independent objects were not separated. Therefore we had to edit and modify the data which took a lot of time, about the 80% of the production time of the project.

145213.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
145213.value: Hong Kong is an extremely rapidly changing city. The old buildings quickly vanish, and with them, so do lifestyles. By the fact that the artists participating in the project attempted to document these spaces with as much detail as possible, and tried to model these objects as precisely as possible, with time-consuming precise work, the visual representation of these spaces will become a part of the material of a general knowledge, and they will be able to live on, and even constitute the basis for further research. The technology employed in this project is not new. Many heritage projects use similar software and hardware. This project perhaps differs from the familiar similar projects in two respects. The first is that I have intentionally tried to use inexpensive technology that is accessible to everyone: for instance, open source software, typical cameras. The second is that while most similar projects present historically important and well-known buildings or locations, this project would like to introduce an everyday lifestyle of people living contemporaneously with us.

147013.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
147013.value: Moving into retirement is a major life event though there are a few local studies assessing retirees’ adjustment in the actual transition. Positive adjustment to retirement provides a nurturing environment for retirees to prepare for a new chapter in later life; alternatively poor adjustment may result in poor health and life dissatisfaction. With a growing number of employees retiring from work in the coming few years, there is a pressing need to identify protective factors for positive adjustment to this critical life transition. Wang, Henkens, and van Solinge’s (2011) resource-based dynamic perspective proposes that tangible, mental and social resources possessed by retirees determine the quality of adjustment to retirement. It is predicted that retirees will maintain their well-being if their resources do not change significantly after retirement; whereas they will experience negative changes in well-being if their resources decline after retirement. Based on this theoretical framework, the proposed project aims at examining retirees' adjustment and longitudinal changes in physical, cognitive and psychological well-being in the actual retirement transition. It also intends to assess the mediating role of retirement resources in the relationship between pre-retirement planning and retirement adjustment. Pre-retirees, who will retire from their current job in the next 6 months, will be recruited to take part in this longitudinal study. The project will consist of an initial study which will be conducted six months pre-retirement, and two follow-up studies which will be conducted six months and one year after the actual retirement. Findings of this project will contribute to the literature on aging and human development for understanding the underlying mechanism of adjustment of Chinese retirees, and provide insights and recommendations to policy makers and health care professionals for promoting retirement preparation and designing intervention programs among middle-aged working adults. 退休是人生中一個重大的階段，但很少本地研究探討退休人士的適應情況。有效的適應能有助退休人士打開生命的新一頁；相反地，倘若未能適應退休生活，可能會導致對生活的不滿及長遠的健康問題。在未來幾年，將會有越來越多的在職僱員進入退休行列，所以探討退休適應的影響因素是十分迫切及重要的。根據Wang, Henkens 和van Solinge (2011) 提出的資源基礎理論，一些實質、心理及社交的資源均會影響退休人士的適應情況。因此，如果僱員於退休前後的資源沒有明顯差別，他們的心理和生理狀態的轉變不會太大；反之，如果他們的資源因退休而下降，他們會因此而經歷負面的轉變。根據此理論框架，本研究的目的為測試退休人士的適應情況，及以縱向方式來探討他們在生理、認知及心理狀態的轉變，亦會探索退休資源在退休前規劃及退休適應之間的中介角色。本研究將會招募六個月後退休的在職人士，在他們退休前六個月、退休後半年及一年進行三次問卷調查。研究結果將有助了解華人適應退休生活的影響因素及機制，研究結果將對老年與發展心理學的文獻作出貢獻。另外，本調查結果可為政策制定者和醫護人員提供有效的建議，以推廣中年在職人士的退休前準備及設計介入計劃。

147013.label: Realisation of objectives
147013.value: The three objectives of this project have been achieved satisfactorily. Objective 1 has been realized through an implementation of a longitudinal study in a sample of 197 Hong Kong Chinese retirees. It consisted of three waves of data collection: Time 1 was conducted 6 months before the actual retirement of the participant; Time 2 and 3 were carried out 6 months and 12 months respectively after the retirement. Among the 197 participants, 146 retirees also completed the T2 assessment, while 132 retirees completed the T3 assessments (response rate as 74% and 67% respectively). Their levels of physical, psychological and cognitive well-being were measured in all three waves using both subjective (e.g., self-reported Short-Form Health Survey, life satisfaction, psychological well-being) and objective (e.g., Mini-mental state examination for measuring cognitive functioning) tests. The latent growth model was conducted to examine the longitudinal changes in physical, psychological and cognitive well-being. Objectives 2 has been achieved through testing the mediation relationship among pre-retirement planning activities, retirement resources, and retirement adjustment. In particular, the amount of pre-retirement planning activities was assessed in Time 1 whereas retirement resources and well-being were measured in the three assessments. The latent growth mediation analyses were performed to test the mediating effect of retirement resources in the relationship between pre-retirement planning and changes in well-being during the transition to retirement. Objective 3 has also been achieved through examining the effects of future time perception and interdependent self-construal on retirement adjustment. Specifically, moderation regression analyses were performed to address whether the retirees’ perception of future time and interdependent self-construal (measured in Time 1) would influence the levels of total resources and retirement adjustment.

147013.label: Major findings and research outcome
147013.value: This longitudinal study examined Hong Kong Chinese retirees’ adjustment to the retirement transition over 18 months. It consisted of three waves of assessment: 6-month pre-retirement (T1), 6-month (T2) and 1-year (T3) post-retirement. Major findings are summarized below: a) The latent growth models were conducted to investigate whether retirees showed poorer well-being after retirement. Results reveal that the mean of the slopes of well-being variables was not significant, though the negative value of the slopes of physical functioning, life satisfaction and psychological well-being implies that there is a general trend of poorer well-being in the current sample of retirees. The significant variance of the slopes of physical well-being and psychological distress also demonstrates the individual variations in the rate of changes in well-being during the transition (i.e., some retirees showed greater declines in well-being while others remained relatively stable over time). These findings are reported in the paper of Yeung and Zhou (2017) in Part C. b) Retirement resources were a significant predictor of psychological adjustment to retirement. In particular, for the retirees with more total resources (including financial, physical, cognitive, social, emotional and motivational resources) after retirement, they reported significant higher levels of physical and psychological well-being in T2 and T3. The slopes of various resources were also significantly correlated with the slopes of psychological and physical well-being. These findings are reported in the papers of Yeung (2017) and Yeung and Zhou (2017). c) To uncover the underlying mechanism of the positive effect of pre-retirement planning activities on retirement adjustment, the latent growth mediation analyses were performed. The results show that pre-retirement planning helped the retirees to maintain (or even improve) their total resources after retirement, which subsequently contributed to better adjustment one year after retiring from their jobs. These mediation results are summarized in the paper of Yeung and Zhou (2017). d) The moderating effects of future time perspective (FTP) and interdependent self-construal on the relationship between resource changes and psychological adjustment were also explored using regression analyses. In particular, the negative effect of resource gain over time on T3 psychological distress was significantly stronger in the retirees with more limited FTP than in those with more open-ended FTP. In addition, the positive effect of resource gain on T3 life satisfaction was stronger in the retirees with higher interdependent self-construal than in those with lower interdependent self-construal (these results will be appeared in a manuscript under preparation).

147013.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
147013.value: This project is the first longitudinal study in Hong Kong to examine the actual changes in well-being and resources over an 18-month transition to retirement among Chinese retirees. It has created a valuable database to evaluate the impact of pre-retirement planning activities on retirement resources and psychological adjustment to retirement. However, the long-term effects of pre-retirement planning and resource changes await further investigation. In view of a growing number of retirees in the next 10 years, it is essential to promote working adults’ preparation for their retirement and to identify the buffering factors to reduce maladjustment in the retirees with fewer preparatory behaviors and resources before retirement. Findings of this project have generated insights for future research: (1) to evaluate the long-term impacts (5 years and above) of pre-retirement planning; (2) to explore whether resource gains in social and cognitive domains can compensate declines in financial resources over time; and (3) to examine whether intervention programs on retirement planning are effective in increasing the amount of resources of retirees in the long run. Based on the data and experiences of the present longitudinal project, an extension study will be proposed in the fall of 2018 to investigate the above-mentioned issues.

147013.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
147013.value: Positive adjustment to retirement is essential for maintaining physical and psychological well-being in later life. This project aimed at identifying the protective factors for successful adjustment to this critical life event. By applying the resource-based dynamic model (Wang et al., 2011), this 3-wave longitudinal project examined the retirees’ actual changes in physical, psychological and cognitive well-being before and after retirement. It also explored the underlying mechanism between pre-retirement planning activities and retirement adjustment. Results of the latent growth models reveal that there is a general trend of experiencing poorer physical health, life satisfaction, and psychological well-being one year after retirement. The retirees also perceive themselves having fewer total resources (especially financial resources) after retirement. Consistent with the prediction, positive changes in well-being are shown in the retirees with resource gains after retirement. The results of the latent growth mediation analyses also reveal that the retirees with more planning activities before retirement acquire greater resources at the initial stage, which consequently contribute to better post-retirement well-being. Findings of this project provide important implications to the policy makers and employers to promote preparation for retirement among middle-aged employees to facilitate positive adjustment to retirement in the future.

157013.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
157013.value: Over thirty years after the Cambodia genocide of 1975-79, which took the lives of an estimated 2.2 million Cambodians, the Extraordinary Courts in the Chambers of Cambodia (ECCC) have begun tribunal hearings for what has been described as “the largest and most complicated prosecution since Nuremberg in 1945” (Andrew Cayley). But as Julie McGonegal notes in her book Imagining Justice, truth and reconciliation commissions have tended towards a “privileging of discourses of forensic truth and a devaluation of stories and literature” (180). My research project entitled “Reframing Human Rights Discourse: Justice and Cambodian Life Stories in English” will consider how Cambodian diasporic life stories (as found in oral history, literature, and film) serve as a rich site for understanding difficult questions about justice in the aftermath of genocide: How are notions of trauma read differently across cultural, national, gendered, and generational divides, and what are the implications of these epistemological differences for thinking about justice? What is the relationship between the mobilization of life stories and the collective work of reconciliation? Finally, how might life stories productively reframe and call attention to the limitations of international human rights discourse in the twenty-first century? My research will explore how Cambodian life stories in English not only bear witness to a truth beyond what is empirically verifiable, but they also have a creative license to imagine potential futures beyond the trauma, a creativity that is not as readily available in anthropological, sociological, and legal texts. Scholars have noted that the need to bear witness “provides one explanation for why there has been more life writing by or about Cambodians than by or about any other ethnic cohort in the United States during the past several decades” (Yamada 147). Trends parallel to the American context are now taking place in other parts of the world, evidenced by the recent emergence of Cambodian literature, film, and oral history in English in places such as Canada, Australia, and Cambodia. This body of cultural production reconstructs a traumatic past that haunts not just the memory of Cambodians, but also twentieth-century collective memory. In analyzing a selection of this archive, my project will contribute knowledge to the overlapping fields of life writing, oral history, human rights cultural studies, critical genocide studies, refugee studies, and the study of Cambodian diaspora. 摘要：在1975年至1979年的柬埔寨種族滅絕中，估計有220萬柬埔寨人喪生。及後超過三十年，柬埔寨法院特別法庭（ECCC）開始了法庭聽證，審理被形容為「自1945年紐倫堡審判以來最大型及最複雜的起訴」（凱利．安德魯）。但朱莉麥格在她的書《想像正義》裡，提及真相與和解委員會傾向視法庭的話語為真理並貶低故事和文學裡的真相（180 ）。我的研究項目名為「重新定義人權話語：正義與柬埔寨人民的生活的英語故事」，將考慮柬埔寨人民的離散生活的故事（包括在口述歷史、文學和電影中找到的故事）如何提供豐富的材料，解答有關種族滅絕後的正義等難題： 不同的文化、國家、性別和時代看待創傷的概念有何不同？而這些知識上的思考正義的差異有何含義呢？離散的生活故事與集體和解又有何關係？最後，這些生活故事將如何有效地的重構人權話語，並呼籲人們關注國際人權話語在二十一世紀所面對的局限？ 我的研究將探討柬埔寨生活的英語故事如何見證了超出經驗可驗證的真理，更作為創意的體現，讓人民以想像的可能的未來超越創傷。這種創造力並非人類學，社會學和法律文本中能找到的。學者們指出，這樣的見證的需要「解釋了為何在過去幾十年的美國，由柬埔寨人所寫的或有關柬埔寨生活的書籍，比任何其他民族的多」（山田147 ）。與美國景況平行的趨勢正在世界各地其他地方發生，英語的柬埔寨文學、電影及口述歷史近來在加拿大，澳大利亞和柬埔寨等地的出現便是證明。這類文化產物重構了慘痛過去，所困擾的不單是柬埔寨人的記憶，更是二十世紀的集體回憶。我的項目，分析了此存檔的一部分，它將有助於提供有關生命書寫、口述歷史、人權文化研究、評論種族滅絕研究、難民研究及柬埔寨離散研究等重疊領域的知識。

157013.label: Realisation of objectives
157013.value: Reframing Human Rights Discourse: Justice and Cambodian Life Stories in English has achieved most of its project objectives. The research addresses the gap in scholarly research about the stories of survivors and refugees of the Cambodian genocide and the Vietnam War, contributing knowledge of relevance to Cambodia's ongoing truth and reconciliation movement, to the ongoing global refugee crisis, and to the topic of asylum seeking in the local Hong Kong context. The research analyses refugee stories in a variety of genres (memoir, film, fiction) and thus offers new methodological approaches in the field of cultural studies for analysing texts across different mediums. This project has made an impact in the fields of human rights, cultural studies, and Asian studies in particular. In total, I have 10 journal publications emerging from this project. This is a substantial research output given the difficulty of the subject matter and the challenges of accessing and working with the archives in a post-conflict setting where history is still being reconstructed. I have hired and trained Research Assistants, Student Assistants, and Postdoctoral Fellows. I have travelled to Phnom Penh, Cambodia to undertake archival and secondary research at the Bophana Audiovisual Centre (http://bophana.org) and the Documentation Centre of Cambodia (http://www.dccam.org). I attended the ECCC Tribunal hearing in Phnom Penh (http://www.eccc.gov.kh/en) and conducted court observation. These research activities contributed directly to the publication of journal articles that derived from the project. Since the beginning of the project, I have attended 14 international conferences/workshops in my field, where I presented my research as a conference panelist or invited speaker. I have also been actively engaged with disseminating my research at my university in the English Department and the Center for Southeast Asian Research. My research for this project has directly benefitted my teaching and has resulted in 1 published journal article on teaching human rights and literature. In March 2015, I was awarded City U's Teaching Excellence Award and received the university nomination for the UGC Hong Kong-wide Teaching Award. I have achieved some additional research/educational outcomes indirectly related to the project, such as the organization of a four-week internship project in Cambodia for Hong Kong students. The video summarizing this project can be found here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HxSolO_bAlg&feature=youtu.be. This internationalization project was funded by a different grant, but would not have been possible without the background and research networks I acquired working in Cambodia through the GRF project. The first problem I encountered was the construction of the online Cambodian archive. After some field research in Cambodia, it was discovered that several archives of Cambodian literary and cultural material already existed and therefore it was not necessary for me to construct another duplicate one. I reverted back to the 5 objectives as per the original application (5.1). The second area of under-achievement is the publication of the book manuscript. Although the manuscript has already been submitted once for review to Temple University Press, the book needed to undergo a significant round of revisions and therefore is still under consideration from Temple UP. Although the manuscript could not be fully completed in the 3 years of the ECS project, I believe my journal articles that derived from this project (many of which are article versions of the manuscript chapters) have made a satisfactory impact in the field and the book manuscript is still forthcoming.
