To investigate the sociopolitical values of individuals who consume commercial nightlife in China.
To examine how nightlife consumption practices in China reinforce as well as disrupt hierarchical socioeconomic structures.

241813.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
241813.value: 夜經濟—一個由城市研究和地理學者提出的,指深夜中的文化消費與生產的名辭—在過去幾十年在西方經濟發達國家快速成長. 目睹夜經濟在歐美助長城市重建.中國政府也從2000年代起大力在國內建立夜經濟.這是一個出人意料的發展,因為政府在1980年代仍有處死搞舞會派對人,而在1990年代仍因禁毒而把很多的廳關掉.本研究計畫探討這新發展怎麼影響中國社會.而探討會集中在三方面: 本地居民怎麼抵抗和利用夜經濟空間,夜生活參與者的社會政治觀,和夜生活消費對現存社會分層的支持和擾亂.

241813.label: Realisation of objectives
241813.value: All three objectives have been fully achieved. Data collection went smoothly. Objective 1: The fieldwork and interviews associated with Objective 1 took place in Beijing’s main nightlife districts: Sanlituan-Gongti, Shichahai-Gulou. The Sanlituan-Gongti district displaces and disturbs local residents to a small degree, and the Shichahai-Gulou district does it to a moderate degree. I find that local and Beijing residents are able to reclaim spaces of these two nightlife districts through practicing non-commercial leisure activities in the two districts. There only problem is the scale of this resistance is limited. Not many local residents do that, and the variety of ways through which they reclaim nightlife districts spaces are also limited. The data is good and the outcome is similar to what I expected, but they are probably not enough for writing a paper. In time meantime, these data are briefly analyzed in a paper in preparation ( ‘Far Eastern formations’) Based on my past research experience, I know that local residents do more to resist gentrification and reclaim space in nightlife districts in Changsha and Wuhan, for example. I therefore plan to write a dedicated paper on this topic through analyzing how local residents appropriate nightlife districts of other cities. I have already done a bit of that in the past and will gather more data very soon. Objective 2: A survey was successfully carried out in May 2016 with 1,000 nightlife participants. It took much planning and redesign. A slight problem here is that the price of doing a survey went up quite a bit since 2013. I was advised to lower the cost (because my budget is limited to HKD 100,500) through switching from phone surveying to online surveying. Eventually I think the pros of picking online surveying outweigh its cons. Random sampling is more fully carried out through online survey. The data collected largely support the argument I originally planned to make in the proposal, which is that sociopolitical values of avid nightlife participants are in some ways more liberal than the average Chinese citizens. Objective 3: Data for Objective 3 were supplied by a subsection of the survey, in-depth and ethnographic interviews, and participant observation (by the RA and PI). I collected good data from all these sources. I was fortunate to have found an excellent RA to do participant observation in dance clubs. She helped to get access to data that were not open to me. She carried out the kinds of observation that I originally planned, which focused on the social interaction among clubbers from different socioeconomic class. Good data on this issue were collected. I will discuss these data in a paper in preparation (‘‘Toward a nocturnal sociology’). Beyond the three original objectives: I extended the scope of investigation to service work and service workers in the Chinese dance club. Most of these workers are rural-to-urban migrant workers. Analysis of these data has led me to new research directions beyond the three planned objectives of the original proposal. I am glad about it because the new direction is both theoretically intriguing and marketable to high ranking journals. I was led to write four papers on service work and rural migrant service workers. Three of them have been submitted and undergoing review. The fourth is being revised because I was dissatisfied with the first draft (the one on ‘Trilateral games’) Let me provide a very short description of the four papers I have written and three papers I am drafting with data of this GRF project. I am the sole author of all of them. All of them are attached with the report. 1. rural migrant workers and consumption: An alternative perspective This study critiques the dominant perspective in current studies on Chinese rural migrant workers’ consumption and constructs an alternative perspective. I construct it partly through borrowing from the ongoing interdisciplinary debate on consumption’s sociopolitical characteristics, and partly through constructing a new conception of sociopolitically progressive consumption that would help re-interpret consumption practices of rural migrant workers 2. Reassessing Chinese rural migrants’ consumption: the case of ‘post-1990s rural migrants’ working in Beijing’s dance clubs This study engages current studies on Chinese rural migrants’ consumption, problematizing their assessment of it as sociopolitically conservative or mere personal empowerment. It empirically challenges current characterization of rural migrants’ consumption through documenting how a group of third generation rural migrants consume and analyzes evidences that show how they subvert the sociocultural hierarchy that discriminates them in urban China. 3. New boundary work of Chinese rural migrant workers: How they contest rural-versus-urban boundary in urban China This study identifies and analyze new types of boundary work that the most recent cohorts of Chinese rural migrants do as they confront this rural-versus-urban boundary. Most studies argue that assimilation is the main type of boundary work and that rural migrants usually fail to carry it out. Some studies refer to universalizing blurring as a secondary type of boundary work. This study aims to challenge these theories and perspectives by illustrating that other types of boundary work are becoming increasingly prominent in China. This new boundary work is more successful, complex, variegated, and subversive of the established rural-versus-urban boundary. 4. Trilateral games, consent, and resistance in service work in a dance club in Beijing This study illustrates that there are shop-floor games that are robustly trilateral in its formation, operation, and impact. I explore how trilaterality in games is and explicate how trilateral games manufacture worker consent and facilitate worker resistance. I find that service workers adopt new, worker-invented service routines, professional identities, and styles of doing service work that are unendorsed by the management and disliked by experienced customers. Most interestingly, they do not only resist pressures to revise these games, but proactively and strategically fight management and customers for a better environment of running them. 5. Neoliberalization of the night-time economy in China This is the first study that focuses on the night-time economy (NTE) in China. It aims to show that the Chinese NTE strongly develops toward a neoliberal orientation and to analyze how this development differs from current neoliberal developments of NTEs in the West. 6. Characterizing and assessing Far Eastern formations of night-time economies: the case of China This study maps out the formation of major commercial and non-commercial nightlife institutions in urban China, analyzes complex interaction and hybridization among them, and assesses Chinese NTE’s sociopolitical implications by comparing with those of familiar Western NTEs. The main findings are that Chinese formation of NTE is even more different from Western ones than current studies suggest, and that although its sociopolitical characteristics are less problematic than those of Western NTEs in some important aspects, they are more problematic in others. 7. Toward a nocturnal sociology: An analysis of nightlife participants’ social behavior and sociopolitical views This study contributes to advancing nocturnal sociology through testing whether individuals act and think in night-time specific social contexts in different ways than they do in familiar daytime contexts.

241813.label: Major findings and research outcome
241813.value: Objective 1: I find that local residents resist, reclaim, and negotiate the gentrified urban spaces of nightlife districts. However, I notice that the scale of resistance is moderate. For example, the scale of resistance in Changsha and Wuhan are larger, and that in Shenzhen and Shanghai is even more limited than that in Beijing. Because the funded research project is based on a single city (Beijing), I have not made dedicated research trips to other cities to do detailed data collection. Objective 2: I find that sociopolitical values of avid nightlife participants are in some ways more liberal than other Chinese citizens. The difference is significant in specific areas including sex, gender, and class. Nightlife participants think that nightlife provides for them a more liberal platform of social interaction than the daytime world. They also believe that their nightlife participation has contributed to transforming some of their (daytime) habits and thinking. Objective 3: I find that commercial nightlife consumption in China can both reinforce and disrupt hierarchical socioeconomic structures. I collected qualitative and quantitative data that elaborate how disruption and subversion of socioeconomic hierarchy is accomplished. Nightlife participants, including middle class and wealthy ones, maintain weak (daytime) ties with lower socioeconomic status friends they make in nightlife settings. Rural migrants, who compose the service workforce of dance clubs, contest socioeconomic hierarchy through tipping the power balance in manager-customer-worker relationship in cathedrals of consumption. They also subvert sociocultural hierarchy through accumulating clubcultural capital and developing the alternative urban identities.

241813.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
241813.value: There is great potential for producing additional papers or books. It is mainly because data I collected with the project complement the data I have collected over the past decade. With new data, I am ready to write at least six paper or chapters on the Chinese night-time economy. Two among the six are attached with this report (in the form of a draft and an abstract).

241813.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
241813.value: The research project finds that local and Beijing residents are able to reclaim the gentrified spaces of nightlife districts. They do it through practicing non-commercial leisure activities in areas designated as public in and near nightlife districts. It finds that sociopolitical values of experienced nightlife participants are in some ways more liberal than other Chinese citizens. The difference is significant in specific areas including gender, sex and class. It finds that commercial nightlife consumption in China contributes to disrupting the established class hierarchy. Nightlife participants, including middle class and wealthy ones, maintain daytime ties with lower status friends they make in nightlife settings. Rural migrants, who compose the service workforce of dance clubs, subvert sociocultural hierarchy through consuming nightlife in knowledgeable ways and developing the alternative urban identities.

242213.label: Project Objectives
242213.value: Analyze the trend of land expropriation protests in China during the last decade, including the changing number of such protests, their scale, repertoire of collective action, and conflict intensity, their geographical location and position in the administrative hierarchy, and the protesters’ demands. The purpose of this exercise is to generate background information for the case studies. Undertake in-depth case studies of four land expropriation protests in rural and peri-urban Guangdong and Sichuan, two of which involve more than one phase of land requisition. Attention will be paid to the contexts in which the protests emerged, the actors involved, and the historical unfolding of the events. Appraise the impacts of China’s changing policies of land development and their uneven implementation at the local level on the dynamics of land expropriation protests. The investigation will extend to how the laws and administrative measures introduced in the last decade have altered the relationships between villagers, other private actors, and officials from different levels of the government in the drama of land requisition. Evaluate whether the oft-noted central-local division of the Chinese state continues to provide the political opportunity for the emergence and “success” of these land expropriation protests or whether there has been a breakdown in the state’s capacity for local leadership among the cases studied. Examine the structures and processes of mobilization, analyzing in particular the social characteristics of the rank-and-file protesters and leaders, the extent to which the protests have emerged spontaneously, whether protesters have networked with outside activists, whether such protests show signs of coalescing into some kind of rudimentary organization, and whether protesters who have lived through more than one phase of land expropriation can use their past experience and prior networks to improve their organizational capability. Delineate the meanings articulated by the villagers through the protests, focusing on the value they attach to land, their understanding of rights and justice, and their perceptions of central and local governments. Investigate whether the villagers’ consciousness has been altered by repeated experiences of land expropriation. Through this exercise, the project will reflect on the ideas of rightful resistance, moral economy, hegemony, and citizenship rights.

242213.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
242213.value: The proposed project will examine protests against land expropriation in China. It will have two parts. The first part will be a longitudinal analysis of such protests over the last ten years. The second part will involve four in-depth case studies of land expropriation protests in Guangdong and Sichuan, two of which involved more than one phase of land requisition. In addition to the analysis of policy papers, statistics and news reports on land expropriation, petition and mass disturbance, this study will entail 100 interviews with government officials, researchers, journalists, non-government organizations and villagers that have engaged in the protests. This project is important for several reasons. First, although China’s land expropriation protests have increased in number since the late 1990s and important policy changes on land development have been introduced, relatively few scholars have studied land expropriation protests as such. This project aspires to fill this gap in the empirical knowledge. Second, existing studies of China’s rural conflicts have either paid insufficient attention to the institutional and structural factors in the emergence of land expropriation protests or treated these factors as static and external to the protests. By contrast, this project will draw attention to the changing policies and, above all, the interactions and negotiations among officials from different levels of the government, villagers and other actors in the conversion of rural land into urban land. As such, it is expected to provide a more dynamic analysis of the institutional-structural processes that underlie the unfolding of the protests. Third, this project will complement existing studies of China’s rural conflicts by providing new observations about the political opportunity for collective action, mobilization process, and cultural meanings that structure the protests. Above all, because this project will involve cases with more than one phase of protest, it will introduce new factors, namely, prior networks and learning from past experiences, with which critical debates in the study of China’s rural conflicts and nascent civil society can be re-examined. The debates include whether the protests have emerged spontaneously and remained disorganized or coalesced into emergent organizations with the benefit of past experiences and prior networks; and whether the protesters may gain a rudiment of rights consciousness when repeated land requisitions lead them to re-consider the meaning of land, justice, and their relationships to the government. The investigator expects to publish several internationally refereed journal articles and, in time, a monograph on the findings.

242213.label: Realisation of objectives
242213.value: OBJECTIVE 1 Objective one involves a tracking of China's trend in land expropriation protests. Reviewers of the project proposal suggested to drop this objective and, in part because of this, funded this project for two years rather than three. Against the advice, I keep this objective. However, given limited time and resources, I did not give priority to this objective and, without committing the RA to the task of reading and coding newspapers, managed to find a few secondary reports that did not turn out to be very informative. As the following will suggest, the Guangdong and Sichuan cases turn out to be very different and I would have benefited from such a broad overview. However, given the circumstances, I would not consider the inability to meet this objective a major failing on my part. In the future, though, internal funding will be applied to undertake this study. OBJECTIVE 2 From the point of view of the number of case studies and interviews completed, I have arguably "overachieved" objective 2. Specifically, the postgraduate student and I interviewed 30 villagers from 5 villages and 10 other informants in Sichuan; and I interviewed 23 villagers from 5 villages and 6 government officials from Guangdong. I also collected villagers' petition/litigation documents and "contracts" allegedly drawn up for the sale of land. Back to Hong Kong, I collected additional documents like court rulings of specific cases, details of the corporations taking over the expropriated land, news reports and secondary studies of the cases. A major concern is that the cases from the two provinces differ tremendously and they depart from the sampling criteria laid out in the proposal. While all 5 cases in Guangdong involved "protests" broadly defined, only one case in Sichuan witnessed overt protests. Having said so, I would still contend that, for a qualitative research inspired by the grounded theory method, it is important to let the phenomena speak for themselves rather than impose the researcher’s prior suppositions on the study. OBJECTIVE 3 In addition to examining changes in the Land Administration Law, I have also collected and examined other national plans on urban expansion, provincial and county level guidelines for land expropriation, and some other region-based initiatives on land development and regulation, all with a view to ascertaining their impacts on the outbreak of protests during land expropriation in these two provinces. To this extent, I would say that this project objective has been achieved. However, it turns out that the number of documents is massive, which makes it risky to claim at this point that my analysis is final. Having said so, I would argue that changes in the Land Administrative Law and other policies did not reflect directly in the level and nature of conflicts in land expropriation (Lin 2009). Instead, the rising importance of "land finance" for the local governments has prompted an across the board surge in land expropriation protests since the 2000s. Furthermore, while the Guangdong-Sichuan difference is real, much of it stems from the fact that most Guangdong cases concern land expropriated in the 1990s when such activities were poorly regulated. It is my tentative conclusion and a postulation that can be investigated further. OBJECTIVE 4 Case materials collected for this study (objective 2) have allowed me to evaluate the significance of political opportunity. First, even in cases that involved vigorous protests (e.g. a few thousand villagers blocking a highway for two days), no evidence pointed to a breakdown in the state's capacity for local leadership (Chen 2007). Second, villagers have often exploited the political opportunity stemming from the central government’s discourse of "rule by law" or concern with rooting out corruption. However, while this strategy might have shielded them from overt and immediate suppression, it has not always led to "success" in their protests (cf. O’Brien and Li 2006). Third, this study finds that the local cadres play an ambiguous role in matters of land expropriation. While they could be the target of villagers' protests (if they "stole" the village land), they could also serve as leaders in the villagers' contention or guardians of villagers' interests in the matter of land expropriation (cf. Michelson 2008). The last point is of interest and can be explored further in a more formal study of China's local politics. OBJECTIVE 5 Again, case materials collected for this study (objective 2) have involved an analysis of the structure and process of mobilization. However, due to differences between Guangdong and Sichuan, it is hard to provide an across the board analysis. The protest in Sichuan was spontaneous, spearheaded by a few outspoken villagers that worked on the land and lived their whole life there. Cases in Guangdong show at least two patterns. Those in peri-urban setting tended to be led by villagers in the late forties or fifties who rely on the land for income (i.e. rentier). Their children who might be well-educated or working on some urban jobs (factory, restaurants, or legal firms) were seldom involved. Those from the peri-rural areas, however, were led by villagers in the thirties, forties and occasionally twenties. Most had either worked in larger cities or were entrepreneurs with some means. In Guangdong, protesters sought help from or were aware of other rights defenders. However, fear of harsh suppression prevented them from forming coalitions. An unexpected finding is that, while most villages used an assortment of tactics, some engaged in petition, and a few ventured litigation (He 2014; Michelson 2007; Zweig 2003). The choice between petition and litigation is a phenomenon worthy of further examination. OBJECTIVE 6 Case materials collected for this study (objective 2) have tapped villagers for the value they attached to land, their understanding of property rights, meanings of justice, and their views of the central and local governments. Views expressed by these villagers through micro-blogs or online forums were also sought out and analysed. To this extent, the study has achieved this objective. The villagers' views are complex and diverse. Focusing on their views on land (and without going into all the details), whereas some villagers hold fundamentally instrumental views and see land as a potential source of income, others have in addition considered land an embodiment of their community and identity. Furthermore, even in Sichuan where rurality seems to be associated with poverty, not all villagers are overly eager to cut off from their land and become "urban residents." For them, land provides a sustainable source of income and urban living entails cash expenditures that make them feel insecure (Sargeson 2011; Lora-Wainwright 2014). In fact, this view has also been expressed by villagers in a relatively affluent chengzhongcun in Guangzhou. Villagers have also given rather divergent views on their ownership rights of land. While some are quite willing to concede that land "ultimately" belongs to the state, some hold a more contentious view and link the matter with the state legitimacy. In short, this study has unveiled ideas and beliefs that go a long way to addressing the issues of moral economy, hegemony, and citizenship rights. Having said so, it remains the case that meanings are not only complex but layered. There is room for a more vigorous and multi-layered operationalization of the idea of "rights" and thus further investigation.

242213.label: Major findings and research outcome
242213.value: (1) CHANGING LAND POLICIES AND REGIONAL VARIATIONS This study finds that whereas land expropriation in Sichuan has been conciliatory, those in Guangdong tend to be conflict-ridden and involve land expropriated decades ago (cf. Sargeson 2011, 2013). This regional variation stems from the cadres' differential compliance with national policies and provincial or county-level guidelines (cf. Lin 2009), which relates to but goes beyond the central-local dichotomy. These ideas have been explored in three conferences (outputs 9.2, 9.5, 9.7), and they will be examined thoroughly in a paper that compares the two regions systematically. A by-product of this project is an analysis of China's practices of urban expansion. One version of the paper has been submitted as a chapter for an edited volume (output 8.2). (2) CENTRAL GOVERNMENT, LOCAL CADRES, AND POLITICAL OPPORTUNITY Just as villagers have strategically utilized the central government's discourse on the rule of law; depending on the nature of land expropriation, they may either protest the village cadres or appeal to them for the advancement of their causes. The finding suggests a need to refine the central-local and state-society dichotomies and unpack the meaning of political opportunity. It contributes to the debate on the relative importance of central or local cadres in addressing the villagers' grievances (O’Brien and Li 2006; Michelson 2008). These ideas have been investigated in several conference papers (outputs 9.1, 9.3, 9.4 and 9.5) and effort will be made to write a paper that engages directly with the debate just mentioned. (3) LEADERS AND TACTICS This study has identified systematic variations in the social characteristics of leaders in the spontaneous Sichuan protest, protests in peri-urban Guangdong, and those in peri-rural Guangdong (see section 5.3 above). Furthermore, it finds that whereas protesting villages tend to use an assortment of tactics that include petition and demonstration, a few cases have ventured administrative litigation. A paper is being drafted (output 8.4) to account for the considerations behind and processes leading to administrative litigation (cf. Chen and Xu 2012; Erie 2012; He 2014). (4) LAND, PROPERTY RIGHTS, LEGITIMACY This study has unveiled meanings attributed by some villagers to land, property rights, and state legitimacy. Preliminary analyses of the data have been reported in two conference papers (outputs 9.3 and 9.6) and an international refereed journal article (output 8.1). A paper that examines this issue more thoroughly has been drafted and will be submitted after another round of revision (output 8.3).

242213.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
242213.value: (1) REGIONAL VARIATIONS AND TYPOLOGIES OF CONTENTION This study has identified a rather striking difference between Sichuan’s peaceful expropriation versus Guangdong’s conflict-ridden ones. While this pattern is somehow supported by existing research (Sargeson 2011) and has been given an explanation (i.e. early versus late urbanization and cadre compliance to land policies), the argument can be strengthened by the examination of new cases drawn from different provinces with divergent characteristics of urban expansion and local governance. (2) LOCAL SOCIETY; LOCAL POLITICS This study's finding concerning the role of the local/village cadres in land expropriation suggests the need to go beyond the simple-minded central-local or state-society dichotomies. As such, there is room for a study of local society and politics that takes into account, among other factors, the complexity of local social relations and the intricacy of village-township interface. (3) LAND, PROPERTY RIGHTS, HEGEMONY This study has unveiled important beliefs expressed by villagers in Guangdong concerning land, property rights, and hegemony. First, it will be important to explore the viewpoints of villagers outside Guangdong and, second, it will be necessary to undertake a more vigorous and multi-layered operationalization of the idea of “rights” and deepen this investigation.

242213.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
242213.value: Land expropriation is the number one reason underlying social protests in China. Despite the large number of news reports on the topic, there have been few academic studies. This project contributes by filling the glaring gap. Four findings are particularly noteworthy. First, there is an intriguing regional difference between Sichuan and Guangdong provinces, with land expropriation in the former being relatively more peaceful. This study attributes the difference to the level of local officials’ compliance with national and local regulations on land expropriation. Second, concerning the debate on whether central government officials or local cadres are more important for redressing villager grievances, this study argues that, instead of abstract debates, it is more important to identify the local cadres’ role in land expropriation. Third, this study finds that most protesting villagers have relied on an assortment of collective actions (e.g. petition, demonstration), yet only a few have resorted to litigation, thus raising the question as to the reasons underlying their choice. Fourth, this study also taps into the ways villagers viewed the significance of land and the nature of their property rights, thus shedding light on the debate on citizenship rights in China.

243313.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
243313.value: Works on history written by women in imperial China have not previously been the subject of systematical and thorough scholarship. The writing and reading of history seems to have been a male-monopolized enterprise in imperial China. There is only one woman historian included in a collective biography of Chinese historians (Zhang 1984). In a widely circulated dictionary of Chinese historians, which offers a total of 2,643 entries, merely 6 entries are dedicated to women (Qiu 1990). Among these 6 women, only 2 lived entirely in the imperial era. This is the first project to rediscover women's under-represented voices in Chinese historiography. The investigator would like to put forth that female scholars in different dynasties did produce historical works, no matter how minimal the total number compared with the huge quantity produced by male historians. The investigator proposes to conduct research on women-authored books and short writings on history in imperial China. She is of the opinion that a thorough examination of women's views on different aspects of history and a multi-angled comparison with men's perspectives would certainly sketch a different picture of the past, even though the total output of historical works by women was relatively limited. The venture of historical writing was certainly dominated by male scholars in the past. However, by appropriately placing women back into the historical scene, we could gain a more balanced understanding of how people in the past recorded and viewed history. We would be able to come across ambitious and interesting arguments presented by women. By going through their works, we could witness how women in the past integrated the public and private spheres, offered unique female perspectives on historical events, engaged themselves in debates on central problems in historiography, and brought up family-oriented and daily-life-based viewpoints to challenge conventional assumptions. In the long-term, this project will add new knowledge to the fields of gender history and historiography. 這是首項以重新發現中國古代女性在歷史閱讀及撰寫中的主體性和能動性為宗旨的研究。過往二十多年來中國性別史的蓬勃研究展現了豐碩的成果。然而﹐中國古代女性的史學著述始終未有成為學者系統研究的課題。在我們既有的知識系統裡﹐寫史論史似乎是男性專利的工作﹐但事實並不如此。這項研究將對女性史觀進行整理﹐以及從多角度與傳統論述比較﹐相信將有利於我們重新構建古人對多種歷史問題的看法﹐並掌握更為全面的歷史景觀。

243813.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
243813.value: Altough postcolonial studies have managed to communicate the bias of Western historiography of the non-West, few attempts have been made to explore the importance of the non-West for the history of Western nations. Stressing the role China and the Vietnam War had for changing its political landscape this project aims for a fundamental revision of Sweden’s contemporary history along this line. By shifting focus from Sweden’s role internationally to the importance of global events for the development of its domestic politics a new understanding for the emergence of radicalization under Olof Palme is pursued. Proceeding from newly opened archives and recently published memoirs this proposed investigation attempts to explain the appearance of an influential Maoist movement in the late 1960s - laying bare the reactions and changes this movement forced upon Swedish foreign and domestic policy of the 1970s. A first hypothesis, already tried in a pilot study, indicates it was the Chinese Communist Party who laid the foundation for a Maoist led united front in Sweden by inviting and training a small number of Swedes. A second hypothesis following directly from the first is that the radicalization of the ruling Swedish Social Democratic Party was directly caused by political provocations and its relentless focus on American atrocities in Vietnam by the United Front. A third idea that follows from this is that the Social Democratic Party came to use the Vietnam War for domestic politics; especially during national political elections. This proposed revisionist narrative of contemporary Swedish history is to be framed by an epistemological discussion about state influence over Swedish historiography during Social Democratic Party rule. Much of the material from Chinese and Swedish archives has been collected already. The part of the project founded by the RGC will run for two years and result in one article, two conference presentations, and a monograph. The general lesson presumptively drawn from this proposed study is that local history is not comprehensible without its global context. This study might become an important first step for a much needed change of focus in historiography from National history to world history and could also bring important new information and insights to the fields of Cold War and China Studies. After all, Sweden was an important proponent on the side of many socialist liberation movements in the Third World during the Cold War era. 殖民研究已成功地傳達西方的偏見 史學的非西方，很少嘗試已作出探索的重要性 非西方西方國家的歷史。強調中國的作用和 越南戰爭改變其政治面貌，該項目旨在為 沿著這條線的瑞典現代史上的根本性的修改。通過轉移焦點 從瑞典的國際作用的全球性事件的重要性 發展其國內政治有了新的認識出現 奧洛夫·帕爾梅下激進追求。要從新開張的檔案館和最近出版的回憶錄這個建議的調查，試圖解釋 一個有影響力的毛派運動在20世紀60年代後期出現 - 一語道破 反應和變化運動硬塞瑞典的外交和國內政策 20世紀70年代。第一種假設，已經嘗試過的試點研究，表明它是 中國共產黨奠定了基礎，為毛澤東領導的統一戰線 瑞典的邀請和培養少數的瑞典人。第二個假設 後，直接從第一執政的瑞典社會的激進化 民主黨直接造成的政治挑釁和不懈的重點 美國在越南的暴行聯合陣線。第三個想法，從 這是社會民主黨上台使用越南國內戰爭 政治，尤其是在國家的政治選舉。此建議的修正主義敘事 當代瑞典歷史是被誣陷狀態超過瑞典史學的影響在社會民主黨執政的認識論討論。許多來自中國和瑞典的檔案材料已經收集了。該項目的一部分，由研資局成立將運行兩年，結果一文中，有兩個 會議介紹，一本專著。一般推定得出的教訓 此建議研究當地的歷史是不理解不其全球 上下文。這項研究可能成為一個急需改變的第一個重要步驟 從國家的歷史史學對世界歷史的焦點，也可能帶來 重要的新信息和見解，冷戰與中國研究領域。 畢竟，瑞典是一個重要的支持者在旁邊的許多社會主義解放 運動在第三世界在冷戰時代。

243813.label: Realisation of objectives
243813.value: 1 To explain the emergence of a Maoist movement in Sweden and China’s role herein. 2 To probe if the Swedish Maoists created a united front against the US by focusing on the Vietnam War. By meticulously puzzling together mainly Swedish, but also some Chinese, sources I have reconstructed the historical structure of events, people, and organisations leading eventually to the establishment of a Maoist political Party; and a united front strategy, led clandestinely by this party, to rally Swedish opponents against the American attempt to hinder a communist takeover of South Vietnam. For the Swedes, to create a broad anti-American Swedish mobilization carried the hope of eventually break up the politically hegemonic Social Democratic Party and garner support for the otherwise minuscule Maoist Sweden’s Communist Party SKP. But for Beijing, which is clear from Chinese Foreign Ministry Archives material and from the archives of SKP as well, the interest was only for Sweden to become a part of an international united front focusing on Indochina. Too late only, did the Swedes realize this fact. The one sided focus on Vietnam and not domestic issues eventually led to the break up and demise of the Swedish Maoist party. 3 To investigate how the ruling Social Democratic Party stymied this united front by making Vietnamese ‘liberation’ their own agenda 4 Explore how Sweden’s Social Democratic Party used the Vietnam War to gain young voters in the national elections of 1968, 1970, and 1973. Party documents, memoirs, and other sources reveals how the Social Democratic Party (in power since the 1930's) from the early 1960's sensed a need of rejuvenation, and was forced to act in that direction when the large cohort of young people coming of age in the 1960's got engaged in the Vietnam War protests channeled skilfully by the Maoists. Starting in 1965 already, and then accelerating in 1967 and 1968 the Social Democratic Party engaged wholeheartedly for Hanoi and the NLF. I the general elections of 1968 and 1970 and also 1973 much focus was on the Vietnam War, and the SAP was victorious. However in 1976, with the war over, they tried to distance themselves from their support of Pol Pot, but this time the 40 plus years of SAP political hegemony is broken. From the Swedish Foreign Ministry Archives and from diplomatic memoirs emerges a picture that shows how the Swedish engagement in the protests against the US has, since the 1980's been misrepresented. 5 Examine to what extent Sweden supported communist movements around the world and how close their politicians stood to Mao’s China and Pol Pot’s Kampuchea. I give particular attention to the two Swedish Ambassador Kaj Björk, Jean Christophe Öberg the first serving in Beijing, the second in Hanoi, proceeding, relying on, among other sources, classified documents transferred to me via the DC Cam archives in Phnom Penh. These documents when consulted reveal a clear support of Kampuchea, from these Swedish ambassadors and their superiors in Stockholm - all the way to the top of the SAP. A special case is made on Kaj Öberg’s unique investigative tour of Kampuchea in 1976. His reports from that journey, not before investigated, reveals an informed theoretical understanding of, and sympathies for, the Socialist experiments undertaken by Pol Pot. The documents from the time also reveals a European attitude in historical consciousness and historiography of the typical traits of orientalism. A similar proclivity to forget, and misrepresent the role of the other described by Said onward figures also in the anti Vietnam War movement. The Swedish documents from the anti war movement (not least openly available proofs from its monthly publication) when read together together with Vietnamese material clearly instructs us in how Hanoi managed the establishment of a Swedish anti American popular protest movement as an important cog in its wider ‘diplomatic’ front of the war. 6 To conduct a critical investigation into the relationship between power and historiography in twentieth century Sweden. 7 Conduct a case study that can help highlight the explanatory deficiencies involved in Eurocentric historiography. The way that the history of the SAP, especially Björk's, Öberg's and Palme’s strong support for brutal East Asian dictatorships has been downplayed and displaced onto the fringe group of Maoists, whose international program they had actually taken over, points to a problematic relationship between power and knowledge. I approach this relationship in Sweden by analyzing and then juxtapose and link causally another morally infected part of Swedish history namely its compliance towards Nazi-Germany demands during World War Two. The historiography of these two events is compromised by a political influence over higher education and research. When from the late 1990's a political campaign paired with an official authority sets out to deal with WW II and with Swedish ultra nationalist and Nazi movements among its young contemporary population this is done in a way that takes attention from, and ultimately displaces the SAP engagement in the 20th century radical communism. In a longer digression, and this was an unexpected discovery, I discuss what could perhaps be described as an unconscious dialectic, arising from the suppressed memories of World War Two and Holocaust with bearing also in the broader European context.

243813.label: Major findings and research outcome
243813.value: In 2014 I presented a paper at the Resisting War conference, organized by the Institute of Contemporary History at Nova Universidade de Lisboa (Part C). The same year I also spoke at the the Tenth European Social Science History conference organized by the International Institute for Social History in Vienna (part C). Suggesting that the Swedish emotional engagement into the Vietnam War might be a projection, or displacement of a still unresolved trauma regarding the horrors of World War Two in Europe, these two presentations grew into an article submitted for consideration to Rethinking History: The Journal of Theory and Practice (see Part C). In 2015 i gave a presentation at the Judging the Past in a Post-Cold War World conference at the Humanities Research Centre, University of Sydney. This paper was based on research regarding how close the political ruling party of Sweden, the Social Democrats, was to Pol Pot’s Kampuchea in the 1970s while also critically investigating the relationship between power and historiography in twentieth century Sweden. This paper argued that in recent decades official political support for the brutal communist revolution of Pol Pot is displaced in official historiography on a small fringe group of Swedish Maoists. Politics has this way been both pacified and historically decontextualized. My paper is selected to appear in a Brill book focusing on the main theme of the conference that will appear in under the editorship of Judith Keene and Elizabeth Rechniewski (see Part C). I have also been working on Sweden’s part in Hanoi’s ‘diplomatic war;’ in order to highlight the deficiencies in some European historiography on the 1960s to deal with Asian agency. It intends to unpack the still untold history of how North Vietnam, as part of its ‘diplomatic war,’ set out to make Sweden a partner in their fight for world opinion.To present my results from this research I was invited to give a paper at the World History Association yearly conference in Ghent, Belgium. For personal reasons I was not able to participate. The same paper was also accepted for a panel at the International Convention for Asia Scholars in Chiang Mai, Thailand 2017, for which because of financial reasons I could not partake However, I continued working on this paper and have now submitted it for an article (Part C) to The Sixties: A Journal of History, Politics and Culture.

243813.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
243813.value: I see three paths for taking this research further. The first deals with the Maoist writer Jan Myrdal, a loyalist to Beijing, played a dominant part in the Swedish Vietnam War protests, but more importantly became Sweden’s leading intellectual voice of the 1960s and 1970s, and also influenced a generation of international China scholars with his Report from a Chinese Village. No biography exists on Jan Myrdal. I am in contact with him and help out with the Chinese material of the newly opened Jan Myrdal Library and Archives. Iam reading through his authorship of around 100 books and will apply for yet more support from the RGC for this. There is a recently opened personal archive of the writer and political activist Sara Lidman, containing corresponde and diaries dealing with her close contacts with the authorities in Hanoi during the Vietnam War. Sara Lidman was incredibly influential in creating a deep popular resentment against the American atrocities in Vietnam. Nothing has been written about this and I want to spend some weeks at her personal archives.

243813.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
243813.value: Using Sweden as a case my research shows how current interpretations of the West European protest movement against the Vietnam War in the 1960 is seriously flawed in a typical orientalist manner. It is in the dominating framework understood that the young protesters rose up on their own accord, reacting with moral indignation against its Western societies, leading to political engagement in order to assist a helpless Third World against imperialist incursions from, mainly, the US. In reality, as I prove, the Third World nations were active players in an effort to turn a young student population in the west onto their side. In Stockholm, as my research for the first time lays out, Beijing, Hanoi, and later also Phnom Penh planned the conversion of the Swedish opinion in the war and then, in various ways, carried this plan out. As I furthermore show, the particular political situation in Sweden at the time made this feasible; with the ruling Social Democrats in need to win over the young leftist voters preoccupied with the Vietnam War. Opportunism thus piggybacked on youthful altruistic idealism channeled by propagandists from Asia.

243913.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
243913.value: As the availability of multichannel and 3D sound systems increases, so will the demand for the diffusion (upmixing) of stereo and 5.1 channel recorded audio to these larger, more immersive systems. In the simplest case, this may be taking mono or stereo audio and making it sound as if it was originally recorded and mixed for 5.1 surround sound, for which there are currently many, though similar methods. The vast majority of these methods, however, are not designed to accommodate larger 16.1 - 22.2 systems, nor concert hall acoustic-adjustment systems, which may employ several dozens channels. Although faithful to their source, these methods may add little to the inherent flatness of the original, 2-dimensional recordings. This proposal is for the evaluation of a completely new method for rendering stereo and 5.1 audio on 3D systems (with height channels), making stereo and 5.1 audio sound as if they were originally recorded and mixed for an arbitrarily large system. It would capitalize on the increased number of loudspeakers to mimic the acoustic complexities that take place in concert halls caused by instrumentalists moving their instruments during performance, resulting in dynamically changing sound directivity. After the listener-informed fine-tuning of the system, test subjects would be brought into a 24.2 channel 3D audio facility for comparison and discrimination tests as it is compared to two other methods currently vying for standardization; Dolby’s ‘Atmos’ and Auro Technologies’ ‘Auro3D’. Aside from evaluating the effectiveness of these competing technologies and thus influencing the outcome of this most recent format war, the comparison to this novel method could contribute to its acceptance in the industry. As such, it may well become an integral part of home entertainment systems, movie theatre sound systems, and concert hall acoustic-adjustment systems, providing listeners with a new, heightened listening experience, even from older stereo and 5.1 recordings. 隨著多聲道及三維音響系統的普及，重混雙聲道錄音的需求變大。現有的混音規則主要是將雙聲道重混音至環迴立體聲，這些混音規則能為平面的雙聲道加一點變化，但不能推至更大的系統例如八聲道或三維音響系統。 這項計劃開發和測試的一種全新重混音規則，目的是重塑往往在現場錄音失去的生命力細節。使用多聲道揚聲器能作為其中一種補足，重現音樂會現場的音效複雜性。這個重混音規則將由多個獨特的混音程序組成，個別程序需要進行反覆的測試。研究結果將可應用於家庭娛樂系統、 數位電影院和音樂會音樂廳聲學等範疇。

244313.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
244313.value: The proposed study examines the modernisation of the Chinese military between 1911 and 1937 using the Fengtian Army (fengjun) of Manchuria and the Chinese National Revolutionary Army (guomin gemingjun, NRA) of the Nationalist Party (KMT) as examples. The period between the end of the Qing Dynasty in 1911 and the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937 witnessed a series of important changes in tactics, weaponry, and the understanding of warfare among the militaries of the world. Fighting techniques on land, sea, and air changed drastically during World War One (WWI) and the years afterwards. Specifically, this study focuses on the attempts of officers from the two armies, many of whom had received modern military education in China and abroad, to respond to outside military changes and to institutionalise modern military science by establishing education infrastructures such as military academies, professional journals and training manuals; constructing a paradigm of warfare and creating an intellectual community; and creating training units such as training regiments (jiaodaotuan). In addition, by critically examining the writings of the officers from these two armies and related archival sources, this study looks at the Chinese attempts to study modern military science and its reception of post-WWI military theories from abroad, such as those on airpower, armoured warfare, combined arms operations, and total war. It elucidates not only the influence from Japan, Germany, and the Soviet Union on the theoretical development of the Chinese military during the period concerned and but also the Chinese officers’ attempt to construct a new paradigm of warfare to suit the situation in China. Such understanding was reflected in how the two armies were trained, organised, and equipped. By looking at the theoretical development and institutionalisation of modern military science in China between 1911 and 1937, this study tries to bridge the gap in our understanding of Chinese military history between the late-Qing period and the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War and to enhance our knowledge of the history of global military change during the interwar period (1919-1939). In a sense, this study also provides an interesting example of how the Chinese organised and institutionalised modern and foreign knowledge and gives fresh insights into the modernisation of China during the early 20th century. 本研究計劃以奉軍和國民革命軍為中心，剖析中國自1911至1937年的軍事現代化。自1911年清朝結束至1937年第二次中日戰爭爆發，世界各國的海、陸、空軍在戰術、武器、以及對戰爭的認識均有重大轉變。 本計劃主要考察上述兩軍的軍人如何應對戰爭的轉變，以及如何實現中國近代軍事科學的制度化。他們建立軍校、專業期刊、以及訓練教範等現代軍事教育 工具，建構關於戰爭的範式，組成軍事學術群體，並成立教導團等訓練部隊。從他們建立的制度以及有關軍事科學的著作，我們可探討民國時期的軍人如何學習現代軍事科學，並吸收第一次世界大戰的軍事經驗，如空軍的應用、裝甲兵理論、多兵種協同作戰、以及總體戰等。本研究不但釐清日、德、蘇等國對近代中國軍事現代化的影響，亦可以發現中國軍官曾嘗試建構所謂切合中國需要的軍事理論。這些軍官在理論和制度上的探索，均影響了奉軍和國民革命軍的訓練、組織、以及裝備。 本研究嘗試研究1911年至1937年的中國軍事理論的發展和制度化，以補充從晚清至抗戰期間的中國軍事現代化論述，並深入對兩次大戰期間軍事轉變的理解。它亦為中國的現代化，以及外來知識如何影響中國，提供一個案例。

244313.label: Realisation of objectives
244313.value: In all, all the objectives as stipulated in the objective has been realized to the satisfaction of the PI, although this also led to more questions that requires further research (please see Part 6.2). The realization of the objectives will be discussed in detail below: The PI has gone through the major publications and training manuals of the Northeast Army and the Chinese Nationalist Army that are currently available in China, Taiwan, and Japan. Quantitative method such as construction of databases is also employed to make sense of the publications in order to gauge the intellectual development of the Chinese officers of the time, hence the attempt to compile lists of military publications during this period. It is found that the Chinese officers were, as initially speculated by the PI, deeply interested in and influenced by the lessons of the First World War. The lessons of the war, from tactical to grand strategic, were being extensively discussed. In sum, the Chinese started to examine the latest army tactics that stressed on dispersion, combined arms warfare, and mechanization. This discussion also led to an interest in organizing the society around military discipline in order to train a population that could withstand modern war as they understood it. It was also during this period that the Chinese started to move away from blindly translating foreign military works and produce original works concerning the latest military developments. By studying the publications of the Chinese officers during the period and the processes which these publications were being produced, the PI has been able to elucidate the ways which the Chinese intellectual officers institutionalized modern military knowledge through professional academic journals, military education institution, as well as training units. The institutions and legislation concerning the dissemination of military knowledge, such as the establishment of the censorship system and copyright laws for military books, were also studied. The PI has also been able to trace the attempt of the Chinese officers to establish a number of paradigms and a common language to discuss military issues, especially through the introduction of military dictionaries and translation works. Through critically reading the publications written by the Chinese officers, especially the articles that could be found in the professional military journals of the two armies as well as their education institutions, the PI found that the Chinese officers at that time were first and foremost influenced by the Japanese, who tried to understand the lessons of the First World War mainly from the perspective of the entente powers. Soviet influence, on the other hand, was limited because of the purge of the communists from the KMT during the Northern Expedition, and the limited support provided by the Soviet Union during the early stage of the development of the Nationalist Army. Surprisingly, the German influence on Chinese military development was considerably less important than it has always been assumed. Previous works on the topic usually assumed that the German advisers, headed by generals von Seekt and Falkenhausen, represented the entirety of German military thought and the Chinese had little understanding of post-WWI warfare without German enlightenment. This study, instead, found that the German advisers came mainly from a highly selected group of officers who were disciples of von Seekt, who preferred a small and mobile elite striking force but had little exposure of the type of fighting that prevailed in the Western Front during the war. One of the objectives of the project is to examine the emergence of and changes in the Chinese professional officer corps before the Second Sino-Japanese War. To achieve this goal, two issues are approach in connection with each other: 1) the infrastructural and institutional changes in the Fengtian Army and the NRA; 2) the composition, world view, and features of the officer corps. The first task is made easier because of the existing literature on the topic, while the second has to be achieved through a detailed prosopographical study of the officers of the time. Data about the birth, education background, training, as well as career of the officers from the two armies were collected and analyzed, especially those who had contributed to the professional military journals during the period concerned. One of the most important findings of this research project is that it offers a new understanding of the state of the Chinese armies during the 1920s and 1930s, with a special focus on the beginning of the Second Sino-Japanese War. It suggests that the Chinese military, at least those under the control of the Chinese Nationalist Government, was deeply influenced by the technological, or even futuristic, approach of war. The influence was so strong that some of the officers were obsessed with the latest military development of the industrialized countries while overlooking the difficulty of implementing these new tactics in China. Some Chinese officers urged for a more prudent approach to military modernization that put the local contexts into consideration and make full use of Chinese military and social traditions. The best example would be the leaders of the Guangxi clique who tried to introduce the baojia system as a means to widen military service and obtain a more stable source of manpower in the areas under their control. However, their success remained limited as by 1937, the Chinese military was an unbalanced force: on the one hand, it was a large and cumbersome force that consisted a large number of infantry who were poorly trained; on the other, the leaders of the Nationalist Army spent a large amount of precious resources to purchase advanced equipment such as tanks and heavy artillery that were too few in number to influence the overall performance of the military. Another impact of foreign military thinking on the Chinese officers was that by 1937, some of the leaders of the Chinese military became very confident of the effectiveness of the new weapons, especially the Air Force. This study successfully elucidated the process which military knowledge were absorbed, produced, as well as disseminated in the major Chinese military forces during the period. It also located the major groups of primary sources about this topic, which have been largely looked by scholars who study the military history of the time. While offering a number of new understanding to the Chinese military development during the first half of the 20th century, this study opens up a number of questions that worth studying in greater detail, which will be discussed in 6.2.

244313.label: Major findings and research outcome
244313.value: This study has several major findings and outcomes that are closely related to the research objectives. The first being the discovery of many publication for the consumption of the Chinese officers produced from the late Qing period to the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War. Many of these publications are original works written by the Chinese officers, instead of merely translated work of foreign pieces. More importantly, when comparing the translations to the original works, it was found that the Chinese officers often altered the original text according to their needs. From the study of these publications, the PI assessed the impact of the First World War on the officers’ theoretical and practical understandings of war, and concluded that although the Chinese officers had not participated in any actual fighting and only a few officers went to observe the War in Europe, their understandings of war were deeply influenced by the war, from basic tactical issues such as the spacing between individual soldiers in an advancing infantry unit to grand-strategic and political issues such as how societies should be organized to survive in a modern war. The PI was also able to gauge the foreign influence on the theoretical and practical developments of the modern Chinese military. This influence was mainly the result of the gradual institutionalization and localization of modern military science since the late Qing reforms. The Qing government and its successors introduced a series of means that would allow the effective influx of modern military learning into China. These means included the passing of copyright legislation, introduction of professional military journals, as well as formation of experimental units to test the next tactics. This project challenges the existing idea that the Chinese military during the 1920s and 1930s were deeply influenced by Soviet or German influences by highlighting the Japanese influence on the Chinese military. Another major finding of the project is that, by 1937, the Chinese officers, at least those who are more outspoken and prolific in the professional military journals and training institutions, were obsessed with the efficiency of modern technology and machines. This made them more overly confident in some of the tools available to them at that time, especially the air force.

244313.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
244313.value: This study allows the PI to have a deeper understanding of the Chinese officers during the period between the Xinhai Revolution and the beginning of the Second Sino-Japanese War, including their background, training, technical efficiency, world view, as well as their understanding of modern war. Thus, the project should continue along several dimensions: the time-frame of future research should cover the development of the Chinese military science during Second Sino-Japanese War, the pivotal conflict that drastically changed the political landscape of China and East Asia. During the war, many theories that were developed and formed believed by the officers would be quickly repudiated, and on the other hand experience of actual fighting and Allied aid would allow the officers to have a new appreciation of the capability of their weapons and the impact of war on the society. The topic can also be further developed by looking at other Chinese armed forces at that time, most importantly the regional warlords such as the Guangxi and Canton cliques, as well as the Chinese Communist forces. The third dimension that worth developing would be to explore the Chinese understandings on the naval and air dimensions of war.

244313.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
244313.value: This research project filled a gap in the military history of modern China during the republican period (1911-1949) by uncovering the intellectual activities of the Chinese officers between the First World War (1914-1918) and the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937-1945). It finds that the Chinese officers at that time were, like their counterparts in other countries around the world, keen on digesting the lessons of the First World War, and their scope ranged from tactical to grand strategic questions. This study also outlines the process which some of the leading intellectual Chinese officers tried to introduce the lessons of the First World War to their colleagues through professional academic journals, military education institutions, and training units. This study elucidates the Chinese understanding of war during the early twentieth century. Such understanding shaped the ways which they reacted to internal and external challenges and the outcome of the wars during the period. It concludes that some of the Chinese officers were deeply influenced by the Japanese military and were so fixated on the perceived modern way of war that they attempted to fight in ways that were not in line with the existing political, economic, and social condition of China.

244413.label: Project Objectives
244413.value: To analyze the narratives of FDH returnees as presentations of self. Themes expected to be identified in these narratives include the reinvention of self in the home context, the adjustment to new identities as mother, wife and daughter, alienation and identity transformation, and the revitalization of their ethnolinguistic identity. To analyze the long-term impact of the traumatic experiences FDHs suffered during their time in Hong Kong. Many FDHs have suffered years of repression and abuse, and the project seeks to explore how these traumas may have affected their self-esteem and identity. To analyze how the concept of ‘home’ is conceptualized in FDH returnee narratives. Migrant workers are denied access to a space they can call ‘home’. Their claim to public space in Hong Kong is controversial, and they have not been able to make their homeland their ‘home’. The project explores how FDHs reorient themselves and attempt to reclaim their national and regional identity, and give new meanings to the concept of ‘home’. To explore the importance of strong social networks and religious faith in empowering FDH returnees to deal with loss of belonging and alienation and to overcome the trauma of separation which, for many, has characterized the better part of their lives. To publish several articles in tier-one international journals in which the findings from this research project are presented and discussed. To bring the findings ‘back to the community’ by sharing with FDHs in Hong Kong how they may prepare themselves for their return. This will be done through talks and discussions at the church shelter where the PI works as a volunteer, and through articles in popular magazines for FDHs (such as HerStory published by the Mission to Migrant Workers).

244413.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
244413.value: There are currently about 285,000 foreign domestic helpers*) (FDHs) in Hong Kong, the majority being from Indonesia and the Philippines. They work as live-in maids on two-year contracts providing much-needed remittances to their families back home. The life of FDHs in the diaspora is relatively well researched. Studies have shown that FDHs are subjected to discrimination and exploitation. They work long hours, are often underpaid, and reports of physical assault, sexual abuse, and hunger are all too common among FDHs seeking refuge in Hong Kong’s church shelters (Constable 2007; Ladegaard 2012a). Recent research has also shown that the separation from their families is an issue many FDHs are struggling with**). Lai (2011: 580) argues that migrant women in the diaspora are often painfully aware of a fractured identity which is separate from, and yet tied to, their families back home. This calls for “compartmentalized forgetting and remembering simultaneously”: forgetting their children and other family members because it is too painful to remember, and yet, remembering because this provides them with the strength to endure their hardships. FDHs, who are an essential part of the city's economy, have been denied the right of abode in Hong Kong, so even if they have spent the better half of their lives in the city, they still need to return home. The present project seeks to explore the identity transformations reflected in FDH narratives when go home after years of service in Hong Kong. No study has looked at identity construction in FDH returnees, so this research aims to fill a gap in the literature. It will revisit some of the migrant women who participated in the PI's current research in a Hong Kong church shelter, and explore what the diasporic homecoming has done to their sense of self. The project will visit former Hong Kong domestic helpers in Indonesia and the Philippines and conduct group interviews in which they share their personal narratives of homecoming. The sharing sessions will focus on questions such as the reinvention of self in the new context of ‘home’, the revitalization of relationships with spouses and children, alienation and the concept of ‘home’, the fear of failure to re-bond and ‘fit in’, and the revitalization of the vernacular language and culture. The data will be analyzed using a narrative analysis approach which combines Toolan’s (2001) attention to linguistic detail with the therapeutic component of narrative research (Payne 2006). 有名無實：從返國外籍家庭傭工敘事體現疏離及身份變遷 香港現時約有28萬5千名外籍家庭傭工(下稱「外傭」)，主要來自印尼和菲律賓。他們以兩年合約形式在本港擔當住家傭工，把薪金匯到家鄉，解決家中燃眉之急。有研究詳細地探究散居香港的外傭生活，顯示他們受着歧視及剝削。根據不少前往香港一家教會收容所棲身求助的外傭指出，他們工作時間甚長，往往薪金不足，甚至遭受人身傷害、性虐待及飢餓(Constable 2007; Ladegaard 2012a)。 近期亦有研究指出，外傭與家人分隔兩地，往往令他們掙扎苦惱。Lai (2011: 580) 指出，流散香港的女性外傭時常清楚自己斷裂的身份，明白自己既與故鄉的家人分離，同時卻與他們緊繫一起。這種心態要求「忘記與念記劃分並存」(compartmentalized forgetting and remembering simultaneously)：每當想起家人子女，份外痛苦，必須把他們忘記，卻不得不念記他們，作為支撐自己忍受艱辛的力量。 外傭是香港經濟的重要一環，政府卻一直否定他們的居留權利。即使外傭在本港工作半生，他們最終仍要返國。本項目希望從於香港工作多年後返國的外傭自述中，探索身份的變遷。迄今並無研究探討返國外傭的身份建構，本研究旨在填補箇中的文獻空隙。我們將重訪一些曾參與首席研究員於教會收容所進行當前研究的女傭，了解她們流散香港後返回祖國，這場經歷如何影響她們對於本我的感覺。我們將前往印尼與菲律賓，探訪一些前香港外傭，並進行集體訪問，分享各人述說回國的故事。分享環節側重一些議題，例如在新「家」的背景下如何重新發現本我，與配偶和子女的關係如何重拾生氣，「家」的概念及疏離感覺，害怕最終難以重新連繫及融入，以及重拾本土語言與文化等。研究將運用敘事分析模式，結合Toolan (2001)注重語言細節的特色，並配合敘事研究的治療元素(Payne 2006)，剖析所得資料。.

244413.label: Realisation of objectives
244413.value: The project objectives have all been achieved. The project has generated a total of six high-impact publications: four tier-one journal articles, two book chapters published by international publishers, a monograph published by an international publisher, as well as six conference papers and several talks and seminars. Some of the publications (not least the monograph) also draw on data that was collected for a previous GRF project on the life stories of domestic migrant workers in Hong Kong. The project has also brought the findings 'back to the community' by giving talks at the migrant worker NGOs who have helped me collect the data (Pathfinders and Mission for Migrant Workers). The findings have also been used by Pathfinders, the Hong Kong-based migrant worker NGO that helped me get data from their clients in Hong Kong and Indonesia. Pathfinders works on reintegrating domestic migrant workers (DMWs) upon their return to Indonesia, and the data collected for this project has been used by Pathfinders in their attempts to improve their education programme. The research has also helped me in the voluntary work I do for Pathfinders as a member of a group that is working to improve the home reintegration programme that the NGO offers to women who are moving back to their home countries. The only problem encountered had to do with identifying competent transcribers/translators to transcribe and translate the Indonesian narratives. There are not many people in Hong Kong who are perfectly fluent in English, Bahasa and Javanese (the three languages used in the stories recorded in Indonesia), and the Research Assistant had to go through training before s/he was able to do the transcription work adequately. One person was hired and went through the training, only to drop out before she did any work. Another translator was hired and she could only work part-time. This delayed the project for some time, but I am pleased to report that I was able to recruit a very competent translator/transcriber who did excellent work for the project. In conclusion, I am happy to report that all project objectives have been met, despite the fact that the project was trying to cover new ground and it was therefore difficult to predict exactly what the outcomes would be. Very little research has been done on DMWs' experience of return to their home towns, and it was therefore more difficult than usual to predict what the field trips would generate. However, my overall predictions turned out to be accurate, but there were also findings that were unexpected. For example, the clear distinction between Filipino and Indonesian returnee narratives was striking: Filipino returnees were generally happy about what they had accomplished as domestic workers overseas and looked upon their life's work with pride and a sense of accomplishment. Many of the Indonesian returnees, on the other hand, were in great distress about what they had experienced and used the storytelling as a way to come to terms with the traumatic experiences they had had while working overseas. The difference between the two groups of women will be addressed in future publications, such as a contribution to a Special Issue of Journal of Language & Social Psychology, which will focus on 'Communication and Transnational Mobilities' (scheduled to appear in 2019). The project generated a total of 107 recorded and transcribed narratives. The data has not been exhausted and I anticipate that at least two additional articles could get published: one for the Special Issue of Journal of Language & Social Psychology, and one for a Special Issue of Language & Intercultural Communication on 'Translating Language and Intercultural Communication Research into Social Action', edited by Hans Ladegaard and Alison Phipps (scheduled to appear in 2020).

244413.label: Major findings and research outcome
244413.value: 1) Indonesian domestic migrant worker (DMW) returnees are engaged in reinventing themselves upon their return to Indonesia. They often see themselves as strangers in their home towns where in particular their struggle to get accepted by their children is a salient theme in many of the narratives (see Part C, publication no. 2, 5 & 7). 2) The women often feel alienated in their own communities. They feel the need to reconceptualize the concept of 'home' and what it means to them. They realise that their values have changed fundamentally during their time in the diaspora and it is therefore difficult for them to 'fit in' back home. This is particularly true for women who have violated the sexual norms of the community and brought back a child and no father (see Part C, publication no. 5). 3) Several of the Indonesian women are suffering from the trauma they experienced while working overseas (particularly in the Middle East). A relatively novel finding is that these women frequently use code-switching in their storytelling. I argue that they do it to create emotional distance to what they have experienced by using English, a language which we assume may serve a more instrumental purpose for them (see Part C, publication no. 1, 6 & 7) 4) The women are often finding comfort in their faith, and in the sacrifices they have made for their families. They went overseas because of their desire to be helpers: they wanted to serve God, help their families, and help the people of Hong Kong, so the sacrifices they have made are for the common good (see Part C, publications no. 3, 4 & 7)

244413.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
244413.value: Apart from the two articles planned for Special Issues of international journals (one for Journal of Language & Social Psychology scheduled for 2019, and one for Language & Intercultural Communication scheduled for 2020), the project has identified at least one additional area that needs to be further developed. The project found that many Indonesian migrant workers are subjected to various forms of abuse while working overseas and they return to their hometowns while still suffering from trauma. The next phase of the project will seek to explore trauma narratives further. Most research on trauma narratives is done by health professionals who pay no attention to language. There is a need therefore to look at the structure and characteristics of trauma storytelling. The narratives that have been recorded can be used as a basis for further research, but the next phase of the project will also record further evidence of FDHs' traumatic experiences, both in Hong Kong and Indonesia. The aim is twofold: first, a more detailed systematic description of trauma narrative as a genre, and second, to identify the women who have been abused before they leave Hong Kong in order that they may receive counselling before they return to their hometowns.

244413.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
244413.value: The project has further documented the widespread abuse of particularly Indonesian domestic migrant workers. All of the 67 Indonesian returnees whose stories were recorded in this project were underpaid for (at least) their first contract, and there were at least five cases of women who had been sexually assaulted while working overseas. There were also several cases of systematic long-term abuse, such as physical assault and starvation, with detrimental consequences for the victims. Not in one single case did the women receive any justice for what had happened to them, more often than not because the abuse happened in the Middle East where there are no migrant labour laws to protect their rights. It is of paramount importance that the abuse of migrant workers is documented. It is also important that their experiences of coming home are documented in order for us to more fully comprehend the extent of the sacrifices they are making to help their families and their country. The stories that were recorded for this project document the immense difficulties experienced by migrant workers who have to reinvent themselves in order to 'fit in' when they return to their home countries.
