340613.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
340613.value: Nowadays, most countries undertaking transitions from authoritarianism to democracy seek to overcome historical divisions and build a more inclusive society based on reconciliation and trust. In Myanmar, currently in the early stages of democratic reform, issues of transitional justice also arise. Given that the military retains considerable political power, the key question is how to deal with an abusive past without compromising prospects for political change. This project examines issues of transitional justice and national reconciliation in Myanmar. It utilizes existing conceptualizations in the growing field of transitional justice and aims to contribute to knowledge on the political sociology of reconciliation. Specifically, it examines the propensity of transitional justice measures, such as reparations, investigations, and apologies, to contribute to reconciliation, forgiveness and trust. In doing so, it will shed light on major policy dilemmas of transitional justice in a largely non-Christian setting. At the core of the project will be a set of in-depth interviews designed to reveal the meaning of reconciliation, trust, and forgiveness in the Myanmar context, plus a survey, which will also embed vignette-based experiments. These vignettes will manipulate scenarios that illustrate policies of transitional justice. The project draws on more than fifteen years of experience amassed by the PI in the field of transitional justice, his expertise in conducting and statistically analysing surveys and survey experiments in six countries, publishing in leading social science outlets, and co-authoring two papers on pre-transitional justice in Myanmar with the CI. It also draws on the extensive expertise of the CI in the area of Myanmar politics, plus his considerable research experience, strong publication record, and contacts in the country. For fieldwork, it will contract two ad hoc research assistants/interpreters with knowledge of local languages. The project is significant in three main aspects. First, it is the first systematic, theoretically-informed empirical study of transitional justice and reconciliation conducted prior to adoption of transitional justice mechanisms. Second, its understanding of key concepts such as reconciliation, justice and forgiveness in a predominantly non-Christian context will be of great relevance to parallel Asian cases. Third, it will generate policy recommendations for the critical Myanmar case. The project will result in one co-authored monograph, two research papers, four presentations in local and international conferences, and one policy brief; a separate funding will be sought for an international conference on the topic. The project will last for 24 months. 緬甸過渡時期的轉型正義與民族和解 現今許多經歷從威權政體到民主政體過渡的國家，試圖在和解與信任的基礎上，解決歷史原因造成的分化，尋求建立更加包容的社會。處於民主改革初期的緬甸，也面臨著過渡時期的轉型正義難題。鑒於軍方仍擁有相當大的政治權力，如何改變其過往濫用權力的歷史並實現政權改革成為了關鍵。 依據現有的轉型正義理論框架，本項目研究緬甸過渡時期的轉型正義與民族和解問題，進而豐富政治社會學中有關民族和解的內容。具體來說，研究主要針對過渡時期的司法措施，如賠償，調查和致歉以及由此引發的和解，寬恕和信任問題。這項研究將揭示轉型正義在一個非基督教國家的主要政策困境。 本項目主要包括一系列旨在揭示有關緬甸政體和解，信任和寬恕意義的深入訪問，同時會進行一項調查，包括一個以插圖為媒介的實驗，圖像內容為各項轉型正義政策的解讀。 本項目的首席研究員在轉型正義領域積累了超過15年的經驗，曾在六個國家進行調查實驗，有著專業的執行和分析調查技能，其研究曾在領先的社會科學刊物發表，包括與研究助手合作的兩篇關於緬甸前轉型正義時期的論文。該研究助手對緬甸政治有著豐富的認知，同時亦有大量的研究經驗和出版記錄，以及在緬甸當地擁有充足的人脈。實地考察方面，項目將聘用兩位熟悉當地語言的特設研究助理/口譯。 此項目在三個方面具有重要意義。首先，它是第一個在未採納轉型正義機制而進行的關於轉型正義與民族和解系統理論的實證研究。其次，研究一個非基督教背景國家對於和解，正義與寬恕的理解，能作為其他類似亞洲國家的借鑑。最後，研究將給處於政改關鍵時期的緬甸提供政策上的參考。項目內容包括：一個共同撰寫的專著，兩篇研究論文，四次本地和國際會議報告，一個政策簡報，以及一個另外尋求資助的相關國際會議。此項目將持續24個月。

340613.label: Realisation of objectives
340613.value: This report is being submitted merely 4 months after the project was completed. In spite of this, I believe that the objectives of the project have been achieved and exceeded: In order to contribute to knowledge in the area of political sociology a new concept "limited liberalism" has been developed. The concept has been applied to transitional justice, national reconciliation and political reconciliation in order to examine major dilemmas and processes at the onset of political transition. The concept has two advantages: it can describe the configuration of Myanmar's political culture; and it can travel to other contexts, including Western societies. In order to examine the prospect for reconciliation, we devised a survey questionnaire and devised three survey experiments simulating variations of real-life situations. The reverse translation of the questionnaire was solicited. The probabilistic survey was conducted among 1614 respondents in five major areas, including Yangon and Mandalay provinces, and Kachin, Kayin, and Shan States. We conducted 76 indepth interviews with members of parliament, civil society groups, former political prisoners, internally displaced populations, and ethnic minorities in order to determine the meaning of critical concepts; the qualitative study was accompanied by a library research to inquire into the etymological origin of these concepts and monitoring of the press. In addition to it, relevant sections of Myanmar laws were translated to English. The qualitative data were translated and fully transcribed; and the quantitative data were analysed in SPSS and Amos. A co-authored book proposal is currently under consideration by the Oxford University Press. The acceptance is subject to referees comments and approval by the Delegates of the Press. Instead of planned two, three research articles were written and submitted; two research papers and an article that popularised the results. Among the academic articles, the first co-authored article on intergroup relations in Myanmar is currently under consideration for a special issue on Myanmar in the Journal of Contemporary Asia. Second, an article written by the PI that uses the path analysis to delineate the role of transitional justice in democratisation is under consideration in the Journal of Peace Research. Third, an article written by the PI that reviews empirical literature in transitional justice has been resubmitted to Advances in Political Psychology, which is an annual supplement of Political Psychology (revise and resubmit). In view of the often protracted review process, which is beyond the authors' influence, the original objective of this project as outlined in its application was to submit these outputs for considerations. Two other working papers were written. The results of the research project were presented internationally at Harvard, Yale, and the Law and Society Association annual meeting; and will be presented at the Intl Sociological Association Forum in Vienna. Locally, the paper was presented at the Hong Kong Sociological Association annual meeting, and 2 universities, Lingnan University and the City University of Hong Kong. In addition to it, I run a workshop on the process of rehabilitation of victims of human rights abuses in Yangon and gave two talks, one at Yangon University and one at AAPP. Additional funding from Lingnan was sought and granted, which resulted in organizing an international conference in December 2015 with more than 20 speakers from the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, Germany, Switzerland, Singapore, Hong Kong, China, and Myanmar. The project has targeted major academic outlets; the Journal of Contemporary Asia ranks 2 in Area Studies and the Journal of Peace Research ranks 6 in Political Science. Should we targeted emerging journals, our work could have probably been already published. We had an invitation to submit our book proposal to a global academic press, which we declined in view of the prospect of being considered by the Oxford University Press.

340613.label: Major findings and research outcome
340613.value: On the theoretical level, the project resulted in developing the concept of limited liberalism. Limited liberalism is a property of political culture whereby an individual's commitment to liberal values are manifested in parallel with illiberal values. Limited liberalism is thus characterised by one or more inconsistencies in the application of liberalism rather than by a degree of liberalism, which could be described as semi-liberalism. Thinking more broadly, we realized that the phenomenon of limited liberalism is not exclusive to Myanmar, but rather is also manifest in contemporary western political cultures. Indeed, although social researchers and government policymakers often use the internal consistency of liberal ideology as a guide to analyse democratic attitudes, the social reality may be more complex. This project explored the concept of limited liberalism in Myanmar's political culture. We focused particularly on the three areas of inclusiveness and democracy, ethnic relations and tolerance, and transitional justice because each manifests an array of liberal, limited liberal and illiberal attitudes. In the sphere of inclusiveness and democracy, liberals support citizenship, voting rights and gender equality, non-liberals seek to suppress such rights, and limited liberals are prepared to extend them to some groups but not to others. In the sphere of ethnic relations, liberals are tolerant, non-liberals are intolerant, and limited liberals express tolerance of some ethnic groups and intolerance of others. In the sphere of transitional justice, liberals promote rectification of historical injustice, non-liberals oppose this, and limited liberals manifest selectivity in doing this. We have also examined whether the concept of limited liberalism carries any predictive value vis-à-vis an emerging political system. We have found that liberal attitudes are associated with the support for democracy and the rejection of the military rule, limited liberals are happy to support a hybrid regime of illiberal democracy. In contrast to the book, our articles were more sectional in their approach. Our first article explored the dynamic of intergroup relations in Myanmar, especially the issue of tolerance, multiculturalism, and respect towards ethnic minorities. The second article examined the role of transitional justice in democratisation by conceptualising transitional justice as a bridge and developing a path model that enabled its empirical examination. The third article summarised a review of empirical literature in the area of transitional justice, which has been frequently driven by advocacy rather than scholarship. We have also written an article that popularized the results, which was published in the interpreter.

340613.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
340613.value: The richness of the data would allow us to deliver a number of conference talks with a possible publication prospect. However, this needs to be carefully balanced in order not to infringe the copyrights of the book manuscript. There is also a possibility of replicating the survey in a few years time in order to observe the changes in political culture in Myanmar.

340613.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
340613.value: Historic elections in Myanmar in November 2015 led to the installation of a new government in March 2016 and saw the country deepen its graduated transition away from entrenched authoritarian rule. Nevertheless, the military forces that for decades dominated national politics remain privileged in a constitutional framework designed to deliver discipline-flourishing democracy. One critical question that therefore confronts the 50 million citizens of this Southeast Asian nation is whether their push for still greater democracy is strong enough to prevail over the resistance of a powerful military machine, buttressed by swelling undercurrents of intolerance. To address this question, this project examined the contours of Myanmar’s political culture in the context of ongoing reform. Drawing on extensive fieldwork, including a survey of 1614 respondents and more than 75 in-depth interviews, it identifies an at times puzzling blend of liberal and illiberal attitudes, which it terms limited liberalism. It explores this concept and its manifestations primarily in the areas of inclusiveness, tolerance and historical justice. It examines the extent to which liberal and illiberal attitudes are associated with adherence to liberal and illiberal democracy. It concludes with a mixed picture concerning Myanmar's future, whereby democracy may not mean support for individual rights.

340713.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
340713.value: Cognitive linguistic research shows that metaphor is not a marginal decorative phenomenon but a fundamental basis to thought in general, and scientific, economic and social modelling in particular (Ortony 1993). The metaphorical structuring of thought can operate at a latent or subconscious level. The proposed research will investigate the origins and spread of the metaphors prevalent in the writings of European “economic philosophers” from the 17th century to the present. These will include Hobbes, Hume, Adam Smith, Ricardo, Malthus, (Darwin,) Marx, Ruskin, Mill, Keynes, Hayek and Friedman. Using computer software for identifying metaphorical items in texts and their frequency and distribution, it will (1) identify the most prevalent semantic domains from which metaphors of economic activity are drawn (2) determine which of these conventional metaphors pre-dated capitalism, and to what extent they were invented or adopted by economic philosophers (3) ascertain whether critics of capitalism such as Marx and Ruskin accepted or contested these metaphors (4) consider whether the findings corroborate the results of a less extensive study carried out by the PI and reported in chapter 8 of his book Washing the Brain: Metaphor and Hidden Ideology (Benjamins, 2007). The PI was prompted to propose this research by a review of this book. The reviewer, Paul Davidson, suggested that further research should examine the metaphors used in critiques of capitalism, notably the writings of Marx (Davidson 2008). The relevance of this study is both theoretical and practical. It will trace the origins and development of cognitive metaphors within economic theory, broadly-conceived. It is a case study in the debate over the universality or cultural specificity of cognitive metaphors. It will address the question of whether metaphors which support the competitive nature of capitalism are unconsciously used by its critics, and whether this undermines their critiques. It will raise awareness among economic and social theorists of the power of metaphor to shape, if not determine, thought. More importantly and practically it may make policymakers more aware of the unstated and unacknowledged metaphors underlying policy, and the alternative metaphors necessary to moderate the recent excesses of late capitalism. The research would hopefully lead to two books. One, an academic monograph explaining the methodology and results of the study. Another, drawing on the research more selectively, targetting a lay audience/policymakers. The latter would raise awareness of the metaphors driving economic and social policy, and the possible alternatives. Oxford paperbacks is a possible publisher of the second book. N/A

341413.label: Project Title(Chinese)
341413.value: 計算社會認識論和科學方法

341413.label: Project Objectives
341413.value: To develop a new software package for examining social epistemological scenarios, by building on the program Laputa. To use this software package to examine a number of social epistemological questions concerning scientific method, including but not limited to: (A) What factors affect how the division of labour in science might best be struck, especially with respect to the different functions of imagination (or theory construction), puzzle solving (or theory development and application), and criticism (or theory testing)? (B) When might it be advantageous to science to have irrational members, e.g. members whose degrees of belief violate the axioms of probability in particular ways? (C) What scientific procedures currently serve, and which additional procedures may be implemented, to counteract or exploit psychologically established tendencies to individual irrationality, such as confirmation bias? (D) What is the relative value of a group concentrating on a research programme, and together abandoning it only at a crisis-point, versus having some members who are ‘dogmatic’, i.e. who focus on articulating and developing the programme, and others who are ‘critical’, i.e. who explore different avenues on the basis of identified weaknesses of the programme, simultaneously? (E) Under what circumstances does flow of information between individual members of different research groups aid the inquiries of the groups of which those persons are a part? And under what circumstances is such a flow detrimental? (F) To what extent does one’s research pedigree, i.e. the communication links with which one starts, determine one’s research trajectory? To produce a minimum of four journal articles, to be published in top-tier journals in philosophy or HPS, and one research monograph, to be published with a leading academic press. (Publication at this rate, in this quality of venue, is in line with my research record.) To produce an open dataset which may be used in future projects.

341413.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
341413.value: How should we organise inquiry, and science in particular? Traditional approaches to this question have two key defects. First, they assume that all scientists should perform similar roles at any given point in time, e.g. focus on testing theories with a view to abandoning those that falter (for Popper), or concentrate on solving puzzles defined by the dominant paradigm with a view to refining current theories (in ‘normal science’ for Kuhn). Second, they assume that rational groups must be formed of rational agents. This research programme eschews both these assumptions, in order to engage with our actual human predicament as inquirers. It proposes that group inquiry succeeds in so far as it involves procedures that serve not only to counteract, but also to exploit, our individual flaws and externally imposed (e.g. economic or political) constraints. To put it simply, it treats how best to organise science as a complex question about what we should do with the resources at our disposal – human and otherwise – given the constraints determined by the context of inquiry. It proposes to investigate the question using computer simulations, which have been applied in other disciplines to great effect but have only recently started to be used in philosophy. Specifically, simulations of group inquiry will be used to help to construct an account of how best to organise science, and to derive testable predictions from the account. The overarching aim of using simulations in this context is to open up a whole new field of research, on the basis of new interdisciplinary connections and investigative methods. It is further anticipated that this project will have practical consequences for the organisation of scientific inquiry in the future. 我們應該如何組織對世界的探知活動, 特別是科學研究? 對這個問題的傳統回答有兩個主要缺陷 . 其一, 它們預設所有科學家應該做的事情是一樣的. 比如, 波普爾(Popper)認為科學家都應該測試科學理論以爭取推翻它; 庫恩(Kuhn)則認為在常態科學裡面, 科學家都應該去解決範式下產生的問題以爭取改進現有理論. 其二, 它們假設理性的群體一定是由理性的個人構成的. 本研究從人類探知活動的真實困境入手, 所以會摒棄這兩個假設. 本研究的出發點是認為成功的群體探知活動之所以成功, 是因為其遵循一些方法或過程, 而這些方法或過程不僅試圖消除個人缺陷和外在限制(比如經濟政治方面的限制)對探知的不良影響, 同時還試圖利用一些個人缺陷和外在限制為群體服務. 簡單的說, 對於科學研究如何組織的問題, 本研究會當作如下的問題來處理:在一定的限制條件下,我們應該如何利用現有的人力和其它資源來進行探知活動. 本研究會用計算機模擬的方法來探索這個問題的答案.計算機模擬的方法在很多領域被有效應用,但在哲學里的應用才剛剛起步.本研究會試圖從對群體探知的計算機模擬中建構關於如何組織科學研究的理論,同時推導出該理論的一些可以被經驗測試的後果. 本研究更大的目的是開啓一個新的跨學科的研究領域.可以預期其研究結果會有助於更有效的組織實際的科學研究.

341613.label: Project Title(Chinese)
341613.value: 信任的符碼─維繫貨幣的社會共識

341613.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
341613.value: Money is a medium for payment, exchange and storage. The flow of money and the flow of goods and services usually occur in opposite directions, but beyond direct transactions there are more subtle, piggybacked social processes ongoing when money circulates: new identities are established, social relationships are shaped, and social institutions are consolidated. For example, China’s Ming dynasty issued a banknote in the 1370s to proclaim the legitimacy of a new empire. The Spanish silver coin peso de ocho marked an important stage of colonialism and global trade starting from the 1570s. Hong Kong’s five transport companies issued a joint ticket in 1996 to carve out spatial access and efficiency as a desirable way of urban life. This study investigates a social phenomenon that enables money to work: social consensus. The essence of money is based on the fact that all parties involved are willing to recognize the value of a common symbolic token, and this willingness is a circular, meta-knowledge. One recognizes a HK$100 banknote because one knows that “other people” will recognize it. The power position of the currency issuer and material properties of a token may influence the consensus-building (or dissolution) process, but these are not straight-forward and sufficient factors to guarantee success. This project will draw concepts and framework from four groups of literature: classical sociology, economic sociology, science studies (especially the group on social studies of finance), and sociologists’ work on power (e.g. Parsons, Lukes). The empirical research comprises two parts. Part I is an in-depth qulitative inquiry of a few contemporary currency tokens by semi-structured interviews and documentary research. People involved with the issuance, implementation, regulation, and daily use of the token will be interviewed to understand important issues on the establishment/dissolution of consensus, and on the success or failure of circulation. Part II is documentary research on a slightly broadened set of 8-12 selected currency tokens from the world, followed by the construction of a coding matrix. Boolean logic analysis will be conducted to test out the currency properties correlated to the status of circulation.

341713.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
341713.value: Occupational safety remains an important concern for organizations especially in high risk industries. We propose an integrative model of workplace safety by adapting the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model. In this model, we will investigate both motivation (engagement in safety) and strain (burnout) processes linking social, organizational and personal factors to safety incident outcomes. We propose 1) resources (e.g., safety climate, work-family enrichment, and psychological capital) will positively influence employee safety motivation (work engagement), which in turn positively influence safety behaviours (more safety compliance and participation and less safety violation); 2) job demands (e.g., risks and hazards, interpersonal conflict, organizational politics, and work-family conflict) will positively influence employee burnout, which in turn negatively influence safety behaviours; 3) safety compliance and participation will negatively relate to safety incident outcomes (less near miss incidents, injuries and accidents), whereas safety violation will positively relate to outcomes (more near miss incidents, injuries/accidents); 4) resources will buffer the impact of job demands on burnout, whereas job demands will strengthen the positive impact of resources on safety motivation; 5) Chinese psychological belief of fatalism will be an obstacle of safety by exacerbating the negative effects of job demands on burnout. As nursing, construction and rail are high risk industries in Hong Kong, we will test this integrative model in nurses, construction and rail workers by two approaches: first, identify social, organizational and personal factors that are most relevant in high risk industries by 120 qualitative interviews (using critical incident technique). Second, we will collect two-wave survey data from 400 nurses, 400 construction workers, and 400 rail workers, using structural equation modelling to test our hypotheses. This study will add to psychology of safety literature dominated by studies in Western societies by exploring what similar and unique antecedents of workplace safety can be found in these industries in Chinese context. The research findings will have implications for nursing, construction, and railway safety for both its customers and passengers, specifically enhancing safety. The CEO and human resource managers of the nursing, construction and rail industries can develop strategic planning to identify what factors cause employees to bypass safety procedures and what factors can motivate them to engage in good safety performance, and also understand how these factors jointly influence workplace safety. Further, by bridging western management theories with Chinese culture on Hong Kong, this study would contribute to searching the most effective cross-cultural management practices for promoting workplace safety. 在現代組織尤其是高風險行業中，職業安全受到很大關注。我們通過修正工作要求-資源（JD-R）模型，提出了一個工作場所安全的整合模型。在這個模型中，我們將探討連接社會、組織和個人因素的動機（參與安全）和緊張（倦怠）因素，及其對安全事故的影響。我們提出1）資源（例如，安全氛圍，工作-家庭增益和心理資本）將對員工的安全動機（工作投入）產生積極影響，這反過來又積極影響安全行為（更多的遵守和參與及更少的違反）； 2）工作要求（例如，風險和危害，人際衝突，組織政治，和工作-家庭衝突）將導致員工倦怠，這反過來對安全行為有負面影響； 3）遵從安全要求和參與安全行為將降低安全事故的發生（更少有驚無險的事故，更少傷害和意外事故），而違反安全要求則增大安全事故的發生（更多有驚無險的事故，更多傷害和意外事故）；4）工作資源將緩衝工作要求對倦怠的影響，而工作要求將加強工作資源對安全動機的積極影響；5）中國人“宿命論”的心理觀念對安全是一個障礙，因為它誇大了工作要求對倦怠的負面影響。由於護理，建築，和鐵路在香港是高風險的行業，我們將在這三個行業中測試這一整合模型。首先，通過對120人進行定性訪談（使用關鍵事件法）來確定高風險行業中與職業安全最相關的社會、組織和個人因素。其次，我們將收集400名護士，400名建築工人和400名鐵路工人的兩撥數據，並利用結構方程模型來檢驗我們的假設。目前安全心理學的研究以西方社會為主導，本研究將通過探討中國社會中影響高危行業工作場所安全的相似或獨特的因素，填補現有文獻的不足。研究結果可以服務於護理、建築和鐵路行業的客戶或乘客，尤其有助於提升安全。此外護理、建築和鐵路行業的CEO和人力資源經理，也可依據本研究的發現來製定戰略規劃，以確定哪些因素導致員工規避安全程序，哪些因素促使員工積極投入安全行為，並理解這些因素如何共同影響工作場所安全。最後，這項研究聯合了西方的管理理論與香港的中國文化，從而有助於找尋促進工作場所安全的最有效的跨文化管理的實踐。

341813.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
341813.value: Prior studies of organizational learning in developing country based subsidiaries of multinational corporations (MNCs), headquartered in developed economies (Clark and Geppert, 2006; Hong and Snell, 2008) assume and portray uni-directional flows of knowledge and practice from the home country, via expatriates, to local employees in the subsidiary units within the host country. Post-colonial theorists argue that the knowledge and practice colonizers can deliberately withhold some key expertise, to maintain their superiority over the dependent knowledge recipients (Frenkel, 2008, Jack et al., 2008). More open and complete sharing of home-based expertise may serve to create a springboard for knowledge flow in the 'reverse' direction. The proposed research will be conducted in subsidiaries, located in the Pearl River Delta, China, of MNCs that are headquartered in developed countries. Through qualitative interviews and observations, we shall identify episodes where local employees are actively involved in improvising organizational practices that their managers endorse as effective for local conditions. Such contributions by local employees may typically be modest in scale and scope. They may be blended with input from the headquarters and expatriates to create hybrid situated practices. They are likely overshadowed by dominant processes of knowledge transfer from the headquarters. They are nonetheless seeds for empowerment scenarios, where local employees legitimately improvise new and appropriate organizational practices. This study will identify the various processes, dynamics and arrangements through which such glocalization may take place and how managements may support them. We shall conduct 60 face to face interviews in 5 case study organizations. Most interviewees will be local Chinese employees at middle or junior levels. Some will be expatriates in senior or middle level posts. We shall gather rich descriptions of incidents and processes that either facilitate or attenuate local contributions to organizational learning. At least two days of prearranged field observations will also be conducted at each site. A qualitative approach is proposed because it is appropriate for understanding the complex dynamics and processes under investigation. One can publish qualitative research in top journals, such as Organization Science, the Journal of Management Studies, and Organization Studies. The Journal of International Business Studies recently published a special issue on qualitative research, calling for more qualitative studies on organizational learning. We expect our study to inspire further research in emerging economies on how to use latent local expertise to address local issues and draw lessons with more universal significance that contribute to reverse knowledge transfer. 摘要 過去對於來自發達經濟體的跨國公司設在發展中國家的子公司的組織學習研究指示(Clark and Geppert, 2006; Hong and Snell, 2008)，其知識和技術的轉移都是單向的，一般是由總公司，通過外派員，轉移至東道國內子公司的本地員工。但後殖民理論家爭論，其外派員，作為知識和技術的殖民者，為了保持自己對本地員工的優勢，往往會刻意隱瞞一些關鍵的專業知識(Frenkel, 2008, Jack et al., 2008)。結論是應有更開放和完整的來自總公司專業知識的共享，創建一個跳板來進行“反向”知識流動。 這項研究的對象是總部來自發達國家的跨國公司位於珠三角的附屬公司。通過定性訪談和觀察，我們會找出一些本地僱員積極參與針對本地情况去改良現有組織措施，而又得管理者贊同的事例。雖然這種本地僱員可作的貢獻只有適度的規模和範圍，它們也可以和來自總部和外派員的意見作整合，創建一種混合的解决方法。他們可能被由總部主導的知識轉移過程所掩蓋。但他們仍然能作為賦權的種子，來讓當地員工湊合一些適當本地情况的組織措施。這項研究將確定各個全球和本地化可發生的過程，動力和安排，和管理層如何能支持他們。 我們將研究五個案例及進行60面對面訪談。受訪者將會是在中低層的中國本地僱員，但有些人會是高級或中層職位的外籍人士。我們將收集一些本地情况促進或削弱組織學習的過程和豐富的事件描述。並在每個站點進行至少兩天的實地觀察。 提出定性方法作為這項研究的調查方法，因為它是能對複雜的動態和進程作出適當的理解。人們可以發布定性研究在頂級學術期刊，例如Organization Science, the Journal of Management Studies, and Organization Studies。國際商業研究雜誌 (The Journal of International Business Studies ) 最近出版了一本關於定性研究的特刋，提出要進行更多組織學習的定性研究。我們希望我們的研究，能激發更多關於在新興經濟體中如何使用本地專業知識以解決當地的問題的進一步研究，並制訂 一些對反向知識轉移更普遍的教育意義。

341813.label: Realisation of objectives
341813.value: We studied 6 foreign-headquartered MNC subsidiaries (Circle, Square, Triangle, Tess, Parker, and Kirin), plus another MNC (Huawei) that is headquartered in China, with subsidiaries located outside China, chosen for comparative purposes. We collected qualitative data from the first 6 organizations mainly through interviews, supplemented with observational and documentary evidence. In 5 of the 6 non-Chinese-headquartered firms, local Chinese employees were contributing proactively to organizational learning (Objective 1 a). However, in one of those 6 firms (Square), we found major barriers to local involvement in organizational learning (Objective 1 b). We drew on documentary evidence and qualitative interviews to study Huawei. We found that both of the contrasting patterns, noted above, were in operation at Huawei. At Huawei's sales/service subsidiaries, local employees were typically confined to routines, with strategic decisions being made by the Chinese cadres. However, documentary data indicated that local employees in Huawei's R&D subsidiaries in various countries were actively involved in organizational learning. The story behind this divergence appears to be that Huawei is strategically separating its R&D subsidiaries from its sales/service subsidiaries in order to maintain tight overall HQ control while nonetheless capitalizing on local talent worldwide to drive product and process innovation. In Huawei, therefore, whether local employees in its diverse foreign subsidies contribute proactively to organizational learning depends on the mandate conferred by the HQ to the particular subsidiary (R&D versus sales), a decision which is based on the identification of local talent pools; Huawei's R&D subsidiaries contribute to innovation with the global market in mind, not the local market. Among the 6 foreign-headquartered MNC subsidiaries in China, key dimensions of enterprise contexts that facilitated proactive engagement by locals in organizational learning included: recognition by the HQ that the PRC is a large and growing local market; a labour supply made abundant by recruiting nationwide, enabling the selection of suitably-qualified employees; and a policy of using local material or component suppliers, the selection of and collaboration with which required locally-specific knowledge. In 3 of the MNCs (Parker, Triangle, and Kirin), the respective HQ took a pragmatic approach to empowering local managers to engage in innovation and entrepreneurship, based on the recognition that the PRC has distinctive consumer needs that must be addressed in timely fashion, recognizing that opportunities may otherwise be lost to competitors. In these firms we found many examples where local Chinese employees had driven process, product, or policy innovations. In one MNC in particular (Triangle), formal recognition by the HQ through prizes and/or career progression was seen as important in encouraging locals' ongoing innovative involvement (Objectives 2 & 3). We found instances in one organization (Triangle) of local employees being able to convince foreign-based headquarters that local changes to imported processes were necessary. In other organizations (especially Tess, and Huawei's sales subsidiaries), the respective HQs were more insistent on compliance with HQ-originated procedures. In one organization (Square) we found instances where expatriate managers refused to admit openly to local employees that the HQ-originated procedures were unsuitable in the circumstances and required local adaptations. In Square, the expatriates turned a 'blind eye' to local adaptations and would not discuss them constructively even among themselves, and such reluctance by senior managers to recognize and reward local initiatives and adaptations led to ill will and lack of commitment among locals, and was reflected in the 'drying up' of local innovations. Nonetheless, there were instances in at least four organizations (Triangle, Parker, Tess, Kirin) where a subsidiary had originated product or process innovations that were being adopted by the HQ or sister subsidiaries. Instances where a subsidiary worked collaboratively with the headquarters to develop hybrid practices that are acceptable to both parties were largely confined to Huawei, where it appeared that the HQ was pushing hard for such joint innovation, and was celebrating this through feature articles in the on-line company magazine, Huawei People (Objective 4). Regarding Objective 5, we found strong evidence in two firms (Triangle and Kirin) of a reservoir of common understanding and psychological safety between the respective Chinese subsidiaries and overseas HQs. In both cases, the Chinese subsidiaries had been operating for two decades or more, and were trusted to develop their own local products, so long as the core expertise of the HQ was not being compromised. At Kirin, the ongoing presence of Japanese expatriates ensured that the strict standards of the Japanese proprietary brand were being upheld. At Triangle, there were very few expatriate managers, and communication was maintained through regular visits and overseas forums, where local process and product innovation ideas and achievements were shared and reviewed. Both organizations emphasized the importance of bodies of factual evidence in establishing and supporting the pragmatic legitimacy of local ideas and achievements, before institutionalizing new processes and products locally, and before the HQ would consider embedding them as worldwide best practices or offerings. No one there mentioned cross-cultural training; it appeared that mutual trust and understanding had been built through collaboration over a prolonged period of years. Regarding Objective 6, we studied whether the inter-cultural dynamics resembled a 'third culture' pattern. Apparently not at Huawei, despite the blend of Western-originated procedures across many functions with a Chinese-style cadre system. Huawei interviewees (whether Chinese or non-Chinese) mentioned that expatriates and locals there tended to operate as separate groups, and this phenomenon was also a point of criticism in the company magazine. Expatriate managers had very limited presence at Circle, Triangle and Parker, and the locals appeared to be content with the freedom afforded to them. These three cases can be construed as representing the emergence of 'third cultures' that were operating in accordance with company norms at a distance from the respective HQs, and which HQ managers felt comfortable visiting. In contrast, at Square, relations between the expatriate Japanese and the Chinese were 'sour'. The locals felt excluded from decision-making and perceived that they had no career progression. At Tess, some groups of local employees had proven their trustworthiness vis a vis the expatriate managers, but the front-line employees were subject to strict regulation. Kirin appeared to constitute something closer to a 'third culture' where the Japanese and Chinese managers were co-present, and where the latter's ideas were adoptable, even when promoting the Japanese brand. There were examples within Triangle, Circle, and Parker where local managers had established that HQ-originated and stipulated procedures were inadequate for the local market, and had developed their own local alternatives. In one case, at Triangle, a team had received prizes from the HQ for their innovation. In other cases at Triangle, teams were in the process of marshalling evidence to establish the validity of their alternative arrangements. So how were the local employees empowered to reach this stage, where they had become sense-givers? Based on the 6 non-Chinese headquartered firms, we observed a general pattern, where the respective local subsidiary had gone through an initial, exportive, stage of assimilating expertise from the HQ. Subsequently, there may then have been a contestative stage, during which the HQ and locally-stationed expatriates tackled local resistance to HQ-stipulated procedures. Only if local employees could demonstrate their 'tame-ability' could the subsidiary enter a final stage of integrative knowledge assimilation, where they were empowered to adopt a sense-giving role vis-a-vis expatriates or the HQ (Objective 7).

341813.label: Major findings and research outcome
341813.value: We adopted qualitative methods to study 6 foreign-headquartered MNC subsidiaries located in China (Circle, Square, Triangle, Tess, Parker, and Kirin), plus another MNC (Huawei) that is headquartered in China, with subsidiaries located outside China. In China, contextual factors that encourage active local involvement in organizational learning include: market demand for locally-designed products, supply of suitably-qualified employees, and the use of local suppliers. Internal factors that encourage local involvement include rewards for innovation, career progression opportunities, and sufficient flexibility to alter standard, HQ-originated routines. These internal factors require a reservoir of mutual trust and understanding between a subsidiary and its HQ to be built up through collaboration over many years. Subsidiaries can eventually become 'third cultures' that operate in accordance with company norms, and which HQ managers may regard as second homes to visit. It remains important that local employees continue to reassure the HQ that its core expertise is not being compromised. We found instances in most of the China-based subsidiaries of product or process innovations that have been embedded by the HQ as worldwide best practices or offerings, and/or being adopted by sister subsidiaries. We also found instances where subsidiaries established that particular HQ-stipulated procedures are unsuitable for local circumstances, and developed alternatives. Scenarios of these types have required the originating subsidiaries to provide substantial factual evidence to establish the pragmatic legitimacy of local ideas and achievements. Huawei is unique in among our case organizations, in encouraging certain types of subsidiary (with specialist R&D mandates) to work collaboratively with the HQ to develop 'hybrid' products. For Huawei, whether local employees contribute to organizational learning depends on the mandate conferred by the HQ, a decision that is based on the identification of local talent pools. A tendency for Chinese and non-Chinese Huawei employees to operate as separate groups remains a challenge to third culture integration. The Chinese retain tight strategic control and keep sales subsidiaries separate from specialist R&D centres. Among the non-Chinese headquartered firms, we observed a general progression toward a subsidiary’s integration as a knowledge and innovation initiator. There is an initial exportive stage of assimilating expertise from the HQ. A contestative stage may follow, when the HQ and expatriates tackle local resistance to HQ-stipulated procedures. A third, integrative stage involving integrative knowledge assimilation ensues if local employees have demonstrated both their capability and their 'tame-ability'. Local employees are then empowered to engage in sense-giving and thought leadership.

341813.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
341813.value: We shall further develop the EGOS conference paper and pursue this, along with the papers in draft or under review, to publication in journals such as Human Relations, Organization Studies, or Journal of World Business. Using existing data, we may also study closely the contrasts between the progression stages of Chinese subsidiaries as knowledge and innovation initiators in the non-Chinese headquartered firms, and the progression stages (if any) of overseas subsidiaries in the Chinese headquartered firm. We can interpret the contrasts through the lenses of cross-cultural trust building, national differences in institutional preferences, and the model of Morgan & Kristensen (2006), discussed in the paper that we have under review in Human Relations. Scholars may study the progression stages as knowledge and innovation initiators of foreign subsidiaries in other Chinese-headquartered MNCs, to see whether this follows the Huawei pattern, or a similar pattern to that of subsidiaries in our non-Chinese headquartered firms, or some other pattern. Huawei has created open innovation centres yet still maintains tight control over its own specialist R&D centres. Scholars may study cases where other MNC subsidiaries are involved in open innovation, and the implications for trust and power relationships between such subsidiaries and their headquarters.

341813.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
341813.value: We studied innovation by 6 China based subsidiaries of foreign-headquartered multinational corporations (MNCs), plus a comparison case of an MNC headquartered in China with subsidiaries outside China. China-based MNC subsidiaries are likely to innovate if there is local market demand, if employees are well-qualified, if suppliers are local, if employees are rewarded for innovating, if there is career progression, and if the headquarters (HQ) allows flexibility. Strong trust and mutual understanding with the HQ is a necessary condition. Even then, subsidiaries must provide comprehensive proof that locally-initiated methods or products are sound and marketable. Their journey towards recognition as knowledge and innovation providers has three stages. The first stage involves demonstrating to the HQ that the subsidiary has successfully absorbed the requisite expertise from the HQ. The second stage involves demonstrating that any local changes to methods or outputs stipulated by the HQ are reasonable and do not jeopardize standards. The third stage involves honoring freedom by providing credible creative ideas and achievements. In the Chinese-headquartered MNC, overseas subsidiaries do not innovate unless the HQ has created them as highly specialized R&D units. The HQ works closely with the latter to develop jointly-created innovations while maintaining tight strategic control.

341913.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
341913.value: A familiar form of explanation is causal explanation. To causally explain an event is at minimum to cite a cause of that event. Not all explanations, however, are causal. We find non-causal explanations at work in philosophy, the sciences, as well as in everyday life. First, consider a philosopher who claims that facts about brain states explain the facts about experience. In this case she isn’t claiming that brain states cause mental states, though a causal connection between them certainly isn’t ruled out by her claim. Second, consider the scientist’s claim that a given isotope of gold has a certain atomic mass in virtue of containing a certain number of protons and neutrons. This claim isn’t naturally interpreted as a causal claim either. Third, suppose you wish to explain to a friend why there was a global economic recession in 2008. One way to do so would be to cite facts that were causally responsible for the economic meltdown such as the occurrence of predatory lending and the deregulation of financial institutions. But another way to explain why there was a recession would be to cite facts that seem constitutively related to the recession, for example the fact that 2008 was marked by severe declines in consumption, investment, government spending, and export activity. While there is an enormous amount of philosophical work on the nature of causation and causal explanation, until very recently philosophers have had relatively little to say about non-causal explanation. Given the important role that such explanations play in philosophy, science, and everyday life, non-causal explanation is a topic worthy of careful study. In my view, each of the non-causal explanations described above is a metaphysical explanation in particular. While a causal explanation is a matter of establishing what causes what, a metaphysical explanation instead is a matter of explaining what grounds what or what obtains in virtue of what. This project has two parts. In the first part I focus on two foundational questions concerning grounding. First, what is the connection between the notions of grounding and essence? Second, in what sense, if any, do grounded facts reduce to the facts that ground them? In the second part I turn to the matter of how we might apply a regimented notion of grounding (one recommended by our discussion of essence and reduction) to address two longstanding philosophical problems concerning the mind: mental content and unified consciousness. 342013.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
342013.value: Numerous policy initiatives have been carried out to improve educational outcomes in both developed and developing countries, but very few have had significant effects. As identified in the huge volume of existing literature, two main factors have hindered efforts to identify effective education policies. First, many policy interventions have been implemented to improve the external inputs in education, such as school resources and teacher quality, with little attention given to student incentives. While external factors may be important, student incentives are more crucial to improving educational outcomes. Second, although student academic performances can be affected both directly and indirectly by these policy interventions, the effects are difficult to isolate. This so-called endogeneity problem can only be properly tackled if policy intervention can be implemented as a randomised experiment. In recent years, much effort has been made to fix these two problems. The proposed project will address them by carrying out a large scale randomised experimental study in rural China to test the effects on student performance of implementing an individual student-based incentive scheme for study, or pay-for-grades scheme, combined with the use of an e-learning tool to assist student learning. The main innovations of the project will be as follows. First, while several studies have already looked at the effects of pay-for-grades scheme the results have been mixed. Moreover, few existing pay-for-grades studies have also considered combining such schemes with means to help student learning. We will combine our scheme with an e-learning tool to assist student learning. Second, the e-learning tool we are going to use not only provides students with many self-learning programmes but also has the function to record the exact usage of the tool by the students in different learning activities. So it can tell us exactly how the incentive mechanism works on students to affect their self-learning efforts. Third, the project will be designed as a large-scale randomised experiment to be implemented in rural China. That will not only enable us to overcome the endogeneity problem but will also generate more policy relevance because it will help to address the lack of education resources in the rural areas of developing countries, such as China.

342013.label: Realisation of objectives
342013.value: Under the support of this GRF project, we have carried out several experimental studies in mainland China in the past several years. The project has also gradually evolved and expanded its scope to education intervention aiming at improving both student study efficiency and motivation. In the process, we have collaborated with five different Education Bureaus at City and County level. They are Nanchang, Shaoyang County, Zhaoqing, Zhongshan and Xinshao County. In total, we have experimented four different types of education interventions. It has helped local Education Bureaus to sharpen their e-learning policy, find out how to increase student study motivation and also how to better deal with problems of inequality in education resources and parental absence issues in rural areas. More specifically, We have following completed or on-going projects: 1. Combining e-learning with Pay-for-grades on Educational Outcome, a two-year experimental project covering 6 primary and middle schools, 58 classes and over 2500 students in Nanchang for the period March 2014 to June 2015; 2. Student Feedback, Parent-teacher Communication and Academic Performance, a one-year experimental project covering 10 primary schools, 70 classes and 3800 students in Shaoyang County from April 2015 to June 2016; 3. E-learning, Intrinsic Motivation for Study and Academic Performance, a one-year experimental project covering 11 schools and over 1500 students in Zhaoqing and Zhongshan from October 2016 to August 2017; 4. Can e-learning resources and incentive for study improve education outcomes in rural schools? An experimental study, this is still on-going project that covers 100 rural schools in Xinshao County. It has started in September 2018 and expected to complete by August 2019. The whole project did not go exactly the way as planned. Hence, there was some delay in both implementation and completion of our research papers. The is mainly due to the fast-changing technologies and e-learning practices in China. The e-learning machine we originally proposed to use for our experiment became obsolete and the market was dominated by pad and laptops by the time we received the funding. We have managed to sign another collaboration agreement very quickly with Nanchang Education Bureau to implement almost the same experimental study (see project 1 above) using laptops (the Bureau had a budget to cover one student one laptop for all students in the 58 experimental classes) instead of e-learning machines to engage e-learning. The Bureau originally agreed to extend the initial six experimental schools to all schools in Nanchang. But due to the funding constraint as well as the desire of the Bureau to further develop its own e-learning resources this was not implemented after two years. This project did not achieve the ideal sample size as we originally hoped . We therefore explored collaboration opportunities with other local education bureaus in China. Due to the resource constraint and needs of different bureaus (not all schools have already been covered by wifi connection and not all students can afford to have their own laptops), we refined our subsequent experimental design accordingly but maintained pretty much the same spirit of searching for the combined effects of adopting new technology in education and incentivizing student learning motivation. Hence, in project 2, we have conducted an experiment in a poor rural county that has not had the internet connection for all its schools. Here the technology used is simply teachers’ mobile phones and the incentivizing mechanism is through regular structured teacher communication with students and their parents on student performances at schools. In project 3, we test directly the relative and combined impacts of e-learning and a training program aiming at improving student intrinsic motivation (more specifically, growth mindset). In project 4, we managed to implement our experiment with the support of Xinshao Education Bureau to a much bigger sample (100 rural schools in total) to revisit the original idea of combined effects of e-learning and motivation for study. In this case, we confine our e-learning to a very specific format (yet much welcomed by these rural schools): i.e. providing recorded lessons taught by experienced teachers in central schools to remote village school students as supplementary e-learning materials to improve their study. On the motivation side, we also change the monetary reward (which is less acceptable to schools and teachers) to honorary awards (the best performance or improvement certificate issued by local education bureau and displayed in classroom). So, it is on basis that we claim that we have carried out a broad range of innovative experiments on the same topic for this project, which has greatly exceeded the original targets of the projects. In addition, the PI has also organized two major KT workshops at Lingnan University to disseminate our results that have attracted well over 100 teachers and educational officials from both the mainland and Hong Kong to attend. We have also presented our research findings in five major international conferences. The PI has also been invited by the National Institute of Education Sciences, the Education Bureaus in Nanchang, Zhaoqing, Zhongshan, Suzhou, Dongguan, Shaoyang and Heyuan to present our findings and give advices on their future development in e-learning. The project has generated significant social impacts. Based on these facts, we believe that we have achieved the intended goals of this project.

342013.label: Major findings and research outcome
342013.value: Our main findings can be summarized as follows: First, our research shows that for e-learnings to be effective, teachers and students need to be given a well-designed learning platform that is both user friendly and tuned towards the individualized teaching and study needs of them. Since many teachers are not trained for the use of the latest technologies applied in e-learning enough training and motivation also need to be provided before it can be utilized effectively. Simply making the technology (such as one student one laptop and wifi accessible campus) available cannot do the magic itself. Second, some simple but well-designed e-learning practices can generate surprising good effects on student learning, such as our well-designed feedback mechanism using mobile technology. It saves teacher time from a lot of paper work but enables them to give constant feedback to students and their parents on student performance in schools. This low-cost intervention can generate 0.15-0.20 standard deviations increase on math scores and 0.09 standard deviation on Chinese scores. It is particularly helpful for left-behind children in rural China. Similarly, our initial findings from a pilot study also shows that making the recorded lessons delivered by more experienced and better quality local central school teachers available to remote rural school students at synchronized pace (using same textbooks and taught at the same pace) can be a very effective. Third, we also find that well-designed programs aiming at raising student intrinsic motivation for study can generate very good short-term results. Our intervention in Zhaoqing and Zhongshan indicates a two-hour training on student growth mindset generated a 0.1 to 0.3 standard deviation increases in English, Chinese and math scores three months later. It can also raise the incentive for student to use e-learning for self-study, although it may not produce additional effects on scores. Furthermore, we find that monetary reward produces insignificant effects on performance. We have so far finished writing one paper (see IZA DP No. 11347), and will soon submit it to a leading education economics or development journal. We are also in the process of writing two other papers. We also expect to write at least one more paper when the final study is completed in August 2019. Our findings have been disseminated in a number of international conferences, including: 2017 Asian Meeting of the Econometric Society and the 2017 Inaugural Conference of the Asian and Australasian Society of Labour Economics.

342013.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
342013.value: We have still an on-going experimental study developed out of this project (project 4 in 5.3). We will complete the project and write another academic paper based on the findings. We will also try to collect more data from schools and students that have received our intervention to see if and what may be the longer-term effects of these interventions. We can also do several follow-up research projects. First, we will further explore the effects of some more advanced e-learning tools developed lately, such as AI learning (the use of AI technology to implement individualized learning). In particular, the big data generated from such kinds of learning can greatly improve our understanding on how and what really affects student learning habits and outcomes. Second, we will also collaborate with psychologists to develop better tools to improve student intrinsic motivation for study. In particular, we have found that they can generate good short-term results, but yet to confirm whether and how the effects can be long lasting.

342013.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
342013.value: Under the support of this GRF project, we have carried out several experimental studies in mainland China in the past several years. They focus on the study of the effects of various education interventions aiming at improving both student study efficiency and motivation. We find that e-learning can be effective tools to close the education gaps created by inequality in education resources. In particular, simple e-learning tools such as better teacher-student communication tools can produce very significant effects on student performance, so as making recorded lessons by more experienced teachers in local central schools available to remote rural school students for self-study. However, much development (such as better and user-friendly e-learning platform), training and sharing of good practices need to be done before the potential benefits of e-learning can be realized in China. We also find that promoting student learning motivation is very important for academic performance. Here, monetary incentive is much less powerful than intrinsic motivation. Our project has helped local Education Bureaus to sharpen their e-learning policies, find out how to increase student study motivation and better deal with problems of inequality in education resources and parental absence issues in rural areas.

342213.label: Project Objectives
342213.value: We aim to bring the new technical results on the identifiability of causal structure from probability distributions to bear on the issue of reductionism in probabilistic causation. Our main objective is to assess the prospect of defending (some version of) reductionism based on these results, and if positive, to present new arguments for a carefully formulated thesis of reductionism. We aim to provide a general unification of the consilience-based methodology and the likelihood-based methodology in the context of causal discovery. In this regard, a secondary objective is to explore the possibility of extending our analysis of the connection between consilience and likelihood to other contexts. We intend to clarify the conceptual connections between the recent important work on causal discovery and the interventionist account of causal laws/generalizations. We aim to develop a general notion of ‘virtual intervention’ and propose some novel methods of causal inference based on the notion. In terms of research output, we aim to produce several substantial publications, at least one for each of the previous objectives, in leading philosophy journals. We also aim to publish at least two articles in premium artificial intelligence and/or statistics journals, and two in top conference proceedings in computer science. There is a chance that the research on the question of reductionism may grow into a book project.

342213.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
342213.value: This collaborative project (between a philosopher and a computer scientist) is in large part motivated by two observations. First, although philosophers of causation have rightly paid considerable attention to (and sometimes contributed to) the literature of causal modeling, some exciting developments in the recent literature have escaped philosophers’ radar. Second, some important ideas in the new developments of causal modeling were anticipated in or connected to philosophical work. In this project we aim to figure out the philosophical implications of the recent advances in causal modeling, and to further explore some new methods of causal inference. We will focus on three issues. First, a set of new theoretical results have revealed that once we go beyond the standard parametric assumptions in causal modeling -- that of linearity and/or that of Gaussianity -- the causal structure can in many cases be uniquely identified from the probability distribution. These results seem very relevant to the issue of reductionism in probabilistic theories of causation, for according to one rendering of the issue, the question is whether the probability distribution over all variables uniquely determines the causal structure. We propose to investigate in detail the extent to which these new results revive the prospect for reductionism. Second, we found that a central method in the recent literature on causal discovery was anticipated by the philosopher Malcolm Forster. Forster interpreted the method as one that is based on William Whewell’s notion of ‘consilience of inductions’, which he argued distinguishes the method from likelihood-based methods. In a working paper, however, we showed that the likelihoods in Forster’s examples did take into account the kind of consilience highlighted by him. In the present project we plan to build on that work and develop a general unification of the consilience-based methodology and the likelihood-based methodology in the context of causal discovery. If successful, the results may also throw light on the consilience-based methodology in general. Third, we would like to clarify the connections between the general modeling assumptions in the recent developments of automated causal discovery -- in which some notion of exogeneity plays an important role -- and the interventionist account of causal laws/generalizations. Among other things, we think it is possible to develop a notion of ‘natural experiment’ or ‘virtual intervention’ that is more general than what follows from interventionism, and based on that notion, some novel methods of causal inference from observational data. 本課題緣起兩個觀察。第一，研究因果的哲學家沒有足夠注意因果建模(causal modeling)領域的最新進展。第二，這些最新成果和哲學文獻里的一些討論頗有關聯。因此，本課題旨在從哲學的角度梳理因果建模和推理的新方法。此跨學科研究會由一個哲學家和一個計算機科學家合作完成。 本研究主要有三個方面。其一， 當下科學哲學的主流意見認為因果不可能還原為概率。但因果建模文獻里的一系列新定理說明，在線性高斯模型之外，很多情況下概率分布可以完全決定因果關係。這讓我們有理由再探把因果還原為概率的可能。本研究試圖重新評估還原論的前景。 其二，一個重要的因果推理的新方法和哲學家福斯特(M. Forster)的一些工作吻合。福斯特認為該方法基於赫維爾(W. Whewell)的归纳一致(consilience of inductions)的方法論，與統計學中的似然(likelihood)法截然不同。但我們有一些初步結果表明，這兩種方法論在福斯特的例子中是可以統一的。我們會嘗試擴展這些初步結果，使這兩種方法論在更一般的情況下統一。 最後，本研究會釐清因果建模新成果所依賴的條件和哲學中最近流行的干預主義理論之間的聯繫。在此基礎上我們會嘗試改進干預主義中的“干預”概念，以啓發一些更新穎和有效的因果推理的方法。

342213.label: Realisation of objectives
342213.value: We believe that we have sufficiently addressed the project objectives and achieved a much better understanding of the original questions that motivated them. Regarding the first objective, the big question was whether the mathematical results on the identifiability of functional causal models could lend support to the philosophical thesis that causality is reducible to probability, or more precisely, to the thesis that the asymmetry between cause (variables) and effect (variables) is identifiable from their joint probability distribution. In connection to this question we had, so to speak, both negative and positive findings. We found that an old result due to Hyvarinen and Pajunen (1999, “Nonlinear independent component analysis: existence and uniqueness results”) could be adapted to suggest a negative answer to the question. The adapted result states roughly that for any continuous random variables X and Y with a joint probability distribution, there always exists a random variable Z such that Z is statistically independent of X, and Y can be written as a function of X and Z (and so there also exists a random variable W such that W is statistically independent of Y, and X can be written as a function of Y and W). In other words, there always exists a functional causal model that points the causal arrow from X to Y and also a functional causal model that points the causal arrow from Y to X, both of which are compatible with the joint probability distribution of X and Y. Therefore, even if it is granted that (variable) causation is in general representable by functional causal models, causal asymmetry is not identifiable from the probability distribution alone. It is then not surprising that all the positive identifiability results that we know impose nontrivial conditions on what kinds of functions are allowed. In part due to this negative finding, our investigation on this issue took a somewhat different direction. Instead of working with functional causal models, we turned to notions of exogeneity that originated in the econometric literature. In particular, we explored the prospect of bridging the gap between a causal notion of exogeneity (that is conceptually linked to causation) and a statistical notion of exogeneity (that is defined solely in terms of probability distributions). The result is twofold. On the one hand, and also in connection to the third project objective, we worked out a novel way to infer the direction of a causal arrow based on statistical tests of exogeneity. On the other hand, we found that our tests could be reinterpreted as testing a special kind of “independence” between local modules in a causal network. This is in a way very similar to the “modularity” condition in the philosophical literature, but “modularity” is standardly defined in terms of interventions and as such is not a non-causal notion that is needed for a reductive account of causation. So the answer to our original question probably remains negative, but our new approach raises a new theoretical question: how to unify it with the approach based on functional causal models under a general philosophical framework? After searching through the philosophical literature on probabilistic causation, we came up with two promising ways to approach the new question: a generalization of Dan Hausman’s independence account of causal asymmetry, or an appeal to the standard “Causal Markov Condition” and “Causal Faithfulness Condition” in an appropriately augmented causal model. (More on these further developments in Section 6.2.) Regarding the second objective, we fixed a number of problems in our treatment of Malcolm Forster’s counterexamples to the likelihood theory of evidence, and extended our unification of the consilience-based methodology and the likelihood-based methodology in Forster’s examples to a theorem that is applicable to the general setting of functional causal models. We also reviewed the philosophical literature on the confirmational or evidential value of consilience or unification, and thought that the various Bayesian accounts might be usefully compared to our likelihoodist account. However, as it turned out, all the cases we found (except for Malcolm’s) already assumed the equality of likelihoods as a presupposition, and then they could only be accounted for by playing with Bayesian priors. Our current conclusion is that our account targets an important class of cases that seem to have been largely overlooked in the philosophy of science literature. Regarding the third objective, we worked out several novel methods of causal discovery, in collaboration with other computer scientists. As already mentioned, we developed an exogeneity-based method for inferring the causal direction between two random variables from purely observational data, which dispenses with the parametric assumptions that are routinely made in the approach based on functional causal models. We also extended the currently most general and powerful method based on functional causal models to deal with the important and widespread problem of selection bias. We showed, among other things, that in the case of “outcome-dependent” selection bias, a situation that is most frequently discussed in the statistical literature, the causal direction between two variables is still generically identifiable in the so-called post-nonlinear causal models. In addition, we designed a method of causal inference from nonstationary time series, where the nonstationarity, despite being a challenge for statistical analysis, also provides an opportunity for causal inference in that changes over time can be exploited as “virtual interventions” or “natural experiments”. Our method took advantage of such “virtual interventions”, and also employed a novel trick by treating time as an auxiliary random variable, so that some traditional causal discovery methods can be readily used to detect nonstationary causal modules and control confounding. Finally, we also worked on some variants of the traditional causal discovery methods that rely on weaker assumptions. Regarding the last objective, we, together with various collaborators, already published 7 relevant papers, 2 in top philosophy journals (“Philosophy of Science”, “Synthese”), 3 in reputable computer science journals (“ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology”, “Applied Informatics”, “International Journal of Data Science and Analytics”), and 2 in premier conference proceedings (“Proceedings of the 32nd conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence”, “Proceedings of the 15th Conference on Theoretical Aspects of Rationality and Knowledge”), all of which were refereed. Moreover, we finished a substantial paper on the method for causal discovery from nonstationary data, which is about to be submitted. We also presented various findings from this project in a number of international conferences.

342213.label: Major findings and research outcome
342213.value: Below is a list of major findings and relevant publications or presentations: 1. We found that a known mathematical result in the literature on nonlinear independent component analysis could be adapted to argue that despite all the impressive identifiability results regarding functional causal models, no general reduction of causality to probability is forthcoming even if causation is assumed to be in general representable by functional causal models. We reported the adapted result and its implications in a paper published in ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology. 2. We worked out a new perspective on causal asymmetry, which not only suggested a generalization of Dan Hausman’s celebrated independence account of causal asymmetry, but also led to a novel method for inferring causal direction from observational data. We presented the former idea on two occasions: The 7th Asian Conference on Machine Learning in Hong Kong and an international workshop on causal inference in Tokyo; a technical report on the latter was presented in the 15th Conference on Theoretical Aspects of Rationality and Knowledge and was published in its refereed proceedings. 3. We refined our earlier treatment of Malcolm Forster’s interesting challenges to the likelihood theory of evidence and derived a general result unifying consilience-based methodology and likelihood-based methodology in the setting of functional causal models. We published our philosophical defense of likelihoodism in Philosophy of Science, and reported the general mathematical result in the paper published in ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology. 4. We extended the currently most general method based on functional causal models to deal with the important and widespread problem of selection bias. The work was accepted for a plenary presentation in the 32nd conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence, and was published in its refereed proceedings. 5. We developed a novel method for inferring causal structure from nonstationary observational data, which to a good extent can also handle confounding due to hidden variables. We are about to submit a paper on this method for review (which is also attached in Part C). 6. The PI also worked with other collaborators on variants of some traditional causal discovery algorithms, some of which were reported in a paper published in International Journal of Data Science and Analytics. Moreover, the PI and the Co-I each coauthored a paper with Peter Spirtes on some general issues of causal discovery, the former published in Synthese and the latter published in Applied Informatics.

342213.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
342213.value: An interesting question that emerged from the project is whether there is a general, plausible philosophical framework that can unify our exogeneity-based approach and the functional-causal-model-based approach (and perhaps also the more traditional constraint-based approach) to causal discovery. As previously mentioned, we thought of two promising ways to approach this question. The first seeks to generalize Hausman’s independence account of causal asymmetries. Instead of claiming that causal asymmetries are grounded in the fact that a cause of an effect is always independent of some other cause of the same effect, we would like to argue for a broader claim, something like: causal asymmetries lie in the fact that causes are independent of some aspect of the cause-to-effect transformations (but effects are usually not independent of effect-to-cause transformations). But this vague claim need be sharpened, especially when the causal relation of interest is confounded. The second way is to treat causal modules or parameters that specify the modules as additional, semi-causal variables and apply standard principles such as the “causal Markov principle” and the “causal faithfulness principle” to the enlarged structure to derive the principles behind the apparently different approaches. We are both interested in further pursuing these lines of inquiry.

342213.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
342213.value: The asymmetry between cause and effect may seem obvious: a cause (say, the tuning of a switch) can be used to manipulate, control, or bring about its effect (say, the volume of a radio), but usually not vice versa. However, notice that the terms just used to describe the asymmetry, “manipulate”, “control”, and “bring about”, are very similar in meaning to the term “cause”, so much so that the description strikes many as tautological or uninformative. Thus many philosophers regard it an important question to characterize causal asymmetry in more informative terms. In practice, too, we often need to figure out the direction of causal influence without the luxury of deliberate manipulation or control. The dictum that cause precedes effect in time can be useful sometimes, but does not help when temporal information is not available. This research built on some recent breakthroughs in the machine learning literature that greatly enhanced the feasibility of inferring causal direction from purely observational data (that is, without appealing to deliberate manipulations or temporal order). The project was interdisciplinary in nature and resulted in what we believe to be significant contributions to both the relevant philosophical literature and the relevant machine learning literature.
