404613.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
404613.value: Superconductors with light elements, such as carbon-based superconductors, have attracted great interests for their element abundance, low cost and non-toxicity, which are important advantages for future applications. The newly discovered alkali metal doped hydrocarbons are of great interest because of their simple molecular structures and possible high Tc. Limited by the powder samples that contain mixtures of many different components/phases used in previous experiments, much information including charge transfer, crystalline structure and transport properties of the superconducting phases remains unclear. Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) experiments require very small sample and are quite suitable for attacking these problems. Especially, with high energy resolution tunneling spectroscopy, superconductivity can be directly measured at low temperatures through tunneling spectroscopy with simultaneous structural information. It is surprising that previous experiments indicate that an optimal doping for hydrocarbon-based superconductors is 3 K atoms (or 1.5 Sr / Ba) per hydrocarbon molecule. It is also a mystery whether both the lowest unoccupied molecular orbitals (LUMO) and LUMO+1 or the LUMO alone is responsible for the superconductivity. Compared with C60, which has 3 degenerate lowest unoccupied molecular orbitals (LUMO) and takes 3 electrons for optimal doping, picene only has one non-degenerate LUMO and one non-degenerate LUMO+1 that is energetically close to LUMO. Other hydrocarbon molecules have similar situations. Thus, the charge transfer from K atoms to the hydrocarbon molecules and the orbital responsible for the superconductivity must be investigated in order to understand the mechanism of the superconductivity. It is expected that identification of the crystalline structure is equally important for the understanding of the superconductivity of hydrocarbon-based superconductors. In this proposal, we will prepare thin film samples through thermal evaporation onto substrate surfaces in vacuum and single crystalline domains can be searched at single or multiple layer thickness. With controlled K deposition, we expect to be able to detect the charge transfer from K atoms into hydrocarbon molecules at both molecular level and thin film level using scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS). With both high spatial resolution images and high energy resolution tunneling spectroscopy, we will also be able to identify the K composition and the structure of the domains that are superconducting. Through our experiments, we expect to bring new understanding to these newly discovered hydrocarbon-based superconductors and may also provide guidance for search of higher Tc organic superconductors. 由于元素丰富、低成本、无毒性等一系列与应用相关的优越性，由碳等轻元素组成的超导体一直吸引着科学家们的兴趣。最近发现的碱金属元素掺杂的碳氢化合物因为它们的简单分子结构和较高的超导温度而备受关注。但是，由于它们的常用样品是粉末，可能含有其他组分或物相，影响了诸如电荷转移、晶体结构、以及超导相中的输运特性的研究。 隧道扫描术实验只需使用很小的样品，所以有可能用于解决上述问题。 这一技术还同时能得到样品结构和高分辨的隧道电流谱，是研究小样品超导的理想工具。 前人的实验表明，碳氢化合物的最佳掺杂是每个分子掺3个K原子（或1.5个Sr/Ba原子）。 这使得人们搞不清楚是分子的最低无占据态（LUMO）还是它与LUMO+1态一起参与超导的。与之对比是C60, C60有3重简并的LUMO态，所以需要获得3个电子以达到最佳掺杂。但picene分子却只有1个无简并的LUMO态和1个在能量上与之相近的无简并的LUMO+1态，原则上只需2个电子就达到最佳掺杂； 其他碳氢分子也与之相象。这明显与实验结果有矛盾。所以，我们必须研究电荷从K原子向碳氢分子的转移以及与超导相关的分子轨道以理解这类分子的超导机制。我们相信对于这类超导体来说，它们的晶体结构的识别对理解超导性也同样重要。 在这个项目里，我们将通过热蒸发的方法来制备超薄的样品。我们将识别单层膜或多层膜中的单晶畴。通过控制K的蒸发量，我们将利用隧道电流谱在分子水平上探测电荷从K原子到碳氢分子的转移。依赖同时具备的高空间分辨率及隧道电流谱的高能量分辨率，我们将可以辨别K原子的组分、单晶畴的结构、以及它是否超导。通过我们的实验，我们期望能对碳氢化合物的超导机制加入新的理解，也期望能为寻找更高超导温度的有机超导材料提供指导。

404613.label: Realisation of objectives
404613.value: The objective of this proposal has been reasonably achieved. Three postgraduate students and a number of other types of researchers including postdoctors have participated in this project. We have used vacuum thermal deposition method to grow the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) including molecular coronene and picene films on various substrates and subsequently doped them by potassium under ultrahigh vacuum (UHV) conditions. The prepared pristine and K doped PAH samples have then been systematically investigated by low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy (STM/STS). On Au(111) surface, we found it was easy to grow monolayer and bilayer coronene. (Picene behaved similarly to coronene so we will not discuss it further). Doping them with various amount of K could also be achieved. Such samples allowed us to systematically study the structures of various phases formed and their electronic properties via simultaneous structure imaging and tunneling spectroscopy measurements. The evolution of the charge transfer from K atoms into the coronene films via filling LUMO and LUMO+1 orbitals was fully revealed, the corresponding morphology of the films with various amount of K was also imaged and found to be strongly governed by the amount of charge transfer. For K3Coronene, in particular, the LUMO orbitals was observed indeed to have been pulled down to the Fermi level by band filling with charges transferred from doped K atoms. Unfortunately, due to the presence of electronic correlation effect and Mott−Hubbard transition in the system, the LUMO orbitals at the Fermi level split into an upper unoccupied part and a lower occupied part, rendering the superconductivity phase in monolayer and bilayer impossible. This was a situation that was not able to predict at the proposal writing stage. The nature way to eliminate the splitting of LUMO at the Fermi level is to reduce the electronic correlation effect and the Mott−Hubbard transition by growing bulk-like coronene films. The lattice constants of the monolayer and bilayer coronene in the pristine or K-doped forms were found to be different from those of the bulk coronene films and were believed by us to be the cause of the above effects. The seemingly simple job of growing thicker films eventually turned out to be extremely challenging. There was a competition between annealing to achieved ordering of the molecular layers and desorption of the molecules at even a relatively low temperature, say ~100oC, due to the high saturation vapor pressure of the relevant PAH molecules. A few approaches were taken to overcome this difficulty. First, we have tried to grow the films at low temperature ~78K by cooling the sample stage with liquid nitrogen. Indeed, it allowed multilayer growth of coronene. However, in the process of doping K afterwards, we had to anneal the sample to somewhat high temperatures. As long as we annealed it at room temperature for extended period of time, the coronene molecules started to evaporate and ended up with only a bilayer on Au(111). The second approach we took was to co-evaporate K and coronene simultaneously to grow KxCoronene films directly. This method lost the monitoring and control of film thickness and eventually led to thicker films that was not suitable for STM imaging. The third approach was to choose different substrates which had weaker interaction with coronene molecules and might result in bulk-like structure with a thin film thickness. We have tried a variety of substrates such as Cu(111), Ag(100), NaCl on Cu(111), and KCl on Ag(100). Interesting knowledge was indeed obtained and the results on the strength of interaction between coronene and substrates formed the basis of a nice paper published. This approach achieved partial success. On a few layer KCl covered Ag(100) surface, a 2 × 1 superstructure of coronene with respect to that of bulk coronene was observed in the multilayer form of coronene. Unluckily, when K was doped on it, no ordered structures could be resolved with STM. With the above effort, we have learned that thin films of KxCoronene do not hold a structure resembling that of the bulk. Instead of developing a superconductivity phase, a phase with the LUMO electronic band splitting appeared. On various substrates, we have manifested that the crystalline structures and molecular orientations of coronene thin films were both thickness-dependent and substrate-sensitive due to the competition between molecule−substrate interaction and intermolecular interaction. Growth of thicker coronene films with and without K doping was attempted but with limited success. Different approaches such as devised in Section 6.2 may help to obtain bulk-like structure. At this stage, no direct observation of superconductivity phase was achieved and thus the objective 3 “To understand the detailed mechanism of superconductivity” is only partially achieved.

404613.label: Major findings and research outcome
404613.value: Using scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy (STM/STS), we have first studied the monolayer and double-layer pristine and potassium-doped coronene films on Au(111) at the molecular level with the doping ratio x ranging from 0 to 4. Both the morphology and the electronic property were found to be strongly governed by the amount of charge transfer. Certain phases of K3Coronene and K4Coronene could be fabricated by controlling the corresponding K doping ratios. While in K4Coronene a doubly degenerate LUMO state of the undoped coronene became fully occupied, in K3Coronene that state was observed to cross the Fermi level and split into an upper unoccupied part and a lower occupied part, implying the presence of electronic correlation effect and Mott−Hubbard transition in the system. The observed four different phases of K3Coronene further showed different strengths of electronic correlation effect and led us to speculate that the superconductivity transition with different Tc in potassium-doped coronene observed elsewhere might have an origin from the electronic correlation effect with different strengths. The above results were published as Publication 1 and presented in Conference 1 as seen in part C. To address the possibility of growing thicker polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) films resembling bulk PAH, molecular coronene films with or without K doping on various substrates including HOPG, Cu(111), Ag(100), NaCl on Cu(111), and KCl on Ag(100) were attempted and investigated by low-temperature STM/STS. The crystalline structures and molecular orientations of coronene thin films were found both thickness-dependent and substrate-sensitive due to the competition between molecule−substrate interaction and intermolecular interaction. While in mono- or bilayer films, coronene molecules are flat-lying on the surface with hexagonal lattice, in multilayer films, the topmost molecules are in a standing-up but tilted configuration with rectangular lattice. In particular, a 2 × 1 superstructure with respect to that of bulk coronene is formed on thick KCl film. For K-doped coronene monolayer, at doping ratio x = 3, similar LUMO and HOMO shifting and splitting behaviors as that for coronene double-layer on Au(111) was observed. By contrast, for potassium doped coronene multilayer on Ag(100) and KCl/Ag(100) surface, no well-ordered structures are obtained. The failure to produce well-ordered K-doped coronene multilayer implies a big challenge of growth of PAH thick films in vacuum and the major difficulties in observing superconductivity in vacuum grown PAH films. The above results were published as Publication 2and presented in Conference 2 as seen in part C.

404613.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
404613.value: To overcome the difficulty of vacuum growth of thick organic films, one may grow the sample in a bulk-like form by placing a suitable substrate in the growth furnace of bulk powders. With appropriate K-doped bulk-like sample grown on the substrate, one can then thin the organic film to a thickness of a few nm to a few tens of nm and use scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy to study the various structural phases and their corresponding electronic transport properties. Superconducting phase may be identified afterwards. Another way to grow thicker organic film is to use CVD-like method by a flow gas to bring the organic molecules to the substrate at relative high pressure in the growth furnace. This may also reduce the desorption of organic molecules during the growth process with a relative high environmental pressure. Controlling the time may lead to a suitable thickness of the sample for STM/STS study that further relates the electronic transport properties to the structural information.

404613.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
404613.value: Superconductivity is a fascinating macroscopic quantum phenomenon. Superconductors with light elements, such as carbon-based superconductors, have attracted great interests for their element abundance, low cost and non-toxicity, which are important advantages for future applications. A new class of alkali metal doped hydrocarbons belongs to this category and may hold high transition temperature Tc. To reveal relation between the molecular structural arrangement and the superconductivity in K-doped hydrocarbon films, we have grown coronene films with various thickness on different substrates and studied them by scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy that can simultaneously uncover structural information and transport properties. While the pristine coronene films are insulators, K doping can clearly shift the energy bands with respect to the Fermi level and potentially make the films metallic and even superconducting. At present, with x = 3 for KxCoronene in their monolayer and bi-layer forms, the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital bands are brought to the Fermi level but split into an upper unoccupied part and a lower occupied part due to the presence of electronic correlation effect and Mott−Hubbard transition. Future work to remove such splitting possibly by growing much thicker films (difficult job) to recover the potential superconductivity is needed.

404813.label: Project Title(Chinese)
404813.value: 關於可壓縮定常跨音速流的研究

404813.label: Project Objectives
404813.value: One of the main objectives is the existence and structure of steady flows in a nozzle which are continuous and contain sonic state. Since the steady compressible Euler equations are strongly degenerate near a sonic state, a smooth transonic flow may be structurally unstable as proved by Morawetz. Indeed, for a finite de Laval nozzle, a Taylor type smooth transonic flow does not exist in general and is structurally unstable even if it exists. So this is very difficult but important issue to study. One major goal is to prove the existence of smooth Meyer type transonic flows in a general 2-dimensional finite de Laval nozzle with physical boundary conditions. This will yield the first rigorous existence of smooth Meyer type transonic flows in a de Laval. We will deal with both irrotational Meyer type transonic flows and Meyer-type transonic flows with none-zero vorticity. Next, we will study the well-posedness and properties of steady subsonic-sonic solutions in a given nozzle of variable sections for the full Euler equations which will generalize our recent special results on irrotational flows in a converging straight nozzle. In this case, the sonic curve is a free boundary where the Euler system becomes degenerate. Finally, we will also investigate general weak subsonic-supersonic flows in a general nozzle. Our next goal is to study transonic flows with shocks in a general nozzle. A particular goal is to continue to investigate the transonic shock problem in a de Laval nozzle due to Courant-Friedrichs: for a given de Laval nozzle, if the upper stream flow remains supersonic behind the throat of the nozzle and the exit pressure is suitably large, then a transonic shock front intervenes at a certain place in a divergent part of the nozzle, and the speed and strength of the shock are automatically adjusted so that the pressure at the exit of the nozzle reaches the given exit pressure. This difficult but interesting problem has been solved successfully only in the two-dimensional case. We would like to study the existence of solutions to this problem in the case of 3-dimensional nozzles. There are essential difficulties in transonic-shocks 3-dimensional nozzle due to the strong coupling of the hyperbolicity and ellipticity of the 3-D compressible Euler system. We will also study the transonic flow pattern in a de Laval nozzle that a subsonic steady flow enters the converging part of the nozzle, speeds up to sonic state near the throat and remains smooth and supersonic after sonic curve, is intervened by a transonic shock, becomes subsonic again, and reaches the suitably given pressure at the exit. This problem is open completely since both the sonic curves and transonic shocks are free boundaries and the governing system is strongly degenerate at the sonic state. Another main objective is to investigate the existence and structures of steady subsonic flows in multi-dimensional nozzle of variable sections. Both finite length and infinitely long nozzles will be studied. Started with the pioneering work of L.Bers, most of the previously works deal with irrotational (or near-irrotaional) steady subsonic flows in infinitely long nozzles with variable sections, which can be handled since the governing equation is elliptic for subsonic flows. However, in the case of non-irrotational steady flows, the governing system is elliptic-hyperbolic type even for subsonic flows. So the problem is much more challenging, and even the formulation of the subsonic flow problem is highly non-trivial. The only available results are concerning the existence of global subsonic steady flow with small vorticity in general infinitely along 2-dimensional nozzles with given mass flux and Bernoulli’s function at upstream. We plan to study the case of prescribing the upstream velocity and to obtain steady subsonic flow with large vorticity in general multi-dimensional nozzles. Another goal is to study general steady subsonic flows in finite nozzles with variable sections, which remains open even irrotational flows.

404813.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
404813.value: Ideal steady compressible fluid-motions are governed by the steady compressible Euler equations. The studies of such a system of partial differential equations give rise to many important and challenging open problems in the theory of nonlinear partial differential equations, and are important in both theory and applications. Since the system is mixed-type in general and highly nonlinear, thus a general well-posedness theory for the steady compressible Euler system with physical boundary conditions is far from being completed. In this research project, we propose to study some special but physically important wave patterns for ideal steady compressible flows in nozzles with variable sections which has important applications in aeronautics and gas dynamics. In particular, we will focus on the following topics: well-posedness of steady subsonic flows in general 3-dimensional nozzles with non-trial vorticity, well-posedness of steady smooth transonic flows in a de Laval nozzle; and well-posedness of the Courant-Friedrich’s transonic shock problem in a finite three-dimensional de Laval nozzle with given exit pressure. These studies will lead to some deeper understanding on degeneracies, nonlinear free-boundaries, and propagation of corner singularities for mixed-type and degenerate partial differential equations. 可壓縮理想定常流體運動是由歐拉方程組來描述的。對這類偏微分方程組的研究是偏微分方程理論中具有挑戰性的公開重要難題，在理論和應用都具有重要意義。由於定常可壓縮歐拉方程組是混合型的，且具有很強的非線性，故其帶有物理邊界條件的解的適定性理論還遠遠沒有完善。這裏我們提議研究在空氣動力學和航空學中具有重要應用的幾類在彎曲管道中的定常可壓縮流動中的特殊但重要的波型。特別是我們將聚焦於下述幾個適定性問題：三維管道中具有非平凡渦度的定常亞音速流動；收一級管道中光滑的定常跨音速流動；及Courant-Friedrich's關於給定出口壓力的有限管道中的跨音速激波問題。這些研究將進一步加強人們對混合型及蛻化偏微分方程組中非線性自由邊值問題、蛻化結構和邊界奇性的傳播等問題的深刻理解。

404813.label: Major findings and research outcome
404813.value: With the main support of this grant, the PI has achieved the objectives of the project by establishing the following results: 1. We have made substantial progress on the studies of smooth transonic flows in general curved 2-dimensional nozzles, which are governed by a nonlinear partial differential equations with degeneracy and singularities at the sonic state. First, we give a complete answer to a problem of L. Bers on the structure of the set of exceptional points on sonic curve by showing that for any C^2-smooth transonic flow of Meyer type, the sonic curve consists at most three connected parts and one of which consists of all exceptional points and is a closed line segment. Second and more importantly, we established the local well-posedness of Meyer type transonic flow with sonic curve containing only exceptional points for a general class of de Laval nozzles which are suitably flat at its throats. This gives the first existence result on the general smooth Meyer type transonic flows in a nozzle with variable sections. Then we derive some necessary and sufficient conditions to extend those local Meyer type transonic flow globally. In particular, we have shown that a global supersonic extension exists in a symmetric nozzle whose upper wall is convex after the throat. Surprisingly, the subsonic extension of the local Meyer type transonic flow is more subtle, we have derive a necessary and sufficient condition for this extension in terms of the geometry and nozzle and height of the throat. All these results are reported in the papers [14, 13, 12, 24]. Furthermore in [24], we established the first well-posedness of Lipschitz continuous subsonic-sonic flows in a general 2-dimensional finite nozzle and have characterized completely the location of the sonic points in such a flow. This solves a long standing open problem. For steady flows with non-trivial vorticity, we have established the well-posedness of 2-dimensional Euler flows past a wall or a symmetric body as long as the upstream vorticity is suitably small. The asymptotic behavior of such a flow is also obtained. This is published in the paper [16]. 2. We have also obtained some significant results on transonic flows with shocks. In particular, we have solved the Courant-Friedrich’s transonic shock problem in a class of 2-dimensional nozzle which are generic perturbations of a flat nozzle. We have design a delicate scheme to prove the existence of single or multiple shock solutions in terms of the exit pressure and the geometry of the nozzle. This is reported in the paper [25]. 3. Besides the works mention above, we have obtained the following results closely related to this project: longtime existence of entropy solutions to the 1-dimensional full Euler system with periodic initial data [1, 23]; uniform estimates for 3-dimensional surface waves independent of both viscosity and surface tension [2, 22]; vacuum dynamic and regularities and asymptotic stability of solutions to the compressible Navier-Stokes equations [3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 11, 17, 20]; stability of viscous boundary layers [9, 21]; blow-up criteria and uniqueness of liquid-crystal flows [5, 15, 18]; non-uniqueness of entropy solutions to the compressible Euler system [19], etc.. Many of these papers are published in top research journals.

404813.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
404813.value: The results, ideas and approaches developed in this project will be extremely useful in the further studies on multi-dimensional transonic flows, where many challenging issues remain to be settled. In particular, our results on the characterization of sonic curve in terms of the topology of the exceptional points and characteristic information should be extremely important for more general Meyer type flows. Our idea of new linearization schemes for determining the local of the possible transonic shock in terms of the geometry of the nozzle and the range of the exit pressure should share more light on the general transonic shock problems. Our formulation and treatment of the steady flow past a wall or symmetric body should also be important for understanding the general steady compressible flow past a general body with non-zero vorticity: our studies in this project also gave rise to many interesting problems such as vacuum phenomena for supersonic flow in expanding nozzles, subsonic or subsonic-sonic jet problems, etc.. We will pursue these and other related problems in future works. These will involve further theoretic studies of mixed-type PDEs with complicated geometry and free boundaries.

404813.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
404813.value: Ideal steady compressible fluid-motions are governed by the steady compressible Euler equations. The studies of such a system of partial differential equations give rise to many important and challenging open problems in the theory of nonlinear partial differential equations, and are important in both theory and applications. In this project, we have studied some special but physically important wave patterns for ideal steady compressible flows in nozzles with variable sections or passing a body which have important applications in aeronautics and gas dynamics. In particular, we have proved the well-posedness of Meyer type smooth transonic flow for a class of de Laval nozzle, solved Courant-Friedrich’s transonic shock problem for a class of nozzles with given exit pressure; the well-posedness of smooth subsonic flow with non-zero vorticities pass a wall or a body, etc.. These studies have led to some deeper understanding on degeneracy, nonlinear free-boundary, and propagation of Corner singularities for mixed-type and degenerate partial different equations.

405113.label: Major findings and research outcome
405113.value: We developed a general threshold model which provide flexible threshold modelling of data. A criterion function based on the minimum description length principle is developed for estimating the number and locations of thresholds and for performing model selection in each regime. We show that the number and locations of the thresholds can be consistently estimated under mild conditions. Efficient computation procedure is also developed for the optimization based on a genetic algorithm. Simulation studies and real data examples are examined to demonstrate the statistical and computational efficiency of the proposed method.

405113.value: This project develops a general threshold model which provide flexible threshold modelling of data. This provides flexible and interpretable ways to describe scientific mechanisms in research studies.

405213.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
405213.value: The local Langlands correspondence is a key ingredient of the Langlands program, which is the most far-reaching and influential philosophy in modern number theory. It concerns with associating Langlangs parameters, which are objects of arithmetic nature, to irreducible admissible representations of p-adic reductive group, which are objects in harmonic analysis. This conjectural correspondence is the major unsolved problem in representation theory for many decades, although many important special cases have been established. The study of irreducible admissible representations can be reduced to those of supercuspidal representations. Under favorable assumptions, all supercuspidal representations have been constructed by earlier work of the PI, and more recently, the construction has become more streamlined. On the other hand, recent work of the PI and others identified important interesting classes of supercuspidal representations such as the epipelagic representations. In an important recent work of Kaletha, Langlands parameters are associated to epipelagic representations. In this projects we propose to study and extend the method of Kaletha to attack more cases of the local Langlands correspondence conjecture. 郎蘭茲綱領是引導近世數論研究影響最深遠的思想，而局部郎蘭茲對應是此綱領的一個關鍵成分。其目的在於把郎蘭茲參數與 p 進約化群的不可約表示配對，使分析意味濃厚的後者聯繫上深具算術訊息的前者。此對應目前是懸而未決的猜想，也是數十年來表示論最重要的未解決問題之一。但是有許多重要的特例已經被了解。 不可約表示的研究可以化約為超尖點表示的研究。在簡單的假設下，所有超尖點表示已經由計劃主持人的先前工作構造出來了。近年來，這個構造更被精簡清晰化。同時，計劃主持人和他的合作者們，更找出了幾類特別重要的超尖點表示，包括淺水表示。 在 Kaletha 最近的重要工作中，郎蘭茲參數可以和淺水表示配對。本計劃將研究擴展此方法來進一步了解局部郎蘭茲對應的更多情形。

405513.label: Project Objectives
405513.value: We will establish the mathematical unique determination of the physical metrics in Maxwell equations using the admittance map. We will establish the mathematical unique identifiability of the two physical metrics of special types in Maxwell equations by a partial admittance map. We will establish the qualitative determination of EM inclusions by either near fields or far fields. We will establish a solid mathematical theory to explore and understand the regular and non-regular behaviors of EM parameters.

We will establish a solid mathematical theory to explore and understand the regular and non-regular behaviors of EM parameters.

405513.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
405513.value: The project aims to conduct a systematic and intensive mathematical investigation into a challenging mathematical inverse problem associated with the Maxwell equations. The inverse problem is motivated by the physical exploration into the interior properties of certain materials or media using some measurement data. Although a great deal of numerical effort has been made to solve the inverse Maxwell problem, still not much has been achieved to understand the problem mathematically, including the unique determination and stability of the solutions. The inverse Maxwell problem of our interest can be formulated mathematically as the geometric problem of determining two Riemannian metrics by the corresponding external data encoded into the boundary admittance map (or Dirichlet-to-Neumann map) or the scattering amplitude. Due to the invariance of the Maxwell system under diffeomorphisms, the best result one can expect in the general case is to recover the metrics in a gauge equivalence class. In the literature, there have been extensive studies on the unique determination of isotropic metrics, i.e., both of them are conformal to the Euclidean metric, whereas very little is known in the general anisotropic case. The main goal of this project is to tackle the uniqueness in determining the anisotropic metrics or in determining the isotropic metrics using the partial admittance map, and also study the invisibility problem due to some non-uniqueness. The proposed research starts with an effort to establish the uniqueness in determining real analytic metric tensors up to a real analytic diffeomorphism, then the unique identifiability of isotropic metrics by partial admittance map. Afterwards we will explore how to qualitatively locating the singularities of non-smooth metrics by the scattering amplitude. Finally we shall derive some approximate invisibility cloaks by non-singular isotropic metrics. All these problems are rather challenging from the mathematical points of view, but the results achieved in this project can answer several fundamental questions and significantly advance our mathematical understanding of the inverse Maxwell problem, as well as provide some insightful guidances to numerical solutions. The mathematical techniques developed in this project are applicable to many other inverse problems. 確定電磁場中度量的數學理論 本研究項目的目的是系統深入地研究與電磁場方程相關的數學反問題，也即利用一些測量的數據， 希望確定某些電磁場環境或介質中的內部物理性態。對這個反問題的數值模擬已有很多工作，但仍未有理論上的探討及深入理解，特別是反問題解的唯一確定和穩定性。 我們將利用一些特別的數學工具，例如DtN映射算子和電磁場中度量的本性結構來研究這個反問題的唯一確定性和穩定性。對於各向同性和各向異性的介質將分別研究。我們的理論結果既有定性的分析，也有定量的數值方法和數值分析。

405513.label: Realisation of objectives
405513.value: We made huge efforts and achieved all the objectives, in fact, much more than we planned in the proposal. We proposed in [1] a fundamental concept of scattering coefficients for inverse electromagnetic medium problems, and it is now proved to be a powerful tool for numerical solution and analysis of various inverse problems, especially the EM medium/inclusion reconstruction in this project. The scattering coefficients have nice features such as symmetric, tensorial and decaying properties, and have a unique relationship with far-field pattern. We related the exponentially ill-posed character of the inverse medium scattering at a fixed frequency to the exponential decay of scattering coefficients. For the numerical purpose, the sensitivity of scattering coefficients with respect to changes in two physical metrics, the permittivity and permeability, was established. We worked out the reconstruction formulas of both permittivity and permeability using the data from scattering coefficients, and demonstrated the improved stability of the reconstruction using multi-frequency measurements. By means of the new fundamental concept, we made a significant mathematical and numerical progress in [2] for the phaseless reconstruction from far-field data. It also enabled us to perform more insightful sensitivity, resolution, and stability analysis of phaseless problems and better understand why the phaseless reconstruction is more severely ill-posed. Furthermore, the new concept allows us to study the stability by estimating the condition number of the inversion process for both the phased and phaseless cases, and to provide an insightful instruction for efficient phaseless measurements in applications. This is the first time to establish the stability in terms of condition numbers for phased and phaseless inverse scatterings, and it opens a promising direction that is well complementary to the existing regularization theory [10]. One main objective of our project is the mathematical and numerical study of recovering physical parameters using partial data, which is the case in most applications. For this we chose to focus our studies on the electrical impedance tomography and diffusive optical tomography in [3,4] when only one or two pairs of Cauchy measurement data is available. These inverse problems form the basic steps in reconstructions of EM parameters and inclusions in our project, and are severely ill-posed mathematically and extremely challenging numerically. Surprisingly, we are able to design a direct sampling method (DSM) to recover inhomogeneous inclusions for both problems, and the DSMs are much less expensive and easier to implement than most existing methods. Our project aims also at a qualitative determination of EM inclusions by either near fields or far fields. In [16], we focused on a general shape reconstruction problem, i.e., to construct, up to scalings and rigid transformations, the optimal shape of an object given either its polarization tensor at multiple contrasts or the partial eigenvalues of its Neumann–Poincare operator. We created a highly novel strategy to recover the eigenvalues from polarization tensor by means of holomorphic functional calculus, and then developed a regularized optimization for shape reconstructions. This new methodology is expected to have other important applications such as in the design of plasmon resonances and in the multi-frequency or pulsed EM imaging of anomalies. Domain decomposition methods (DDMs) are proved to be the most natural numerical methods that are highly efficient in parallel solutions of many direct problems of PDEs. Inverse problems are much more time-consuming and challenging, especially the reconstructions of two EM metrics and inclusions in our project. So fast solvers like DDMs are essentially more significant and necessary to develop than for direct problems. However, little has been done yet due to the strong ill-posedness and nonlinearity of inverse problems. We derived in [3,13,14] a series of DDMs for some typical inverse problems, including the identification of fluxes, source strengths and initial temperature in general elliptic and parabolic systems. The methods converge globally, are highly parallel, and nearly optimal in terms of meshes and time steps. These DDMs provide essential building blocks to most numerical solvers for recovering the physical metrics in Maxwell system or EM inhomogeneous inclusions in our RGC project. In order to use least computational efforts to achieve optimal efficiencies and accuracies, adaptive finite element methods (FEMs) were proposed in [5,8] for two highly ill-posed inverse problems, recovering the Robin coefficient and electric conductivity in diffusion systems from boundary measurements. Unlike for direct problems, a posteriori error estimators can not be derived for this ill-posed nonlinear inverse problem, instead they were established from our convergence analysis of adaptive algorithms. We proved the convergence of discrete solutions generated by adaptive FEMs through general least-squares minimizations with appropriate regularizations. Inverse problems are known to be numerically unstable and expensive. In [12] we proposed two randomized algorithms for solving large-scale inverse problems with general Tikhonov regularizations. The first algorithm can reduce large-scale systems to much smaller-scale systems and seek their regularized solutions in combination with some existing choice rules for regularization parameters. The second approach can essentially reduce the sizes of the original large-scale ill-posed systems, and the reduced systems can provide approximate solutions with same numerical accuracy as the ones by the classical generalized SVD, but they are much more stable numerically and much less expensive. In order to speed up the entire numerical solutions of inverse problems, one effective strategy is to design fast solvers for all direct problems involved in the inversion processes. In this direction we managed to make several important progresses [6, 7, 9, 15, 16] related to this RGC project. First in [7], we derived an adaptive edge element method to an optimal control problem associated with a magnetostatic saddle-point Maxwell’s system, and proved the reliability and efficiency of the a posteriori error estimators and the desired convergence of the adaptive method. PML is a popular and efficient strategy to approximate a PDE over an infinite domain by a finite domain. But there is little work to build up efficient preconditioners for solving the PML system of an electromagnetic system. We proposed in [9] block triangular preconditioners for a PML system of an electromagnetic wave scattering problem and analyzed the spectral behaviour of the preconditioned systems. Furthermore, we provided in [6] a mathematical and numerical framework for the analysis of the effects of pulsed electric fields on physical media that have two physical heterogeneous permittivity and conductivity. A fully discrete finite element scheme was proposed for numerical approximations of the interface problem with general pulses, and demonstrated to enjoy the optimal convergence in both space and time. The new results and numerical scheme have potential applications in many fields like electromagnetism, medicine, food sciences, and biotechnology, especially in numerical inversion processes involved in these applications. Practically, it is often very helpful and important to effectively visualize and understand the numerical reconstructions for various inverse problems. In [15] we proposed a powerful nonnegative matrix trifactorization (NMF), based on a sparse low-rank approximation of positive data and images in terms of tensor products of positive vectors. The NMF can extract major components in the given data and images representing structures of different resolutions but still preserve the positivity of the basis and sparsity of the approximation. We emphasize that for all numerical reconstruction methods we developed in this project, sufficient numerical experiments were conducted to check and demonstrate their effectiveness and stability.

405513.label: Major findings and research outcome
405513.value: We presented in [1] a fundamental concept of scattering coefficients for inverse electromagnetic medium problems. Several nice features were discovered for scattering coefficients. The exponentially ill-posed character of inverse medium scattering is revealed to be closely related to the exponential decay of scattering coefficients. Reconstructions of both permittivity and permeability were proposed using far-field data, and demonstrated the improved stability using multi-frequency measurements. The fundamental concept led to more insightful sensitivity, resolution, and stability analysis of phaseless problems with respect to far-field data and explained the severe ill-posedness of the phaseless reconstruction [2] [10], by using the condition number of the inversion process. We investigated electrical impedance tomography and diffusive optical tomography in [3,4] when limited data is available, and designed computationally very cheap direct sampling methods to recover inhomogeneous inclusions. In [16], we studied a general shape reconstruction problem to construct the optimal shape of an object given either its polarization tensor at multiple contrasts or the partial eigenvalues of its Neumann–Poincare operator. We derived in [3,13,14] a series of domain decomposition methods (DDMs) for several typical inverse problems. The methods are shown to converge globally, highly parallel, and nearly optimal in terms of meshes and time steps. Adaptive finite element methods (FEMs) were proposed in [5,8] for recovering the Robin coefficient and electric conductivity in diffusion systems from boundary measurements. And the convergence of adaptive FEMs was proved through general least-squares minimizations with appropriate regularizations. In [12] we proposed two randomized algorithms for solving large-scale inverse problems with general Tikhonov regularizations. Both algorithms reduce large-scale systems to much smaller-scale systems, and still provide approximate solutions with the same accuracy as the best existing methods, but being more stable and less expensive. We derived an adaptive FEM to an optimal control of Maxwell’s system, and proved its reliability, efficiency and convergence [7]. We proposed block preconditioners for PML systems of electromagnetic scatterings and analyzed the spectra of the preconditioned systems [9]. In [6], we provided a mathematical and numerical framework for analyzing the effects of pulsed electric fields on heterogeneous physical media. A full FEM was proposed for the interface problem, and demonstrated to enjoy optimal convergence. We proposed a powerful nonnegative matrix trifactorization [15], which can extract major components in the given data and images representing structures of different resolutions but still preserve the positivity of the basis and sparsity of the approximation.

405513.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
405513.value: We proposed in [1] a fundamental concept of scattering coefficients for inverse electromagnetic medium problems, and it is now proved to be a powerful tool for numerical solution and analysis of various inverse problems [2]. Scattering coefficients are shown to have several nice features, and have a unique relationship with far-field pattern. It would be important to study and understand detailed stability behaviors of a nonlinear inverse problem in terms of scattering coefficients. This understanding can guide us how to better measure the data and to what more general inverse problems scattering coefficients can apply. We have achieved several important results in this project in mathematical and numerical study of recovering physical parameters using partial data, which is of great interest to most applications. For the severely ill-posed nonlinear inverse problems, electrical impedance tomography and diffusive optical tomography, we designed direct sampling methods (DSMs) to recover inhomogeneous inclusions, and the DSMs prove to be much less expensive and easier to implement than most existing methods. It is a highly interesting and significant topic to explore how to develop similar DSMs for more general inverse problems. The two topics above are the PhD research projects of two of my current PhD students.

405513.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
405513.value: This three-year RGC project has made a systematic and intensive mathematical and numerical investigation into a challenging mathematical inverse problem associated with the electromagnetic Maxwell system. Inverse problems of this type have wide applications in many areas, and are motivated by the exploration into the interior properties of physical materials or media using measurement data from the partial boundary of the physical domain. The main objective of the project is to study the numerical and mathematical reconstruction of physical heterogeneous electric permittivity and magnetic permeability. We have explored in depth how to locate the inclusions and singularities of physical parameters by the scattering amplitude qualitatively and quantitatively, and developed adaptive methods and fast parallel algorithms for the reconstructions. Sufficient numerical simulations were conducted to check and demonstrate the effectiveness and stability of our numerical reconstruction methods against the noise in measurement data. These inverse problems are mathematically ill-posed and highly challenging from the numerical points of view. The results achieved have provided answers to several fundamental mathematical issues, significantly advanced our understanding in the inverse Maxwell problem, and presented insightful guidance to efficient numerical solutions. The mathematical methods and theories established are applicable to other physically important inverse problems.

409513.label: Project Objectives
409513.value: Obtaining the critical temperature of a spin-orbit coupled Bose-Einstein condensate. Using Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov approach to study how spin-orbit coupling suppresses the critical temperature through suppressing the kinetic energy of the system along multiple directions. Exploring interaction induced corrections to the critical temperature beyond mean field approximation. Formulating an effective theory for emergent novel normal states at low temperatures. We will derive an effective theory to characterize the relevant low energy excitations and study the dependence of the parameters in the effective theory on microscopic variables of spin-orbit coupling. Deriving correlation functions and thermodynamic quantities of the normal state from the effective theory in different parameter regions. Exploring possibilities of creating novel normal states via spin-orbit coupling, such as a three-dimensional algebraic boson liquid. Obtaining correlation functions of the emergent algebraic boson liquid at zero temperature in two dimension in both the spatial and frequency space. 409513.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
409513.value: Weakly interacting condensates persist up to a critical temperature in three dimension, because of the small condensate depletion at low temperatures. It is also known that, if one is able to destroy a condensate at low temperatures or at the ground state, interesting many-body states with novel correlation functions may emerge. Conventional methods for achieving this goal include enhancing interaction and reducing dimension. The recent exciting developments of realizing synthetic spin-orbit coupling for ultra cold atoms have inspired intensive interest to study the interplay between spin-orbit coupling and condensates. PI and coworker, and other researchers, recently found that spin-orbit coupling significantly enhances condensate depletion of weakly interacting bosons even at sufficiently low temperatures in three dimension. This discovery indicates unprecedented opportunities of suppressing condensates and generating novel many-body states via spin-orbit coupling. The study on using spin-orbit coupling to suppress condensates is still at its early stage. Results of condensate depletion at low temperatures cannot directly tell one what is the critical temperature to destroy a spin-orbit coupled condensate. It is unclear neither whether the condensate can be destroyed by spin-orbit coupling at the ground state. An even more important question is, what are the emergent many-body states of these uncondensed bosons at very low temperatures or at the ground state? In this project, we will systematically study how spin-orbit coupling controls the critical temperature of an interacting condensate. When the critical temperature is strongly suppressed, we will study the correlation functions and thermodynamics of the normal states. We expect that novel normal states will emerge, such as algebraic boson liquids, due to interaction induced correlation effects in these low temperature regions. To study the critical temperature, we will generalize the well established methods for ordinary condensates to spin-orbit coupled ones. Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov theory will be used within the mean field framework and many-body Green's function formalism will be applied to explore beyond mean field effects. To study the emergent normal states at low temperatures, we will adopt the standard approach of the effective theory to explore the low energy excitations, correlation functions and thermodynamics. The outcome of this project will provide guidance for experimental efforts to search for novel many-body states of spin-orbit coupled bosons. It will suggest to the cold atom physics community a new approach to enhance correlation effects in a high dimensional system using spin-orbit coupling, without resorting to enhancing interaction nor reducing dimension. 由於凝聚體在低溫下具有很弱的虧損，弱相互作用的三維波色－愛因斯坦凝聚體在一個臨界溫度以下存在。眾所周知，如果能夠在低溫下甚至於是在基態上抑制凝聚的發生，具有新奇關聯性質的多體相將可能出現。實現這一目標的常規方法包括增強相互作用和降低系統的維度。 近期在超冷原子中實現合成自旋軌道耦合的這一進展激發了對自旋軌道耦合和凝聚體之間的相互作用進行研究的極大興趣。本課題的研究者和合作者，以及其他研究人員最近發現，自旋軌道耦合即使在極低的溫度下也能顯著增大三維弱相互作用體系裡的凝聚體虧損。這一發現展示了利用自旋軌道耦合來抑制凝聚並產生新奇多體相這樣一個前所未有的機遇。 對利用自旋軌道耦合來抑制凝聚體的研究仍處於早期階段。對低溫下凝聚體虧損的研究結果不能直接告訴我們凝聚體的臨界溫度。目前也不清楚自旋軌道耦合是否可以在基態上抑制凝聚體。一個更重要的問題是，當凝聚體在低溫下或者基態上消失以後，出現的多體相是什麼。 在這個課題中，我們將系統地研究如何利用自旋軌道耦合來控制有相互作用的凝聚體的臨界溫度。我們將研究當臨界溫度被降低以後，正常態的關聯函數和熱力學性質。我們預計，由於相互作用在這些低溫區域裡引起的關聯效應，包括代數玻色液體在內的新奇正常態將產生。 我們將把研究普通體系裡臨界溫度的理論方法推廣到自旋軌道耦合的體系中。在平均場框架裡，我們將應用哈特里- 福克－玻戈留玻夫理論。在超出平均場框架以外，我們將應用多體格林函數方法。為研究在低溫下的正常態，我們將採用有效理論來探討低能激發，關聯函數和熱力學性質。 這個課題的成果將對實驗上搜尋自旋軌道耦合的玻色子的新型多體相的研究提供理論指導。這個課題會給冷原子物理領域提供一個新的方法，用以提高在高維體系中的關聯效應。這個基於自旋軌道耦合的方案將不依賴於加強相互作用或者降低維度這些傳統的方法。

409513.label: Realisation of objectives
409513.value: The critical temperature of a spin-orbit coupled Bose-Einstein condensate was first obtained for non-interacting systems, in which the Density of States was significantly enhanced by spin-orbit coupling. Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov approach was then used to explore interaction effect. The microscopic variables of spin-orbit coupling have been explored to suppress the critical temperature down to zero in three dimensions. An effective theory was derived to characterise spin-orbit coupled bosons. When the condensate vanishes, correlation functions and thermodynamic quantities of the non-condensed state were studied to characterise the emergent new quantum liquid. Signatures in experiments were also explored. Besides spin-orbit coupled bosons stated in the objectives, fermions were also explored, and a novel topological d-wave superfluid induced by the interplay between interaction and synthetic spin-orbit coupling was discovered.

409513.label: Major findings and research outcome
409513.value: Though textbook results tell one that bosons condense at the ground state in two dimensions, we discovered a new quantum state of bosons, which does not condense. Our results were summarised in the publication, A two-dimensional algebraic quantum liquid produced by an atomic simulator of the quantum Lifshitz model, Nature Communications 6, Article number: 8012 (2015) doi:10.1038/ncomms9012. Inspired by the effects of the interplay between interaction and synthetic spin-orbit coupling, we also explore a fermonic system and found out a novel d-wave superfluid. The results were summarised in a publication, Chiral d-Wave Superfluid in Periodically Driven Lattices, Phys. Rev. Lett. 115, 225301 (2015) One Mphil and one PhD students were trained. Three invited talks were given in international conferences. Seminars were given in a number of universities, including University of Chicago, Purdue University, South University of Science and Technology of China.

409513.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
409513.value: We may explore synthetic spin-orbit coupling in large spin systems. The interplay among condensation, synthetic spin-orbit coupling, and the large spin degree of freedom may bring us a lot more new quantum states of bosons.

409513.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
409513.value: Half particles in the universe, the so called bosons, condense at sufficiently low temperatures. In this project, we discovered new quantum states of bosons, which do not condense due to the influence of synthetic spin-orbit coupling. By significantly enhance the single-particle Density of States, the critical temperature of bosons gets suppressed. It is even possible that at zero temperatures, the ground state becomes an algebraic quantum liquid in two dimensions, instead of the conventional condensate.

409613.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
409613.value: My research interests focus on various problems in mathematical physics and geometry. There are quite close relationships between these two areas. Particularly, I am working on problems about fluid dynamics (Navier-Stokes and fractional Navier-Stokes equation), coupled harmonic map flow (gauged harmonic map flow and Ricci harmonic map flow), Ginzburg-Landau vortices, Maxwell-Chern-Simons-Higgs vortices and Yang-Mills-Higgs monopoles. My goal is to understand the geometry and the motion law governed by each different model. The starting point of my research is mathematics. But I plan to find some important applications and discover some interesting phenomena in physics. The study of these problems involves techniques from various areas of mathematics for instances: geometric analysis, nonlinear Partial Differential equations, nonlinear functional analysis, variational methods, etc. Of course it also requires intuitions from physics to understand fully both physics and mathematics behind these models. I believe that my research will have direct impacts not only in mathematics but also in different fields of physics, for instances: quantum field theory, quantum mechanics, fluid dynamics etc. 本人的研究兴趣主要集中在数学物理以及几何学中的一些问题。这两个领域间有着非常紧密的联系。特别的，我正在研究的领域包括流体动力学，耦合的调和映照，Ginzburg-Landau涡旋，Maxwell-Chern-Simons-Higgs涡旋以及Yang-Mills-Higgs单极子。我的目的是能够理解这些模型背后的几何本质以及基本粒子的动力学描述。研究这些问题需要运用数学中很多分支领域的技巧。比如几何分析，非线性偏微分方程，非线性泛函分析和变分法。当然我们也需要运用物理学中的直觉去了解这些模型背后的数学问题。我相信这些研究会对数学以及物理学中的不同领域带来直接的影响。这些领域包括量子场论，量子力学以及流体动力学。

409613.label: Realisation of objectives
409613.value: For item 1 in Sect. 5.2, we have accomplished this objective by successfully building up a partial regularity theory on solutions of the steady fractional Navier–Stokes equations in 3D. In fact we find that 5/6 is a critical threshold for 3D steady fractional Navier-Stokes equation. If the order s of the fractional laplacian satisfies 1/2 < s < 5/6, any steady suitable weak solution is regular away from a relatively closed set with zero (5−6s)-Hausdorff measure. Solution is regular throughout the whole domain when 5/6 ≤ s < 1. For item 2 in Sect. 5.2, we have studied some static problems related to Chern-Simons-Higgs theory. Chern-Simons-Higgs theory is a simplified theory, which decouples neutral fields from the original MCSH theory. In a submitted article, we have found singular solutions to Chern-Simons-Higgs equation. These singular solutions correspond to fractional vortex filament solutions of CSH theory in 2D. Not only existence theory of singular solutions, we also considered its boundary layer phenomenon as a small dielectric constant approaches to zero. This problem is also partially motivated from the so-called Poisson-Boltzmann equation. We have just finished this manuscript. Large efforts have been devoted to studying dynamical problems related to items 2 and 3 in Sect. 5.2. But due to difficulties from the associated coupled system, problems in these items are extremely hard to tackle. Moreover increasing dimension from 2 to 3 also provides a difficulty since the geometry of singularities becomes complicated. In order to reduce the difficulties and meanwhile keep all these interesting problems under consideration, I have tried to find solutions to Ericksen-Leslie system, which is a hydrodynamical system for nematic liquid crystal flow. Ericksen-Leslie model shares some similarities with gauged harmonic map, Ginzburg-Landau equation and Yang-Mills-Higgs equation. One can see that gauged harmonic maps is a coupled system between Yang-Mills fields and harmonic maps, while Ericksen-Leslie model is a coupled system between Navier-Stokes equation and harmonic map heat flow. Our achievements in Ericksen-Leslie system are as follows. In fact we have focused on some instability phenomena in Ericksen-Leslie system. Three instabilities have been addressed in this project. They are oscillation instability, concentration instability and Fréedericksz transition. For the oscillation instability, we found that when circulation Reynolds number is non-trivial, the orientation variable of liquid crystal material will not approach to any m-equivariant harmonic maps while time goes to infinity. The orientation variable will circulate around the z-axis with angular variable diverging according to a logarithm function. For the concentration instability, we studied a twisted solution to the Ericksen-Leslie system. We found that solution will blow up exponentially if the twist rate is non-zero. The optimal blow-up rate is also found. For the Fréedericksz Transition, we focused on the effects from external magnetic field. We successfully showed the existence of a critical threshold for external magnetic field. Below the threshold, there is only one constant equilibrium state and no transition will happen. But above the threshold, constant solution is no longer stable. It will transit to another equilibrium state with lower energy. Moreover as it is well-known that Ericksen-Leslie system is a limiting system of Beris-Edward system, we also tried some problems related to the Beris-Edward system. In particular we considered a simple model without fluid dynamics. That is the so-called Landau-de Gennes theory. This Landau-de Gennes theory can also be compared with Yang-Mills-Higgs theory. Studies of static solutions to Landau-de Gennes theory will help us to tackle static problems in item 3 of Sect. 5.2. Recently we have made a breakthrough to find solutions to Landau-de Gennes theory in 3D with axial symmetry. We find that solutions to Landau-de Gennes theory in 3D may have hedgehog, ring (half degree) and split-core (strength 1) type singularities which can be compared with vortex filament solutions in Ginzburg-Landau theory and monopole solutions to Yang-Mills-Higgs equation. More than Ginzburg-Landau theory and Yang-Mills-Higgs theory, Landau-de Gennes theory contains richer phases while temperature varies. The method that we have used to find these solutions to Landau-de Gennes theory relies on a successful study of a Signorini problem for S^4 valued harmonic maps. Signorini problem is a free boundary problem which has been well studied for scalar functions. But in our resolution, we generalize the standard Signorini problem from scalar case to system case. Indeed this resolution partially gives some answers to problems in items 3 of Sect. 5.2. But we just finished our article on Aug. 2018. It is impossible to submit the manuscript before the deadline of the current project. Here in the following are some details about the methodology used in this manuscript. In this article we firstly studied the instability of hedgehog solutions to the Landau-de Gennes theory. This result also tells us that monopole solutions to Yang-Mills-Higgs equation are not stable neither in some parameter regime. Then we study in details the instability mode for the hedgehog solution and build up a bifurcation theory which allows us to bifurcate two different solutions from the Hedgehog solution in the Landau-de Gennes theory. Moreover one bifurcated solution has half-degree ring singularities, while another bifurcated solution contains split-core singularity with strength 1. Our bifurcation theory is novel. It is based on a Signorini free boundary problem for harmonic maps. The results in this article also solves a long standing open problem in the theory of nematic liquid crystals. Indeed we also have tried effective dynamics of gauged harmonic maps related to dynamical problems listed in items 2 and 3 of Sect. 5.2. Because problems that we have considered are quite closely related to problems in ferromagnets and Gorkov-Eliashberg equation, the original problem listed are not worth of further studying. So we have changed to study disclination dynamics arising in Beris-Edward system/Ericksen-Leslie system. In other words we changed fields from Yang-Mills fields to fluid governed by Navier-Stokes equation. But this change makes problems much harder than before due to the lack of compactness for associated tensor fields. We have tried well-posedness for limiting theory while some parameter approaches to zero. But to justify rigorously the effectiveness of the limiting process is hard. Such problems are indeed related to many open problems in complex fluid, e.g. global well-posedness on weak solutions to Oldroyd B system. So far the project is of great success. The impact is far-reaching. Not only it leads to resolutions of many important problems in mathematics and physics. But also it opens several new streams for our future study. During the period of the project, some problems listed in the original objectives are switched to related problems in nematic liquid crystal theory. PI believes that such changes are necessary. On one hand the problems solved under this project essentially focus on the original objectives and provide answers to the original objectives listed in the project. On the other hand to our surprise, solutions to these new problems also provide contributions to more important problems in both mathematics and physics.

If the order s of the fractional laplacian satisfies 1/2 < s < 5/6, any steady suitable weak solution is regular away from a relatively closed set with zero (5−6s)-Hausdorff measure. Solution is regular throughout the whole domain when 5/6 ≤ s < 1. In [2]-[4], we have studied a hydrodynamical model arising in nematic liquid crystal theory. That is the so-called Ericksen-Leslie system. This system is a coupled system between transported harmonic map heat flow and Navier-Stokes equation. For such coupled system, we have focused on some instability phenomena observed by physicists. Indeed three instabilities have been addressed in this project. They are oscillation instability, concentration instability and Fréedericksz Transition. For the oscillation instability, we found in [2] that when circulation Reynolds number is non-trivial, the orientation variable of liquid crystal material will not approach to any m-equivariant harmonic maps while time goes to infinity. The orientation variable will circulate around the z-axis with angular variable diverging according to a logarithm function. For the concentration instability, we studied a twisted solution in [4] to the Ericksen-Leslie system. We found that solution will blow up exponentially if the twist rate is non-zero. The optimal blow-up rate is also found. For the Fréedericksz Transition, we focused on the effects from external magnetic field. In [3] we successfully showed the existence of a critical threshold for external magnetic field. Below the threshold, there is only one constant equilibrium state and no transition will happen. But above the threshold, constant solution is no longer stable. It will transit to another equilibrium state with lower energy. We also have studied some static problems related to gauged harmonic maps and Chern-Simons-Higgs theory. In a submitted article, we have found singular solutions to semi-linear elliptic equations with exponential nonlinearities. This type of semi-linear equations contains Chern-Simons-Higgs equation and Born-Infeld gauged harmonic map equation in the case when the Born-Infeld parameter equals to 1. The solutions are found with a novel shrinking hole argument and inverse-problem method. However this manuscript is finished after the deadline of this project.

409613.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
409613.value: Since the problems considered under this project are quite closely related to several problems in nematic liquid crystal theory, in the future PI wants to address the following potential problems: (1). Stability of equilibrium solutions in 3D Landau-de Gennes theory. In particular we are interested in the stability issue on solutions with ring and split-core singularities; (2). Hausdorff dimension of the preimage set of harmonic maps/harmonic maps with potentials. Typically we want to provide a lower and upper estimates on the Hausdorff measures of the preimage set of solutions to some harmonic maps into sphere; (3). Parabolic hausdorff dimension of the preimage set of harmonic map heat flow. This is a generalization of problem (2) to dynamical system of parabolic type; (4). Signorini problem for vector-valued mappings. Particularly we are interested in the regularity of free boundary and their stratification. (5). Dynamics of disclinations in Landau-de Gennes theory.

409613.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
409613.value: The project is of great success. The impact is far-reaching. As one can see, the solved problems are all closely related to essential problems in both mathematics and physics. We have already studied several instability issues in the theory of nematic liquid crystals. These instability issue are even new in physical world. For example we rigorously prove the logarithm divergence on the angular variable in Ericksen-Leslie system when circulation Reynolds number is non-trivial. This result reveals the relationship between orientation variable and fluid. We also show that the liquid crystal material will blow up according to an explicit exponential function. Moreover our results also justify the so-called Fréedericksz Transition, which provides a quantitative study on the Fréedericksz Transition. For the fractional Navier-Stokes equation, our research generalizes partial regularity theory for stationary Navier-Stokes equation to the fractional case. This result fits well in the current main stream of mathematical studies. Moreover our study on semi-linear elliptic equations also provides a new method (shrinking hole + inverse-problem method) to find solutions with singularities. Meanwhile we have justified the effectiveness of Born-Infeld approximation to singular solutions of Maxwell-Higgs equation. PI believe that these researches are significative in both mathematics and physics.

409713.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
409713.value: The project aims to understand how bacteria interact with their physicochemical microenvironment when they settle on surfaces during the early stage of biofilm formation. Bacteria are the most abundant form of life on the Earth. It is believed that the majority of bacteria live in communities on a range of biotic and abiotic surfaces. Such surface-associated bacterial communities, also known as biofilms, play important roles in ecological systems and in human health. We propose to investigate a fundamental question in biofilm research, i.e. how bacteria sense and adapt to the surface environment at the onset of biofilm formation. Surface sensing, or the “bacterial sense of touch”, is fundamental to biofilm formation. Elucidating the mechanism of surface sensing has been a long-sought goal; yet neither the molecular basis nor the environmental signal for surface sensing has been identified. A major difficulty is to probe the physicochemical microenvironment that dictates the physiology and behavior of surface-attached cells. In this project we aim to reveal the physical basis of bacterial surface sensing. We will measure the dynamic changes of the physicochemical microenvironment near surface-attached cells while monitoring the cellular differentiation process, using a combination of novel fluorescence sensors, genetic engineering and quantitative analysis of time-lapse microscopy. We will further quantify how the motile behavior of cells adapts to the surface environment, since motility is an important aspect of bacterial behavior during biofilm formation and during pathogenic infections. Our study will provide key insights to the physical basis of biofilm formation. The results will substantially advance our understanding on microbe-environment interactions, and may help to design new clinical strategies to prevent the formation of pathogenic biofilms. The interdisciplinary nature of our research will also promote collaborative efforts between physical and biomedical research communities in Hong Kong.

409713.label: Realisation of objectives
409713.value: With the funding from this grant, the PI has been investigating the role of two important physicochemical parameters, namely osmolarity and viscosity, affect the differentiation of bacteria upon surface contact. We measured the temporal dynamics of osmolality in swarm cell differentiation, and measured how environmental viscosity affects bacterial physiology behavior. For Objective 1, our work revealed that the osmolarity in the microenvironment of surface-attached cells is not constant, but experience non-trivial temporal dynamics during surface-associated cellular differentiation. In further studies to be supported by future grants, we plan to find out the genetic factors responsible for this change. For Objective 2, we have measured cell’s physiological response in viscous environment, and found that the transient physiological adaption can be attributed to metabolites in viscous agents. We further found that cells in viscous fluids perform two novel forms of collective motion, one being non-contact cohesive swimming between nearby cells, and the other being collective oscillatory motion. See Research Outcome below and Research Output Publication #2&3 in Part C for details.

409713.label: Major findings and research outcome
409713.value: There are two major research outputs arising from this project: 1. Collective oscillation in bacterial suspensions. Publication #2 in Part C: Chen C, Liu S, Shi X, Chaté H, Wu Y (2017) Weak synchronization and large-scale collective oscillation in dense bacterial suspensions. Nature 542: 210–214. In this study we discovered a novel mechanism of biological collective oscillation. Collective oscillatory behavior plays a vital role in many biological processes, such as embryogenesis, organ development, and pace-making in neuron networks. Collective oscillations in multicellular systems studied to date often arise from coupling between individual cells that display inherent oscillations. In stark contrast, we discovered a mechanism of collective oscillation that does not require inherent oscillation of individual cells: We found that millions of motile cells in dense bacterial suspensions can self-organize into highly robust collective oscillatory motion, while individuals remain moving in an erratic manner. This phenomenon presents a fundamentally new mechanism of oscillatory behavior in multicellular systems, and it constitutes a new type of ordered active matter that will advance the field of non-equilibrium physics. 2. Bacterial swimming in two dimensions. Publication #3 in Part C: Li Y, Zhai H, Sanchez S, Kearns DB, Wu Y (2017) Noncontact cohesive swimming of bacteria in two-dimensional liquid films. Physical Review Letters 119, 018101. The study provides new insight for understanding how single cell behavior lead to collective dynamics in bacterial colonies, such as in bacterial swarms. Steric repulsion and flagellar intertwining were believed to dominate individual interactions between swimming bacteria in proximity; in particular, steric repulsion was suggested to be a key mechanism responsible for self-organization in quasi-2D bacterial suspensions. By contrast, the noncontact cohesive swimming we report in this paper is mediated by hydrodynamic interaction, involving neither steric repulsion nor flagellar intertwining. Therefore cohesive swimming may be another key factor that gives rise to collective motion and self-organization in 2D bacterial colonies.

409713.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
409713.value: The mechanism of collective oscillation we uncovered may find applications in biomaterial self-assembly and in controlling robotic swarms. The novel form of cohesive swimming of cells in confinement merits further studies by physicists in the fields of active matter and low-Reynolds number hydrodynamics. To the extent that cohesive swimming may promote bacterial dispersal in natural and clinical environments, our results may interest microbiology and medical communities.

409713.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
409713.value: Bacteria are the most abundant form of life on the Earth. Contrary to the conventional view that bacteria lead a single-celled life, it is now believed that the majority of bacteria live in surface-associated communities called biofilms. In the natural environment, biofilms play an important role in global carbon and nitrogen cycles. Biofilms found in the human body and on medical devices usually cause chronic infectious diseases, while some of them may benefit human metabolism and immune response. Biofilms have also attracted increasing attention from the physics community because of their relevance to nonequilibrium pattern formation, active matter, and complex fluids. It is therefore important to achieve a comprehensive understanding on the biofilm lifestyle of bacteria. Here we investigated how bacteria sense and adapt to the surface environment at the onset of biofilm formation. We found that cells in viscous fluids perform two novel forms of collective motion, one being non-contact cohesive swimming between nearby cells, and the other being collective oscillatory motion. The obtained results will provide essential information to understand the surface-associated lifestyle of bacteria. The results may find applications in biomaterial self-assembly and in controlling robotic swarms.

409813.label: Project Objectives
409813.value: Developing VSS to evaluate multiple substitutions of small functional groups simultaneously. The key to the efficiency of VSS is the sampling of multiple target states, rather than a single state as in traditional FEP techniques. In our preliminary work, we have evaluated the substitution involving four functional groups, Cl, CH3, OH, and OCH3. The results indicate that VSS provides significantly higher computational efficiency compared with traditional FEP techniques. Based on these data, we will further investigate four additional groups that are frequently considered in lead optimization. Through this development, substitutions at all sites by multiple functional groups can be evaluated in a single VSS calculation. Implementing the VSS method. The open-source program VMD is chosen as the platform. A major challenge in implementing VSS is the efficient calculation of non-bonded interactions. We plan to employ a fast, geometric criterion to determine whether such calculation can be replaced by a heuristic measurement for a given simulation frame — our preliminary data shows that this approach can eliminate over 80% of the computation without affecting the accuracy of the results. Applying the VSS method to optimize lead compounds for an anti-TB drug target. With over one million new cases estimated every year, TB is a serious public health problem in China. We have recently identified a series of inhibitors against an enzyme target in anti-TB drug discovery. Using VSS, we plan to examine substitutions that may enhance the activity of these inhibitors.
