446213.label: Major findings and research outcome
446213.value: We have constructed a comprehensive framework within which a general uncertainty propagation formulation with multiple inputs and multiple outputs under non-linearity and non-normality as well as full and partial information can be implemented (Xue et al., 2015) (Leung et al., 2016) (Chen et al., 2017). Objective 1 is achieved. We have built an a more general error propagation law for full and partial information via high-order Taylor series expansion method in which the first-order Taylor series expansion is admissible or the nonlinearity of the transfer function f can be accommodated. The theoretical arguments are supported by empirical results (Xue et al., 2015) (Leung et al., 2016) (Chen et al., 2017). Objectives 2 and 5 are achieved. The general framework for uncertainty propagation has been successfully applied to study the characteristics of the intersection point of two line segments propagated from the uncertainties of endpoints via high-order Taylor-series expansion (Xue et al., 2015). The uncertainty of overlaying two or more polygons, in the form of potential interaction areas, has also been studied and characterized using our novel methods (Leung et al., 2017). The framework and algorithms have also been applied to solve more complicated problems in space-time prism involving different types of uncertainties over the starting and ending time, activity time and velocity of individual movements. Experimental results support the effectiveness of our proposed general framework of uncertainty propagation (Leung et al., 2017). Objective 6 is achieved. We introduce a Monte Carlo simulation method, an extended Taylor-series expansion method and the interval-slope extension method for uncertainty analysis of interval-valued information. We then employ them to calculate the length of a line, the intersection of two lines and the area of a polygon and the associated uncertainty when information is interval in value. We show that the extended Taylor-series expansion method offers a theoretic support to the study of uncertainty propagation of interval-valued spatial data. Our analysis results show that the extended Taylor-series expansion method performs the best in applications (Jin et al., 2017). Objectives 3 and 4 are achieved.

446213.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
446213.value: Our research lays the foundation for the analysis and propagation of uncertainty in geographical information in general and GIS in particular. The framework is rigorous and powerful in handling uncertainty of spatial data of various types and with various kinds of distributions. The propagation methods are flexible enough to accommodate linear and non-linear transfer functions of complete or partial information. The approach has great potential to tackle error analysis and propagation of the ever evolving geographical information. We will attempt to extend it to uncertainty analysis and propagation of voluntary geographical information which is more complex and embedded with various kinds of uncertainty.

446213.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
446213.value: Uncertainty is ubiquitous in decision making with geographical information. It might be due to randomness in data acquisition and processing, or it might arise from vague judgments or measurements. Furthermore, the uncertainty-laden data might not be normally distributed as assumed by most error models. Complicating further the uncertainty problem is the non-linearity of the transfer function that we use to propagate uncertainty from inputs to outputs. To effectively and rigorously handle such situations, we have successfully formulated a general framework within which uncertainties of various kinds can be analyzed and propagated through operations in geographical information system (GIS) and time geography. We have also built into the framework novel and powerful methods for uncertainty propagation when the transfer function is nonlinear, and the inputs and outputs are multidimensional. A series of numerical and real-life applications have supported the efficacy and applicability of the general framework for uncertainty analysis and propagation. By providing a solid foundation, our study will advance the research frontier and applications of uncertainty analysis and propagation in general and GIS in particular.

446513.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
446513.value: The research will analyze the causes, dynamics and consequences of proactive collective violence in contemporary China. In the past thirty years, especially the last decade, protesters in China have initiated violence when contending with local authorities. Without facing suppression, demonstrators destroy police vehicles, ransack government offices and attack local officials. Proactive collective violence is effective. The central government is swift to intervene, local decisions are often withdrawn and local leaders dismissed. Proactive collective violence, however, is also costly. Ultimately, taxpayers have to pay for the destruction and key activists often end up in jails. The phenomenon of proactive collective violence presents a challenge to theories of contentious politics. Unlike what Charles Tilly and William Sewell have observed in Europe, proactive collective violence in contemporary China has targeted exclusively local governments rather than the state writ large. It is not rightful resistance in that it involves law-breaking activities, but it bears partial family resemblances with rightful resistance in that its organizers and participants insist - not without legal or constitutional grounds - that their claims are lawful. Proactive collective violence, so it seems, combines boundary-spanning and thinly-disguised proactive claims with clearly transgressive claim-making activities. It involves far more aggression than “rights defense campaigns” suggests, but it is neither typical rioting nor a precursor to revolution. Scholars have examined how government authorities handle and cover up incidents of proactive collective violence. Several important questions, however, remain to be systematically addressed. How to conceptualize proactive collective violence? Why has it occurred more frequently in the last decade than in the first twenty years of the reform? Is it only a tactical move to alarm and goad the central leadership or does it portend a growing undercurrent of anti-system sentiments? How to contain violence and promote peaceful participation? The project addresses these issues. Drawing on archival sources and in-depth interviews, it will reconstruct major incidents of proactive collective violence occurred in the reform era. It will then compare incidents occurred in the last decade with earlier ones to see how claims, dynamics of interactions and government responses have evolved. It will also explore what political reforms may help contain violence by facilitating peaceful pursuit of lawful rights and interests. The project will be carried out from 1st September 2013 to 31st August 2016. It is expected to produce several articles in peer-reviewed academic journals. 過去三十年﹐特別是近十年﹐在一些地區﹐中國民眾在針對地方政府的抗議活動中採取了諸如燒警車﹑衝擊破壞政府辦公樓甚至攻擊政府工作人員的暴力行動。本研究從抗議者的訴求特質和政治信任模式兩個方面分析抗議行動激進化的社會心理和政治心理根源。同時﹐本研究從本土政治精英與外來黨政領導的矛盾﹑新生代對地方政治權威的蔑視以及新媒體的信息溝通功能等方面分析暴力事件發生的過程和機製。此外﹐本研究探討如何通過政治參與制度的改革和法治建設避免公民與地方政府發生暴力衝突。

447513.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
447513.value: There is much evidence that East Asians are more sensitive to failure than success, whereas North Americans are more sensitive to success than failure. This difference has been described as reflecting an East Asian self-improvement orientation and a North American self-enhancement orientation. Some studies suggest that the different responses to performance are socialized in children by parents. East Asian parents respond to children’s performance by highlighting their failures and downplaying their successes. In contrast, North American downplay children’s failures and highlight their successes. Notably, parents’ responses predict children’s academic and emotional functioning, such that the East Asian pattern appears to facilitate academic but undermine emotional functioning, whereas the North American pattern may have costs to academic and benefits to emotional functioning. The proposed research aims to identify why East Asian and North American parents respond differently to children’s performance. The idea is that parents in the two regions have distinct socialization goals, which shape their responses to children’s performance. Whereas East Asian parents are concerned with children improving themselves (self-improvement goals), North American parents are concerned with promoting children’s self-esteem (self-enhancement goals). Focusing on Hong Kong and the United States, the proposed research will test three key hypotheses: (1) Chinese parents hold self-improvement goals for children more than do American parents, who hold self-enhancement goals more; (2) these two goals drive the different patterns of Chinese and American parents’ responses to children’s performance; (3) parents’ socialization goals via their responses to children’s performance facilitate children’s academic and emotional functioning. Two studies employing correlational and experimental methods will test these hypotheses in a real world context while detecting the causal role of socialization goals. In Study 1, 400 Chinese and American parents will report on their socialization goals and responses to children’s performance in the academic arena. Their elementary school children will report on both their own and their parents’ responses to their performance; parents and children will also report on children’s academic and emotional functioning at the same time and a year later. In Study 2, 320 Chinese and American mother-child dyads will visit the laboratory. Mothers’ socialization goals will be manipulated to focus on either children’s self-improvement or self-enhancement; their responses to elementary school children’s failure and success will be observed and children’s own responses will be assessed. The two studies will provide insight into culturally distinct parenting practices that contribute to the achievement and affect gaps between cultures. 大量証據顯示，東亞人對於失敗的敏銳程度比成功高，而北美洲人則剛剛相反，對成功比失敗更敏感。這差異一直被指反映出東亞人注重自我完善，而北美洲人則注重自我提升。研究顯示東亞人與北美人對失敗和成功有著不同的敏銳程度可能源於兩地家長對於孩子的表現會有不同的回應：東亞家長回應孩子表現時傾向於強調其失敗的地方，並淡化其成功之處，北美的家長則傾向於淡化孩子失敗的地方，並強調其成功之處。值得一提的是家長的回應方式或會影響孩子的學習和情緒：東亞模式雖有助孩子學習，但容易令他們感到不快樂；北美模式雖不能幫助孩子學習，卻可以令他們生活得更快樂。 本研究旨在了解東亞和北美兩地家長為何會用不同的方式來回應孩子的表現。我們相信兩地家長在教養孩子方面有不同的目標，因而令他們對孩子的表現有著不同的回應方式。東亞家長希望孩子不斷追求進步 (自我完善目標)，而北美家長則著眼於增強孩子的自信(自我提升目標)。本研究會在香港和美國兩地，嘗試驗證三項重要假設：1) 香港家長比美國家長更著重要孩子力求進步(自我完善目標)，而美國家長則比香港家長更著重提高孩子的自信(自我提升目標)。2) 這兩個目標令兩地家長回應孩子表現時會出現兩種不同的模式。3) 家長的育兒目標會透過其對孩子表現的回應影響孩子的學習和情緒。 本研究同時採用相關法和實驗法驗證上述假設，既能有效辨認因果關係，同時貼近現實處境。研究分兩部分：在第一部分，合共四百名居於香港和美國的家長會獲邀告訴我們他們的育兒目標以及平日對孩子的學術表現的回應；其就讀小學的孩子亦會描述自己以及父母對自己表現的回應。另外，在該學期以及一年後，家長和孩子均會告訴我們關於孩子在學習和情緒方面的情況。第二部分的研究會邀請三百二十個香港和美國的家庭參與實驗。我們會嘗試暫時改變母親的育兒目標，使其注重自我完善或自我提升，然後觀察這些母親對其正就讀小學的孩子的表現有什麼回應，以及孩子對自己表現的回應。我們相信這項研究將有助我們了解育兒理念在兩地孩子於學習及情感方面的差異上所扮演的角色。

447513.label: Realisation of objectives
447513.value: The project comprised a set of two complementary studies that focused on comparing Chinse and American parents and their children (for details, please refer to the Objectives). Study 1 was a one-year longitudinal survey study involving about 1000 families, whereas Study 2 was an experimental study involving about 330 families. The two studies used complementary methodological approaches, as reflected by the age ranges and geographical locations of the samples, as well as the use of survey, laboratory observations, and behavioral assessments. Overall, the three objectives described in the grant application were achieved successfully. There were two modifications in the design of Study 1. First, as described in the proposal, we were originally going to just compare Chinese families in Hong Kong to European American families in the United States. At the end, we had a Hong Kong Chinese sample, but we added a Mainland Chinese sample. A major reason is that as we conducted the first wave of data collection in Hong Kong and the United States, we realized that the two samples were quite different in terms of demographic background. Whereas our Hong Kong sample resided in a metropolitan city, our American sample resided in the suburb of a mid-size city in the United States. Indeed, in our proposal, we motivated the current research by drawing on the literature that compared how individuals in East Asian societies (including Mainland China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Japan, etc.) and North American (including the United States and Canada) societies respond to their performance, as well as the literature on East Asian and North American parents’ responses to their children’s performance. As such, the initial plan to focus on Chinese families residing in Hong Kong rather than other Chinese societies was mostly out of practical concerns. Given this research background and the fact that Hong Kong is more westernized than Mainland China, the sample of Hong Kong Chinese families may not be as representative of Chinese families in general when compared to families from the average city in Mainland China, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. As such, we added a sample from the suburb of a mid-size city in Mainland China to match the demographic background of the European American sample and allow for greater generalizability. The second modification to Study 1 was that, we originally planned to focus on the age range of fourth- and fifth-grade in both studies. We decided to focus on seventh grade in Study 1 and fourth- and fifth-grade in Study 2 to cover a wider age range and yield a more complete developmental picture. We also believe that this change would lower the attrition rate, as fifth-graders would be in sixth grade in the second wave of data collection and we have consistently found in the past that families in graduating classes tend to be reluctant to participate in research. Unlike Study 1, Study 2 was conducted as planned without modification, but there were two major challenges. We encountered much difficulty in getting families to come to our laboratories for the experiment, possibly because of overwhelming requests for research participation received by families. Another challenge concerned the coding of videotapes featuring Chinese and American parent-child interactions and children working on the task by themselves. Several teams of coders had to be trained to code different aspects of the videotaped interactions and behaviors, with each team comprising native coders from each site as well as bicultural coders. Although we had successfully used similar procedures in the past, this time, a few of the coding teams had difficulty establishing reliability, such that we had to redo the coding by recruiting and training new coders, resulting in substantial delay in our coding work and hence data analyses. In terms of the achievement of the first objective, based on survey data, although Chinese parents held self-enhancement goals to a lesser extent than did American parents as expected, surprisingly, Chinese (vs. American) parents also held self-improvement goals to a lesser extent, which might be due to a reference group effect and the social desirability of items in the self-improvement goals scale. Further analyses within each country revealed the expected pattern, with Chinese parents endorsing self-improvement goals more than self-enhancement goals and American parents showing the opposite pattern. We also successfully achieved the second objective. In the laboratory experiment in Hong Kong and the United States, we manipulated parents’ goals such that they would temporarily hold more of a self-improvement or a self-enhancement goal by random assignment, then we observed their responses to children’s performance (manipulated so that children would have a success or a failure by random assignment as outlined in the proposal) in the laboratory, such that there was a 2 (culture) x 2 (socialization goal) x 2 (performance) design. We then analyzed both parents’ responses to children’s performance as observed in the lab and as reported by parents afterwards. Regarding parents’ responses to children’s performance as observed in the laboratory, we found that across cultures, parents in the self-enhancement goals and self-improvement goals conditions differed in their responses to children’s performance in terms of the proportion of positive versus negative statements made to children, suggesting a causal relation between parents’ socialization goals and their responses to children’s performance as hypothesized. The interaction between socialization goals and type of statements, however, was only marginally significant in our analyses. This interaction, however, was significant when we analyzed parents’ reports of how they responded to children’s performance in the lab: Across countries, mothers in both goal conditions reported themselves as making more positive than negative statements to children, but the difference between positive and negative statements was larger in the self-enhancement goals condition than the self-improvement goals condition. Besides these findings from the experimental study, the survey data similarly revealed the expected longitudinal relations between parents’ socialization goals and their responses to children’s performance. The third objective was also successfully achieved. In the experimental study, so far we have only found weak effects of parents’ responses to children’s performance on children’s subsequent academic and emotional functioning in the lab, which could be because the effects of parents’ responses to children’s performance on children are more cumulative than immediate. There was evidence that across countries, the more parents responded to children’s performance by making positive statements, the greater children’s subsequent positive emotional functioning and perceptions of competence and task importance, but some of these effects were no longer significant when controlling for basement assessments of these constructs. Parents’ responses to children’s performance also failed to predict children’s subsequent performance. In our survey data, guided by the growing body of research on social cognitive development, we took a slightly different approach in our data analysis by focusing on children’s reports of their parents’ self-enhancement and self-improvement goals for them, given that such reports reflect children’s perceptions, which represent a major mechanism by which parents’ practices influence children’s development. Indeed, we found that the differences between Chinese and American parents in their responses to children’s performance contributed to the differences in their children’s views about themselves and their lives as well as emotional distress overtime through children’s perceptions of parents’ self-enhancement and self-improvement goals for them.

447513.label: Major findings and research outcome
447513.value: Although there are a number of studies on the socialization goals of parents from different cultural backgrounds, prior research has not tested the idea that Chinese and other East Asian parents may hold more self-improvement than self-enhancement goals for children, whereas American parents may hold more self-enhancement than self-improvement goals for children. This represents a knowledge gap given that research in cross-cultural psychology has consistently shown that East Asians tend to downplay their achievement, whereas Americans tend to emphasize their achievement, but it remains unclear whether and how these differences may originate from parental socialization, especially parents’ socialization goals and the way they respond to children’s performance. The current research was an initial step to fill this gap and yielded empirical evidence that Chinese parents tend to prioritize self-improvement over self-enhancement for children, whereas American parents tend to show the opposite pattern. We also replicated prior research and found that Chinese parents tend to respond less positively to children’s performance than American parents. Another major finding is that, in our cross-cultural experimental study with manipulations of parents’ socialization goals as well as children’s performance, there was evidence that parents’ goals influence the way they respond to children’s performance regardless of parents’ cultural background. Although this effect was only marginally significant using laboratory observations of parents’ responses, it was evidenced in parents’ perceptions of their responses to children’s performance, which might reflect their intended responses. We are currently conducting additional analyses and about to write up the findings. In addition, the current research also contributed to the literature by revealing that differences in Chinese and American parents’ responses to children’s performance accounted for the differences in their children’s views about themselves and their lives as well as emotional functioning both directly and indirectly through children’s perceptions of parents’ goals for them (please refer to Part C). Specifically, the findings point to American (vs. Chinse) parents’ greater use of responses that focus on what children has done well as a major reason why American (vs. Chinese) children feel that their parents value their self-enhancement, thereby contributing to American (vs. Chinese) children’s more positive views about themselves and their lives as well as reduced emotional distress. Moreover, comparisons of such pathways in the two countries revealed generally similar mechanisms, albeit with differences in specific longitudinal links. These findings add to on our understanding of universal and culture-specific processes in parental socialization.

447513.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
447513.value: Building on the findings of the current research as well as prior studies, an intervention study has been designed with the goal of promoting more effective parenting and ultimately enhancing parent-child relationship as well as children’s academic and emotional functioning. A grant proposal has been written for this intervention study and it is currently under review. The intervention will target parents in Hong Kong with children studying in the senior grades of primary school. As part of the intervention, parents will learn about different parenting approaches and their pros and cons. For example, they will learn about different ways of responding to children’s performance. They will also be trained to be more sensitive to the messages that they conveyed to children through their responses to children’s performance. By providing parents with evidence-based advice on parenting in a variety of formats such as written materials and coaching, it is expected that the intervention may help parents expand their knowledge as well as repertoire of parenting skills, enabling parents to engage in more effective parenting and thereby promoting children’s development.

447513.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
447513.value: Prior research has shown that individuals from East Asia tend to respond more strongly to their failures than successes, whereas individuals from North America tend to respond more strongly to their successes than failures. Focusing on how these differences develop, this research examined whether East Asian and North American parents may have different concerns for children, such that they respond to children’s performance differently, thereby contributing to children’s academic and emotional functioning. We conducted a longitudinal survey study and a laboratory experiment, involving about 1300 families of youth in China and the United States. We found that Chinese and American parents were concerned about their children’s orientation to improving themselves and developing positive self-regard, respectively; such concerns appeared to underlie why Chinese and American parents tended to focus on children’s failure and success, respectively. These differences in parents’ concerns and responses to children’s performance contributed to Chinese (vs. American) children’s less positive views about themselves and their lives and greater emotional distress. These findings highlight the importance for professionals working with families to understand parents’ goals for children and responses to children’s performance, pointing to these aspects of parenting as directions for interventions aimed at promoting optimal development in children.

447613.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
447613.value: This project will study the relationship between public space and social capital in the context of urban governance. With a focus on Sham Shui Po, a District Council District in Hong Kong, the project will study whether the availability of public space and facilities such as markets, parks, sidewalks, libraries, and recreation centers within walking distance affects the level of social capital, which is understood as encompassing social networks, trust, and reciprocity at the community level. It will also examine the ways in which people use public space, and whether the use of public space affects the development and maintenance of social ties, trust, and mutual support between and among the members of a community. The project will also examine the factors that mediate the impact of public space on social capital in various forms and at various levels, including the type of public space (e.g. markets, parks, recreation centers, shopping malls and sidewalks), the nature of public space (e.g. physical openness, a long association with local history, the physical and economic layout, and flexibility of use), any stigma associated with specific places, the organization of activities in public space by civic associations and government agencies, the motives and behavior of individuals using public space, the working hours of individuals and the time they spend commuting, and the socio-cultural and historical specificity of communities. After assessing the causal linkage between this list of variables and the level of social capital, it should be possible to ascertain whether the availability and accessibility of public space is sufficient to explain and predict the development and maintenance of social capital, or whether external interventions in the form of government-organized and NGOs-initiated activities are required to exploit the social functions of public space to the maximum. The results of the project should shed light on the social functions of public space in urban life and should increase our understanding of the relationship between public space and social capital. The findings should help policy-makers to make well-informed decisions on urban planning and development. In particular, they should enable policy-makers to make the most of public space to enhance social capital and life satisfaction at the community level. 本計劃探討在城市管理中公共空間與社會資本的關係。以香港的深水埗區為個案研究，本計劃將研究公共空間和公共設施 (如市集、公園、行人道、圖書館、綜合活動中心) 的建立，是否會影響社會網絡、社會信任和互相關顧等社會資本的產生。本計劃亦會研究 市民使用公共空間的情況及其使用會否影響社區關係、互信及互助等社會資本的建立和維持。在這些命題的基礎上，我們將會着力探討各種可能影響公共空間產生不同形式和水平的社會資本的背後因素，當中我們會考慮的因素包括：(1)公共空間的類型 - 例如市集 、公園、康體中心、商場和行人路；(2)公共空間的性質 — 如其開放程度、與該社區的歷史聯系、環境及經濟層面的規劃、使用的彈性；(3)該公共空間是否帶有任何負面標籤；(4)社區團體或政府機構會否利用該公共空間組織和進行社區活動；(5)市民使用公共空間的動機和行為；使用者日常用於工作和交通的時間；社區的文化和歷史特徵。經過評估以上各種因素和社會資本水平之間的因果關係後，本研究將能夠確立公共空間的設立和使用本身是否足以影響社會資本的產生及維持；或是公共空間的社會功能，只有在政府和民間團體所舉辦的社區活動等外力的協助情況下，才能達到明顯效果。當研究完成後，結果將能反映公共空間在城市生活中的社會功能和價值，亦能增加大眾對公共空間和社會資本的理解。這些發現盼能有助決策者在進行城市規劃和發展時，能夠充分利用社區的公共空間來加強該區的社會資本和提升市民的生活素質。

447613.label: Realisation of objectives
447613.value: The central research question in the project is: “Does the availability of public space and facilities promote the development of social capital?” It aims at studying the relationship between public space and social capital in the context of urban governance, with a focus on Sham Shui Po. The project has a total of five objectives and all of them are achieved with the major tasks and analysis of the project. In terms of division of labor and organization, this section would describe the major research tasks to explain the steps taken in achieving all these research objectives while the following section would concentrate on presenting the research findings and how they meet the research objectives. In summarizing all five objectives, they examine the ways in which people use public space, and whether the use of public space affects the development and maintenance of social ties, trust, and mutual support between and among the members of a community. The project also examines the factors that mediate the impact of public space on social capital in various forms and at various levels, including the type of public space (e.g. markets, parks, recreation centers, shopping malls and sidewalks), the nature of public space (e.g. physical openness, a long association with local history, the physical and economic layout, and flexibility of use), any stigma associated with specific places, the organization of activities in public space by civic associations and government agencies, the motives and behavior of individuals using public space, the working hours of individuals and the time they spend commuting, and the socio-cultural and historical specificity of communities. Besides, it investigates whether external interventions in the form of government-organized and NGOs-initiated activities are required to exploit the social functions of public space to the maximum. As a first step, a list of variables and different levels of social capital were determined during fist stage literature review and used to structure focus group discussion and interviews questions, with the aim of finding the causal linkage between public space and social capital stated in the central research question, major area asked includes: • Does use of public space affects the development and maintenance of social ties, trust and mutual support between and among the members of a community? • Does accessibility of the space and its flexibility of use affect popularity of usage? • Does external interventions (e.g. organization of activities), socio-cultural and historical specificity of communities’ matters in usage of public space and the corresponding building of social capital? Based on the literature review, interviews with 25 community leaders/ district officials and a total of 16 focus group discussions with local residents were carried out. Below summarized scope of investigations with regard to objectives: Interview with Community Leaders/ NGOs/ District officials: • The nature ( accessibility and flexibility) of targeted types of public space • The effect of external interventions ( e.g. activities organized ) on facilitating the use of public space • The frequency of usage of public space and the social-mix ( gender, ethnicity, social class) of users Focus Groups Discussions with Residents of Different Socio-Demographic Mix: • Assessing the variables (e.g. the type, the nature and external intervention) illustrated by affecting the use of public space • Examining the factors (e.g. the type, the nature and external intervention) influencing the development and maintenance of social capital in its various forms and at various levels • Explaining the general usage and the motivation of individuals in accessing a particular public space. • Identifying the ways in which residents use the corresponding public space and whether there is a consistent mix of visitors from different socio-demographic backgrounds Data was collected on four major themes including: flexibility of public space (i.e. management and rigidity of regulations), accessibility of public space, external interventions (i.e. NGOs and government influence) and social-mix of public space users. Attention is also given to questions which include how social mix is found in some public space but rarely in others. Telephone Survey A telephone survey of about 1,000 citizens, aged 18 or above, of random sampling in Hong Kong has been conducted. In the survey, we study (1) the respondents’ social demographics (e.g., age, gender, race/ethnicity, language, birth origin, length of residence, household income, and education); (2) work pattern (e.g., working hours, days of work, and time spent commuting); (3) availability of public space; (4) use of public space; and (5) stock of social capital. In the telephone survey, it will draw on the index of trust, norms and reciprocity (TNR) devised by Curley (2010, pp. 55-56) to measure the stock of social capital. The index of TNR is based on the mean score for 11 items (Cronbach’s α = 0.78). The respondents are asked whether (1) they want the same thing as their neighbors; (2) they care what their neighbors think of their actions; (3) most of their neighbors are respectful of each other; (4) people in the neighborhood can be trusted; (5) people in the neighborhood share the same values; (6) people in the neighborhood generally get along with each other; (7) they can influence what the neighborhood is like; (8) if a problem arises in the neighborhood, then local people can solve it; (9) people are willing to help their neighbors; (10) they recognize most people in the neighborhood; and (11) many of their neighbors know them. The respondents will be required to give a true or false response to each item, which will be coded on a 5-point scale (with reverse coding if necessary). Index scores range from a low of 1 (a very low level of social capital) to a high of 5 (a very high level of social capital). Having collected these data, statistical methods are used to assess the relationship between the availability and use of public space, and the level of social capital, with intervening variables such as social demographics and work patterns controlled. In completing the project, some problems are encountered but fortunately they are all overcome in the process. One major problem is the unexpected departure of the original PI, Professor Ng Kai-hon, to a non-UGC funded institution in August 2014. Due to the leave of former PI, a few changes from the original plan have been to make sure all original objectives can be achieved. An application for 6 months project extension and transfer of PI were made. A shift in activity order is also made. As stated in the research proposal, this preliminary study on relationship between public space and social capital consist of two main parts 1) telephone survey 2) focus group/ interviews, to be completed in sequence. They are done in reversed order under the decision of former PI Prof. Ng Kai-hon as focus groups/ interviews with officials requires more original/ in-depth knowledge, both of which he is most suitable for. A third problem is related to the implementation of the telephone survey. Originally, the telephone survey is confined to Sham Shui Po. Due to technical difficulties and cost consideration, it is expanded to the entire Hong Kong, which has actually enhanced the representation of the findings of the study. With these changes and adjustments, all objectives are achieved as planned.

447613.label: Major findings and research outcome
447613.value: The major research tasks in the project include interviews, focus groups and surveys. In interviews and focus groups, it uses Sham Shui Po as the major focus. For telephone survey, due to technical difficulties and other concerns, it is expanded to the entire Hong Kong. With this expansion, it actually has enhanced the scope, credibility, and generalizatbility of our findings. As some of the findings have been mentioned in the section above, it would mainly summarize the aggregate research outcomes here. In interviews and focus groups with local residents, NGOs, and local leaders, many of the hypotheses are supported. They include the importance of the availability of public space and facilities such as markets, parks, sidewalks, libraries, and recreation centers within walking distance to the level of social capital. Furthermore, the ways in which people use public space, and the purpose assigned to it also matter. In the process, the NGOs and social leaders also play a key role as they have influence on the design and the regulation of public space in the community. External interventions in the form of government-organized and NGOs-initiated activities are required to exploit the social functions of public space to the maximum. Overall, the close relationship between public space and social capital has been confirmed. In the telephone survey, it draws on the index of trust, norms and reciprocity (TNR) devised by Curley to measure the stock of social capital. Major items are all measured on a scale of 1-5. The score for availability of public space index, consists of eight different types / purposes of public space, is 3.08. The level of availability of public space is the weakest in areas of three major purposes (public libraries and cultural facilities; place to meet different people and friends; place for friends’ communication and gathering). These results clearly show that the availability of public space for consumption is totally different from the availability of public space for intellectual activities and community building, including meeting friends and different people, which are important for establishing contact, trust and mutual support, and eventually the formation of social capital. A contrasting mindset is also found in which citizens are committed to their community but are feeling incapable of making an impact in it. Finally, an empirical correlation is found between TNR and the public space index, which is consistent with the qualitative findings from interviews and focus groups.

447613.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
447613.value: The theoretical development and empirical findings in this project should have both academic and policy implications for future action. It has provided support for a relationship between public space and social capital. In research, the next step is to shift more attention in future research of good governance to the non-institution-based and society-centered inputs such as public space which may not produce good governance directly but are still contributing to good governance by generating the facilitating process which enables the formation of social capital. In terms of policy, the proposed future action is to educate policymakers on urban planning and governance with the project findings. One tough dilemma is the trade-off between private space and public space. Hong Kong serves as a good case demonstrating the dilemma faced by many global cities worldwide - the shrinking of public space with the triumph of market economy, symbolizing a standoff between civil society and capitalism. While private space, being available for sale, generates more economic return to powerful business interests, social benefit generated by social capital via public space must never be ignored. Although more information does not necessarily bring an easier choice here, it would make it a more informed one.

447613.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
447613.value: This project studies the relationship between public space and social capital in the context of urban governance, with a focus on Sham Shui Po, a District Council District in Hong Kong. It finds the availability of public space and facilities such as markets, parks, sidewalks, libraries, and recreation centers within walking distance does enhance the level of social capital, which is understood as encompassing social networks, trust, and reciprocity at the community level. Factors that mediate the impact of public space on social capital include the type and nature of public space, the physical and economic layout, and flexibility of use, any stigma associated with specific places, the organization of activities in public space by civic associations and government agencies, the motives and behavior of individuals using public space, and the socio-cultural and historical specificity of communities. Support for these findings is also generated from a territory wide telephone survey. The study sheds light on the social functions and importance of public space in urban life and the close relationship between public space and social capital. It informs policy-makers that the design, access and availability of public space is important for enhancing urban governance at both community and city levels.

447713.label: Project Title(Chinese)
447713.value: 香港城市規劃制度的盲點：社區能力、社會資本、公民價值觀及社會影響評估

447713.label: Project Objectives
447713.value: The aim of this study is to demonstrate that the urban planning system and the development process in Hong Kong have been blinded to the existence of community capacities and values. Through a number of strategic case studies, the aim is to investigate the social impact development projects have made, or will make, on the capacities, social capital and values held by local communities. The research findings will be analysed to examine how community-based planning can be introduced into the current urban planning system in Hong Kong. Specific objectives are: “Making the invisible community capacities, social capital and citizen values visible”: through in-depth case studies in the urban and rural contexts of Hong Kong, identify systematically the “hidden capacities, social capital and values”: • To examine factors contributing to or hindering the sense of community of local residents. • To undertake a “capacity mapping” of the community through community profiling, identifying their assets and social capital, as well as needs and issues. • To undertake “citizen values assessment” to ascertain the key community concerns and values. “Explicating social impacts”: to undertake ex-ante or ex-post social impact assessments of the (proposed) development initiatives on the identified community capacities and values. To carry out a systematic audit of local “planning” and administration and to examine how community capacities, social capital and values, as well as concerns can be nurtured and acknowledged either by the existing administration or by the setting up of innovative institutions within or beyond the government. To interrogate the research findings and address the following under-researched aspects related to people’s right to city planning: • The social costs of an urban planning system without a community-based component. • The difficulties and importance of community-based planning in a non- democratic polity that is seen to privilege certain interests. • Techniques and challenges in identifying local capacities, social capital and values in a dense and highly urbanized context. • Technical and methodological issues on conducting social impact assessment in a place with high development pressure.

447713.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
447713.value: This study will argue that the “bulldozing” approach adopted by most development projects in Hong Kong has been sustained by an ignorance of their impacts on local communities. Through detailed mapping of community capacities, social capital and values, and identification of social impacts of development projects in four communities, the research is intended to demonstrate the importance of institutionalising community-based planning to guarantee people’s right to the planning of their local communities. Urban planning in Hong Kong is basically a top-down process. Although in recent years, the government has tried to engage communities in the planning process, the top-down nature of the system remains intact. Development projects in the city are often implemented through razing established communities to make way for “growth”. Affected community members, when eligible, will receive cash compensation but the community networks, social capital, economic ties and trust that take many years to accumulate, will “dissipate” as “development” proceeds. To make visible these “invisible” capacities, social capital and values, four in-depth community studies in rural and urban Hong Kong will be carried out: two that have been impacted by development initiatives and two that are facing imminent changes. Through summoning a number of proven research tools on community development, the research will identify systematically individual and collective capacities and social capital within the community; carry out a “citizen value assessment” exercise to identify key concerns and values held by these communities; and based on these, undertake a social impact assessment exercise to evaluate the social impact of the imposed development projects on the studied communities against the identified capacities and values. The research team will carefully examine whether or not the existing planning and governance mechanisms could be transformed to address this social impact and how community-based planning can be instituted within or beyond the government to building, rather than destroying, local capacities. The research will be a unique Asian contribution to the field of community development and social impact assessment that has been dominated hitherto by Western literature. It will provide evidence on the state of social capital in densely populated Hong Kong. The research findings will challenge the local development approach that is blind to the existence of valuable community assets and provide convincing evidence for the urgent institutionalisation of community-based planning. It will also contribute to the further theorisation of alternative development that advocates for the rights of local communities in shaping urban spaces. 可以說，香港「推土機」式的發展得已持續的其中一個原因是社會未能掌握這種開發模式對社區所造成的影響。這項目希望通過對四個社區的能力、社會資本、公民價值觀及發展項目的社會影響的詳細研究與評估，展示以社區為本的規劃的重要性，從而倡議市民參與規劃設計地區的權力。 香港的城市規劃基本上是一個由上而下的制度。雖然近年政府一直試圖讓市民參與規劃，但是規劃制度由上而下的本質並沒有改變。在城市開發的過程中，傾向把社區夷為平地，以現金補償那些受影響和合資格的居民。可是，那累積多年「無形」的社區網路，社會資本，經濟關係和信任等，往往在「開發」的過程中「悄然消逝」。 爲了使人們看到這些「無形」的社區能力，社會資本和公民價值觀，本研究將開展兩個位於市區和兩個位於新界等四個案例；而市區和新界均各有一個已受發展項目影響的個案和一個即將面臨發展影響的個案。通過採納各種行之有效的研究工具，本項目將搜集資料以鑑定社區内個人和集體的能力和社會資本，開展「公民價值觀評估」工作，以確定這些社區重點關注的議題，並根據這些議題，來進行社會影響評估，以評審或估計發展項目如何衝擊社區的能力和社會資產。研究小組亦會仔細研究現有的規劃和治理機制，查看是否可以轉化及解決發展項目對社會的影響，甚至把社區為本的規劃制度化，好使地區的能力和資本得以建立而不是被拆毁。 由於社區規劃和社會影響評估的文獻大都出自西方學者的手筆，這項研究將提供一個獨特的亞洲視野。它將為人口稠密的香港把脈，彙報其社會資本的狀態。研究結果亦會提供有說服力的證據，挑戰香港一直以來對寶貴的社會資產的存在視而不見的發展陋習，以證明社區規劃制度化的迫切性。研究也將有助倡議地區人士有權規劃設計城市空間等另類發展模式的理論建構。

447713.label: Realisation of objectives
447713.value: The project has four objectives and the following paragraphs summarise how and the extent these objectives have been achieved. Objective 1: “Making the invisible community capacities, social capital and citizen values visible”: through indepth case studies in the urban and rural contexts of Hong Kong, identify systematically the “hidden capacities, social capital and values”: The project has carried out research works on the Blue House in Wanchai and the Choi Yuan Village in the New Territories. To a less extent, the project has also studied Kwun Tong and the Northeast New Territories. Through archival research, questionnaire surveys and intensive interviews with different stakeholders, factors contributing to or hindering the sense of community of local residents have been identified. For urban communities, the length of residents and the existence of place-based charity organisations as well as “system-transforming” intellectuals (enlightened elites) who extend their help to the affected communities seem to be essential for explicating community capacities and their social capital and values. However, in the case of Kwun Tong when redevelopment was announced in 1998 but was not implemented until 2010, the sense of continuous uncertainties made it almost impossible to sustain a cohesive community. The situation in the new territories is even more complicated. While the government has a policy to maintain the integrity of indigenous villages in the planning process, it does not recognise the rights of non-indigenous villagers in rebuilding their lived space when affected by urban expansion. Hence, non-indigenous villages are usually bull-dozed to make way for “development”. The irony from our site investigation is that few indigenous villagers actually live in the “indigenous villages” while non-indigenous villagers usually live and practise farming in their place for generations. Our questionnaire survey and interviews prove that community members have great capacities and knowledge that, however, have not been accounted for or visible in the planning process. It is because urban planning in Hong Kong does not start with understanding the capabilities and needs of existing communities. These untapped resources have been instrumental to the “success” of saving the Blue House for continuing its time-honoured function to serve the community as well as the eventful reconstruction of the New Choi Yuan Village in face of displacement. To a large extent, the existence of enlightened elites helped boost the bonding, bridging and linking social capital of the two communities to address their key concern—the right to live and use the place to build a community. However, for those affected by the Kwun Tong Town Centre Redevelopment and the indigenous villages in the Northeast New Territories, they seem to concern more about monetary compensation that they can receive—the exchange value of a place. Objective 2: “Explicating social impacts”: to undertake ex-ante or ex-post social impact assessments of the (proposed) development initiatives on the identified community capacities and values. The results are very obvious. For the Blue House and the New Choi Yuan Village, the fight to retain a right to use their lived spaces and the challenges involved have continuously boosted their capabilities and reconfirm the importance of exerting their right to use a place for their community building and human flourishing. However, for Kwun Tong, the community has disintegrated in face of redevelopment uncertainties. In the New Development Areas in the Northeast New Territories, it is very difficult to identify the indigenous villagers as many who are living within the indigenous villages are from other urban areas. On the contrary, the non-indigenous population who have fought for their rights to continue farming have received little empathy as the institutional and legal set up in the city does not recognise their assets and their right to a different style of living. Objective 3: To carry out a systematic audit of local “planning” and administration and to examine how community capacities, social capital and values, as well as concerns can be nurtured and acknowledged either by the existing administration or by the setting up of innovative institutions within or beyond the government. Through the in-depth case studies, the PI has tried to advocate three ways to nurture and boost community capacities, social capital and use value of a place: • The government of Hong Kong should develop community planning, either within the Planning Department or through the appointment of community planners in each District Council or local charity or social work organisations. • There should be local market places in each district of Hong Kong. Local economic development is the most effective means to nourish entrepreneurship, mutual support, social capital and community building. • In any planning exercise, the starting point should be a thorough understanding of the existing communities, their capacities, social capital and assets. Unless these are probably considered, acknowledged and further enhanced in the new plan, nothing should be done to destroy an existing community with strong social networks. Objective 4: To interrogate the research findings and address the people’s right to city planning in a non-democratic polity without community planning, nor proper means of identifying and assessing local capacities, social capital, values and social impacts. To guarantee people’s right to the city and to urban planning, it is very important for Hong Kong to reconsider its planning system, especially the Hong Kong Planning Standards and Guidelines and the various administrative policies that determine who gets what, where, when and how. Not only should the relevant ordinances and regulations be carefully reviewed to ensure people having equitable rights to the city, it is also important to design a procedure for different stakeholders to come together and deliberate on people’s rights/duties, privilege/no right, power/liabilities and immunities/disability. These continue to be heavily under-researched areas in Hong Kong.

447713.label: Major findings and research outcome
447713.value: The project helps identify macro-socio-economic and structural factors including a top-down urban planning system for the absence of community-based planning in Hong Kong (papers 1, 3-4, 7-10). The detailed case studies confirm the theoretical relationships between the right to place-making and individual as well as community well-being (papers 2 and 7). The project points to the need of local public spaces for community members to interact, utilize their capacity and assets to foster positive human relationships and actualise themselves through working together (papers 2-4, 7). However, with a growth at all cost development ideology, planning exercises seldom afford to have a thorough understanding of how communities use local spaces for their life and livelihood (papers 3-10). The case studies of the Blue House and Choi Yuan Village reveal the important roles of “enlightened elites” or “system-transforming” intellectuals in articulating the assets and accumulated social capital in the local communities (papers 5-10). They are also instrumental in exposing the social impacts of a “community-blind” development process, empowering local communities to mobilise and fight for the use values of their lived environment (papers 5, 6, 8-10). They help organise the affected communities through intensive knowledge exchange (translation) processes among different stakeholders. Communities aided by “enlightened elites” are much more resilient than those communities that face redevelopment uncertainties for a long time or with internal conflicts and little outside assistance (papers 5, 6, 9, 10). It is only through the detailed investigation of people’s lived experiences in space over time can we generate a plan that nurtures a sustainable community where people’s capacities and assets can be respected and utilized. The research findings show that instead of imposing territory-wide needs onto local communities, planning should start with acknowledging people’s time-honoured place-making efforts and results. Otherwise planning would bring a lot of harm and suffering to closely knit communities (papers 5-10). The research project also highlights a blind spot in Hong Kong: the importance of local economic development. Community planning is not just for providing housing and related community infrastructure. More importantly, it is about developing local economic activities that can utilise local talents and nurture social networks. It is about re-embedding economic transactions in social relations (papers 8 and 10). This is probably the best way to guarantee people’s right to use the city (papers 2 and 7).

447713.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
447713.value: While these case studies are extremely important to guide transformative planning practices in the local context, it is equally important to set the discussions in theoretical frameworks that connect to contemporary academic discourses in other contexts. To integrate community planning with “re-commoning” practices that focus on the development of local or moral economy, stressing the need for economic transactions to serve people’s well-being and a sustainable environment could be one research direction that can be further explored. The “community-blind” planning culture in Hong Kong has led to many social and spatial justice issues especially in the New Territories where two “classes” of citizens exist—the indigenous and non-indigenous villagers. The situation should be further investigated regarding the protection of the indigenous villages which actually are housing a very small indigenous population—most of the residents are from outside the villages. Further research in these areas will not only enrich our theoretical understanding of socio-spatial justice, the research findings will also provide be very important pointers for transforming the institutional, legal and administrative set up of planning and development-related regimes in Hong Kong.

447713.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
447713.value: With the absence of community planning in Hong Kong, the “growth-at-all-cost” development ideology has blinded us to recognise the capacities and assets accumulated in the city’s many neighbourhoods. However, “enlightened elites” have aided residents in the Blue House and the new Choi Yuan Village to mobilise their social capital to emphasise the use values of their lived experiences and fight for their right to plan and develop their community. A thorough understanding of people’s relationships to one another and to their surrounding environment, therefore, should be seen as the very first step of an urban planning process. Indeed, community planning should be in place to help develop community members’ capabilities, fostering their social networks and social capital as well as utilising their talents and creativity to meet one another’s socio-economic needs. Depriving people’s right to use local space will adversely affect their well-being. The research findings also underscore the importance of community spaces such as local markets in nourishing bonding, bridging and even linking social capital for community building. These findings demand a review of the Hong Kong Planning Standards and Guidelines, the statutory planning process and urban management policies and protocols adopted in the city.

448313.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
448313.value: The implementation of the Model Play (yangbanxi) project accompanied the commencement of the Cultural Revolution, and the Jiang Qing regime worked to ensure that they were to become models of the new revolutionary culture. But very few works could pass the harsh censorship apparatus, making the list of the officially-approved stories, at least in the first few years, extremely short. The scarcity and rigidity of these Model Plays encountered the obvious problem of communicating to the vast Chinese population with such cultural and linguistic diversity. It was clear that these approved works, primarily Peking Operas and a few ballets and musical pieces, had to be re-enacted in other cultural forms and media for further dissemination. Although the Model Plays were meant to serve primarily the ambitions of certain political leaders, the wide adaptation of these works was much more difficult to control. This research aims to study precisely this dynamic of hegemony, in which top down coercion cannot work without some bottom up supports. These adapted works were situated in an ambiguous position between the two extreme ends of, on the one hand, officially-endorsed propaganda arts and, on the other hand, the many underground and unofficial cultural activities also took place then. While both the Model Plays and the underground works have been widely studied, these adaptations have not been examined carefully. This research will fill in this gap and help construct a more comprehensive picture of Cultural Revolution’s cultural scene. In addition to its significance to our understanding of this history, this research also aspires to construct a more complex model to analyze the relationship between politics and aesthetics as manifested in these works. This research, more specifically, aims to read these adaptation works as arts, and explore if they were able to challenge the status quo, break down boundaries, and introduce new ways of thinking. The research, therefore, foregrounds how the repressed aesthetic power of the Model Plays might be unleashed during the adaptation process. By comparing how the same work is represented in different forms, this research could reveal the aesthetic dimensions of these works. Although the cultural scene during the Cultural Revolution was so politicized, this was also a time when radical democracy existed side by side with extreme party control on people’s everyday life – identifying the pluralization effects of these adaptations might help us take an alternative stance for re-examining the Cultural Revolution’s national politics. 「樣板戲」計劃乃伴隨著文化大革命的開始而實施，它是江青用以確立新的革命文化樣板的政治手段。然而很少作品可以通過苛刻的審查機制，這導致了至少在最初幾年裡，獲得官方認定的樣板戲名單相當匱乏。樣板戲的匱乏性及刻板性，致使其在文化和語言均多樣的龐大的中國人口傳達上出現了顯而易見的困難。很明顯地，主要是京劇、芭蕾舞劇和交響音樂的官方認可作品都不得不以其他文化形式和媒介重演，以作進一步的傳播。雖然樣板戲意味著主要為某些政治領導人的野心而服務，但由於這些作品被廣泛改編，使它們更加難以被控制。本研究的目的，正正是分析這種自上而下的動態霸權運作絕不能缺少自下而上支持。這些改編的作品位處於兩個極端之間的曖昧位置上，其一方是官方認可的宣傳藝術，另一方是許多隨之而洐生的地下和非官方文化活動。雖然樣板戲和地下作品都已被廣泛研究，但這些改編作品還沒有被仔細分析。這項研究將填補這一空白，並有助於建立一個對文化大革命場景更全面的了解。 本研究除具有認識這段歷史的意義外，亦希望透過建構一個更複雜的模型，以分析這些作品表現出來的政治與美學之間的關係。更具體地說，本研究的目標是把這些改編作品看作藝術，探討它們是否能夠挑戰現狀、打破規限和引進新的思維方式。因此，這項研究將關注樣板戲所壓抑的美學如何在改編的過程中被釋放。通過比較同一作品的不同形式的再現，本研究將可揭示這些作品的審美維度。雖然文革期間的文化場景相當政治化，但在極端政黨控制著人們日常生活的同時，亦並存著激進的民主精神，確立這些改編作品的多元化影響，或將有助我們採取另一種立場來重新審視文革的國家政治。

448313.label: Realisation of objectives
448313.value: This research examines a wide variety of cultural forms produced during the Cultural Revolution, and it also locates a rich set of materials demonstrating how people engaged and created propaganda culture at that time. This research shows that the Cultural Revolution propaganda culture was given the mutually contradictory tasks of agitating revolution and providing order. On the one hand, the new revolutionary subject was conceptualized as an active component in a collective movement, and each subject was viewed as liberated and enlightened. On the other hand, the entire revolutionary community was extremely conformist, and there was no room for anyone to deviate from the model. The project examines how such chaos and order could manifest at the same time. The PI characterizes the dominant logic of subject formation during that time by the notion of “singularity,” taking advantage of the two opposite meanings that could be derived from that term. On the collective level, the entire body of the Chinese people could be seen as a singularity, the component parts of which followed each other and contrasted themselves from the rest of the world as a people; individually, however, many Chinese people at the time truly believed that they were independent and enlightened subjects. The conflicts between these two levels of the subject define the tragic dimensions of the event. Although “self-reliance” was a widely promoted dominant value, the notion of the self was highly problematic, as the self was asserted only to be suppressed, and there was a strong sense of insecurity prevalent throughout society.

448413.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
448413.value: In speech signals, talker-specific characteristics such as the size and configuration of one’s vocal apparatus, emotional mood and speaking rate modulate the acoustic realization of an identical linguistic content. Such talker variation in speech signals poses a challenge for rapid and accurate speech perception. Nevertheless, listeners show extraordinary success in recovering the intended linguistic message. How listeners manage to map variable acoustical signals onto invariant linguistic categories is a fundamental question in speech perception. The process of recognizing intended words despite the acoustic variation induced by talker variability is called talker normalization. Context plays an important role in such a process. Listeners tune to a particular talker’s phonetic space based on contextual phonetic cues, which can provide important frames of reference for normalizing talker variation in spoken word recognition. Specifically, listeners may achieve phonetic constancy in lexical tone perception by estimating the relative pitch location within a particular talker’s pitch range estimated from the context. Moreover, previous studies demonstrated that different types of context (speech vs. nonspeech) with identical pitch information contributed unequally to talker normalization. In particular, nonspeech context hardly facilitated talker normalization, though it contained the same pitch information as the speech context did. So far, it is still unclear what the necessary requirements are for an effective context effect in talker normalization, and what the neural bases of talker normalization are. In this project, behavioral and electroencephalographic (EEG) experiments will be conducted to systematically examine the psychological and neural bases of context-dependent talker normalization in lexical tone perception. We aim to identify the necessary requirements for the context effect by examining the effect of speech intelligibility and congruency in talker identity on talker normalization. Moreover, we will investigate the psychological bases of talker normalization in tone perception by examining its relation to non-linguistic tasks such as pitch location judgment. We will use EEG experiments to investigate the neural mechanisms of context-dependent talker normalization. In particular we will examine whether context-dependent talker normalization is an actively controlled process that requires attention and voluntary control, or an automatic process. Findings of this project will shed important light on the mechanisms and bases of phonetic constancy in speech perception. Moreover, this project will lead to a richer understanding of perceptual constancy in general. 說話人的特征對產生的語音信號有很大的影響。由於說話人在情緒，語速，發聲器官的大小、形狀等方面的差異，同樣的話由不同的人說、在不同的情境下說，會呈現為不同的聲學信號。這種由說話人不同而造成的聲學信號上的不確定性為快速、准確的語音感知提出了挑戰。然而，聽眾卻能夠非常順利地獲取說話人想傳達的語音信息。這個過程是如何實現的，即，聽眾如何將具有紛繁變化的聲學信號映射到某些特定的音類上，這是言語知覺研究中的一個基本問題。 從帶有說話人特征的聲學信號中識別出說話人想傳達的詞，這樣的過程就是“說話人歸一化”。上下文在這個過程中起著重要作用。正是依據上下文的語音線索，聽眾得以確定說話人所特有的語音空間，並且建立相對音高的參照系—這一步對實現口語中的說話人歸一化至關重要。換言之，聽眾可以從上下文估計出說話人的音高范圍，進而得到相對音高的位置，從而在聲調感知中達到知覺恆常的狀態。前人的研究表明，上下文的類型（語音或非語音）是影響說話人歸一化的一個因素。非語音的上下文即便與語音類型的上下文具有同樣的音高信息，對聽眾實現說話人歸一化也幾乎不會有任何促進作用。目前，上下文具有哪些必要條件才能有效地促進說話人歸一化，以及“說話人歸一化”的神經機制是怎樣的，都有待研究。 我們的研究項目將通過行為和腦電實驗來系統檢測不同上下文環境中，聲調感知的“說話人歸一化”的心理和神經機制。我們的目標是通過研究語音清晰度和前后說話人身份一致與否對說話人歸一化的影響，從而確定上下文能夠促進說話人歸一化所需的必要條件。此外，我們將通過研究諸如音高位置判斷等非語言的任務與聲調感知中說話人歸一化的關聯，來探討說話人歸一化的心理基礎。我們將使用腦電實驗來研究依賴於上下文的說話人歸一化的神經機制。具體來說，我們將檢驗依賴於上下文的說話人歸一化是一個需要注意力且要求主動控制的自主控制的過程，還是一個自動實現的過程。 我們研究項目的成果將為揭示語言感知中的語音恆常性的機制提供重要信息，也將加深我們對一般知覺恆常性的理解。

448413.label: Realisation of objectives
448413.value: Talker variability in speech signals poses a challenge for rapid and accurate speech perception. Nevertheless, listeners show extraordinary success in recovering the intended linguistic message. This phenomenon is known as talker normalization. How listeners manage to map variable acoustical signals onto invariant linguistic categories is a fundamental question in speech perception. This project aims to achieve a fuller picture of tone perception. Phonetic cues in the context play an important role in talker normalization. According to the context tuning mechanism, listeners tune to a particular talker’s phonetic space based on contextual phonetic cues, which can provide important frames of reference for normalizing talker variation in spoken word recognition. Specifically, listeners may achieve phonetic constancy in lexical tone perception by estimating the relative pitch location within a particular talker’s pitch range estimated from the context. In this project, behavioral and event-related potential (ERP) experiments have been conducted to systematically examine the psychological and neural bases of context-dependent talker normalization in lexical tone perception. As for behavioral experiments, subjects were instructed to identify the target words given different types of context precursors. For instance, the recorded sound of syllable /i33/ (意, meaning) is likely to be perceived as /i55/ (醫, doctor), a word with high level tone, when it is preceded by a context whose over pitch level has been shifted down to an extent, and likely to be perceived as /i22/ (二, two), a word with low level tone, when it is preceded by a context whose over pitch level has been shifted up to an extent. The manipulation of the experimental conditions was mainly on the context part. Such a linguistic task (i.e., word identification with context) was adopted for Experiments 1, 2 & 3. As for the nonlinguistic task (Experiment 4), the subjects were asked to rank the pitch level of the target with reference to the pitch range of the context. As for the ERP experiments (Experiments 5 & 6), electroencephalographic (EEG) signals were recorded when the subjects were instructed to conduct the task. Then ERPs were obtained by averaging the EEG epochs which were time-locked to the onset of the target words. By comparing the ERPs across different context conditions, the detailed time course of neural processes in tone normalization has been discovered.

448413.label: Major findings and research outcome
448413.value: 1. Our findings indicate that the context effect is a product of multiple levels of processing, with the primary contribution from phonological cues (meaningless speech context). The contribution of auditory cues is negligible, and that of phonetic cues and semantic+syntactic cues is both moderate. Phonological cues likely enable listeners to calibrate the acoustic-to-phonological mapping of speech sounds for each talker, facilitating the categorization. 2. Our findings indicate that the superior temporal gyrus (STG) is activated bilaterally during the processing of talker changes when listeners attended to lexical tone changes in the stimuli and during the processing of lexical tone changes when listeners attended to talker changes, suggesting that lexical tone and talker processing are functionally integrated in the bilateral STG, providing evidence for a general neural mechanism of integral phonetic and talker processing in the bilateral STG. Our results also show that interactions of lexical tone and talker processing occur 500–800 ms after auditory word onset (a simultaneous posterior P3b and a frontal negativity). Such findings have implications for understanding the neural encoding of linguistic and talker information. 3. Our findings suggest that speech and nonspeech sounds are partly processed by domain-specific mechanisms and that information from the same domain can be integrated more effectively than that from different domains. Therefore, domain-specific processing of speech could be the most likely cause of the unequal context effect. Moreover, focal attention is not a prerequisite for extracting contextual cues from speech and nonspeech during perceptual normalization. This finding implies that context encoding is highly automatic for native listeners.

448413.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
448413.value: Tone is a supra-segmental feature. Whether the findings regarding tone normalization are applicable to talker normalization of segments merit further study. We have already been awarded another GRF project which systematically compares the normalization mechanisms of tones versus vowels. Moreover, we are also interested in further extending this line of research to consonant normalization. Pitch is also a prominent feature of music. How pitch processing in speech interacts with that in music is also an interesting topic which attracts our interests. By far, literature (including our research work) has provided rich evidence that the pitch information in nonspeech (e.g., triangle waves) is hardly useful for tone normalization. However, whether pitch information in music is helpful for tone normalization is still an open question.

448613.label: Project Objectives
448613.value: To study the records about ghosts in early China. To analyze the records in their historical and social contexts, and explore the agencies that produced these records. To look at the continuity and change of the conception of ghosts and explain the changes in terms of social, political, and intellectual transformations. To summarize the cultural and religious significance of ghosts in ancient China, and in comparison with other early cultures.
