448613.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
448613.value: One of the central concerns of any religious system is the need to explain the destination of life. Is the end of life the end, or is there something more to it? For those belief systems that postulate a life beyond this one, a certain form of existence, be it called soul, phantom, or ghost, has to be assumed simply because the human cognitive faculty usually could not imagine an existence without any attributes. Once this is done, ghost became a real entity in society and profoundly affected the growth and development of human culture. It would be somewhat inappropriate to say that ghosts affected the development of religion, since ghosts are part of the religious phenomenon. Yet without an understanding of how ghosts functioned in a religious system, we may not be able to comprehend the system, nor the society in which religious beliefs were nurtured. Ancient China is a place where ghosts thrived. Where did they come from? How did they look like? How did people recognize and treat the ghosts? How did they affect people’s lives? How did people imagine their relationship with human beings? What was their role in the belief systems? How did they affect literature, art, and transform people’s idea of the world? By asking and answering these questions, this project intends to offer an alternative view of the religious culture of ancient China, when most studies concentrate on Confucianism, Daoism, ancestor worship, ritual, or divination. Methodologically, this project will use textual and archaeological evidence to portray the development of the phenomenon of ghosts in ancient China, beginning from the Shang Dynasty and down to the Six Dynasties period. Within each sub-period, I shall articulate a theme that could characterize the nature of the development. I shall discuss how a discourse on ghosts emerged in early China, how the imperial government sought to regulate the activities of ghosts, how ghosts became prominent in literary representations, and how, in the Six Dynasties, the taming of ghosts became the contesting ground for Daoist and Buddhist advocates. Finally, I shall make some comparison with ghosts in other parts of the ancient world, to show the universality and particularity of the phenomenon of ghosts in human society. The goal of this study is to produce a book that could provide a fresh understanding of ancient Chinese religion and society, one that walks the path that is less traveled. 任何一個宗教系統的主要關切點不外是要解釋生命的去向：生命的結束果真是完全結束，或者還有什麼其他的可能性？對於那些認為死後仍有某種存在的信仰系統而言，必須得假設某種存在的形式，不論是稱為靈或鬼，因為人的認知能力一般很難想像一種沒有任何性質的存在狀態．一旦這一點成立，那麼鬼或魂的概念在人類社會中就成為一種實際存在的東西，對人類文化的成長和發展有重要的影響．我們也很難說鬼魂影響的宗教的發展，因為鬼魂的概念跟本是宗教現象的一部分．如果不瞭解鬼魂如何在宗教系統中發生作用，我們也就不能全面瞭解這個宗教系統，也不能瞭解它所成長的社會． 古代中國社會中，鬼魂無所不在．它們從何而來？有什麼面貌？人們如何可以辨認鬼的形象？又如何對待或處理鬼魂？鬼魂如何影響了人們的生活？它們與人有什麼樣的關係？它們在信仰系統中的角色是什麼？它們對文學，藝術有何影響，又如何轉化了人們的世界觀？這些都是本研究計畫打算探討的問題，也是本研究與一般有關中國宗教文化的研究不同之處．我們希望能藉此研究提出一些前人較少探討的問題，並且提出對中國宗教性質的新看法．在研究方法上，本研究擬應用文獻及考古資料來重建古代中國鬼的現象的發展．討論將從商代一直到六朝時代．在這中間又可分為一些小的段落，每一段落都各有其發展特色．我們討論的問題包括先秦時代鬼的概念的出現，帝國時代政府如何規範鬼的活動，鬼的概念如何成為六朝文藝作品中的新元素，而在佛道兩教的發展中，馴鬼術又如何成為兩者彼此競爭的要點．最後，我們也將從比較的觀點來檢視中國的鬼與世界其它文化中的鬼有何異同，又是否能因此對中國宗教和社會的性質有新的瞭解．

448613.label: Realisation of objectives
448613.value: The project objectives have been achieved in the following way: 1. The PI has several articles published (or forthcoming) with international academic presses. (See Research Outcome). 2. The PI has been given invited talks and participating in international conferences to disseminate research results. (See Research Outcome) 3. A monographic study is being prepared to be published in a major academic press. The title of the book is Search the Dark City: The Culture of Ghosts in Ancient China. All the objectives in 5.1 have been dealt with in this book, as shown in the chapter titles: Chapter 1 Introduction: Ghost as a Subject of Human Experience The central thesis of this study is that since the idea of ghosts is a persistent factor in the religious beliefs, it could serve as an index of the interactions, mutual accommodations, or even syncretistic fusions, between the more institutionalized religious systems, be it Daoism, Buddhism, or other forms of beliefs, and the indigenous Chinese beliefs. Chapter 2 Confront: The Emergence of a Discourse on Ghosts Chapter two examines pre-imperial documents that have to do with the origin, nature, function, and image of ghosts, and the reaction and accommodation ghosts received in the forms of ritual propitiation, prayer, or exorcism. It will be basically a text-oriented study of the ancient documents, from the Shang Dynasty oracle bones to the Classical texts, including such recently excavated texts as the Shuihudi Daybook and the Baoshan bamboo text, to establish a basic outline of the phenomenon of ghosts in early China. I shall also discuss the emergence of a discourse of the significance of ghost in society, mainly among thinkers such as Zhuangzi, Xunzi and Mozi.Towards the late Warring States period, as shown in texts such as Lushi chunqiu (Master Lu’s Spring and Autumn Annal呂氏春秋) and Zhouli (The Rite of Zhou周禮), there was an intellectual trend to systematize the gods and ghosts into a more coherent structure. The texts foresee a centralized structure of the spiritual world after the establishment of the universal empire. Chapter 3 Regulate: Imperial Order and Local Variations Chapter three examines various textual and iconographical expressions of the idea of ghost in the Qin and Han Dynasties, and investigates how the official and the private spheres interacted with one another and affected the development of ghost and related ideas such as the netherworld. Chapter 4 Humanize: Stories that Reveal the Dark Corner Chapter four discusses the rise of literary representation of ghosts from the end of the Han dynasty to the era of disunity, the Six Dynasties period (3rd-6th centuries CE). A special literary genre, the Zhiguai (志怪)“anomaly stories,” that emerged at the end of the Han dynasty and flourished during the subsequent Six Dynasties period made ghost stories one of the central themes. The motif of ghost received literary embellishment and conceptual refinement and had great influence on the idea of ghost in the subsequent Chinese religion and culture. This chapter therefore explores this literary world of ghosts and study their images, characters, behavior, malice, benevolence or even vulnerability, and their possible influence on the worldview and religious and emotional life of the period. Chapter 5 Contain: Ghosts in Early Daoist Religious Culture Chapter five concentrates particularly on a number of early Daoist texts, and also compare Daoist ideas of the nature and origin of ghosts, their images and functions, and the exorcistic rituals, with those of the pre-Daoist Chinese popular religion. This comparison could delineate more clearly the difference, or the lack thereof, between Daoist religion and popular religious cults. Chapter 6 Incorporate: Ghosts in Early Buddhism Chapter six discusses early Buddhist views and treatment of ghosts. When Buddhism came to China, it did not come into a religious vacuum. Besides trying to win over the attention of the literati class, Buddhist advocates also needed to confront whatever popular beliefs they encountered. Early Buddhist texts, therefore, also abound with references to popular religious activities, including the worshipping of ghosts and spirits. An examination of the idea of ghost in the early Buddhist literature and accounts about the activities of Buddhist monks could therefore provide a concrete focus for our understanding of at least part of the extent of the Sinicizaton of Buddhism. Chapter 7 Compare: Chinese Ghosts in a Comparative Perspective Since the phenomenon of ghosts is universal, our illumination of the significance of ghosts in early China will constitute a basis for further comparison with ghosts in other parts of the world. The similarities and differences among ghosts of China, India, Ancient Near East, Japan, Greece, and Medieval Europe will be my subject of investigation, for only through comparison can one appreciate the individual characteristics of each culture.

In order to do this, there should be a collective effort by scholars in each field to discuss the possibility of an in-depth investigation of ghosts in different societies, with common questions to ask and to answer.

448613.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
448613.value: This project studies the changing conception of ghosts in ancient China from the Shang Dynasty to the end of the Han Dynasty, at the beginning of the development of Buddhism and Daoist religion. By establishing the basic change of the concept of ghosts, from malicious evil force to becoming a more human-like being, we can trace the changing cultural and religious environment in which the concept of ghost was developed. This understanding can serve as a basis to understand the later development of Buddhism in China, as the Buddhists needed to deal with the indigenous ideas of ghosts in order to persuade and disseminate their messages to the common people. When Buddhism tried to incorporate the Chinese ghosts into its system, what exactly happened in the process is an important issue. This study provides the basis to further understand this issue.

448713.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
448713.value: Yan Shigu 顏師古is a historian and master of Confucian Classics (jing經) in the period of late Sui dynasty and early Tang dynasty. However, his achievements of Confucian Classics was always neglected by previous scholars. In view of this, the present project will survey Yan Shigu’s works, i.e. Commentaries of Hanshu漢書注, Kuangmiuzhengsu匡謬正俗 and Ji Jiu Pian Zhu急就篇注, in order to study his achievements of Confucian Classics in Tang dynasty: First, investigate the quotations that Yan Shigu cited from the Classics and its commentaries in his commentaries on the Hanshu. Ban Gu, the historian who compiled the Hanshu, was a scholar of the Han dynasty steeped in the classical studies. Yan Shigu followed Ban's practice of citing the Classics in his writings. Yan's quotations fall into two general categories: (1) his interpretation of Hanshu's quotations from the Classics, and (2) his own quotations from the Classics to explain texts in the Hanshu. The study of Yan’s quotations is also a way to discover the other explanation of the Classics. Second, since Yan Shigu was the grandson of Yan Zhitui顏之推, author of the Yanshi jiaxun顏氏家訓, and nephew of Yan Youqin顏遊秦, author of the Hanshu queyi漢書抉疑, it is only natural that his family had a profound influence on his works. A comparison between Yan Shigu and his ancestors will be done in this project. The development of the commentaries of Classics from Six dynasty to Tang dynasty will also discuss. Third, the role of Yan Shigu in the edit of the Wujingzhengyi五經正義. This project will discuss the difference between Yan Shigu’s works and Wujingzhengyi in the commentaries of the Classics. Fourth, Lu Deming陸德明’s Jingdianshiwen經典釋文 is a phonetic explanation monograph annotating, by phonetic notation, 14 classic works in pre-Qin dynasty. This project will investigate different explanation of the Classics between Lu Deming and Yan Shigu. Fifth, Kuangmiuzhengsu reflects the Mainstream Characters Concept 正字學of Yan Shigu. This project will also study the character concept of Yan Shigu from his works, such as Wujing Dingben五經定本, Yanshiziyang顏氏字樣, and also the Commentaries of Hanshu. Finally, compares the same chapters or passages found in the Commentaries of Hanshu, the Three Commentaries on the Shiji史記三家注, Li Shan’s commentary on the Wenxuan文選李善注, so to discuss the citations of the Classics and its commentaries within these works.

448713.label: Realisation of objectives
448713.value: 本計劃以兩年時間，全面考察唐代顏師古在其著述中用經之概況，並藉此勾勒顏氏於唐代經學史之地位，計劃已大抵完成，並已達致以下成果。 首先，本文以顏師古《漢書注》為據，考察《漢書》引經之時，顏氏如何援引經書及經注以作解釋。本計劃以《詩》、《書》、《易》為例，全面考證顏氏引經解經之實。據此得知雖至唐代，經學定於一尊，然顏氏解經仍不拘一家，博採眾說，能集大成，如《詩》不主毛、《易》不主王，惟《書》則幾乎皆用偽孔，此其大較也。又，《漢書》未必援引經書，而顏氏仍多引經文、經注以作解說，可見顏氏飽讀經書，出口成章，實唐代經學之大家。 其次，取司馬貞《史記索隱》為例，比對顏師古《漢書注》與此書之關係。《史記》錄三千年史事於一書，而《漢書》只載前漢一代史事，惟漢興至武帝百年之間，《史》《漢》互見篇幅甚眾，顏注或參裴駰《集解》，而《索隱》又有取資顏注者。本計劃亦已作細緻考察顏氏《漢書注》與司馬貞《史記索隱》之關係，兩兩校之，互有佳處，各擅勝場。 再者，顏師古先奉皇命，校正五經文字，有訂正當世文字之功，並有《顏氏字样》傳世。《顏氏字样》久佚，惟本計劃勾沉史料，搜得遺文，補足顏氏正字學之成就。又，顏氏於《漢書注》、《匡謬正俗》、《急就章注》等，皆有訂正當時文字之說法，此等材料，同為本計劃加以利用，構成顏氏正字學之重要部分。 接著，顏師古究竟有否參與唐代《五經正義》之編撰，前賢素有爭議，眾說紛紜，莫衷一是，其中尤以「五經文字」曾否成書，以及撰者孰誰最受關注。據本計劃仔細比對，諸經正義援引「定本」者，未必能與顏氏其他著述之說法相合。且五經以外亦有「定本」，顯非顏氏所能參與，準此而論，今《五經正義》所引「定本」，未必即為顏氏所定。 最後，顏師古因其《漢書注》之作，《新唐書》譽之為班固功臣，後世遂多以史學家名之。本計劃通過以上考察，知悉師古不單以史學名家，在經學方面亦多有所得，既有考訂經籍文字，亦有援引經文、兼引經說者，且其數量不在少數，解說成林，日後重寫唐代經學史者，自當補足師古之一頁。

448713.label: Major findings and research outcome
448713.value: 經過兩年時間，本計劃大抵完成。其中最重要之發現，約有以下數端： 1. 顏師古《漢書注》所見經學資料。得知顏氏引經、用經注多不拘一家，擇善而從，在定於一尊之唐代經學尤顯重要。 2. 顏師古與「定本」。前人或謂《五經正義》所引「定本」為顏氏《五經定本》，或不以為然。經過本計劃考查，可知《正義》所引「定本」之字詞或釋義，未必與顏氏其他著述所見者相同。加之以《五經正義》以外諸經亦有「定本」云云，則「定本」未必為顏氏所撰可以推知。 3. 顏師古嘗為《五經》訂正文字，又有《字样》之撰，輔之以《漢書注》、《急就篇注》、《匡謬正俗》等就經書文字之討論，可知顏師古實有功於唐代正字學。此舉不單為師古一人之學，更是顏氏一族自隋至唐之家學。 4. 顏師古應在唐代經學佔一席位。經過本計劃考察，顏師古之學問實不當以史學囿之，就其諸書注釋所見，其人深於經學，當可以經學家名之。

448713.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
448713.value: 顏師古在《漢書注》、《急就篇注》、《匡謬正俗》等皆就個別字詞釋義，勝處頗多，亦每為後世詞書編者所採。因此，即在本計劃完成以後，本人仍然繼續廣泛蒐集顏師古在各書的釋義，合成一帙，命名之為「顏師古釋義詞典」，希望能在訓詁學上彰顯顏師古之重要性。

448713.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
448713.value: 在有唐一代，顏師古不應只被視為史學家，而當以經史名家者目之。利用《漢書注》、《急就篇注》、《匡謬正俗》、《五經正義》等，可知顏師古實深諳經學，解說不拘一家，能博採眾說，並化繁為簡。至其解說，每為後世學者所採，影響深遠。唐代經學史往往缺乏顏師古之一頁，據本計劃考證，實可重寫相關部分，並重新突顯顏師古之經學地位，以及其承先啟後之作用。

449013.label: Project Title(Chinese)
449013.value: 中國2000-2005年區間技術移民和非技術移民的比較研究

449013.label: Project Objectives
449013.value: The overall objective is to identify the difference between skilled and unskilled migration in China in terms of spatial patterns and determinants of interregional migration. To use quantitative methods to examine the difference between skilled and unskilled migration in China in terms of migration asymmetry, relative emissiveness and top regions of in-migration via the testing of four hypotheses. To identify and compare the determinants of interregional skilled and unskilled migration using migration models. The roles of different determinants in skilled and unskilled migration will be examined via the testing of three hypotheses in the context of China.

449013.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
449013.value: In the age of globalization, advanced producer services are concentrated in leading cities attracting many skilled migrants regionally and internationally. Skilled migration has become an increasingly important part of international and internal migration in contrast to general labor migration in many countries. The spatial patterns and determinants of skilled migration will be different from unskilled migration due to their different origins, human capital and the destination choice. Many quantitative and qualitative studies have been made on internal migration as well as temporary migrants in China. But most previous studies do not distinguish skilled migration from unskilled migration, leaving a significant research gap in the literature. A few related studies have been conducted on the distribution of talents. From the perspective of migration studies, the number of talents or the skilled people is a stock variable which is related to both the production of talents by universities and the migration. Having many talents is not the same as attracting many skilled migrants. To assess the effects of various factors on attracting talents from other regions, it is important to analyze the migration instead of the distribution of skilled migrants directly through this project. Some important research questions need to be answered regarding the possible difference between skilled and unskilled migrants in China. First, does migration asymmetry exist among both skilled and non-skilled migration? Is there any difference in the extent of asymmetry between two kinds of migration? Second, is the relative emissiveness of skilled migration more evenly distributed than that of unskilled migration? Are the top regions of relative attractiveness for skilled migration different from that of unskilled migration? Third, are skilled migrants less affected by distance than unskilled migrants? Fourth, are there any differences in the main determinants of skilled and unskilled migrants? How would manufacturing, trade and foreign investment, openness and amenities affect unskilled migration and skilled migration differently? This project will conduct a systematic comparative study to reveal different spatial patterns and determinants of skilled and unskilled migration in China using the data from 1% population sampling survey in 2005. The approaches of migration spatial structure and eigenvector spatial filtering will be used in migration analysis. With the ageing of China’s population, unskilled migration may reach its peak in the near future. The pattern of skilled migration will become more and more important. The findings have important implications to population distribution and regional development in China. 在全球化時代，高級生產服務業多集中在世界主要城市，吸引許多跨區域和國際技術移民。相比於一般的勞動力遷移，技術移民在國際和跨區域遷移中扮演越來越重要的作用。由於移民的來源地、人力資本、遷移目的地不盡相同，技術移民的空間格局和影響因素不同於非技術移民。中國國內人口遷移與暫住人口方面，已做了很多定性和定量研究，但是很少有研究將技術移民與非技術移民區分開來，這是現有文獻中研究不足的地方。 已有一些研究涉及技術人才的空間分佈。從移民研究的角度看，一個地區技術人才的數量是一個存量指標，受到當地大學畢業生的數量和人口遷移兩方面的影響。擁有很多技術人才不同於吸引大量的技術移民。本研究評估各種因素如何影響各地對區外技術人才的吸引力，進行移民分析極其重要，而不僅僅是關注技術人才的分佈。 針對技術移民與非技術移民的差別，需要回答一些重要的研究問題。首先，技術移民和非技術移民中是否都存在遷移不均衡現象？如果都有遷移不均衡，兩者的不均衡程度有什麼差別？第二，技術移民遷出地分佈是否比非技術移民更加均衡？技術移民的主要遷入地是否不同於非技術移民？第三，距離對技術移民的影響是否小於非技術移民？ 第四，影響技術移民和非技術移民的因素有什麼不同？製造業、貿易、外國投資、城市的開放度和宜居環境怎樣影響技術移民和非技術移民？ 本研究利用2005年1%人口抽樣數據，對中國技術和非技術移民進行系統的比較研究，揭示兩者在空間格局和影響因素上的差異。遷移分析將會使用移民空間結構與特徵向量空間過濾等方法。隨著中國人口老化，非技術移民的數量在不遠的將來會達到頂峰，技術移民的格局將會變得越來越重要。研究結果對於中國的人口分佈和區域發展將有重要的啟示作用。

449013.label: Major findings and research outcome
449013.value: Earlier studies have treated migrants as a homogenous group when modelling interregional migration flows in China (Fan, 2005; Yang et al., 2015). Only a few recent studies have attempted to model the migratory behaviours of skilled individuals (Fu & Gabriel, 2012). This project has advanced our knowledge of internal migration in China by analyzing the difference in the determinants of skilled and less-skilled migrations. Comparative analysis shows that migration asymmetry exists among less-skilled migration in the period 2000-2005. The degree of migration asymmetry is less severe among skilled migrants than less-skilled migrants. The relative emissiveness of skilled migration is less evenly distributed than that of less-skilled migration. Results from descriptive analysis show that both skilled and less-skilled migrants tend to move away from the interior to the coastal region. Comparing with the migration of less-skilled people, the migration of skilled people is less influenced by the friction of distance, the regional unemployment rate, and the concentration of foreign investment but is more affected by the regional wage disparity. With respect to the effect of amenities, climatic amenities exert a strong influence on the skilled migration but have a positive effect on the less-skilled migration at origin and no effect at destination. The medical services are influential in the migration of less-skilled people to destinations but turn out to have no effect on skilled people. Our findings suggest that the decisions of migrants in China increasingly resemble those in Western developed countries. First, Chinese skilled migrants tend to be more capable of overcoming the friction of distance than their less-skilled counterparts, therefore are more likely to move a long distance than the latter. Second, the self-selection model suggests that migrants tend to relocate to regions where the returns to skills are more compatible with their skill endowments. Our findings verify the applicability of the self-selection model in the Chinese context. Third, consistent with prior studies on developed countries, less-skilled migrants are more responsive than skilled migrants to regional differentials in the possibility of employment. The migration decisions in China are also different from those in Western countries. The foreign investment plays a critical role in influencing the migration decision of Chinese people. China’s skilled people tend to prioritize employment-related issues over amenity-related issues in their migration decisions, and their attitudes toward life and work are different from those of their counterparts at this stage of development.

449013.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
449013.value: The major destinations of skilled migration in China are expected to differ from those of less-skilled migration in the future, because there is a divergence between the distribution of skill-intensive industries and that of labor-intensive industries. Skilled people will continue to be highly concentrated in major metropolitan cities such as Beijing and Shanghai which provide competitive salaries and high-quality public goods and services. Less-skilled workers, especially those from the central and western regions, may find jobs in their home provinces. Thus the new patterns of migration may emerge in China and call for new migration policies. More recent census microdata are useful for further comparison between skilled and less-skilled migration in terms of spatial patterns and determinants. Research advancement in this direction will also benefit studies on urbanization, urban housing issues, and unbalanced regional development in China. Further research grant will be sought to engage new research in this area.

449013.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
449013.value: Leading cities are attracting many skilled migrants regionally and internationally. Skilled migration has become an increasingly important part of migration in contrast to general labor migration in many countries. The spatial patterns and determinants of skilled migration will be different from unskilled migration due to their different origins, human capital and the destination choice. Many quantitative and qualitative studies have been made on internal migration as well as temporary migrants in China. But most previous studies do not distinguish skilled migration from unskilled migration, leaving a significant research gap in the literature. This project has conducted a systematic comparative study to reveal different spatial patterns and determinants of skilled and unskilled migration in China. Comparing with the migration of less-skilled people, the migration of skilled people is less influenced by the friction of distance, the regional unemployment rate, and the concentration of foreign investment but is more affected by the regional wage disparity. With the ageing of China’s population, unskilled migration may reach its peak in the near future. The pattern of skilled migration will become more and more important. The findings have important implications to population distribution and regional development in China.

449813.label: Project Title(Chinese)
449813.value: 手勢對於空間關係的有益作用

449813.label: Project Objectives
449813.value: 1. To examine the impact of embodied movements, i.e., spontaneous hand movements, on learning and remembering spatial relation. 2. To investigate whether gesturing while thinking silently (i.e., co-thought gestures) and gesturing while producing spatial language (i.e., co-speech gestures) would yield the same facilitating effect on learning and remembering spatial relation. 3. To compare the effectiveness of gestures on learning and remembering spatial relation to that of spatial language. 4. To illustrate the moderating effects of gesture frequency, task complexity, and individual differences in spatial skills on learning and remembering spatial relation.

2. To investigate whether gesturing while thinking silently (i.e., co-thought gestures) and gesturing while producing spatial language (i.e., co-speech gestures) would yield the same facilitating effect on learning and remembering spatial relation.
3. To compare the effectiveness of gestures on learning and remembering spatial relation to that of spatial language.
4. To illustrate the moderating effects of gesture frequency, task complexity, and individual differences in spatial skills on learning and remembering spatial relation.

449813.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
449813.value: When we navigate in an environment, we form a spatial representation regarding relation between locations, objects, and paths. Therefore, developing techniques to improve spatial relation learning and memory is crucial. This research asks whether producing embodied movements, specifically hand gestures, enhance memory for spatial relation. Gestures are spontaneous hand movements, e.g., right hand swipes horizontally that represents a movement to the right. They are produced in space, and thus, are inherently spatial. However, little research investigates whether gestures improve spatial relation learning and memory. Recently, the PI (So) has conducted the first study discovering gesturing while thinking silently (co-thought gestures) is an effective embodied technique in enhancing recall accuracy of steps in a navigation task (So, Vong, Ching, 2012; in preparation). However, there are three critical issues remain unaddressed. First, it is uncharted whether gestures accompanying spatial language (co-speech gestures) result in the same facilitating effect on memory for spatial relation as co-thought gestures. Co-speech gestures in fact are produced more often than co-thought gestures. Second, it is unknown whether spatial language is as effective as co-thought and co-speech gestures in improving memory for spatial relation, yet spatial language is commonly used among majority of learners. Third, it is unclear whether the beneficial effects of co-thought and co-speech gestures vary with task complexity, gesture frequency, and levels of spatial skills. Three-hundred and sixty participants will perform the spatial sequence learning task in which they study routes with 10, 13, and 16 steps and later reconstruct them with sticks during recall. They are randomly assigned to one of the six conditions where we manipulate encoding methods (co-thought gestures, co-speech gestures, or spatial language alone) and gesture frequency. Participants will also perform three spatial skill assessment tasks that examine different aspects of their spatial skills. Separate regression analyses will be conducted to examine the effects of rehearsal methods, gesture frequency, levels of spatial skills, and their interactions on the number of steps recalled at each level of route complexity. We expect that co-thought and co-speech gestures would yield stronger beneficial effects on recall than spatial language but the beneficial effects would be weakened when encoding less complex routes and for participants with weaker spatial skills. The findings will help to construct more comprehensive theories of embodied cognition and develop education intervention, which uses gestures to facilitate spatial relation encoding in those with weak spatial skills, like children and patients with dementia. 當我們在身處的環境中，我們會形成了一個對於對象和路徑之間的關係的空間畫像。因此，開發技術以提高空間關係的學習和記憶是重要的。這個研究會探究身體動作，特別是手勢，會否增強空閻記憶力。手勢是自發性的手部動作，例如，右手向橫移動表示向右移動。手勢也是在空間產生。然而，很少有研究調查手勢是否提升空間關係的學習和記憶。近年， 我們已經進行了第一次研究發現在默想時產生的手勢能加強被試者記起路線的部驟（So, Vong, Ching, 2012; in preparation)） 。然而，有三個關鍵的問題仍然沒有得到解決。首先，我們不知道在說話時產生的手勢是知是否與在默想時產生的手勢都能加強被試者記起路線的部驟。在說話時產生的手勢比在默想時產生的手勢普遍。其次，用來描述空間的語言未知是否跟手勢一樣有效提高空間記憶力。這些語言大多數學習者使用。第三，目前還不清楚路線的複雜性，手勢頻率和空間技能水平是否影響手勢的作用。本研究有三百六十被試者參加，他們將學習不同的路線(分別為 10 ，13 ，和16個步驟)，後來他們用棍棒重建路線。他們被隨機分配到6個不同的實驗情況去排練，以用來區分空間語言， 不同類別的手勢，和手勢頻率的影響。被試者還將執行空間技能的評估。不同的回歸分析會在每個級別的路線複雜性研究不同的排練的方法，手勢頻率，空間的技能水平，和它們之間的相互作用對路線記憶的影響。我們預計，相對描述空間的語言，在默想時產生的手勢和在說話時產生的手勢會對路線記憶產生更強的有益作用，但其有益作用會在排練不太複雜的路線和在空間技能較弱的被試者了減低。該研究結果將有助於手勢和空間關係構建更全面的理論，並幫助教育界發展干預方法來促進空間兒童和老年癡呆症患者的空間記憶。

449813.label: Realisation of objectives
449813.value: All four objectives stated in the proposal were all achieved. Objective 1. Two experiments were conducted. Adult participants were asked to study routes shown in four diagrams, one at a time. Participants reproduced the routes (verbally in Experiment 1 and non-verbally in Experiment 2) without rehearsal or after rehearsal by mentally simulating the route, by drawing it, or by gesturing (either in the air or on paper). The findings have shown that producing gestures facilitates route learning in a navigation task and its facilitation effect is comparable to that of hand movements that leave physical visible traces. Objectives 2 to 4. A single experiment was conducted. Adults studied routes with 10, 13, and 16 steps and reconstructed them with sticks, either without rehearsal or after rehearsal by producing gestures with speech, gestures alone, or speech only. The findings have shown that producing gestures with and without speech facilitates route learning at different levels of route complexity and in learners with different levels of spatial skills. In addition, the number of steps rehearsed in gesture, but not that rehearsed in speech, predicted the recall accuracy. Thus, gesture is more effective than spatial language in encoding spatial information, and thereby enhancing spatial recall.

449813.label: Major findings and research outcome
449813.value: In the first study, we focused on gestures produced without accompanying speech, i.e., co-thought gestures (e.g., an index finger traces the spatial sequence of a route in the air).Adult participants were asked to study routes shown in four diagrams, one at a time. Participants reproduced the routes (verbally in Experiment 1 and non-verbally in Experiment 2) without rehearsal or after rehearsal by mentally simulating the route, by drawing it, or by gesturing (either in the air or on paper). Participants who moved their hands (either in the form of gestures or drawing) recalled better than those who mentally simulated the routes and those who did not rehearse, suggesting that hand movements produced during rehearsal facilitate route learning. Interestingly, participants who gestured the routes in the air or on paper recalled better than those who drew them on paper in both experiments, suggesting that the facilitation effect of co-thought gesture holds for both verbal and nonverbal recall modalities. It is possibly because, co-thought gesture, as a kind of representational action, consolidates spatial sequence better than drawing and thus exerting more powerful influence on spatial representation. In the second paper, adults studied routes with 10, 13, and 16 steps and reconstructed them with sticks, either without rehearsal or after rehearsal by producing gestures with speech, gestures alone, or speech only. For all levels of route complexity and spatial skills, participants who were encouraged to gesture (with or without speech) during rehearsal had the best recall. Additionally, we found that number of steps rehearsed in gesture, but not that rehearsed in speech, predicted the recall accuracy. Thus, gesture is more effective than spatial language in encoding spatial information, and thereby enhancing spatial recall. These results further corroborate the beneficial nature of gesture in processing spatial information.

449813.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
449813.value: Producing co-thought gestures allows us to construct the spatial information and retain it in our memory with relatively little effort. Further research could address whether such encoding method can be applied to other spatial tasks and how long its mnemonic effect is. The current findings can also paves the way for future research developing educational or clinical interventions using hand movements to facilitate the encoding of spatial relations in children who have weaker spatial skills than adults, and in patients with dementia, whose spatial skills are declining over time.

449813.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
449813.value: Gestures are spontaneous hand movements produced while speaking or thinking. Producing gesture with or without speech helps learners to encode spatial sequences, and its facilitating effect is even stronger than spatial language. Our research enriches our understanding of the role of different kinds of hand movements (gestures with speech and gestures without speech) in encoding spatial information. More importantly, it can fill the gap in the literature by looking at the circumstances in which hand movements are effective for encoding spatial information. It also guides clinicians or educators to develop effective intervention programs using gestures to help those with weak spatial skills to find their ways.

450013.label: Project Objectives
450013.value: To ascertain how INGOs gain entry into China and how they negotiate political uncertainties. 450013.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
450013.value: This project examines the influx of international nongovernmental organizations (INGOs) into China since the country’s opening to the outside world began in the early 1980s. Over the past three decades, INGOs have worked across China to address issues of rural poverty, educational inequality, environmental degradation, access to healthcare, and a host of other social concerns made more prominent by (or resulting from) wide-sweeping economic reforms. Despite the widespread acknowledgement of an INGO presence in China, to date there is little broad-based scholarship on this subject. This project will be the first study to document the size, characteristics, and survival strategies of INGOs in contemporary China, empirically ‘mapping’ the landscape by identifying which INGOs are there, what issues they take as their focus, and where in China they operate. This project will also create a database documenting INGO personnel structures, governance practices, legal status, funding sources, expenditures, and organizational networks. These data will allow for comparison of INGO practices across country of origin (including organizations based in Hong Kong) as well as other variables, with the end goal of helping establish a baseline understanding of INGO experiences upon which future research can build. Theoretically, this study will break new ground by pushing forward our understanding of global civil society and authoritarianism. Extant theory suggests that the Chinese government should either reject INGO entry or seek to control INGOs centrally. The presence of over 200 INGOs currently at work in China at least complicates the first supposition, while the second – centralized government control over INGOs – has yet to be substantiated. My prior research into relations between grassroots NGOs and the Chinese government gives reason to question the assumption that the government in Beijing is able to fully control INGOs. Through in-depth interviews with INGO staff, I will analyze the ways in which INGOs negotiate space to work in what is generally presumed to be a hostile political environment. At the same time, interviews with Chinese government officials will shed light on the calculations state agents make when deciding whether – and to what extent – INGOs will be allowed to operate. Assembling insights from these varied data sources will help delineate the dynamics that shape INGO relations with the Chinese state and offer reference points for understanding INGO-state relations in other authoritarian regimes. 本項目將會研究自20世紀80年代初中國對外開放而大量湧入的國際非政府組織。在過去三十年，國際非政府組織在中國各地致力于解決農村貧窮、教育不平等、環境退化、獲得醫療保健以及一系列由大規模經濟改革而加劇或造成的社會問題。 雖然國際非政府組織在中國的存在被普遍承認，但至今對這個題目有廣泛的研究卻並不多。本研究將會在學術上首次記錄現時中國存在的國際非政府組織的規模、特點和生存策略并進行區域性統計，指出有哪些國際非政府組織，它們關注的議題以及它們在中國哪裡開展項目。本研究同時會建立一個國際非政府組織的數據庫，記錄它們的人事架構、治理常規、法律地位、資金來源、支出和組織網絡。這些數據將允許研究者把國際非政府組織的做法、它們來源國家的做法（包括以香港為基地的組織）以及其他變因進行比較，數據庫最終的目標是希望建立對國際非政府組織一些最基本的瞭解，讓以後的研究可以建基在這些瞭解之上。 理論上，本研究將會有新的突破，推進学术界對全球公民社會以及威權主義國家的理解。現存的理論提出中國政府應拒絕國際非政府組織的進入或集中控制這類組織。但現存在中國境內超過200個國際非政府組織令第一個假設變得複雜，而第二個假設——中國政府會集中控制國際非政府組織，仍然有待被證實。透過與國際非政府組織的員工進行深入訪問，本研究者將分析這些組織怎樣在一個普遍被認為是紧张的政治環境下協商它們的工作空間。與此同時，本研究者將探索去了解中国政府在決定是否或在什麽程度上允許國際非政府組織在中國運作有哪些考量。整合不同數據的啟示將能勾畫出國際非政府組織與中國政府的關係，并同時能夠為關於國際非政府組織與其他威權主義國家關係的研究提供參考。

450013.label: Realisation of objectives
450013.value: The first two objectives – “To ascertain how INGOs gain entry into China and how they negotiate political uncertainties” and “To ascertain how local-level and higher-level governmental authorities view and interact with INGOs” – were achieved through months of fieldwork, including intensive interviews with INGO leaders, INGO staff, and government officials. While government officials were sometimes reluctant to meet – as had been anticipated – the ones who did were generally quite helpful, and INGO staff members themselves were fantastic sources of insight into the dynamics of the INGO-government relationship. The third objective – “To empirically ‘map’ INGO activities in China, including identifying what issues they take as their focus (e.g., literacy, HIV/AIDS, environmental protection), their geographical distribution, personnel structures, governance practices, legal status, funding sources, and expenditures” – was achieved through a combination of internet searches, networking with pre-existing contacts, expanding contacts by asking for new introductions at the end of interviews, a survey of INGOs conducted online, and at the very end of the project by the Ministry of Public Security’s own online database of registered INGO activities and representative offices. Collectively, these sources have allowed me to collect the most comprehensive data possible, saving in some cases for sources of funding (which, again, was as expected, especially for more politically sensitive groups). The fourth objective – “To deepen the theorization of global civil society and its operations in authoritarian regimes” – was achieved through not only the analysis of the data described above but also through extensive exchanges with theoretically-minded practitioners as well as presentations at conferences (as detailed in the ‘outputs’ section below).

450013.label: Major findings and research outcome
450013.value: One finding is that, prior to the introduction of the INGO Law in 2016, a majority of INGOs in China were working in a legal grey zone, outside of any official regulation. For clearly political INGOs – those seeking to promote political liberalization and human rights, for example – a common approach was to minimize contact with the state. Yet even for these groups, they were not ‘unknown’ to state agents. These were typically led by foreigners, although they may also employ some Chinese staff. Other less obviously ‘sensitive’ groups enjoyed closer, if informal, ties with government agencies, a strategy they believed won them some measure of freedom to pursue their goals. A few of these had formal memoranda of understanding with particular government agencies, but these arrangements could be fragile and were sometimes allowed to lapse with neither side seeking renewal. Many, if not most, of the INGOs in China were almost fully staffed by Chinese people – a clear change from the foreign-dominated teams that predominated in the late 1990s. Some INGOs also consciously cultivated relations with government by employing former Chinese government officials, a strategy seen as offering a measure of ‘insider knowledge’ and political protection should it be needed. While one or a combination of these strategies allowed INGOs access to China, their effectiveness was not guaranteed. Some groups believed their efforts to be consequential and ultimately beneficial to China. Other INGO staff openly admit they are uncertain how great a role they can play in effecting meaningful change on the ground given the multiple restrictions they face. The situation above was dramatically transformed by the INGO Law first proposed in December 2014, approved in 2016, and which formally took effect in January 2017. Facing a new regulatory system that requires all INGOs to register even one-off activities, INGO leaders are learning to navigate a new institutional legal structure. Some groups have pulled out of China due to uncertainty over their ability to find a ‘supervisory agency’ within the government. Many agency heads, despite having supported INGOs in the past, proved noncommittal during the lead-up to the law and preferred to wait for instructions from higher levels of the state before vouching for their long-term partners.

450013.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
450013.value: At the time of writing (mid-2017), around 150 INGOs have registered offices in China, but that number is far fewer than the 7,000 official estimate announced by the government leading up to the law’s announcement. The law has had major implications for China’s relations with the outside world, and time will tell whether the number rises or whether obstacles persist to keep a larger number of INGOs out of the country. One future direction for my research will be to follow up periodically with groups active in China prior to the law to see which ones have remained, which have modified their work, and which have left altogether. The government’s own database and other nonprofits documenting the law’s implementation will be excellent sources of data for future quantitative and qualitative analyses.

450013.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
450013.value: This project aimed to understand how international non-governmental organizations (INGOs) operate in mainland China, where – prior to 2017 – there was no clear legal structure regulating their work. Through interviews with dozens of INGO leaders, staff members, and government officials, I established that prior to the INGO Law taking effect in January 2017, these groups worked on a range of issues, including trade, humanitarian aid, education, health, political freedoms, etc. For most groups, this was achieved through a patchwork of ad hoc relationships with government agencies at the provincial or lower levels of the Chinese state. In late 2014, the government began considering a nationwide law to regulate all such groups, passing the law in 2016 and requiring that by 2017 INGOs register with the Ministry of Public Security. In the interim, many groups pulled out of the country and others curtailed their operations, finding that their long-term government partners were reluctant to vouch for them in the absence of clear guidance from the central government. Only a tiny percentage of groups have registered since the law passed, creating quandaries for them as well as for the Chinese government and its international reputation.

450013.label: Other impact (e.g. award of patents or prizes, collaboration with other research institutions, technology transfer, etc.)
450013.value: Knowledge Transfer: Through a series of interviews, focus groups, and private consultations with INGOs, Chinese legal scholars, Chinese and non-Chinese government officials, and other stakeholders, in the course of this project I produced four policy feedback documents that were widely distributed to Chinese policymakers and other relevant parties concerned with the drafting and promulgation of China's first-ever national Law on International Nongovernmental Organisations. These documents were produced at two different stages. In the first stage, roughly May 2015, the law was still being drafted and circulated for public comment. In the second stage, around September 2016, the law had been finalised but relevant governmental authorities were still drafting implementation guidelines. Each stage produced a set of two documents, one in Chinese and one in English. Aside from being distributed through my personal and professional networks, these policy feedback documents were also made publicly available for download on my personal website (www.anthonyjspires.com) and on the website of Beijing-based China Development Brief, a nonprofit clearinghouse for information about civil society in China.

450113.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
450113.value: Sign linguistics first emerged in the States in 1960s and has gradually expanded across the globe. Research findings in the past five decades show that sign languages used by deaf people are natural instantiations of humans’ innate linguistic ability on a par with spoken languages. One significant value of studying sign languages is that they provide an invaluable testing ground for existing linguistic theories which are based primarily on spoken languages. The major difference between sign and spoken languages lies in the modality by which linguistic messages are perceived and conveyed; the former make use of the visual-gestural mode; the latter the audio-vocal mode. By investigating the structures of sign languages, and comparing them with those of spoken languages, one can tease apart modality-specific linguistic properties and linguistic universal patterns not restricted to specific modality. This proposed research project aims at contributing to this line of inquiry by investigating the basic word orders of four sign languages in Asia, namely, Hong Kong Sign Language, Japanese Sign Language, Jakarta Sign Language (in Indonesia) and Sri Lankan Sign Language. Generally speaking, the basic word order of a language refers to the most frequent and unmarked order of a transitive verb and the two noun phrases denoting the core arguments in a simple clause. In spoken languages, there are interesting typological findings that relate the basic word order to other aspects of word order and morphological characteristics (e.g. case, agreement) in a language. These findings shed light on how humans process languages in general, offering a solid basis for linguistic descriptions and the development of linguistic theories. Against this background, this study aims at finding out: i. whether a basic word order exists in the four selected sign languages; ii. whether the correlations between the basic word order and other word order characteristics identified in spoken language typology are also attested in these four languages; iii. whether word order interacts with other morphological features in identifying grammatical relations in these four languages; and iv. whether there are characteristics unique to sign languages that result in word order patterns different from spoken languages. This project will generate a database and detailed descriptions of the word order of these four sign languages that will support the future linguistic research of these languages as well as verification of the existing linguistic theories on word order typology. 450313.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
450313.value: Our intense fieldwork in the past has led us to realize the unique importance of ritual specialists in local social life and the great varieties of their ritual in Chinese villages. While local ritual traditions by definition are local, in the course of our research we were able to identify two local ritual traditions, namely Lüshan Daoism and Pu’an (1115-1169) Buddhism, which inform the ritual traditions in many important ways in southeast China. While studying these two ritual traditions, we have also identified in the field a third tradition that plays an important role in the formation of local ritual traditions, to wit the Zhengyi, but not the Zhengyi to which we are accustomed. Our previous project on local rituals specialists has shown that the Daoist liturgical framework, especially the one that Dean found in Putian,Fujian (Dean 1993), is only one element in a complex whole that makes up the local ritual traditions of southeast China. The Buddhist contribution, notably the ‘white’ funeral and yankou (flaming mouth) rituals, is now well recognized but has still not been adequately studied, primarily because local ritual studies have, so far, been mostly undertaken by Daoist specialists. We have found that in the literary sketches and encyclopedias of the Ming-Qing period, lay household Buddhist ritual specialists known as ‘hearth-dwelling monks’ or ‘huozhai seng’ were as popular as the lay household Daoist ritual specialists known as ‘hearth-dwelling Daoists’ or huoju dao. The huoju dao has received due attention by scholars, while the study of huozhai seng has been largely ignored. This project is in part an attempt to fill the gap. We aim at studying select local ritual traditions from both a synchronic and diachronic viewpoint. Our research questions include: how was a local tradition formed and how did it evolve? What were the parent ritual traditions that inform a local ritual tradition and how did they interact? Were there identifiable structures of local ritual tradition? To what extent does the dichotomy between ‘red’ Daoist exorcistic ritual and ‘white’ Buddhist funeral ritual apply to local ritual tradition? What were the contributions of Buddhism to local ritual tradition? This project is a systematic study of the three main constituents of Chinese local ritual traditions: Zhengyi, Lüshan and Pu’an, to see how they interact to form a local ritual tradition. 過往密集的田野調查使我們認識到中國農村中儀式的多樣性和儀式專家對地方社會生活的重要性。雖然地方儀式傳統的地方性非常強烈，在我們研究的過程中我們仍能辨認到對中國東南部儀式傳統影響甚深的兩種地方儀式傳統——閭山道教和普庵佛教。在研究上述兩種傳統的同時，我們又識別出第三類對中國東南部地方儀式影響至巨的儀式傳統——正一道教，但它和我們一向所熟悉的正一道教又大有不同。在我們過往的課題中已發現道教儀式傳統，特別是丁荷生於褔建莆田所研究的傳統，只是中國東南部眾多複雜地方儀式傳統的一種。我們現在已能容易辨別佛教對中國儀式傳統的貢獻，特別在白事（喪葬）和瑜伽焰口法事（超度亡魂用）方面。可是佛教對地方儀式的貢獻仍未被充份認識。主要的原因之一是地方儀式傳統的研究者主要仍以道教專家為主。我們在明清時期的小說和類書中發現，在家的佛教儀式專家被稱為「火宅僧」。他們與道教的「火居道」同樣流行。火居道一直很受學者的重視而火宅僧則基本被學界所忽略。本計劃擬於此填補空間，從歷時和共時兩方面對地方儀式傳統進行研究。我們的研究問題包括：一個地方儀式傳統如何形成和演變？地方儀式傳統有那幾種原型或母體，它們互相如何交涉？地方儀式傳統有否可辨認的結構？道教驅邪（紅事）、佛教度亡（白事）的說法能否應用到地方儀式傳統中？佛教對地方儀式傳統有那些貢獻？本研究計劃希望系統地研究中國地方儀式傳統中三個組成部份：正一、閭山和普庵，並嘗試了解它們之間如何交涉從而形成地方的儀式傳統。

450313.label: Realisation of objectives
450313.value: Our project applies the ethnographical methodology developed by the P.I and Co-I for the study of local rituals. This methodology of working with a research team of collaborators enables us to cover a comparatively large area and has been proved to work well in previous projects supported by different competitive grants. (Objective 1: Pu’an in Jiangxi) Prof. Yang Yongjin of the Yichun University in Jiangxi works with the P.I. on Pu’an in northwest Jiangxi. We have completed a study of the Pu’an ritual tradition in northwest Jiangxi. (Objective 1: Pu’an in Fujian) Ms. Zhong Jinlan, a researcher at the Hakka Research College of Jiaying University in Guangdong, works with the P.I. on Pu’an ritual tradition in Guangdong and western Fujian. As the only female fieldworker in our team, Zhong has brought in a gender perspective for our project. Part of her research is on the Hakka women in western Fujian. She has completed a study on the Pu’an ritual tradition in western Fujian. (Objective 2: Zhengyi in Jiangxi) Prof. Lü Pengzhi of the Southwest Jiaotong University works with both the P.I. and the Co-I on Zhengyi Daoism in western Jiangxi. Lü has completed his study of a Zhengyi ritual tradition in western Jiangxi and has made an important discovery of a lost tradition of registers used in the Zhengyi tradition. To receive a register in Taoism is to be initiated. The level of initiation was in direct relation to the number and types of registers received. As early as the Tang, there was a system of twenty-four ritual registers created by the medieval church of the Heavenly Masters, also known as the Zhengyi School. This is mentioned and discussed in many Taoist texts but the actual ritual registers were no longer available after the Cultural Revolution. In 1999, with the help of government officials, four ritual registers of the Zhengyi School were recovered from Jiangxi and were re-introduced to Mt. Longhu, the headquarters of the Zhengyi School. After years of fieldwork, our team was able to recover 27 kinds of Zhengyi registers as well as the instructions on how to use them. Another important discovery is that among the 27 kinds of registers of the Taoist Zhengyi school, we have discovered a register for the Pu’an Buddhist school. Based on the evidence we collected, we believe that the Zhengyi School started to incorporate the teaching of Pu’an School through its system of registers. This happened not later than the late Qing. Our research team member, Lü Pengzhi has a thorough discussion of our discovery of the lost Zhengyi ritual registers and its significance for the studies of ritual traditions in China in his two articles published in top journals in China. Dr. Lin Chen-yuan of the National Chengchi University in Taiwan works with the the P.I. and Co-I on Zhengyi Daoism, Lüshan Daoism and Xianghua Buddhism in southern Fujian. (Objective 3 Lüshan in Fujian) Prof. Huang Jianxing of the Fujian Normal University and his mentor Mr.Ye Mingsheng, a researcher in Fujian Art Academy, works with the P.I. and Co-I on Lüshan Daoism in Mindong, Fujian. Our fieldwork concentrates on two sites: a) Yongfu of southwest Fujian which was an ordination center for Lüshan local Taoists in southwest Fujian and thus is important for us to understand the Lüshan ritual tradition that still has an extensive influence to ritual in south China. b) Fu’an in eastern Fujian which is known for its a large number of spiritual mediums. The mediums themselves are a special kind of ritual specialist. Huang finds that they work closely with local Taoists in the region. Huang’s research has opened up a new dimension for the study of local ritual.

450313.label: Major findings and research outcome
450313.value: We have completed our study on the Pu’an school of ritual and are in the process of preparing a monograph on the topic to be co-authored by the P.I. and a research team member Prof. Yang Yongjin. It will be published a volume in our ritual series. Dr. Lin Chen-yuan of the National Chengchi University in Taiwan works with the P.I. and Co-I on Zhengyi Daoism, Lüshan Daoism and Xianghua Buddhism in southern Fujian. He has finished his dissertation Le rituel taoïste du sud-est du Fujian (The Taoist ritual of southeast Fujian) and is working on publishing it as a monograph in Chinese. Our project has made two important discoveries (1) Discovery of a set of lost ritual registers of the Zhengyi School in Jiangxi In 1999, with the help of Chinese officials, four ritual registers of the Zhengyi School were recovered from Jiangxi and were re-introduced to Mt. Longhu, the headquarters of the Zhengyi School. After years of fieldwork, our team was able to recover 27 kinds of Zhengyi registers as well as the instructions on how to use them. Another important discovery is that among the 27 kinds of registers, we have discovered a register for the Pu’an school. Based on the evidence we collected, we believe that the Zhengyi School started to incorporate the teaching of Pu’an School through its system of registers. This happened not later than the late Qing. Our research team member, Lü Pengzhi has a thorough discussion of our discovery of the lost Zhengyi ritual registers and its significance for the studies of ritual traditions in China in his two articles published in top journals in China. (2) Discovery of a transmission center for the Lüshan School It has been found that the Lüshan Taoist ritual school was widely practiced in southeast China, especially among the Hakka (guest people). We also know that the ritual school was inherited within families. In Yongfu of southwest Fujian, we discovered an ordination center for Lüshan local Taoists for the neighboring five counties. This changes our conception of the Lüshan school, especially on the way it was transmitted. Our research team member, Ye Mingsheng has written a monograph on the Yongfu transmission center for the Lüshan School.

450313.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
450313.value: Our extensive fieldwork has led us to link the Pu’an ritual tradition in Jiangxi to the ritual traditions in mid-Hunan, northwest Yunnan and Minnan (southern Fujian). We have found in Minnan, mid-Hunan and northwest Yunnan both close collaboration and competition between the Buddhist and Taoist ritual traditions. We also found a ‘Taoization’ of Buddhism in ritual in the three areas. A follow-up project has been developed along this line and an application for the follow-up project has been submitted for the next round of the General Research Fund.

450413.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
450413.value: 樹皮布是一種植物性的無紡布，曾在熱帶地區十分流行，用木拍或石拍打制而成。近幾十年來，大量的史前石拍在東南亞大陸上出土，結構特徵與樹皮布石拍有共通之處。迄今已知最古老的石拍在距今七千至六千年前於香港及環珠江口一帶出土。這些考古發現為樹皮布體系的起源提出很多重要的問題。 該研究項目從多學科角度調查東南亞史前石拍的功能。我們將對蘇拉威西島（印尼）的樹皮布製作方法和樹皮布石拍進行民族學調查、使用痕分析、以及澱粉粒殘留物分析。合作專家們分工如下： - 考古學：鄧聰教授是石器技術專家。有近三十年的東亞史前考古研究經驗。是首位就東南亞史前石拍文化圈體系分布和分類進行了全面整理的考古學家。焦天龍教授有豐富南中國、太平洋考古研究的經驗，對太平洋樹皮布的民族資料熟悉。 - 民族學：蘇拉威西博物館的Iksam Djorimi先生是蘇拉威西樹皮布文化專家。蘇拉威西是世上絕少數見到仍用石拍打制樹皮布的生產地之一，適合與南中國史前石拍進行比較分析。 - 古植物學：葛威教授是澱粉粒殘留物分析的專家。葛教授將負責找出土石拍和樹皮布樹種關係的證據。這是首次用澱粉粒殘留物來分析史前石拍功能的研究計畫。 此項研究計畫首次試圖以民族考古學的角度，研究樹皮布在東南亞史前的起源。蘇拉威西最後一代的樹皮布製作者現在已達老齡，必須儘早訪問調查。香港和東南亞地區史前石拍的功能，從以上的合作定能增進瞭解，對此地區甚至全球樹皮布衣服體系的歷史有很重要的貢獻。

450413.label: Realisation of objectives
450413.value: Applying a multidisciplinary approach, this project employed ethnographic and archaeological studies to achieve significant results regarding the function of prehistoric stone beaters in Hong Kong and Southeast Asia. Firstly, PI conducted long-term ethnographic research in Sulawesi and Java islands of Indonesia on the barkcloth variety. He comprehensively documented stone beaters, wooden bats, and manufacturing processes of barkcloth. PI conducted an in-depth comparison between barkcloth tools in regional settlements. PI also investigated the production of Dluwang (bark paper). Secondly, PI examined the use-wear of over 100 ethnographic stone beaters from the Palu museum in Sulawesi and Bada village. This data was combined with archaeological data on the use-wear of hundreds of excavated stone beaters along the Pearl River Estuary, Vietnam and Sulawesi for comparison. As the unearthed artifacts share similar use-wear as the ethnographic stone beaters in Indonesia, the project’s outcome demonstrates the functions of prehistoric stone beaters. PI also observed the hafting process made by barkcloth specialists, which enriched our understanding of prehistoric stone beaters. The third objective was achieved through capturing close-up photography of ethnographic and unearthed stone beaters with a Nikon DSLR D800 and a Dino-Lite. PI focused on the production technology, use-wear, and the hafting method reflected on the barkcloth beaters. Over 2,000 photographs had been recorded, demonstrating the use-wear characteristics of modern and prehistoric beaters. This first-hand data provided crucial insights of the unearthed stone beaters functionality. The last objective was to provide direct evidence of the function of excavated stone beaters. Starch grain analyses were performed on ethnographic barkcloth in Laos, Thailand, Yunnan and Hainan provinces in China, and Taiwan. Samples of plant fiber and starch were also taken from the ethnographic stone beaters from Sulawesi, Indonesia. Furthermore, different starch and plant fibers have been identified from the unearthed stone beaters in Tai Wan, Fu Tei Wan, Yung Long, Man Kok Tsui in Hong Kong, Baojingwan in Zhuhai, and Shuichong. The outcome of these analyses provided extremely valuable information that prehistoric stone beaters once served as a barkcloth production tool. For the ethnographic research, PI compared the stone beaters found in Lore Lindu National Park, and beaters found among Pandere Kaili People, Lengkeka Tuare People and Toraja People. The combination of wooden bats and stone beaters was the majority of these ethnographic beaters, with one exception of a wooden composite beater used by the Pandere People. In the Gintu village in Sulawesi, PI observed a mother and a daughter, named Hungkeke Pole and Elizabeth Role respectively, producing barkcloth. PI documented videos and hundreds of photographs from the production technology perspective. Ethnic minorities in Central Sulawesi produce barkcloth by combining multiple tools. This highly developed process begins with tree felling, the Paper Mulberry (Broussonetia papyrifera vent. Sieb) being the most commonly used tree. Paper Mulberry can be logged in two to three years, while the bark is approximately 3-5mm. People plant it in their backyard, and harvest when necessary. Production is performed at a workshop outside people’s houses. A wooden platform is set in the middle, with two banana tree trunks as a support on the side. As banana tree trunks are soft and flexible, they are ideal supporting pads. The trunks are usually 2 meters tall. The outer bark is removed by knife. The inner bark is peeled off , rinsed under water, and transferred into earthenware with banana leaves for three days of fermentation. The barkcloth producer then neatly stacks barkcloth that is approximately 1m in length and 7-8cm wide on a rectangular wooden surface. The bark is layered in four to five layers, until approximately 1cm in thickness. Barkcloth tools used for beating consists of three wooden bats and five stone beaters. The bark is repeatedly beaten to 2-3mm. Initially, two wooden bats with 3 to 5 grooves will be used to loosen bark fibers. The bat is effective in quickly stretching the bark. A stone beater is then employed for evenness for precisely controlling the thickness of the barkcloth. The grooves found on stone beaters can range from 7-70. As soft bark receives prolonged beating by stone beater, the surface is smooth. Producers use one or both of their hands for beating. Balance is hard to maintain when using one hand, resulting with damage to the top and side of the stone beaters. Contrarily, using both hands result in the stone beaters being broken in half due to excessive force while beating. The last step involves using a wooden bat to beat dried barkcloth for a softer finish. Currently, only stone beaters have been unearthed in archaeological record. However, the possible usage of wooden bat in prehistoric times should not overlooked. As the excavated stone beaters dated to 6000 to 7000BP in the Pearl River Estuary have been found with use-wear on both the top and side, and some being broken into half, this strongly indicates that these excavated stone beaters shared similar production technology as the modern ethnographic samples. We found the following common characteristics of the use-wear on ethnographic and excavated stone beaters. We first divided them horizontally and vertically into four sections. It is evident that stone beaters are polished at the top, whereas the grooves on the sides show wide range of breakage. Only minimal damage has been shown on the bottom. In terms of weight, ethnographic stone beaters in Sulawesi are roughly 30 grams. Unearthed stone beaters, however, have a larger variation in its weight, ranging from 20 grams to 1 kilogram. The weight have changed significantly through time. In terms of the hafting method, the ethnographic stone beaters in Sulawesi have grooves on the sides installed with rattan. Interestingly, the stone beaters in Zhongshan in Pearl River Estuary, Baojingwan in Zhuhai, Gexinqiao in Guangxi, and Fengyuan in Vietnam are also found with grooves, possibly for hafting. Applying use-wear analysis, weight comparison, and traces of hafting to our comparative studies, we concluded that various use-wear found on unearthed stone beaters resulted from prolonged beating of barkcloth. PI systematically documented over 100 barkcloth beaters unearthed in the Pearl River Estuary and over 200 ethnographic stone beaters found in Makassar, Manado, Palu and Jakarta in Indonesia. They were categorized by use-wear and traces of hafting. Photographs were captured by separating the stone beaters into the aforementioned four sections. The general phenomenon is severe damage to the top and edge, where over 60% of excavated stone beaters share such use-wear. A lack of damaged ethnographic stone beaters may have resulted from damaged stone beaters not being collected. Bark fibers and starches of Paper Mulberry were identified on the Sulawesi ethnographic stone beater. In Hong Kong, the three stone beaters excavated in Tai Wan dated to 6,000BP have also been found with intriguing results. Stone beaters DW01 and DW03 were found with flat-shaped tree fiber and starch, whereas DW02 had tube-shaped fiber. The stone beaters unearthed in Fu Tei Wan and Yung Long were identified with substantial evidence of starch and fiber. Moreover, the stone beaters found in Zhuhai have been detected with large amount of starch. The lack of systematic databases of prehistoric starch and tree fibers in China creates obstacles in determining the species of these plant fibers and starch. An in-depth comparative study thus requires further work.

450413.label: Major findings and research outcome
450413.value: 1. There has been an ongoing debate on the functionality of prehistoric stone beaters unearthed from over twenty sites in the Pearl River Delta dated to 6,000 to 7,000 BP. PI Tang advocated that we must analyze through the techno-typologies of these artifacts, as the form of an artifacts must have a strong correlation to its application. In the book TAPA: From Tree Bark to Cloth: An Ancient of Oceania From Southeast Asia to Eastern Polynesia, PI discussed the prehistoric stone beaters excavated from the Pearl River Delta through their techno-typologies and evidence of use-wear. After he combined these studies with the ethnographic materials he collected, he concluded that the stone beaters were indeed for barkcloth production. TAPA is the leading multilingual book regarding barkcloth in recent years, compiled with international scholars. PI’s paper was published in English and French (abstract), and it can be regarded as the most representative academic work in Europe and the Americas on the origin of barkcloth. PI also conducted an in-depth discussion on the origin of unearthed stone beaters and their dispersion in prehistoric East Asia. This is a significant contribution to the study of the history of barkcloth culture and the study of the origin of human clothing. 2. PI published an article in the book Beaten Bark: Hidden Treasure Fuya, Tapa, Daluang along with the Beaten Bark Exhibition held at the Jakarta Textile Museum in 2016. The book is compiled with international scholars of barkcloth culture in English and Indonesian. 3. In this project, PI had the opportunity to document over 200 ethnographic and excavated stone beaters in Indonesia, especially in the island Sulawesi. He created a systematic database with large amount of photographs and materials of these stone beaters according to the production technology and use-wear of the stone beaters for analysis. These academic materials have proven that the barkcloth stone beaters in Sulawesi are originated from Southeast Asia, and especially Vietnam. 4. PI conducted a comprehensive and in-depth study on prehistoric stone beaters unearthed from the Neolithic Age to the Bronze Age in the Pearl River Estuary. He collected a large quantity of first-hand data regarding the production technology and functions of these stone beaters. As the earliest stone beaters were unearthed in this region, the data PI collected has tremendous significance in the research of barkcloth history.

450413.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
450413.value: 1. With the significant outcome from this project, a monograph regarding the origin of barkcloth culture is being planned to be published in the next two to three years. 2. Renowned scholars of the origins of paper in the world have always speculated the raw materials and production technology of barkcloth-making are the important basis for the origin of true paper. Through this project, PI had the opportunity to observe extremely rare ethnographic materials of bark paper in Bandung, Java. In 2017, PI presented the topic “From Bark Paper to Barkcloth” in the Department of Archaeology at the Jilin University. PI hopes to explore the origin of paper in the future based on the research of barkcloth history.

450413.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
450413.value: From the perspective of ethnoarcheology in the history of human clothing, it is speculated that the origin of non-woven fabric barkcloth originated in southern China. Since 1990, a significant amount of prehistoric stone beaters with grooves on its sides have been unearthed in the Pearl River Estuary. These were new discoveries that the Chinese archaeological community had never experienced in the past. This kind of stone beater is also absent in the ethnographic data in China. Through this project, PI investigated the complete process of barkcloth manufacturing in Bada village in Sulawesi, Indonesia, where it is the only place in the world with people still using stone beaters to produce barkcloth today. He was able to document various use-wear found in the production of stone beaters and throughout its usage. With the living fossils of stone beaters in Indonesia today, PI collected the ethnographic data and compared it with the archaeological materials in the Pearl River Delta. PI concluded that the prehistoric stone beaters unearthed in this region were barkcloth stone beaters. The outcome of this research is crucial for the study of the origin of non-woven fabric, and the history of human clothing.

450513.label: Project Objectives
450513.value: The overall objective is to conduct a systematic documentation of the basic grammar of HKSL. Current research on HKSL is rather sketchy and lacks collaborative efforts to uncover systematically the properties of the language at different linguistic levels. The proposed project is timely as previous findings offer a point of departure enabling the researchers to further uncover the grammatical properties intrinsic to HKSL, leading to the compilation of a reference grammar of HKSL. At the level of sign language phonetics/phonology, a primary goal is to ascertain the number of contrastive handshapes and locations in HKSL. The accuracy of descriptions will facilitate the organization of sign language dictionaries that usually involve handshape and locatoin to be the primary index for sign categorization. Identification of the types of phonological processes and nonmanuals at different linguistic levels will fill a major gap in the study of sign language phonology. At the level of lexicon and morphology, the proposed project aims to identify a list of word classes in HKSL, and to examine under what categorical membership may occur within the grammar. Word formational processes such as compounding is another focus at this level, in particular, how meaningful units are combined in a sequential or simultaneous fashion during the process, and which sublexical unit(s) are being deployed for what types of word formation in HKSL. At the level of morphosyntax, the project will confirm how different phonological components of sign formation are deployed to encode morpholocial, syntactic or semantic functions in HKSL, namely pronouns, verb agreement, aspectual modulation, number incorporation, classifier constructions, etc. We aim to derive a set of descriptively adequate criteria in the analysis of these prominent components of the language. At the level of syntax, the project will ascertain the word order of a variety of syntactic structures such as negation and modals, nominal structures, and verbal structures. Clause combining strategies in subordination and coordination will also be analyzed. Parallel to this analysis is to identify the obligatoriness and spread of nonmanuals that accompany these syntactic structures, to ascertain whether the use of nonmanuals to mark syntactic structures is a universal phenomenon among sign languages.
