450513.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
450513.value: The proposed project aims to compile a reference grammar of Hong Kong Sign Language (HKSL), a language used by members of the HK Deaf community. Historically, linguistic research on HKSL started in 1993 when attempts were made to document individual signs for purpose of compiling a sign language dictionary to support local Deaf developments. This led to a series of small scale research projects examining the linguistic organization of HKSL at the phonological, morphological and syntactic level. To date, we understand that HKSL demonstrates natural language properties in terms of linguistic structure and interpretation, and that simultaneity and use of space in linguistic organization are characteristic of the language. These properties manifest themselves in how phonological parameters of handshape, location, movement, palm orientation and lexical non-manuals are combined in individual sign formation; how morphological units are “stacked up” in compounding, verb agreement, aspectuality, and classifier predicates; and how certain nonmanuals co-occur with constituent structures articulated manually but serially. To a linguist, it is most exciting to see how linguistic theories may be applied to analyzing languages occurring in the visual modality, and whether certain properties internal to the language are modality specific. While celebrating the emergence of this research discipline in HK, the scattered studies conducted so far in no way justify an adequate description of the HKSL grammar. Indeed, it is time to take stock of the current findings and to verify the controversial linguistic phenomena observed in the literature. The proposed project promotes collaboration with members of the Deaf community in the systematic documentation of the grammar of HKSL, with a view to ultimately enriching the linguistic accounts of HKSL. Examples of gaps of linguistic descriptions are many, namely contrastive phonological units involving handshapes and location and types of phonological processes; the relationship between movement modulation and sign language morphology; the issue of hierarchical structure as demonstrated in coordination and subordination; the lexical, morphological, syntactic and prosodic functions of nonmanuals; and finally the semantics of HKSL which is left largely unexplored. These phenomena form the basis of investigation in the current project. Significantly, the findings of this unprecedented research project will be translated into some basic linguistic descriptions in the form of a reference grammar, a long-awaited output to benefit developments in sign language teaching, deaf education, speech and language rehabilitation, as well as sign interpretation, research areas that are still underdeveloped in Hong Kong. 本提議研究項目旨在按香港聾人社區所使用的香港手語(HKSL)編制一套參考語法。有關香港手語的語言學研究開始於1993年，當時研究人員記錄了各個手語，用以編制一本手語詞典來支持本地聾人發展。這些研究進而發展出一系列小型的研究項目，從音系、形態及句法層面探究香港手語的語言學組織形式。 目前，無論是從語言學結構的角度還是從釋義的角度，我們經已知悉香港手語展示出的自然語言性質，并瞭解了這一語言在語言學組織形式上的特點：同時性及使用空間。這些特徵通過以下這些方式得到表現：手型、位置、動作、手掌朝向及詞彙非手控特徵這些音系參數的組合的；形態單位在詞素複合、動詞一致、體態以及量詞謂語中的疊加；某些非手控特徵是如何與連續性的手控的成份結構共現。對於語言學家而言最令人興奮的是，語言學理論是如何被運用在分析這些視覺模式的語言的，以及一些手語內在的特徵是否具有其模式獨特性。 儘管這一研究學科在香港的出現是值得慶賀的，目前為止所做的研究仍十分分散，尚不足以完整描述香港手語語法。的確，我們需要對現有的發現進行盤點，并確認文獻中觀測到的一些語言現象。本提議研究項目將會推進與聾人社區成員的合作，并系統性地記錄香港手語語法，以冀最終豐富有關香港手語的語言學解釋。暫缺的語言學解釋尚有許多，例如包含手型及位置的對比性音系單位以及音系變化過程；動作調節與手語形態的關係；在並列及從屬結構中體現的層級結構問題；非手控特徵在詞彙、形態、句法及韻律的功能；以及最終，香港手語的語義系統，其中大部份的問題都尚未探索。這些現象構成了本研究項目的調查基礎。 本研究項目最終會通過參考語法的形式轉化為一些基本的語言學描述，這一期待已久的產出將會使得手語語言教學、聾人教育、言語及語言康復訓練以及手語翻譯等一系列在香港尚未發展完備的研究領域受益。

450513.label: Realisation of objectives
450513.value: The overall objective of the project is to conduct a systematic documentation of the basic grammar of Hong Kong Sign Language (HKSL) (i.e. objective 1), in particular, to document the basic linguistic properties at the phonetic/phonological, lexicon and morphological, morphosyntactic and syntactic level (i.e. objectives 2 to 5). To achieve these objectives, the following strategies have been adopted: 1. Training of hearing students and especially Deaf researchers in Sign Linguistics to facilitate (a) collection of sign language data, (b) design of elicitation materials, (c) transcription of HKSL data; 2. Examining the linguistic properties of HKSL at the level of phonetics and phonology, lexicon and morphology, morphosyntax as well as syntax (i.e. objectives 2-5); and 3. Disseminate findings of the linguistic properties of HKSL through presentations at conferences and publications, as well as the construction of a publicly accessible portal ‘Hong Kong Sign Language Corpus’ to facilitate future research and training developments in HKSL. In what follows, we will report on how and to what extent the overall objectives have been achieved. As for Strategy (1), the project has funded a full time research assistant position for a student who concurrently pursues part-time PhD study in Sign Linguistics. In addition, three more PhD students, one MA student, and two undergraduate Deaf students have received training in Sign Linguistics during the course of project implementation. They were invited to investigate specific domains of HKSL that interest them. The full time research assistant/part-time PhD student is compiling her PhD thesis on ‘reflexivity in HKSL’. The second PhD student is compiling her PhD thesis on ‘classifier realization in sign languages’. She is writing up a paper on causativity and transitivity in HKSL and Tianjin SL. The third PhD student is developing her research on the psycholinguistic processing of HKSL at different linguistic levels. Currently, she is writing up a paper on categorical perception of HKSL handshapes. The fourth PhD student is writing up a paper on the syntactic structure of nominal expressions. One MA student is completing her research paper justifying the existence of noun classifiers in HKSL. Two Deaf undergraduate students of linguistics have completed their BA graduating papers. One paper examines reduplication in HKSL and the other on the morphological realization of the marked and unmarked distinction with degree adjectives in HKSL. For this specific project, a novice Deaf adult has been recruited and trained to support the development of the HKSL Corpus; he is responsible for identifying Deaf adults in HK, organizing data collection activities with them, transcribing and coordinating the transcription of corpus data, checking the accuracy of data transcription, and collaborating with hearing researchers in the design of elicitation materials for specific grammatical components. Overall speaking, the project has achieved its objectives of generating a team of Deaf and hearing expertise to support Sign Linguistics research and training developments in HK, and the HKSL data will contribute to the call for data from understudied sign languages globally. As for Strategy (2) (Objectives 2-5), which is the documentation of HKSL at the levels of phonology and phonetics, lexicon and morphology, morphosyntax and syntax. Data documentation through video archives is complete 100%. The glossing of signing data is complete 100%: all video data (12 narratives, 16 dyads of spontaneous conversational data totaling 18 hours of recordings, and some other data generated through international collaboration) have been transcribed and glossed, and accuracy of transcription checked. While fieldnotes on the basic properties of HKSL phonology, phonetics, morphosyntax and morphology are 100% complete (objectives 2-4), fieldnotes on HKSL syntax are just 95% complete. Specifically, detailed fieldnotes of some of the basic properties, including nominal structure, pronouns and impersonals, syntactic position of certain functional elements, and word order variation with verb types have been confirmed; however, the project has yet to confirm properties associated with coordination and subordination as well as nonmanuals. Our strategy was to gloss all the signing data as the first phase of development when the training with the Deaf researchers was done. On average it took 3 to 4 months to gloss one hour of free conversations between two signers. As for nonmanuals, the original plan was to recruit two Deaf researchers who have some initial experience in supporting Sign Linguistics research at the Centre for Sign Linguistics and Deaf Studies to conduct this analysis. The project planned to give them additional training to help them distinguish linguistic nonmanuals from emotional expressions because their boundaries could be blurred even to native signers sometimes. Coincidentally, the two Deaf researchers that the project planned to recruit were admitted to CUHK to do a full-time top up BA in Linguistics, which prevented them to engage in the coding of nonmanuals. The PI regarded giving them priority to their study was more important than the project. Given the Deaf situation in HK, it was difficult to replace with another two Deaf researchers who had already had some initial experience in Sign Linguistic research. It turns out the coding of nonmanuals is complete for narratives but not for conversational data. Additionally, the Co-Pi, Dr. Scholastica Lam, who pledged to focus on some complex syntactic constructions of HKSL involved in coordination and subordination, decided to leave the Centre, due to family reasons. All these happenings have prevented the project from advancing the syntactic analysis (i.e. objective 5) to cover nonmauals and some complex constructions, to an extent that the project has originally intended to achieve. Since the two Deaf researchers have just completed their BA in Linguistics study, to be graduated in 2018 fall, the Project plans to recruit them to cover the nonmanual component of the HKSL data. The project has led to 13 conference presentations, 2 journal papers (in press), and 2 book chapters (one in press and one under revision). All have acknowledged the support of the GRF grant. The project hopes to generate a few more papers on the following topics, classifier realization, reduplication, degree adjectives, and nominal structure. Agreement to formally publish a reference grammar of HKSL has been reached with Mouton de Gruyter under the Sign Language Typology Series and a book contract is being prepared. The submission of the manuscript is scheduled to be 2020 fall. We hope to advance our analysis of the syntax of HKSL in the interim and to embark on some semantic analysis of HKSL in order to enrich the book contents. Additionally, a publicly accessible portal ‘Hong Kong Sign Language Corpus’ (www.cslds.org/hkslcorpus) will be announced at The Sign Language and Linguistics Society. The portal presents different types of data, including narratives elicited by animated cartoons and picture books, naturalistic data from free conversations, and experimental data from different elicitation materials. All types of data contain video recordings with multiple synchronized video cameras and annotations created by ELAN (https://tla.mpi.nl/tools/tla-tools/elan/, Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics, The Language Archive, Nijmegen, The Netherlands; Crasborn & Sloetjes, 2008). The project has also generated a set of elicitation materials for phonological handshape recognition, locative existentials, motion and location predicates, transitives, causatives and resultatives, telicity and agentivity, whole-entity versus handling classifiers, person and spatial agreement, syntax of modals, negators, and auxiliary HAVE, wh-interrogatives, as well as nonmanul adverbials. These materials pave the way for future projects especially the construction of sign language assessment for clinical, social and educational purposes.

450513.label: Major findings and research outcome
450513.value: By constructing a corpus with a relatively larger set of data from native Deaf signers, we can systematically examine HKSL grammar at different levels systematically, namely phonetics/phonology, lexicon and morphology, morphosyntax, and syntax. For phonetics and phonology, we have conducted both qualitative and quantitative analyses of 2,293 signs from the HKSL Corpus, we managed to reanalyze the contrastive handshapes and location parameters. Additionally, the quantitative analysis of movement and lexical nonmanuals further confirm our previous findings. In terms of morphology, a total of sixteen word classes have been identified in the lexicon of HKSL. Compounding is a very productive morphological process in sign formation in HKSL. Other morphological processes confirmed are numeral incorporation and affixation for classifiers, agreement, quantification and aspectuality. By examining the narrative and free conversation data, we have confirmed that different phonological parameters are employed to encode morphological, syntactic, and semantic functions in HKSL. Among which, handshape is adopted to refer to arguments of predicates, number and plurality, manner of manipulation, and object delimitation. Movement as a parameter often undergoes modulations to encode person and spatial agreement, event quantification, aspectuality, and predicate meaning. At the level of syntax, word order in different structures has been examined. It shows that functional elements in HKSL often appear at the sentence-final position. Two mechanism of combining clauses, coordination and subordination, have been further studied in this project. In addition to presenting the findings at conferences, two journal papers have been accepted for publication this year. One of them examined a sub-type of impersonal constructions, R-impersonals, in HKSL. Three strategies of encoding R-impersonals are reported: the use of a non-specific and indefinite determiner ONEdet-path (someone/anyone), null forms, and a character sign PERSON/HUMAN. Among which, the use of ONEdet-path (someone/anyone) is the most preferred one for HKSL native signers. The study provides supporting evidence that R-impersonals generally receive arbitrary interpretation, and impersonal subjects have quantificational and anaphoric properties. In the other journal paper, we developed a formal account for classifier constructions in HKSL and applied this analysis into explaining bimodal bilingual Deaf children’s acquisition of classifier constructions, in terms of crosslinguistic influence from spoken languages into sign languages. A third paper co-authored by Li Jia and Tang, Gladys offers an overview of sign language grammar based on HKSL and Chinese Sign Language data, covering phonology, morphology and basic syntax.

450513.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
450513.value: The current GRF grant has enabled the PI and her Deaf and hearing team of researchers to develop a corpus of HKSL, to confirm some preliminary observations of its linguistic properties, and to initiate analysis of grammatical domains that have not been tapped previously. The PI will recruit the two Deaf BA graduates to complete the coding of nanmauals. With the corpus set up, the team of researchers will continue to investigate the syntax of HKSL, especially the properties associated with complex sentences as exemplified in coordination and subordination, topics and focus, and other related phenomena such as ellipsis. There is still a domain of HKSL grammar that awaits investigation, which is the semantics of HKSL. Recent advances in sign linguistic research have begun to probe into quantification of objects and events, telicity and spatial pointing, etc. The PI hopes to apply for further funding to support this line of research in future. Additionally, the data from the corpus will serve as a reference for the adult grammar in our investigation on how deaf children acquire HKSL. Acquisition research has been hampered by a lack of adult grammar. With the corpus in hand, an obvious advantage is to consult the data for the adult grammar as baseline for comparison. The corpus will also be used to support Deaf instructors in developing teaching materials, and sign interpreter trainers to extract naturalistic data for sign interpretation training.

450513.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
450513.value: The project is the first ever attempt in Hong Kong to document a visual-gestural language - Hong Kong Sign Language (HKSL) – to justify its linguistic status and social as well as education value. It aims at producing a record and a description of the linguistic properties of HKSL. The record comprises videos capturing and preserving the language that is expressed in the visual-gestural modality, through transcriptions of the language into glosses and annotations in English to facilitate international access. More specifically, the annotations leave a record for future identification of analyzable grammatical properties. The descriptions also demonstrate how an annotation system may be employed to show the language functions in how signs are formed with handshape, movement, location and orientation, and how signs are combined to form compounds, phrases and sentences; how signers make use of nonmanuals to encode grammatical and discourse functions. The project also demonstrates the benefits of collaborative research involving both hearing and Deaf researchers trained in Sign Linguistics. This team of experts will continue to unravel the grammatical properties of HKSL at deeper levels. The set of elicitation materials created in the process of data collection has strong application value, especially for the construction of sign language assessment for clinical, social and educational purposes. To allow public access for local and sign language research purpose worldwide, a portal ‘Hong Kong Sign Language Corpus’ will be announced at the Sign Language and Linguistics Society.

450813.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
450813.value: To address issues of climate change, traffic congestion and decreasing fossil-fuel resources, policy makers, planners and designers are looking at Hong Kong as a model which links high density areas with an efficient public mass transport system. Locally speaking, however, residents’ concerns about the model’s effects on affordability, everyday culture and community life have grown. As a long-term study, this research project will investigate the impacts of the West Island Line, a soon to be completed Mass Transit Railway (MTR) project, on public spaces and community life. It builds on the applicant’s current GRF project, Measuring Community Benefit in Public Space Transformation in Sai Ying Pun, which collects and examines a range of analytical data, mappings, video documentations, ethnographic observations, surveys and interviews. The proposed project would start in 2014, after the completion of the current Sai Ying Pun research and in the year when the new MTR West Island Line begins to operate. The West Island Line is a westbound extension of the existing Island Line, connecting the districts of Sai Ying Pun, Shek Tong Tsui and Kennedy Town with Hong Kong’s financial center and the wider territory. A western extension of the Island Line was planned for the first time as early as in the late 1960s (Freeman, Smith and Associates, 1967), but only in 2009 did the construction of a revised project commence. Until now, the district has been served mainly by means of road transportation, including buses, mini-buses and taxis. However, a different way of living in the Western District is expected upon the opening of the West Island Line. A comparison between the district's earlier conditions and the changes brought about by the new MTR line will further the understanding of the long-term impacts of infrastructure developments on quality of living in dense urban areas. The West Island Line development is of particular interest also because here the MTR Corporation Limited has integrated public participation into its planning process from the very beginning. The research project will therefore include an examination of the results of this approach, as an important test case for community-based infrastructure planning in Hong Kong. The project will conclude with the definition and evaluation of the “Hong Kong model” of infrastructure-related urban design and planning. This model then can be used as a reference in the international discussions on sustainable urban development. 此項計劃旨在研究港鐵西港島綫為香港公共空間和社區生活所帶來的轉變，在優配研究金(GRF)計劃“Measuring Community Benefit in Public Space Transformation in Older Urban Districts: A Case Study of Sai Ying Pun＂的基礎上，提供一系列數據分析、繪圖統計、照片和錄像資料，再配以民族誌式的考察和訪問，進行全面性的研究。計劃將於上述優配研究金計劃完成後展開，主要紀錄港鐵西港島綫在2014年落成後產生的影響。此研究計劃透過比較西環在新港鐵綫通車前後的社區面貌，深入了解基建發展對本港生活質素的長遠影響。 新的研究不會重覆早前GRF計劃所做過的，而會在其基礎上延伸出來，評估港鐵西港島綫的規劃模式。西港島綫有異於港鐵以前的項目，在於這條新鐵路將啟用於香港最古老的城區，並相應引入了很多社區參與、共融的理念。研究將分析西港島綫對社區帶來的影響，以評估港鐵的新方向能否成為香港城市規劃的里程碑。研究的結論不但有助於香港日後的城市規劃發展，同時亦給予中國內地一個參照的對象：北京正在籌劃中的地鐵擴建工程，便影響到城內多個舊區，以及當中的市井文化、社區生活。

450813.label: Realisation of objectives
450813.value: The longitudinal nature of the research project allowed capturing the changes of the public spaces and their usage before and after the completion of the MTR West Island Line. The research project also permitted the comparisons with the finding of an earlier General Research Fund project in Sai Ying Pun. As previously mentioned in the mid-term report, due to the significant reduction of the funding (HK$ 100,000 for three years), the research objectives were adjusted and subsequently approved by the UGC to focus mainly on the Sai Ying Pun area. With a range of research activities and a parallel conducted community outreach project (“Magic Carpet”) the revised objectives could be achieved. Starting out with the broad objectives to understand the impact of the newly opened metro line, the research project first focused on the investigations of the urban spaces and community life and then addressed the development of a district community benefit plan for a more holistic and community oriented planning in Sai Ying Pun. Built upon interdisciplinary approaches, research methods included the photo survey of local stores, interviews with residents, and analytical drawings and three-dimensional models to evaluate spatial design of old and new public spaces and surrounding buildings. Specifically, to capture the changes of the urban environment induced by the new infrastructure development, activities in various streets and public spaces were filmed. The physical changes in the district were documented in the photo survey of local businesses during and after the completion of the metro line. The photo survey of local shops was important as these shops are seen as an essential part of the local culture and places of much of the social interaction in the district. In 2012, the research team had photographed around 300 shop-fronts. These shop-fronts were photographed again in 2015 after the opening of the metro. 25 video interviews with shopkeepers and residents were conducted in 2013 as part of the “Magic Carpet” community outreach project and five of them were retaken in 2016. The video interviews are freely accessible online on the project website and constitute an oral history archive of the fast changing district. The website also includes drawings and photos of the district’s public spaces. Community benefits were achieved through collaborations with the local school King’s College (as part of the Magic Carpet project) and with social workers and volunteers from Caritas Hong Kong. With the social workers and volunteers, the team organized annual community workshops and a District Council Election Forum to facilitate discussions on public spaces and community development. The continuing collaboration with Caritas provides deeper insights about the changing conditions and concerns of the people working and living in the district, particularly those residents with low income and special needs. Additionally, the co-organized place-making events allowed testing interventions of alternative spatial arrangements and gathering residents’ feedback and insights. These interventions enhanced the understanding of who decides – on the ground – how the public spaces are designed, managed and used. Furthermore, the research objective of connecting research and teaching activities was realized by incorporating students in the research and community activities. Students of the BSSc in Urban Studies and MSc in Urban Design programmes participated in the project through activities in a range of courses (URSP2300 Urban Design and Placemaking, URBD5710 Urban Design Studio, URBD5731 Urban Processes & URBD 5732 Urban Transport Networks). The joint efforts of the research team, students, social workers, volunteers, and secondary school students (supported by an additional Knowledge Transfer Fund for the Magic Carpet project) have produced a range of multi-media materials e.g., physical and digital models, drawings, photos and videos to capture the relationships between the physical environment, public space and the social activities in the area affected by the new MTR line.

450813.label: Major findings and research outcome
450813.value: The interdisciplinary approach enabled the understanding of how urban transformation has been evolved and how the new MTR West Island line affected community life. Our survey showed that residents generally appreciate the convenience and faster commute brought by the new metro line. However, some expressed concerns of the sharply rising rental prices and others concerned the loss of community cohesion. Mappings and photo surveys showed not only an increasing vertical growth of buildings but also increasingly impermeable ground floor levels, adversely affecting the district’s streetscape. Detailed drawings and 3d models highlighted the differences of spaces provided by the different stakeholders involved in regards to the provided accessibility and amenities. The government had promised that the new MTR line would reduce vehicular traffic and thus create a better living environment. Thus the project investigated particularly how walkability was improved. However, in Sai Ying Pun the newly created public spaces of the MTR and URA were not linked to an overall strategy to improve the pedestrian environment, instead, 1) More handrails were put-up reducing the widths of sidewalks and obstruct freer pedestrian movement; 2) pedestrianized parts of Centre Street continued to lack basic amenities such as seating; and 3) no solutions were developed to provide safe pedestrian access to the health cluster and public space across Eastern Street, leaving substantial obstacles for walkability, particular for disabled, elderly, and young families. In sum, there appears to have been missed opportunities for a more fundamental upgrading of public spaces and the pedestrian environment. At the same time, the sharp increase of property prices and the replacement of old buildings by high-rise towers put significant pressure on the existing community. To optimize Hong Kong’s model of using large transport infrastructure projects to boost urban renewal the following steps are suggested: - Draft a district-based community benefit plan based on local aspirations and needs, considering local characteristics, spatial challenges and opportunities. - Develop an integrated public space network to maximize the full potential of vehicular traffic reduction and achieve overall an improved pedestrian environment. - Consider proactively inclusiveness and special needs of disabled, elderly and young families. - Address proactively the sharp rise of property prices to ensure a fairer share of the created improvements. - Create spaces and activities to foster community cohesion and social interaction to counteract socio-spatial polarisation during the dynamic transformation process.

450813.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
450813.value: The idea of the community benefit plan was developed by the PI and Associate Prof. Min Jay Kang at the National Taiwan University. The joint book book discusses the approaches in both cities: M.J. Kang & H. Tieben, Magic Carpet - Towards Community Benefit Plans for Urban Regeneration in Taipei and Hong Kong, Taipei: Tonshan (in print / Dec 2017), 457 pages. The team of the PI, Caritas Hong Kong and the Conservancy Association Centre for Heritage applied successfully for an Urban Renewal Fund and started in 2017 with a pilot project for a public space project in Sai Ying Pun (Magic Lanes) realising ideas of the envisioned community benefit plan. As Hong Kong's MTR system is further expanding, the PI could participate as academic consultant in a consultancy study of Kowloon City, commissioned by the URA, using the same study approach. He combined this research also here with the same kind of community and placemaking project (here supported by a Quality Education Fund of Hong Kong SAR Government). The extension of the research to other areas offered the opportunity to compare the findings of different districts and understand better the impact of Hong Kong's infrastructure driven development model.

450813.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
450813.value: The project was set to evaluate impacts of the MTR West Island Line on public space in the Western District, with a scope to increase community benefit for districts that may undergo similar urban transformation in the future. The findings showed that while the new metro line significantly increases the mobility of the residents and visitors, opportunities to seize the benefits of such a large infrastructure project and investment to fundamentally improve the living environment of the district have been missed, e.g., improvements of the streetscapes and public space access. Based on the research findings, steps to create community benefit plans as a basis for an integrated planning are proposed.

451113.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
451113.value: The goal of this project is to examine how word-level and character-level lexical variables influence skilled readers’ recognition of two-character Chinese compound words. Understanding basic lexical processes is a critical perquisite for an in-depth investigation of higher-order lexical activities, e.g., reading. Following the procedures adopted in Balota et al.’s (2007) English Lexicon Project, we will obtain norms for participants’ lexical decision performance using 6,000 widely-known two-character words varying on various lexical variables, e.g., word frequency. In the lexical decision task, one of the gold standards for testing lexical processing models, participants decide whether two characters form a Chinese word, e.g.,朋友(friend), or a non-word, e.g.,形忌. Words’ mean reaction times and accuracies will be analyzed via item-level regression models and participants’ reaction-time distributions will be analyzed by fitting their trial-level data to the ex-Gaussian distribution. This project will make three major contributions to the literature. First, performing item-level multiple regression analyses of reaction-time and accuracy data will shed light on the main effects of various lexical variables and their potential interactions. These goals are difficult to accomplish within factorial-design studies due to the difficulty in matching correlated extraneous lexical variables. The normed data based on a much larger word pool, relative to those in factorial-design studies, will clarify some ambiguities in the literature, particularly those involving higher-order interactions between variables. Second, a fine-grained analysis of the effects of lexical variables on the characteristics of participants’ reaction-time distribution, which has rarely been examined in the literature, will provide additional insights into effects that cannot be observed when only mean reaction-time data are examined, e.g., the nature of morphological decomposition. Third, an online database will be established and made freely available to the research community to provide normed lexical decision reaction-time and accuracy and descriptive statistics of lexical variables for Chinese compound words. By comparing this database with those in other languages, e.g., English, psycholinguists may better understand cross-linguistic differences in lexical processing, e.g., whether morphological decomposition is language-specific vs. language-universal in compound word processing. The normed data can also be used to run virtual experiments to test whether some findings derived from factorial-design studies can be replicated using different sets of stimuli. Overall, the proposed Chinese Lexicon Project will further our knowledge of Chinese word recognition processes and provide the research community with a timely online database of lexical variables and normed lexical-decision performance that will make a significant contribution to psycholinguistic research. 這個方案的目的是研究詞匯水平和漢字水平如何影響熟練閱讀者對漢語雙字詞的再認。理解詞匯基本水平的加工是深入研究高級詞匯加工（例如，閱讀）的一個關鍵的先決條件。繼Balota等人（2007）研究中採用的英文詞匯方案，我們採用六千個常用雙字詞，讓被試進行詞匯判斷任務，從而可以得到這些詞匯在不同變量水平的標準（例如：詞頻）。詞匯判斷任務是測試詞匯加工模式的黃金標準之一，在這個任務中，被試的任務是判斷兩個字是否能夠組成一個詞。例如，“朋友”是一個詞，而“形忌”則不是一個詞。對詞匯判斷的平均反應時和正確率進行基於項目的回歸分析，將反應時的分布進行試次水平的前高斯（ex-Gaussian）分布擬合。現方案對文獻有三個主要的貢獻。 首先，對反應時和正確率進行項目水平的多元回歸分析可以揭示詞匯的不同變量的主效應和交互作用。然而使用因素設計的研究很難達到該目的，因為匹配額外的詞匯變量是幾乎不能實現的。源於大量詞匯庫的標準數據與以往因素設計的研究中的數據庫不同。這些標準的數據可以澄清文獻中的一些含糊之處，尤其是對那些涉及到高水平的變量之間的相互作用。 第二，文獻中幾乎沒有研究對詞匯不同變量對被試反應時分布的影響進行研究，現方案通過精細的分析，能夠提供除了通過平均反應時所觀察到的效應外其他額外的效應，例如，形態分析的性質。 第三，現方案可以實現建立一個在線數據庫，可以免費的供研究界使用，可以提供漢語復合詞的標準化的反應時，準確率和詞匯變量的描述性統計。心理語言學家通過與其他語言（如英文）的數據庫進行比較可以更好的理解詞匯加工中跨語言的差異，例如，在混合詞匯加工中，形態分解是否是語言特異化的。這些標準化的數據還能被用於進行虛擬實驗進而探討如果採用不同的研究材料，因素研究中的發現是否能夠得以重複。 總而言之，我們提議的漢語詞匯方案能夠進一步地使我們了解漢語詞匯再認加工過程以及給研究團體提供這樣的一個及時的在線數據庫，這個數據庫中包含了不同的詞匯變量，以及詞匯判斷的標準化數據，這些對語言心理學的研究有著非常重要的意義。

451113.label: Realisation of objectives
451113.value: To achieve Objective 3, we used a megastudy approach to develop a repository of lexical variables and lexical decision behavioral measures (reaction times and accuracy rates) for more than 25,000 Chinese two-character compound words, which involved 594 native Cantonese Chinese-speaking participants in Hong Kong. After establishing this database, we performed three analyses to illustrate its potential uses. First, we compared the proportion of variance in lexical decision performance accounted for by six word frequency measures and demonstrated that the best predictor was Cai and Brysbaert’s (2010) contextual diversity subtitle frequency. Second, we ran virtual replications of three previously published lexical decision experiments (e.g., Leong & Cheng, 2003; Peng et al., 1999). We found very close convergence in the findings between the original experiments and the present megastudy. Finally, we conducted item-level regression analyses to examine the main effects of theoretically important lexical variables, such as character frequency and word frequency, in our normative data. The preliminary results were reported in our poster (Tse, Yap, Chan, Sze, & Lin, 2016, International Congress of Psychology) and the full set of analyses was reported in our manuscript (Tse, Yap, Chan, Sze, Shaoul, & Lin, 2017, Behavior Research Methods). More importantly, we make this database online available in Excel format (see http://dx.doi.org/10.3758/s13428-016-0810-5). This is the first publicly available large-scale repository of behavioral responses pertaining to Chinese two-character compound word processing, which should be of substantial interest to psychologists, linguists, and other researchers. This resource should also provide a valuable adjunct to influential mega-databases, such as the Chinese single-character, English, French, and Dutch Lexicon Projects. To achieve Objective 1, we utilized the data in the abovementioned repository to examine the main and interactive effects of lexical variables on two-character Chinese compound word processing. Specifically, we performed item-level hierarchical regression analyses on lexical decision megastudy data of more than 18,000 two-character Chinese compound words, with the multiple, typically correlated, lexical variables being controlled for. The first analysis determined the main effects of lexical variables and unique item-level variance explained by orthographic (frequency and stroke count), phonological (consistency, homophonic density), and semantic (transparency) variables. Both character and word variables were considered. Results showed that orthographic and semantic variables, respectively, accounted for more collective variance than phonological variables, suggesting that Chinese skilled readers rely more on orthographic and semantic information than phonological information when processing visually presented words. The second analysis tested interactive effects of lexical variables and showed significant semantic transparency × cumulative character frequency and word frequency × cumulative character frequency interactions. The effect of cumulative character frequency was stronger for transparent words than for opaque words and was stronger for low-frequency words than for high-frequency words. However, there was no semantic transparency × word frequency interaction in reaction time. All these analyses were reported in our manuscript (Tse & Yap, in press, Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology). Collectively, these findings cannot be easily accommodated by the extant models of Chinese compound word processing, and will serve as important benchmarks for informing new models. To achieve Objective 2, we utilized the data in the abovementioned repository to reveal the influences of lexical variables on Chinese two-character compound word processing and examine their relationship with participants’ individual differences in lexical performance, e.g., whether participants with better performance would show stronger word frequency effect in lexical decisions. The individual difference markers include (a) self-rated proficiency on the knowledge for traditional characters and spoken Cantonese and their grade-point average and Chinese language university entrance score, (b) mean lexical decision response time, (c) d-prime (based on lexical decision hits and false alarms), (d) ex-Gaussian RT distributional characteristics: µ and σ, mean and SD of leading edge, and τ, tail of the distribution, and (e) diffusion model parameters, such as drift rate (rate of accumulation of information). The ex-Gaussian RT distributional characters and diffusion model parameters (i.e., d and e) were estimated via fine-grained quantile analyses of reaction-time distributions. We found that effects of word frequency, character frequency, and number of strokes were moderated by lexical processing fluency, as reflected by d-primes and drift rates. Specifically, higher fluency participants showed larger effects of word frequency but smaller effects of stroke number and character frequency. Skilled readers are generally less sensitive to most word properties (e.g., character frequency and stroke number) but they can also flexibly attend more to word frequency (correlated with familiarity), which is diagnostic of the distinction between words and nonwords. These analyses were reported in our poster (Yap, Lim, & Tse, 2017, Annual Meeting of the Psychonomic Society). We are now working on a manuscript, which will report the full details of these analyses (Lim, Yap, & Tse, in preparation).

451113.label: Major findings and research outcome
451113.value: Using a megastudy approach, Tse, Yap, Chan, Sze, Shaoul, and Lin (2017, Behavior Research Methods) developed a database of lexical variables and lexical decision reaction times and accuracy rates for more than 25,000 traditional Chinese two-character compound words. To illustrate the potential uses of the database, we compared the proportion of variance in lexical decision performance accounted for by six word frequency measures and found that the best predictor was Cai and Brysbaert’s (2010) contextual diversity subtitle frequency. Also, we ran virtual replications of previously published lexical decision experiments and found convergence in the findings of original experiments and the present dataset. Finally, we examined the effects of theoretically important lexical variables, such as character frequency, in our dataset. This large-scale repository of lexical variables and behavioral measures is made available publicly to psychologists, linguists, and other researchers. In Tse and Yap (in press, Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology), we examined the effect of lexical variables on Chinese lexical processing by performing item-level hierarchical regression analyses on lexical decision megastudy data of 18,983 two-character Chinese compound words. First, we found that orthographic and semantic variables, respectively, accounted for more collective variance than phonological variables, suggesting that Chinese skilled readers rely more on orthographic and semantic information than phonological information when processing visually presented words. Second, we demonstrated significant semantic transparency × cumulative character frequency and word frequency × cumulative character frequency interaction effects. The effect of cumulative character frequency was stronger for transparent words than for opaque words and was stronger for low-frequency words than for high-frequency words. However, there was no semantic transparency × word frequency interaction in reaction time. These findings as a whole could not easily be accommodated by any models of Chinese lexical processing. In Lim, Yap, and Tse (in preparation), we examined the relationships between the influences of lexical variables on Chinese two-character compound word processing and participants’ individual differences in lexical performance, which were defined by various markers, including ex-Gaussian RT distributional characteristics and diffusion model parameters, as estimated via fine-grained quantile analyses of reaction-time distributions. We found that skilled readers showed larger effects of word frequency but smaller effects of stroke number and character frequency, suggesting that they were generally less sensitive to most word properties (e.g., character frequency) but they could also flexibly attend more to word frequency (correlated with familiarity), which is diagnostic of the distinction between words and nonwords.

451113.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
451113.value: After developing a repository of lexical variables and lexical decision behavioral measures for more than 25,000 Chinese two-character compound words, we plan to perform at least two additional sets of analyses to further our understanding of Chinese lexical processing. First, the linear and/or nonlinear of effect of targeted variables, such as number of strokes, could be captured more easily, which could not be observed in factorial-design experiments where variables are dichotomized. Second, the data in this database could be compared with those in other Lexicon Projects (e.g., English in Balota et al., 2007) to test cross-linguistic differences in compound word processing and help identify language-specific versus language-universal processes in lexical processing. To further utilize the current repository of lexical variables, we plan to run analogous megastudy using word naming reaction-time and accuracy as behavioral measures. This would allow a comparison of the effects of lexical variables on participants’ lexical decision and naming performance, which in turn demonstrates whether the lexical effects obtained in the current normative data would be specific to lexical decision or task-general phenomena.

451113.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
451113.value: In the lexical decision task, one of the gold standards for testing lexical processing models, participants decide whether two characters form a Chinese word, e.g., 朋友 (friend), or a non-word, e.g., 形忌. In our project, we developed a database of lexical variables, such as character frequency, and lexical decision reaction times and accuracy rates for more than 25,000 traditional Chinese two-character compound words. Using this database with a word pool much larger than previous studies, we found significant semantic transparency × cumulative character frequency and word frequency × cumulative character frequency interactions, but not semantic transparency × word frequency interaction in reaction time, which could not easily be accommodated by any Chinese lexical processing models. Skilled readers showed larger effects of word frequency but smaller effects of stroke number and character frequency, suggesting that they were generally less sensitive to most word properties (e.g., character frequency) but they could also flexibly attend more to word frequency (correlated with familiarity). Other than advancing our knowledge of Chinese word recognition processes, the database established in our project provides research community with a timely online database of lexical variables and normed lexical-decision performance.

451513.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
451513.value: The aim of the project is to investigate the frontispiece to the Ming-dynasty Daoist Canon and its different editions since its first printing in 1447 so as to bring to light the formation and changes in composition, artistic images and affiliated traditions of the imperially patronized Daoist pantheon in late imperial China. The Daoist Canon of the Ming dynasty was the only extant imperially sponsored woodblock edition of Daoist works collected from all parts of China. In sharp contrast to the texts of the Canon that were the subjects of critical analysis in the past century, its frontispiece has been neglected. The frontispiece of 1447 is a highly important historical document pictorially representing the Daoist pantheon endorsed by the imperial court of the fifteenth century. Its subsequent editions resulting from re-carving and reprinting of the Daoist Canon also shed light on the changes in conception and imagery of the orthodox Daoist pantheon among various circles in later times. The proposed project aims to explore the formation and organization of the imperially endorsed Daoist pantheon as shown in the frontispiece of 1447 and to explicate visual variations among different editions of the frontispiece so as to establish the histories of all extant copies of the Ming Daoist Canon and their frontispieces from 1447 to the present day. The outputs of the proposed project will include an archive of literary materials on the Ming Daoist Canon and the histories of all extant copies, and a database of images of different editions of the frontispiece and other visual representations of the Daoist pantheon from the Ming dynasty onward. A series of academic papers on the following topics will be produced: (1) The organization and intention of the imperially endorsed Daoist pantheon as shown in the frontispiece to the Ming Daoist Canon of 1447 and its relationship with the broader religious and visual culture (2) Visual variations in different editions of the frontispiece to the Ming Daoist Canon and their links to the changing conception and imagery of Daoist deities and pantheon among patrons who commissioned re-carving and reprinting of the copies in later periods. (3) Histories of extant copies of the Ming Daoist Canon and their frontispieces from 1447 to the present day 本研究計劃以刊刻於1447年的明《道藏》扉畫以及後世為該書重刻的扉畫為研究對象，通過對比不同版本中道教神譜的組合，神祗的藝術形象以至相關道派的轉變，從而探討明清道教神譜的變遷。 中國歷代帝皇雖曾多次進行全國性的道經收集並將之結集成藏，但惟獨明朝刊刻的《道藏》能流傳至今。過去一百年，學界對明《道藏》所藏的各種經籍進行了深入研究。然而，有關《道藏》扉畫的研究卻一直沒有展開。事實上，明《道藏》扉畫描繪了十五世紀明皇朝認可的道教神譜，為重要的歷史資料，而其後多次補刻和重印的《道藏》扉畫，更反映了歷代皇朝認可的道教神譜在觀念和藝術形式上的轉變。本研究計劃旨在探討1447年明室認可的道教神譜的組織和構成原因，並通過分析它與其後為明《道藏》重刻的扉畫的不同，藉以建立傳世幾套明《道藏》及其扉畫由1447年至今的流傳歷史。 是項計劃的研究成果將包括一個蒐集各種傳世明《道藏》的歷史文獻資料庫，以及一個明《道藏》扉畫及相關的道教視覺文化圖像資料庫。此外，本計劃亦會就以下課題出版論文： (一) 刊刻於1447年的明《道藏》扉畫所呈現的道教神譜的組成和設計目的，以及其與明代宗教和視覺文化的關係。 (二) 不同版本的明《道藏》扉畫的圖像差異，以及這些差異如何體現後代贊助《道藏》扉畫重刻和重印者對道教神祗的觀念和意像的改變。 (三) 幾套傳世明《道藏 》以及其扉畫自1447年刊印至今的流傳和修整的歷史。

451513.label: Realisation of objectives
451513.value: Objective 1: 1. In the past 3 years, the PI made 9 research trips and many online requests to collect images of about 50 copies of extant frontispieces for the Daozang, as well as those of related Buddhist and Daoist artefacts. Through comparing the Daozang frontispieces in different extant copies, the PI found that there exist only two versions of the Daozang frontispiece, namely the Ming version and the Qing version. 2. Through a comparison between the Daozang frontispiece and Yuan and Ming temple murals, the PI argues that the Daoist pantheons shown in Daozang frontispieces basically share the same principle of arrangement as that depicted on the murals of the Yuan-dynasty Daoist temple, Yongle gong. 3. Historical texts concerning the Ming court and the editor of the Daozang was carefully studied. The PI found that the imperial support of thunder rites and the affiliation of Zhao Yizheng 邵以正, the chief editor of the Daozang, to the Quanzhen 全真 and the Qingwei 清微 sects contributed to the choice of some key figures, especially thunder marshals, to be depicted in the frontispiece. 4. A long article focusing on the underlying principle of the Daoist pantheon shown in the imperially endorsed frontispiece of the Ming Daozang has been completed and submitted to a referred journal. 5. The first objective is, thus, achieved. Objective 2: 1. To understand how Daozang frontispieces related to the broader religious and visual culture, the PI studied a large amount of Ming Buddhist sutra frontispieces. Further research on the arrangement of figures in Daoist scripture frontispieces and how they are different from that found in extant early Buddhist frontispieces was conducted. 2. To explore how the printing of the Daozang frontispiece and its depiction of thunder marshals is linked to worship of thunder gods in the imperial court in the early Ming, the PI examines a wide range of Daoist scriptures, books and relics. She argues that these scriptures and books contributed to the imperial endorsement of the thunder gods as the Dark Troops safeguarding the Ming Empire. Further, she establishs that the printing and distribution of the Daozang and its frontispiece was a means of consolidating their important position. 3. Through a thorough study of the relationship between the Daozang frontispieces and the Buddhist sutra counterparts, and between the images shown in the frontispiece and those in artefacts of the Ming period, the second objective is achieved. Objective 3: 1. Since there exist the Ming and the Qing versions of the Daozang frontispiece, a comparative study was conducted to explicate their visual differences. 2. The PI found that the Qing version concerns more about visual effect of the frontispieces and ignores some important Daoist symbols. For example, in the Qing version, the number of deities on both sides of the frontispiece is made exactly the same while the Ming original is not; more symbols are depicted as decoration on the gowns of major Daoist deities while a critical motif on the back of the central kneeling figure was removed. The PI argues that such visual differences point to the ignorance of the Qing designers about Daoist religion and their eagerness to enhance the visual quality of the frontispiece. The fruit of this investigation is presented in an article which is currently under review. 3. The third objective is achieved. Objective 4: 1. The PI made research trips to examine important extant Daozang copies in person so as to collect images of representative extant copies of the Daozang and data related to their respective history of transmission. These copies include the reprint of 1598 in the Qingdao Provincial Museum; a few original copies of 1447 and some reprint of 1598 in Tai’an County Museum, Shangdong; the earliest Qing version of Daozang frontispiece printed in 1708 collected in Nanyang County Library in Henan; a reconstruction of the Qing reprint of the Ming Daozang in 1845 in the National Library of China; a reprint in 1866 in Shanghai Library; some loose copies of various dates in the Kyoto University Library, as well as some loose copies collected in the Palace Museum, Beijing. The PI also acquired images of the Daozang frontispiece from important copies collected in the White Cloud Monastery in Beijing, those in the Shoryobu (Imperial Library) of Imperial Household Agency and those in Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris. 2. Based on the PI’s personal contact with staff at the above institutions and her research, she has written up a summary of how different copies mentioned above were passed down and a detailed account about their present condition. This fruit of this research will constitute a part of her book draft on Daoist Scripture Frontispieces. 3. The fourth objective is completed.

A paper was delivered in an international conference (Part C , 9 no. 3) and published in an edited book (Part C, 8 no. 2) 6. The project has clarified the history of transmission and the present condition of representative copies of the Daozang. The fruit of this study will be integrated in my book draft on Daoist Scripture Frontispieces.

451513.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
451513.value: 1. An in-depth comparative study of Buddhist and Daoist scripture frontispieces is much needed, especially because the present project has already shown that Daoist frontispieces had their own trend of development. Given that Daoist art has long been considered as modelling on Buddhist art, such a comparative study will be essential for correcting this conventional view. The PI has been conducting a pilot project on Ming-dynasty Buddhist scripture frontispieces and seeks to build up a database to further develop this topic. 2. The project has indicated that many Daoist images popular in the late Ming period actually made their first appearance in the frontispieces of the Daozang. A further study on the connection between the mid-Ming Daoist visual culture and that of the late Ming will be important for explaining the popularity of some Daoist figure images in the late Ming period. The PI has planned to compose a book on this topic.

451513.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
451513.value: The project aims to investigate the different versions of the frontispiece to the Ming-dynasty Daoist Canon, so as to bring to light the formation and changes in composition, artistic images and affiliated traditions of the imperially patronized Daoist pantheon in late imperial China. The project has achieved the followings: First, it has proved that there exist only two versions of the Daozang frontispiece: the Ming version and the Qing version. Second, it has uncovered the principle that underlay the composition of the Daozang frontispiece. It has showed that the Daoist pantheon shown in the Daozang frontispiece basically shares the same principle of arrangement as that depicted on the murals of the Yuan-dynasty Daoist temple, Yongle gong. Meanwhile, the imperial support of thunder rites and the affiliation of its chief editor to the Quanzhen and the Qingwei sects contributed to the choice of some key figures to be depicted. Third, it has established that the Daozang and other Daoist scripture frontispieces place extra emphasis on the sacredness of the scene in comparison with their Buddhist counterparts. Fourth, it has reconstructed the history and current condition of representative extant copies of the Daozang.

452313.label: Project Title(Chinese)
452313.value: 翻譯與中英兩次鴉片戰爭，1838-1860

452313.label: Project Objectives
452313.value: To collect firsthand material from both the Chinese and British sides related to translation in the First and Second Anglo-Chinese Wars To establish and analyze the role in Sino-British relations played by translation and translators/interpreters in these two very important wars To identify and examine the different kinds of issues and the impacts on historical developments caused by mistakes or distortions in translations To reinterpret and reevaluate the two wars and the historical figures involved with an emphasis on translation

To establish and analyze the role in Sino-British relations played by translation and translators/interpreters in these two very important wars
To identify and examine the different kinds of issues and the impacts on historical developments caused by mistakes or distortions in translations
To reinterpret and reevaluate the two wars and the historical figures involved with an emphasis on translation

452313.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
452313.value: Without doubt, the first Anglo-Chinese War in 1838-40 and the second one in 1856-60, commonly known as the Opium Wars, were among the most important events in China in the 19th century. Badly defeated, China was forced to open to the West, marking the key turning point in early modern Chinese history. Because of their significance, there are large numbers of books and articles on the two wars, covering the political, military, economic and social aspects. While we agree that many distinguished works have been produced, our understanding of the two wars is not comprehensive and may not be accurate, because one factor has long been neglected: the role of translation. Translation always plays an important part when two countries are engaged in diplomatic and military intercourse. This is particularly true for the two parties involved in the Opium wars because of the huge gap in their languages and cultures. Fighting on alien soil, Britain had to depend on the translators/interpreters for military intelligence, procurement of provisions and handling the Chinese in occupied regions. Apart from translating the diplomatic exchanges before and during the war, the translators were also heavily involved in the negotiations for peace settlement and the preparation of the peace treaties. Unfortunately for a long period of time, both sides suffered from a lack of competent translators. This severely hindered communication and caused long term consequences in Sino-British relations. The present project looks into the translation issues involved in the two Anglo-Chinese Wars. By digging out and delving into firsthand original material from both sides, the PI hopes to identify the problems caused by the lack of competent translators/interpreters. It will explain the backgrounds and constraints of the translators; the mistakes, deliberately made or not, found in the translations of official diplomatic exchanges; and the implications and consequence on subsequent historical developments of such mistakes. By working out the role of translation, we may be able to supply a different interpretation of the two wars. The activities and contributions of some key historical figures of the period can also be reevaluated from a new perspective – their involvement in Sino-British politics in the capacity of translators or translation patrons. In this way, we are writing a chapter for the translation history of China at the same time as we are rewriting a chapter in early modern Chinese history. 毫無疑問，中英第一次及第二次鴉片戰爭（1838-42；1859-60）在中國近代史上佔有極重要的位置，中國其後的歷史發展，在很大程度上直接受到這兩次戰爭的影響。因此，中外歷史學家都對這課題作過不少深入的探討。不過，長久被忽略的是翻譯在這重大歷史事件中的扮演的角色。 中英兩國交戰，無論在戰爭準備（如收集情報）、戰爭期間（如管治佔領地區，收購物資、戰略運用、處理戰俘）以至停戰和約談判以及執行和約條款等，都面對嚴重的語言障礙，須倚賴準確的翻譯才能有效溝通，而翻譯上的錯誤，往往造成嚴重的後果。由於中英雙方在當時都嚴重缺乏合格的翻譯人才，這問題變得尤其嚴重。因此，沒有理解翻譯的功能，對鴉片戰爭的理解也不可能全面和準確。 本項目深入探研翻譯在兩次鴉片戰爭中所扮演的角色。我們會透過全面搜集中英雙方有關鴉片戰爭的原始資料－－包括英國國家檔案館所藏外交部檔案以及中國歷史檔案館相關資料──深入探討和分析如下的一些問題： 1. 中英雙方長期以來所面對的語言障礙問題如何影響中英關係，怎樣直接或間接地導致戰爭的爆發？ 2. 中英雙方的譯者是誰？他們是如何僱用的？他們的背景和資歷（尤其是語文能力）是怎樣的？他們在戰事中有什麼活動？他們的翻譯活動面對什麼樣的制約以至制肘？他們的活動對戰事的發展可有產生什麼影響？他們如何參與停戰的和約談判？他們的貢獻是否受到確認？這背後的語言、政治及文化元素又是怎樣的？ 3. 中英雙方（包括國家以及戰場上）的領袖如何面對語言障礙問題？他們的指令怎樣影響翻譯行為，從而又影響戰事和歷史的發展？ 4. 中英雙方往來文書、照會以至和約是怎樣進行翻譯的？翻譯的過程是怎樣進行和監管的？當中可有出現什麼的錯誤？這些錯誤出現的原因是什麼？翻譯上的問題（包括誤譯）對戰事以至隨後的歷史發展產生什麼影響？ 透過對以上問題的深入探討，我們不但希望能夠重新認識翻譯在中英近代史上所扮演的重要角色（這對翻譯研究有重大的意義），更有可能對兩次鴉片戰爭作出不一樣的詮釋，從而對中國近代史以及中英交往史有更準確的理解。

452313.label: Realisation of objectives
452313.value: Objective 1 deals mainly with the research materials. During the project period, extensive research was conducted locally and overseas for first-hand material on the Opium Wars. A research trip of over two weeks was made in 2016 to London to conduct research at the National Archives at Kew and the British Library, where very important archival material have been found. These include the diplomatic exchanges, both the originals and the translations, between the Chinese and British before, during and after the Wars. Manuscripts of recollections on the wars by their participants were collected. I would like to stress in particular that I have found a manuscript entitled "Draft Official History of the China War 1840-42," prepared by the War Office, UK. Apart from 195 pages of narration, there are over 150 pages of statistical tables, illustrations and hand-drawn rough war maps. In my knowledge, this very important piece of material has never been mentioned by any historian. I will explain on how this would be made available to scholars in Section 6.2 below. Apart from the UK research trip, I have also made research trips to Guangzhou, Beijing and Taipei. In Guangzhou, I visited and researched at the libraries of Sun yat-sen Univeristy and Guangzhou University. In Taipei, I spent much time at the libraries of the Academia Sinica, in particular that of the Institute of Modern History. In Beijing, it was principally the First Historical Archives of China. I am confident to say that I have now in my possession a very rich set of first-hand materials of the two wars, a substantial portion of which have not been consulted or used by scholars of the Opium Wars. And again in Section 6.2 below, I will further talk about the possibilities of making the materials available to a bigger readership. The attainment of objectives 2-4 is mainly carried out by conducting research on the materials and write up papers for publication. With the huge volume of first-hand materials, a very challenging task is to read them and analyze them. With the help of some capable research assistants and student helpers, I have gone through most of them to identify the more important and relevant ones. Since the project, as demonstrated in objectives 2-4, focuses on the role of translation and translators in the two Wars, special attention has been paid to those diplomatic exchanges available both in Chinese and English. For diplomatic dispatches sent by the British, the originals are in English and the Chinese translations are available; while for diplomatic dispatches sent by the Chinese, the originals are in Chinese and the English translations are available. It is most fruitful to compare and analyse the two different versions of the same document to identify translation issues and communication problems. As the linguists from the Chinese side were not capable of doing translations (they might be able to do some interpreting in broken pidgin English), most of the translation work was handled by the translators of the British side. Unfortunately, even the translators/interpreters of the British side were not entirely qualified. On many occasions, we find that they made mistakes not only in expressing themselves in Chinese but also in understanding Chinese. The accuracy of their translations is questionable. Moreover, there is little doubt that they were by no means “impartial” translators/interpreters to provide an objective communication link between the two sides because they steadfastly and only served the interests of the British. In the project, I have studied the two most important and active interpreters/translators of the British camp, John Robert Morrison and Charles Gutzlaff. I have analysed the Chinese standard of the former and specifically written a paper on the latter. I focus on the multiple roles played by the translators/interpreters, that apart from providing translation/interpreting services, they participated actively in negotiation, gathered military information and even acted as magistrate of the conquered areas. This demonstrates that at a very special moment in history, the activities undertaken by the translators/interpreters were very different from the general understanding. By consulting first-hand materials, I have been able to make some important discoveries. For example, I have studied in great details the first round of negotiation over the cession of Hong Kong and came to a conclusion that at the initial stage, the two sides had a very different understanding of “Hong Kong”. Even the concept of “cession” was not clear to the Chinese negotiator. I have also written a couple of articles on the “mistranslation” of the Treaty of Nanking, highlighting the historical consequences of the mistakes and/or ambiguities in the translation. One important paper is on the so-called “Canton Question,” which troubled Sino-British relations after the First Opium War for almost two decades and was generally regarded as one of the major causes of the reopening of the hostilities in the Second Opium War. I have argued against the prevailing assertion that the controversy was brought about by a mistake in translation in the Treaty of Nanking. I agree that there was a discrepancy between the two versions on the opening of Guangzhou as a treaty port, and I discuss the reasons for the discrepancy. On the other hand, by citing the diplomatic exchanges, I argue that the negotiators of both sides had a clear understanding of the treaty terms and agreed that the British were entitled by the Treaty to enter and live inside the City. It was only because of the severe opposition from the Cantonese people that they could not enforce the treaty term. With these publications, I believe that the objectives of the project have been achieved.

452313.label: Major findings and research outcome
452313.value: Altogether six journal articles and two book chapters, which are directly from project, have been published or accepted for publication. They are in-depth studies of the different aspects of the Opium Wars. For example, Articles 1, 3 and 8 (as in Part C) examine the negotiation process and explain how the two sides misunderstood the key terms “Hong Kong” and “cession”. Article 2 studies the Chinese translation of the declaration of war from the Foreign Secretary of Britain, Lord Palmerston, explaining why the Chinese were led into believing that the disputes could be solved very easily. Articles 4 and 6 studies the discrepancies between the English and Chinese versions of the Nanking Treaty and the serious consequences. Article 5 explains how the Chinese translations of the designation of the British chiefs in China changed over time and reflected the shift of power status between the two particles. Article 7 is a study of the key translator, Charles Gutzlaff. They are all ground-breaking because firstly no serious study has ever been made on the role of translation in the two Opium Wars; and secondly, the PI has made the best use of the first-hand materials in the research. These findings would make serious and long-term impact on translation studies and the historical study of the Opium Wars because they are providing very different explanations to the prevailing views of some important issues of this major historical event. Last but not least, those first-hand materials on the two Opium Wars I collected should be seen as a major contribution of the project, because they have long been neglected and very few people have ever used them. If they are eventually published, they will benefit many researchers in the field.

452313.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
452313.value: 1. First-hand materials on the Opium War. No doubt, they are very important and useful for researchers in this and other related topics. I have been approached and authorized by the Shanghai People’s Press to negotiate with the National Archives UK to publish them. Funding may be sought from the Shanghai Municipal Government and even to the Education Ministry of China. It is going to be a big publishing project that may last for 5 to 10 years. 2. "Draft Official History of the China War 1840-42": I have gathered a team of translators (mainly my PhD students) to translate the manuscript. It is hoped that the translation work will be completed soon for submission for publication to the Fudan University Press, which has already indicated strong interest. It is hoped that the book can come out in late 2018 or early 2019. 3. The project has been identified by the Department of Translation, CUHK as an impact case for submission to the 2020 RAE exercise because it has also attracted the attention of people outside the academic circle. More publicity will be made and hopefully it will make some societal impact.

452313.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
452313.value: The project aims at studying the significant impact of translation on one of the most important events in modern Chinese history, the two Opium Wars. In the course of the project, the PI has secured a large volume of first-hand materials of the war, which have been rarely consulted. They consist of diplomatic exchanges between the Chinese and the British before, during and after the wars. By making use of these invaluable materials, the PI has been able to write up several papers on the topic and make many presentations at regional and international conferences. These papers highlight the contributions of the interpreters/translators and explain how they in fact played multiple roles. Apart from providing translation/interpreting services, they participated actively in negotiation, gathered military information and even acted as magistrates of the conquered areas. Overall speaking, taking the Opium wars as a case study, the project aims at manifesting the importance of translation in shaping the course of history.
