452613.label: Project Title(Chinese)
452613.value: 文化融匯與協商：香港穆斯林社群中的華人婦女

452613.label: Project Objectives
452613.value: To review the historical development of the Chinese Islamic community in Hong Kong; To reconstruct the history of the growth and decline of the Chinese Islamic community from the fifties; To analyze the process of women's negotiation between Chinese and Islamic traditions and among their multi-ethnic fellow believers; To analyze women's changing roles in the society and their negotiation with Chinese and Islamic teachings; To theorize women's identity and subjectivity in doing Islam between many cultures--Chinese, Western, South Asian and beyond.
rows: To review the historical development of the Chinese Islamic community in Hong Kong;
To reconstruct the history of the growth and decline of the Chinese Islamic community from the fifties;
To analyze the process of women's negotiation between Chinese and Islamic traditions and among their multi-ethnic fellow believers;
To analyze women's changing roles in the society and their negotiation with Chinese and Islamic teachings;
To theorize women's identity and subjectivity in doing Islam between many cultures--Chinese, Western, South Asian and beyond.

452613.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
452613.value: With the exception of a few studies of South Asian Muslims, the growing Islamic population in Hong Kong has not been documented. This is partly because of the colonial policy of not including religious affiliation in the census and partly because of the low profile adopted by the Islamic community itself. The estimated population of 90,000 to 100,000 Muslims in Hong Kong is only an impression held by a responsible Islamic organization. Except for the stylish Moorish mosque at Tsimshatsui and the escalating number of the veiled Indonesian domestic workers, Muslims are generally invisible in Hong Kong. Among Muslims in Hong Kong, the estimated 30,000 Chinese Muslims have received the least attention. Despite some general accounts that trace the arrival of Muslim traders from the China mainland to Hong Kong in as early as the seventeenth century, the presence of Chinese Muslims had always been overshadowed by their Indian fellow believers through the preferential rule of the British colonial government. Considered as part of the Chinese migrant population, Chinese Muslims have been treated as part of the local Chinese community but never separately as an ethnic community or the hui as they are identified in the mainland. How do they practice their religion amidst the dominance of British Protestantism, capitalistic modernity, and the strong and long-held Chinese customs and traditions in Hong Kong? And specifically, how have the Chinese Muslim women negotiate their role and place between Islamic and modern (Western) values in their daily living? This project will be the first study on the Chinese Muslim women in Hong Kong. Building on my earlier research on religion, family and Chinese patriarchy, this project will analyze how Islamic teaching is negotiated, within the context of British colonialism and Chinese traditions, by Chinese women in the Hong Kong Muslim community. Changing gender roles and women’s place have been identified as some of the most fiercely contested issues in recent cultural and political debate worldwide. Key to the paradigm of a “clash of civilizations” is the concept of a democratic West, with its liberated women, in conflict with autocratic Islamic cultures, with their patriarchal structures and subjugated women. Whether or not, or to what extent, have the Chinese Muslim women been affected by the global contestation in terms of their understanding of gender roles and women’s place in Hong Kong will be an important question to be answered. 除了零星的個別研究，香港穆斯林的歷史從來沒有被記錄在案。由於殖民政策，定期的人口普查並沒有包括宗教一欄，因此沒有官方資料顯示香港人口的宗教組成。直到今天，政府也沒有系統地統計香港的穆斯林人口。2011年《香港年報》中10萬穆斯林的數字也是一個估計值，每年由香港回教信託基金總會提供。除了座落於九龍半島市中心尖沙咀的優雅摩爾式建築的清真寺，以及周日街頭湧現披戴頭巾的印尼家傭外，穆斯林多年來保持低調，在城市中不為人所注意。 根據上述估計，華人占在港穆斯林人口雖然不少於三萬，他們一直更少為人注意。儘管有學者已就穆斯林在香港定居的歷史追溯到17世紀那些來華阿拉伯商人的後裔，在港的華人穆斯林始終生活在以印度裔同儕的影子之下。一方面，基於英國殖民地管治的因素，南亞裔穆斯林在香港一直占據主導地位；另一方面，與中國的情形不同，香港的穆斯林並沒有歸類為「回民」這樣一個民族。那麼，這些少數的華人穆斯林社群是如何經歷英國新教、資本主義現代性、和源遠流長的中國傳統習俗在香港的主導性影嚮？在高度西化的香港，這些少數派的穆斯林婦女又怎麼協調日常生活中伊斯蘭教與現代社會中對女性地位和角色的不同要求？ 此計劃是首項設定以香港華人穆斯林婦女為焦點的研究。建基於我早前就宗教、家庭及中國父權制度的研究之上，是項計劃會分析香港穆斯林社群中的婦女如何就伊斯蘭訓導，在英國殖民主義及中國傳統之間進行協商。性別角色與地位的轉變被視為是世界上最具爭議的議題之一。而撒母耳‧亨廷頓（Samuel Huntington）的「文明衝突論」正環繞自由婦女所代表的「民主西方」價值，與受父權宰制所壓制的婦女所代表的「古老、專制的」伊斯蘭世界文化之間的衝突。究竟這個全球性的論爭如何影嚮香港華人穆斯林婦女對性別角色和地位的理解和實踐仍有待解答。

452613.label: Realisation of objectives
452613.value: All five objectives have been achieved and summarized as follow. 1. A basic understanding of the historical development of the Chinese Islamic community in Hong Kong was achieved. This understanding was achieved through two channels. First, primary materials such as newsletters, annual reports and yearbooks are collected from Islamic Union of Hong Kong (IUHK) and Hong Kong Islamic Youth Association (HKIYA), and the archive of Chinese Muslim Cultural and Fraternal Association (CMCFA). Given the limited and fragmented nature of these information, supplementary materials were collected through the second channel, that is, personal interviews with some of the senior leaders of the Chinese Muslim community. These members did not only provide us with some first-hand information from their recollection about the general landscape of the life of Chinese Muslims, but also their family genealogies, personally kept copies of newsletters from HKIYA and IUHK, news clips on major Islamic activities in Hong Kong, reports and speeches made in the 70s and 80s, and the Bulletin of the Association Building Redevelopment published in 1998. Together with the overall library research, a general history of the Chinese Muslim community in Hong Kong is reconstructed for the first time. 2. Likewise, a basic historical outline for the growth and decline of the Chinese Muslim community in Hong Kong is successfully developed. Through the genealogies of two families, the origins and the history of Hong Kong-Chinese Muslims are shown to be highly complex. They are results of not only the interwoven relationship between Muslim families in China and Hong Kong over a long period of time, but also the multilateral relationships between the Chinese Muslim families and the South Asian and Arab families through interracial marriages. According to the Hong Kong Yearbook 2016, there were about 300,000 Muslims (including 150,000 Indonesian domestic helpers) in Hong Kong, about 4% of the total Hong Kong population. Considering only the residential population, Chinese Muslims comprised the largest group of 40,000, about 13% of all Hong Kong Muslims. Pakistani Muslims, about 30,000 and 10% of the total Muslim population in Hong Kong, have served as the official Muslim representation during the colonial times. The Chinese Muslim community is comprised of Mainland immigrants, Hong Kong born and interracial progenies who have been identified as “local boys” (本地仔). Gleaning the benefit of possessing both Chinese and English language proficiency, “local boys” have fared relatively well in Hong Kong and have dominated IUHK’s governance structure until today. Lacking English, the early Chinese settlers had maintained very low profile in the community and were mostly confined to low-income jobs. Since 1980s, due to the vast urbanization and economic growth of Hong Kong, Chinese Muslims have dispersed to all corners of the territory and a large number of the new generations are secularized. 3. Analysis of the negotiation taken by the Chinese Muslim women between their identities—gender, ethnic and religious—and their life in a modern, urban city of Hong Kong was completed. There were a total of 33 Chinese Muslim women interviewed between 2014 and 2016. Among all interviewed, 31 are descendants of only Chinese ancestry (as far as they know) and two of mixed descents with Chinese mothers and fathers with Pakistani ancestry. By religion, 12 out of the 33 interviewees are converts married into Muslim families. Among the 21 born Muslims, 14 of them share 3 surnames which are all referred to as very prominent historical Chinese Muslim families. Rather than the static image of a submissive Muslim woman, all interviewees have lived their life to the best they can from their respective positions, statuses and as far as circumstances permit. For the born Muslim women, they tried to live by the teaching of putting marriage and family first although their efforts are not always justly rewarded. Given the tight family allegiance because of traditional endogamous practices, one of the biggest challenges for them has been the management of relationships among the multiple extended families. For the Islam converts whose marriages are often interracial—Chinese women married with Pakistani men, their devotion to Islamic practices is the key to earning them respect and legitimate authority within their marital families. Despite the fast changing landscape of Islam as religion and a collective identity in Hong Kong, one major characteristic common to all is their loyalty to their Islamic identity even if two of them have decided to move away from their inherited faith. Analysis is about to completed by the book under preparation. 4. Analysis of the changing roles of Hong Kong Muslim women and their negotiation between their Chinese and Islamic identities is completed with categorization of their experiences into three groups. The first group—essentially the first generation of Muslims from the Mainland—is those who followed their families to migrate to Hong Kong during the fifties, after Communist takeover in the Mainland, and the late seventies, after the end of the Cultural Revolution in China. They are mostly above 60 year of age and usually inherited what was being practiced when their families were in the Mainland. The second group—primarily constituted of daughters of the early generation and some originally non-Muslim wives married into the Muslim families—is culturally highly diverse. Some of them are descendants of prominent Chinese Muslim families with genealogies went back to several hundred years, others are progenies of interracial marriages between Chinese and Pakistani who tended to be big business men or professionals such as lawyers and doctors. Although they are all aged in the forties or fifties, they varied greatly in terms of their marital status, gender roles and the practice of veiling. The last group which is consisted of the youngest includes basically daughters of the second generation Chinese Muslims. These young women from the age of twenties to the thirties, either married or single, were usually educated in Christian schools (the better schools in Hong Kong’s context) are in pursuit of their careers independently, and have travelled or resided extensively overseas like many other Hong Kong young people of their age. They are the ones who are struggling with the meaning of their born Muslim identity in the midst of largely practical, secular Chinese friends. Analysis is about to completed by the book under preparation. 5. Theorization of the women’s subjectivity is an ongoing project in my writing. This project, together with my previous studies on Chinese women of other religious traditions, has given me much insight about the much deceived notion of a modern subject. The modern project of conceiving a subject of free will, liberated from the bondage of slavery from “his” master or religion, is at its best, an ideal to be pursued with the best human intention. The agent who is able to persist with a single integrated mind to make changes to “his” circumstance and therefore collectively changing the world is played out not without the convergence of many conditions and not without sacrifices of many others. The real subject in charge of its life is one who may exercise “change” to make things more bearable or livable at a given time in a given place, for oneself and/or others around them, at the moment. More analysis will be submitted in the summary of findings of Part 6.1 below. Analysis is about to completed by the book under preparation.

452613.label: Major findings and research outcome
452613.value: Major findings can be summarized as two. First, the history of the Chinese Muslims in Hong Kong is highly complicated. Because of British colonization until 1997, the official representation of Hong Kong Muslims has been dominated by Indian-Pakistani, some of the settlers in Hong Kong since the mid-19th century. Pakistani-Chinese marriages gave birth to “local boys” (and girls) who constituted a unique “ethnic” community in Hong Kong. Chinese Muslims who came from Southern China and especially Guangdong in the 1950s after the Communist takeover stayed largely in the low income strata as either manual laborers or small businessmen. The second crop of Chinese immigrants coming after the late 1970s are greatly diversified in terms of ethnicities (Xinjiang, Uygurs, Manchurians, etc.), geographical origins (Northeast and Central China) and most of all, economic statuses and political affiliations. These many diverse backgrounds of “Chinese” Muslims converged in Hong Kong for different reasons provided a profoundly multifaceted platform for women’s negotiation with their gender and religion. Second, as highlighted in point 5 of the summary of the “Objectives Achieved” in Part 5.3 above, rather than the modern subject of free will, the real “subject” of change is one who constantly makes adjustment to make life bearable or livable within given circumstances. In the case of women, they are often both sacrificial wives and mothers and at the same time bold and transgressive of their “predestined” gender roles as the circumstances called for. To push Chandra Talpade Mohanty’s critique of the Western notion of the woman’s subject further, I find religious identities of women further complicate their daily negotiation with gender roles and familial practices. Their narration defies demarcation between the individuals and the collective, independence and dependence, or submission or resistance. Recent psychological studies argue for the necessary existence, in an individual, of a plurality of qualitatively distinct selves as well as an “interpenetrative, dialogical constellation of subselves.” Rather than one unified self, there is a unified position as a Self, encounters her world from a plurality of positions, through a plurality of voices, and yet retains a meaningful coherence. It echoes Kristeva’s early proposal of the subject-in-process, portraying a “coherent” constellation of multiple “subselves” that could be called to the surface according to demands of specific contexts. Through women’s narration of their selves, they define afresh a composite woman’s subject who, in constant negotiation in practices, is in process through living the moments.

452613.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
452613.value: The research has been extended to a comparative study of the Muslim women in two cities--Hong Kong and Guangzhou through the South Asian Program of Hong Kong Institute for Asia-Pacific Studies. Several papers are in preparation jointly by Dr. Zhou Shuyan, a postdoctoral scholar at Sun Yat Sen University and myself.

452613.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
452613.value: Except for the stylish Moorish mosque at Tsimshatsui and the increasing presence of the veiled Indonesian domestic workers, Muslims amounted to about 300,000 are generally invisible in Hong Kong—and the least of all, the estimated 30,000 Chinese Muslims. Despite traces of Chinese Muslim traders in Hong Kong to the early seventeenth century, Indian-Pakistani dominated the official Muslim representation during the colonial time. This project is the first study of Chinese Muslims in Hong Kong which fills an important historical gap not only for Chinese Muslims but also the multiethnic Hong Kong Muslims as a whole, with a focus on Chinese Muslim women. With careful delineation of the complex history of the community, the project provides new insight to how Islamic teaching is negotiated by Chinese women in the Hong Kong Muslim community. Despite their various Chinese ethnicities and variant timing and reasons for settling in Hong Kong, they managed to interpret their religious and gender identities in light of the changing urban landscape of the territory and demonstrated a subject that is both composite and dynamic.

452713.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
452713.value: This study aims to answer the key question of how the Internet affects political participation and transforms public governance by using Hong Kong as a case study. Diffusion of the Internet technology attracts so much attention in political science and public administration because it has the potential to significantly transform governance through altering the traditional relationship among government, citizens, and the civil society by creating a new and virtual interface and empowering different political actors. This new interface exists in terms of both economic sense of public service delivery and political sense of participation and policy-making. Internationally, it is increasingly common for citizens to utilize the Internet actively for political action. In Hong Kong, the Internet also plays a key role in many events and movements, particularly in terms of e-mobilization, which have successfully influenced the policies of the government. Ironically, many studies of the Internet in politics or e-government still focus more on its technological capacity rather than its governance aspect. The impact of the Internet on political participation is still subject to debate. For example, does it increase the participation for all citizens or only magnify the voices and influences of a particular group of citizens, such as the young and the technologically-advanced, creating problems of digital divide and uneven representation? Similarly, is it used only in some particular forms of political actions instead of all forms of political participation? The pessimistic view of “politics as usual” that the Internet is not going to lead to any significant change in governance still cannot be eliminated. This study turns these competing views into testable hypotheses by integrating the major research in this area and our own works. As an international and economically-advanced city ranked highly in terms of the usage of the Internet, Hong Kong provides an ideal setting for addressing these research questions. This study has two major research components. First, it would conduct a citizen survey to find out the use of Internet and Non-Internet means in political participation and construct a political activism index. Second, it will conduct interviews and focus groups to obtain more indepth information regarding Internet use and its deployment in major political events and social movements in recent years. Findings of the project should improve our understanding of the evolving nature and impact brought by the Internet on governance and help to resolve many of the major theoretical debates in the literature. 這研究的目標是以香港作為個案,解答互聯網如何影響政治參與及改變公共管治這個主要的問題。互聯網的科技在政治及公共行政學上,吸引了如此多的注意,是因為它有潛力創造新的界面及加大政治角式的權力,以改變政府、市民和民間社會的傳統關係。這新界面存在於公共服務的提供的經濟層面及政策制定參與的政治層面。國際上,市民也越來越多透過互聯網進行政治活動。在香港,互聯網也在很多事件及運動中,特別在電子動員上,成功影響政府的政策。但很諷刺,很多有關互聯網與政治或政府的研究,仍然聚焦於科技而非管治的層面。 互聯網對政治參與的影響,仍然是具爭議。例如,互聯網是增加了所有•巿民的參與,還是只放大了某些巿民,特別是年青及善於使用科技的一羣,的聲音及影響力,造成電子分隔及不均的代表性?同樣地,互聯網會否只用在部份,而非所有的政治參與上?認為互聯網不會為政治帶來任何轉變的悲觀想法仍不能被排除。透過整合有關的研究,本研究把這些有競爭的看法變成可驗証的假設。作為在經濟及互聯網科技上發達的國際城巿,香港提供了一個理想的環境,來解答這些研究的問題。這研究分成兩個部份。首先,它透過市民的調查,找作互聯網使用者及非使用者的政治參與,和制定一個政治活躍指數。第二.,它透過訪問及聚焦小組,收集有關互聯網在政治事件及社會運動上被使用的深入資料。本研究的結果有助改善對互聯網在管治上影響的認識,及解開很多在文獻上的理論爭辯。

452713.label: Realisation of objectives
452713.value: With the background, major puzzles and key research questions in mind, the research questions of this project are transformed into five major objectives of the project. All objectives are fully met in the completion of the project. This study aims to answer the key question of how the Internet affects political participation and transforms public governance by using Hong Kong as a case study. Diffusion of the Internet technology attracts so much attention in political science and public administration because it has the potential to significantly transform governance through altering the traditional relationship among government, citizens, and the civil society by creating a new and virtual interface and empowering different political actors. This new interface exists in terms of both economic sense of public service delivery and political sense of participation and policy-making. Internationally, it is increasingly common for citizens to utilize the Internet actively for political action. In Hong Kong, the Internet also plays a key role in many events and movements, particularly in terms of e-mobilization, which have successfully influenced the policies of the government. Since many studies of the Internet in politics or e-government still focus more on its technological capacity rather than its governance aspect, this study would like to fill this important gap in the literature. The impact of the Internet on political participation is still subject to debate. More specifically, it is unsure how and to what extent it increases the participation for all citizens or only magnify the voices and influences of a particular group of citizens, such as the young and the technologically-advanced, creating problems of digital divide and uneven representation. Similarly, it remains uncertain whether the Internet is used only in some particular forms of political actions instead of all forms of political participation. Despite the popular belief that the Internet is revolutionize the mode and nature of political participation, the pessimistic view of “politics as usual” still cannot be eliminated totally and empirically. This study turns these competing views into testable hypotheses by integrating the major research in this area. As an international and economically-advanced city ranked highly in terms of the usage of the Internet, Hong Kong provides an ideal setting for addressing these research questions. All the above issues and concerns identified are reflected in the five project objectives. With regard to the first objective, a citizen telephone survey was conducted. Administered by the Centre for Communication and Public Opinion Survey (CCPOS) of the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), the survey was carried out in mid-November 2014 and achieved a response rate of around 40%. With a sample size of 1,006 Cantonese-speaking Hong Kong citizens above the age of 18, the survey covered questions on the use of Internet and Non-Internet means in political participation. Based on this survey, a political activism index (PAI) was constructed. In respect of the second objective, post-survey investigations were carried out. By comparing the social-political variables (e.g., age, education and income) between high-users of e-participation and the low users / non-users, the characteristics of different groups of citizens and their relationships with key variables including Internet use and political participation were studied. For the third objective, interviews and focus groups were conducted. First of all, participants of focus groups were recruited from telephone survey and were grouped by various levels of Internet usage. They are divided into three major groups: low-level, intermediate level, and upper-level, according to their usage of the Internet. Moreover, representatives of interest groups were invited to our interviews, of which many are important politicians, such as legislative council members who are active in social movements and political events. To balance the different viewpoints, politicians across the political spectrum, including both pro-democracy and pro-establishment camps are included in the interviews. Last but not the least, as the Umbrella Movements of 2014 was an important event in terms of social movement and the use of social media and the Internet for political communication and political mobilization, key student leaders involved in the Umbrella Movement are also included in our interviews. Based on the findings and outputs in the tasks in objectives 1-3, policy implications concerning the Internet and public governance of Hong Kong has been drawn and reflections are made on addressing the major debates in the literature, which are the fourth and fifth objectives of the project respectively. In meeting the fourth and fifth objectives, the Internet is found to be transforming public governance worldwide by creating new interfaces of interaction which empower political actors and expand their scope of influence from locality to around the globe. E-participation, particularly e-information and e-mobilization effects, are more obvious among the young and the educated because of their higher digital literacy. Like the new generations in many other countries, the young in Hong Kong are also very concerned about the future and development of Hong Kong and many of them are eager to express their views and feelings through the Internet. As witnessed by many critical events and new social movements in Hong Kong in recent years, such as the anti-express rail movement and the anti-national education movement before the outbreak of the Umbrella Movement, the young and the educated are playing a leading role through the use of Internet in them, which have been so successful in influencing government policies and seeking attention of the international community. The understanding of the impact of Internet on governance is enhanced by the fulfilment of all five objectives of the project as they are all interrelated and building on each other. In term of lessons for public governance, findings of the project carry important policy significance and implications for Hong Kong and other economically-advanced and post-industrial countries. With the rise of the Internet worldwide, the trend of e-participation and its influence in politics and policy-making will only be increased in the foreseeable future. How policy makers should embrace this challenge, such as evaluating the representation of public views expressed through e-participation and the e-feedback on policy proposals, is a tough judgmental call which has been informed by the research findings. In terms of research significance, this study presents a great opportunity for integrating theory and research to provide a better understanding of the governance implication of the Internet, which is highly inadequate before this study as many findings are still normatively-driven, not empirically-based. In meeting its objectives, particularly objective 5, the project has made contributions in at least two major areas in its literature. First of all, the examination of whether the Internet can really enhance democratic governance through empowering citizens. Secondly, the effect and the extent of the Internet in altering state-individual relationship and triggering social and institutional changes. In completing the project, some problems are encountered but fortunately they are all successfully overcome in the end. One major problem is the unexpected departure of Professor Ng Kai-hon, a colleague in my department, to a non-UGC funded institution. Due to his departure, I have to pick up another on-going RGC project from him. Because of this unexpected increase in workload, an application for 6 months project extension was made. With the extension and other adjustments, all objectives are achieved as planned.

452713.label: Major findings and research outcome
452713.value: Does the Internet, particularly the social media such as Facebook, enhance or hinder political participation, including involvement into a social movement? What are its major implications of on public governance? These important questions are examined critically in this project with the case and context of major social movements, including the Umbrella Movement in Hong Kong. The study is based on the analysis of data from a territory-wide telephone survey, interviews and focus groups. It is found that there are some significant differences between the youth and the older age groups in terms of their political preferences and values. In general, the young people are more supportive of democracy and the Umbrella Movement. This difference cannot be fully explained by the global trend of a shift towards post-modernization values. Media usage, particularly the use of Internet, has helped to magnify these differences. The young generation often uses social media such as Facebook to form their views and perceptions of public affairs while the other generations still depend more on the traditional media on this aspect. Based on the findings, it can be argued that the dividing views and contrasting cultures between the young and the rest caused by the Internet make political participation, including social movements both easier and more difficult, a seemingly contradictory outcome. On the one hand, it is easier because the cost of political communication and political mobilization has been significantly reduced. However, on the other hand, it makes political participation more difficult and more challenging to be sustainable because it becomes harder for participants to reach a common vision while weakening the bonding between leaders and followers in a movement or a political organization. In the theories of public governance and citizen participation, it is commonly believed that more political participation should be good and desirable. However, what is being observed from this study seems to defy this common belief. With the rise of political activism in Hong Kong, a problem of “alone together” has emerged. Citizens often participate in collective political action as individuals rather than members of organized groups, making organized political actions and social movements more vulnerable to self-conflicts and internal tension. It shows with the Internet, we are actually facing a more divided and polarized world. This can easily lead to the problem of “more is less”, meaning more political participation can create little or even negative political and institutional changes.

452713.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
452713.value: The findings in this project have both academic and policy implications for future action. In research, the next step is to shift more attention to future studies of the impact on public governance in the Internet age, particularly with the rise of non-institutional participation and the seemingly contradictory outcome of “alone together”, that is, more political participation with less institutional bonding among participants. It should lead to some deeper reflections in terms of both theory and practice. In the theories of public governance, more active participation is commonly perceived as positive. However, what is being observed from this study seems to defy this common logic turning the traditional theories of this area upside down. As observed from the rise of political activism in Hong Kong, citizens often participate in collective political action as individuals rather than members of organized groups, making organized political actions and social movements more vulnerable to self-conflicts and internal tension. It shows that with the Internet, particularly the use of social media, we are actually facing a more divided and polarized world between different generations with potential disruptive impacts. This new pattern of political participation should lead to more research on all these critical issues discovered.

452713.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
452713.value: Does the Internet, particularly the social media such as Facebook, enhance or hinder political participation, including involvement into a social movement? This project finds there are dividing views and contrasting cultures between the young and the rest caused by the Internet, making political participation, including social movements both easier and more difficult, a seemingly contradictory outcome. On the one hand, the cost of political communication and political mobilization has been significantly reduced. On the other hand, it becomes harder for participants to reach a common vision while institutional linkage between leaders and followers is weakened. The rise of political activism in Hong Kong also sees the emergence of a problem of “alone together”. Citizens often participate in collective political action as individuals rather than members of organized groups. We are increasingly living in a more divided and polarized world. When people may be more connected in the Internet age, they are actually more connected to their own and self-constructed conceptual and subjective world rather than to a real community with shared values and common norms. This can easily lead to the problem of “more is less”, meaning more political participation can create little or even negative political and institutional changes.

452813.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
452813.value: An understanding of the cognitive and motivational factors that shape how social communications are generated and interpreted is a necessary precondition for identifying differences in the communication patterns that characterize interactions among representatives of different cultures. The present research will explore these factors. We distinguish between two general dimensions along which cultural differences in processing appear to exist. We examine the influence of differences along these dimensions at several stages of processing that come into play in interpersonal communication, including comprehension, memory, reasoning, perspective-taking and inference. The findings of research will not only provide insight into the cognitive processes that underlie cultural differences but lay the foundation for future examinations of these processes in the context of intercultural communication. 代表不同文化的個體之間的交流是以不同的溝通模式來描述的；識別這些溝通模式的不同之處的一個必要前提，即是要理解塑造社會溝通的產生和解讀的認知方面和動機方面的因素。本研究將探討這些因素。我們區分了信息處理中顯現出文化差異的兩個普遍的維度。我們檢驗了在這些維度上的文化差異在人際溝通的幾個階段所帶來的影響，這些階段包括：理解，記憶，邏輯推理，角度選取和推論等。本研究之發現不僅將洞悉文化差異背後的認知過程，並且為將來針對人際溝通背景下的認知過程方面的研究奠定了基礎。

452813.label: Realisation of objectives
452813.value: Research on cultural differences in behavior has had at least two thrusts. Some research has attempted to characterize cultural differences in social orientation (Triandis, 1995; Markus & Kitayama, 1991). This research seems to converge on the conclusion that Western and Asian cultural representations differ along two related dimensions. One, individualism-collectivism, concerns the disposition to define oneself oneself as a unique individual or to construe oneself in terms of the groups to which one belongs, without regard to the individual members. The second, independence-interdependence, concerns whether individuals perceive themselves as independent of other persons or, evaluate oneself in relation to others. The two dimensions are often treated as equivalent but in fact are conceptually different. The other stream of research, exemplified by the work of Nisbett (2003) and his colleagues, has focused on cultural differences in thinking style, as reflected in the performance on tasks that require it. This research suggests that Asians are disposed to process information “holistically” whereas Westerners have a more analytic style of thinking. It is tempting to speculate that differences in social orientation and more general differences in thinking style are related and may in both be traceable to cultural differences in early childhood socialization (Miller, Fung & Koven, 2007). In fact, however, both differences in social orientation and differences in thinking style may be multidimensional. In fact, Na et al. (2010) found that within-culture correlations among alternative measures of social orientation were close to zero. Moreover, performance on tasks that were assumed to reflect holistic thinking were also virtually uncorrelated with a given culture. The initial research we conducted in the present research confirmed these conclusions. Over a period of several weeks, 200 British and Hong Kong participants were asked to perform over 20 different tasks that had been used in other research as indices of holistic vs. analytic thinking. Although British and Hong Kong participants significantly differed in their performance on many of these tasks, the within-culture correlations among the measures was generally low and nonsignificant, indicating that differences in thinking style fell along more than one dimension. Moreover, the correlations between these measures of social orientation were equally low. We speculated, however, that the failure for measures of social orientation to be related to differences in thinking style was due to two factors. First, as noted above, holistic thinking might not reflect a single process but rather, multiple processes. Second, measures of social orientation reflected differences in individuals’ cognitive state and not differences in process. A more diagnostic procedure that would assess individual and cultural differences in process might be more useful in understanding the generalizeability of thinking style. To this end, we constructed a single task that could be used both to assess and to induce differences in four types of processing: piecemeal processing (a disposition to think of stimulus features independently), global processing (a focus on the stimulus as a whole without considering its individual features), and two types of relational processing (a consideration of stimulus features in relation to their context and a consideration of them in relation to one another. Specifically, representatives of four different cultures—India, Hong Kong, England and the United States—were asked to evaluate a number of paintings that varied in style and content. After doing so, they were asked to indicate which of the four strategies they had generally used to evaluate the paintings. Intercorrelations among the use of the strategies were generally low. However, Indians were typically higher than other cultural groups in global thinking and both types of relational thinking, followed by Hong Kong Chinese and then the two Western cultures. In a third study, we induced each of these processing strategies experimentally by instructing Hong Kong participants to use one of the procedures to evaluate the paintings. After doing so, they performed tasks that had been used as indices of holistic thinking but seemed likely to differ in the particular processing that was required. We found that inducing global processing affected performance on tasks that required consideration of stimuli as a whole but did not affect performance in tasks that required relational thinking. On the other hand, priming item-item relational thinking affected performance on the latter tasks but not the former. Thus, holistic thinking appeared to be multidimensional. A final study replicated these findings using both Indian and United States participants. In the absence of priming, Indians differed from Westerners in their performance of tasks that required each of the four thinking styles we considered. However, experimentally priming these thinking styles overrode these cultural differences and produced effects similar to those observed in Experiment 3. In summary, we found that a process measure that more effectively distinguished between piecemeal, global and relational thinking not only distinguished different cultures but induced differences in task performance, and accounted for cultural differences in this performance.

452813.label: Major findings and research outcome
452813.value: As noted earlier, we found that: 1. Measures of performance on measures of holistic thinking that have often been used as indications of cultural differences in holistic thinking are virtually uncorrelated. 2. A task that was able to identify four different types of thinking style--piecemeal processing, global processing, thinking about items in relation to their context, and thinking about items in relation to one another--distinguished representatives of four different cultural groups (Indians, Hong Kong Chinese, British and North Americans). 3. Inducing differences in processing using this task affected performance on different measures of holistic thinking, indicating that "holistic" thinking was multidimensional. 4. Although Asian and Western participants differed in performance on these measures, experimentally inducing differences in thinking style eliminated these cultural differences. In summary, cultural differences in both social orientation (individualism-collectivism and independence-interdependence (are both multidimensional and more diagnostic process measures are necessary to identify their relationship.

452813.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
452813.value: Our procedure for both assessing and manipulating differences in processing style, which involves a single task that is unconfounded with extraneous task features, is successful in both distinguishing among representatives of different cultures and distinguishing performance on different measures of thinking style. It therefore is potentially useful in examining more clearly the potential antecedents of this processing and the factors that account for cultural differences.

452813.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
452813.value: Representatives of Western and Asian cultures are assumed to differ both (a) in their social orientation (e.g., the tendency to think of themselves as part of a collective rather than as single individuals, and the tendency to think of themselves in relation to others rather than independently) and (b) the type of thinking that underlies their performance on nonsocial tasks. However, current procedures for identifying the relationship between social and nonsocial thinking have been ineffective. By developing a procedure that distinguishes between four different styles of thinking (thinking about features of a stimulus independently, thinking about the stimulus as a whole without considering its individual features, thinking about features of a stimulus in relation to their context, and thinking about features in relation to one another), we were able to identify cultural differences in these processes and also to show that these processes had different effects on the performance of of tasks that require "holistic" thinking. The research therefore provides a more refined understanding of cultural differences in social and nonsocial behavior and how they are related.

452913.label: Project Title(Chinese)
452913.value: 中國證券法律公力執法研究

452913.label: Project Objectives
452913.value: To articulate the historical, economic and political contexts in which public enforcement of securities laws has operated and evolved in China; To examine empirically the manner in which the Chinese public enforcement agencies, in particular the CSRC and the Stock Exchanges, have taken enforcement actions against violations of securities laws; To discern empirically the determinants, as well as the impact, of public enforcement activities and actions by Chinese enforcement agencies, in particular the CSRC and the Stock Exchanges; To advance the understanding of the complex dynamics between Chinese securities enforcement agencies, the affected firms and individuals, as well as other concerned state agencies at both central and local levels, which help to shape actual enforcement processes and outcomes in China; and To propose a more grounded theory for understanding the role that public enforcement of securities laws plays, relative to private enforcement, in the development of national securities markets, with particular reference to China.

452913.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
452913.value: The aim of this project is to explore the ways in which Chinese securities enforcement agencies have taken enforcement actions against violations of securities laws. Effective enforcement of securities laws helps to deter securities fraud and to offer protection for minority investors. Securities enforcement actions can be brought by public and regulatory agencies such as the securities regulator and the stock exchange (“public enforcement”) or by private parties through civil lawsuits (“private enforcement”), or both. Recent comparative studies show that the nature and the structure of securities enforcement actions vary greatly from country to country. In the case of China, public enforcement actions are evidently greater in number, and possibly also in intensity. Academic attention has so far, however, concentrated primarily on the enforcement of securities laws by private lawsuits. Public enforcement of securities laws in China remains relatively understudied and under-theorized. The particular focus of this project will be on the enforcement actions, both formal and informal, by the China Securities Regulatory Commission (“CSRC”) and the Shanghai Stock Exchange and the Shenzhen Stock Exchange (“Stock Exchanges”). Drawing on two unique datasets to be constructed on formal enforcement actions, as well as qualitative data on public enforcement activities to be obtained with the support of a network of collaborating PRC securities regulators, this project will present new insights into, among other things, the intensity of public securities enforcement, the determinants of the public enforcement agencies’ regulatory activities, and the impact of public enforcement actions on regulated firms and individuals in China. It is anticipated that this project will, based upon its systematic, empirical and comparative analysis of public securities enforcement actions in China, propose a more grounded theory for understanding the role that public enforcement of securities laws plays, relative to private enforcement, in the development of national securities markets, with particular reference to China. The theoretical and empirical findings of this project will also contribute to the optimal design of the securities enforcement regime in China and, more generally, to the growing comparative literature on securities regulation, law and finance, and law and development. 本課題旨在研究中國證券執法機關對於證券法律違法行為的執法問題。 證券法律的有效執法，對於遏制證券欺詐和保護中小投資者，發揮著舉足輕重的作用。證券執法既可以由公共執法機關和監管機關（例如證券監管部門和證券交易所）執行，也可以由私人通過民事訴訟的方式實現。前者稱為“公力執法”，而後者稱為“私力執法”。近年的比較證券法研究表明，世界各國證券執法制度的內涵和模式迥異。在中國，公力執法案件在數量上遠高於私力執法案件，公力執法的執法力度似乎也強於私力執法。然而，對於中國證券法律執法的現有學術研究，主要集中於通過民事訴訟方式實現的私力執法。對於中國證券法律的公力執法，研究深度和理論化程度，尚有待提升。 本課題的研究，著重於中國證券監督委員會、上海證券交易所和深圳證券交易所的正式和非正式的證券執法行為。本課題將致力於建立中國證券法律正式公力執法資料庫。同時，本課題將依託與中國主要證券監管機關的合作網路，深入實際瞭解證券公力執法行為。在此基礎上，本課題將推動對中國證券法律公力執法現狀、證券執法機關執法行為的決定因素、證券執法機關執法行為的影響等重要問題的研究。 同時，本課題對於中國證券法律公力執法系統化的、實證性的和比較視野的研究，還將推動相關領域理論研究的發展，特別是證券公力執法和證券私力執法在一國證券市場發展過程中的相互作用關係的研究問題。此外，本課題的理論和實證研究成果，還將對中國證券執法體系的最優制度設計，以及比較證券監管、法律與金融、法律與發展等學術領域的發展，發揮積極的促進作用。

452913.label: Realisation of objectives
452913.value: The quantitative and qualitative investigation undertaken for this project was guided by, and directed towards fulfilling, the project’s five objectives, which were achieved in full. The research achievements are summarised below in the sequence of the five objectives. Objective 1: Methodologically, this component of the project relied primarily on materials derived from secondary sources. It resulted in the creation of a unique archive that traces documentarily the evolution and operation of the public institutions/bodies tasked with the enforcement of securities laws. This archive includes not only readily accessible published materials, such as monographs, yearbooks, journal articles and newspaper entries, but also materials that are ‘internal’ in nature and yet unclassified or otherwise confidential. These materials are thus particularly useful for gaining insight into the development of the securities enforcement regime as it existed in the early days of China’s securities markets. Another valuable feature of the archive is that the secondary materials it houses are supplemented by elite interviews. Interviews were conducted with senior and rank-and-file officials, both serving and former, of the public bodies involved in the set-up and reform of China’s securities enforcement regime. They thus shed light on the underlying, often times undocumented, considerations that account for the institutional changes seen in that regime. The findings arising from this component of the research laid a solid foundation for the successful achievement of the project’s other four objectives. They were also drawn upon in the peer-reviewed publications and conference presentations resulting from the project. Objectives 2 & 3: These objectives were successfully achieved through the construction of a proprietary dataset (‘Dataset’) containing all enforcement actions, both formal and informal, taken by the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), its regional offices and the Shanghai and Shenzhen Stock Exchanges from 1998 to 2016. As a matter of fact, what has been achieved considerably EXCEEDS the specific objectives set out in the original proposal (‘Proposal’) in two important respects. First, the period of investigation stated in the Proposal was 1998-2012. The Dataset has, however, significantly extended the period by four years, stretching to 2016. That significant extension in effect DOUBLES the size of the Dataset. In number terms, the additional four-year period (2013-2016) contributed around 3,900 enforcement actions, more than the nearly 3,800 recorded during the whole of the original period of investigation (1998-2012). Second, the proposed datasets as stated in the Proposal did not seek to systematically collect data on the informal enforcement activities carried out by the CSRC and its regional offices (vis-à-vis the two Stock Exchanges), owing to issues with data availability at the time of the Proposal’s drafting. Thereafter, however, concerted efforts were made to identify and access new data sources, with considerable success. The Dataset thus records various categories of such informal enforcement actions as oral warnings and ‘supervisory talks’, which to the best of my knowledge had not hitherto been captured in a sophisticated manner in the existing literature. Another important feature of the Dataset is its comprehensiveness. It is considerably more comprehensive than any commercial, subscription-based database currently available. The Dataset contains close to 8,000 publicly accessible enforcement actions. By contrast, CSMAR and WIND, the two leading commercial databases that are widely used in the related literature, record just over 4,400 and 1,300 enforcement actions, respectively, during the same period. Although wide-ranging, the Dataset’s enforcement actions did not, in their original form, include many of the variables needed to address the research questions posed in this project. Therefore, a very large body of additional data was collected on a cohort of selected independent variables. These include each culpable firm’s characteristics, e.g. market capitalisation, ownership structure, industry, financial performance, identity of the ultimate controller, and relationship with the regulatory authorities, as well as the personal profiles of its senior office holders. They also included such external factors as the level of media scrutiny the alleged violations received. The identification and selection of these explanatory variables were guided by the research questions the project sought to address. Due to the significantly increased size of the Dataset and the uneven quality of the data sources, data processing was a time-consuming and labour-intensive process. Feedback from conference presentations and elite interviews, whilst constructive, also led to additional steps being taken to further improve data-processing, which entailed a further significant time investment. Despite these many challenges, the project was successfully completed. The empirical findings resulting from a methodologically robust analysis of the proprietary Dataset successfully addressed the many specific research questions that the project set out to answer in relation to its objectives. They also provided robust empirical evidence, on which the project’s peer-reviewed publications and conference presentations relied. Objective 4: Elite interviews were the primary method adopted to elucidate the complex dynamics between the enforcement agencies and regulated firms and individuals, as well as the other stakeholders involved. My interviewees included two selected cohorts of CSRC and Exchange officials in consideration of the formal and organisational separation between the ‘investigative’ and ‘adjudicative’ roles within their enforcement programmes. Thus, the first cohort comprised CSRC/Exchange officials involved in the investigation of securities violations, whilst the second comprised officials and CSRC/Exchange-appointed ‘judges’ responsible for adjudicating allegations of securities violations based on the investigation outcomes. Interviews were also conducted with a variety of stakeholders to determine how they had been affected by, and had reacted to, enforcement actions and how they had attempted to influence the decision-making of the enforcement agencies. These stakeholders included the state agencies concerned at both the central and local levels, as well as the providers of legal, accountancy and financial services. The elite interviews proved to be particularly useful for successfully achieving Objective 4. They helped to gain otherwise unobtainable insight into a number of under-documented, yet important, aspects of enforcement activities. These include for example, the nature and forms of interaction with, and intervention by, regulated firms and individuals, as well as concerned government agencies at various levels, that may have inhibited the CSRC/Exchanges from making decisions as independently as they would have liked. The interview results thus added important nuances to the findings pertaining to Objectives 1, 2 and 3. Objective 5: The quantitative and qualitative findings described above laid a solid foundation for conceptualising and generalising the case of public securities enforcement in China, thereby helping to successfully achieve the project’s final objective. In particular, the unparalleled scope and scale of the project’s data on enforcement actions, both formal and informal, enabled this research to challenge conventional wisdom, which is based largely on a narrower conceptualisation of securities enforcement actions and a considerably smaller pool of enforcement activities.

452913.label: Major findings and research outcome
452913.value: The major findings of this research can be summarised as follows. - It shows empirically that firms of a larger size, firms that are controlled by the state, firms that are more politically embedded, and firms that cooperate with the securities regulators face a lower probability of being targeted for enforcement and a higher likelihood of lenient enforcement. It also demonstrates that, counter-intuitively, a closer personal bond with the securities regulators is likely to intensify the severity of enforcement actions and unlikely to reduce the likelihood of being targeted in the first place. - It demonstrates empirically that investors’ reactions to information on enforcement actions taken against the firms in which they have invested are crucially dependent on the manner in which that information is released and disseminated. More specifically, Chinese investors react negatively to such information when it comes directly from their invested firms. When it is channelled through the regulators taking the actions, in contrast, investors remain indifferent until the financial media take an interest. - It shows empirically that weak public enforcement of the corporate governance code by the regulatory authorities is an important contributing factor to the failure of corporate governance initiatives (e.g. cumulative voting) intended to protect minority shareholders from a cohesive majority. - It demonstrates that the evolutionary trajectory of China’s public securities enforcement programme has been shaped by the complex dynamics between the programme’s aspiration to adopt a US-style, enforcement-led securities regulatory regime and the Chinese securities regulators’ traditional developmental role. - It depicts the changing patterns of the CSRC’s formal enforcement activities, suggesting that the CSRC has emerged as an adaptive regulator willing and able to develop new strategies and shift its enforcement priorities as market conditions evolve. - It posits that the public enforcement of securities laws has played a much greater role than private securities enforcement in the development of China’s securities markets, although its effectiveness is conditional upon various institutional constraints and dynamics. The research outcomes of the project include: - Five articles published/accepted for publication by prestigious peer-reviewed journals and edited volumes published by prestigious academic publishers; - Three keynote addresses and three invited public lectures; - 20 presentations at internationally recognised conferences organised by premier research institutions; and - Three articles under review by prestigious peer-reviewed journals.

452913.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
452913.value: As elaborated above, the project’s Dataset is considerably more comprehensive than the leading commercial, subscription-based databases widely used in academia and industry. It thus presents a much fuller, more nuanced picture of China’s public securities enforcement regime. The Dataset therefore has significant potential for knowledge transfer activities. Potentially interested parties include Chinese legislators and policymakers (as Chinese securities legislation is undergoing a major overhaul), Chinese securities regulators, Chinese investors (both retail and institutional), and Chinese listed firms and their service providers. Global investors are also likely to be interested, for they are gaining more significant exposure to China’s securities markets as the country steps up its efforts to open up its markets to overseas investors, as most recently manifested by the addition of mainland Chinese listed firms by global index provider MSCI to its widely followed emerging market index. Preliminary discussions have been undertaken with potential collaborators in full compliance with RGC and University rules should knowledge transfer activities materialise.

453113.label: Project Title(Chinese)
453113.value: 尋找民間基督教：中國內地福音廣播聽眾來信研究（1959-2004）

453113.label: Project Objectives
453113.value: It is customary to understand the contemporary development of Christianity in China under the outdated dichotomous framework, but this neglects the role of popular Christian communities. When we analyze the letters, we will use the four interrogatives of “who, when, where, and why”, which will help us listen to the voices of these grassroots Christians. The regional diversity of the vast territory of China should not be overlooked in the study of Chinese Christianity. Such regional differences are best illustrated by the well-known fact that Protestant Christianity in China experienced remarkable progress in certain provinces such as Henan, Anhui, Fujian, Zhejiang, Jiangsu, Yunnan and Guangdong. The proposed project will contribute to remedying the deficiencies of the grand narrative of ‘all-China’, by analyzing the temporal and spatial features of the letters and showing the characteristics and regional differences in the development of Protestant Christianity. The plurality of the audience helps us to understand the interactive relationship between Christianity and Chinese society. How does the social composition of the audience change over time? How do the letters reflect the concerns of Christians and non-Christians from differing backgrounds? In what way does the reception of the Christian message reflect the changing social and religious background of Chinese society? How did Christians indigenize the concept of ‘mission’ during and after the Cultural Revolution when they were completely cut off from global Christian organizations? How did they achieve the gospel commission with regard to evangelization, pastoral care and theological education? What were the difficulties, struggles and doubts facing them? What did they do to overcome these obstacles and redefine the challenges facing Christianity in the midst of rapid political, social and economic changes? The numerous letters itself could be considered as a set of new released primary historical materials with significant contributions to the development of Chinese public and popular history. The digitization, transcription, and translation of the radio audience letters will help to set up an electronic database that will be freely accessible to all scholars and research students in the field of Chinese studies.

453113.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
453113.value: Christianity has faced acute institutional and ideological challenges since the establishment of the People’s Republic of China. The government’s closed-door policy led the Church in China to take the road to ‘independence’ which highlighted the appeal of ‘anti-imperialism’. The expulsion of Western missionaries marked the end of the “Missionary Era” in China. Under the banner of building a new socialist state, Christian Enterprises were targeted by the Communist government for reform. To break through the Bamboo Curtain, the Far East Broadcasting Co. (FEBC), an American- funded-based transnational Christian radio organization, established its studio in Hong Kong in 1958 to convey the religious message via shortwave radio to Red China during the peak of the Cold War. This represented part of the Free World’s cultural strategy to employ Christianity to subvert the Mainland. Over half a century, the message from the “underground” strived to respond to the changing needs of Chinese society and Protestant churches in China, and more than 350,000 letters from the Mainland audience were mailed to the FEBC office in HK. Once processed and classified, these letters will throw light on what Raymond Williams calls ‘the structure of feeling’ among Chinese Christians under Communist rule, the changing modes of religious conversion and the development of spirituality after the end of the missionary era. These issues are essential for understanding the Christian renaissance in China today, a controversial topic that attracts much academic and public attention. The research project plans to investigate these 350,000 letters received from 1959 to 2004 for qualitative and quantitative analysis, and to create the first electronic database of Chinese Christians’ letters for research. Covering different geographical regions and many diverse subjects, these letters are indeed rare and valuable primary, historical documents, that will help to rediscover the scenarios of a huge number of rank and file Chinese Christians and spiritual inquirers from the Mao era to Reform China. The project is expected to construct a comprehensive account of those unheard and unseen grassroots Christians, which will not only greatly contribute to the rewriting of the history of popular Chinese Christianity, but also help to improve our understanding of the spiritual, cultural and social landscapes of the Chinese people of that time. These insights should enable us to go beyond the old dichotomy of suppression and resistance in the study of church-state relations, and embrace the current social scientific theory of an unregulated religious market. 中華人民共和國成立後，中國基督教不論在體制或思想上，均面對嚴峻的挑戰。隨著國門緊閉，中國教會走上反「帝國主義」的「獨立自主」的道路。西方傳教士的撤離，意味著在華傳教時代的終結。在建設社會主義新國家的旗幟下，基督教事業成為政府致力改革的目標。 1958年，為了突破「竹幕」籓籬，遠東廣播公司在香港成立錄音室，在冷戰的高峰期仍通過短波向中國內地進行宗教廣播。這代表自由世界企圖以基督教來顛覆紅色中國的文化策略。半個世紀以來，這些來自「地下」的信息致力回應中國社會及教會的不同需要，在港的辦事處合共收到30多萬封中國大陸的聽眾來信。有關信函經處理後，可對共產統治下中國基督徒的「情感結構」，傳教時代結束後宗教改宗的模式與靈性發展帶來啟迪。這也有助認識今天中國基督教的復興這個備受學術及公眾關注的爭議課題。 本研究對1959至2004年間約35萬封來自內地的信函作定量及定質分析，並建立首個中國基督徒信函的數據庫。這些信件涵蓋全國不同地區，涉及廣泛內容，成為發現不同時代中國基督徒及尋道者面貌的珍貴史料。研究亦有助為大量基層信徒重構其面貌，不僅對我們從民間基督教的角度來重寫當代中國基督教史，有重大貢獻；也能提昇我們對期間中國民眾的靈性、文化及社會狀況的認識。本研究突破舊有二元對立的政教關係框架，並期望能對宗教社會科學探究中國未規範的宗教市場理論有所裨益。

453113.label: Realisation of objectives
453113.value: The project objectives have been fully achieved in the following ways: I. RESEARCH TEAM 1. Post-doctoral Fellow. Since a huge number (over 350,000) of listeners’ letters are involved in the research project, it is absolutely necessary to employ a full-time Research Fellow to assist the research. The PI has secured a grant from the Research Committee of CUHK to employ a Postdoctoral Fellow (Dr. YUEN Hao) for 12 months (1 August, 2014 – 31 July, 2015). 2. Co-I. Prof. Joseph LEE of the Pace University, NY, USA visited HK in August 2014 and May 2015 respectively to join the working meeting of the research project. In June 2016, the PI and Co-I were invited to attend an international conference held in Tokyo. We then discussed the project over there. All digitized letters has been shared with the Co-I on the Cloud-platform. 3. Research Student. The PI has supervised a Bachelor of Divinity student on her graduation thesis on the FEB letters. II. DIGITALIZATION of Primary Materials 1. According to the research proposal, all letters (the total amount is over 350,000) is expected to digitize by the professional services agency. Since the service charge of the agency is quite expensive, the PI decided to outsource the digitalization job to student helpers starting from 2017 in order to scan more letters within the limited budget. 2. The research team discovered that the letters of some years are either total lost (1969-1972, 1980-81, 1983-85) or partially lost (1982, 1986-87). Upon the completion of the project, 80% of the letters has been scanned. The reason for not being able to scan all letters (over 350,000) is due to the fragile and vulnerable nature of the letters. It can only be conduced piece by piece and handled with special care. The PI will apply for the Knowledge Transfer Grant to complete the remaining digitalization job. III. COLLECTION of Research Documents 1. Taipei FEB office. The PI visited the FEB office in Taipei during his conference trip. The letters were originally transferred from HK and stored in Taipei before 1997 for security reason. 2. Hong Kong FEB office. The Research student conducted the research works in the FEB office in HK. All related documents for the project have been identified and reproduced, including the internal reports, newsletters, publications, etc. 3. Archival Research in USA. The PI has originally planned to visit the FEB archives in California, USA. Since most of the related primary materials has been kept in the archives of Billy Graham Centre, Wheaton College, USA, a research trip was conducted in June 2017 over there. 4. Radio Taiwan International (RTI). The RTI is originally named Central Broadcasting System (CBS). After the KMT government had retreated to Taiwan, the CBS launched Mandarin program (Voices of Free China) broadcast over shortwave into Mainland China. The PI visited the RTI headquarter during his sabbatical leave in Taiwan in 2018 to collect research materials of the Voices of Free China. IV. PROJECT OBJECTIVES 1. The four interrogatives of “who, when, where, and why” have been employed to investigate the voices of these grassroots Christians as reflected from the audience letters. 2. The plurality of the audience has been investiagated, with special emphasis on the distinish characteristic on the development of Urban and rural churches in China. 3. Textual and contextual analyses have been applied to interpret the audiences’ letter from the age of revolution to the age of reform and opening. 4. The cultural and religious strategy to employ Christianity to subvert the Communist China during the Cold War era has been identified by revisiting the archives of the FEB. V. USPENT BALANCE: The justification for the unspent portion (24.65%, $87754.4) of the total balance) is: 1. The expense of the research trips of the Co-I to HK has been reimbursed by other funding sources. Eventually, only one out of three trips was supported by the project budget. 2. Since one of the conference trips (Rome 2014) has been reimbursed by the conference organizer, the conference expense was unspent. 3. All letters is expected to digitize by the professional services agency. Due to the fragile and vulnerable nature of the letters, it can only be conducted piece by piece and handled with special care. Therefore, the service charge of the agency is quite expensive and beyond our limited budget. In order to scan more letters within the original budget, we decided to fine-tune the budget and reallocate more resources on digitization.

453113.value: The project has contributed to long-term impact brought by the following research findings and outcomes: 1. The project is contributed for the study of contemporary Chinese Christianity, as it departs from the existing ‘Three-self Church versus House Churches’ dichotomous framework, revising the characteristics and development of popular Christianity and the challenges it faced in the PRC. [See research output: 8:1, 8:2, 8:3, 8:4, 8:5, 8:6, 8:7, 8:8, 8:9] 2. The numerous listeners’ letters are the absolutely authentic voices of the common people that will serve as rare first hand historical accounts for reconstructing the social, cultural, ideological and spiritual landscapes of grassroots Chinese society. [See research output: 8:1, 8:5, 8:8, 8: 9, 9:1, 10:1] 3. This research project highlights a qualitative change in the church-state encounters from the Maoist era to the Reform period, using the radio audiences’ letters to capture the dramatic transformation of China’s religious landscape from one solely monopolized by the one-party state to a more pluralistic domain semi-regulated by the state and the market. 453513.label: Project Objectives
453513.value: To identify a predictive model which explains the health outcomes of family caregivers of Chinese dementia sufferers. To explain how and why the predictive factors influence health outcomes of family caregivers of Chinese dementia sufferers.
