597213.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
597213.value: This study can be further developed in several other ways. First of all, it should be noted that acquirers do not select targets randomly. We do not expect that the selection of targets would seriously confound our results. This is because this study focused on the negotiation and integration process of a given takeover. Researchers can incorporate additional characteristics of acquirers and targets in the analytical framework in future efforts. Future research should also look at how status differentials affect another important aspect of corporate takeovers, namely the acquisition premiums. On the one hand, lower-status targets have stronger desires to be purchased by higher-status acquirers and hence they may accept lower acquisition premiums. On the other hand, when acquirer-target status differentials are greater, transaction costs are lower and if we hold the overall cost associated with any corporate takeovers constant, acquirers may be willing to offer higher premiums. Future research should explore how firm status differentials affect acquisition premiums. It should also be meaningful to explore any boundary conditions of the studied relationship by identifying important moderators. This can deepen our understanding of the underlying mechanisms. Future research can try to confirm these speculations.

597313.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
597313.value: ABSTRACT Intercultural service encounters (ICSEs) involve interactions between customers and employees from different cultures. With growing immigration and international tourism in recent years, there has been a rapid increase in intercultural service encounters. However, there are relatively few studies researching the underlying satisfaction evaluation process in these encounters. Moreover, prior research focuses mostly on customers with little attention to employees, despite the dyadic nature of these encounters and evidence of differences in the expectations and perceptions of customers and employees. The proposed study is an attempt to fill this important knowledge gap. In this study, we use expectancy-disconfirmation and attribution theories to explain satisfaction evaluations in intercultural service encounters. Customer satisfaction with a service encounter is an emotional state experienced in response to an evaluation of their service experience. We propose that service employees, just like customers, will form some expectations towards a service to be delivered, and these expectations will serve as reference points when evaluating their satisfaction with the service. We have developed a research framework based on an extensive literature review and in-depth interviews with thirty consumers. We plan to conduct thirty more in-depth interviews with service employees in Hong Kong to find out their views and experiences in intercultural service encounters. We hypothesize several differences in satisfaction evaluation process between service employees and customers using attribution theory. We will use scenario-based field experiments to assess the research framework across different service categories with service employees and customers from diverse cultural backgrounds to enhance the generalizability of the results. Linear structural equation modeling (LISREL) will be employed to assess the hypothesized relationships. The evidence will provide useful insights for managers to identify their staff’s training needs and develop programs to enhance their staff’s intercultural competence such that they can deal with the cause of a service outcome effectively. Moreover, the research will also provide useful insights for managers to design effective strategies to influence customers’ attribution process and develop education programs to improve their customers’ intercultural competence so as to minimize the impact of perceived culture distance on customer satisfaction.

597313.label: Realisation of objectives
597313.value: The research objectives are mostly achieved. 1) We have investigated the effects of perceived cultural distance, disconfirmation, attributions and intercultural competence on satisfaction from the perspective of customers. The findings offer some insight for the managers to design effective strategies for managing customers. The study and findings were presented in an International Business Conference in 2015. 2) We have also revised the initial research model based on the comments provided by an external reviewer on the RGC review panel. The revised model included personal cultural orientations as moderators. Data were collected from customers in a restaurant setting to assess the hypothesized relationships in the revised model. The study, findings and implications were reported in a refereed article in Journal of Services Marketing in 2016. 3) We have also collected data from both employees and customers in a retail setting to examine the effects of perceived cultural distance, disconfirmation, attributions and intercultural competence on satisfaction evaluations. Because the time to conduct the interviews with the foreign customers and service employees was longer than we expected, we got the approval from RGC to extend the project completion date. We eventually obtained an adequate of responses from service employees, foreign and local customers to perform advanced statistical analysis. Multivariate analysis of variance was performed. The findings suggest that service employees and customers make different attributions when encountering a service delivery success vs failure. We are performing more data analysis with structural equation modeling to find out the differences in attributions and satisfaction evaluations between service employees and customers. When the data analysis is completed, the findings will offer more insights for the managers to design effective strategies for managing both employees and customers. Then, all research objectives will be achieved.

597313.label: Major findings and research outcome
597313.value: 1) Presentation at an International Business Conference in London 2015. We found that customer satisfaction was positively related to cultural attribution and self-attribution, but negatively related to attribution to employee. The results suggest that cultural attribution may serve as a buffer when a service failure occurs in an intercultural service encounter. Customers will be more likely to attribute the cause of the failure to cultural differences when perceived cultural distance is large, and high cultural attribution would lead to higher satisfaction. The results also showed that when customers perceived that they were responsible for the outcome, they would feel less dissatisfied. But when they perceived that the employee was responsible for the outcome, they would feel more dissatisfied. We also found that intercultural competence mitigated the negative effect of attribution to employee on customer satisfaction. 2) Refereed article published in Journal of Services Marketing 2016. We included personal cultural orientations as moderators in the research model and examined the role of customer attribution in service delivery success vs. failure. Our results showed that customers tended to hold service employee and firm responsible for service delivery failure rather than themselves and cultural differences, compared to service delivery success. The results also showed that the four personal cultural orientations partially moderated the mediating influencing of the four customer attributions in the process by which service outcome affected customer satisfaction. Specifically, customers with high interdependent orientation tended to take credit for a successful service delivery while customers with high social inequality orientation (IEQ) tended to give credit to service employees and firm in a successful service delivery, and they felt responsible for an unsuccessful service delivery. 3) The major findings have also been covered in a refereed book chapter entitled “Intercultural Service Encounters (ICSEs): Challenges and Opportunities for International Services Marketers. In Leonidas C. Leonidou, Constantine S. Katsikeas, Saeed Samiee, and Bilge Aykol (Eds.), Advances in Global Marketing: A Research Anthology. Springer AG in 2017.

597313.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
597313.value: We will continue the research to examine the roles that attribution and intercultural competence play in satisfaction evaluation with the data collected from service employees, local and foreign customers. The results of multivariate analysis of variance showed that service employees and customers have different attributions when encountering a service delivery success vs. failure. We are performing more data analysis with structural equation modeling to determine these differences because this modeling approach is more rigorous and can account for the measurement error. We will write up the findings and develop a manuscript, which will be submitted to a high quality journal for publication.

597313.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
597313.value: Intercultural service encounters are growing importance due to rapid increases in immigration, international tourism and globalization of service businesses. This research has advanced our understanding of attribution and satisfaction evaluation process in these encounters. The findings offer useful insights for service firms to design effective strategies for managing employees and culturally diverse customers. Considering that intercultural service encounters are becoming more common, it is important for service firms to develop customer education program to educate their culturally diverse customers about local norms and practices such that the customers will form appropriate expectations towards a service prior to consumption. Service firms should also design strategies to influence customers to make more attributions of positive encounters to service employees and firms through marketing communication and customer appreciation program in an effort to achieve high customer satisfaction. On the other hand, service firms should also provide intercultural education and training to improve the knowledge and attitudes of their service employees such that they can adapt services and behaviors to meet the diverse needs of multicultural customers.

597413.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
597413.value: The literature on CEO turnovers typically focuses on the turnover sensitivity to firm performance and how the internal governance structure and quality affects such sensitivity. Two recent papers, Jenter and Kanaan (forthcoming) and Kaplan and Minton (2012), document a surprisingly interesting fact that CEOs are more likely to be dismissed upon poor industry performance. Jenter and Kanaan conclude that boards mistakenly credit and blame CEOs for performance beyond their control. In sharp contrast is a recent paper by Cornelli, Kominek, and Ljungqvist (forthcoming), which shows that CEOs will not be fired when performance deteriorates due to factors beyond their control, nor are they fired for making ‘honest mistakes.’ They also find that following forced CEO turnover, companies see performance improvements. Although the sample setting for these studies is different, the message behind these two sets of results still looks conflicting. Therefore, it is not all clear whether CEOs will be fired for factors beyond their control. The main objective of this project is to help understand the issue of why firms would fire their CEOs based on poor peer performance and whether such decision is made in a rational way. We plan to achieve this goal by examining the short-term announcement effect of the turnover decision and the long-term performance change upon CEO succession. We will also focus on testing one plausible rationale behind such turnovers. We postulate that when the whole industry is in setback and exit is called for but the CEO is reluctant to make the necessary changes, such as layoffs, investment cutbacks, and divestitures, due to agency conflicts (Morck, Shleifer and Vishny, 1989; Jensen, 1993), an effective board will play the role of the takeovers market and fire the incumbent CEO (Kaplan and Minton, 2012) and make necessary changes. Such an explanation carries rich testable implications for us to test in the project. We expect that only firms with effective boards would fire their CEOs upon bad peer performance and replace by external, “powerful”, “generalist” CEOs to revitalize the business under a declining industry through corporate downsizing and/or innovative changes. As a result, the subsequent performance of these firms would be improved. To the extent that governance quality and board effectiveness increase through time, we would also expect increasing turnover-industry performance sensitivity over time. As such, Jensen’s (1993, JoF) earlier concern about the problem of failure to exit will dissipate through time. 在CEO更换这一课题上，金融文献通常重在分析CEO更换对公司业绩的敏感性以及公司内部的治理机制如何影响这种敏感性。在最近的两篇论文中，Jenter and Kanaan （即将发表）和Kaplan and Minton （2012）发现了一个有趣但令人诧异的事实，即一个公司的CEO更有可能因为行业同辈们的拙劣业绩而被自己的公司开除。Jenter and Kanaan 总结到，董事会错误地依据CEO能力范围之外的事宜而对CEO进行奖励和惩罚。然而，与此截然相反，在最近的一篇文献中，Cornelli, Kominek, and Ljungqvist （即将发表）发现，如果公司业绩恶化是因为CEO控制范围之外的事宜导致的，或者CEO犯了一些无意中的“诚恳的错误”，CEO不会因此而被开除。他们同时发现，在CEO被开除之后，公司的业绩得以提升。这些文献采用的样本数据固然不同，但他们传达的信息却非常的矛盾，即，对于CEO是否会因为自己能力范围之外的事宜而被开除，我们是不清楚的。

597413.label: Realisation of objectives
597413.value: All the stated objectives have been achieved despite some unforeseeable difficulties during the course of our investigation. For the first objective, our results do indicate that both earnings (measured by ROA) and stock returns improve from a year before the forced turnover to one and up to three years after the turnover. Such improvements are both absolute as well as relative to the industry peers. Regression analysis using annual data confirms such improvements. However, we acknowledge an inherent difficulty that it is very hard to cleanly accredit such improvements to those forced turnovers purely due to poor industry performance and not also due to firm-specific performance. We hence put a caveat in our paper. For the second objective, we examined two types of changes in sensitivity. The first type is the change in the relative weightings between firm-specific performance and industry performance on a firm’s turnover decision. For this, we found that in industry recessions the sensitivity of firm-specific performance to forced departure is much larger than that of industry peer performance. In many cases, the coefficients of industry peer performance are even not statistically significant, indicating that industry peer performances are completely filtered. This evidence significantly discounts the role of industry performance in turnover decisions when the whole industry falls into a setback. On the other hand, the sensitivity of industry peer performance to forced departure is larger in industry booms than in industry recessions. This evidence suggests that industry peer performance has a larger effect on forced CEO departure in industry booms than in industry recessions. A surprisingly interesting finding is that in many cases the sensitivity of industry performance to forced departure in industry booms is even larger than that of firm-specific performance. This result holds, no matter the CEO leaves the firm for retirement or being fired. Note that for all of the tests in Jenter and Kanaan (2015), the magnitude of coefficients on industry peer performance is smaller than that on firm-specific performance. Our evidence indicates that industry performance is at least as important, if not more so, than firm-specific performance in turnover decisions when the whole industry is in booming. While this evidence confirms that firm-specific performance in industry booms is less revealing about a CEO’s ability, it may also indicate that the board fails to fulfill its monitoring role in good times, as argued by Jenter and Kanaan. The second type is the change in sensitivity over time. For this, we found that the sensitivity of firm-specific performance to forced departure is larger in industry recessions than in industry booms. This evidence confirms again that firm-specific performance plays a determinant role in CEO turnover decisions in industry recessions. For the third objective on firm governance, we examine the impact of large shareholders and CEO power. Specifically, we examine the impact of large shareholders on the pattern of CEO turnover decisions upon industry condition. Our results show that there are more forced CEO departures in firms with one or more large shareholders, irrespective of industry condition. Particularly, in industry recessions, the sensitivity of firm-specific performance to forced CEO departure is greater for firms with large shareholders. These pieces of evidence confirm an active monitoring role of large shareholders, consistent with prior literature (e.g., Shleifer and Vishny, 1986). However, we do not find evidence that the industry peer performance is completely filtered in industry booms. Actually, the results show that the performance-departure sensitivity is strengthened in good times for both industry peer and firm-specific performance measures for firms with large shareholders. The other aspect we look at is CEO power. Jenter and Kanaan (2015) suspect that more powerful CEOs should be better able to defend themselves against “unfair” dismissals in bad times, weakening the effect of peer performance on forced turnovers. But they couldn’t find supportive evidence by measuring CEO power with factors such as whether the CEO is a founder, having large equity stakes, or the board being less independent, etc. We try to look at CEO power from another perspective. Following Adams, Almeida and Ferreira (2005), we measure CEO power with the concentration of titles in the hands of the CEO. Specifically, we measure CEO power as whether a CEO has any position in the board, or if the CEO is also the Chairman of the board, and if the CEO holds the positions of Chairman and President together. The more important position(s) the CEO holds in the board the more power she is assumed to have. As such, we find that forced CEO departures are significantly less for powerful CEOs. Furthermore, we observe that in industry recessions when firm-specific performance plays a determinant role in turnover decisions, the sensitivity of forced departure to firm-specific performance is significantly weakened by powerful CEOs whereas in industry booms, when industry peer performance becomes important in turnover decisions, the sensitivity of forced departure to industry peer performance is also weakened significantly by powerful CEOs. Our results are consistent with the findings in Morse, Nanda and Seru (2008). They document that powerful CEOs can induce the boards to shift the weight on performance measures towards the better performing measures, thereby rigging the incentive part of their pay. About the fourth objective of examining CEO succession patterns and characteristics following forced turnovers due to poor peer industry performance, we ended up deciding not to work on it in this paper as we have another project which specifically examines CEO succession patterns and characteristics following forced turnovers with a special focus on CEO confidence attributes. Such spinoff investigation is triggered by Goel and Thakor’s (2008) CEO promotional tournament model and has been developed into a separate working paper. We focus on and observe distinctive attribute transition patterns between forced turnovers and retirements. Specifically, firms show a correctional pattern of attribute convergence by replacing their fired CEOs with rational CEOs whereas firms with retiring CEOs show an attribute continuity pattern with retiring and succeeding CEOs sharing the same attribute. Importantly, disproportionately more overconfident CEOs work and retire in innovative industries. For the last objective, we focus on two aspects of restructuring, i.e. the possible change in the investment rate and the number of business segments before and after the forced turnovers. Our results indicate a significant drop in the investment rate from a year before the forced turnover to one year and up to three years after the turnover. Regression analysis using annual data confirms such drop. However, we do not observe any significant changes in business segments after CEO turnovers.

597413.label: Major findings and research outcome
597413.value: Our studies have the following major findings. 1. We confirm that industry performance contributes to the likelihood of CEO forced turnovers. 2. However, the importance of industry performance towards CEO forced turnovers differs between industrial upturn and downturn. Specifically, industry performance as a forced turnover decision factor is more important during industrial upturn than downturn. 3. Following the spirit of Engel, Hayes, and Wang (2003), we use the adjusted R2 of the regression of individual stock return against the industry stock return as a proxy on the relative information precision between stock return and industry return in capturing CEO performance ability. We found that the adjusted R2 is significantly higher during industrial upturn than downturn. We interpret such result as that individual stock return (relative to industrial peer stock return) as a reflection of CEO performance ability is weaker in information precision and hence less indicative during industrial upturn than downturn. 4. Combining the above two findings, we conclude that the reason why a firm relies more on industry performance during industrial upturn and relies more on firm-specific performance during industrial downturn when it makes a forced turnover decision is because firm-specific performance is a clearer signal of CEO performance ability during industrial downturn than upturn. As such, the turnover decisions are rationally made. 5. We confirm the above conclusion by finding that after forced turnover, firm’s return on assets (ROA) improves from one year to three years relative to the year before the forced turnover, and such improvement is not only relative to the firm’s own performance but relative to its peers. Furthermore, the investment rate of firms upon forced turnovers reduces in the subsequent three years. 6. Finally, we confirm that governance matters. Even though poor firm performance during industrial downturn is a stronger indicator of the incompetence of the incumbent CEO, a powerful CEO weakens the ability of the board to fire her under such circumstance. On the other hand, a firm with more institutional ownership strengthens such linkage.

597413.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
597413.value: As mentioned earlier, our fourth objective has been spun off to a new project that focuses on CEO attribute transition. There is a recent line of study that looks at the link of finance and corporate culture. In 2015, the Journal of Financial Economics contribute a special issue to look at the “cultural revolution” in finance (Volume 117, Issue 1). We view that CEO attribute transition comes from but also contributes to the company’s corporate culture. Hence, it is interesting and important to look at a specific type of corporate culture which is the CEO confidence attributes and how CEO turnovers change or perpetuate such attributes. We also want to explore if such attribute transitions via CEO turnovers differ between turnovers that are driven by firm-specific performance and turnovers driven by industrial performance. To appreciate the relevance of such research agenda, it is worth noting that there are already studies looking at how corporate culture affects CEO turnover (Fiordelisi and Ricci, 2014) and affects corporate risk-taking behaviors (Li et al., 2013). Hence, we believe that such research development is worthwhile and meaningful.

597413.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
597413.value: Studies found that CEOs could be forced to leave companies upon poor industry performance. However, it is unclear the rationale behind such turnover decision and hence it is equally unclear if such forced turnover decisions are correctly made or not. Instead of searching for economic explanations for such turnover decision, we try to explain through the angle of information precision between firm and industry performance on CEO ability. Specifically, we argue and show that during industrial downturn, firm-specific performance provides more precise information about the CEO ability whereas under industrial upturn, industry performance can reveal better the CEO ability. As such, forced turnovers upon poor industry performance are optimal decisions. Our study hence makes two major contributions. First, we go deeper to contrast the relative weightings of industry versus firm performance used by the board on CEO turnover decisions. We show that during industry boom, the forced turnover decision is based more on (poor) industry performance whereas during industry downturn, such decision is based more on (poor) firm performance. Second, we provide explanation to such switching of weights by showing that firm-specific performance information is more precise during industry downturn than upturn.

597713.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
597713.value: 此項目研究的是強權首席執行官(CEO)的個人能力在多大程度上能解釋他們超高的薪酬。根據管理權力假說(managerial power hypothesis), 強權CEO會使用他們的權力通過榨取股東的租值來獲得過量的薪酬。但是如果強權CEO的超高薪水確實是其超強能力的反映，那麼他們的天文高薪或許就不是過量的。在現有管理權力假說的實證研究中，CEO的能力因素經常被忽略。 為了弄清究竟是管理權力假說(managerial power hypothesis)還是管理能力假說(managerial ability hypothesis)使強權CEO獲得天文高薪, 這個項目旨研究CEO權力的來源。具體來說，就是研究為什麼 CEO是有強權的。我們用市場競爭激烈性以及替換現任CEO的繼任者的稀缺性來作為標杆將CEO的權利分為獲得型(acquired type)和繼承型(inherited type)。獲得型的CEO面對公開競爭，通過他們的高超能力來獲得權利。繼承型的CEO面對來自潛在繼任者的較小威脅，他們的權力是通過能力以外的其他因素獲得的。所以，如果CEO是獲得型的，他們的超強能力使得他們理應得到超高的薪酬；相反，如果CEO是繼承型的，那麼他們的超高薪酬可能就是管理者根深蒂固(managerial entrenchment)權力的一種表現。 為了進一步對管理能力假說進行實證研究， 我們研究獲得型CEO的總薪酬是否大於繼承型CEO的總薪酬。根據管理能力假說(managerial ability hypothesis)，為了隱藏過量的薪酬，強權CEO傾向於獲得一份模糊的薪酬合約來降低股東不滿的可能性。 所以此項目進一步探究是否獲得型CEO的激勵型薪酬(incentive-based compensation)相比繼承性CEO的激勵型薪酬低得多。這是因為激勵型的薪酬比現金型(cash-based compensation)的薪酬更掩人耳目。 此外，我們還將研究CEO權力在文獻中的傳統量度在多大程度上能被CEO權力的來源所解釋。我們預測CEO的能力(即獲得型CEO的能力)是CEO權力量度的一個重要決定因素。此項目還研究獲得型CEO的事前(ex-ante)合約比繼承型的合約更加透明清楚。最後，我們還將研究兩種類型CEO事後(ex-post)合約。我們預期繼承型的CEO事後更改合約情況較獲得型CEO普遍。

597713.label: Realisation of objectives
597713.value: This project has four objectives. To address these objectives in a complete and satisfactory manner, we wrote two research papers. The first paper is “Compensation and Employment Contracts of Powerful CEOs” and the second one is “Explicit Employment Contracts and CEO Compensation”. The first paper is written to address mainly the first three objectives and partially the last objective. The first paper first identifies the source of CEO power into two major types: acquired and inherited (Objective 1). CEO power is said to be acquired if CEOs attain power endogenously by competing with many would-be successors for the leadership position. CEO power is said to be inherited if CEOs attain power endogenously by the lineage with the founding family. Empirically, we use the founder-CEO status as our proxy for acquired CEO power because founder CEOs can make the most relevant corporate decisions due to their significant ownership and long-term interactions with the board. Besides, founder CEOs compete with a large pool of professional executives (potential successors) for the CEO position. The competition is deemed to be intense as many founders have been replaced by professional executives long before their firms go public. We use the heir-CEO status as our proxy for inherited CEO power. Heir CEOs are descendants of the founding family who succeed their parents or relatives to become the leader of the company. Heir CEOs have low perceived ability because they are less immune to competition in the labor market for the leadership position. In unreported results, we also try other measures of acquired vs. inherited CEO power, e.g., professional CEOs in firms with a high pre-existing entrenchment index (E-index) and professional CEOs in firms with a low pre-existing entrenchment index. However, the results are much weaker than our initial expectations and not statistically significant at the conventional levels. Thus, we delete these results from our paper. Additionally, recommendations from audiences in seminars and conferences also suggest that our current classification (founder-CEOs vs. heir-CEOs) is reasonable to capture acquired and inherited CEO power. The first paper examines the relation between conventional measures of CEO power and our measures of acquired and inherited CEO power (Objective 2). Specifically, we empirically examine the effect of the founder-CEO status and the heir-CEO status on CEO leadership, a widely-used and conventional measure of CEO power. The CEO leadership is a binary variable and takes the value of one if the CEO is also the chairman of the board. The CEO leadership is a relevant measure of CEO power because a key function of the board is to remove non-performing CEOs. Thus, allowing the CEO to also serve as the chairman weakens the board’s ability to replace non-performing CEOs. In unreported results, we also try other measures of concentration of CEO title, the degree of board independence, and CEO pay slice. We find that our results on CEO leadership are very consistent. In addition, the estimated effect of CEO leadership is meaningfully large in an economic and statistical sense. Thus, we report only the results of CEO leadership in our paper. The first paper also examines whether CEOs with inherited power are paid more in total pay and more in incentive-based compensation relative to CEOs with acquired power (Objective 3). Specifically, we first use ordinary least squares regressions to estimate whether heir-CEOs and founder-CEOs are paid more in total compensation and in total equity compensation, relative to professional CEOs. However, least squares estimates are expected to be biased because CEO power is endogenously determined by whether it is inherited or acquired. To address the endogeneity issue, we follow Adams, Almeida, and Ferreira (Journal of Empirical Finance, 2009) to use a two-stage instrumental variable approach to estimate the true effect of the heir-CEO status and the founder-CEO status on the level of compensation. The first paper also partially address whether practices of contract renegotiation are less prevalent for CEOs with acquired power relative to CEOs with inherited power (Objective 4). Specifically, we empirically examine whether the use and characteristics of CEO employment agreements (e.g., contract duration and contract explicitness) vary significantly between founder-CEOs and heir-CEOs. This empirical test is relevant as it provides empirical evidence on whether the use and characteristics of CEO employment agreements vary meaningfully between founder CEOs and heir CEOs. The second paper is written primarily to address the last objective of the project. This paper empirically investigates whether renegotiation of CEO employment agreements (EAs) varies between acquired vs. inherited CEO power (objective 4). We believe that this is the most novel research question and adds depth to the literature. It also involves very tedious data collection as we have to collect data on ex-ante CEO employment agreements for S&P500 firms between 1993 and 2012. Specifically, we collected data on (i) the presence of EAs and (ii) terms specified in these employment contracts, e.g., duration, base salary, bonus, and equity grants. In sharp contrast to our expectations, we find that CEO power has NO effect on renegotiation of CEO employment agreements. This result was included in the first draft of the second paper when we submitted our paper for publication consideration at the Journal of Corporate Finance. As our results are weak and the second paper is already lengthy, we ended up cutting this result entirely from the second paper. In unreported results, we also find that the founder-CEO status and the heir-CEO status have no effect on renegotiation of CEO employment agreements. To conserve space for more interesting results, this result is also not reported in our first paper. As we cannot perfectly predict our empirical results when we submit the proposal, the non-result is a natural outcome of doing original and interesting research.

597713.label: Major findings and research outcome
597713.value: In our paper titled “Explicit Employment Contracts and CEO Compensation”, we find that CEO explicit employment agreements are used to induce CEOs to make firm-specific human capital investments that are vulnerable to opportunistic behavior. This finding is consistent with the predictions of Klein, Crawford, and Alchian (1978). We also find that compensation is higher when CEOs have employment agreements that are written, longer in duration, or more explicit in terms. We also find that powerful CEOs are paid more in total compensation. This result is consistent with both the efficient contracting hypothesis and the managerial power hypothesis. To disentangle these competing hypotheses, we examine whether the origin of CEO power affects total compensation in our paper titled “Compensation and Employment Contracts of Powerful CEOs”. Our OLS estimates indicate that founder CEOs are paid on average 12.4 percent more in total pay than professional CEOs, compared to just 4.6 percent more based on the instrumental variable estimates. This indicates that a significant portion of the additional compensation is a premium for the founder-CEO’s superior ability. In contrast, our results indicate that heir CEOs are paid considerably less in total compensation than professional CEOs. Moreover, our IV estimates on the heir-CEO status are significantly smaller than those OLS ones. These results imply that heir CEOs receive a large compensation discount to penalize them for having the inherited CEO power (or actual power to make key corporate decisions). Additionally, founder CEOs are significantly more likely to serve as the board-chair than non-founder CEOs. However, heir CEOs are equally likely to serve as the board-chair as professional CEOs. This result implies that heir CEOs are entrenched and consume private benefits in control. Last, our instrumental variable results indicate that founder-CEOs prefer employment contracts that are disclosed publicly and rigid in contract terms. Broadly, these results are consistent with the efficient contracting hypothesis but inconsistent with the managerial power hypothesis. Two academic papers are produced from this project. The paper titled “Explicit Employment Contracts and CEO Compensation” is forthcoming at the Journal of Corporate Finance. The paper titled “Compensation and Employment Contracts of Powerful CEOs” is currently under revising and will submit for journals for publication consideration in the near future.

Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
597713.value: This project contributes to the executive compensation literature by addressing the contentious debate on whether higher executive pay is determined by managerial power to extract shareholder rents, or the managerial power hypothesis. Alternatively, the higher pay is a premium to reward managers for their exceptional ability, or the efficient contracting hypothesis. As managerial ability is difficult to quantify, findings in extant studies could be biased because CEO power is endogenously determined. This project fills this void to address the endogenous nature of CEO power and its relation with CEO compensation. Our results are broadly consistent with the efficient contracting hypothesis. Specifically, founder CEOs who acquire power endogenously are more likely to serve as the board-chair and be paid significantly more in total compensation than professional CEOs. Heir CEOs who inherit power from their families are paid significantly less in total compensation than professional CEOs. This paper is among the first to conduct an extensive study on the use and complexity of employment contracts by powerful CEOs. This issue is relevant because a core tenet of the managerial power view is that powerful CEOs prefer concealed compensation contracts to camouflage excessive pay.

597913.value: Roll (1988) 指出对于美国公司来说，从市场模型得出较低的R2反映或者公司层面的信息较多，或者噪声较多。尽管有大量研究证据支持这样一个观点：较低的R2表明股价包含更多的公司信息，但是也有越来越多的研究持有不同的观点：较低的R2说明股价中包含更多的噪声。 现在对公司层面R2的研究大多数是静态的，其实质是横断面的研究，而 Dasgupta, Gan and Gao (2010) 却是一个特例。 与以前研究不同， 他们证实公司层面R2 在公司信息披露强度较大期间比在公司信息披露强度较小期间要低。他们的发现意味着将R2与一个静态的和横断面为主的信息环境联系起来是危险的，这是因为如下的情况完全可能发生：平均来讲，信息披露良好的公司其R2可能反而会高，从而导致研究人员（错误地）做出结论，较低的R2 是由于噪声而非信息所致。 按照 Dasgupta 等的方法， 我们考虑在更一般的动态框架下，公司层面R2 所能扑捉到的信息披露强度的不同。 特别是，我们检验公司层面R2在公司年报公布期间（收益季节）和其它时间的差异（其它季节） （见图1）。 我们的假设是 R2 在收益季节相对比较低，此意味着较低的股价同步性的确与股价所包含更多的公司信息相一致。 为了进一步区分股价同步性的解释， 我们也采用其它信息环境的测度对这一问题做出研究，例如 Amihud (2002) 的非流动性测度，买卖差价，和依据信息买卖的概率 （PIN）. 同样与 Dasgupta 等一样， 我们假设这些测度在收益季节会偏低。如是，我们则建立了股价同步性与信息环境测度之间的一个正向关系，支持公司层面R2 的信息假说。 此项研究的贡献有两点. 第一，通过在更一般框架下对R2的动态检验，它扩展了 Dasgupta 等的研究，同时旨在强调现行文献中广泛采用的静态和横断面方法在这一问题上的局限性。第二， 与 Dasgupta 等的研究不同， 我们的关注点是对争论不休的股价同步性的解释做出新的阐述。我们的发现强调在股价同步性的研究中，控制信息强度是极为重要的。

597913.value: The first objective is well realized in two ways. First, we developed a theoretical model to show how cross-asset Bayesian learning can reduce firm-level R squares. Second, we offer robust empirical evidence to support the above theoretical prediction. The second objective is realized in the following sense. Our findings partially explain the dispute between two streams of viewing firm-level R square, since the previous studies do not take the dynamics of firm-level R square into account.

597913.label: Major findings and research outcome
597913.value: Firm-level R square decreases when the general information environment improves. We theoretically demonstrate that if investors can learn the firms’ future performance based on all noisy signals in the market, the systematic volatility would be substantially reduced even when the incremental information content for each particular firm is modest. Empirically, we find that the stock return synchronicity is lower in the earnings season when the information disclosure intensity is dramatically increased. The dominant effect for this dynamic pattern is coming from the systematic volatility rather than the idiosyncratic volatility, and this pattern is more pronounced for older firms whose firm-specific uncertainty is relatively lower. The research has generated a working paper and was presented in 29th Australasian Finance and Banking Conference 2016 held in Sydney on 14-16 Dec., 2016.

597913.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
597913.value: This research can be further extended to an international study by looking at the dynamic patterns of firm-level R squares across different countries. We are interested in the differences of the phenomenon between developed markets and emerging markets. In addition, we may consider the changes of firm-level R squares before and after the implementation Hong Kong and Shanghai stock market connection scheme. The effect of this exogenous shock to two different A-shares - connected stocks and non-connected stocks - would be interesting to investigate. This is another way of looking at the firm-level R squares dynamically while we are working somehow along the direction now too.

597913.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
597913.value: The stock return synchronicity decreases when the general information environment improves. We model the phenomenon theoretically by demonstrating that if investors learn a firm’s future performance from noisy signals in all the other firms, the firm's systematic volatility would be largely reduced. We then empirically find that the stock return synchronicity is lower in the earnings season when the information disclosure intensity is dramatically increased. The dominant effect for this dynamic pattern is coming from the systematic volatility rather than the idiosyncratic volatility, and this pattern is more pronounced for older firms whose firm-specific uncertainty is relatively lower.

598813.label: Project Objectives
598813.value: To derive the expected victim loss function for a specific location after the onset of a disaster, model the ESI deployment decision as a stochastic programming model minimizing the total expected victim loss, and prove that the optimization problem has a unique solution. To design a computationally efficient algorithm to find the optimal ESI allocation, derive the characteristics of the allocation rule, and develop simple heuristics that can be easily implemented. To investigate ESI pre-positioning under the best and worst case scenarios to gain a full picture of the victim loss once disasters occur. To investigate the impact of ESI availability and delivery lead time on victim life saving, derive the value of ESI stockpiling at a given location and determine if more funds are available for ESI pre-positioning, which locations should be given priority. Based on the foregoing analysis, to provide advice and suggestions to humanitarian relief organizations and government emergency management agencies on ESI pre-positioning.

598813.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
598813.value: Over the past decade, the world has witnessed a series of large-scale natural disasters, including the Indian Ocean tsunami (2004), hurricane Katrina (2005) and earthquakes in Sichuan, China (2008), Haiti (2010) and Japan (2011), with associated unprecedented devastation and loss of life. Given increasing global population growth and rapid urban spread, natural disasters tend to create humanitarian crises, which often require complex and coordinated relief operations. Efficient humanitarian relief action can save the lives for thousands of people each year (Australian Agency for International Development, 2011). How to strategically and effectively deploy/pre-position emergency supply inventory (ESI), including pharmaceuticals, medicine, food, water and equipment, is an urgent issue for humanitarian organizations, government agencies and academics. Studies on disaster operations management, particularly, humanitarian relief, are especially important for the densely populated countries such as China. Pre-positioning or stockpiling ESI in potentially disaster-affected locations raises challenging questions. (1) How can performance of ESI management be measured from a humanitarian perspective? (2) How much ESI should a government agency/humanitarian organization deploy at specific locations, considering factors such as the likelihood of disaster happening and the delivery lead time distribution among ESI deployment locations? (3) What are the bounds—the worst and best case scenarios—for the ESI allocation optimization problem? (4) Can we design a simple, efficient algorithm to derive the optimal ESI allocation that can be easily applied by the humanitarian organizations such as the International Federation? (5) How much total ESI should a government agency/humanitarian organization stockpiles in advance? Answering these questions is not easy because the ESI allocation decision involves multiple locations and the number of disaster victims is random and hard to predict in advance. In the project proposed herein, we will study the above questions by building a stochastic programming model. We will first derive the expected number of victims lost for any given ESI allocation, and will then solve the stochastic programming model to derive the optimal ESI allocation. Subsequently, we will study the value of adding more ESI at a location, and how that can reduce the number of victim lost. Finally, we will derive simple heuristics and allocation rules for stockpiling ESI. 在过去的十几年里，世界经历了无数的大规模自然灾难，例如，2004 年印度洋大海啸，2005年颶風卡崔娜，2008年汶川大地震，2010年海地大地震和2011年日本大地震。这些灾难带来了前所未有的破坏和人员伤亡。随着全球的人口增长和城市化的快速发展，自然灾难常常带来人道危机。如何战略地，有效地预先部署紧急救援物资，包括医药，食物，水和设备，已经成为人道救援组织，政府机构和学术界迫切研究的问题。 在可能受灾的地方预先部署紧急救援物资面临以下一些问题：（1）如何从人道的角度对紧急救援物资的管理进行评估？（2）考虑到每个地方灾难发生的概率和它们之间互相运送紧急救援物资的提前期长短，人道救援组织/政府机构应该在各个地方部署多少紧急救援物资？ （3）如何算出紧急救援物资优化问题的界限？ （4）如何设计一个简单有效的算法来帮助人道救援组织预先部署紧急救援物资？ （5）人道救援组织/政府机构应该预先总共部署多少紧急救援物资？ 我们将建立一个随机规划模型来研究以上问题。首先，给定任意一组紧急救援物资的预先部署，我们将推导相应的期望人员死亡数目。然后，我们对随机规划模型进行求解算出最优的紧急救援物资的预先部署。其次，我们将研究在一个地区增加紧急救援物资的价值以及其对减少人员死亡的贡献。最后，我们将设计简单的算法和分配原则来进行人道救援物资的预先部署。

598813.label: Realisation of objectives
598813.value: All the objectives proposed in this project have been successfully achieved. Specifically, in this project, we have successfully modelled the government/firm’s reserved emergency inventory pre-positioning and deployment problem as a two-stage stochastic optimization problem with uncertainties coming from both the supply side (such as the geographical locations of the warehouses, delivery lead times, and partial or complete inventory losses) and demand side (such as the geographical distribution, magnitude, demand variability and arrival patterns). In the deployment stage, we are able to express the expected aggregated unmet demand (that is, the total victim loss) in closed form and derive its first- and second-order properties by using a novel ranking function that characterizes the arrival sequence of reserved emergency inventories. Our investigation shows that the structure of the optimal deployment policy given a set of affected locations is similar to a ‘nested’-type policy with respect to the shadow price at each location. We have considered the best and worst case scenarios. The best case occurs when everything is certain, which is trivial. Thus, we ignore this trivial case. The demand process that results in the worst maximal expected total loss is when the surge demand always occurs at time zero (when the surge occurs). This upper bound is also the solution of a corresponding robust optimization problem when the demand process cannot be effectively estimated due to the lack of historical demand data. A comparison of the solutions of the original and robust problems shows that under the robust setting, both the number of locations and the reserved inventories allocated to each location are increasing in the total number of available reserved inventories. We also derive upper bounds for the expected total unmet demand under commonly observed demand processes. Similar insights are also observed when pre-positioned reserved inventories may be partially lost. We have examined the impact of ESI availability and delivery leadtime. Our results are as follows: when the delivery lead time from a location m to an affected location n increases, the central planner should either increase the deployment amount from the location(s) that is (are) closer to n than m to cover for the increment of demand during the lead time, or decrease the deployment amount from the location(s) that is (are) at or farther away from n than m because of the reduction of the future demand. We find that when the total amount of reserved emergency inventories increases, it may be optimal to reduce the reserved emergency inventories at certain locations and particularly, the reserved emergency inventories may be pre-allocated at fewer locations. Also, it can be optimal to pre-position more reserved inventories at locations with a low probability of demand surge or with a low post-surge inventory survival rate. When the probability distribution of the demand surge locations is more dispersed, the surge may occur at a wider range of locations. Thus, the inventory reserves need to be stocked so that the delivery time to each possible demand location can be balanced, yet the time it takes to deliver the inventories to each location may be on average longer. As a result, the expected total unmet demand becomes larger. Meanwhile, when the demand surge occurs only at certain locations, the inventory reserves can be placed at or near these locations to increase the responsiveness of the supply network and hence reduce the total unmet demand. When more demand arrives at early times, the amount of inventory reserve that can be used to satisfy the demand is less due to the positive delivery lead time and thus, results in a larger unmet demand. Moreover, when the arrival demand is more volatile, the probability of larger arrivals within shorter time periods is larger, which leads to a larger unmet demand. We have designed a computationally efficient one-dimensional binary search algorithm to get the optimal allocation of the reserved emergency inventories. We have also conducted an extensive large-scale numerical study based on the real data under three commonly observed demand surge processes. We find that the optimal pre-positioned reserved emergency inventories at a location can decrease in its own inventory survival rate or its demand surge occurrence probability. Our counter-intuitive results imply that, in a complex supply network with demand surges, such as hurricane, flooding and tsunami, making pre-positioning decision by simply relying on inventory managers’ intuition is not enough, and our model can help them find a better solution.

598813.label: Major findings and research outcome
598813.value: In this project, we study the optimal pre-positioning of reserved emergency inventories in a supply network that faces random demand surge, with the aim of minimizing the expected total unmet demand (that is, minimizing the potential humanitarian loss). We first characterize the matching process between the post-surge delivery of the reserved inventories and the corresponding demand surge process and derive the corresponding expected total unmet demand. We show that the optimal deployment policy is a 'nested'-type policy with respect to the shadow price at each location. Specifically, the set of locations with the highest shadow price is a subset of the affected locations, and they retain all their reserved inventories under optimality. The optimal allocation policy balances the expected shadow price at each location. We show that the expected total unmet demand is larger when one of the following is true: the demand surges tend to occur simultaneously at more locations, the probability distribution of the demand surge location is more dispersed, the post-surge delivery takes a longer time, more demand arrives at the early times, or it has a higher volatility. We then study an equivalent robust formulation of the problem, which provides the upper bond on the expected demand loss, and obtain the closed-form solution under certain conditions. Finally, we conduct an extensive large-scale numerical study based on the real data under three commonly observed demand surge processes. We find that more total reserved inventories do not necessarily lead to more pre-allocation of the inventory at a particular location. Particularly, increasing the amount of total reserved inventories may reduce the number of locations that are pre-allocated with reserved inventories, leading to “inventory pooling". The optimal pre-positioned reserved inventories at a location can decrease in its own inventory survival rate or its demand surge occurrence probability. The related research outcome has been undergone two rounds of review with Production and Operations Management, and is now under the second round revision. Humanitarian relief is not just related with the disaster but also related with other social issues such as poor living conditions and income inequality. Towards that end, we also consider whether the government should provide information to the poor farmers to improve their living conditions.The research outcome has been published by Production and Operations Management in 2015. The other two related research outcomes have been accepted/published by Journal of the Operational Research Society in 2016 and Operations Research in 2018, respectively.

598813.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
598813.value: This research investigated the optimal pre-positioning of reserved emergency inventories via a two-stage stochastic optimization problem with uncertainties coming from both the supply and demand sides. Current results are derived analytically by considering that the following parameters are given and independent of each other: the geographical locations of the warehouses, the delivery lead times, the geographical distribution and magnitude of disaster occurrence, its duration, variability and arrival patterns after disaster strikes. In the real practice, those parameters need to be estimated before applying our optimization model. One very important further development of our research is to statistically estimate those parameters based on the historical data. Note that demand surge belongs to the random rare events. The data may be limited and fragmented, and the collected data may be structured or unstructured depending on the availability. The statistic estimation thus may be based on the parametric or nonparametric modelling methods. Currently, we consider a situation where governments/NGOs/firms have an earmarked budget for purchasing the emergency inventory. However, what shall be the appropriate amount of emergency inventory that the government/NGO/firm needs to pre-purchase? This is worth further investigation. A robust optimization model then needs to be constructed for that purpose.

598813.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
598813.value: Taking into account the potential occurrence of disasters such as a hurricane and tsunami, organizations and firms such as Johnson and Johnson and the IFRC usually keep a certain amount of reserved inventories as a reactive buffer at warehouses in different geographical locations. One critical issue facing those organizations is how to strategically allocate and deploy reserved emergency inventories at designated locations so as to mitigate the impact of demand surges and achieve the humanitarian relief goal when disaster strikes. This is the aim of this research project. We find that the optimal allocation policy balances the expected shadow price of the reserved emergency inventory at each location. We show that when the total amount of reserved inventories increases, the inventories may be pre-allocated at fewer locations, leading to “inventory pooling”. Also, it can be optimal to pre-position more reserved inventories at locations with a low probability of demand surge or with a low post-surge inventory survival rate. We also derive the maximum potential mismatch between the humanitarian needs and the emergency inventory supply. This gives the practitioner a guide over the magnitude of the potential loss and how to allocate the emergency inventories in the most effective way.

599013.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
599013.value: Travel advisory systems (TAS), despite their growing importance in the increasingly volatile travel industry, receive significantly less research effort than warranted. To date, no clear academic definition of TAS exists, and the constituents of an effective TAS remain unclear. In addition, the accountability and neutrality of the information provided by the TAS have recently been questioned because of concerns related to political manipulation. Apparent variances are observed in the TAS across countries, the reasons for which are yet to be explored. In Hong Kong, the newly established Outbound Travel Alert (OTA) system, along with its supplementary services, has not been well received by various groups of stakeholders. The system is either unknown to or not valued by potential outbound tourists. Moreover, the ambiguity of the OTA has been reported to cause confusion to the business operation of outbound tour operators and insurance companies. Therefore, exploring how the various groups of OTA users perceive the effectiveness, including the usability and functionality, of the OTA in Hong Kong and how the OTA has affected these users since its inception are valuable research areas. Recommendations for improving Hong Kong’s OTA to cater to the needs and preferences of related stakeholders are to be provided. Theoretically, a long tradition of study has examined the relationship between perceived risk and travel intentions. However, the author challenges that perceived risk alone may not be a strong predictor of behavioral intention and may not advocate the operationalization of the protection motivation theory (PMT) in the tourism context. Protection motivation, as a result of the evaluation of factors including the severity and vulnerability of threats as well as response efficacy and self-efficacy in performing protective behavior, would perhaps be a better predictor of travel decision. The role of TAS, as a kind of persuasive communication, within a travel risk assessment model will be identified. This research proposes a conceptual model that examines the relationships among perceived risk, protection motivation, and protective behavior, as well as the mediating effect of the effectiveness of TAS on the causal relationship between perceived risks and protection motivation. This research contributes by way of testing the utility of PMT outside the field of health and psychological studies and by providing a theoretically sound approach to studying the phenomenon of TAS. 旅遊行業不穩定性日趨增加, 旅遊預報系統（ TAS ）的重要性也隨之增長, 儘管如此，這方面的研究工作卻明顯較少。到今天為止，TAS還未有明確的定義，而一個有效的TAS應包含哪些內容，仍然模糊不清。此外，最近亦有人質疑TAS所提供之信息的可靠性和中立性，擔心涉及政治陰謀，而各國的TAS存在明顯的差別，當中原因還有待探討。 在香港，新設立的外遊警示制度（ OTA ） ，連同其附帶服務，仍未被各持份者廣泛接受，有些外遊人士根本不知道有這個警示制度，有些則覺得制度沒有實際用途。此外，有報導指OTA內容不明確，造成混亂，影響出境遊行社和保險公司的業務經營。因此，探討不同持份者對OTA的有效性（包括可用性和功能性），以及制度推出以來各種影響，都是值得研究的領域。是項研究將提出改善本港OTA制度的建議，以迎合不同持份者的需要。 長久以來，學術界都有研究風險感知和旅行意向之間的關係，然而，作者質疑在旅遊情況下，風險感知並非一個強而有力的單一因素去影響行為意圖，也不一定引發保護動機理論（ PMT ）。透過評估不同的因素，如風險嚴重程度和脆弱性、反應效能和自我保護能力，識別保護動機，或許能更準確預測旅遊決策。 TAS提供有說服力的信息，其在旅遊風險評估中的作用將被識別。是項研究提出一個結構方程模型來驗證感知風險、保護動機和保護行為之間的關係，以及TAS功效在風險感知和保護動機之間的仲介作用，藉此測試PMT在醫療保健及心理學外的應用，並提出一個理論上合理的方法來研究TAS現象。

599013.label: Realisation of objectives
599013.value: Realisation of objective 1 and 2: Objective 1 and 2 have been successfully achieved through a content analysis study of 19 travel advisory websites of the world's top tourist-generating markets. The findings exhibited that summary of destination security situation, justification of travel warnings imposed, and recommendations, are the most frequently appeared elements and considered the key components of a travel advisory website. Some websites were outperformed in the aspects of incorporating exhaustive destination coverage, providing various communication channels in relation to travel advice, such as contact numbers and addresses of embassies, provision of travel plan registration and travel advisory subscription services as well as the use of mobile apps and social media, and encompass a wide range of travel tips on laws, local culture, religion, entry requirements, health and transportation with the exception of Hong Kong, Singapore and the US travel advisory websites. Therefore, the study suggests that travel advisory information varies across countries, with different focuses on destination laws, culture, region, entry requirements and health. Moreover, it was relatively common for the governments to organize their travel advisory information on the basis of tourist destinations (country/region) rather than presenting ad hoc travel announcements on their websites. The former is believed to be more user-friendly in assisting users to navigate the advisory information of their intended destinations. In presenting travel alerts and warnings, text description supplemented with distinctive levels or symbols in attractive colours and a travel advisory map is preferred as it could easily grasp readers’ attention. Realisation of objective 3: This objective has been fully achieved through an exploratory qualitative study. To review the performance of the Hong Kong’s OTA system from the perspective of outbound tourists, tour operators, and insurance companies. Eight focus group sessions with 46 Hong Kong residents and 11 individual interviews with representatives of tour operators and insurance companies were conducted in May 2015. The results revealed that the OTA system was not a significant source of information used by outbound tourists. Many focus group participants indicated they rarely paid attention to the OTAs and mainly used Google and other online forums and news sources for travel information. Participants representing travel agents and insurance companies offered a different view indicating that OTAs were useful although all agreed that it did have shortcomings. It is apparent that in its present form, the OTA system is not performing the tasks it was established for, particularly from the consumers’ perspective. The research indicated a number of reasons for this situation including perceived bias, failure to constantly update information, lack of ongoing publicity, poor user-friendliness and competition from other news sources. While the research did canvass suggestions for improving the OTA system, it is apparent that the Hong Kong authorities need to reevaluate the purpose of the OTA system, their resourcing of the system, the role travel intermediaries and insurance firms can play and how it is promoted. Realisation of objective 4-7: Objective 4 to 7 have been fully achieved through an exploratory quantitive study. The concepts of risk perception, effectiveness, and the Protection Motivation Theory (PMT) were employed in identifying the predictors of adherence intention of OTA advice. Prior to the main survey, a pilot study was conducted via the Qualtrics software and 345 responses were received to confirm the validity of the measurement model. Main survey was then carried out at the Departure Hall of the Hong Kong International Airport from 20 February 2016 to 27 February 2016 with prior approval from the Airport Authority. 15 helpers were recruited as interviewers and a sum of 710 valid questionnaires were obtained for further analyses. Objective 4: The results of multiple regression analysis suggested that self-efficacy, response efficacy, perceived severity, and benefit of maladaptive behaviors were significant predictors of OTA adherence intention. In other words, a traveler is likely to follow OTA advice if he/she is confident to follow the recommendation, believes that the advice is effective in reducing the potential risk, perceives the risk is severe, and views the benefit of not following the advice is negligible. The findings echoed with most of the past PMT studies. Objective 6: The results of structural equation modeling (SEM) revealed that the higher the perceived effectiveness, protection motivation, and perceived travel risks with the mediating effect of perceived effectiveness, would result in greater OTA adherence intention. Perceived effectiveness of the OTA system was the most influential factor amongst all. The government was therefore suggested to strengthen the perceived effectiveness of the system by including more travel destinations, providing detailed travel advisory information, such as emergency contact numbers abroad, and maintaining an up-to-date TAS. Objective 7: The results of One-way ANOVA and independent t test indicated that sociodemographic and travel-related characteristics influenced travellers’ likelihood in travel advisory adoption differently. Specifically, travellers who are female, in the age of 46-65, high-income, retired, married with children below 18-years old, travelled infrequently, preferred package tours, and would definitely or always purchase travel insurance are more likely to consult and follow travel advice. Recommendations for the Security Bureau: First, China, being one of the most popular travel destinations among Hong Kong travellers, should be incorporated into the OTA system. Further, the government was recommended to expand the destination coverage of the OTA system and update the list of travel destinations regularly. Second, the government was proposed to be more responsive on the issuance, adjustment, or removal of OTAs. The date and time information should be clearly specified. Third, a travel advisory map which indicates the safety and security levels of a destination can be provided on the destinations with OTAs. Fourth, photos or video clips which capture the situation of travel destinations can be presented on risky destinations. This would not only provide better information to travellers, but also encourage travellers to comply with OTAs. Finally, it is crucial for the government to promulgate OTA messages in different channels, such as at the Hong Kong International Airport and extensive use of mass media and social media, to raise public awareness on OTAs.

599013.label: Major findings and research outcome
599013.value: The major findings and research outcome from the three research stages are as follows: Stage 1: Content analysis study of travel advisory websites This stage of study identified the popular practice of organizing travel advisory information on the basis of tourist destinations (country/region) and determined the key components of a travel advisory website, including summary of destination security situation, justification of travel warnings imposed, and recommendations. The study also revealed there are variances in the aspects of destination coverage, travel advisory presentation, provision of travel tips, and issuance of travel advisories across countries. A manuscript entitled "An evaluation of the effectiveness of travel advisories with a specific focus on Hong Kong’s Outbound Travel Alert system" has been submitted to the Journal of Vacation Marketing. Stage 2: Exploratory qualitative study The findings of this stage of study revealed that the OTA system was not a significant source of information used by outbound tourists whereas participants representing travel agents and insurance companies generally found it useful. Nonetheless, greater attention must be given to the needs of various user groups and address the shortcomings of the system. A manuscript entitled "A cross-national analysis of travel advisory websites" has been submitted to Current Issues in Tourism. Stage 3: Explanatory quantitative study The findings of this stage of study signified the importance of perceived effectiveness on the OTA system of travellers as it is the strongest predictor of adherence intention. The effect of individual PMT variables on compliance intention were also fully tested. The findings concur with majority of the PM studies that factors of coping appraisal, including self-efficacy and response efficacy, are the most important factors that influence compliance intention of OTA and the study has successfully confirmed the utility of PMT within the TAS context.

599013.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
599013.value: Future studies may adopt a qualitative approach to seek the opinions from TAS policy makers, and discern their rationales and difficulties in devising and operating a TAS. In addition, future research may also attempt a multi-national study involving a number of economies to examine and compare their travellers' intention to comply with TAS or to confirm and/modify the travel advisory components identified in the first stage of this study.

599013.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
599013.value: Travel advisory system (TAS) is a service designed to provide recommendations on the suitability of travelling to a foreign destination. Previous studies have noted that TAS is an critical determinant of tourist destination choices by potential travellers and serves an important purpose for tourism and insurance companies. Nonetheless, TAS has apparently received far less research attention than it deserves with only nine previous studies identified; empirical studies in this field are particularly rare. The findings of this study indicated that from a Hong Kong perspective, the OTA system is not performing the tasks it was established for, particularly from the consumer’s perspective. The research indicated the reasons for this situation including perceived bias, failure to constantly update information, lack of ongoing publicity, poor user-friendliness and competition from other news sources. While the research did canvass suggestions for improving the OTA system, it is apparent that the Hong Kong authorities need to reevaluate the purpose of the OTA system, their resourcing of the system, the role travel intermediaries and insurance firms can play and how it is promoted. The problems identified with the OTA system are not unique and the insights may be valuable to the TAS used in other countries.

599213.value: 地位性竞争之下收入分配,流动性和经济增长

599213.label: Project Objectives
599213.value: To incorporate the element of positional competition in a dynamic economic model of inequality and mobility. To examine the ways inequality, mobility and economic growth vary with different degrees of positional competition.

To examine the ways inequality, mobility and economic growth vary with different degrees of positional competition.

599213.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
599213.value: Hong Kong is well known for her prosperity, as well as for income inequality which regularly ranks among the highest in the developed economies. Now inequality in itself, as has been argued, need not be much of a concern, provided sufficient amount of economic and social mobility exists. Indeed for many, the story of Li Ka-shing fittingly symbolizes Hong Kong precisely because it is a story both of the inequality in income and of the availability of opportunity; a story of the secret that lies right behind Hong Kong’s economic dynamism; and a story which all who find Hong Kong’s economic success enviable shall, by implication, do well to emulate. In more recent years, however, concerns arose that economic mobility, at least from the level of popular perception, has experienced decline; such concerns are felt not only in Hong Kong, but also in other “tiger economies” in East Asia, and further afield. If valid, such concerns are as much about the potentials for future economic successes as they are about the equity of economic opportunities. If the bright young people today are more likely to be inhibited from economic successes by their backgrounds, the resulting misallocation of talent cannot help but adversely impinging on economic growth in the long run. Thus, mobility is crucial to whether the “Hong Kong model” of economic success can be replicated and sustained. Some of these concerns relate to new technologies such as the ICT. New technologies are known to generate increased degrees of concentration. It is also true that new technologies can raise the sensitivity of payoffs to the ranking, or relative position, of an agent among her fellow competitors. Have new technologies fundamentally altered the structure of competition? How might competition for relative positions affect income distribution, mobility and economic growth? One current gap in the literature is a unifying theoretical framework that grounds the phenomenon of inequality, mobility as well as economic growth on the basis of maximizing economic agents and the economic environment in which they operate, which include, in particular, possible existence of technology-induced positional competition. This is the gap we seek to fill. Our project, if successful, provides a theory that accounts for the phenomenon of inequality, mobility and economic growth by focusing on the economic and technological mechanisms behind them, and also provides a unifying theoretical framework for future examinations on these highly important issues by other researchers. 即使在平等机会的条件下, 收入仍然可以不平等的. 这种与流动性共存的不平等很可能对香港的发展起过重要的作用. 然而, 流动性的缺乏同样可以造成收入不平等的增加, 而这种不平等则会对经济发展产生负面的影响. 科技的发展可以产生不同程度的地位性竞争. 在地位性竞争中, 竞争者的收入不单取决于绝对表现, 也取决于相对表现. 这项研究的目的是从理论的角度理解收入分配,流动性和经济增长如何随着地位性竟争的程度而改变.

599213.label: Realisation of objectives
599213.value: This project sets out to investigate the impact of positional competition on inequality and mobility in a dynamic economic model. The project objectives have been partially achieved. In the research reported in the four working papers under this project, inequality and mobility are endogenous determined in a dynamic economic framework. Being outcomes of the underlying economic structure, inequality and mobility respond to changes of the underlying structure differently. In this research, the distinction between inequality and mobility is clearly drawn. Mobility is defined in the relative sense, as the joint distribution of income ranks across consecutive generations (known as the mobility copula). While inequality in defined in terms of the marginal distributions. This set up is conceptually clean in that any arbitrary combination of mobility copula and marginal income distribution is achievable as a steady state of some Markov process. In other words, when inequality and mobility are shown to be related to each other, those relationship are more than mere connections inherent in the definitions. This project has analysed various ways through which changes in the economic structure can impact inequality and mobility. Some of these changes are shown to impact inequality without changing mobility, while other changes affect both inequality and mobility. Where this project could have achieved more is a more explicit way of modelling positional competition. This task is to be carried out in future research. Analysing inequality and mobility in a dynamic framework has turned out to be more challenging than initially anticipated. Moreover, I have felt it necessary to understand how inequality and mobility respond to changes in the underlying economic structure more generally, and how inequality and mobility are related to fairness and meritocracy, before focusing more explicitly on positional competition. The issue of positional competition continues to fascinate me, and results obtained in this project make it possible for a more explicit analysis of the issue to be carried out in future research.

599213.label: Major findings and research outcome
599213.value: Research conducted under this project builds a series of dynamic economic models where inequality and mobility are endogenous determined. Inequality of outcomes are the results of differences in background, and differences in ability and work efforts. Mobility refers to the persistence of relative social position across generations. Given the empirical findings of the ‘Great Gatsby curve’, which shows inequality and intergenerational social immobility are positively related in many countries around the world, as well as across states in the U.S., our framework makes it possible to investigate channels by which inequality and mobility might be related. Two papers in this research address this issue. In “Inequality, Mobility and the 'Great Gatsby Curve'”, we find the relative efficacy of talent to family background plays a key role in determining the relationship between inequality and mobility. When inequality is fixed, raising the relative efficacy of talent leads to higher mobility. Conversely, we find that when the relative efficacy of talent is fixed, any change in the economic environment that leads to higher inequality will also result in lower mobility, consistent with the ‘Great Gatsby curve’. The paper “Comparing Inequality and Mobility in Linear Models” investigate the 'Great Gatsby Curve’ from a different angle. It is shown in that paper that the origin of inequality matters. Income risk in itself need not affect mobility; on the other hand, capital risk will necessarily affect both inequality and mobility, in the direction consistent with the ‘Great Gatsby curve’. Further, this project has investigated fairness and meritocracy. In the paper “Dynamic Fairness: Mobility, Inequality, and the Distribution of Prospects”, we show that dynamic fairness is jointly determined by inequality and exchange mobility. Overall, inequality reduces fairness, while exchange mobility enhances fairness. Moreover, any particular degree of dynamic fairness can be obtained by one of the many pairs of inequality and exchange mobility. Further, the paper “Is Meritocracy Fair?” identifies two components of meritocracy, which are related to fairness in opposite ways. First, meritocracy, in terms of the degree by which reward rank depends on an agent’s choice, is directly related to mobility and is good for fairness. Second, meritocracy, in terms of the reward schedule (or ex-post inequality), would, in the absence of perfect mobility, reduce fairness. Taken together, meritocracy and fairness can move in either the same direction or the opposite direction, depending on the extent to which each of the two components changes.

599213.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
599213.value: In a time when inequality of outcomes has been rising, it is often not clear if and how the distribution of opportunities has been affected. In general, the ways inequality of outcome and inequality of opportunities may or may not be related is an important topic on which much work still needs to be done. The framework provided in this project provides a basis for these investigations. More specifically, our framework can be used to study the different channels by which changes in inequality may lead to changes in mobility. Now inequality may change for various different reasons. Whether any of these changes will result in changes in the distribution of economic opportunities can be identified. Further, comparisons in terms of on fairness and meritocracy of social outcomes corresponding to these economic changes can be made accordingly.

599213.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
599213.value: To what extent to differences in economic outcomes reflect differences in efforts, talent or family background? How is the distribution of outcomes related to the distribution of opportunities? How do economic and social changes affect the degrees of fairness and meritocracy? This project provides a theoretic framework to analyse these issues. The framework allows inequality and mobility to be joint outcomes of economic forces, in a dynamic setting. Consequently, the nature of inequality and mobility reflects the nature of the underlying social and economic forces. This research has identified situations where changes in the economic structure lead to change in equality of outcome without changing the way economic opportunity is distributed, as well as situations where both the distribution of economic outcomes and the distribution of economic opportunities respond to the underlying structural change. These changes turn out to impact fairness and meritocracy differently.
