605413.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
605413.value: Magnetization dynamics is one of the key subjects in nanomagnetism. Both spin waves (SWs) and domain walls (DWs) are fundamental excitations of a magnet. The purpose of this project is to theoretically study interplay between SWs and magnetization dynamics in nanostructures, especially how magnetic DW propagation in a nanowire emits SWs, and how DW propagation is affected by externally generated SWs. A good understanding of this interplay should generate new knowledge about magnetization dynamics in nanostructures. It is anticipated that magnetic DWs can be used as non-volatile memory cells such as race-track memory with extreme high density, as well as all-magnetic logic circuits and magnetic sensors. Outcomes of this project could have a significant impact in condensed matter physics in general and in the field of spintronics in particular. 磁动力学是纳米磁学中的一个关键题目。自旋波和磁畴壁是磁性材料中的基本激发态。本项目计划对自旋波和磁畴壁运动的相互作用和影响进行系统的理论研究，研究的问题包括：畴壁运动引起的自旋波发射，磁振子导致的畴壁运动和畴壁-畴壁相互作用。本项目的将加深我们对磁畴与畴壁动力学的认识，为更好地在高密度磁存贮和信息处理中使用畴壁与畴壁运动提供坚实的科学基础。

605413.label: Major findings and research outcome
605413.value: We have launched investigations in areas related to our objectives. In particular, we have investigated the interplay of domain wall (DW) propagation and spin waves. A new concept of magnonic spin-transfer torque is proposed. It was predicted that spin wave can efficiently drive a domain wall to propagate along a wire. The prediction was confirmed by experiments. Spin waves are emitted during domain-wall propagation (References 2 and 8). As a result, the well known Walker solution of rigid-body DW propagation is not stable Reference 3). Furthermore, a DW can propagate along a dissipationless nanowire through spin wave emission (References 2). We propose a thermodynamic theory for thermally driven DW motion. This theory explains also naturally a well-known experimental fact: the width of a domain decreases as the temperature increases (Ref. 6). In the studies of geometry effects of DW motion, we found many interesting consequences of notch-assistant antivortex formation including 1) such as relationship between pinning field, notch geometry and DW structures (Ref. 4); 2) notch-assistant antivortex formation so that notches can boost DW motion (Ref. 10) and deepen a DW (Ref. 9). We found also how to use nano-second current pulses to control magnetic skyrmions that was nicely realized in recent experiment (Ref. 11). In addition, three new galvanomagnetic effects were discovered that are yet to be confirmed by experiments (Ref. 12). In addition, we show electronic states of two-dimensional electron gases under strong magnetic field and random spin-obit interaction form bands of critical states (Ref. 7) and extended states floating down as magnetic field approach zero (Ref. 1). All of our results generated from this project should be important for future developments of magnetic nanodevices based on DW propagation.

605413.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
605413.value: It shall be interesting to experimentally confirm many predictions obtained in this project. More detailed studies are definite needed to understand thermal driven DW motion and the interplay between spin waves and DW motion in particular, and other spin textures such as skyrmions in general.

605513.label: Project Objectives
605513.value: Develop a phase field model and an efficient numerical method for three-phase flows with fluid-solid interface boundary conditions. The approach will be based on the two-phase model developed previously by us with special attention on setting up and implementation of the boundary conditions. In particular, we will study the effect of surface tension, contact angle and the roughness of the surface on the deformation.

605513.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
605513.value: Many biomedical, chemical, and industrial processes involve mixtures of three or more components. For example, the behavior of the gas-oil-water system in porous media is a major problem dealt with in petroleum engineering. The adhesion of both single and compound liquid drops to a substrate is another important three phase problem with biomedical applications. There have been few theoretical and numerical studies of flow containing three or more liquid phases compared to the large body of research for two-phase fluid flow, partly due to the difficulties in dealing with hydrodynamics associated with interfaces and triple junctions (where the three interfaces meet), especially when the triple junction meets the solid boundary. In this project, we are interested in the modeling and simulation of the wetting and dynamics of the three-phase flow on a solid surface. We will first develop a phase field model for the three-phase flow capable of studying the flow-solid interactions. Efficient numerical methods will also be developed. We will then study two important problems in three phase flow on solid surface: (1) Wetting, spreading and impaction phenomena of an oil drop on solid surface partially submerged in a film of water, and (2) Dynamics of adherent drops (single and compound drops) under shear flow. The results obtained will provide a deeper understanding of the fluid-solid interaction of three-phase flow with potential for application. 三相和多相混合体是很多生物，化学以及工业领域里常见的现象。比如石油开采中的多孔介质里的水，气，油。现代理论对两相流问题已经有了很深入的研究。但三相和多相问题的理论研究仍然很缺乏。在本项目里，我们将建立一个三相和多相问题的相场模型并发展一套相应的高效数值方法。以此模型，我们将研究两个有深刻应用背景的课题：（1） 油滴在固体表面水薄膜上的性态及撞击效果 (2) 复合液滴在固体表面上的运动机理。

605513.label: Realisation of objectives
605513.value: We have developed a phase field model for the three-phase flows. One of the key results is that we proposed a projection approach for the derivation of a consistent free energy functional for the three-phase Cahn–Hilliard equations. The Cahn–Hilliard equation is then coupled with the Navier–Stokes equations to describe the three-phase flow on solid surfaces with moving contact line. An energy stable scheme is developed for the three-phase flow system. The discrete energy law of the numerical scheme is proved which ensures the stability of the scheme. Therefore the Objective 1 is completely realized. To carry out the research in Objective 2, we study the interface dynamics and contact angle hysteresis in a two dimensional, chemically patterned channel described by the Cahn-Hilliard equation with a relaxation boundary condition. A system for the dynamics of the contact angle and contact point is derived in the sharp interface limit. We then analyze the behavior of the solution using the phase plane analysis. We observe the stick-slip of the contact point and the contact angle hysteresis. We have realized most of what we want in Objective 2. We also developed an efficient adaptive mesh refinement technique to solve the phase field model. Several numerical results are given, including the buoyancy-driven droplet through a fluid–fluid interface, formation of four-phase contact line and dynamics of a compound droplet on solid surface under shear flow. The objective 3 is therefore completely realized.

605513.label: Major findings and research outcome
605513.value: We have developed a phase field model for the three-phase flows. We proposed a projection approach for the derivation of a consistent free energy functional for the three-phase Cahn–Hilliard equations. The system is then coupled with the Navier–Stokes equations to describe the three-phase flow on solid surfaces with moving contact line. An energy stable scheme is developed for the three-phase flow system. The discrete energy law of the numerical scheme is proved which ensures the stability of the scheme. We also show some numerical results for the dynamics of triple junctions and four phase contact lines. A paper with my Ph.D student Qian Zhang is published on Journal of Computational Physics. We also developed an efficient adaptive mesh refinement technique to solve the phase field model. Several numerical results are given, including the buoyancy-driven droplet through a fluid–fluid interface, formation of four-phase contact line and dynamics of a compound droplet on solid surface under shear flow. A paper with my Ph.D student is published on Japan Journal of Industrial and Applied Mathematics, 31 (2014), pp 611-631 We study the interface dynamics and contact angle hysteresis in a two dimensional, chemically patterned channel described by the Cahn-Hilliard equation with a relaxation boundary condition. A system for the dynamics of the contact angle and contact point is derived in the sharp interface limit. We then analyze the behavior of the solution using the phase plane analysis. We observe the stick-slip of the contact point and the contact angle hysteresis. As the size of the pattern decreases to zero, the stick-slip becomes weaker but the hysteresis becomes stronger in the sense that one observes either the advancing contact angle or the receding contact angle without any switching in between. A paper was published on Discrete and Continuous Dynamical Systems (A), 37 (2017), Pages: 1061 - 1073 We simulate a droplet impacting on a solid surface using a phase field model consisting of the Cahn-Hilliard and Navier Stokes equations with the generalized Navier boundary condition. An efficient gradient stable scheme is used to solve the system in axisymmetric coordinates. Our objective is to understand numerically the mechanisms leading to different impacting phenomena such as adherence, bouncing, partial bouncing, and splashing. In particular, we study how various processes are affected by the relevant dimensionless parameters: the Reynolds number, Weber number, density ratio, viscosity ratio, and the wettability of the solid surface. We also compare our numerical results with the experimental results and observe almost quantitative agreement. A paper is published on PHYSICS OF FLUIDS 28, 022103 (2016)

605513.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
605513.value: We would like to implement our three phase model in three dimensions and on general domains. An efficient finite element method on unstructured meshes is needed to cope with the complex geometry of the solid surfaces. To simulate the three dimensional problems, we need to develop a highly parallel algorithm based on domain decomposition techniques.

605513.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
605513.value: In this project, we have developed an accurate mathematically model for simulating the three-phase flows, an important phenomena in many biomedical, chemical, and industrial processes involve mixtures of three or more components, such as gas-oil-water system in porous media. The results obtained in this project provide a deeper understanding of the fluid-solid interaction of three-phase flow with many potential applications.

605813.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
605813.value: The modern world relies very much on networks to provide us daily necessities. So breakdowns in networks can create serious inconvenience in our lives. How to maintain the stability and robustness of networks is a scientifically challenging issue. The robustness refers to the ability of networks to remain operational in resource transportation when nodes or links are removed. Since network structures are often heterogeneous, they can be very fragile when their hubs fail. Furthermore, when one node fails, the load is redistributed among other parts of the network, which can cause a cascade of failures. Message passing is a distributive computational technique with a statistical mechanical basis. In passing messages containing beyond-neighbor information among the nodes, the nodes can make optimal control decisions. The purpose of this project is twofold. First, it aims at proposing message-passing algorithms for remedial actions that reduce the resource provision in a network immediately after a network breakdown so that the remaining structure will not be overloaded, and the occurrence of cascade failures is reduced. Second, it aims at proposing optimization that homogenizes the workload at the distribution hubs of the network and the margins of the links, and diversifies the routes for resource provision to the consumers, as proactive measures to enhance the robustness of the network. 現代社會的日常所需，都常依靠網絡提供，所以網絡損壞可以造成嚴重的不便。如何維持網絡的穩定性和穩固度，在科學上是一個非常具有挑戰性的課題。穩固度是指網絡在節點或連線被移除時，網絡仍能保持運作的能力。網絡結構一般是不均勻的，所以當網絡的樞紐損壞時，網絡就變得很脆弱。而且，當一個節點損壞時，負載便分配到網絡的其他部份，可能造成連鎖性的崩潰。 信息傳遞是一種分散式計算的技術，具有統計力學的基礎。每個節點接收的信息包含相鄰節點以外的狀況，節點接收以後，就可以作出優化的調控決定。本計劃有兩個目的。第一，是提出信息傳遞的算法，在網絡剛損壞時，能及時作出補救行動，減低網絡的供應，使網絡餘下的部份，不至於過載，從而減少連鎖性崩潰的可能性。第二，是提出優化方案，使網絡的分配樞紐的負載和連線的後備容量能均勻化，也把接收點的路徑多元化，作為增加穩固度的預防措施。

605813.label: Realisation of objectives
605813.value: First objective: The achievement of the objective of improving network stability requires us to understand the nature of network instability. While short-term dynamics of single-event cascading failures have been extensively studied, less is understood on the long-term evolution and self-organization of power grids. Hence we introduce a simple model of evolving power grid and establish its connection with the sand pile model and earthquakes, i.e. self-organized systems with intermittent strain releases. We found that these systems share characteristics similar to the cascade failures in power. Hence evolving networks without stability precaution measures may have cycles of blackouts with a wide range of sizes and time scales. We also studied models that exhibit self-organized critical states but with finite-size cutoffs. The coexistence of scale-free avalanches and oscillations appear to be theoretically contradictory without considering finite-size effects since the former is scale-free and the latter indicate typical scales. Yet the contradiction is reconciled by including finite-size effects. In networks with heterogeneous distributions of supply and demand in the nodes, we considered how the demands of the nodes are related to the resource level in the presence of fluctuations in the form of inventory. This demand can be reflected by considering the resource price were the resources treated as a freely traded commodity. We observed that when resources are scarce, prices rise sharply below a turning point that marks the disappearance of excess producers. This shows that the population structure of the network affects the flow of resources. We approached network stability problems by breaking them into local components, arriving at distributive algorithms for optimization. Compared with centralized algorithms, distributed algorithms have the advantages of lower computational complexity, and lower communication overhead. Since they have a faster response to local changes of the environment, they are especially useful for networks with evolving conditions. We applied message-passing techniques to predict how steady-state fluctuations of the node resources drive fluctuations of flows in the links, supported by simulations in benchmark IEEE networks. It provides guidance on how link resources should be allocated to enhance network stability. Using the message-passing approach to allocate bandwidth in the power grid for the purpose of minimizing the current overload or the fraction of failed links, we found that they drops dramatically when compared with the traditional approach. Second objective: The power grid with alternating current can be considered as a network of coupled oscillators analogous to the Kuramoto model. We found that network stability depends on the dominant eigenvalue of the state Laplacian matrix, commonly known as the algebraic connectivity. Note that the state Laplacian matrix is different from the usual graph Laplacian matrix in that the matrix elements depend on the power supply and demand of the nodes. Hence we developed methods to optimize the synchronization stability of the model by minimizing the algebraic connectivity. Using the recently proposed cut-set space approximation of the steady states, we greatly simplified the objective function, and further derive its gradient and Hessian with respect to power supply and demand of the nodes, which leads to an efficient algorithm. It is also viable to adjust the coupling strength of each link to improve the stability of the system. Various operational constraints can also be easily integrated into our scope by employing the interior point method in convex optimization. The properties of the optimized networks were also discussed. Among other interesting properties, the eigenvectors revealed that decentralized networks are more stable. We applied the developed approach to two network modules bridged by a small number of links. We found that the network obtained by minimizing the synchronization stability is much more robust than the one obtained by merely maximizing the phase coherence. We tested our method with the benchmark RTS96 system, using realistic ranges of power supply and demand. Our method can solve the problems satisfactorily. A comprehensive coverage of serving supply nodes is a proactive measure for network stabilization. We considered the problem of selecting the source locations to supply resources on a network. Hence we drew an analogy between spins in antiferromagnet and outlets in supply networks, and apply techniques from the studies of disordered systems to elucidate the effects of balancing the coverage and supply costs on the network behavior. A readily applicable, coverage optimization algorithm is derived. Simulation results show that magnetized and antiferromagnetic domains emerge and coexist to balance the need for coverage and energy saving. The scaling of parameters with system size agrees with the continuum approximation in two dimensions and the tree approximation in random graphs. Due to frustration caused by the competition between coverage and supply cost, a transition between easy and hard computation regimes is observed. We further suggested a local expansion approach to greatly simplify the message updates which shed light on simplifications in other problems.

605813.label: Major findings and research outcome
605813.value: (1) Nature of network instability To understand the nature of network instability, we modeled evolving power grids and found that they share many characteristics with avalanches of sand piles and earthquakes – self-organized systems with intermittent strain releases [13]. Hence evolving networks without precautionary measures may have cycles of blackouts with a wide range of sizes and time scales. We also studied finite-sized models that exhibit self-organized critical states [7]. We found that scale-free avalanches and oscillations coexist due to finite-size effects. We considered networks with heterogeneous resource distributions, and observed a turning point when resources are scarce due to a change in the population structure of the network [14]. (2) Stability of networks We approached network stability problems using distributive algorithms for optimization [10]. We applied message-passing techniques to predict how steady-state fluctuations of the node resources drive fluctuations of flows in the links, supported by simulations in benchmark IEEE networks [9]. We obtained an optimal allocation of bandwidth in the power grid, resulting in a drastic drop of the current overload or the fraction of failed links when compared with the traditional approach. (3) Stable modes in networks of coupled oscillators The power grid with alternating current can be considered as a network of coupled oscillators analogous to the Kuramoto model. We developed methods to optimize its synchronization stability by minimizing the dominant eigenvalue of the stability matrix [12]. We found an efficient algorithm, supported by tests on the benchmark RTS96 system. (4) The source location problem As a proactive measure for network stabilization, we considered the problem of selecting the source locations to supply resources on a network. We introduced antiferromagnetic interactions to increase the coverage, and found that magnetized and antiferromagnetic domains coexist to balance the need for coverage and energy saving [1]. (5) Fluctuation-response relations We generalized the fluctuation-response relations in statistical physics to relate the intrinsic fluctuations and extrinsic driven response of dynamical systems [5]. (6) Complex network dynamics We studied the dynamics of networks whose efficacy weakens after prolonged usage [2]. We found that they can achieve perfect or anticipative tracking. We also found a rich spectrum of network behavior, broadening their capacity to carry information [3,6]. Hence continuous attractor networks may serve as a canonical model for neural information representation [8]. We further proposed modular networks processing multisensory information with the capacity to integrate or segregate information depending on input disparity [11].

605813.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
605813.value: (1) Stability of networks Message-passing techniques calculate network flows accurately, but since they usually assume that networks have tree structures locally, they are less accurate when calculating flow fluctuations when loops are present in the networks. We will develop generalized belief propagation algorithms to deal with loopy networks. (2) Stable modes in networks of coupled oscillators To extend the study of minimizing the dominant eigenvalue for enhancing network stability, we propose to generalize the approach to calculate the eigenvalue averaged over probabilistic network conditions. We propose to test the formalism in model networks and benchmark networks. (3) Complex network dynamics In networks with two or more modules, the modules compete with each other to yield the optimal output consistent with the prior distribution of information and the likelihood of the actual input. We propose to implement an optimal competition mechanism for this purpose. We will further consider the optimal network structure for time-dependent inputs. Next we will consider how features of the input information can be extracted from the dynamics of networks with multiple layers. This will be useful in the design of deep neural networks in artificial intelligence.

605813.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
605813.value: Stability is an important issue for transportation networks such as power grids, since fluctuating network traffic may cause links and nodes to overload and fail. These failures often cascade through the network resulting in system breakdowns. To understand the nature of network instability, we found that evolving power grids without precautionary measures share many characteristics with avalanches of sand piles and earthquakes, which release strains intermittently. Hence cycles of blackouts will occur with a wide range of sizes and time scales. Drastic changes were also found in other networks with heterogeneous resource distributions. To improve network stability, we proposed distributive optimization algorithms to predict how supply and demand fluctuations drive traffic fluctuations, and found that they yield superior allocation of bandwidths compared with the traditional approach. Since power transmission in power grids depend on the phases of the alternating current, we considered networks of coupled oscillators. We developed an efficient algorithm to optimize the synchronization stability of the networks by minimizing the decay time of phase disturbances. To enhance network stability proactively, we considered the problem of selecting the source locations on networks, obtaining structures that balance the need for coverage and energy saving.

606313.label: Project Objectives
606313.value: To derive a continuum representation of orientation-dependent dislocation densities in three dimensions. To derive a continuum model for dislocation motion and interactions in three dimensions that accurately incorporates the long-range interaction and various important short-range interactions. To derive a new continuum plasticity theory in three dimensions based on the above simple representation of dislocation densities and accurate continuum model of dislocation motion and interactions.

606313.label: Realisation of objectives
606313.value: The three objectives of this project have been fully achieved. Objective 1: A simple continuum representation of the orientation-dependent dislocation densities in three dimensions has been developed. In this method, the dislocation substructures are represented by two families of dislocation density potential functions (DDPFs). The slip planes of dislocations are thus characterized by the isosurfaces of one DDPF, while the dislocation curves on each slip plane are identified by the contour curves of another DDPF on that plane. By adopting such a way in representing the dislocation substructures, the geometries and density distributions of dislocation ensembles are simply expressed in terms of the spatial derivatives of the DDPFs. More importantly, one can use the DDPFs to explicitly write down a system of evolution equations, which is the result of upscaling from the underlying discrete dislocation dynamics. Objective 2: We have addressed the following aspects for developing three dimensional continuum dislocation dynamics model incorporating short-range dislocation interactions. These continuum short-range interaction models are derived from discrete dislocation dynamics model. (1) We have derived a three dimensional continuum dislocation dynamics model incorporating the multiplication of dislocations by Frank-Read sources. (2) We have derived continuum dynamics models of the formation, migration and dissociation of dislocation dipoles and self-locked dislocation structures on parallel slip planes. (3) We have derived a continuum expression for the short-range interaction of distributions of parallel straight dislocations using asymptotic analysis, and studied the stability of perturbed regular array of dislocation walls. (4) We have derived two dimensional continuum models for the energy and dynamics of low angle grain boundaries incorporating their dislocation structures. Stabilities of a planar low angle twist boundary subject to perturbations of the constituent dislocations of the grain boundary have been examined, and a proper function space is defined for the analysis. (5) We have derived a multiscale model for the structure and morphology of bilayer graphene. Objective 3: (1) Based on the representation of DDPFs for dislocation distributions and accurate model for the dislocation motion and interactions, we have proposed a dislocation-based three-dimensional continuum model to study the plastic behaviors of crystalline materials. The derived system includes i) a constitutive stress rule, which describes how the internal stress field is determined in the presence of the dislocation networks and applied loads, and ii) a plastic flow rule, which describes how the motion of the dislocation ensemble is driven by the existing stress field. The size effect observed in the compression tests of single-crystalline micropillars is studied and an explicit formula between the flow stress and the pillar size is derived. (2) Flow stress relation with dislocation densities due to various types of inter-plane interactions between perfect dislocations in face-centred-cubic crystals has been formulated. Compared to the widely used Taylor-type hardening relations, the derived formulae resolve more details from the underlying discrete dislocation dynamics. With the derived formulae, the roles played by dislocations belonging to different slip systems in strain hardening are further clarified.

606313.label: Major findings and research outcome
606313.value: Firstly, we have developed a simple continuum representation of the orientation-dependent dislocation densities in three dimensions (Y.C. Zhu, Y. Xiang, J. Mech. Phys. Solids 2015). In this method, the dislocation substructures are represented by two families of dislocation density potential functions (DDPFs), and the geometries and density distributions of dislocation ensembles in three dimensions are simply and accurately expressed. Secondly, we have derived continuum models for dislocation motion and interactions in three dimensions that accurately incorporate the long-range interaction and various important short-range interactions, from the discrete dislocation dynamics model. A continuum dislocation dynamics model incorporating the long-range dislocation interaction, the local line tension effect, and dislocation multiplication has been developed (Y.C. Zhu, Y. Xiang, J. Mech. Phys. Solids 2015). We have derived continuum dynamics models of the formation, migration and dissociation of dislocation dipoles and self-locked dislocation structures on parallel slip planes (S.J. Chapman, Y. Xiang, Y.C. Zhu, SIAM J. Appl. Math. 2016; Y.C. Zhu, N.X. Niu, Y. Xiang, J. Mech. Phys. Solids 2016). (3) We have derived a continuum expression for the short-range interaction of distributions of parallel straight dislocations and studied the stability of perturbed regular dislocation walls (X.H. Niu, Y.C. Zhu, S.Y. Dai, Y. Xiang, arXiv 2017). (4) We have derived two dimensional continuum models for the energy and dynamics of low angle grain boundaries incorporating their dislocation structures (L.C. Zhang, Y,J. Gu, Y. Xiang, Acta Mater. 2017; L.C. Zhang, Y. Xiang, arXiv 2017). Stabilities of a low angle twist boundary subject to perturbations of its constituent dislocations have been analyzed (Y. Xiang, X.D. Yan, Dis. Cont. Dyn. Sys. B, accepted 2017). (5) We have derived a multiscale model for the structure and morphology of bilayer graphene (S.Y. Dai, Y. Xiang, D.J. Srolovitz, Phys. Rev. B 2016; S.Y. Dai, Y. Xiang, D.J. Srolovitz, Nano Lett. 2016). Finally, based on the representation of DDPFs for dislocation distributions and accurate model for the dislocation motion and interactions, we have proposed a three-dimensional continuum model to study the plastic behaviors of crystalline materials, an explicit formula between the flow stress and the size of an compressed micropillar is derived (Y.C. Zhu, Y. Xiang, J. Mech. Phys. Solids 2015). (2) Flow stress relation with dislocation densities due to various short-range dislocation interactions has been formulated, and the roles played by different types of dislocations in strain hardening has been clarified (Y.C. Zhu, Y. Xiang, K. Schulz, Scripta Mater. 2016).

606313.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
606313.value: The continuum models for dislocation dynamics developed in this project provide efficient and accurate tools for the study of mechanical and plastic properties of crystalline materials. Further development of the research may include generalizations of the current models to more complicated dislocation structures such as self-locked structures of curved dislocations in multiple slip planes and energy and dynamics of grain boundaries in polycrystals in three dimensions. The current continuum models can also be generalized towards further understandings of the materials properties such as formation of the persistent slip bands in fatigue metals induced by cyclic loads.

606313.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
606313.value: Dislocations are line defects in crystals. The collective motion and interaction of large numbers of dislocations inside the crystalline materials determine their plastic behaviors. Developing accurate continuum plasticity theories that incorporate detailed formation of local dislocation structure and motion and interactions of dislocations is a very challenging task. We have proposed a continuum representation of orientation-dependent dislocation densities in three dimensions. These method uses dislocation density potential functions and enables simple and accurate expressions for the geometries and densities of dislocation ensembles in three dimensions. We have derived continuum models for dislocation motion and interactions for various dislocation configurations in three dimensions. These continuum models accurately incorporate the long-range interaction and different important short-range interactions. We have also derived a new continuum plasticity theory in three dimensions based on the above simple representation of dislocation densities and accurate continuum model of dislocation motion and interactions. The developed continuum models provide efficient and accurate tools for the study of mechanical and plastic properties of crystalline materials.

606513.label: Project Objectives
606513.value: Study the replacement problem for typical examples, such as the multiaxial O(n)-representation sphere, and the representation sphere of the semi-direct product of cyclic groups. Extend the result of the typical examples to the more general case, where the typical examples are the local versions of the more general case. Apply the replacement results to better understand the homotopy classification of equivariant topological manifolds.

Extend the result of the typical examples to the more general case, where the typical examples are the local versions of the more general case.
Apply the replacement results to better understand the homotopy classification of equivariant topological manifolds.

606513.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
606513.value: Manifold is the basic mathematical language that often describes mathematical models in the natural and social sciences. The symmetry of manifolds, usually described as group actions on manifolds, plays a very important role in the study of such models. For example, various conservation laws in physics are essentially due to actions by certain types of Lie groups (or quantum groups in the case of quantum physics). The field of geometric topology revolves around the most important problems of analyzing the structures of manifolds, comparing different manifolds (the classification problem), and studying the symmetries of manifolds. The classification problem has largely been settled by the solution to the Poincare conjecture and related technique (surgery theory for high dimensions, Thurston's geometrization in dimension 3). However, there are still many problems to be settled about the symmetry of manifolds. We know similar (equivariant homotopy equivalent, to be technical) symmetries will have similar fixed points. The converse problem asks whether something similar to the fixed point of a symmetry is actually the fixed point of another similar symmetry. The investigation of this converse problem is closely related to other problems about the symmetries of manifolds. We already have a fairly good knowledge on the converse problem for the fixed point of the whole symmetry in the case where the K-theoretical obstruction is trivial. The purpose of this project is to extend the knowledge to the fixed point of part of the symmetry, and in the presence of nontrivial K-theoretical obstruction. This will shed some light on the symmetric version of the classification of manifolds.

606513.label: Realisation of objectives
606513.value: For the first objective, we prove homotopy replacement for the examples of multiaxial U(n)- and Sp(n)-manifolds. We still do not have the complete result for the semi-direct product of cyclic groups. For the second objective, we showed that homotopy replacement can be achieved when the link in the quotient space has certain generalised pi-pi structure. Therefore it happens to some other actions by connected Lie groups. For the third objective, we interpreted the homotopy replacement as the calculation of the structure set of some equivariant manifolds. When it comes to finite groups such as Z/2 or semi-direct product of cyclic groups, we are forced to investigate the more fundamental problem of the non-simply connected version of the converse of the Smith theory as developed by Lowell Jones and Robert Oliver. We find that parts of the old theory can be extended, and we also find some counterexamples. These set up the foundation for further investigating the objectives.

606513.label: Major findings and research outcome
606513.value: We are able to show that the homotopy replacement of the fixed point of a subgroup can be achieved when the link in the quotient space has certain generalised pi-pi structure. Such a generalised pi-pi structure appears in multiaxial U(n)- and Sp(n)-manifolds. It also easily appears for some other actions by connected Lie groups. We try to investigate the similar pi-pi structure for finite groups such as Z/2 or semi-direct product of cyclic groups by constructing some basic examples. We find that related problem of obstructions from the Smith theory was only addressed for the simply connected case. This forces us to address the more fundamental problem (for complexes instead of manifolds) of the non-simply connected version of the converse of the Smith theory as developed by Lowell Jones and Robert Oliver. We have found that for groups of not prime power order, Oliver's theory should be largely extendable to non-simply connected case. We also found some interesting examples and counterexamples that help us understand the issue of Smith theory.

606513.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
606513.value: We find the problem of the project to be related to the non-simply connected version of the Smith theory. Further work along this direction can be interesting.

606513.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
606513.value: The project extends the earlier results on homotopy replacement of fixed points. It identifies some key structures that make this happen, and therefore earlier ideas can be applied to more examples. It also identifies the role played by Smith theory, and suggests the need to study the non-simply connected version of the converse of Smith theory. It is surprising that the converse of Smith theory is such a fundamental problem is equivariant topology, and yet little is known about its non-simply connected version.

606813.label: Project Objectives
606813.value: The architecture of an “artificial leaf” must create synergy between form and function, and should provide not only a platform for the “artificial photosynthesis” conversion of CO2 to “methanol solar fuel” but also the infrastructure for CO2 capture, passive fluid flows as well as heat and water self-management. Computational modelling and biomimicry will be important guides in the design of the “artificial leaf”. The selection of materials for the structure and “skin” of the “artificial leaf” and their modifications will be important in implementing a robust design with self-regulating/management system 1D photoactive titania nanotubes with electronic dopants on the surface, core and interlayer spaces will be the basis for the nanostructured photoelectrochemical cell (nPEC) with the anodic and cathodic catalysts incorporated at opposite ends of the nPEC. Catalysts based on non-precious, Earth-abundant metals will be considered a priority in catalyst development. Cathodic catalysts that combine CO2 capture and conversion will be based on catalysts such as Cu and CuAu/ZIF-8. Appropriate methods for nPEC assembly on the H+/e--conducting membrane will be developed “Artificial leafs” will be fabricated and assembled, and the operating device investigated by in situ and operando techniques to obtain valuable information not only on the operation but also the underlying processes and mechanisms. A prototype unit will be field deploy to obtain real operational data under practical condition. The information would be vital for further improvement in design and system optimization.

Computational modelling and biomimicry will be important guides in the design of the “artificial leaf”. The selection of materials for the structure and “skin” of the “artificial leaf” and their modifications will be important in implementing a robust design with self-regulating/management system

1D photoactive titania nanotubes with electronic dopants on the surface, core and interlayer spaces will be the basis for the nanostructured photoelectrochemical cell (nPEC) with the anodic and cathodic catalysts incorporated at opposite ends of the nPEC. Catalysts based on non-precious, Earth-abundant metals will be considered a priority in catalyst development. Cathodic catalysts that combine CO2 capture and conversion will be based on catalysts such as Cu and CuAu/ZIF-8. Appropriate methods for nPEC assembly on the H+/e--conducting membrane will be developed

“Artificial leafs” will be fabricated and assembled, and the operating device investigated by in situ and operando techniques to obtain valuable information not only on the operation but also the underlying processes and mechanisms. A prototype unit will be field deploy to obtain real operational data under practical condition. The information would be vital for further improvement in design and system optimization.

606813.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
606813.value: 資源的快速消耗和環境的日益惡化是人類未來幾十年面臨的兩個最大的挑戰，基於非再生化石燃料的能源開採、生產、轉化和使用過程是污染物和溫室氣體的主要來源。當前，科學界已經達成了共識：過量的二氧化碳的產生導致了自然界碳循環的不平衡，使得二氧化碳在大氣中含量逐步增加。衆所周知，二氧化碳作為一種主要的溫室氣體，是導致氣候變化的幕後黑手，氣候變化不但威脅全球經濟和環境，而且也導致了極端天氣和新的病原體的出現，嚴重影響了公共和個人健康以及人類生活質量。雖然捕集二氧化碳並將其進一步封存于地下或海洋花費不菲且不可持續，但作為一種可行的減少二氧化碳排放的策略，仍然得到多國政府的支持。另一種更可行和可持續的途徑是利用二氧化碳作為原材料去生產燃料和化學品，當前二氧化碳已被用來生產尿素（肥料和塑料工業原料），水楊酸（製藥工業原料）以及聚碳酸酯塑料，如果二氧化碳能夠被轉化為燃料，其需求量將大大增加。本項目的目的是探索工程技術及材料方面的創新，構建太陽能驅動的“人工樹葉”去實現二氧化碳到燃料的轉化，本項目的突破將創造巨大的商機，減少污染并保證未來的能源安全。

607013.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
607013.value: We aim to study some stochastic spatial models that are widely used in epidemiology and physics, which have variants that are also used in information science and marketing. Motivated by the practical consideration that the world is not homogeneous, we consider the models when the space is equipped with a random environment given by random conductances. The random conductances can be used to model, for example, how likely/how quickly a contagious disease or a piece of information can spread from one location to the other, and spatial inhomogeneity is reflected in that different pairs of locations are associated with different conductances. The main theme of the research will be the effect of the random environment on the behavior of these models, at or near the critical states. We shall study the distribution of particles (e.g., infected individuals, individuals with certain characteristic of interest, etc.) over space and time, by estimating various occupation statistics, focusing both on the macroscopic picture, like the spread of the population and the number of occupied sites, and the microscopic picture, like whether there will be clustering phenomenon when there are unusually large number of particles in small regions. We will also seek possible scaling limit theorems, which describe the asymptotic behavior of the systems as the number of particles gets large. Closely related to these studies are the intersection properties of random walks in random environments (mainly random conductance models), which is also a main target of this project. 我們致力於研究一些在流行病學和物理學上皆有廣泛應用的隨機空間模型。類似模型也被用在信息科學和市場學中。基於現實世界中各個地方存在差異的考慮，我們考慮這些模型在隨機傳導率影響下的隨機環境下的行為。傳導率可被解釋為比如有多大可能或者多快一個傳染病或一則消息會從一個地點傳到另外一個地點。當傳導率是隨機給定的時候，各個地方就可能被賦予不同的傳導率，空間差異性因此被體現出來。此項研究的主旨是去理解隨機環境對這些模型在臨界或近臨界狀態下會造成哪些影響。針對某些具有某種特性的粒子，比如傳染病模型中患某種疾病的個體，我們會研究它們在空間以及時間中的分佈情況。具體來說，從宏觀的角度上看，我們會估計比如這些粒子分散得多廣泛；從微觀的角度上看，我們會研究比如是否會有在一個小區域裡有很多粒子聚集的情況發生。我們也會去證明可能的極限定理。這些極限定理能幫助我們理解這些模型在涉及大量粒子情況下的性質。跟這些研究緊密相關的是隨機游動在隨機傳導率環境下的相交性質。這些性質的研究也是這個項目的一個重要組成部分。

607013.label: Major findings and research outcome
607013.value: Jointly with my postdoc Eyal Neuman, in [C1], we study the maximal displacement of subcritical branching random walks. Precise asymptotics of the tail probability are established. The paper has been published in Probability Theory and Related Fields. Still with Eyal Neuman, in a working paper [C2] which is close to finish we consider the near-critical case. This case is much more difficult. We again establish asymptotics of the tail probability. In another working paper with Yuqiang Li [C3], we study the occupation statistics of the critical branching walks in a random environment given by random conductances. Our results extend the corresponding results in [Lalley and Zheng (2011), Annals of Probability], where only simple random walks are considered.

607013.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
607013.value: One of our motivations for studying the maximal displacement of branching random walks is to prove a phase transition result for the spatial SIR epidemic model. In an ongoing work with Eyal Neuman, we consider this question. Good progress has been made towards a positive answer to a question raised in my earlier paper [Lalley, Perkins and Zheng (2014), Annals of Probability], showing that in dimensions two and three, there exists an extinction-survival phase transition. Another closely related model is spread-out percolation. Jointly with Ed Perkins, we consider this model and aim to establish second order asymptotics of the critical probability.

607013.value: The project, in general, is about discrete particle systems. These systems can be used to model various phenomena arising from physics, biology, information science etc. Our results provide important insights into long time behavior of these systems.

609513.value: 本研究方案由两项研究课题组成。第一个课题研究的是关于一大族循环码的重量分布问题。最近作者成功地完成了新的三族循环码的重量分布的计算，看起来文中的思路可以应用于更一般的情形。作者计划把这些结果推广到其他相关的循环码族上并计算码的重量分布。这个研究有可能使得我们对一般循环码的重量分布计算有更多地了解。第二个课题研究的是数字信号的设计。在2008年三位数学家和工程师Shamgar Gurevich, Ronny Hadani 和NirSochen用群的表示理论提出了一个非常天才的数字信号的设计，这个设计满足很多很好的性质，特别的，信号具有很强的抵抗时间和相位的干扰的能力。这个设计可能具有非常广的应用前景。受他们工作的启发，作者基于数论发现了另外一个设计。新的设计有一些优势。建立在这项工作之上，作者希望研究相关的一些问题，也希望研究别的设计办法。作者也将研究这个数字信号设计的应用。

609513.value: The theory of error-correction codes is an important research area, and it has many applications in modern life. One of the major challenges in coding theory remains to construct new error-correction codes with good parameters and to study various problems such as finding the minimum distance and designing efficient decoding and encoding algorithms. 609813.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
609813.value: Molecular recognition plays important roles in numerous biological processes including gene regulation, cell signaling and enzymatic activity. There are various theoretical frameworks on molecular recognition, ranging from induced fit to conformational selection. However, it is still difficult to dissect the chemical details of molecular recognition because this requires a detailed understanding of the dynamic conformational ensemble of proteins and how ligands may alter this ensemble. Markov state models (MSMs) constructed from Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations have the potential to provide an atomically detailed picture of protein-ligand recognition that would be difficult to obtain experimentally. However, applying MSMs to protein-ligand binding is challenging because one must capture both the protein’s conformational changes and the heterogeneous timescales of ligand dynamics due to interactions with the protein. To better understand the details of binding mechanisms, we propose a novel algorithm, Automatic state Partitioning for Multi-body systems (APM), for constructing MSMs for the protein-ligand two body systems. The APM algorithm effectively models the impact of protein conformational changes and the drastic differences in the timescales for ligand dynamics between bound and unbound states. This is achieved by directly incorporating kinetics into geometric clustering when identifying the metastable conformation states in a manner that yields tremendous enhancements in the computational efficiency of MSM construction and the accuracy of the models for two-body systems. Preliminary results show that the APM algorithm greatly outperforms existing algorithms for constructing MSMs for two-body systems. For example, we are able to obtain comparable results using less than a fifth of the sampling when constructing MSMs for the aggregation of two hydrophobic particles in water. We will use a selection of Periplasmic Binding Proteins (PBPs) as model systems to understand the fundamental elements of protein-ligand recognition, because PBPs have highly conserved tertiary structures but a diversity of binding mechanisms. Using MSMs, we can compare equilibrium thermodynamics before and after binding, calculate kinetics, identify the major binding pathways, and examine intermediate state structures along these pathways. An important emphasis of our theoretical work will be to generate hypotheses that will be tested by our experimental collaborator, and these experiments will further help refine our theoretical models. In this way, we will reveal relationships between protein structures, their dynamic conformational ensemble, and the mechanisms of molecular recognition. 分子識別在包括基因調控，細胞信號傳導和酶活性等眾多生物過程中起著重要的作用。現在存在從誘導契合到構象選擇等一系列分子識別的理論框架。然而，解剖分子識別的細節是很困難的，因為這需要對動態的蛋白質構象集合及配體分子怎麼改變這個集合有詳細的了解。馬爾科夫態模型（MSMs）有潛力對實驗很難直接研究的蛋白質配體識別機理提供一個原子層面的細緻的圖像。然而，應用MSM來研究這個問題是具有挑戰性的，因為我們必須捕捉到蛋白質的構象變化及其配體分子由於與蛋白質相互作用的引起的複雜動力學變化。 為了更好地理解分子識別的機理，我們提出新的對多體系統自動劃分構象態（APM）的算法來對蛋白質配體體系構建MSMs. APM算法有效地處理蛋白質的構象變化和配體分子在與蛋白質結合與未結合狀態時間尺度的大幅差異的影響。這是通過直接將動力學與基於幾何信息的聚類結合在一起來高效快速的尋找亞穩態的構象狀態。初步結果表明，APM算法在構建兩體體系的MSM能大大優於現有的算法。例如，在研究兩個疏水顆粒在水中的聚集時，我們可以僅僅用五分之一的數據得到和以前的方法可比較的結果。 我們將使用一系列週質結合蛋白（PBPs）作為模型系統來了解蛋白質配體識別的基本要素，因為PBP蛋白具有高度相似的三級結構但非常不同的結合機理。通過MSM我們可以比較結合前後的平衡熱力學，計算動力學，確定主要的結合路徑，並得到這些路徑上的亞穩中間態的信息。我們的理論工作的一個重點是產生可以被實驗合作者檢驗的預測，這些實驗將有助於進一步完善我們的理論模型。以這種方式，我們將揭示蛋白質結構，動態的構象集合，和分子識別機理之間的關係。

609813.label: Realisation of objectives
609813.value: All three objectives of the proposal have been fully achieved: For objective 1: We have developed the Automatic State Partitioning for Multi-body Systems (APM) method, a novel algorithm that can effectively construct Markov State Models (MSMs) from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to elucidate the protein-ligand recognition mechanisms (J. Chem. Theor. Chem.,11, 17, (2015)). The APM algorithm effectively models the impact of protein conformational changes and the drastic differences in the timescales for ligand dynamics between bound and unbound states. This is achieved by directly incorporating kinetics into geometric clustering when identifying the metastable conformation states in a manner that yields tremendous enhancements in the computational efficiency of MSM construction and the accuracy of the models for multi-body systems. We have shown that the APM algorithm greatly outperforms the popular splitting-and-lumping algorithm for constructing MSMs for a number of multi-body systems. We believe that our novel APM algorithm holds great potential in understanding the mechanisms of many multi-body processes including the recognition between protein and ligands. Based on APM, we have further proposed a general framework for constructing MSMs to investigate multi-body recognitions (Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys., 18, 30228, (2016), Highlighted as Inside Front Cover & Methods in Enzymology., 578, 343, (2016), Book Chapter). Finally, we have developed a GPU-based fast clustering algorithm for MD simulation trajectories, which could greatly facilitate the MSM construction for protein-ligand binding systems (J. Comput. Chem., 38, 152, (2017)). For objective 2: We have constructed MSMs to elucidate the molecular recognition mechanisms for three selected periplasmic binding proteins: LAO, Choline binding protein (ChoX), and Glutamine binding protein (GlnBP). In particular, we have quantified the recognition mechanism of ChoX to be ~90% conformational selection dominant under experimental conditions, and these results have been published in PLOS Comp. Bio. 10(8):e1003767, (2014). To elucidate these mechanisms, we have applied a new three-pronged approach of flux analysis, MSMs, and MD simulations to determine the contribution of induced fit and conformational selection to a particular protein-ligand recognition process. This is achieved by recovering all the necessary parameters for the flux analysis in combination with available experimental data. Our results also suggest that ChoX has several metastable conformational states, of which an apo-closed state is dominant, consistent with previous experimental findings. Moreover, using MSMs, we show there exists four metastable states for apo-GlnBP, where both open and closed conformations are substantially populated. These observations suggest a conformational selection mechanism in ligand recognition of GlnBP (published as: Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., 55, 13990, (2016)). Finally, our previous work already elucidated that LAO adopts a more complex binding mechanism with a combination of conformational selection and induced fit (PLOS. Comp. Bio., 7, e1002054, (2011)). These studies have successfully revealed a variety of ligand recognition mechanisms of selected PBPs. For objective 3: We have successfully revealed critical structural features in a protein’s intrinsic dynamics on protein-ligand binding mechanisms. For ChoX, we show that diminishing the hydrogen bond between N229 and G232 can greatly accelerate transitions between two metastable states. Furthermore, we show that ligands can not only directly bind to the closed ChoX conformation, but also induce the conformational changes of the partially open metastable state to reach the bound state (PLOS Comp. Bio. 10, e1003767, (2014)). For GlnBP, we have applied the NMR Residual Dipole Coupling (RDC) experiments to provide direct validations of our simulation results (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., 55, 13990, (2016)). In addition to PBPs, we have widely applied MSMs to investigate the impact of protein’s intrinsic dynamics on protein-ligand and protein-protein recognition mechanisms on a series of other systems: e.g. elucidating a two-step recognition process for the dimerization of human islet amyloid polypeptides (Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys., 18, 29892, (2016)), and an induced-fit mechanism for recognition between DNA and Ago protein (J. Phys. Chem. B, 120, 2709, (2016)).

609813.label: Major findings and research outcome
609813.value: Molecular recognition such as protein-ligand binding plays crucial roles in many biological processes. Molecular recognition events can employ a variety of mechanisms, ranging from induced fit to conformational selection. Dissecting the chemical details of molecular recognition is still a difficult task because this requires a detailed understanding of protein conformational changes and how ligand may induce these changes. With the support of this grant, we have developed the Automatic State Partitioning for Multi-body Systems (APM) method, a novel algorithm that can effectively construct Markov State Models (MSMs) from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to elucidate the protein-ligand recognition mechanisms (J. Chem. Theor. Chem., 11, 17, (2015)). We have further proposed a general framework for constructing MSMs to investigate multi-body recognitions (Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys., 18, 30228, (2016)). Using MSMs, we have elucidated molecular recognition mechanisms for three periplasmic binding proteins with distinct recognition mechanisms: Lysine-, Arginine-, Ornithine-binding protein (LAO), Choline binding protein (ChoX), and Glutamine binding protein (GlnBP). Specifically, we quantified the recognition mechanism of the ChoX to be dominant by the conformational selection (PLOS Comp. Bio. 10, e1003767, (2014)). For apo-GlnBP, we discovered that there exist four metastable states, where both open and closed conformations are substantially populated. These observations suggest that a conformational selection mechanism in ligand recognition of GlnBP (published as: Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., 55, 13990, (2016)). Using these PBPs, we have further revealed critical structural features in protein’s intrinsic dynamics on protein-ligand binding mechanisms. For example, we show that removing a single hydrogen bond between N229 and G232 can greatly accelerate transitions between two metastable states of ChoX (PLOS Comp. Bio. 10, e1003767, (2014)). For GlnBP, we have applied the NMR Residual Dipole Coupling (RDC) experiments to provide direct validations of our simulation results (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., 55, 13990, (2016)). Other than PBPs, we have widely applied our methodology to investigate recognition mechanisms for a series of other systems (PCCP, 18, 29892, (2016), J. Phys. Chem. B, 120, 2709, (2016)). Due to the above findings, the PI has been invited to give talks in prestigious international conferences including the American Chemical Society (ACS) national meeting, and the Pacific Chemistry conference. Moreover, due to his development of the APM algorithm, the PI won the 2014 OpenEye Outstanding Junior Faculty Award in Computational Chemistry from ACS Division of Computers in Chemistry. Three graduate students partially supported by this grant have successfully obtained their Ph.D degrees.

609813.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
609813.value: Understanding molecular recognition between protein and ligand is of critical importance in understanding many biological processes such as enzymatic catalysis and cell signaling. MSMs constructed from extensive computer simulations hold great potential to study kinetics of molecular recognition. Although MSMs have been successfully applied to protein folding, protein-ligand binding is still a major challenge due to the complexity of the ligand dynamics and its coupled protein conformational changes. Our APM algorithm can efficiently deal with the complexity of the ligand dynamics due to two-body interactions. We show that the APM algorithm can achieve significant improvements on the efficiency and accuracy of MSM construction for two-body systems. By constructing MSMs, we have elucidated relationships between protein structure, conformational dynamics and binding mechanisms for selected Periplasmic Binding Proteins. In the further development, our understanding of protein-ligand recognition mechanisms may greatly help protein engineering and rational drug design. MSMs are a powerful tool that can automatically identify metastable conformational states along protein-ligand binding pathways, and calculate equilibrium thermodynamics and kinetics for them. In addition to protein-ligand recognition, our APM algorithm holds great potential to be widely applied to investigate other important processes such as protein-protein interactions, protein-RNA recognition, peptide aggregation, and hydrophobic collapse.

609813.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
609813.value: Molecular recognition between a protein and ligand is fundamental to many biological processes. Experimentally probing the atomistic details of this kinetic process is challenging. Computer simulations may complement experimental techniques to provide dynamic information at atomic resolution. However, it is still difficult for all-atom simulations to reach the experimental timescales of the protein-ligand recognition. Markov state models (MSMs) are powerful kinetic network models that can predict long timescale dynamics from many short simulations. Although MSMs have been successfully applied to protein folding, protein-ligand binding is still a major challenge due to the complexity of the ligand dynamics and its coupled protein conformational changes. We developed a new algorithm, Automatic state Partitioning for Multi-body systems (APM), that can efficiently deal with the complexity of the ligand dynamics due to two-body interactions. We show that the APM algorithm can achieve significant improvements on the efficiency and accuracy of MSM construction for protein-ligand recognition. By constructing MSMs, we successfully elucidated molecular recognition mechanisms for several Periplasmic Binding Proteins with distinct binding mechanisms. In the long term, our understanding of protein-ligand recognition may greatly help protein engineering and rational drug design.

609913.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
609913.value: The goal of these studies is to develop biomarkers of the oxidative stress associated with many human diseases, biomarkers that could be used to predict the risk of disease. Epidemiological studies have revealed a cause-and-effect relationship between chronic inflammation caused by infection, smoking, radiation and other insults, and human diseases such as cancer and age-related diseases. When a tissue is damaged by these insults, white blood cells move into the tissue and release reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS) that cause damage to all types of biological molecules. Damage to DNA, for example, causes mutations, while damage to lipids and proteins induces cell death that ultimately leads to mutations and pathology linked to human disease. In addition to direct damage to biomolecules, the chemical stresses also induce an indirect form of damage in which oxidation of biomolecules leads to the generation of reactive electrophiles. The bulk of these electrophiles are reactive carbonyl-containing species that can further react with nearby DNA, RNA and protein to produce covalent adducts that pose additional adverse health effects. The goal of the proposed studies is to exploit the generation of these reactive carbonyl species and their resulting adducts to develop clinically useful biomarkers of oxidative stress and inflammation. We will approach this problem by developing novel, highly sensitive and selective liquid chromatography-coupled mass spectrometry (LC-MS) methods to identify and quantify the conjugated metabolites of reactive carbonyls for correlation with the extent of inflammation pathology and disease risk. Using a well studied rat model of toxicant-induced oxidative stress, we will initially focus on urinary excretion of the glutathione, cysteinylglycine, cysteine, and glycine-conjugated metabolites generated from aldehyde- and ketone-containing electrophiles that are formed from oxidative damage to biological macromolecules. The expectation is that the degree of exposure-induced oxidative stress will correlate directly with the excretion of these conjugated reactive carbonyl metabolites. The results of the proposed studies will be translated to other animal models of oxidative stress, such as rats treated with dichromate and paraquat. It is expected that the proposed studies will serve as a foundation for future studies in humans and with untargeted metabolomic analyses of blood and urine biomarkers of oxidative stress. We also anticipated that the proposed metabolomics platform will be applicable to many other oxidative stress-related human diseases, including atherosclerosis, Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s diseases, with unique signature metabolomic profiles useful in early diagnosis and therapeutic monitoring of the disease state. 本课题的目标是研究与许多人类疾病相关的氧化应激过程中产生的生物标志物，这些标志物可以用于该类疾病的预测和诊断。流行病学的研究已经阐明了由感染、吸烟、辐射以及其他一些损害会导致慢性炎症，这些慢性炎症会诱发人类的疾病如癌症和老年痴呆等。当组织遭受到这些损害后，白细胞会向受损组织迁移并释放出对生物分子造成损伤的活性氧和氮，例如，对DNA的损伤会导致其突变，对脂类和蛋白的损伤会诱导细胞凋亡并最终导致基因突变，诱发各类疾病。除了直接损伤生物分子外，这些氧化后形成的活泼亲电性化学物质也会间接损伤生物分子。这些亲电物质是含有活性羰基的化合物，它们能够和邻近的DNA、RNA及蛋白形成共价键加合物，对健康造成不利影响。我们的研究目的是寻找这些含有活性羰基的化合物以及他们在体内形成的加合物，从而发现氧化应激过程以及炎症所产生的生物标记物。 我们将开发出新的、灵敏度高和选择性强的液-质联用（LC-MS）方法，来定性和定量分析这些与感染病理和疾病相关的活性羰基加合物。我们用已经成熟的氧化应激大鼠模型，研究大鼠排泄物尿液中的谷胱甘肽、半胱氨酰甘氨酸、半胱氨酸以及甘氨酸加合物，这些加合物是由氧化应激反应破坏生物大分子所产生的醛酮亲电物质生成后，在体内进一步代谢产生的，通过检测大鼠尿液中这些加合代谢产物的含量，来探索它们与炎症病理以及疾病的相关性，我们预测炎症的程度和活性羰基的加合代谢产物含量是成正相关的。研究结果可被应用于其它氧化应激动物模型上，如用重铬酸盐和巴拉刈处理大鼠所建立的模型。我们的研究将为以后的氧化应激反应动物血液和尿液中生物标志物的代谢组学分析奠定基础。我们建立的代谢组学平台将可用于其它氧化应激疾病，如动脉粥样硬化、帕金森症和阿尔茨海默病，这些代谢组学轮廓的特殊印记在疾病的早期诊断和治疗监测中具有重要作用。

609913.label: Realisation of objectives
609913.value: The project objectives listed above have been achieved completely. Project objective implementation details are as follow: Firstly, we have developed high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), HPLC coupled with high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-MS), and HPLC coupled with tandem MS/MS (LC-MS/MS) methods for studying the metabolic fate of formaldehyde, which being one of the predominant oxidative stress-induced reactive carbonyls. The products formed from conjugation reactions of formaldehyde with amino acids (e.g. lysine and cysteine), N6-formyllysine and thioproline, respectively, in both extracellular fluid and in proteins were quantified using our developed LC-MS/MS coupled with isotope dilution methods. The studies reveled dose-dependent formation of the adducts in oxidative stress exposed cells. The results from these studies were published in peer-reviewed journal, the Chemical research in Toxicology and are listed in Part C of this Report. Secondly, we have developed in vitro protocols for the synthesis of major metabolites of formaldehyde, i.e. N6-formyllysine and thioproline. The method entails reacting formaldehyde with an excess of lysine or cysteine in physiological conditions to form the derivatives, and the products formed were purified by HPLC. The heavy isotope-labeled form of the metabolites was also synthesized using the developed synthetic method. The metabolites and their respective metabolites were characterized by UV absorption spectrophotometry, high-accuracy MS, and MS/MS techniques. To cope with the challenge of analyzing the highly polar aldehyde/ketone metabolites in the complex sample matrix of biofluid (e.g. extracellular fluid), we develop sample pretreatment methods for the trace analysis of N6-formyllysine and thioproline. To this end, we chemical derivatized the adducts using 9-fluorenylmethoxycarbonyl chloride (Fmoc-Cl) to increase their hydrophobicity facilitating their extraction and cleanup using solid-phase extraction and liquid-liquid extraction methods. The conversion of N6-formyllysine and thioproline to their Fmoc derivatives facilitate their extraction from the sample matrix as well as for subsequent HPLC or LC-MS/MS analysis. Using the developed method, we investigated the dynamic change in concentration of thioproline, the condensation product formed by reacting intracellular cysteine with formaldehyde in extracellular fluid of oxidative stress exposed cells. The study revealed a dose-dependent formation of the adduct in oxidative stress exposed cells, indicating thioproline maybe a good biomarker for assessing the extent of oxidative stress and related human disease. These findings, with the objectives realized, were published in two peer-reviewed journals papers, Chem. Res. Toxicol., 2015, 28 (3), pp 394–400 and Chem. Res. Toxicol., 2016, 29 (11), pp 1865–1871.

609913.value: Using our developed LC-MS/MS-based analytical method, this study revealed a dose-dependent formation of thioproline formed by reacting formaldehyde with cysteine in both the extracellular fluid and in protein of oxidant (Fe2+) exposed cells, which has not been reported before. Because thioproline is also being used as a health supplement, taken together with anti-oxidative stress glutathione and cysteine, the study discovered the production of thioproline as an interesting antagonistic response to oxidative stress-induced toxicity. These novel findings were published in two peer-reviewed journals papers, Chem. Res. Toxicol., 2015, 28 (3), pp 394–400 and Chem. Res. Toxicol., 2016, 29 (11), pp 1865–1871.

610113.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
610113.value: 在過去十年中無線通信經歷了一個飛速發展的過程，並且已經影響到我們生活的方方面面。對於接入各種無線服務的持續要求，以及無線因特網和其他服務的成長（例如3D因特網，擴展實境，社交網絡，物聯網），都產生了對新型的可以實現無縫接入的無線網絡的強烈需求。在過去幾年里無線數據量每年都成倍的增長，並且這個趨勢會持續下去。這就意味著在未來10年內無線數據量將會增加驚人的1000倍。這種無線寬帶數據的爆炸式增長對無線運營商滿足并提高用戶體驗帶來了挑戰。為解決這個問題，世界各地的運營商開始佈設4G網絡系統。但4G系統帶來的性能提升并不足夠滿足無線數據增長的需求，特別考慮到數據量到2020年會增加1000倍。 我們急需發展新技術來應付快速的無線數據增長。最近無線異構網絡被認為是可以極大增加網絡容量并提高用戶體驗的一種有效方案。在這種網絡中，很多小型基站會佈設在原來的宏基站附近來增加容量。因為各種類型的基站需要很好的協同工作, 這種新型的網絡結構提高了系統的複雜度,也帶來了很多新的挑戰，包括回程線路，干擾，移動管理，同步等問題。這其中干擾管理尤為重要。但由於網絡的異構特性，各種不同的接入點有不同的傳輸功率，不同的覆蓋範圍，以前在單層網絡結構下發展的干擾管理方案都難以應用。在這個研究項目中，我們的主要目標是研究在下一代異構蜂窩網中的干擾管理。我們會開發有效的干擾管理技術來提高網絡容量并改善用戶體驗。我們會尤其關注在異構網絡中同層或者層間的干擾控制。我們提出的研究計劃包括分析異構網絡的容量增益；開發微小區的感知頻譜分享和接入技術；設計有效的降低同層和層間的干擾方法；設計異構網絡中的基站接入方法；並且研究利用中繼來提高異構網絡的頻譜效率.

610113.label: Realisation of objectives
610113.value: With the explosive growth of smartphones and mobile applications, we have entered an era of mobile data deluge. Mobile data traffic particularly has been almost doubling every year, and this trend is forecast to continue. This implies that the 5G network, which will be deployed about 10 years after 4G LTE networks, will need to have 1000 times the capacity! Traditional techniques to increase the capacity have reached their limits, and innovative approaches will be needed. Heterogeneous networks (HetNets), which compose of densely deployed radio access points with different coverage/power, provide a cost-effective way to boost the network capacity, as the spatial reuse efficiency of the radio spectrum can be significantly increased. The heterogeneous structure of HetNets, however, will introduce non-trivial complexities for network implementation and operations, when compared with a homogeneous network. In particular, intercell interference will be the limiting factor for the achievable throughput in HetNets. This project investigated the effect of intercell interference in HetNets, and developed effective interference management methods. Our research objectives covered key technical challenges in HetNets, including evaluation of the effect of intercell interference and the achievable capacity gains in HetNets (Research Objective 1), cross-tier spectrum sharing and access (Research Objective 2), as well as developing efficient interference coordination techniques (Research Objective 3). Our investigation closely followed the stated research objectives. • First, to understand the effect of interference and evaluate the achievable performance of HetNets, network analysis based on spatial random network models was performed, where locations of base stations are modeled as Poisson point processes. Stochastic geometry was applied as the main mathematical tool for network analysis, which not only helped to accomplish Research Objective 1, but also provided valuable analytical results to carry out Research Objectives 2 and 3. • To address Research Objective 2, we developed effective algorithms for cross-tier spectrum sharing and access. Compared with the conventional orthogonal and full spectrum sharing schemes, we investigated the cognitive ability of small-cells to sense available channels, and our proposal allowed femtocells to dynamically access the available macro-tier spectrum in addition to their dedicated femto-tier spectrum. This helps to maximize the area spectral efficiency. The investigation built heavily upon the analytical results developed for Research Objective 1. • While Research Objective 2 mainly considered cross-tier interference, Research Objective 3 targeted interference caused by macro-tier base stations, as they are more powerful (transmit power of a macro BS can be 10-20dB higher than that of a small BS). Based on analytical evaluation of network performance, we first proposed a user-centric intercell interference nulling scheme, which effectively cancel interference for cell edge users. To reduce the requirement of channel state information, we also developed a topological interference management method, which only needs the network connectivity information. This significantly reduces the overhead for obtaining instantaneous channel information. • Considering the recent development in wireless communications and networking, we also investigated two other important research problems in HetNets, i.e., device-to-device (D2D) communications and cache-aided content delivery. D2D communications help to further increase the spatial reuse efficiency of spectrum, and thus increase the network capacity. We developed efficient resource allocation algorithms for D2D assisted HetNets. Caching popular files at the wireless network edge is an effective method for wireless content delivery, and we developed cache placement algorithms, as well as mobility-aware cache methods for D2D content delivery. Overall, we believe that we have satisfactorily completed this project. By covering all the research objectives in the project (Research Objectives 1 to 3), we are able to produce academically and practically significant research while contributing meaningfully to the training of students in this important area (Research Objective 4). Specifically, as a result of this project, three PhD students (Chang Li, Lu Yang, and Rui Wang) have been trained and graduated. In addition, with fruitful research outcomes, we were able to publish 8 journal papers, as well as 10 conference papers in IEEE flagship conferences. In particular, one conference paper [conference paper #8] received the Best Paper Award at IEEE International Conference on Communications (ICC) in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, May 2016.

610113.label: Major findings and research outcome
610113.value: Major findings and research outcome of this project are summarized as follows. As for references, [C1] and [J1] represent conference paper #1 and journal paper #1 in Part C, respectively. • Analytical Evaluation of HetNets: Our investigation on HetNet performance analysis in [C1, J3] demonstrated that changing the base station density in different tiers in HetNets would affect both the link reliability and area spectral efficiency (ASE), and it revealed a new kind of tradeoffs between these two important performance metrics. Our analytical results helped to optimize such tradeoff. Moreover, the coverage probability of millimeter wave (mmWave) networks was analyzed in [C7] via stochastic geometry, which showed that a large antenna size is critical for a good coverage. • Cross-tier Cognitive Spectrum Sharing and Access: Interference between different tiers of HetNets is the main bottleneck to achieving high spectral efficiency. In a series of works [J2], [C2, C3, C4], we developed algorithms for efficient cross-tier spectrum sharing and access. By allowing femtocells to dynamically access the available macro-tier spectrum in addition to their dedicated femto-tier spectrum through cognitive spectrum underlay, our method helps to maximize the area spectral efficiency. • Interference Coordination Techniques for HetNets: Due to the large transmit power and wide coverage, interference from macro base stations play a dominant role in HetNets. To suppress such intercell interference, we developed a user-centric interference nulling method in [J1], and a topological interference management (TIM) method based on low-rank matrix completion in [J4, C6]. Device-to-device (D2D) communications is an important component in HetNets, which increases spatial reuse of spectrum efficiency. In [C5, C10, J6], we have developed effective resource allocation and interference coordination algorithms for D2D communications. • Cache-aided HetNets: It has been observed that wireless content delivery dominates the mobile data traffic, and wireless caching, by storing popular content at access points and mobile devices, has been recently proposed as an effective approach for content delivery. In HetNets, cache can be deployed at different access points, and its optimization will be critical for the achievable performance. In [C8, C9, J8], we investigated cache content placement and cache size allocation at radio access points, which can effectively reduce the backhaul traffic. Moreover, in [J5, J7] we also investigated mobility-aware device caching, assisted by proximate D2D communications. Such schemes can effectively exploit the user mobility information and reduce the traffic load at base stations.

610113.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
610113.value: This project has produced promising results on interference management for heterogeneous networks (HetNets). HetNets will be the key network architecture for 5G networks, and there are lots of future research directions. In particular, wireless caching, i.e., caching popular content at access points or mobile devices, has been demonstrated as an effective approach for mobile content delivery. Cache-aided HetNets will bring additional design challenges. It is of critical importance to jointly consider such design aspects as cache placement, interference management, user association, and network cooperation. As demonstrated in [journal paper #5, #7], user mobility will also be important side information to exploit for performance improvement of content delivery. On the other hand, millimeter-wave (mmWave) communications will be a key supporting technique for 5G, due to its great potential in solving the spectrum crunch problem in current cellular systems. Thus it is important to investigate HetNets with both mmWave layers and sub-6GHz layers. Due to the high directivity in the mmWave transmission, interference will have different features and new methods will be needed. Built upon our previous work on network analysis for mmWave systems in [conference paper #7], it will be interesting to further investigate HetNets with mmWave communications.

610113.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
610113.value: We are witnessing an exponential growth of mobile data traffic, thanks to the proliferation of smart mobile devices and the popularity of various mobile applications. However, the current 4G LTE network does not provide enough capacity to catch this demand, and thus the wireless industry has been actively working on 5G networks. As physical-layer techniques are approaching their limits, there is a need for the network architecture evolution. Heterogeneous networks (HetNets) stand out as a promising solution, where small base stations are overlaid within the macro network based on traffic/coverage demand. It represents a new networking paradigm that can enhance network capacity, as well as providing a uniform user experience. This project investigated interference management in HetNets, and has produced fruitful research results. In particular, a new set of analytical results has been derived to characterize the effect of interference, and evaluate the network performance. Innovative interference management techniques have been developed, including interference nulling and topological interference management. Effective algorithms for cross-tier cognitive spectrum sharing and access have also been proposed. Overall, this project has shed new light on designing and optimizing HetNets, and the developed methodologies will also be valuable for other types of wireless networks.
