660513.label: Major findings and research outcome
660513.value: We have a long standing interest to understand how animal communication is controlled by the neural hardwiring and signal processing steps so that specificity is ensured. Such communication event would impose selection on biological features and ensure reproductive success. In this project, we have successfully utilized the calcium imaging approach at the single cell level to monitor the neuronal activities in live animals over an extended period to document the time delay between chemical input and electrical excitation output. The approach allows us to define both at single cell level and at the animal behavioral level a correlation of neuronal excitation and behavioral response, leading to the definition of amphid neuron, AWA, and male specific neuron, CEM, as key neuronal players in this process. We have demonstrated for the first time that CEM is a chemosensory neuron, and have mapped its connection with an interneuron required for integrating motor function from chemosensory input. Along this line, we showed that the chemical input is dependent of the TRPP channel components, unknown in the past to display chemoreceptor property. We further defined four key signaling molecules acting within CEM as relay molecules. We have successfully characterized the chemical composition and identified a key chemical as the signal for sexual communication. Its molecular specificity would be important for the next phase of research to facilitate our hunt of critical metabolic process, alteration of which can facilitate the evolution of hermaphroditism, which defines the holy grail of speciation studies. The identification of this SRD-1 as the volatile pheromone receptor in AWA neuron and the definition of its structural domains allow us to concentrate on the C-terminal region and characterize the detailed mechanism of the intracellular relay of signaling. This molecule and its sequence variations in different species also provide an alternative path to address how lack of selection pressure (in the absence of compulsory requirement of sexual reproduction) can lead to degeneration of functions at the molecular level. Part of this work, including those in the imaging part above, is reported in the manuscript under revision. Although the original objectives of the proposal were slightly modified in the course of this study, the outcomes indeed have led us to an equally significant biological understanding of the biology of the neural architecture and function. The focus was shifted towards evolution at the molecular level, and selective process driving sex-specific behavioral output and animal speciation.

660513.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
660513.value: The project has generated a lot of potential leads for research expansion; from (1) the characterization of the SRD-1 receptor at the molecular level to define the possible binding features between the pheromone with the receptor at a biochemical level, (2) exploring new single cell RNA seq technology to identify additional components acting in CEM to fully described the signaling event in this neuron, or (3) exploring a more evolutionary dimension to identify enzymes in the pheromone production process, the loss of which would facilitate hermaphroditism establishment. While each of these would go into a very different domain, (3) will be our core future direction since it will offer answer(s) to a bigger question in biology allowing us to compress the evolutionary process from a longer time frame to experimentally manageable window. Particularly when we have already established the technology for stable RNAi transgenesis in C. remanei, have the assay in place, and necessary molecules identified, our lab would be in a unique position to take on this speciation question few other labs have capability to explore.

660513.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
660513.value: Experimental biologists have examined how the biological world is constructed and functions executed. This project started off by examining how animal communication is controlled by the key sets of neurons, their interconnection, requirement of important components and how they would be able to make a living animal tick. In this study, we clearly defined individual cells required in one animal to read signals from another. We experimentally proved the connectivity of these cells and visualized their activities upon stimulation. We have identified multiple molecular components essential for this perception. We identified the chemical signal and the receptor on one of these neurons that are essential for the initiation of a dialogue. Characterization of this receptor revealed how its property has changed in time, and offered insight about how these biological functions evolved leading to the formation of a distinct species. Having these elements identified opens up a venue for us to consider a controlled evolution process in the laboratory by experimentally manipulate these genes in a systematic stepwise manner to get a good understanding of the mechanisms and constraints.

660813.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
660813.value: The neurons of the adult central nervous system must constantly suppress their cell cycle. When suppression fails, a pathway of cellular events initiates that ends with the death of the cycling neuron. However, neurons that have started a cell cycle can survive for months in a ‘half-dead' state where they have replicated their DNA but cannot progress to M-phase and complete cell division. This is clinically relevant as in diseases such as Alzheimer’s, 10% or more of the neurons in affected areas are trapped in this condition. We propose to use a unique marking system to identify cycling neurons while alive in culture, and assess how their physiological and structural properties are altered. We predict that the cell cycle events change both the structure and the electrophysiology of the cells and that these deficits lie at the root of many early disease symptoms. We will test this idea using patch clamp physiology and structural analysis of the ‘half-dead’ neurons. Our second objective is to stop and/or reverse the cell cycle changes and determine which of the functional deficits are restored. The findings will have direct impact on the clinical picture and should offer important predictions about effective therapeutic strategies based on reversing some or all of the cell cycle events in Alzheimer’s disease. 在成年的中樞神經系統裡，神經元必須時刻透過壓抑細胞周期以維持正常的功能。當此抑制系統失效時，細 胞內的信號便會引起連鎖反應，然後導致神經元的凋亡。然而，不少實驗數據皆顯示，已開始了細胞周期的神經元並不會在短時間內死 亡，反之它們會把脫氧核糖核酸復製後，在有絲分裂期前停留，以一種＂半死活＂的狀態生存。阿爾茨海默氏症，正是一種與此神經元變 化現象有密切關係的臨床疾病。臨床數據指出，在病人腦部受影響的區域，會有不少於10%的神經元產生以上的變化。為對有關的現象進行仔細的研究，我們建議使用一種獨特的標籤系統，先在活神 經元中分辨出已進入細胞周期的細胞，然後對其生理及結構上的變化進行分析。我們預測，細胞周期會對神經元的結構及其生理電學功能 會帶來不良的影響，而這些變化正是導致各種神經系統疾病早期徵狀的主要原兇。因此，我們亦會利用膜片箝制的技術，對這些處於＂半 死活＂狀態的神經元進行結構上的分析。與此同時，我們的另一研究目標，是阻止和／或逆轉细胞周期對神經元產生的變化，以及確認有哪些功能可被修復。這項研究的成果，不但會對疾病的臨床認知帶來重要的 突破，更會為以逆轉细胞周期為治療基礎的發展帶來重要的啟示。

660813.label: Realisation of objectives
660813.value: The project objectives have been met. The tangible evidence of this can be found in the list of publications that were supported in whole or in part by this award. Equally important, there are several major publications that are yet to come for which this grant served as the foundation and for which its support will be acknowledged. Our pursuit of the first objective led to the discovery that, as we predicted, the structural and physiological properties of the neurons that have entered the cell cycle are altered. By every measure that we anticipated, these cells are not functioning properly. These changes are not just losses of function, but do active damage to the neuronal circuitry and the cell biology of the surrounding healthy neurons. We showed that the trigger for the unscheduled neuronal cell cycling often comes from GSK3β, driven by a rise in the small cyclin-like activator, p25. The GSK3β:p25 interaction leads to enhanced phosphorylation of tau, but decreased phosphorylation of β-catenin. A partial explanation for this situation comes from in silico modeling, which predicts that the docking site for p25 on GSK3β is the AXIN-binding domain; be- cause of this, p25 inhibits the formation of the GSK3β/AXIN/APC destruction complex, thus preventing GSK3β from binding to and phosphorylating β-catenin. Coexpression of GSK3β and p25 in cultured neurons results in a neurodegeneration phenotype that exceeds that observed with p25 and CDK5 (the tradtional target of p25). When p25 is transfected alone, the resulting neuronal damage is blocked more effectively with a specific siRNA against Gsk3β than with one against Cdk5. We propose that the effects of p25, although normally attributed to activate CDK5, may be mediated in part by elevated GSK3β activity. This work has been published in the PNAS. In pursuing the physiological and structural properties of the neurons, we discovered an unexpected property that has profound implications for neurodegenerative disease, Alzheimer's disease (AD) in particular. We discovered that global reductions in β-catenin protein occur in human AD brain and its mouse models. In both human and mouse we find discrete patches of prefrontal neurons with robust, nuclear-localized β-catenin staining. Once again, we traced the driver of this phenomenon to the p35 fragment, p25. Stabilized β-catenin then drives the expression of cell cycle-related genes. With these oncogenic properties, nuclear β-catenin not only drives the neuronal cell cycle that we were exploring, it unexpectedly stabilizes p53 and enhances its activity. The result is the appearance of neuronal senescence. The senescent neurons release Dkk1, a canonical Wnt antagonist, in a p53-dependent manner and trigger apoptosis in nearby, otherwise healthy bystander neurons. Inhibition of Dkk1 and nuclear p53 activity attenuated this bystander killing effect. As neurons are fully differentiated post-mitotic cells, we propose that the normal oncogenetic activity of β-catenin cannot drive a true cell cycle. But this same process can drive a type of senescence known as oncogene-induced senescence, and the finding that neurons in the Alzheimer's disease brain adopt this second senescent phenotype prior the deposition of extracellular plaques is significant. The idea that the degeneration of neurons in the AD brain is due to their neighbors imposing a bystander killing, rather than from their own intrinsic deficiencies changes our perspective and our disease models in important ways. These findings have been submitted, but the manuscript is under revision as of this date. A second manuscript which has been submitted and is awaiting a decision documents that profound physiological changes associated with the cycling neurons. The second objective was to use anti-inflammatories and HDAC inhibitors to alter the phenothpe of the cycling neurons and hence the neurodegeneration in clinically relevant ways. Pursuit of this objective has also led to several unexpected findings. We first discovered that the prinicples behind the loss of ATM activity (the cause of neurodegneration in ataxia-telangiectasia – A-T) are very much at work in the seemingly unrelated condition of AD. Ataxia telangiectasia (A-T) is a multisystemic disease caused by mutations in the ATM (A-T mutated) gene. It strikes before 5 years of age and leads to dysfunctions in many tissues, including the CNS, where it leads to neurodegeneration, primarily in cerebellum. Alzheimer’s disease (AD), by contrast, is a largely sporadic neurodegenerative disorder that rarely strikes before the 7th decade of life with primary neuronal losses in hippocampus, frontal cortex, and various subcortical nuclei. Despite these differences, we found that a failure of ATM signaling is involved in the neuronal death in individuals with AD. In both, partially ATM-deficient mice and AD mouse models, neurons show evidence for a loss of ATM. In human AD, three independent indices of reduced ATM function—nuclear translocation of HDAC4, trimethylation of histone H3, and the presence of cell cycle activity—appear coordinately in neurons in regions where degeneration is prevalent. These same neurons also show reduced ATM protein levels. And though they represent only a fraction of the total neurons in each affected region, their numbers significantly correlate with disease stage. This previously unknown role for the ATM kinase in AD pathogenesis suggests that the failure of ATM function may be an important contributor to the death of neurons in AD individuals. It also is proof of principle that that inhibition of HDAC4 activity or nuclear translocation would have value in human diseases beyond A-T. These findings have been published in eNeuro. Our exploration of the role in inflammation in the neurodegenerative phenotype also returned significant findings. For these studies we returned again to A-T as our model system. We found that the inflammatory changes associated with A-T show both cytokine and brain region specificity. The CNS changes induced by broad-spectrum immune challenges, such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS) injections are a complex mixture of neuroprotective (TNF ) and neurodegenerative (IL1β) cytokine responses that change over time. For example, LPS first induces a protective response in A-T neurons, activating tissue repair genes. This is followed over time by a set of more degenerative responses. Additional phenotypic complexity arises because the neuronal response to an immune challenge is regionally variable; cerebellum and cortex differ in important ways in their patterns of cellular and biochemical changes. Our findings suggest brain responses to cytokine challenges are temporally and regionally specific and that both features are altered by the absence of ATM. This implies that management of the immune status of A-T patients might have significant clinical benefit and also carries implications for the progress of AD. These findings were published in PLoS One. We are now pursuing these findings to learn whether anti-inflammatory regimens such as ibuprofen can delay the symptoms of the A-T as it does for AD. Conditioned medium from LPS stimulated monocyte cells (LM) applied to cultures of dissociated cortical neurons leads to numerous degenerative changes. Pretreatment with ibuprofen, however, blocked this damage. Systemic injection of LPS into either adult wild type or adult Atm-/- mice produces an immune challenge that leads to profound behavioral, biochemical and histological effects. Ibuprofen pretreatment of young presymptomatic Atm-/- mice appeared to completely block the appearance of the neuronal cytological changes. These findings are under review in Molecular Neurodegeneration. The project also helped support a number of high profile review articles that provide a well-cited context in which the basic science findings should be seen in relationship to human neurodegenerative disease.

660813.label: Major findings and research outcome
660813.value: The project has advanced our understanding of the curious relationship that fully differentiated non-mitotic cells such as neurons have with cell cycle regulation. We show that the cell cycle initiation can be triggered by molecular triggers such as a loss of ATM activity, or by a p25-stimulated activation of β-catenin (a known oncogene). Whatever the trigger, entrance into an impossible cell cycle triggers a variety of structural and physiological responses. The most unexpected of these is the induction of an oncogene induced senescence phenotype in the cycling neurons. This literally turns these neurons into silent killers. In their sensescent state they secrete all manner of senescence associated secretory products that kill otherwise healthy surrounding cells. These findings significantly change our perspective on neurodegnerative disease and suggest several important new approaches to preventative therapy. The findings that manipulation of the immune environment can materially alter the course of neurodegenerative disease while not unexpected still has important implications for disease altering therapies. We have shown that the inflammatory process that accompanies the neuronal cell loss is complex and regionally variable. The therapeutic potential therefore comes with both hope that substantial differences can be made in people's lives, as well as caution that the therapies must take both regional and temporal responses into account.

660813.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
660813.value: The project laid the groundwork for some signficant advances that will be pursued. The first is the nature of the senescent phenotype and the possibility of working to contain not inflammation in general, but senescence associated cytokines in particular. A second approach would be to further explore the mechanisms leading up to the p25/GSK3β disregulation. The creation of p25 would seem to hold an important key to these mechanisms and this linkage will be pursued. The altered physiology of the senescent/cycling cells will also be explored further.

660813.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
660813.value: Neurodegenerative disesase remains a major public health challenge. Geratricians often remark that of all the conditions that they deal with in their practice, cognitive decline and ensuing dementia are the ones in greatest need of clinical advances. By studying the molecular mechanisms behind age-related neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, we have taken a few steps in that direction. We have developed evidence that the body's immune response can be an important factor determining the onset and the rate of progression of neuronal cell loss. This has suggests several important and relatively inexpensive clinical applications. Drawing the connection between the loss of cell cycle regulation in mature neurons with the appearance of a senescent phenotype has the potential to change our conceptualization of several diseases. The cycling neurons change their physical and biochemical properties and act almost like zombies. They themselves cannot die, but they slowly cause the death of otherwise healthy surrounding neurons. Attacking both the initiation of the senescent phenotype and its consequences is a new and promising therapeutic approach to diseases such as Alzheimer's where such neurons are found in the regions undergoing degeneration.

660913.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
660913.value: 腺苷環化酶（AC）把ATP轉化成一個非常重要的第二信使，cAMP。cAMP 調節很多生物進程，包括細胞生長和分化，學習和記憶，嗅覺，生殖，心臟壓力以及表皮的分泌。到現在，人們已經在哺乳動物中發現了九個跨膜的和一個可溶性的腺苷環化酶。泛素是一個調節細胞中蛋白量的重要的調節因子。Mono-或multi-ubiquitination一般導致膜蛋白內吞，並運送到內吞小泡中。內吞小泡中的蛋白會再次運回細胞膜或運到溶酶體降解。人們還發現泛素化還調節GPCR信號通路中的其它蛋白的運輸和降解。不過，雖然腺苷環化酶在cAMP信號通路中的作用非常關鍵，幾乎所有的關於腺苷環化酶的研究都集中在它們本身的活性上。而對泛素化或其它機制介導的腺苷環化酶蛋白降解卻沒有研究。 我們最近意外發現TRIP-Br1會減少所有測試過的5個腺苷環化酶isoform的表達量，包括AC1, 2, 5, 8和sAC。上述功能通過物理的相互作用實現。我們同時發現TRIP-Br1結合併穩定一種含有RING-domain有E3泛素連接酶, XIAP (X-linked inhibitor of apoptosis)。XIAP也能夠降低AC1和AC2的表達。 根據以上發現，我們提出一種假設：TRIP-Br1可以作為一種adaptor，把XIAP和其底物，所有的AC isoform聯繫起來。而XIAP介導腺苷環化酶的泛素化和降解。另一種可能是，TRIP-Br1與AC的結合是XIAP介導的，而TRIP-Br1通過穩定XIAP來降低AC的表達。 另外，通過影響XIAP，TGF信號能夠減少AC表達。我們提出三個目標以及相應的實驗來驗證這些猜想。 這個研究想要研究TRIP-Br1和XIAP介導的泛素化是否影響AC的蛋白表達水平。這是一個至關重要的問題，而且以前沒有人探討過。這個工作的完成將大大加深我們對AC調節的認識，並且為通過控制AC的功能來設計一些醫療方法展開一個新的方向。

660913.label: Realisation of objectives
660913.value: 1) To determine whether TRIP-Br1 binds to all AC isoforms and decreases their protein expression in vitro and in vivo Because TRIP-BR1 potentially interacts with multiple AC isoforms, thorough studies of its interactions with multiple AC isoforms is impractical in the 3-year period of the grant. Therefore, our strategy was to carry out a thorough study on AC1 and perform a few key experiments on other AC isoforms. a. AC1 interacts with TRIP-BR1. We found that AC1 interacts with TRIP-Br1 in coimmunoprecipitation and GST pull-down experiments. Further mapping of the binding site of AC1 on TRIP-Br1 suggested that the SERTA domain of TRIP-Br1 was required for the binding. On the other hand, the C1b domain of AC1 alone was sufficient for interacting with TRIP-Br1. In addition, our pair-wise pull-down experiments indicated that AC1 directly bound to TRIP-Br1. b. TRIP-Br1 reduced AC1 stability and its cAMP production. To examine the functional impact of TRIP-Br1 binding to AC1, we monitored AC1’s forskolin-stimulated cAMP production. cAMP production by AC1 was measured in HEK293T cells with or without stably co-expressing TRIP-Br1. Intriguingly, co-expressed TRIP-Br1 suppressed the activity of AC1 by 70%. Agreeing well with the functional data, stable expression of TIRP-Br1 in cells also decreased the protein levels of transiently co-expressed AC1 by 60%. More importantly, knocking down and knocking out endogenous TRIP- Br1 significantly enhanced endogenous AC1 expression. Moreover, our surface biotinylation assays suggested that TRIP-Br1 diminished plasmalemma AC1, and our CHX experiments indicated that TRIP-Br1 reduced AC1 stability rather than its transcription and synthesis. c. TRIP-Br1 might be a general regulator of multiple AC isoforms. Furthermore, we found that TRIP-Br1 bound to other isoforms of adenylyl cyclases, including AC2, AC4, AC5, AC6, AC8, and soluble AC. Protein levels of these isoforms of adenylyl cyclases and cAMP production by these adenylyl cyclases were also reduced by TRIP-Br1, implying that TRIP-Br1 may be a general regulator for adenylyl cyclases. The data on TRIP-Br1 knockout mice also support the notion (also see below). 2) To examine how interaction with TRIP-Br1 regulates AC expression, particularly a. if TRIP-Br1 binding leads to the ubiquitination of ACs and if this requires XIAP; b. if TRIP-Br1 acts as an adaptor or a modulator of XIAP in regulating AC levels. a. if TRIP-Br1 binding leads to the ubiquitination of ACs and if this requires XIAP. It was reported by other labs that TRIP-Br1 bound to XIAP, a RING E3 ligase. We examined the role of XIAP in AC1 degradation. We first verified the interaction of TRIP-Br1 and XIAP by GST pull-down and co-immunoprecipitation assays. Further mapping the binding site of XIAP on TRIP-Br1 indicated that XIAP binds to the N-terminus of TRIP-Br1. Interestingly, XIAP was immobilized by AC1-M-FLAG-HIS only in the presence of TRIP-Br1. These results suggested that TRIP-Br1 acts as an adaptor for XIAP and AC1. Overexpression of wild-type XIAP in Hela cells reduced AC1 while overexpression of XIAP mutants, H467A and F495A, which abolish E3 ligases activity of XIAP, had minimal effect on AC1 level. Significantly, knocking down and knocking out XIAP increased AC1 protein level, further confirming the role of XIAP in AC1 degradation. Similar results were obtained for AC2 and AC5/6. b. TRIP-Br1 and XIAP collaborate to ubiqutinate AC1. In vitro, AC1 was immunoprecipitated and blotted for ubiquitin in HEK293T cells with overexpression or knockdown of XIAP. Over-expressing XIAP dramatically enhanced AC1 ubiquitination and knocking down XIAP reduced AC1 ubiquitination. Co-transfection of TRIP- Br1 and XIAP further enhanced AC1 ubiquitination. It is noticeable that over-expression of TRIP-Br and knocking down XIAP at the same time failed to promote AC1 ubiquitination. Similarly, over-expressing XIAP while knocking down TRIP-Br1 had no effect on AC1 ubiquitination, further confirming that TRIP-Br1 and XIAP collaborate to ubiquitinate AC1. To examine whether XIAP actually catalyzes the ubiquitination of AC1, we assembled an in vitro ubiquitination system that contained ATP, the E1 Ub-activating enzyme (Uba1), the E2 Ub conjugating enzyme (UbcH5b), the substrate AC and the E3 ub ligase (XIAP). XIAP catalyzed polyubiquitination of AC1 only in the presence of TRIP-Br1. In addition, we also identify that the XIAP-induced polyubiquitination of AC1 is predominantly K27-linked. Moreover, we identified a highly conserved lysine residue (K1047 in AC1) in the N-terminus of ACs as an XIAP-mediated ubiquitination-conjugation site. 3) To test if TGF-β controls the ubiquitination and degradation of ACs via XIAP/TRIP-Br1. We looked at the the effect of TGF-beta’s effect on the ubiquitination and degradation of AC. However, we did not observe any reproducible changes. Instead, we looked at other physiological regulations of XIAP-TRIP-Br1 and their effect on AC levels. Because AC-cAMP-PKA signaling pathway is known to stabilize XIAP through CREB or PIK3-Akt signaling, we hypothesized that an increase in AC and PKA activities upregulates XIAP protein expression and subsequently downregulates AC protein expression in a negative-feedback manner. We tested this hypothesis in mouse primary cells, specifically in macrophages, because they reportedly upregulated XIAP upon forskolin stimulation and are relatively easy to culture. 6 h treatment of either isoproterenol or forskolin, two commonly used AC/cAMP agonists, increased XIAP protein expression, and, more importantly, markedly decreased AC1 protein expression in the macrophages of wild-type mice in a PKA-inhibitor-sensitive manner. Significantly, ablation of TRIP-Br1 gene nullified the regulatory effects of the cAMP agonists on AC1 protein expression while had little impact on the agonists’ effects on XIAP protein expression. These observations indicated that cAMP-PKA signaling regulates AC1 expression through increasing XIAP in a negative-feedback manner and TRIP-Br1 is an indispensable part of this negative-feedback loop.

660913.label: Major findings and research outcome
660913.value: Major Findings: Adenylyl cyclases (ACs) generate cAMP, a second messenger of utmost importance that regulates a vast array of biological processes in all kingdoms of life. However, almost nothing is known about how AC activity is regulated through protein degradation mediated by ubiquitination or other mechanisms. Here, we show that TRIP-Br1, a newly identified protein with poorly characterized functions, acts as an adaptor that bridges the interaction of multiple AC isoforms with XIAP, a RING-domain E3 ubiquitin ligase. XIAP ubiquitinates a highly conserved Lys residue in AC isoforms and thereby accelerates the endocytosis and degradation of multiple AC isoforms. XIAP/TRIP-Br1-mediated degradation of ACs forms part of a negative-feedback loop that controls homeostasis of cAMP signaling. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism for degrading multiple AC isoforms and modulating the homeostasis of cAMP signaling. Research outcome: 1 paper submitted to eLife 1 conference paper 2 students trained.

660913.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
660913.value: Our study can potentially open up new avenues of research and development for designing therapeutic approaches to control AC functions in health and disease. We will explore if TRIP-BR-1 and XIPA mutation would affect other physiological processes that are regulated by ACs and cAMP signaling, such as hearing and olfaction.

660913.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
660913.value: Adenylyl cyclases (ACs) are enzymes that produce cAMP, a small chemical that regulates numerous biological processes in all kingdoms of life. However, almost nothing is known about how AC activity is regulated through protein degradation mediated by ubiquitination (a type of chemical modification of proteins) or other mechanisms. In this proposal, we show that TRIP-Br1, a newly identified protein with poorly characterized functions, acts as an adaptor that bridges the interaction of multiple AC isoforms with XIAP, a ubiquitin ligase that carries out ubiquitination of proteins. XIAP ubiquitinates a highly conserved lysine amino acid residue in AC isoforms and thereby accelerates the endocytosis and degradation of multiple AC isoforms. XIAP/TRIP-Br1-mediated degradation of ACs forms part of a negative-feedback loop that controls homeostasis of cAMP signaling. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism for degrading multiple AC isoforms and modulating the homeostasis of cAMP signaling.

661013.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
661013.value: Growth of dendritic arbors and dendritic spines, the synaptic specialization where excitatory neurotransmission takes place, is essential for proper functioning of the brain and needs to be precisely regulated during development. Defects in dendrite development and abnormal spine morphogenesis have been implicated in many neuropsychiatric disorders including autism, a heterogeneous genetic disorder in which rare mutations in many genes crucial for dendritic growth and spine development have been identified. While the serine/threonine kinase Cdk5 is emerging as a key player in the regulation of dendrite morphology and spine formation, the underlying mechanism is not clear. We have previously identified the scaffold protein Axin as a novel Cdk5 substrate. Phosphorylation of Axin by Cdk5 at Thr-485 is induced by the neurotrophin brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and this phoshorylation is essential for axon formation. Interestingly, de novo variation of the Axin gene has been identified in Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) individual. Given the important role of BDNF and Cdk5 in dendrite and spine development, these observations together led us to hypothesize that Axin might represent a novel signaling protein that interacts with Cdk5 to promote dendritic growth and spine formation, and dysfunction of Axin might lead to impaired social interaction observed in autism. To test our hypothesis, we will first determine whether Axin is required for dendrite development and spine morphogenesis in cortical and hippocampal neurons by knocking down Axin expression using shRNA. We will then address whether Axin function requires its phosphorylation by Cdk5. Moreover, the signaling pathway by which Axin promotes dendritic growth and spine formation will be elucidated. In particular, we plan to examine if Axin mediates the effect of BDNF on dendrite morphology through the Rho-GTPases Rac1 and Cdc42. Finally, we plan to investigate the functional consequences of Axin knockdown or expression of phospho-deficient Axin in vivo. The neocortex of mouse embryos will be depleted of Axin by introducing shRNA using in utero electroporation. Social behaviors of the mice in adulthood will be tested using a variety of behavioral tests. 661013.label: Realisation of objectives
661013.value: Dendrites are highly polarized neuronal structures that transmit signals between neurons. Neuron populations have specific dendritic arborization associated with their specific functions. Dendritic spines are small protrusions along neuronal dendrites and are the key structures at the postsynaptic sites of glutamatergic synapses that mediate excitatory neurotransmission. The dynamic morphology and protein composition of dendritic spines are implicated in higher-order cognitive functions. Dendrite development and spine morphogenesis are regulated by the activation or inactivation of small Rho-GTPases driven by extracellular signaling, for example, by brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). Disturbances of these processes may lead to neuropsychiatric disorders such as autism. We previously found that BDNF stimulation causes cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (Cdk5) to phosphorylate Axin, a multi-domain scaffold protein, at Thr485. However, the role of this Cdk5-dependent phosphorylation at later stages of neuronal development is unclear. The present study revealed that Axin is essential for dendrite development and spine morphogenesis. To investigate the roles of Axin in dendrite and spine development (objective 1), we examined its expression in hippocampal neurons. Axin and p-Axin were enriched in cell soma and dendrites. Moreover, Axin and p-Axin puncta along the dendrites were co-localized with postsynaptic density (PSD)-95 at synapses. Furthermore, Axin and p-Axin were concentrated in the postsynaptic density fractions of the mouse brain, suggesting that Axin and its phosphorylation might play a role at synapses. The shRNA knockdown of Axin expression in mature hippocampal neurons significantly reduced dendritic spine density. More importantly, lentivirus-mediated Axin knockdown in the CA1 region in vivo similarly reduced dendritic spine number. Re-expression of RNAi-resistant Axin partially rescued spine morphology, while expression of the T485A mutant of Axin fully restored the dendritic spine density in Axin-knockdown neurons. Overexpression of Axin or its T485A mutant in wild-type neurons clearly increased dendritic spine number. These results suggest that Axin level and its phosphorylation by Cdk5 play critical roles in dendritic spine morphogenesis. Furthermore, silencing Axin in mature neurons reduced the number and total length of dendrites as well as the complexity of dendritic trees, indicating that Axin plays an essential role in maintaining dendritic structures. To investigate how altering endogenous Axin level affects dendritic spine morphogenesis and synaptic functions, we treated neurons with XAV939, a tankyrase inhibitor, to stabilize Axin. Treating neurons with XAV939 significantly increased dendritic spine density and the number of PSD-95–positive clusters, indicating the increase of postsynaptic structures. In addition, XAV939-treated neurons exhibited an increased frequency of spontaneous miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) and a dose-dependent increase of the phosphorylation of AMPA receptor subunit GluA1 at Ser831. Live-imaging analysis further demonstrated that stabilizing Axin decreased the spine elimination rate without affecting the spine formation rate. These findings collectively suggest that Axin stabilization increases the number of functional synapses and synaptic transmission. To further understand the molecular basis underlying the actions of Axin in dendrite and spine development, we performed mass spectrometry analysis to search for Axin-interacting proteins in the synaptosomal fraction of the mouse brain (objective 2). Among the list of candidate Axin-interacting proteins, we identified 7 and 8 unique peptides that are CaMKIIα and CaMKIIβ, respectively. We subsequently confirmed the interaction between Axin and CaMKII in HEK293T cells and the mouse brain. Because the activation of Cdc42 within dendritic spines depends on CaMKII, we investigated if Cdc42-mediated cytoskeletal dynamics is involved in Axin-dependent dendritic spine morphogenesis. Interestingly, the expression of Cdc42 but not Rac1 (another small Rho-GTPase) in Axin-knockdown neurons restored dendritic spine density. These results collectively indicate that Axin provides a scaffold for CaMKII in dendritic spines to enable Cdc42-mediated cytoskeletal reorganization. BDNF is a critical mediator of activity-dependent dendrite development. We previously demonstrated that Thr485 phosphorylation of Axin is increased by Cdk5 activation stimulated by BDNF. We also previously identified that several proteins, liprinα1, calmodulin kinase-like vesicle-associated [CaMKv], and p70 ribosomal S6 kinase [S6]), are the substrates of Cdk5. Intriguingly, the activity of these proteins are regulated by their Cdk5-dependent phosphorylation following induced neuronal activity/BDNF, which are critical for activity-dependent dendrite development. Together, orchestrated regulation of Cdk5-dependent phosphorylation of Axin and these proteins may be involved in mediating the neuronal activity-dependent dendrite development. The physiological roles of Axin in regulating dendrite and spine development was further characterized in vivo. Interestingly, injecting XAV939 into embryonic mouse brains resulted in the expansion of the intermediate progenitor population; this consequently increased the number of pyramidal neurons in the upper layers of the neocortex and ultimately resulted in increased brain size and weight. The increased number of excitatory neurons in the adult brain also led to aberrant morphology and disorganization of neurons in the neocortex. In mouse brains treated with XAV939, the excitatory neurons exhibited reduced dendrite arborization and spine density. In addition to the morphological changes of excitatory pyramidal neurons, the laminar distribution of interneurons was altered; specifically, we observed increased interneuron density in layer 2/3 of the neocortex. The density of excitatory synapses was significantly reduced, but there was no change in inhibitory synapses compared to the control mice, indicating that the overproduction of excitatory neurons abolished the balance between excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission. In addition, the overproduction of excitatory neurons was associated with autism-like behavior in mice. The XAV939-treated mice exhibited social behavioral deficits, namely reduced interaction with unfamiliar mice in a three-chamber social interaction test. Compared to the control mice, they exhibited enhanced repetitive behaviors, namely more self-grooming and digging activities. These results collectively demonstrate the importance of maintaining proper Axin levels during neuronal development.

661013.label: Major findings and research outcome
661013.value: The aim of this study is to understand the signaling pathways that shape neuronal morphology In particular, we specifically examined the Cdk5/Axin signaling complexes in regulating dendrite development and dendritic spine formation. 1. Axin is prominently expressed at synapses Axin and the phospho-Thr485-Axin proteins were found to be enriched in the postsynaptic density fractions of the mouse brain. They were colocalized with postsynaptic density (PSD)-95 in cultured hippocampal neurons (Chen et al., 2015). 2. Axin regulates synaptogenesis Silencing the Axin protein expression significantly reduced the dendrite spine density in cultured hippocampal neurons. Re-expression of wildtype or Cdk5-phosphorylation deficient mutant of Axin restored the spine morphology (Chen et al., 2015). These results suggest that Axin level and its phosphorylation by Cdk5 are essential for dendrite development and spine morphogenesis. 3. Identification of downstream signalings for Cdk5-Axin-mediated dendrite and synapse development To decipher the signaling mechanisms underlying the role of Cdk5-Axin signaling complex in dendrite and spine development, we performed mass spectrometry analysis to search for Axin-interacting proteins and Cdk5-interacting proteins in the synaptosomal fraction of the mouse brain. Collectively, we identified a number of signaling proteins such as CaMKII. CaMKv, liprinα, and S6K that are important mediators of Cdk5 or Axin-dependent dendrite and spine morphogenesis (Lai, et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2016 and Huang et al., 2017) 4. Increased Axin led to autism-like behavior in mice To further understand the physiological role of Axin in shaping neuronal morphogenesis, we pharmacologically increased endogenous Axin levels by injecting XAV939 into the mouse embryonic brain. We found that increased Axin resulted in an increase in the number of functional synapses and synaptic transmission, and led to autism-like behavior in mice (Fang et al., 2014). These findings suggest that an optimal level of Axin is required for normal neuronal development

661013.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
661013.value: In the current project, the roles of Axin and its Cdk5-dependent phosphorylation in dendrite and spine development have been identified. One key issue that should be addressed by future studies is the involvement of Axin in the regulation of neuronal communication at the circuit level. To this end, we can examine the regulation of dendritic arbors and synaptic morphology in the hippocampal excitatory neurons of Axin knockout or its phosphorylation mutant mice; the results would elucidate the roles of Axin in postsynaptic regulation in vivo. Another topic of interest is the association between Axin and human diseases, specifically autism. The XAV939-injected mouse model can be used to examine the imbalance of excitatory and inhibitory neurons, which can provide insights into the pathological mechanisms underlying the neurodevelopmental disorders that are associated with excitatory and inhibitory imbalance.

661013.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
661013.value: Growth of dendritic arbors and dendritic spines, the synaptic specialization where excitatory neurotransmission takes place, is essential for proper functioning of the brain and needs to be precisely regulated during development. Disturbance of these processes may lead to many neuropsychiatric disorders including autism. Our project aimed to better understand these developmental events by investigating the functional roles of a protein Axin, which serves as a scaffold for signaling complexes, in dendritic development and spine morphogenesis. Interestingly, we found that Axin is enriched in synaptic fraction. The phosphorylation of Axin, which is induced by Cdk5, regulates its roles in spine morphogenesis. In addition, we found that Cdk5-Axin signaling complexes play a key role in orchestrating various cellular signals to direct the dendritic development and spinogenesis. Increased Axin expression in the cerebral cortex led to the enhanced neurotransmission, which resulted in autism-like features in mice. Our findings have elucidated the roles of Axin in brain development and its underlying molecular mechanisms. They provide insights into the molecular mechanisms of brain development and the pathological basis of various neurodevelopmental disorders.

661113.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
661113.value: The dried fruits of Schisandra chinensis and Schisandra sphenanthera, which are commonly used Chinese herbs, are clinically prescribed for the treatment of inflammatory diseases, such as viral hepatitis. Schisandrin A (Sch A) and schisandrin B (Sch B) are the active ingredients isolated from the fruits of Schisandra sphenanthera and Schisandra chinensis, respectively. Earlier studies have found that Sch A-enriched extracts of Schisandra sphenanthera possess anti-inflammatory activity. In this connection, we hypothesize that Sch A possesses anti-inflammatory activity which involves the modulation of inflammatory signaling pathway(s) through acting directly on respective signal molecules. In addition, recent studies in our laboratory have demonstrated that Sch B elicits a glutathione-dependent antioxidant response via a redox-sensitive signaling pathway. Given that inflammation is a process that typically involves oxidative stress, we further hypothesize that Sch B can produce an anti-inflammatory action indirectly through altering the redox status of immune cells. If the anti-inflammatory actions afforded by Sch A and Sch B are mediated through independent pathways, it is also possible that the combined treatment with Sch A and Sch B could produce synergistic anti-inflammatory effects. With these notions in mind, we propose to investigate the anti-inflammatory actions of Sch A or Sch B alone or in combination using cell models – namely, lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages and concanavalin A (Con A)-stimulated lymphocytes. The findings in cultured cells will be reinforced using the mouse model of carrageenan-induced ear inflammation. 661313.label: Realisation of objectives
661313.value: Revised objectives 1 and 2 in B5.2 have been completed. The results have been published in Lau et al. “Long-term, passive exposure to non-traumatic acoustic noise induces neural adaptation in the adult rat medial geniculate body and auditory cortex.” NeuroImage, 107 (2015). Below is a summary of the findings: We employed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to study noise-exposed adult rats. We found that passive, pulsed broadband noise exposure for two months at 65 dB SPL leads to a decrease of the sound-evoked blood oxygenation level-dependent fMRI signal in the thalamic medial geniculate body (MGB) and in the auditory cortex (AC). This points to the thalamo-cortex as the site of the neural adaptation to the moderately noisy environment. The signal reduction was statistically significant during 10 Hz pulsed acoustic stimulation (MGB: p < 0.05, AC: p < 10^−4), but not during 5 Hz stimulation. This indicates that noise exposure has a greater effect on the processing of higher pulse rate sounds. The findings are very similar to our original hypotheses. As hypothesized, the AC fMRI signal was reduced following noise exposure. The MGB signal post-exposure however was reduced while the inferior colliculus signal was not significantly affected. Together, these findings suggest that the thalamus and the cortex adapt their function to the noisy environment.

661313.label: Major findings and research outcome
661313.value: This project has enabled the discovery that long-term moderate noise exposure has a multi-faceted and multi-level impact on the auditory brain. Sound temporal processing in the auditory cortex (AC) and medial geniculate body (MGB) is affected (See Lau et al., NeuroImage, 2015a). Specifically, responses to high temporal modulation rate sounds are reduced while responses to low modulate rate sounds are unaffected. This is likely related to behavioral observations that subjects are less able to identify high modulation rate sounds after exposure. Sound frequency processing in the inferior colliculus (IC) is also affected (See Lau et al., NeuroImage, 2015b). Specifically, responses to tones are shifted towards IC regions that normally respond to lower frequencies. This is likely related to previous observations that high frequency regions not chronically exposed to noise have expanded while low frequency regions exposed have contracted. The pyramidal tract (PT) is anatomically affected (See Abdoli, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 2016). Fractional anisotropy is increased, which is related to increased organization of white matter fibers. This is likely related to chronic psychomotor agitation.

661313.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
661313.value: There are many directions for further development of this important research area. First and foremost, human studies should be performed to relate these animal findings to humans. Subjects can be recruited from occupations and living environments with chronic background noise at moderate levels. Audiometric studies should be performed to test different aspects of auditory processing. Further, brain imaging can be performed to identify brain regions affected. Second, animal studies can be performed with invasive, but more specific methods such as electrophysiological recordings and immunohistochemistry. This will identify cellular and molecular changes in different brain regions. These animal studies will benefit from the results of this project, which have effectively identified the brain regions to target. Third, imaging and behavioral studies can be performed on the same subjects to directly relate brain changes to hearing deficits.

661313.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
661313.value: Long-term exposure to moderate intensity noise, such as noise pollution, affects hearing in multiple ways. Unlike loud noise, which damages primarily the ear, moderate noise’s primary effect is on sound processing in the brain. In this project, we showed that long-term moderate noise affects the processing of sound frequency and timing. Multiple levels of the brain are affected, extending from the brainstem up to the auditory cortex. These brain changes likely affect our ability to properly interpret speech in noisy environments and to distinguish sounds with fine pitch differences. In turn, these will negatively affect learning and verbal communication. In summary, this project has made significant advancements towards understanding the impact of long-term moderate noise on hearing. It has also opened many directions for further research towards understanding and treating this important problem.

661413.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
661413.value: Escherichia coli is a highly versatile species capable of surviving and reproducing in a wide range of habitats of highly contrasting conditions. In addition to being traditionally known as a natural inhabitant of the large intestines of warm-blooded animals, many recent studies have reported that E. coli is able to persist in many different types of external habitats (e.g. sediment and soil) independent of fecal input. These findings have led to concerns about not only the validity of using E. coli as an indicator of fecal pollution but also environmental matrices acting as reservoirs of enteric pathogens. Besides the practical concerns, those findings have also unveiled a previously unknown facet of the biogeography of E. coli, and led to many interesting questions about the ecological niche, lifestyle, metabolic capability, and stress resistance of the species that are yet to be resolved. The nutrients and physical stresses associated with a habitat are the most fundamental factors delimiting the ecological niche of a species. Thus far, the nutritional requirement for E. coli to colonize external habitats remains largely unexplored. In this project, we will focus on marine sediment as an external habitat and investigate for the first time the nutritional basis for E. coli to establish a niche therein (i.e. nutritional niche). We will use interstitial water extracted from the sediment of a tide flat as the sole source of nutrients, and test for the growth response of E. coli strains previously isolated from various environmental and fecal sources. The types of substrates in interstitial water supporting the growth of E. coli, and the genes and metabolic pathways being involved will be identified using transcriptomic, proteomic and phenotypic analysis. We will also investigate if and how such traits vary across strains of different sources and genetic background so as to understand nutrient exploitation as a selection pressure for E. coli populations invading marine sediment. The persistence of E. coli in external habitats is a widely reported but poorly understood phenomenon. The results obtained in this project would make an important step towards the understanding of the mechanisms that allow E. coli to invade and persist in marine sediment. The results will also establish a knowledge foundation for future investigations of the nutritional relationship (e.g. competition and co-metabolism) between E. coli and bacteria that are indigenous to marine sediment. 大腸桿菌具有很高的多樣性，並且能夠在多種差異巨大的環境中生存和繁殖。早期研究普遍認為大腸杆菌生只能存在恒溫動物的腸道內，但是近期許多研究報告指出，在沒有動物排泄物存在的情況下，也能夠在多種不同類型的腸道外環境（如沉積物和土壤）中檢測到大腸桿菌的存在。這些發現不僅對繼續使用大腸桿菌作為糞便污染指示菌的合理性提出了質疑，同時也揭示了某些環境可能作為腸道致病菌的來源的可能性。此外，這些發現還開啟了大腸桿菌在生物地理學方面的相關研究，包括其生態位、生存方式、代謝能力、抗逆性等。環境中的營養成份和物理條件是決定一個物種生態位的最基本因素。到目前為止，大腸桿菌在腸道外環境中生存時對營養物質的需求情況還不為所知。在本課題中，我們研究了以海洋沉積物作為大腸桿菌生存的腸道外環境時，其在該生態位中所需的基本營養物質。我們將會使用從海岸潮間帶沉積物中提取的孔隙水作為營養物質的唯一來源，研究從多種環境和糞便中分離到的大腸桿菌在其中的生長情況。通過對大腸桿菌的轉錄組、蛋白組和表型分析，確定孔隙水中能夠支持大腸桿菌生長的營養物質種類，以及參與相關物質利用的基因和代謝途徑。同時，我們還會對不同來源和遺傳背景的大腸桿菌的差異性進行分析，以研究當營養物質利用成為一種選擇壓力時，大腸桿菌群體在海洋沉積物中如何應對。大腸桿菌在腸道外環境中的存在已經被多次報導，但關於該方向的深層次研究卻很少。本課題的研究將會使我們進一步了解大腸桿菌在海洋沉積物中的生存機理。並且，還會對進一步研究大腸桿菌與海洋沉積物中內源細菌的營養關係（例如種間競爭，共代謝）提供依據。

661413.label: Realisation of objectives
661413.value: Objective 1 We tested water salinity as a source of stress as well as dissolved molecules in the interstitial water of marine sediment as a source of nutrient to the survivorship and growth of E. coli, respectively. For this purpose, a total of 160 presumptive E. coli isolates were collected from raw sewage and marine sediment. The isolates were classified into genotypes using REP-DNA fingerprinting and subsequently analysed for phylogenetic affiliation using multi-loci sequence typing. Notably, some of the sediment isolates were identified as belonging to the cryptic clade II of Escherichia, instead of E. coli. Cryptic Escherichia refers to previously unidentified monophyletic clades of strains, which are phylogenetically divergent yet taxonomically largely indistinguishable from E. coli sensus stricto. Currently, a total of five cryptic Escherichia clades (I to V) have been described in the literature. There is mounting evidence indicating that cryptic clade I is a subspecies of E. coli sensus stricto and is likely associated with human hosts as a potential pathogen whereas cryptic clades II to V are more likely to be environmentally adapted. The isolates were tested for (i) respiratory activity under six different levels of water salinity (0, 7, 14, 21, 28 and 35 ppt), (ii) respiratory activity under 96 osmolyte conditions, and (ii) growth in 100kD-filtered interstitial water. The isolates exhibited large variations in their tolerance to salinity and osmolytes and in their growth in interstitial water. Such variations had no apparent relationship with the phylogenetic affiliation of the isolates tested. Notably, the isolates from sediment, particularly those belonging to cryptic clade II of Escherichia had slower growth in interstitial water than the sewage isolates. But the slow growers generally had stronger glycogen accumulation phenotype. The results suggest that the resources utilization strategy of the cryptic clade II of Escherichia was more geared to storage than immediate growth, which may benefit long term survival in the generally less stable and less predictable external environments as compared to the enteric environment in mammalian hosts. Objective 2 Transcriptomics and shotgun proteomics analyses were used to identify genes and proteins expressed in the bacterial cells in response to high water salinity as a stress or to interstitial water as the sole source of nutrient. The isolates involved in the investigation were chosen using two criteria: 1) the isolates had close phylogenetic relationship yet contrasting growth / decay rate in the same test condition, or 2) the isolates had similar growth / decay rate in same test condition yet relatively distant phylogenetic relationship. Four E. coli isolates sensus stricto from raw sewage were involved in the test for the effects of salinity. The cells of each isolate were exposed to the M9 minimal medium with an intrinsic salinity of 15 ppt and to the M9 minimal medium supplemented with NaCl to reach a final salinity of 35 ppt (equivalent to that of full strength seawater), respectively. Contrarily, a total of seven isolates together with E. coli K12 as a reference were involved in the test for the effects of interstitial water as the sole source of nutrient. The seven isolates included three members of the cyptic clade II of Escherichia from marine sediment and four members of E. coli sensus stricto (three from sewage and one from sediment). The cells of each isolate were given the M9-glucose medium and 100 kD-filtered interstitial water, respectively. Gene and proteins that were differentially expressed under the contrasting salinity and nutrient conditions were identified. The gene and protein expression in response to salinity stress differed substantially among the four E. coli isolates involved in the investigation. In contrast, the expression profiles observed for growth in interstitial water were more consistent among the seven isolates of E coli and cryptic Escherichia. These results suggest that the differences observed between E. coli and the cryptic clade II of Escherichia with respect to growth in interstitial water could be due to differences in the coordination of post-transcriptional events. Objective 3 E. coli and the cryptic clade II of Escherichia growing in interstitial water and M9-glucose medium had different expression levels for many genes and proteins. The genes that were up-regulated in the interstitial water were associated with amino acid metabolism and transport, indicating amino acids may be utilized as one of the carbon sources in interstitial water. On the contrary, when the isolates were cultured in the M9-glucose medium, they had all up-regulated the genes associated with iron acquisition and B-vitamins biosynthesis, indicating the presence and utilization of these substrates in interstitial water. Nonetheless, the cells growing in interstitial water had up-regulated the genes associated with stress response and curli formation, suggesting that the interstitial water was a resourceful yet at the same time a more stressful environment than the minimal medium of M9-glucose. The results of proteomics analysis were in support of those of the transcriptome analysis. Lysogeny plays important roles in the diversification of the ecologic characters of E. coli. We investigated the possible roles of lysogeny in the survivorship and nutrient utilization profile of E. coli. For this purpose, we induced the prophages of an E. coli strain from marine sediment and took the induced phage particles to infect a strain of fecal E. coli. An isogenic lysogen of the latter was thus obtained. Genome sequence analysis indicated that a P2-like prophage was transferred from the sediment strain to the isogenic lysogen. This lysogenic infection led to tractable changes in many of the ecophysiological attributes tested. Incubation experiments in seawater and sediment microcosms indicated that the isogenic lysogen had higher survivorship than the wild type fecal strain, although it was not as high as that of the sediment strain from which the P2-prohage was originated. The comparison of carbon utilization profiles indicated that the isogenic lysogen had increased the utilization of 37 carbon sources (mostly carbohydrates) and reduced the utilization of 12 other carbon sources (mostly carboxylic acids) in comparison to the wild type fecal strain. In addition, the isogenic lysogen grew faster than the wild type in high salinity and in the presence of six types of compatible solutes, suggesting that osmotic regulation was a possible survival benefit conferred by the P2-like prophage. Nonetheless, the isogenic lysogen appeared to be less acid tolerant. Generally, the isogenic lysogen had better survivorship in the sediment and seawater, and had a substrate utilization and stress resistance profile resembling the sediment strain more than the wild type fecal strain. The molecular mechanism causing the observed changes are yet to be investigated. None of the 46 genes carried by the P2-like prophage (31 phage structural genes, 6 phage regulatory genes, 1 putative reverse transcriptase and 8 genes of unknown functions) have been reported to have effects on bacterial survival or nutrient utilization. Nevertheless, these results provide a new insight to phenotypic attributes, including nutritional requirement and stress resistance, that enable E. coli to survive marine in sediment.

661413.label: Major findings and research outcome
661413.value: Emerging evidence indicates that the cryptic clades of Escherichia should represent novel species rather distinct ecotypes of E. coli. Nonetheless, their co-existence in many environmental matrices, especially those that are perceived pristine, provokes many interesting questions about the differences / similarity in lifestyle that are yet to be resolved. This project started with E. coli sensus stricto and subsequently extended to the cryptic clade II of Escherichia because we found a number of strains of the latter in the marine sediment samples. Currently, very little is known for the member of cryptic clade II due to their rarity in the samples of the studies elsewhere in the world. The results of this project are filling in some of the knowledge gap. One of the major findings of this project is that when E. coli and Escherichia cryptic clade II were grown under the same condition, they appeared to have different global expression profiles; however, the differences largely reduced when they were compared for differentially expressed genes between the growth in sediment interstitial water and M9-glucose medium. This suggests that, although E. coli and Escherichia cryptic clade II had many inherent differences in their metabolic capabilities, they both appeared to be having similar behaviour in interstitial water with respect to amino acid metabolism, trace nutrients utilization and stress response. For instance, they both appeared to be utilizing methionine, glycine, proline, cysteine and taurine but not tryptophan when given interstitial water. They were also utilizing propionate and L-fucose, iron siderophores and B vitamins in interstitial water. In addition, they both had expressed a variety of genes (e.g. ydcS, csiD, aldB, acs, actP, aldA, gltA and glpF) to overcome the stresses associated with growing in interstitial water. E. coli and Escherichia cryptic clade II appeared to share a lot of similarities with respect to growth in interstitial water as the sole source of nutrient. This finding could provoke a new debate of whether their differences in ecological characteristics are as pronounced as previously thought. Another major finding of this project is that lysogeny is a possible mechanism for an E. coli strain to acquire a new nutrient utilization profile that may help diversify its niches from the wild type strain. This may also provide an opportunity for E. coli to rapidly adapt to a new environment, for instance, during the transfer from the enteric environment to an external habitat.

661413.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
661413.value: Previous studies have investigated the ecological and physiological characteristics of the cryptic clades of Escherichia, such as their principal habitats, growth requirements, and ability to form biofilms and colonize gut surfaces. Although there is compelling evidence that the members of clade I are associated with humans and the members of clades II to V are adapted to the external environments, their actual ecological niches remain largely not known. Knowledge of cryptic clade II is particularly scarce, partly due to the rarity of their members (only two strains reported so far). For unknown reasons, cryptic clade II appears to be abundant and widespread in Hong Kong. We have obtained 16 isolates of cryptic clade II from marine sediment during this study and many more from soil, periphyton and freshwater stream in another study. This provides us with a good opportunity to compare the nutritional niches and other ecological characters of the members of cryptic cades II dwelling in different environments. The interstitial water used in this study was a relatively simple environment in comparison to the entire sediment matrix. Therefore, further investigations should aim to use a whole matrix of sediment, soil or periphyton, although it would be technically very challenging.

661413.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
661413.value: Marine sediment is a complex matrix with conditions very different from the mammalian guts. How E. coli, as a gut bacterium, is able to grow in marine sediment is a question of fundamental importance. This study investigated the metabolic pathways that enabled E. coli to cope with water salinity as a stressor and utilize the dissolved molecules in sediment interstitial water as a source of nutrient. In addition, the nutrient utilization strategy of E. coli was compared to that of cryptic Escherichia, which is a group of bacteria closely related to E. coli and is adapted to survive in the natural environments. The analysis of gene and protein expression profiles indicated that different E. coli strains had different strategies to cope with salinity stress. However, E coli and cryptic Escherichia had rather similar nutritional requirements for growth in interstitial water. Particularly, they both appeared to utilize amino acids in interstitial water as a source of carbon. In addition, the interstitial water appeared to be a resourceful yet stressful environment to both E. coli and cryptic Escherichia. The results in this study provide new insights to phenotypic and metabolic attributes that enable E. coli and cryptic Escherichia to survive in marine sediment.

661613.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
661613.value: Reversible protein phosphorylation plays a central role in cell signaling, regulation of gene expression, controlling organismal growth and development and adaptation to environmental changes. With the advent of powerful and robust phosphoproteomics, we are now able to profile phosphoproteins at a large scale and to determine the phosphorylation sites associated with an environmental inducer, touch. Knowledge gained from the phosphoproteome analysis provides a basis for further study of the functions of these phosphorylated proteins in diverse touch-induced responses and signaling. Being non-motile creatures, plants must perceive diverse environmental stimuli and respond in ways that enable acclimation to their local environment. Plants sense and respond to touch, probably because such physical perturbation is associated with stimuli such as wind, herbivore attack, and plant neighbor crowding. Indeed, in response to touch, plants undergo the touch-induced developmental and morphological changes called thigmomorphogenesis, which confer enhanced herbivore and wind resistance. Furthermore, root growth is also guided by touch and normally moves away from physical barriers through thigmotropism. Many plant organs display thigmonasty, touch-induced movements important for tendril curling and/or leaf movements. Despite the fundamental nature of the mechanical stimulus of touch and that over 2.5% of genes of Arabidopsis, a model plant species, are rapidly up-regulated in expression in response to touch, the signaling pathways responsible for plant touch responses have not been elucidated yet. However, numerous secondary messengers have been implicated in the touch-response pathway. In this proposed project, phosphoproteomics will be applied to study phosphor-relay-mediated signaling in the Arabidopsis touch response. To that end, we hereby propose 1) to globally profile and identify phosphoproteins upon touch stimulation for 0, 0.5, 1, 2, minutes; 2) to determine the biological functions of phosphoproteins in touch signaling pathways using multidisciplinary approaches, including transgenic plants, epistasis analysis, physiological measurements and protein biochemistry and 3) to search for putative phosphosites-binding proteins (kinases and phosphatases) and putative phosphorylation-interacting proteins in order to construct the post-tranlational modifcation (PTM) networks during Arabidopsis touch responses. This research is expected to decipher the intricate networks of plant cell signal transduction pathways mediated by phosphor-relay and to provide information on the molecular mechanisms underlying mechano-sensing, thigmotropism, thigmonasty and thigmomorphogenesis. The outcome of this research will contribute to the development of a model system for molecular systems biology and will be applied toward improving crop productivity for food and bioenergy and removing environmental carbon dioxide.

661613.label: Realisation of objectives
661613.value: To elucidate the dosage effect of touch on morphogenesis, we treated six groups of Arabidopsis plants with one touch per second for 10–80 s. The touch response increased with increasing treatment period, reaching the maximum at 40 s of touch treatment. We confirmed the cellular effect of such a 40-s treatment in both BRET-based GFP::Aequorin fusion protein transgenic plants and ProCML39::LUC/Col-0 transgenic plants (LUC plants). The 40-s touch treatment triggered both a rise (spike) in cytoplasmic calcium concentration [Ca2+]cyt in AEQ plants and an increase in the expression of the touch-responsive recombinant gene ProCML39::LUC, consistent with a previous report (Lee et al., 2005). The strength of both cotton swab and finger touch treatments was 84.1 ± 79.8 mg/touch . No wounding effect was observed in leaves under this strength of repetitive touch treatment . A repetitive 40-s touch (1 touch/s) with either a cotton swab or gloved finger resulted in delayed bolting in both agar- and soil-grown plants. We selected LUC plants for PTM proteomics analysis, as these plants report dynamic touch responses . We employed 14N- and 15N-labeled plants as either the control or touch-treated plant samples in both forward and reciprocal mixing experiments. A total of six biological replicates (four forward and two reciprocal replicates, see Methods) were performed with aerial tissues upon 40 seconds of touch. As a result, 4,895 phosphopeptides from 2,426 phosphoprotein groups were repetitively (n > 2) detected, among which 579 phosphopeptides represented novel phosphosites of the 509 protein groups according to the phosphopeptide repertoire in the PhosPhAt 4.0 database following the previously described method. The number of unique phosphopeptides detected from two replicates was 50% higher than that from a single replicate (3,362 vs. 2,237), whereas the number increased by only 4% (from 4,712 to 4,895) when the total number of unique phosphopeptides from six replicates was compared to that from five replicates , indicating that increasing the number of replicates to more than five contributed little to the total number of unique phosphopeptides identified using the current quantitative phosphoproteomics approach. Although over 80% of the phosphopeptides were detected in both the control and touch-treated samples, the number of touch-specific phosphopeptides (603) was approximately 2.4-fold higher than that of the untouched control (250) . This result indicates that a 40-s touch treatment increased the number of overall protein phosphorylation sites. According to the substrate sequence specificity of Ser/Thr protein kinases (O'Neill et al., 2000), 28%, 9%, and 27% of the phosphorylated Ser/Thr are found in acidophilic (p[S/T][D/E] or p[S/T]xx[D/E]), basophilic (Rxxp[S/T]), and proline-directed (p[S/T]P) motifs, respectively. Moreover, we identified six touch-specific phosphorylation motifs via bioinformatics analysis of the phosphoproteome, suggesting that some phosphorylation events may be catalyzed by related kinases. We performed quantitative analysis of the ratios of isotope-coded peptides in 750 strictly selected, quantifiable pairs of light and heavy phosphopeptides, leading to the identification of 23 touch-enhanced phosphopeptides and one touch-suppressed phosphopeptide , corresponding to a total of 24 phosphoprotein groups (in which several phosphoproteins may share the same phosphosite). The greatest increase (15.2-fold) in phosphorylation level was found at either the T29 position of MAP KINASE KINASE1 (MKK1, AT4G26070) or the T31 position of MAP KINASE KINASE2 (MKK2, AT4G29810), whereas the most highly downregulated (-1.4-fold) phosphosite was found at T30 of the Light-harvesting chlorophyll-protein complex II subunit B1 (LHB1B1, AT2G34430). These results are consistent with the observed difference between the number of phosphopeptides in the control versus touch-treated samples (i.e., touched > untouched phosphopeptides). Touch treatment increased both the concentration and diversity of phosphopeptides. This list of phosphopeptides includes MKK2 (AT4G29810), CALCIUM-DEPENDENT PROTEIN KINASE1 (CPK1, AT5G04870), CALMODULIN-DOMAIN PROTEIN KINASE5/6 (CPK5/6, AT4G35310/AT2G17290), and Protein phosphatase 2C (PP2C) family proteins, which are all well-known protein phosphorylation/dephosphorylation enzymes that function in cell signaling (Hunter, 1995). In addition, we identified eight touch-enhanced phosphopeptides from eight phosphoproteins of unknown function. We named these proteins Touch-Regulated Phosphoproteins (TREPHs). The levels of two similar peptides, VNpSLLSIPR and VNpSLVQLPR (derived from distinct members of the PP2C family), increased 1.8- and 1.4-fold, respectively, in response to touch treatment. These results, in combination with the results of the bioinformatics analysis, revealed a touch-regulated phosphosite motif in PP2C family proteins. Bioinformatic analysis of those touch-regulated phosphosites predicted a number of putative touch-regulated phosphosites, producing a list of phosphosite motifs. One of these motifs is the S625 phosphosite motif of TREPH1, which shares sequence similarity with a putative phosphosite in RECEPTOR LIKE PROTEIN 47, (RLP47, AT4G13810) and L-TYPE LECTIN RECEPTOR KINASE III.1 (LECRK-III.1, AT2G29220). These results suggest that these putative kinases might play a role in protein phosphorylation changes following plant touch stimulation. To investigate the role of touch-induced protein phosphorylation in thigmomorphogenesis, we screened both homozygous and heterozygous T-DNA insertional mutant lines of the six phosphoproteins, including mkk2 and treph1-1 , to screen for plants with defective touch-induced delay of bolting. The treph1-1 and mkk2 mutants showed a conspicuous defect in the delayed bolting time touch response compared to the remaining candidates, including several control plants. The three other phenotypic changes associated with the touch response, including changes in rosette leaf number, average rosette radius, and inflorescence stem height, was not abolished in the mutants treph1-1 and mkk2 although the touch effects on these phenotypes were reduced by the stimulus . These results indicate that both treph1-1 and mkk2 are defective in demonstrating touch-delayed bolting and therefore MKK2 and TREPH1 are essential for this aspect of thigmomorphogenesis. To investigate the functional role of S625 phosphorylation of TREPH1 in the touch response, we performed force stimulation on two groups of transgenic plants: dPro35S::His::YFP::TREPH1/treph1-1 , expressing the phosphorylatable YFP::TREPH1 fusion protein ; and dPro35S::His::YFP::TREPH1S625A/treph1-1, expressing YFP::TREPH1S625A protein isoform with a point mutation predicted to prevent site-specific phosphorylation. In the transgenic TREPH1-complemented lines, the bolting time response of the loss-of-function mutant treph1 was rescued, with the bolting time significantly delayed from 23.3 ± 0.2 to 24.7 ± 0.2 days , whereas the TREPH1S625A protein-complemented lines showed no significant delay in bolting , even though the expression levels of TREPH1S625A were similar. To determine whether S625 phosphorylation of TREPH1 was required in both the regulation of touch-inducible gene expression and the touch response, we performed both transcriptomics and RT-qPCR analysis and bolting time measurements in transgenic lines TREPH1/treph1-1 and TREPH1S625A/treph1-1. We detected an association between touch-inducible gene expression and the touch response. The single point mutation S625A resulted in reduced expression levels of TCH2K1, CML38, ERF11, and JAZ7 . We also investigated TREPH1 subcellular localization. At the cellular level, the YFP::TREPH1 fluorescence was localized primarily to the cell periphery, consistent with cytosolic localization . The distribution of YFP::TREPH1S625A was similar to that of wild-type protein. The cytoplasmic localization of TREPH1 was further confirmed by cellular fractionation, with the bulk of TREPH1 found in the soluble, not membrane, fraction. The interatomic analysis of the phosphoproteins using the bioinformatics program STRING, we identified two protein–protein interactomic modules among these touch-related phosphoproteins. BLAST analysis of the amino acid sequence of TREPH1 against the proteomes of both plants and animals revealed homologs of the TREPH1 C-terminus in mammals, monocots, and dicots .

661613.label: Major findings and research outcome
661613.value: Plants can sense both intracellular and extracellular mechanical forces and can respond through morphological changes. The signaling components responsible for mechanotransduction of the touch response are largely unknown. Here, we performed a high-throughput SILIA (stable isotope labeling in Arabidopsis)-based quantitative phosphoproteomics analysis to profile changes in protein phosphorylation resulting from 40 seconds of force stimulation in Arabidopsis thaliana. Of the 24 touch-responsive phosphosites identified, many were kinases, phosphatases, cytoskeleton proteins, and ion transporters. Both MAP KINASE KINASE2 (MKK2) and TOUCH-REGULATED PHOSPHOPROTEIN1 (TREPH1) became rapidly phosphorylated in touch-stimulated plants, and both are required for touch-induced delayed flowering, a major component of thigmomorphogenesis. The loss-of-function treph1-1 mutant also exhibited defects in touch-inducible gene expression. A non-phosphorylatable site-specific isoform of TREPH1 (S625A) failed to complement treph1-1, providing evidence for the functional relevance of the touch-regulated phosphorylation of TREPH1. Fluorescence microscopy of a tagged TREPH1 protein and subcellular fractionation analysis indicate that TREPH1 is primarily associated with the cytosol. Altogether, these findings identify new protein players and indicate that protein phosphorylation is an essential component in mechanoresponses in Arabidopsis.

661613.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
661613.value: In the following research, we intend to (1) further analyze the membrane-bound PTM proteins associated with touch, (2) to focus on the genetic, molecular and cellular analysis of these newly identified membrane and cytosolic phosphoproteins, kinases, phosphatases, including ion channels, responsive to touch treatment and (3) to establish molecular network of mechanotransduction.

A novel protein TREPH1 has been found to play a key role in regulation of the touch-delayed flowering, one of the important plant touch responses. This important protein may be responsible for deliver the force signals, like wind, rain, insect bite or even self-touching by plant leaves, to gene activities and plant appearance development.
