661713.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
661713.value: DNA replication is a fundamental cellular process in the development of organisms and cancer. While obligatorily expressed in cancer cells, some replication-initiation proteins are not expressed in non-proliferating normal cells. Furthermore, inhibiting DNA replication-initiation proteins induces apoptosis in cancerous but not normal cells. Therefore, replication-initiation proteins are attractive targets for cancer detection and intervention. Understanding the mechanism and regulation of DNA replication will help combating cancer. Initiation of eukaryotic DNA replication is regulated by a two-step mechanism: replication licensing and origin activation. In replication licensing, several replication-initiation proteins are loaded into replication origins to form pre-replicative complexes (pre-RCs) at the M-to-G1 transition. Since ORC (origin recognition complex) is required for loading other pre-RC components onto chromatin, ORC plays a central role in replication licensing. ORC forms an asymmetric structure in which Orc1p/4p occupy the upper half while Orc2p/3p/4p/6p form the lower half. However, how this asymmetric structure loads the symmetric MCM (minichromosome maintenance) double-hexamers is unknown. In addition, DNA replication results in doubling of origins. It remains a fundamental question when and how ORC associates with the newly replicated origins to protect them from histone invasion. More importantly, it is unknown whether a regulated process of loading ORC to the duplicated origins is essential for DNA replication. We have discovered that ORC self-interacts and forms dimeric complexes (double-hexamers) at origins before pre-RC formation in budding yeast. Furthermore, upon initiation, each ORC double-hexamer separates into two single-hexamers, each to bind one of the two duplicated origins until late M phase. At the M-to-G1 transition, non-chromatin-bound ORC associates with the chromatin-bound ORC single-hexamers to re-form double-hexamers. Importantly, preventing ORC dimerization abolishes pre-RC formation, DNA replication and cell proliferation. Our findings uncovered a cell cycle-dependent ORC ‘dimerization cycle’ which critically regulates DNA replication. However, we know little about how ORC dimerization is regulated. It is also unknown if ORC dimerization occurs in other eukaryotes. We propose to further investigate ORC dimerization and its regulatory mechanisms in budding yeast. We will determine if ORC phosphorylation, other factors, ATP metabolism, and/or origin DNA control ORC dimerization. We will also examine if human ORC dimerizes and if hORC dimerization regulates human DNA replication. These studies will shed new light onto the exquisite control mechanism of genome duplication. Furthermore, if ORC dimerization proves essential for human DNA replication, this will suggest that ORC dimerization is a potential anticancer target since its disruption will inhibit cell proliferation. 661713.label: Realisation of objectives
661713.value: The overall goal of this project is to study the functions and regulation of the ORC dimerization cycle in yeast and human cells. We have employed cell biology, genetics, molecular biology and biochemistry approaches to achieve the following objectives: Objective 1: Determine the precise timing of the ORC dimerization cycle and confirm the semi-conservativeness of ORC dimerization in budding yeast As described in the Background section of the proposal, we found that ORC forms double-hexamers in G1 but not S or M phase cells. To determine the precise timing of ORC being single- and double-hexamers, we performed chromatin binding assays to determine the timing of ORC becoming double- from single-hexamers during the M-to-G1 transition by harvesting cells every 10 minutes for 1 hour after the cells were released from a nocodazole block in M phase. The results show that ORC dimerizes at the M-to-G1 transition right before MCM loading to the chromatin. Similarly, we have also determined that ORC begins to become single hexamers at the G1-to-S transition using cells that were released from the G1 block. Using a different strategy, we expressed epitope-tagged ORC subunits under the control of the GAL promoter in G1- and M-synchronized cells, respectively, and released them into the cell cycle to examine the time of their association with chromatin. The data again show that newly synthesized ORC binds to chromatin in late M phase. These data further support that function of the ORC dimerization cycle in the once-per-cell cycle control of DNA replication. Furthermore, our data suggest that upon S phase entry, each double hexamer ORC separates into two single hexamers to bind each pair of nascent origins until late M phase. The non-chromatin-bound ORC then associates with the chromatin-bound ORC to reform double hexamers at the M-to-G1 transition. Preventing ORC dimerization by depleting non-chromatin bound ORC proteins in M phase, or by Orc6p point mutations that disrupt ORC self-interaction, abolishes pre-RC formation, DNA replication and cell proliferation and viability. Our findings from the yeast-two hybrid analysis, co-IP, chromatin binding assay, re-ChIP, sucrose gradient sedimentation, and several function assays uncovered an essential, cell cycle-dependent and semi-conservative ORC ‘dimerization cycle’ that may play three fundamental roles in the regulation of DNA replication: providing a symmetric platform to load the symmetric pre-RCs, marking and protecting the nascent sister replication origins until the next licensing, and providing the first guard against origin re-licensing within the same cell cycle. Objective 2: Investigate the mechanisms controlling ORC dimerization in budding yeast It is known that ORC is required for the loading of other initiation proteins onto replication origins. In contrast, no factor is known to recruit ORC onto origins. However, it is not known if some proteins are needed to promote ORC dimerization. We have used conditional mutants of initiation proteins to determine if any of them affect ORC dimerization. We found that Noc3p forms dimers and is required for ORC dimerization. These data not only shed light on the regulation of ORC dimerization, but also provide a new role of Noc3p in replication licensing. In addition, we found that ORC dimerization is regulated by ORC phosphorylation and de-phosphorylation, and the chromatin loading of Cdc6p and ORC dimerization is independent of each other. Objective 3: Examine ORC dimerization and determine its significance in human cells Given the conservation of ORC and other initiation proteins in eukaryotes, we hypothesize that hORC dimerization may also occur to regulate DNA replication in human cells. We have used the yeast two-hybrid system to determine that three human ORC subunits have self-interactions similar to the findings in the yeast ORC. We further mapped the self-interaction domains of some of the hORC subunits. Importantly, we found that human ORC double hexamers co-localize on stretched chromatin fiber bundles from G1 phase, but not M phase, human cells. These data provide visualization of ORC dimerization on stretched human chromatin fibers, further supporting the conclusion on ORC dimerization. Together, these results further confirmed the physiological significance of ORC dimerization and revealed its control mechanisms in budding yeast, and identified a similar ORC dimerization cycle in human cells. These studies shed new light onto the intricate control mechanism of genome duplication in eukaryotes. All proposed goals of this grant have been achieved by our studies. A manuscript has been submitted.

661713.label: Major findings and research outcome
661713.value: Eukaryotic DNA replication licensing, which is a prerequisite for genome duplication and also plays a critical role to ensure that all chromosomal DNA is replicated exactly once per cell cycle, involves the recruitment of many replication-initiation proteins by origin recognition complex (ORC) to form pre-replicative complexes (pre-RCs) at replication origins. ORC binds to and marks replication origins throughout the cell cycle. However, some fundamental issues in the regulation of ORC remain unsolved. We found that ORC self-interacts and dimerizes (forming a double hexamer) before MCM loading in budding yeast. Our data also suggest that upon S phase entry, each double hexamer ORC separates into two single hexamers to bind each pair of nascent origins until late M phase. The non-chromatin-bound ORC then associates with the chromatin-bound ORC to reform double hexamers at the M-to-G1 transition. Preventing ORC dimerization by depleting non-chromatin bound ORC proteins in M phase, or by Orc6p point mutations that disrupt ORC self-interaction, abolishes pre-RC formation, DNA replication and cell proliferation and cell viability. Similarly, human ORC subunits also self-interact and the ORC double hexamers co-localize on stretched chromatin fiber bundles from G1 phase, but not M phase, human cells. Our findings uncovered an essential, cell cycle-dependent and semi-conservative ORC ‘dimerization cycle’ that may play three fundamental roles in the regulation of DNA replication: providing a symmetric platform to load the symmetric pre-RCs, marking and protecting the nascent sister replication origins until the next licensing, and providing the first guard against origin re-licensing within the same cell cycle. A manuscript with the following highlights has been submitted for publication: 1. ORC self-interacts and dimerizes (forming a double heterohexamer) in a semi-conservative and cell cycle-regulated manner. 2. ORC dimerizes in an early step of pre-RC formation, providing a symmetric platform to load the symmetric pre-RC. 3. During DNA replication, each ORC double hexamer separates into two single hexamers, thus protecting the two nascent replication origins at each locus and helping to prevent re-licensing in the same cell cycle. 4. The ORC dimerization cycle is essential for pre-RC formation and plays a critical role to ensure that DNA replication occurs exactly once per cell cycle.

Potential use of human ORC self-interactions as anticancer drug targets for drug research and development.

661713.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
661713.value: Eukaryotic DNA replication licensing, which is required for genome duplication, involves the regulated recruitment of many replication-initiation proteins by the hexameric origin recognition complex (ORC) at replication origins. ORC binds to, marks and protect replication origins. However, some fundamental issues in the regulation of ORC remain unsolved. We found that ORC interacts with itself and dimerizes (from a single hexamer to a double hexamer) before the loading of other replication initiation proteins in budding yeast. We also find that upon DNA replication, each double hexamer ORC separates into two single hexamers to bind to and thus protect each pair of nascent origins. Preventing ORC dimerization abolishes DNA replication and cell proliferation and cell viability. Similarly, human ORC subunits also self-interact and the ORC double hexamers co-localize on stretched chromatin fiber bundles from G1 phase, but not M phase, human cells. Our findings uncovered an essential, cell cycle-dependent and semi-conservative ORC ‘dimerization cycle’ that may play three fundamental roles in the regulation of DNA replication: providing a symmetric platform to load the symmetric replication machinery, marking and protecting the nascent sister replication origins until the next licensing, and providing the first guard against re-replication within the same cell cycle.

661813.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
661813.value: 聚球藻是海洋中丰度很高並且具有重要生態學意義的一類單細胞藍青細菌，是海洋初級生產力的主要貢獻者。聚球藻因細胞內包含的色素蛋白的種類及數量的多寡不同會呈現從藍綠色到橙紅色不同的顏色，如捕光复合体中的藻膽蛋白。含有高濃度的藻紅蛋白（PE）的聚球藻能夠高效地吸收綠光並且細胞顏色呈現紅色，而僅僅含有藻藍蛋白 （PC）的聚球藻則主要吸收紅光而呈現藍綠色。紅色聚球藻主要分佈在藍光及綠光能夠穿透的外海水域，而綠色聚球藻主要分佈於渾濁的紅光爲主的水域，例如河口區域。根據分子分類學方法，聚球藻具有很高的基因多樣性，至今已經發現了超過20種的不同進化類羣的聚球藻。這些類羣代表了不同的生態分佈或者是生態型，但是有研究表明聚球藻的生態型與色素分佈不具有必然的聯繫。最近的研究顯示編碼色素蛋白的基因具有相對獨立的進化方向。不同類羣的聚球藻可能通過水平基因轉移獲得不同的色素蛋白基因，而能夠快速地適應於不同的生態位。因爲不同生態型的聚球藻經常同時出現在相同的海域，因此聚球藻是研究同一功能類羣的微生物是如何共存和佔據不同的棲息地的理想生物。 河口通常是渾濁的，半鹹水的水域。它在海洋的營養鹽及有機質的輸入過程中具有重要的作用。由於透光性差，靠近陸地的河口地區通常是高營養鹽，但低葉綠素及初級生產力的水域。隨着懸浮顆粒物的沉澱，在距離陸地較遠的河口區域，當光線適合時，浮游植物會爆發生長並達到最大生物量。我們預測含PC爲主的聚球藻主要分佈在靠近岸邊，低鹽，渾濁的水域，而含PE爲主的聚球藻主要分佈在遠離陸地，高鹽，陸架水域。因此，對不同基因型及表型的聚球藻在大型河流河口的時間空間分佈變化的研究有助於認識河口及近岸地區的微食物環和碳及營養物質的生物地球化學循環。 在該項目中，我們將研究聚球藻在珠江口水域及香港近岸水域的丰度和系統發育多樣性的季節性變化。圍繞香港的海水具有完全不同的水文條件，香港的西部水域主要受珠江的影響爲高污染的水域，而香港東邊的水域主要是相對乾淨的近岸海水。我們計劃每個月從河口及近岸站位採集樣品，我們的研究將集中在： 1） 香港水域聚球藻系統發育多樣性的研究，重點關注PC爲主的聚球藻，因爲這類聚球藻在亞熱帶河口區域的重要性還是未知數。 2） 應用定量PCR的方法研究主要的聚球藻生態類羣在河口及近岸地區的時空變化，及研究引起生態類羣分佈差異的環境因素。 3） 從河口地區分離聚球藻菌株，並且研究它們的生理生態特性，例如它們最佳的生長條件（如光線，鹽度，溫度，營養鹽等）。 我們預期發現聚球藻類羣在河口及近岸站點具有顯著不同的色素組成及系統發育結構，同時我們預期看到聚球藻主要類羣在河口及近岸的時空變化。這些發現將更好的讓我們瞭解聚球藻不同類羣的生態位及他們在多變的河口環境中的生物地球化學循環中所扮演的角色。

661813.label: Realisation of objectives
661813.value: We achieved all objectives and exceeded what we have proposed to do. We have conducted monthly sampling in Hong Kong coastal waters and used flow cytometry, next generation sequencing and qPCR to study the composition, diversity and seasonal variation of Synechococcus in Hong Kong coastal waters. We have isolated dozens of unique stains of Synechococcus from Hong Kong coastal waters and studied their physiological and ecological characteristics and its implication in environmental adaptation, biogeochemical cycling and response to climate change. We have expanded our study to China Seas and the Pacific Ocean. We are still working on the genomic study of some interesting strains. We are also working on cyanophage that infect our strains. Overall, I consider this is one of the most successful project I have done in a decade.

661813.label: Major findings and research outcome
661813.value: Seasonal variations of Synechococcus abundance and community composition in two contrasting stations of Hong Kong waters were also studied by using FCM and 454 pyrosequencing of rpoC1 gene. We found that the Hong Kong coastal water is a hot spot of high Synechococcus diversity containing almost all known clades and novel new strains. Temperature and salinity are the main factors influencing the Synechococcus community composition in Hong Kong waters. Unlike most PE-type Synechococcus which cannot survive in low salinity estuarine waters, we found that some clade IX Synechococcus strains that were common in our study sites can grow at a range of salinities. We expanded our study area to reveal niche differentiation of Synechococcus lineages and pigment types, and the biotic and abiotic factors affecting Synechococcus abundance and diversity in the western Pacific Ocean. Our data showed the highest Synechococcus abundance occurred in the East China Seas and Japan Sea. Synechococcus pigment genetic composition also showed as latitudinal differentiation. CA4-B and/or high phycourobilin-containing cells are the most abundant at SCS, type 3a is dominant pigment type in ECS, while CA4-A type chromatic acclimaters are major pigment type in the Synechococcus community in the subarctic Ocean. Furthermore, we developed a new primer set, named peBF/peAR, for PCR of cpeBA gene. The superior coverage and efficiency of this primer set is proved in a study of Synechococcus community pigment genetic diversity in ECS and SCS. The impact of freshwater from the Pearl River on taxonomic structure and pigment composition of Synechococcus communities was studied along a salinity gradient in Pearl River estuary. Several novel PE euryhaline Synechococcus were isolated from Hong Kong waters, and their genome was sequenced and compared with oligotrophic ocean strains. For example, the high ability of HK01 (one of the PE containing euryhaline isolates) to deal with salinity variations may be due to the presence of Na+/H+ antiporter. Coastal strains have markedly different genome structure from oceanic strains. For example, coastal strains have more regulators to adapt to relatively unstable coastal waters. Moreover, genes related to type IV pilus and cell wall synthesis are quite different between coastal and oceanic strains.

661813.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
661813.value: There is a great potential to further develop research in this topic. I will try to develop proposals to unveil niche differentiations of Synechococcus lineages through whole genome analysis and metagenomic analysis. Synechococcus strains belonging to clades II, III, V, VIII, IX and S5.2 with different pigments have been isolated from different regions of Hong Kong waters. It is interesting that some PE Synechococcus isolated from Hong Kong waters are identified as clade VIII and S5.2 that are traditionally recognized as groups of PC Synechococcus. Analyzing genome sequences of those strains will develop our understanding about the evolution history of Synechococcus and also provide insights into reasons of niche differentiation of Synechococcus lineages. Further research on the genome of euryhaline PE-type Synechococcus, especially clade IX, may help us to better understand how these Synechococcus cells deal with salinity changes. We also collected 10 metagenomic samples from the Sea of Okhotsk, the Pearl River estuary and the northern South China Sea. Using those sequences, we will study functional gene composition of Synechococcus community in different environments.

661813.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
661813.value: Marine Synechococcus is a group of unicellular cyanobacteria that contributes a great proportion of the primary production in global oceans. Synechococcus cells span a range of different colors from blue-green to pink-orange depending on their pigment composition. Red Synechococcus dominate in oceanic waters where green and blue light penetrates deep into the water column, while green cyanobacteria dominate in turbid waters such as in estuaries, where red light prevails. Molecular phylogeny has revealed great genetic diversity amongst Synechococcus, with more than 20 distinct genetic lineages or clades.In this project we have studied phylogenetic diversity and seasonal variations of Synechococcus in the Pearl River estuary and Hong Kong coastal waters, as well as the western Pacific Ocean. Our results showed that the Hong Kong coastal water is a hot spot of high Synechococcus diversity containing almost all known clades and novel new strains. Synechococcus phylogenetic lineages and pigment genetic composition also showed a latitudinal niche differentiation. Several novel red euryhaline Synechococcus were isolated from Hong Kong waters, and their genome was sequenced and compared with oligotrophic ocean strains. Research on the genome of euryhaline PE-type Synechococcus help us to better understand how they deal with salinity changes.

662013.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
662013.value: In obese individuals, chronic elevation of circulating lipids can increase cellular fatty acid influx, induce cellular stress and lipotoxicity, and cause insulin resistance and cardiomyopathy. Synthesis and deposition of triglycerides (TAG) into lipid droplets (LDs) is a protective mechanism against excess fatty acids. LDs are evolutionarily conserved organelles where cellular fat storage is regulated in response to cell growth and energy demand. Increase in TAG can be accommodated by an increase in the number or size of LDs. Although many conserved enzymes for fatty acid metabolism and TAG synthesis have been identified, the molecular mechanisms that couple TAG synthesis with its deposition into LDs are poorly defined. Our long-term goal is to understand how fat deposition and mobilization are regulated at LDs in fed and fasted states. The objective of this proposal is to elucidate the molecular mechanisms by which a conserved protein, TMEM-SLE, facilitates LD expansion in C. elegans and mammalian cells. TMEM-SLE is found only in metazoans and it is predicted to contain multiple transmembrane alpha-helices. Our preliminary results led us to formulate a central hypothesis that TMEM-SLE can simultaneously engage the phospholipid monolayer of LD surface and the phospholipid bilayer of the endoplasmic reticulum via distinct helices and play a structural role in the assembly of a TAG synthesis protein complex. Live imaging in C. elegans revealed TMEM-SLE in discrete puncta at the ER-LD interface. TMEM-SLE physically associates with FATP1 and DGAT2, two known proteins that promote TAG synthesis and LD expansion at the ER-LD interface. The aims of the proposed experiments are to (1) define the molecular determinants of TMEM-SLE localization and the functional significance of TMEM-SLE localization; (2) determine how TMEM-SLE interacts with FATP1 and DGAT2 and whether the stability, localization or inter-molecular interactions of TMEM-SLE is nutrient dependent; (3) determine the function of TMEM-SLE in mammalian adipocytes and hepatocytes. The proposed studies will provide fundamental insights on physical and functional coupling of intracellular organelles. Specifically, we will address how the terminal step of TAG synthesis is coordinated between LDs and specialized sub-domains of the ER. Our research should reveal new regulatory nodes that limit or accommodate the flux of TAG biosynthetic intermediates, which are known to cause insulin resistance. 662113.label: Project Objectives
662113.value: Primary Objective #1: To develop, as major tools to help facilitate our study, transgenic lines of mESCs and Xenopus laevis frogs, which express the bioluminescent Ca2+-sensitive protein aequorin, or the ultra-sensitive fluorescent Ca2+ reporter, YC-Nano50. Primary Objective #2: To fully characterize the Ca2+ signalling signatures that occur during neurogenesis in both vertebrate models. A first step in this process will be to advance our understanding of Ca2+ signalling during neurogenesis in mESCs to the same level as we currently have reached for amphibians. This will include investigating the effect of noggin, chordin and BMPRs on neurogenic Ca2+ signalling, as well as the role(s) played by LTCs, ryanodine and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptors. Primary Objective #3: To investigate the role played by TRPC1 in regulating/generating Ca2+ signalling during neurogenesis, and determine the possible interactions it may have with BMPR2 at the plasma membrane. Secondary Objective #1: In the case of mESCs, where entry of Ca2+ across the plasma membrane has been reported to be mainly via SOCs rather than VOCCs [10], we plan to investigate, via a knock-down strategy, the various possible SOC channel complexes that TRPC1 might form in combination with STIM1 and ORAI1, either together or alone.

662113.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
662113.value: 神經發生初期的步驟包括神經誘導、神經祖細胞分化為神經元和神經膠質細胞的轉換。一般認為此早期神經發育過程中的時間序列於脊椎動物中廣泛保存，而控制每個步驟的因果調控網絡已有許多研究探討過。我們感興趣的是鈣離子信號所扮演多樣化的角色，通過被描述作細胞內”鈣離子信號工具箱”的特定元素組合，如何參與和相互作用的信號通路以調節神經發生中每個步驟。 我們提議把鈣離子信號在兩棲類和哺乳類動物的神經發生過程中所扮演的角色作為重點，從而確定哪些元素於這些不同的脊椎動物之間是保守的。經已有許多研究使用兩棲類胚胎去探討早期階段的神經發生。例如，有報告指出鈣離子信號對於子宮外非洲爪蟾胚胎發育時的神經誘導起著直接的作用。然而，要使用在子宮內發展的哺乳類動物胚胎去研究神經發生卻甚為困難。其中的一種解決方法是使用胚胎幹細胞。 所以，本研究的重點為結合非洲爪蟾動物帽外植體的使用，與老鼠胚胎幹細胞的基因順從程度，從以表徵鈣離子的存庫，以及鈣離子的釋放和攝取機制（即“開”和“關”的開關）之間的相互作用，如何在調節脊椎動物神經發生上擔演重要的角色。為了實現這目標，我們計劃創造一條前體內表達發光和熒光鈣離子指示劑的轉基因株系動物模型。 根據這些研究結果，我們將能夠識別哪種鈣離子介導的信號是保守於策劃神經發生的因果監管網絡中。我們假設這些保守的鈣離子工具元素可能對產生所需的信號是非常重要的，鑒定這些要素將有助於我們全面了解脊椎動物神經發生的調控。 最後，更深入的理解鈣離子於胚胎幹細胞的分化過程中所扮演的角色，首先是神經幹細胞，然後是神經元和神經膠質細胞，將有助於發展操控細胞內和細胞核內的鈣離子的技術，致使胚胎幹細胞的分化到特定的細胞命運，以及最終分化的結果比目前有更好的結果。

662113.label: Realisation of objectives
662113.value: Primary Objective #1: We have made considerable and significant progress with regards to Primary Objective #1. Xenopus laevis: We have established two populations of transgenic X. laevis, one “holding population” at the National Xenopus Resource (NXR) located at the Marine Biological Laboratory (MBL), Woods Hole, MA, USA, under the management of Dr. Marko Horb (Director of the NXL, and Co-I of GRF662113), and one “working population” at the Animal and Plant Care Facility (APCF) at HKUST. At the NXR, we have the following germline positive and functional aequorin-tested X. laevis individuals, where aequorin is either ubiquitously expressed throughout the embryo using the cytomegalovirus (CMV) as a promoter, or specifically targeted to neurons using the beta-tubulin 2 (TUB2) promoter: Adults: F0 CMV-aeq - 5 mixed; F1 TUB2-aeq -15 mixed, plus additional F1 TUB2-aeq-GFP individuals that have been sexed: 10 males and 10 females. Juveniles: At this stage of the project, we have not crossed any more frogs at the NXR due to the expenses incurred keeping them there. At the APCF, we have the following germ-line frogs that express functional aequorin: Adults –TUB2-aeq-GFP: 6 males and 6 females (offspring of founder male M1), and TUB2-aeq-GFP-aeq: 5 males and 13 females (offspring of founder male M25). These animals were shipped from the NXR to HKUST in April 2016. Juveniles: We subsequently crossed a WT male frog with a TUB2-aeq-GFP female frog (offspring of M25) and identified 32 potentially transgenic individuals from their fluorescent signal. These juvenile frogs are currently 11 months old, and there are 16 females and 16 males. When they are sexually mature, their offspring will be tested for functional aequorin. These two populations of transgenic X. laevis will serve as a resource for our own planned experiments, as well as for the international community. As required, we will ship additional frogs from the NXR to HKUST, while maintaining the holding population at the NXR. As we have many years of experience using the bioluminescent Ca2+ sensitive reporter aequorin, and due to the expenses involved (both manpower and materials) and resources required to generate transgenic lines of Xenopus, we decided to focus on aequorin, rather than the fluorescent reporter YC-Nano50. We consider that this has been a major factor in us being able to achieve this aspect of Primary Objective #1. Mouse Embryonic Stem Cells (mESCs): During the course of GRF662113 we constructed the following Sox1-GFP 46C mESC lines that expressed a variety of proteins that helped in our investigation. These were as follows: tdTomato-Apoaequorin, NanoLantern(Ca2+)150, R-GECO, G-GECO, GEM-GECO, CRISPR/Cas9-mTRPC3 knockout, hTRPC3 overexpression, mouse TRPC1 shRNA knockdown and mouse TRPC3 shRNA knockdown. For the first seven of these lines we used the EF1-alpha promoter, whereas for the shRNA knockdown lines, we used the human U6 promoter. The R-, G- and GEM-GECO are red, green and ratiometric Ca2+ indicators, respectively. We consider, therefore, that by the end of funding provided by GRF662113 we have met Objective #1 with regards to both Xenopus laevis and mESCS in that we have generated powerful models to continue this project. Primary Objective #2: At the time of grant submission, our understanding of the role(s) of Ca2+ signalling during neural induction and early neurogenesis in amphibian embryos was recognised to be more advanced than that of mammals due to the in-utero development of the latter. Thus, considering the progress made in identifying the Ca2+ signalling toolkit members that are involved in the induction, initiation, and subsequent regulation of early neurogenesis using mESCs as a model system, we believe that we have made significant strides in bringing our understanding of neurogenesis in mammals up to a level much closer to what we currently understand about amphibians. For example, we have recently published a review considering the role of Ca2+ signalling on the self-renewal and neural differentiation of ESCs (see Part C8, Publication#12), and we have presented our latest findings at numerous local and international meetings (see Part C9, Conference#19,22,23,32,33). Furthermore, we have recently submitted a research paper to Science China Life Sciences (SCLS) describing our latest data (see Part C8, Publication#10). With regards to advancing our understanding of the possible interaction between L-type voltage-activated Ca2+ channels (LTCs), BMPRs, and noggin during neurogenesis in amphibians, we demonstrated that the expression of the LTC subunit, Cav1.2 is restricted to the dorsal mesoderm and the inner layer of the ectoderm (i.e., the first ectoderm layer to be induced to a neural fate) in gastrula-stage embryos. We also report that XITRPC1 transcripts and TRPC1 protein are both expressed in the ectoderm of blastula- and gastrula-stage embryos. We also showed via MO-mediated knock-down that TRPC1 is required for the generation of the noggin-induced Ca2+ transients generated in isolated ectoderm at the start of gastrulation. These data have been presented at a number of conferences (see Part C9, Conference#13,15) and are currently being written-up as a research paper. We have also developed (and published, see Part C8, Publication#7) a hypothesis, which suggests that the signalling pathway that regulates neural determination might involve a Ca2+ influx through TRPC1 channels. We suggest that this initial rise in Ca2+ might then induce a depolarization of the plasma membrane, which in turn activates Cav1.2 channels. This subsequent influx of Ca2+ serves to multiply the signal and might result in the expression of Ca2+-sensitive neural genes and/or transcription factors. Thus, in the increasingly complex and integrated field concerned with understanding Ca2+- mediated regulation of neurogenesis, we believe that we have made a significant contribution in identifying several of the Ca2+ signalling tool-kit members responsible for this process in both amphibians and mammals. Primary Objective #3: Out of the other Ca2+ toolkit members that might be involved in neural induction and early neurogenesis, we were particularly interested in the role played by TRPC channels as well as their possible interaction with BMPRs. One of the major findings to emerge from our study is that in amphibians, TRPC1 appears to be most involved in generating (in association with other toolkit members) the required Ca2+ transients, whereas in mammals (at least in mESCs), TRPC3 appears to be the major player involved. This might reflect the finding that amphibians appear to rely on extracellular Ca2+ crossing the plasma membrane to generate their neurogenic signals, whereas mammals rely more on Ca2+ released from intracellular stores. We are currently preparing a review about this significant and intriguing difference. There is a degree of overlap between Primary Objectives #2 and #3. Thus some aspects of our realization of Primary Objective #3 are covered in our response to #2. Secondary Objective #1: Unknown to us, between submitting GRF662113 and being awarded funds to carry out the work, Dr. Helen Hao (the postdoc hired with funds from GRF662113), had already knocked-down (KD) STIM1 and Orai1 in mESCs using shRNAs during her PhD thesis. In these KD mESC lines, SOCE was impaired when compared with Scr control cells. These results have already been published (Hao et al (2014) Stem Cell Research 12:452-446). Furthermore, Hao et al also reported that shRNA-mediated KD of TRPC1 had no significant effect on Ca2+ entry into mESCs. As this objective was considered to be a Secondary Objective, and as the work had been published, we focused on the three Primary Objectives of the proposal.

662113.label: Major findings and research outcome
662113.value: As mentioned previously, one of the major findings to emerge from our study is that in amphibians it is TRPC1 that appears to be most involved in generating (in association with other Ca2+ toolkit members) the required Ca2+ transients required for neural induction, whereas in mammals (at least in mESCs), TRPC3 appears to be the major player involved. This might reflect the finding that amphibians appear to rely on extracellular Ca2+ crossing the plasma membrane to generate their neurogenic signals, whereas mammals tend to rely on Ca2+ released from intracellular stores. It will take further studies and comparisons between other amphibian and mammalian species to establish if this is a general feature. Furthermore, during the course of the funding period we also confirmed the important interplay between the various Ca2+ toolkit elements (in both amphibians and mESCs) that contribute to the complex signalling networks that regulate neural induction and early neurogenesis. There is clearly much more to discover before we fully understand these essential developmental processes. Our findings are reflected in the following output that resulted from this funding: 1. 662113.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
662113.value: We consider that with the establishment of the transgenic CMV-aeq-GFP and TUB2-aeq-GFP lines at the NXR and APCF, we are poised for the next phase of this long-term research project. This will focus on using the transgenic models to further and extend the research goals initially outlined in GRF662113. To this end, we plan to apply for a new GRF grant to continue this project. We also believe that what we have achieved (and the experienced gained) with regards to the other objectives outlined in GRF662113 will provide a solid foundation on which to build a new application. Our collaboration with Drs Moreau and Leclerc in Toulouse, and Dr Marko Horb at the NXR, remain strong and active, and thus bodes well for our future productivity. Furthermore, we just received internal funding from HKUST to purchase a second Andor iXon 897 back-illuminated EMCCD camera, which we are now installing on one of our Photon Imaging Microscopes (PIMs). This will help to double our potential bioluminescent imaging output. We have also recently purchased (one again via internal HKUST funding) a Lonza AAB-1001Nucleofector 2B electroporator and preliminary tests have shown that it is most suitable for electroporating aequorin plasmids into mESCs.

662113.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
662113.value: Investigating the early signalling events that regulate the induction and differentiation of neural cells that form our central nervous system (CNS) is of paramount importance for extending our understanding of diseases associated with its degeneration or damage, and for developing possible therapies for its regeneration/repair. A key component in the highly integrated signalling networks that regulate neurogenesis is the Ca2+ ion, the so-called universal second messenger. Cells have the potential, especially during early development, to assemble a variety of elements from what has been called a “Ca2+ signalling toolkit,” which allows them to generate specific signalling signatures that help undifferentiated cells to develop into a particular cell type, be it a heart or liver cell, or indeed a cell in the CNS, such as a neuron or glia. Identifying the Ca2+ toolkit elements (receptors, channels, buffers or pumps) involved in the differentiation of the CNS (e.g., TRPCs, BMPRs, LTCs, IP3Rs, and RyRs), will provide us with the opportunity to identify malfunctioning components in the Ca2+ signalling pathways, to develop means of compensating for the resulting deleterious effects, and to design drugs to help treat such malfunctions. With the increasing prevalence of neurodegenerative diseases, this research is of great socioeconomic value.

662213.label: Project Objectives
662213.value: To study the balance of CDK1 inhibitory phosphorylation in checkpoint maintenance and recovery • Once DNA damage is repaired, the checkpoint has to be silenced to allow the cell cycle to resume. Although inhibitory phosphorylation of CDK1 is now firmly established as a key mechanism for normal cell cycle control and checkpoint maintenance, several outstanding issues continue to intrigue and baffle. Using specific inhibitors to uncouple the CDK1 autocatalytic feedback loops, we aim to demarcate the contribution of different kinases and CDC25 isoforms during both checkpoint maintenance and after the checkpoint is abrogated. To identify novel players in checkpoint recovery pathways • An emerging concept is that not all regulators of the G2–M transition are involved in checkpoint recovery, and vice versa. Using a target screening approach, we plan to discover novel components that affect checkpoint recovery. Knockdown of key components should accelerate or delay entry into mitosis after checkpoint silencing. Preliminary testing indicates that these experiments should yield interesting and unexpected checkpoint-silencing components and define new research directions. To elucidate if distinct mechanisms are involved in checkpoint abrogation and adaptation • It is likely that distinct regulators are involved in normal checkpoint recovery, checkpoint adaptation, and forced checkpoint silencing. These various processes of checkpoint recovery have significantly different outcome and implication in vivo. Using multiple approaches that include the use of checkpoint defective cells lacking ATM or Artemis, we plan to elucidate the mechanisms in which the checkpoint is silenced under physiological and non-physiological conditions. To investigate the translational potential of checkpoint abrogation on hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) • A potential anti-cancer therapy approach involves DNA damage followed by checkpoint abrogation. HCC and NPC provide a unique opportunity for translational studies of this approach. These projects aim to investigate if there is synergism between radiotherapy and checkpoint abrogating agents on these cancers. Cell line and animal studies will be used to test if the combination treatment triggers higher cytotoxicity in cancer cells than in normal cells. In addition, whether the checkpoint components are biomarkers or of prognostic value, and whether they affect checkpoint control in these cancers will also be investigated.

662213.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
662213.value: DNA double-strand break is one of the most harmful DNA lesions in human cells. Checkpoint mechanisms are essential for providing opportunities to repair damaged DNA. Once repair is completed, the checkpoint has to be silenced to allow the cell cycle to resume. Although remarkable progress has been made in our understanding of individual checkpoint pathways, many outstanding basic issues concerning checkpoint recovery remain to be deciphered. This project aims to investigate both basic and translational aspects of checkpoint recovery. Experiments are designed to uncover the detailed mechanisms that balance the CDK1 inhibitory phosphorylation in checkpoint maintenance and recovery. The functions and regulation of several established players including MYT1, WEE1, and CDC25 will be investigated. Moreover, we also aim to discover new components of the checkpoint recovery network. As checkpoint silencing under physiological conditions and after checkpoint abrogation have significantly different outcome and implication in vivo, we plan to establish the distinct mechanisms involved in silencing the checkpoint under different conditions. Remarkably, checkpoint abrogation is also used as a chemotherapeutic approach to eliminate cancer cells by mitotic catastrophe. Thus emphasis is also placed on the translational aspects of checkpoint abrogation, in particular the opportunities provided by cancers including hepatocellular carcinoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Collectively, a more complete understanding of checkpoint recovery should have far-reaching implications for basic and translational research. DNA雙鏈斷裂是對人類細胞傷害最大的DNA損傷。檢查點是修復受損DNA的必要機制。在完成修復後，檢查點需要被關上，以恢復細胞週期的運轉。雖然在個別檢查點的傳導途徑已經取得了確切的理解，但是在恢復檢查點的傳導途徑上仍然有很多基本問題還未被詮釋。本項目主要在基礎研究和轉化研究層面上對恢復檢查點的機制作出考證。其中的實驗會涵蓋CDK1的抑制磷酸化，在維持和恢復檢查點上如何取得平衡的機制。亦會對WEE1， MYT1，和CDC25這幾個經典因素的功能和調控進行研究。此外，我們會尋找在恢復檢查點途徑網絡上的新成員。另外，由於在生理條件下和壓制檢查點後的檢查點恢復有不同的結果及影響，我們計劃找出其背後的機制。更重要的是，壓制檢查點亦在用作引發有絲分裂災難以消除癌細胞的化療方法。因此，本項目亦會強調對肝癌和鼻咽癌的化療方法上的轉化研究。總括而言，對檢查點恢復有一個更深入的理解應當對基礎和轉化研究可以產生深遠的影響。

662213.label: Realisation of objectives
662213.value: Understanding CDK1 inhibitory phosphorylation in DNA damage checkpoint Once DNA damage is repaired, the checkpoint has to be silenced to allow the cell cycle to resume. To mimic checkpoint recovery, we have used a CHK1 inhibitor and a WEE1 inhibitor to bypass the checkpoint, forcing the damaged cells into mitosis. Given the current paradigm that DNA damage checkpoint is believed to act on both CDC25 and WEE1/MYT1, it is paradoxical that inhibition of WEE1 alone can lead to CDK1 activation, as CDC25 is still being inactivated by CHK1/CHK2 (Mak et al., 2014; 2015). We have now established that in the presence of WEE1 inhibitor, the newly synthesized cyclin B1 was responsible for mitotic entry. As WEE1 was inhibited, these newly synthesized cyclin B1 formed complexes with CDK1 and could not be turned off by WEE1-dependent phosphorylation. These newly made cyclin B1 then entered the nucleus to drive mitosis. Using a PLK1 inhibitor, we further found that nuclear accumulation of this population of cyclin B1 was dependent on PLK1 activity. Hence this also explained why the checkpoint abrogation by WEE1 inhibitor was abolished by PLK1 inhibitor. Using conditional cyclin A-knockout cells, we further discovered that WEE1 inhibitor-mediated checkpoint abrogation requires cyclin A (manuscript in preparation). Taken together, these mechanistic studies revealed a complex picture of how mitotic entry is driven after the DNA damage checkpoint is overcome. Checkpoint recovery: identification of novel players By using a target siRNA library to knockdown different components that known to regulate G2–M, we found that several potential regulators could accelerate or delay entry into mitosis after checkpoint silencing. These include known regulators of checkpoint recovery such as PLK1 and Aurora A, and previously unrecognized players such as MASTL and salt-inducible kinase 3 (SIK3). The kinase MASTL promotes normal G2–mitosis transition by inhibiting PP2A via ARPP19 and ENSA. We demonstrated that MASTL is critical for maintaining genome integrity after DNA damage. Although MASTL did not affect the activation of DNA damage responses and subsequent repair, it determined the timing of entry into mitosis and the subsequent fate of the recovering cells. These results established that precise control of MASTL is essential to couple DNA damage to mitosis through the rate of mitotic entry and APC/C regulation (Wong et al., 2016). How cells are killed during mitosis (mitotic catastrophe) once they recover from checkpoint is an important issue to understand. Many mitotic kinases are both critical for maintaining genome stability and are important targets for anticancer therapies. We provided evidence that SIK3, an AMPK-related kinase, is important for mitosis to occur properly in mammalian cells. Downregulation of SIK3 resulted in an extension of mitosis did not affect the DNA damage checkpoint. Moreover, both mitotic arrest and cell death caused by spindle poisons or pharmacological inhibition of mitotic kinases including Aurora A, Aurora B, and PLK1 were enhanced after SIK3 depletion. These results establish the importance of SIK3 as a mitotic regulator and underscore the potential of SIK3 as a druggable antimitotic target (Chen et al., 2014). Another key family of players in mitotic catastrophe are the anti-apoptotic proteins. We performed a systematic study to determine which members of the anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family are involved in determining the duration of mitotic block before cell death. Depletion of several anti-apoptotic BCL-2-like proteins significantly shortened the time before apoptosis. Among these proteins, BCL-W has not been previously characterized to play a role in mitotic cell death. Although the expression of BCL-W remained constant during mitotic block, it varied significantly between different cell lines. Disruption of the BCL-W gene with CRISPR-Cas9 speeded up mitotic cell death. Conversely, overexpression of BCL-W delayed mitotic cell death, extending the mitotic block to allow mitotic slippage. These results showed that BCL-W contributes to the threshold of anti-apoptotic activity during mitosis (Huang et al., 2016). Mechanism of checkpoint abrogation versus adaptation It is likely that distinct regulators are involved in normal checkpoint recovery, checkpoint adaptation, and forced checkpoint silencing. These various processes of checkpoint recovery have significantly different outcome and implication in vivo. We found that in addition of modulating the timing of mitosis after checkpoint abrogation, MASTL also affect checkpoint adaptation. Using long term live-cell imaging (>48 h) of cells expressing either histone-GFP markers or the FUCCI cell cycle reporter, we have tracked checkpoint adaptation after DNA damage. For example, we found that a constitutively active mutant of MASTL accelerated checkpoint recovery in the absence of checkpoint abrogator. Conversely, knockdown of MASTL delayed checkpoint recovery. More interestingly, the APC/C (an ubiquitin ligase that drives mitotic exit) was activated in MASTL-depleted cells after DNA damage. As this occurred in the absence of mitosis, this mechanism may be responsible for genome instability after downregulation of MASTL (Wong et al., 2016). Checkpoint abrogation: translational potential A potential anticancer therapy approach involves DNA damage followed by checkpoint abrogation. As radiotherapy is the primary treatment for NPC, this offers a rationale to investigate if uncoupling the DNA damage responses can sensitize this cancer type. The G2 DNA damage checkpoint is controlled by three levels of kinases: ATM/ATR, which phosphorylates CHK1/CHK2, which in turn phosphorylates WEE1. A number of small molecule inhibitors have been developed against these kinases as potential therapeutic agents. We demonstrated that compare to that in immortalized nasopharyngeal epithelial cells, ATR, CHK1, and WEE1 were overexpressed in NPC cell lines. Inhibitors of these kinases were unable to promote extensive mitotic catastrophe in IR-treated cells, indicating that they are not very effective radiosensitizer for this cancer. In the absence of prior irradiation, however, mitotic catastrophe could be induced with inhibitors against CHK1 or WEE1. Targeting CHK1 and WEE1 together induced more extensive mitotic catastrophe than the individual components alone. Taken together, our results show that NPC cells depend on CHK1 and WEE1 activity for growth and that inhibitors of these kinases may serve as potential therapeutics for NPC (Mak et al., 2015). Unexpectedly, partial inhibition of WEE1 and CHK1 had the opposite effect of accelerating the cell cycle without inducing apoptosis, thereby increasing the overall cell proliferation. This was also corroborated by the finding that cell proliferation was enhanced by kinase-inactive versions of WEE1. We demonstrated that these potential limitations of the inhibitors could be overcome by targeting more than one components of the ATR–CHK1–WEE1 simultaneously. These observations reveal insights into the complex responses to pharmacological inactivation of the ATR–CHK1–WEE1 axis (Mak et al., 2014). Mitosis is choreographed by a number of protein kinases including PLK1 and Aurora kinases. As these kinases are frequently dysregulated in cancers, small-molecule inhibitors have been developed for targeted anticancer therapies. Using concentrations of inhibitors that did not induce severe mitotic defects on their own, we found that both the metaphase arrest and mitotic slippage induced by inhibitors targeting Aurora A and Aurora B were enhanced by a PLK1 inhibitor. We found that PLK1 is overexpressed in NPC. Cells were more sensitive to PLK1 inhibitor as a single agent or co-inhibition with Aurora kinases than normal cells. These observations underscore the mechanism and potential benefits of targeting PLK1 and Aurora kinases to induce mitotic catastrophe in cancer cells (Li et al., 2015).

662213.label: Major findings and research outcome
662213.value: We have performed mechanistic studies on checkpoint abrogation, which revealed a complex picture of the ATM/ATR-CHK1/2-WEE1 axis is regulated and how mitotic entry is driven after the DNA damage checkpoint is overcome (Mak et al., 2014; 2015). We further identified several potential regulators affect either the entry into mitosis after checkpoint silencing or the subsequent mitotic catastrophe. These include known regulators of checkpoint recovery such as PLK1, Aurora A (Li et al., 2015), SGO1 (Wong et al., 2015), and previously unrecognized players such as MASTL (Wong et al., 2016), SIK3 (Chen et al., 2014), BCL-W (Huang et al., 2016), and TRIP13 (Ma et al., 2016). Our studies also substantiate the idea that distinct regulators are involved in normal checkpoint recovery, checkpoint adaptation, and forced checkpoint silencing. Finally, we demonstrated that checkpoint abrogators and several mitotic kinases are potential drug targets, acting as radiosensitizers in cancers including nasopharyngeal carcinoma (Mak et al., 2014; 2015; Ma et al., 2014; Li et al. 2015).

662213.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
662213.value: Several potential drug targets have been characterized or newly discovered to be important for either checkpoint abrogation or mitotic catastrophe. These include classic checkpoint components including, ATM, ATR, CHK1, CHK2, and WEE1, as well as mitotic regulators including MASTL, SGO1, PLK1, and Aurora kinases. Further understanding of their network of regulators and substrates will extend our understanding of this important subject. Further development of drugs against these targets will have far-reaching implications for translational research for many types of cancer.

662213.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
662213.value: The DNA damage checkpoint arrests cells in G2 phase and is critical for the maintenance of genome stability. Abrogation of the checkpoint induces mitotic catastrophe, a common strategy for cancer therapies. This project elucidated several basic and translational aspects of checkpoint abrogation to mitotic catastrophe. We have elucidated that the mechanistic basis of how the checkpoint is maintained after DNA damage. Several novel players of the checkpoint were discovered, including MASTL and SIK3. We also discovered that drugs that inhibit components of the G2 DNA damage checkpoint (including ATM, ATR, CHK1/2, and WEE1) promoted mitotic catastrophe in cancers including nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Drugs that target mitosis also enhanced the cancer cell killing affect after the DNA damage checkpoint is abrogated. Further development of drugs against these targets will have far-reaching implications for translational research for many types of cancer.

662413.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
662413.value: 大部分海洋底栖动物都具有复杂的生活史，包括营浮游生活的幼体和营固着生活的成体两个阶段。这种由幼体附着生活向成体固着生活不可逆的转变称为幼体附着变态，包括附着和变态两个部分。幼体附着变态的发生需经历如下三个阶段：幼体对环境因素进行探测识别、信号转导通路对探知的信号进行级联放大和基因转录和蛋白表达调控产生生理变化。正是在附着变态这个过程中，很多污损无脊椎动物会聚集性附着、侵蚀船体等设备或工程。这些位于水面以下的生物聚集体也因此被称为“生物污损”，对海洋产业造成巨大的经济损失。了解污损生物的附着变态机制，并进一步研发新的、环境友好型抗污损试剂是相关科研人员的最终目标。 过去十年，我们的研究主要集中在藤壶、管虫和苔藓虫等污损生物附着变态的分子机制上。特别是如下三个方面的研究，我们已经积累了丰硕的研究成果。1）诱导生物附着变态的环境因素；2）调节幼体附着变态的功能基因；3）诱导或抑制附着变态的天然活性产物的分离鉴定和作用机制。但是，对于附着变态过程中起信号转导作用的内源性分子的研究却一直很少，部分原因在于缺乏幼体生态学和分子生物学等多学科交叉整合分析的能力。近期，我们研究组将幼体生态学、分子生物学和生物信息学研究人员有机整合到一起，并成功建立了“组学”（转录组学和蛋白组学）研究平台。通过该平台，我们获得了高信息量的“组学”数据库。这将有助于我们深入研究藤壶、管虫和苔藓虫附着变态的分子机制，进行弥补这方面研究的不足。 通过“组学”研究的近期成果，我们发现在幼体附着变态前后，一些新的蛋白会表达；但是在附着变态发生转变的短时间内，新蛋白的合成表达不太可能是调控这一过程的主要机制。另外一种可能，幼体通过蛋白翻译后修饰来进行信号转导，并调控之后的附着变态。根据我们之前“比较组学”研究获得的初步结果，以及接下来的基因转录和蛋白表达分析，加之幼体附着能力测试，我们发现了一些可能参与幼体附着变态的信号转导通路。现在，我们需要做的是对这些信号通路的功能作用以及它们之间可能存在的相互关联进行研究。本研究计划假设幼体通过一氧化氮通路传递外部信号，并通过p38 MAPK通路来调控其附着变态。为验证这一假设，本计划拟进行如下研究：1）p38 MAPK在幼体附着变态过程中的直接调节作用；2）寻找p38 MAPK与幼体附着变态直接相关的下游底物；3）以重要的污损生物兼模式生物纹藤壶为对象，研究p38 MAPK和一氧化氮通路之间可能存在的相互关联。这一系列实验旨在弄清促使和调节幼体附着变态的分子信号通路网络。结合我们近期已经获得的一些初步研究结果，这一计划将有助于我们深入了解藤壶的附着变态机制，进而为新的抗生物污损试剂的研发提供资料。

662413.label: Realisation of objectives
662413.value: To realize the first objective, we first cloned the full-length coding sequence of the MEK3 in the barnacle. Briefly, based on the partial sequence of the homologue in our A. amphitrite database, we designed specific primers and used them to clone the target gene from barnacle cDNA using 5’race and 3’race methods. Based on the full-length coding sequence, we characterized the MEK3 sequence in the barnacle and compared the sequence with that of MEK3 in other species, such as humans and Drosophila, to determine the degree of conservation of the MEK3 protein in A. amphitrite. A phylogenetic tree was constructed by the maximum likelihood statistical method with MEGA software to understand the possible evolutionary relationships among MAPK kinases. Then, we confirmed the kinase-substrate interaction by in vitro kinase assay. The dominant-activated and dominant-negative mutants of MEK3 in A. amphitrite were generated by replacing Ser and Thr residues, which corresponded to Ser-189 and Thr-193 for MEK3 in humans, with Glu and Ala residues, respectively [67]. Pure recombinant wild-type (WT) MEK3 with its various mutants and WT p38 MAPK protein were obtained in an E. coli over-expression system. The in vitro kinase assay was performed, and the results were examined by autoradiography after sodium dodecyl sulfatepolyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) to determine whether the MEK3 can really and directly activate p38 MAPK in A. amphitrite. We then examined whether the phosphorylation of p38 MAPK by MEK3 in A. amphitrite occurred. Recombinant proteins of WT p38 MAPK and its various mutants were obtained by over-expression in E. coli. and then used to perform the kinase assay with dominant-active mutants of MEK3 in A. amphitrite. The results from mutants with one or two mutations were compared with the WT p38 MAPK. Because there were two other members of the MAPK family including ERK and JNK in our barnacle transcriptome database, it was necessary to examine whether the MEK3 was specific to p38 MAPK in A. amphitrite. We first cloned the full-length coding sequence of ERK and JNK using the method mentioned above, generated the recombinant proteins of ERK and JNK from E. coli, and then used them with p38 MAPK as substrates for in vitro kinase assay to examine the specificity of the regulating kinase. We then examined whether the MEK3 in the barnacle activated p38 MAPK in vivo and was involved in larval settlement. To achieve this goal, we measured the pp38 MAPK and phosphor-MEK3 (pMEK3) levels to determine whether pp38 MAPK and pMEK3 had similar expression patterns during larval development. Our results showed that pp38 MAPK was expressed at the highest level in the cypris stage among all developmental stages of A. amphitrite. We conducted immnunoprecipitation (IP) assay using a barnacle extract and then identified the the target protein. We also used Western blotting to determine the protein level of pMEK3 in cyprids treated with adult an barnacle extract and used the pMEK3 antibody and found that the MEK3 in A. amphitrite was involved in cypris response to the adult barnacle extract. To realize the second objective (identification of p38 MAPK substrate related to larval settlement), we carried out a substrate screening experiment. First, we conducted experiments at 40C to minimize the phosphorylation and used the kinase-dead mutant of p38 MAPK by replacing the Thr and Tyr on the TGY motif with Ala and Phe, respectively. Both the kinase-dead mutant of p38 MAPK and the WT were cloned into pGEX vector and over-expressed in E. coli. The recombinant glutatione S-transferase (GST)-tagged p38MAPK WT and mutant proteins were used as bait to perform pull-down assay from a cypris extract to identify the proteins associated with p38 MAPK. The beads incubated with GST protein were used for negative control. The isolated proteins were retrieved and subjected to SDS-PAGE. The bands appearing only in p38 MAPK or its mutant samples, but not in the control samples, were extracted for identification by mass spectrometry (Zhang et al. 2012). To identify the substrate of p38 MAPK in A. amphitrite, cyprids were treated with SB203580, and those not treated with this inhibitor served as the controls. Both the treated and untreated cyprids were collected for protein extraction and proteomic analysis. Differentially expressed phosphoproteins were then selected and identified. To make sure the effect due to SB203580 treatment was not a side effect, we used the second p38 MAPK inhibitor, SB202190 in parallel. Furthermore, to confirm whether the two compounds indeed inhibited p38 MAPK activity, we performed in vitro kinase assay with or without these two compounds using the p38 MAP kinase assay kit. To identify the non-conserved substrate of p38 MAPK, we constructed a barnacle cDNA library expressed in yeast which served as the prey while p38 MAPK WT and kinase-dead p38 MAPK (T181A/Y183F) were cloned into pGBKT7 DNA-BD vector and transformed into yeast AH109. To confirm the kinase-substrate interaction, in vitro kinase assays were performed as described above. The phosphorylation site on the p38 MAPK was determined by generating various mutants. Based on the substrate gene sequence, digoxigenin (DIG)-labeled antisense and sense RNA probes were prepared and used during hybridization. For immunostaining, the recombinant his-tag protein was used as an antigen and injected into rabbits. The GST-tagged protein was used to purify the particular antibody from serum. After identification of the phosphorylation site in the substrate, a specific phosphorylation substrate antibody was generated. Finally, we used Western blot to examine the pp38 MAPK and phospho-substrate protein levels after treating the cyprids with an adult barnacle extract. To realize the third objective (cross-talking between NO pathway and p38 MAPK pathway), we conducted the following experiments. First, we treated cyprids with another NOS inhibitor, SMIS (S-methylisothiourea sulfate), and then used Western blot to examine the pp38 MAPK protein level with the pp38 antibody. To further prove that the NO level in larvae affects p38 MAPK activity, we treated cyprids with NO donor SNP (sodium nitroprusside dehydrate) that releases NO in vivo and then measured the pp38 MAPK level. However, the results have not been very consistent. Then, we obtained the antibody that recognized the pMEK3 in A. amphitrite. We used the antibody to measure the pMEK3 level in larvae after treating cyprids with NO donor and NOS inhibitors. Furthermore, we checked if the NO affected thep38 MAPK through cGMP by comparative proteomic analysis and Western blotting with their respective antibodies after treating cyprids with guanylate cyclase inhibitors (ODQ, 6-anilino-5,8-quinolinedione (LY83583)) and activators (A350619,41-2272). Finally, we examined the pp38 MAPK and pMEK3 protein levels by Western blotting using their respective antibodies in larvae pretreated with NO synthesis inhibitors and then with the adult barnacle extracts.

662413.label: Major findings and research outcome
662413.value: In the present study, we tested our working hypothesis that the nitric oxide (NO) pathway responding to external signal regulates barnacle larval settlement mediated by activation of an p38 MAPK in a barnacle species, Balanus amphitrite. We demonstrated that 1) the p38 MAPK pathway regulated the larval settlement of B. amphitrite (Zhang et al. 2013). To study the signaling pathway associated with p38MAPK during larval settlement, we sought to identify the upstream kinase of p38MAPK. Three MKKs (MKK3, MKK4 and MKK7) and three MAPKs (p38MAPK, ERK and JNK) in A. amphitrite were cloned and recombinantly expressed. MKK3, but not MKK4 or MKK7, phosphorylated p38MAPK. Furthermore, MKK3 activity was specific to p38MAPK, as it did not phosphorylate ERK or JNK. Consistent with the patterns of p38MAPK and phospho-p38MAPK (pp38MAPK), pMKK3 and MKK3 mainly localized to the antennules of the cyprids. Western blot analysis revealed that pMKK3 levels, like pp38MAPK levels, were elevated at the cyprid stage. Moreover, pMKK3 levels increased after treatment with adult barnacle crude extracts. 2) P38 MAPPK cross-talks with the NF-kB pathway (Zhang et al. 2015, Zhang G's PhD thesis). We applied label-free proteomics to analyze changes in the proteome of cyprids treated with a p38 MAPK inhibitor and found that the expression levels of 80 proteins were significantly modified (p < 0.05) and nine pathways were significantly enriched. Further analysis revealed that p38 MAPK might regulate the energy supply and metamorphosis. Two potential regulatory proteins, CUBserine protease and PKAα, were both down-regulated in expression. Importantly, they were co-localized with the neuron transmitter serotonin, suggesting that the CUBserine protease was present in the neural system. PKAα was highly expressed during the cyprid and juvenile stages, and it was co-localized with phospho-p38 MAPK (pp38 MAPK) to the cement gland, suggesting that PKAα might have some functions in cement glands. 3) there was cross talk between p38 MAPK and NO/cGMP pathways (Zhang Y et al. 2012 Zhang G et al. 2015). We analyzed changes in the proteome of A. amphitrite cyprids in response to different concentrations of the NO donor sodium nitroprusside. The expression of 106 proteins differed in all three treatments. These differentially expressed proteins were assigned to 13 pathways. SNP treatment stimulated the expression of heat shock proteins and arginine kinase, which are functionally related to NO synthases, suggesting NO/cGMP pathways cross-talk with a number of other pathways (including p38 MAPK pathways, NF-kB pathway, and cGMP/AMP pathway).

662413.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
662413.value: In this project, we found that a number of pathways are involved in the larval settlement of barnacles but it remains unclear how these pathways interact. A network analysis approach may be required to decipher the roles of particular pathways in larval settlement. We may conduct further studies on individual pathways first before working on the network. Comparative larval transcriptomics and proteomics have provided substantial information on proteins and genes involved in larval settlement. We will take advantage of proteomic and transcriptomic databases developed in house in the future.

662413.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
662413.value: Most marine animals that attach to both the man-made or natural surfaces have a complex life cycle that consists of a free-swimming larval stage and a sessile juvenile/adult stage. The transition between these two entirely different life stages, called larval settlement (including both larval attachment and metamorphosis), is directed and controlled by environmental cues. It is accomplished through the recognition of environmental cues, amplification of those cues through signal transduction pathways, and subsequent physiological alterations mediated by differential gene expression and protein regulation. It is during this critical period that the larvae of many fouling invertebrate species gregariously attach to man-made structures such as ship hulls. The accumulation of these species on underwater surfaces, known as biofouling, causes great economic loss to marine industries. Identification of the key signaling molecules involved in larval settlement, their interaction (cross talk), networks, and pathways will facilitate the design of targeted antifouling strategies and the development of novel, environmentally friendly antifouling solutions.

662513.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
662513.value: Cancer is a leading cause of death worldwide and early diagnosis of cancer is of crucial importance in cancer treatment and management. Here, we propose a research project aiming to explore the diagnostic value of keratin fluorescence for noninvasive and early detection of squamous epithelial cancer. Keratin, a fibrous and insoluble protein in cells, constitutes type I and II intermediate filaments with at least 20 subtypes, named keratins 1–20. Certain keratin subtypes are only expressed in normal human tissues, but not in diseased ones, and vice versa. Various tissues have been subclassified according to their keratin profiles. Since keratin expression varies so greatly among different tissues, they have been widely used in the fingerprinting of various cancers. Human tissues have multi-layered structures. Over 90% of early cancers originate from the epithelium, the most superficial tissue layer. Recently, the PI’s group discovered that there is a large aggregation of keratin filaments in the topmost epithelial layer, which, importantly, emits strong keratin fluorescence. Our preliminary study indicated that keratin profile and expression in tissue can be determined based on the spectral and temporal characteristics of fluorescence of individual keratin subtypes. Furthermore, the temporal characteristics of keratin fluorescence measured from animal model in vivo showed strong correlation with the precancer development in epithelial layer. Because keratin naturally exists in cells of human tissues and tissue fluorescence can be measured remotely, it can potentially be used for non-invasive diagnosis of early cancer development in squamous epithelium. In the proposed research, we will use hamster cheek pouches, the commonly used model for the human squamous epithelium, to study keratin fluorescence and profiles of normal and precancerous epithelial tissues at different stages. The normal and precancerous epithelial tissues will be analyzed by immunohistochemical staining methods with available antibodies for specific keratins for keratin profiling. The keratin profiles from the panel of normal immortalized epithelial cell lines and their matched cancer cell lines will serve as a baseline for further analysis of clinical specimens. Success of the proposed research will develop an insightful understanding of diagnostic value of keratin fluorescence and lead to large scale study of early cancer diagnosis of human squamous epithelial cancers using keratin fluorescence signals. This is a re-submitted proposal. The reviewers’ major comments and the detailed responses to the comments are presented in section 6. The total requested funding for the proposed research is HK$1,600,000 (US$205,000). 在全球範圍內，癌症是導致人類死亡的最主要原因，癌症早期診斷對癌症控制和治療至關重要。我們在本文中提出了一個嶄新的研究計劃，旨在通過角蛋白熒光這種無創的方法，探索其在早期發現鱗狀上皮癌的診斷價值。 在細胞中，角蛋白是一種不溶性的纖維蛋白， 是中間纖維的一類，分為I和II型，包括至少20個亞型，命名為角蛋白1-20 。 某些特定的角蛋白亞型只在正常人體組織中表達，但在患病的組織中不表達；類似的，另外一些特定的角蛋白亞型只在患病的組織中表達但是在正常的組織中不表達。根據角蛋白在組織中亞型的不同，組織也可以被分成不同的種類。由於角蛋白在不同的組織中表達差異性很大，它們已經被廣泛使用去診斷各種癌症。人體組織一般呈現多層結構，超過90％的早期癌症起源於皮膚最淺表的上皮組織。最近，PI的研究小組發現，上皮組織的最上層覆蓋有大量的能發出熒光的角質蛋白纖維。 我們的初步研究表明，組織中角蛋白的組成和表達可以根據單個角蛋白亞型在頻域和時域上的螢光特徵加以區分。此外，從活體動物模型中測量的角蛋白熒光時域特徵與發生於上皮細胞層的早期癌症有很強的相關性。因為角蛋白天然存在於人體組織的細胞並且組織熒光可以遠程測量，它有可能被用於非侵入式早期鱗狀上皮癌症的檢測。 在提議的研究中，我們將使用常用的人類的鱗狀上皮模型——倉鼠頰囊模型，來研究上皮組織正常情況及早期癌變不同時期角蛋白的螢光及其組成。我們將使用免疫組織化學染色方法，通過現有的特定角蛋白抗體來分析正常和早期癌症的的上皮組織中角蛋白的組成。正常永生化上皮細胞株和其相應的腫瘤細胞株庫中的角蛋白組成將作為基準，進一步分析臨床樣本。提議研究的成果， 將深入瞭解角蛋白螢光診斷價值， 並且引導大規模使用角蛋白螢光早期檢測人類鱗狀上皮癌的研究。

662513.label: Realisation of objectives
662513.value: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), arising from various human anatomic sites, including esophagus, oral cavity, lung, and cervix, is the most common cancer capable of metastatic spread worldwide. Early diagnosis and localization of SCC is of crucial importance in cancer treatment and management. In this research project, we aimed to explore the diagnostic value of keratin fluorescence for noninvasive and early detection of squamous epithelial cancer. Particularly, we developed a multi-channel time-correlated single photon counting (TCSPC) detection technique and multi-color excitation sources. By integrating the advanced detection and excitation technology with a home-made two-photon microscope system, we achieved in vivo measurements of multiple endogenous nonlinear optical (NLO) signals from the epithelial tissue (epithelium of the oral cavity and skin) of small animal models (hamster and mouse) in time and spectral domains simultaneously. We explored diagnostic utility of this multimodal NLO microscope technology for noninvasive detection of squamous epithelial precancer in vivo. The induced precancer lesions at hamster cheek pouch was used as an animal model of carcinogenesis. The NLO microscope system employed was equipped with the ability to collect multiple tissue endogenous NLO signals such as the two photon excited fluorescence (TPEF) of keratin, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH), flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), collagen, hemoglobin and tryptophan, and the second harmonic generation (SHG) of collagen in spectral and time domains simultaneously. High resolution label-free NLO images were acquired from stratum corneum, stratum granulosum-stratum basale, and stroma for all tissue measurement sites. Our work demonstrated for the first time (to our knowledge) that multicolor excitation based multimodal NLO microscopy system produced a great wealth of diagnostic information ranging from tissue architecture, cellular/subcellular morphology, to biochemical information emanating from different stratified tissue depths. In particular, our results elucidated stratum corneum to contain significant diagnostic information for identifying precancers in vivo. The previous work conducted by other groups and PI’s group have demonstrated the diagnostic values of various endogenous optical signals from tissue, such as the autofluorescence of keratin, NADH, FAD, collagen, and tryptophan, and the SHG of collagen. However, these signals are distributed in different layers of superficial tissue. Our study showed that the diagnostic information from the different tissue layers can be effectively integrated to provide high performance diagnostic algorithm for identifying squamous epithelial precancer. These results affirm the efficacy of the novel multi-wavelength excitation and detection to produce a wide range of TPEF and SHG signals for clinical squamous premalignancy diagnosis application in vivo. We further demonstrated that the two-photon optical spectroscopy and microscopy can provide important biochemical and morphological information on epithelial tissue where most of precancers originated. Our findings revealed that the squamous epithelium is generally more or less keratinized. However, although the keratin fluorescence in the topmost keratinizing layer with 20-50µm thickness provides diagnostic information, it causes serious interference in seeking the correlation between other endogenous optical signals and tissue pathology because the keratin fluorescence overlap with other signals in wavelength and time domains. Therefore, the depth-resolved optical detection provided by two-photon excitation can effectively reduce the interference and isolate the optical signals of diagnostic values from the underlying non-keratinized epithelial layer. We found that the ratio of NADH over FAD fluorescence measured in the non-keratinized epithelium is strongly correlated to tissue pathology. The fluorescence lifetime of tryptophan fluorescence in the keratinized layer is a biomarker of precancer development in epithelium. The TPEF imaging based on NADH autofluorescence provides the morphological information of non-keratinized tissue layer that also produces significant diagnostic value. These results provide profound insight into the biological basis of the inherent differences in NLO signals of normal and precancerous epithelial tissue. Overall, the depth-resolved TPEF spectroscopy and microscopy are sensitive techniques to detecting as keratin and other proteins in epithelium. Out study not only revealed the diagnostic value of keratin, but also demonstrated how to integrate the keratin signal with other endogenous NLO signals to achieve higher diagnosis accuracy in the detection of SCC.

662513.label: Major findings and research outcome
662513.value: Our work demonstrated for the first time (to our knowledge) that the multimodal nonlinear optical (NLO) spectroscopic microscope system could not only extract significant diagnostic information from keratin fluorescence in the topmost keratinized layer of epithelial tissue, but also produced a great wealth of diagnostic information ranging from tissue architecture, cellular/subcellular morphology, to biochemical information emanating from different stratified tissue depths. In particular, our results elucidated keratinized stratum corneum, the topmost epithelial layer to contain significant diagnostic information for identifying early squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in vivo. More importantly, although the keratin fluorescence in the topmost keratinizing layer with 20-50µm thickness provides diagnostic information, it causes serious interference in seeking the correlation between other endogenous optical signals and tissue pathology because the keratin fluorescence overlap with other signals in wavelength and time domains. To apply the keratin fluorescence for early diagnosis of SCC, a depth-resolved fluorescence detection, such as two-photon NLO spectroscopy or microscopy, must be used to separate the endogenous optical signals from different tissue layers. Our study showed that the diagnostic information from the different tissue layers can be effectively integrated to provide high performance diagnostic algorithm for identifying squamous epithelial precancer. These results affirm the efficacy of the novel multi-wavelength excitation and detection to produce a wide range of TPEF and SHG signals for clinical squamous premalignancy diagnosis application in vivo. Out study not only revealed the diagnostic value of keratin, but also demonstrated how to integrate the keratin signal with other endogenous NLO signals to achieve higher diagnosis accuracy in the detection of SCC.

662513.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
662513.value: The use of keratin fluorescence for epithelial cancer detection provides a few clear advantages. The keratinized epithelium is located at the top layer of epithelial tissue. Therefore, the keratin fluorescence can be effectively excited because there is no optical attenuation to excitation light and emission fluorescence to this topmost keratinized epithelial layer. The laser power level can be significantly reduced in comparison with the excitation of two-photon fluorescence from underlying normal epithelial layer and stromal layer. This could be critical for translation of the diagnostic technology to human subject. This could ultimately lead to the development of new technology with improved sensitivity and accuracy for the detection of SCC and significantly reduce costs associated with unnecessary biopsies, and treatment delays.
