758413.label: Major findings and research outcome
758413.value: The findings reveal that opposition to public housing tends to fall into two different categories. The first type involves neighbourhoods dominated by private homeowners, who tend to frame their opposition as concerns for environmental quality, echoing findings in the international literature. The case findings also suggest the importance of taking into account the political context of Hong Kong, to achieve a more nuanced interpretation of opposition behavior. Existing governance arrangements mean that although elected district councilors are consulted on planning matters, they only play an advisory role, whereas the government enjoys strong decision-making powers. Nevertheless, district councilors tend to bargain for compensatory infrastructure, since these represent significant political gains for individual councilors. In other words, what appears to be NIMBY opposition can be understood as political tactics by which local politicians score points with their electorate. The government tends to entertain these negotiations, even though it has no statutory obligation to do so, given that the dampening of opposing voices may confer legitimacy to government decisions. These findings have been detailed in a journal paper which is under review, entitled "Analysing the Dynamics of Planning Conflicts: Framing Processes in a Housing Project in Hong Kong". The second type of opposition presents interesting contradictions, since it involves neighbourhoods dominated by public housing residents. Further research reveals that these neighbourhoods tend to be characterized by existing high density of public housing flats, as well as under-provision of open space. Furthermore, some of the newly planned housing projects involve rezoning of open space to residential use, which triggers resistance from local residents. Although there are legitimate reasons behind opposition, the delays caused by these bargaining processes mean that opponents are easily labelled as NIMBYs and blamed for housing undersupply problems. These findings are detailed in another journal paper under review, entitled “Trade-offs between open space and housing development in hyper-dense neighbourhoods in Hong Kong”. Drawing on theories from the political literature, it is argued that the notion of NIMBYism has been strategically deployed in recent years to attribute the cause of housing undersupply to neighbourhood resistance. This may divert attention away from alternative interventions that could increase land supply for public housing, but which may materially interrupt the status quo and alter existing power relations. Apart from the abovementioned journal articles, major findings of the study were presented in three international conferences in 2014 and 2015.

758413.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
758413.value: The research findings highlight an interesting issue which has potential for further investigation. As indicated in the summary of major findings, different actors involved in planning conflicts are keen to establish the legitimacy of their claims and actions. Opposing homeowners seek to establish the legitimacy of their concerns through appealing to notions of environmental quality, while the non-elected administration seeks to boost the legitimacy of its siting decisions through negotiated compensation with locally elected politicians. Given that the struggle to establish political legitimacy constitutes a significant part of the dynamics of planning conflicts, it is worth exploring the range of norms and principles which actors deploy to establish or challenge the legitimacy of governance processes and outcomes, including both private and public housing supply conflicts, which could help explain why housing supply conflicts escalate or de-escalate over time. In terms of the proposed course of action, the Principal Investigator has prepared a new research project proposal which seeks to explore legitimacy constructions in different types of housing supply conflicts in Hong Kong. Subject to availability of further research funding, more in-depth investigation on this topic is expected to be carried out over the coming year.

758413.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
758413.value: Opposition to planned housing projects presents major challenges for governments under pressure to meet supply targets, a phenomenon which has been examined in international studies on NIMBYism. This study contributes by examining opposition behaviour in a less familiar context, namely Hong Kong. Opposition to public housing is rather unexpected, since public housing constitutes a large tenure in Hong Kong. Furthermore, one might expect less room for planning delays since the executive-led government enjoys strong decision-making powers. Interestingly though, there has been increasing resistance to public housing projects in recent years. This project contributes to better understanding of the reasons behind emergent opposition, through qualitative case studies which investigate negotiation processes underpinning controversial projects. Through detailed analysis of documentary evidence and in-depth interviews with key actors, the study reveals that opposition is often a political tactic to bargain for infrastructure improvements in high-density neighbourhoods. The study also provides a more critical interpretation of the NIMBY label, highlighting its use as a political strategy to blame neighbourhood actors for undersupply problems, which diverts attention away from alternative solutions. Thus, the study adds value to ongoing debates by going beyond site-specific controversies and pointing towards broader political factors behind housing supply delays.

758713.label: Project Title(Chinese)
758713.value: 學校教科書中少數民族及宗教的呈現：多元文化與通識教育

758713.label: Project Objectives
758713.value: To analyze how ethnic and religious minorities in mainland China and Hong Kong are represented in textbooks and officially recommended supplements for Senior Secondary Liberal Studies.
rows: To analyze how ethnic and religious minorities in mainland China and Hong Kong are represented in textbooks and officially recommended supplements for Senior Secondary Liberal Studies.

758713.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
758713.value: This research will reduce the gap in knowledge about curriculum content in Hong Kong education related to ethnic and religious minorities of mainland China and Hong Kong. Specifically it examines Senior Secondary Liberal Studies textbooks and officially recommended supplementary resources to assess the degree to which they align with the stated aim of enabling students to “appreciate…diversity in cultures and views in a pluralistic society.” By ethnic and religious minorities, this study includes groups living in mainland China or Hong Kong who are recognized in the resources as being not part of the Han ethnic group (i.e. Chinese ethnic groups other than Han, Indonesians, Indians, Whites, etc.); and/or are portrayed as religious, as part of a religious group, or as involved in religious practice (Buddhists, Muslims, Christians, and so on). The main objective of this study is to analyze how ethnic and religious minorities in mainland China and Hong Kong are represented in textbooks and recommended supplements for Senior Secondary Liberal Studies. The aim of the analysis is to develop more substantive understanding of the content of Senior Secondary Liberal Studies textual resources related to multicultural diversity in society. The project will employ quantitative and qualitative analyses of the content of Liberal Studies Senior Secondary resources that discusses ethnic and religious minorities in mainland China and Hong Kong. This includes textbooks, resources provided by the Curriculum Development Institute, and resources collected and made available through the Hong Kong Education City Web-based Resource Platform (which is a recommended website by the Education Bureau). The content will be found chiefly in 2 of the 6 modules of the Liberal Studies curriculum, “Modern China” and “Hong Kong Today.” The quantitative analysis will measure coverage of these subjects within the resources overall, while the qualitative analysis will examine how the minorities are discussed, using Key Words in Context and text and pictorial coding. The qualitative analysis will consider if various minority groups are regarded favorably or negatively overall, or as part of society or separate from the majority. Reliability of findings will be tested using teacher surveys. The results of this study will have several impacts. The findings will build knowledge on the content of the Liberal Studies curriculum and the multicultural content of Hong Kong education, inform teacher training and education programs for Liberal Studies, and increase capacity for local cross-cultural and comparative research on multicultural education. 研究致力於填補香港通識教育課程中關於內地及本港少數民族與少數宗教的知識空白。具體地講，本講究主要分析現行香港高中通識教育教科書及官方推薦的補充資料，以此評估通識教育能夠在何種程度上配合實現“讓學生學會理解多元社會中的文化與觀點多樣性”的教育目標。關於少數民族和少數宗教的定義，本研究中的少數民族主要指那些生活在內地及本港的非漢族群體（如非漢族華裔、印度尼西亞人、印度人、白人等）；本研究中的少數宗教主要指那些被描述為帶有宗教性質及參與宗教實踐活動的群體（如佛教徒、穆斯林、基督徒等）。 本研究的主要目的在於分析內地及本港的少數民族及少數宗教是如何在香港通識教育教科書及補充資料中被呈現的。此分析將提升更多對通識教育文本資料中涉及香港社會文化多樣性問題的實質性理解。 本研究項目將採用定量分析與質性分析兩種方法，分析香港通識教育文本資料中關於內地及本港少數民族和少數宗教問題的課程內容。其中涉及通識教育教科書，由課程發展處提供的文本資料，及香港教育城市網絡資源平台（此網絡平台為香港教育局推薦）上可用的文本資料。分析對象主要集中在通識教育課程六大模塊中的兩個模塊，即“當代中國”與“今日香港”。定量研究的部分將綜合考量在全部文本資料中對少數民族和少數宗教問題的討論情況；質性研究的部分將通過語境關鍵詞法、文本編碼及圖片編碼，分析少數民族及宗教是如何在教科書及補充資料中被討論的。質性分析還將分析各個少數群體是否被賦予積極或消極的意義，以及他們被認為是社會的一部分還是與多數群體相分離的少數。本研究的信度將通過教師調查得以驗證。 本研究將在以下幾個方面作出貢獻：為香港通識教育課程及其他多元文化課程構建知識基礎，為通識教育師資培訓及其他項目提供參考依據，以及充实本土跨文化研究及多元化教育的比較研究。

758713.label: Realisation of objectives
758713.value: The analysis of how ethnic and religious minorities in mainland China and Hong Kong are represented in textbooks and officially recommended supplements for Senior Secondary Liberal Studies has been fully achieved. During the time of the project, 28 books from Liberal Studies, including books from several publishers, were obtained, representing the marketplace of Liberal Studies textbooks from the time the subject began to the time of the project completion. Roughly 200 discrete entries from the texts, including textual data and pictoral data, were fully coded and transcribed and analysed using qualitative and quantitative means. Hundreds of official recommended supplements, namely web links from the Hong Kong Education City website, were examined, with relevant materials extracted for transcription and coding. Additionally, as officially recommended supplements for Liberal Studies include news media clippings, more than 100 relevant articles each from South China Morning Post, Apple Daily, and Oriental Daily from 2004-2015 were extracted through comprehensive research of the news websites, coded, and analysed. As mentioned in the proposal a reliability process which involved a teacher questionnaire was effectively implemented, and together with the parallel analysis system for text coding validity and reliability, an appropriate degree of reliability and validity were demonstrated. Furthermore, the researchers developed a more robust picture of the situation and analysis via questionnaires and surveys of practicing and pre-service teachers about their views and practices in relation to the research objectives.

rows: To analyze how ethnic and religious minorities in mainland China and Hong Kong are represented in textbooks and officially recommended supplements for Senior Secondary Liberal Studies.

758713.label: Major findings and research outcome
758713.value: Liberal Studies, according to the Hong Kong Education Bureau, should help students understand diversity and pluralism, and appreciate and respect different views in society. However, our study has found that representations of ethnic and religious diversity in Hong Kong and the world provided by Liberal Studies resources are not adequate for students to develop balanced or accurate views of how different experiences, cultures, and values play a role in people’s lives and society. Textbook coverage was scarce on these topics. In terms of the nature of coverage, representations tended to echo stereotypical views that have been found problematic in Hong Kong society and media in the past. Ethnic minorities are regarded most often as a homogeneous group despite the high degree of internal diversity of minorities not only from South Asia (a highly diverse region itself), but from around the world, who permanently reside in Hong Kong. Religion and ethnicity were primarily discussed in an abstract sense. When their import was addressed, a deficient or problematic framing was most frequently used, which regarded their differences as problematic or causing social challenges. While such statements may be accurate for some or many ethnic minorities, a reductive treatment risks enabling students to conflate all ethnic minorities with South Asian, grassroots residents. The role of religion in people’s lives was hardly addressed; when it was, Islam was conflated with sexism and anti-Western sentiment, reducing a diverse community to an extreme minority of the faith. Beyond textbooks, local media was found wanting. Teachers and student-teachers agree such sources are satisfactory at best, and problematic in relation to multicultural teaching and learning. Interdisciplinary social studies curricula in other parts of the world similarly deemphasize multiculturalism compared to other topics, such as economics and politics. In this case, an incidental de-emphasis in resources (perhaps caused by attempts to decrease social studies curriculum as a whole) may result in overgeneralizing statements that obscure rather than illuminate multicultural perspectives.

758713.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
758713.value: Currently several articles and a book are in production to publicise the findings. The project will also be further developed and expanded with a new GRF project examining multiculturalism throughout Hong Kong's social studies' curriculum, which includes History and General Studies. In terms of action, the following are recommended: First, teachers should help students develop a critical orientation toward textbooks and media via critical media literacy. Text publishers should work with multicultural groups and/or consultants with expertise to develop textbooks to be substantive when it comes to discussing diverse members of society. Policy makers and teacher trainers can support efforts to enhance resources for teaching toward multicultural aims. Developing space for teachers and students to learn about issues in-depth from multiple perspectives should be emphasized. Educational leaders should help teachers empower themselves as social science researchers in relation to such issues. As our study found that teachers did not see their knowledge as a major strength, work can be done through teacher education and professional development to equip teachers with research skills, which they can provide in turn to students. Local policy makers and teacher trainers may also benefit from more sustained thinking regarding the requirements of multicultural education.

758713.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
758713.value: Liberal Studies, according to the Hong Kong Education Bureau, should help students understand and appreciate diversity. However, our study has found that representations diversity provided by Liberal Studies resources are not adequate for students to develop balanced views of how different cultures and values play a role in people’s lives. Textbook coverage was scarce, and representations tended to echo stereotypical views that have been found as problematic. Ethnic minorities are regarded often as a homogeneous group despite the high degree of diversity of minorities. Religion and ethnicity were discussed with a problematic framing, which regarded differences as problematic or causing challenges. The role of religion in people’s lives was hardly addressed. Beyond textbooks, local media was found wanting. Teachers feel that such sources are satisfactory at best, and problematic in relation to multicultural teaching and learning. Interdisciplinary social studies curricula in other parts of the world similarly deemphasize multiculturalism compared to other topics, such as economics and politics. In this case, much more work needs to be done in terms of pedagogy, policy, curriculum development, educational leadership, and textbook and resource production to align Liberal Studies with its multicultural aims.

758913.label: Project Title(Chinese)
758913.value: 共同建構適當的小班教學法: 連結中學師生的對話

758913.label: Project Objectives
758913.value: To develop a deeper understanding of student perceptions and experiences of learning in reduced-size classes, and the nature of the developmental process of teachers’ reflection and pedagogical change based upon that student voice. To understand teaching and learning processes in large and reduced-size secondary school English classes where the teacher is the same. To formulate a set of guiding principles for effective pedagogy in reduced-size classes.
rows: To develop a deeper understanding of student perceptions and experiences of learning in reduced-size classes, and the nature of the developmental process of teachers’ reflection and pedagogical change based upon that student voice.
To understand teaching and learning processes in large and reduced-size secondary school English classes where the teacher is the same.
To formulate a set of guiding principles for effective pedagogy in reduced-size classes.

758913.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
758913.value: In Hong Kong secondary schools there is a move towards the widespread use of reduced-size classes as a strategy for better teaching and learning. This study sets out to build upon recent studies in Hong Kong (Galton & Pell, 2010; Harfitt, 2012a) by investigating under-researched aspects of class size reduction (CSR), namely the developmental process of teachers’ pedagogical change, and hearing the student voice on teaching and learning processes in smaller classes. Apart from there being a paucity of research on CSR in the secondary school context, the significance of this study is threefold. Firstly, it examines whether and to what extent teachers vary their pedagogy in large and small classes. Research suggests that teachers do not change their pedagogy from one class to another (Stasz & Stecher, 2002), but without saying why. Secondly, the student voice has been largely overlooked in previous studies. This student voice furnishes us with crucial insights from within the classroom as students’ perspectives might lead to a better understanding of the significance of class size in relation to teaching and learning processes. Thirdly, insights gleaned from the complex relationship between class size and teaching and learning facilitate theory building; and carry significant implications for practice in relation to teaching, teacher education and policy. The study adopts a predominantly qualitative methodology by conducting case studies in 6 secondary schools, with one teacher from each school teaching a reduced-size class and a regular size class at the same year level (grades 10-12). It also makes strategic use of quantitative data by eliciting students’ perceptions on their teaching and learning experiences through a baseline questionnaire to over 1000 students. This represents the first of three main research phases. Interviews with over 400 students will be conducted to seek their voice on teaching and learning in large and small classes, and elicit their suggestions for improving the teaching and learning in their respective context. After triangulating the questionnaire and interview data with lesson observations, teachers will be provided with the questionnaire findings and student interview transcripts to elicit their reaction to their students’ feedback. The final phase of the study includes examination of school achievement scores, follow-up lesson observations to explore if, and how, students’ ideas have been incorporated into each teacher’s pedagogy as well as further interviews with participants. Data collection will be conducted over two academic years, with the study expected to last for 34 months. 香港中學普遍傾向減少每班人數, 作為提升教與學質素的策略。本研究以現有研究為基礎 (Galton & Pell, 2010; Harfitt, 2012a)，探討「減少每班人數」(Class size reduction (CSR)) 這議題內, 尚欠研究的範疇, 即教師教學法改變的發展過程，以及學生在教與學過程中的「聲音」。 在中學 縮減每班人數的策略, 現時仍然缺乏充份研究。本研究針對這個不足, 具備三方面的意義。首先，本研究旨在探討教師在教授大班和小班時 , 會否及如何改變教學法。現有研究曾經提出, 教師不會因應每班人數而改變教學法 (Stasz & Stecher, 2002) 。然而，這些研究並沒有指出這種現象的原因。第二，以往的研究很大程度忽視了學生的聲音。這些源自課堂內的學生聲音及角度，可幫助我們更了解每班的人數在教與學過程中的意義。第三, 探討每班的人數和教與學的關係, 不僅促進學術理論的建構, 更具有教學，師資培訓和政策實踐的涵義。 本研究以質性方法學為主, 在六所中學進行個案研究。每所學校有一位教師, 在同一年級裡(10-12年級), 教授一班人數已減少的班和一班常規班。此外, 會為超過1000名學生進行基線問卷調查，從中獲取學生教與學的觀感, 進行量化數據分析。這是三個主要研究階段的第一階段。這階段也會為超過400名學生進行訪談, 藉以聽取學生對大班和小班教學的「聲音」,以及他們對改善教與學的建議。問卷及訪談也用來三角測定檢示課堂觀察的資料。然後, 會把問卷調查結果及學生訪談記錄交給教師, 藉以取得老師對學生反饋的反應。研究的最後階段，包括審查學校的成績及跟進課堂觀察，藉以探討每位老師有否及如何把 學生的想法融入自己的教學方法。另外, 也會進一步採訪參與者。本研究資料收集將超過兩個學年進行，整項研究預計持續34個月。

758913.label: Realisation of objectives
758913.value: Three objectives underpinned the project and were successfully achieved. The first was to develop a deeper understanding of student perceptions and experiences of learning in reduced-size classes, and the nature of the developmental process of teachers’ reflection and pedagogical change based upon that student voice. This was achieved through the stated research design and a close relationship forged with selected secondary schools, English teachers and pupils. Through research output e.g., sole-authored book (Harfitt, 2015), international refereed journal articles (Harfitt, 2014; Harfitt, 2015; Harfitt, 2017) and book chapters (e.g. Harfitt, 2016), the first, second and third objectives were fulfilled. This output demonstrates a better understanding of teaching and learning processes in large and reduced-size secondary school English classes where the teacher was the same. These publications also articulated a better understanding of student perceptions and experiences of learning in reduced-size classes (Harfitt, 2015; 2017), and the nature of the developmental process of teachers’ reflection and pedagogical change based upon students’ feedback (Harfitt, 2014). I wish to thank the teachers and schools who participated in my study. There were two schools which changed their original schedules (from my initial research plan) but both were able to accommodate me in the second year of the study. One teacher left her school but the school was able to point me towards another teacher in the English panel. I was very appreciative of this as it meant I was able to keep the same number of teachers as I originally planned and did not have to find another school which was my initial thought and worry. In two schools the size of the small class changed due to changes in student numbers (In School 5 the small class of 25 became a class of 24 while school 6 became a small class of 21 and not 18). To realise the first and second objectives I conducted a student questionnaire and this was administered to 1035 students across six secondary schools. This questionnaire provided me with a platform from which to build my knowledge base on the students' perceptions of small classes. The data shows that students are overwhelmingly in favour of small classes and are able to articulate the differences in the way that class size reduction can mediate their learning. Focus group interviews with all students in the 6 reduced-size classes were then completed to add to my data on the student voice. In total I interviewed 128 students from the small classes and 145 students from large classes in the same schools to elicit their opinions and perceptions. Students from all six small classes spoke at length about how they enjoyed a different class atmosphere once the class size had been reduced, as seen from the following interview extracts: 'It’s much better in this small class because we know each other now. We are like a group of friends. Before, (in a large class) we do not have good relations with the others.' (School 1) 'I have not studied in a class like this before. We help each other a lot…it’s different to before…I mean we are closer together as classmates. We talk to each other and work together.' (School 2) 'This is the best class I have been in. We work together and help each other. (School 2) I want to study in the small class next year (again). It helps me a lot. I can ask the teacher questions and she helps me. I also get help from my friends in the class. They are willing to help me.' (School 3 – translated from L1) 'Last year I studied in a class of 39. I like this class (the small class) more because the teacher knows me more…I can see she can help me. Before this I was on my own.' (School 4) 'I feel more included in this class. I have more friends and we work better than other classes I have studied in. I think small classes make us closer.' (School 6) 'I like learning in a small class because I am more able to participate and I am confident than before. I think the small class makes me more confident. I don't know why.' (School 6) The students were a huge part of this study and they gave me so much information and insight into their experiences of teaching and learning in reduced-size classes. The student voice gathered in each school / research site was entirely constructive (as above) and enabled the research to develop a focus on teachers' professional development. The final objective of the study was to formulate a set of guiding principles for effective pedagogy in reduced-size classes. This was based on more than 75 class observations over a two-year period. I have proposed in my workshops for teachers and in my publications as well as in-service teacher training courses that if teachers and teacher educators focus on salient pedagogical strategies such as questioning, collaborative work and feedback (Harfitt, 2015) then small classes can bring important academic and social benefits. The following features of students' learning were noted in smaller classes: Students participated more often in classroom dialogue in the small classes; Students displayed more humour in the smaller classes (with each other as well as with their teachers); Students were more sociable and communicative with each other in and out of the small class; Students were more aware of the learning opportunities inherent in small classes; Students asked more questions to their teachers as well as to their peers; Students engaged in more out-of-class meetings to discuss learning and share materials as well as knowledge; Students in the small classes developed a stronger rapport with their teachers and accepted them as a member of the class community; Students engaged in more peer tutoring in and out of class; Students asked for more work in class; Students accepted more responsibility from their teachers in the small classes (answering questions, students forming their own groups, choosing their own seats, working together, finding their own learning resources, shaping their own class assignments etc.); and, Students helped each other more in the smaller classes and the small classes in general were found to be more supportive learning environments; The following pedagogical approaches were seen to be key (Harfitt, 2015) through my study: Teachers made their small classes less threatening through the use of students’ names and routines aimed at encouraging participation and pupil talk; Teachers gave students more responsibility in the small classes (students forming their own groups, helping peers, finding their own learning resources, shaping their own class assignments etc.); Teachers displayed better quality interaction patterns in the small classes (dialogic talk, more open questions, prompts, scaffolds, extended wait-time, extended discourse, exploratory talk, etc.); Teachers were more aware of spatiality in the small classes, making more use of the physical resources in these classes (rearranging the classroom layout for different tasks and learning activities etc.); Teachers employed more cooperative and collaborative learning activities in small classes through the use of group and pair work; Teachers’ feedback in the small classes moved away from corrective feedback (where teachers point out errors in students’ work) to a more informing and evaluative type of feedback that allowed the teacher to pose questions for students so that they could reflect. This supported students’ self-regulation and engagement.

758913.label: Major findings and research outcome
758913.value: A number of major findings emerged from this project. They relate to (1) student perceptions of teaching and learning in small or reduced-size classes (Harfitt, 2015; Harfitt, 2017); (2) an overview of good practices and pedagogy in terms of teaching and learning in small classes (Harfitt, 2015); and (3) the need for further research and professional development in HK secondary schools on the issue of effective teaching in small or reduced-size classes (Harfitt, 2015). Detailed interviews were carried out with multiple cohorts of students who studied in small and large classes in six participating schools. Data illustrated the perceptions of students towards learning in small classes. I found the students to be confident and constructive in their comments on the teaching and learning they were experiencing in the reduced-size classes. Each student reflected in a mature way, often drawing on their previous experiences of studying in larger classes. At no point in the interviews did students make personal criticisms of their teacher, or their schools. The students also displayed a keen interest in developing their own learning potential as reflected in their feedback on teaching. For example, some of the students wanted to see more group work integrated into their classes as they appreciated the opportunity for peer-learning. Some wanted more individual feedback from their teachers, suggesting that students were well aware of the importance of feedback in the teaching and learning cycle and saw the opportunities for individualised pedagogy in smaller classes. Others noted that they needed more time to engage with tasks and work, a point which was supported by the teachers in each school but who also noted the constraints of the curriculum. Another finding was that most teachers in the study were also able to accept the comments and feedback from their students to initiate change in their pedagogy and it was observed how some teachers varied their questioning techniques, offered more group work opportunities and provided more quality feedback in class. The issue of a heavy workload and pressure to cover the curriculum was still raised by teachers and seemed to act as a brake on teacher change. The study also produced a set of guiding principles based on multiple classroom observations of teachers and students working in small classes. These principles and best practices were outlined in Harfitt (2015) and highlighted some of the salient features of students' learning and teacher's pedagogy in small classes.

758913.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
758913.value: Further school-based research about how class size reduction mediates teaching and learning processes is certainly needed. While this study focused on multiple classes and students in six secondary schools, further research may investigate how a class of students makes the transition from primary 6 to secondary one (in small classes) to understand how benefits (if any) transfer when students move to a different level of schooling. Equally it would be interesting to research how one class develops over a period of 2-3 years if they stay in a small or reduced-size class. This would allow researchers to understand more about the process of learning that is fostered by small classes. A renewed focus on small classes might also shed light on the personal aspects of student development rather than the academic development which has characterised previous research of class size reduction in HK and elsewhere. A focus on wellness would allow researchers to examine how and why small classes benefit personal growth in young learners. The focus on wellness, character building and all-round, whole-person development is a feature of EDB reforms and it would be interesting to see if small classes can assist these noble aims.

758913.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
758913.value: The project sought to use the student voice in HK secondary schools to promote teachers’ pedagogical innovation in small classes. The study examined whether pedagogical change can be brought about through brokered dialogue with students. Findings suggest the student voice is a powerful catalyst for teachers’ professional development. One teacher incorporated her students’ comments on teaching and learning in small classes to adopt alternative approaches including pedagogy, assessment and classroom layouts. Another teacher employed more group work and collaborative learning for pupils. A third teacher built on her students’ feedback to give more ‘voice’ in the classroom instead of dominating lessons with teacher talk. Another teacher adapted her questioning techniques to promote a more dialogic approach in class. A negative message from the project was that the teachers saw ‘curriculum coverage’ as an insurmountable obstacle to pedagogical change in small classes. Worryingly, too, they had not received any professional development on how to maximize the opportunities inherent in small classes. The results of the project made significant contributions to our understanding of how small classes benefit teaching and learning and how the student voice is invaluable in promoting teacher change. The project makes a strong case for more effective small class pedagogy.

759213.label: Project Objectives
759213.value: To investigate the physical injury patterns associated with male IPV victims presenting to AEDs in Hong Kong to enhance our knowledge of early identification strategies for this population. We hypothesize that the injury patterns of male IPV victims presenting to AEDs are different from those of men suffering accidental injuries (non-IPV victims) in term of (1) injury location, (2) injury cause, and (3) injury severity. To gain an understanding of the healthcare needs of male IPV victims in terms of public healthcare services and chronic physical and mental illness to develop appropriate services to meet those needs. We hypothesize that the healthcare needs of this population are different from those of male accidental injury patients (non-IPV victims) presenting to AEDs. To examine the help-seeking characteristics of male IPV victims and their correlation with the factors of gender, age, healthcare needs, and injury indicators to inform the design of an appropriate intervention approach and services for these victims and their families. We hypothesize that men’s help-seeking characteristics are different from women’s, and we also expect to find differences among male victims of different ages and with different healthcare needs.

759213.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
759213.value: Intimate partner violence (IPV), particularly violence against women, is a global public health issue (Krug et al., 2002). Previous IPV studies focus primarily on female victims, neglecting the experience of male victims. In fact, in IVP, men may play the role of perpetrator of intimate terrorism, victim of resistant violence during women’s self-defense, or party to common couple violence caused by tension leading one or both partners to resort to violence rather than coercive control (Johnson, 1995, 2006), as well as victim of violence perpetrated by women (Hines & Douglas, 2010). Men and women can be both the victims and perpetrators of IPV, and a multidimensional understanding of such violence thus requires a gender-inclusive approach (Hines & Douglas, 2011). Studies exploring the male victims of IPV are vital to the prevention of family violence (Lau et al., 2008). Such studies have never been conducted in Hong Kong, and the aim of the proposed research is to explore the injury patterns, healthcare needs, and help-seeking characteristics of male IPV victims to better detect these victims and develop appropriate preventive strategies. Men are generally less likely than women to seek help (McKelley, 2007; Noone & Stephens, 2008; Tsui, Cheung, & Leung, 2010), and hence male IPV victims may be reluctant to disclose their victimization. They may perceive a threat to their masculine identity (Rentoul &Appleboom, 1997; O’Brien, Hunt, & Hart, 2005; Tsui, Cheung, & Leung, 2010) and fear losing face (Chan, 2006, 2009). Accident & Emergency Departments (AEDs) may be the only place that male IPV victims seek help (Chan et al., 2012), and thus exploring AED records should prove a valuable resource in furthering our understanding of the profile, injury patterns, healthcare needs and help-seeking characteristics of these victims in Hong Kong. A retrospective cohort study will be carried out in collaboration with the AEDs of two regional hospitals, Tuen Mun Hospital and Pok Oi Hospital. Data on male victims of IPV will be collected from the hospital computer databases and from the patient medical charts filled out by physicians. The findings of this study will fill the gap in our empirical knowledge of male IPV victims in Hong Kong.

759213.label: Realisation of objectives
759213.value: 1. To investigate the physical injury patterns associated with male IPV victims presenting to AEDs in Hong Kong to enhance our knowledge of early identification strategies for this population. We hypothesize that the injury patterns of male IPV victims presenting to AEDs are different from those of men suffering accidental injuries (non-IPV victims) in term of (1) injury location, (2) injury cause, and (3) injury severity. • This objective has been achieved. The medical records of all intimate partner violence victims presenting at the AEDs of TMH and POH between 2010 and 2014 were retrieved and reviewed as proposed. Data analysis was conducted to explore the injury patterns of IPV male victims, in terms of injury location and injury cause, and it implications to the healthcare needs of male IPV victims. The results shown that, as compared to female IPV victims, male IPV victims are more likely to be presented with bites, abrasions, and laceration injuries, they usually attend the AED after midnight, and they are mostly older than 40 years old. In terms of demographics, male IPV victims are more likely to be employed, are native or permanent residents, and with low motivation to seek help from social services. We suggested that health care and helping professionals should be aware of such gender differences among IPV victims, and be sensitive in identifying male IPV victims, and develop early IPV detection cum intervention program especially for this target group accordingly (Choi et al., 2015). 2. To gain an understanding of the healthcare needs of male IPV victims in terms of public healthcare services and chronic physical and mental illness to develop appropriate services to meet those needs. We hypothesize that the healthcare needs of this population are different from those of male accidental injury patients (non-IPV victims) presenting to AEDs. • This objective has been achieved. The past health history of male IPV victims from 2010 to 2014 (5 years) and randomized sampling of male non-IPV victims from 2010 to 2014 were retrieved by research nurses from hospital databases. The results showed that male IPV victims tend to be relatively older (>40 years old), more attend AED or other public healthcare services (e.g., hospital or in-patient wards), more attend AED after midnight in past 5 years, as compared to male non-IPV victims (Choi et al., manuscript in preparation). 3. To examine the help-seeking characteristics of male IPV victims and their correlation with the factors of gender, age, healthcare needs, and injury indicators to inform the design of an appropriate intervention approach and services for these victims and their families. We hypothesize that men’s help-seeking characteristics are different from women’s, and we also expect to find differences among male victims of different ages and with different healthcare needs. • This objective has been achieved. The help-seeking characteristics of male IPV victims and their correlation have been explored. In the comparison between male and female IPV victims, males were less likely to receive on-site counseling in AEDs. Considering such gender difference in preference of receiving help, male-specific intervention service approach is necessary to help more male IPV victims accept and receive services. Currently, most of victims who refused on-site counseling services return home after discharge and no referral to medical social worker to follow their needs, and a large proportion of them refuse help. It means these victims return to the same risky situation of IPV. Therefore, healthcare professionals must go through further training on dealing with these cases and their situations. Victims’ awareness of the risk and harm of IPV must also to be raised, especially for those who been through ongoing multiple abuses (Choi, et al., manuscript under review on Preventive medicine).

759213.label: Major findings and research outcome
759213.value: The records of IPV victims presented to the AEDs of two regional hospitals in Hong Kong between 1 January 2010 and 31 December 2014 were retrieved. 1,112 IPV cases (male = 183; female =929). As compared to male IPV victims, more female IPV victims reported having contusions/bruising, tenderness, and swelling (p<.001) from IPV. On the other hand, more men reported having abrasion or scrape, laceration or cutting (p<.001). If focused on female IPV victims, cohabiting women were about 2.1 times more likely to have head, neck, or facial injuries (OR=2.1, 95% CI=1.30–3.40, p=.002), almost twice the risk of having multiple injuries in different locations (OR=1.82, 95% CI=1.25–2.65, p=.001), and twice likely to experience more than one method of physical abuse (OR=1.72, 95% CI=1.18–2.51, p=.005) (Wong et al., 2016). In comparison to non-IPV male victims, male IPV victims were mostly more than 40 years of age, more attend public healthcare services, and attend AED after midnight (Choi et al., manuscript in preparation). Gender-related differences in victims’ demographic characteristics, injury patterns, and help-seeking behaviours, were well observed in the study. Male IPV victims are more likely to be presented with bites, abrasions, and laceration injuries, they usually attend the AED after midnight, and over 66% of them are older than 40 years old. In terms of demographics, male IPV victims are more likely to be employed, are native or permanent residents. Besides, male victims of IPV are more likely to refuse on-site counselling services in AEDs than female IPV victims. (Choi, et al., manuscript under review on Preventive medicine). As mentioned above, 73 mutual violence cases (13.13%) were identified. Among the mutual abuse cases, 59% of the female victims had been abused multiple times, and this is more than twice as the males (27.4%, p<.05). Women had more contusions or bruising than men (p<0.01) while more men than women had abrasion or scrape (p<.05) in mutual IPV episodes. These multiple incidences have demonstrated the higher risk of further IPV in these mutual abuse couples (Choi et al., manuscript under review at Violence and victims). We suggested that health care and helping professionals should be aware of such gender differences among IPV victims, and be sensitive in identifying male IPV victims, and develop early IPV detection cum intervention program especially for this target group accordingly (Choi et al., 2015).

759213.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
759213.value: There is a need to further development of the research on screening tools and development of a valid measurement in identifying male victims of IPV. This study focused on male IPV victims visiting an emergency department, who may have more severe injuries than those in the community. Therefore, the findings may not be generalized to other populations. Therefore, study on male IPV victims in the community is one of potential study areas for further research development of male IPV victims. Moreover, further research in different locations around the world is important to explore the similarities and differences across different countries and cultures. Additional research focus should be given to different types of mutual IPV where male victims are usually involved; this will enable future development of more effective intervention and prevention for IPV. Multidisciplinary collaboration is needed and must be established formally to help IPV victims, their families, and their motivations to seek help, followed by studies of the effectiveness of newer intervention and prevention strategies for male IPV victims.

759213.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
759213.value: The records of victims of spouse abuse presenting at Accident and Emergency Departments (AEDs) of two regional hospitals in Hong Kong, between 1 January 2010 and 31 December 2014 were retrieved. A total of 1,112 IPV partner abuse cases (male = 183; female =929) were identified; of these, there were in total 73 “couple cases”, that is, where both partners in a relationship were admitted. About half of the female victims (49.7%) reported having been physically abused in mutual IPV multiple times (more than twice); this was more than twice as often as in males (27.9%). More men than women reported having abrasion or scrape, laceration or cutting in episodes of IPV. Unlike female IPV victims, male IPV victims tend to be employed and native or permanent residents, and with low motivation to seek help from social services. Professionals should be aware of gender differences in the characteristics of IPV victims, especially the sensitivity to identify male IPV victims, who are often difficult to be identified. The development of a comprehensive early IPV-detection program should take gender differences into account, and services for male victims should be specifically designed to put a stop to IPV.

759413.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
759413.value: Rivers provide key environmental goods such as water supply, habitats for diverse wildlife, and wholesome recreational opportunities for citizens. Human activities have significantly altered, degraded or damaged river ecosystems worldwide. The situation calls for restoring their environmental-ecological integrity to sustain environmental goods. River restoration is thus an expanding area of public concern and investment in both developed and developing countries. However, such work has been hampered by inadequate understanding of stakeholder preferences of various restoration options and the lack of benefit measurement of restoration alternatives. In this context, a critical knowledge gap could be filled regarding public attitudes, preferences and willingness-to-pay (WTP) for river restoration in monetary terms. The results could serve as an input for cost-benefit analysis to gauge the efficiency of public investment and maximize welfare in the social domain. The contingent valuation method (CVM) is a major valuation technique for non-market goods and services. It relies on people’s statement of their preference to infer the gain or loss of social welfare induced by hypothetical changes in an environmental asset. CVM has been widely applied to estimate the benefits of river restoration. Most relevant research has focused on developed countries, with few attempts in developing countries where river degradation is severe, demanding pressing restoration efforts but constrained by shortage of funding and in-depth studies. Moreover, it has been acknowledged that social, cultural, and institutional factors may affect public preference and willingness-to-pay for environmental goods. Comparing the contingent valuation of environmental goods between developed countries and developing countries could shed light on the underlying causes of discrepancies between these two groups of countries and the transferability of empirical CV results in a globalizing world. However, very few studies have adopted such a comparative perspective. This proposed study will work at the interface of two main strands of scholarly inquiry, integrating economic analysis into river restoration and validating the institutional and cultural sensitivities of the CVM, to investigate the social welfare of river restoration in both Guangzhou (China) and Flanders (Belgium). The objectives are to (1) quantify the social welfare of river restoration by applying CVM; (2) investigate how people’s environmental attitudes affect their payment decisions; and (3) test whether different institutional and cultural contexts could influence WTP. This study will contribute new knowledge to fill a gap in the effects of culture and institution on CVM. In practical terms, the findings will inform decision-making on environmental management in China.

759413.label: Major findings and research outcome
759413.value: Major findings: 1. In Brussels, econometric analysis based on the mixed logit models revealed that overall public would like to have a more natural river (open and naturalized channel, good water quality, and with rich species diversity), while achieving good water quality was the most preferred attribute. 2. In Guangzhou, river restoration could reverse negative externalities associated with polluted urban river stretches to positive externalities, and the positive externalities of river restoration is attributed to riverine greening. 3. An in-depth comparative analysis using both generalized multinomial logit models and latent class models revealed fairly similar preference heterogeneity regarding various attributes between respondents from two cities, and there exists a highly significant scale heterogeneity and hence large degree of uncertainty amongst Guangzhou respondents when making their WTP decisions. 4. Another significant finding shared commonly by respondents from two cities is that those who could not appreciate urban river’s ecosystem services adequately were not in favor of moving away from the status quo. Thus, cultural difference between developed Brussels and transitional Guangzhou would generally not affect residents' decisions to support urban river restoration, but rather than shape their preferences and valuations of more nuanced attributes and associated levels regarding urban river restoration.

759413.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
759413.value: 1. To structure the interactions between institutional and cultural context with people’s attitudes and understanding of what in urban landscape is valuable, and tie them with policy and management alternatives so as to facilitate benefit transfer between developed and transitional nations. 2. To explore the linkage between environmental information transparency, sensory experiences and respondents' comprehension of ecosystem services provided by restoring urban river stretches. 3. To investigate the distance decay effects of respondents' preferences and WTPs for river restoration. 4. To delve the underlying reasons for Guangzhou respondents' highly significant scale heterogeneity.

759413.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
759413.value: The discrete choice experiment (DCE) approach has been widely applied in developed nations to examine individual preference heterogeneity regarding the provision of ecosystem services, and thereby a wealth of empirical evidence has been generated. Knowledge about how to inform and benefit the DCE studies in developing countries remains limited because of a lack of direct cross-country comparisons between developed and transitional nations. Using two duplicate DCE surveys executed in Brussels (the capital city of Belgium) and Guangzhou (the capital city of Guangdong province, China), where both local municipal governments are intending to restore heavily modified and polluted river stretches in densely-populated urban settings, this study provides an in-depth analysis and comparison between two groups of respondents’ preferences and influencing factors. Contributing to the new knowledge and growing literature that recognizes and explores residents’ preference heterogeneity as well as the scale heterogeneity in environmental and ecological goods, this comparative study provides information to policy makers and practitioners for optimizing strategy to restore impaired urban river ecosystems, facilitate benefit transfer between developed and transitional nations, and to generate a robust and resilient supply of ecosystem services in cities where concentrations of people, environmental deterioration, and demand for diverse ecosystem services are highest.

759513.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
759513.value: This research explores issues concerning the continuing struggle for restoring the social order and defending the Confucian culture among the Han Chinese literati who collaborated with the alien regime during the Manchu conquest of Ming China, 1644-1662. Although the significant role of these surrendered Chinese in the conquest history is acknowledged, their perspective and interpretation of collaboration have not been systematically studied. Inspired by the works of Michel Foucault (1926-1984) and the cultural theorists, the research attempts to employ discourse analysis to reexamine the collaborators’ ideas and acts of collaboration revealed in the social discourse regarding the restoration of social order and the defense and transmission of Chinese culture under the alien rule. It aims to shed new light on the study of Ming-Qing cultural and intellectual history and provide a useful alternative for future studies. Instead of regarding former Ming officials’ taking office under Manchu rule as a political realignment of personal choice, the research will reconsider collaboration from a wider socio-cultural angle to evaluate how late-Ming and early-Qing individuals were influenced by the social perception and social interaction of their time. The findings are expected to deepen our understanding of the nature of collaboration and its relation to the Qing rise in late seventeenth-century China. The research will also analyze how the important Confucian doctrines were addressed in the intellectual discourse during the dynastic transition and to what extent they in reality shaped the political behavior of the scholar-officials. In addition, it will explore how these early-Qing historical figures interpreted and reinterpreted the Confucian teaching in identifying their roles and duties as responsible officials, filial sons and able community leaders, especially when there was a role conflict. The historical evaluation of the submitted Ming officials after the post-conquest period will be discussed to see how it changed as a result of the socio-political development. The research will be conducted through an intensive inter-textual examination of a variety of primary sources, including official and private histories, court memorials, gazetteers and other archival materials, as well as the biographies, autobiographies, letters, poems and writings of the literati concerned. Apart from the discourse analysis, reference will be made to the recent social and cultural theories, such as Foucault’s power/knowledge analysis and Antonio Gramsci’s (1891-1937) idea of hegemony, with a view to providing a convincing narrative of an era of crisis and transformation in late imperial China. 降清明臣在明（1368－1644）、清（1644－1912）易代史中的重要角色備受關注，惟他們對變節一事所持的觀點和詮釋，卻一直缺乏有系統的研究。本研究計劃旨在重新審視這方面的問題，探討漢族士大夫在鼎革之際，如何通過與滿洲征服者合作，恢復明亡後的社會秩序和延續世代相傳的儒家文化。 借鑑福柯（1926－1984）及其他學者的文化研究理論，我們會利用話語分析重新解讀當時的社會話語，從異族統治下重整綱紀和保存文化等迫切社會議題中，揭示仕清者的具體想法和由此而來的實際行動。這將會為明清文化和思想史帶來新的視角，並為未來研究提供新的路向。 本研究會從較廣的社會文化角度，評估社會認知和人際互動對明清士人的影響，而避免將問題過分簡化，把他們的仕清抉擇，一概視為純粹的個人投敵行為。研究結果將有助加深我們對明臣降清，以及其與十七世紀滿清興起關係的認識。此外，我們亦會深入分析鼎革時期的士人話語，探討當中有關儒家教化的論述，以及它們在實際生活中，如何左右士大夫的政治行為。與此同時，我們更會討論，這些清初歷史人物在界定本身作為人臣、人子及社會領袖的角色和責任時──特別在角色出現衝突的情況下──怎樣重新詮釋先賢的教誨。 我們也會梳理易代後降清者評價的轉變，以見歷史褒貶與社會政治環境變遷的關係。本研究將以跨文本研究方法，對現存各種史料，包括官、私記載、官方奏摺、方志、檔案，以及時人的傳記、書信及詩文等資料進行深入的分析。 除了話語分析外，我們亦會利用其他社會文化理論，如福柯的權力／知識理論、葛蘭西的文化霸權理論，為這段中華帝國晚期的易代歷史，提供一個較為合理可信的敘述。

759613.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
759613.value: Ever since the inception of the Bill of Rights Ordinance (‘BORO’) in 1991, courts in Hong Kong have been reviewing executive and legislative acts for compatibility with human rights. These powers of review were enhanced after the handover by the Basic Law 1997, which entrenched an extensive list of fundamental rights. The availability of constitutional rights as a ground of judicial review has enabled courts to scrutinise policy decisions that were traditionally difficult to challenge and to review such decisions using the proportionality test – a standard of review higher than that warranted under orthodox principles of judicial review. The increased judicial powers that rights review introduced has caused concerns that courts, in exercising these powers, would interfere with policy questions that they lack the expertise or information to decide, or moral issues that they as unelected institutions lack the democratic legitimacy to resolve. Courts have repeatedly expressed these concerns in judgments, including most recently cases where they had to determine the constitutionality of policies limiting welfare benefits to certain groups of people, and laws barring transsexual persons from marrying in their desired gender. Judgments that struck down long-standing laws have sometimes attracted criticisms that courts were usurping policy-making functions that properly belonged to the government; that Hong Kong was experiencing ‘judicial tyranny’ (e.g. regarding the Court of First Instance’s striking down of laws banning foreign domestic helpers from attaining permanent residency, see Wong Yau-kar, ‘How the authors of the American Declaration of Independence would view the Vallejos judgment’ [in Chinese] Mingpao, 01/11/2011). To allay these concerns, Hong Kong courts have sometimes exercised their powers of constitutional review with restraint, by ‘deferring’ to the views of the executive or legislature in rights cases. In the last decade, the extent of deference that courts grant increasingly determines the outcome of rights litigation in Hong Kong. Despite this, there has been a dearth of studies of the concept of deference in Hong Kong. This project will provide the first comprehensive and systematic study of post-handover higher courts’ attitudes on deference. It aims to ascertain how deferential courts have been in adjudicating constitutional rights claims and factors that affected their degree of deference, evaluate whether existing judicial attitudes towards deference enable courts to accommodate concerns about their institutional and constitutional limits, and outline an approach to deference that courts should adopt in light of Hong Kong’s unique institutional and constitutional context. 自從《香港人權法案條例》於1991年生效，香港法院便有權覆核行政和立法行為是否合乎人權標準。由於《基本法》保障人權的範疇甚廣，司法覆核的權力於1997年回歸後得以擴大。此權力容許了法院審核一些傳統上難以挑戰的決策，並以比例原則 -- 一項被公認為更嚴格的審查標準 -- 來審核這些決策。法院廣大的司法覆核權力使人關注法院在行使有關權力時，會否干預政策等法院欠缺專門知識和資訊去處理的問題，或道德等法院作為非民選機構因而欠缺認受性去處理的問題。法院曾在判辭中多次表達有關的憂慮。最近，法院審理政府只把福利派發給某些群組的做法是否合憲一案，和另一宗不許變性人以其所選定的性別結婚的法例是否合憲案件時，再次重申法院對干預政策的憂慮。法院裁定某些由來已久的法例違憲的決定，時而被批評為「司法篡權」，指司法干預侵佔了政府制訂政策的功能；亦有評論形容香港正經歷「司法暴政」（指原訟庭裁定禁止外傭取得永久居留權的法例為違憲，見黃友嘉：美國《獨立宣言》的作者會怎樣看外傭居港權判決，2011年11月1日明報) 為息疑慮，法院有時會採取克制的態度，在審理案件時遵從行政或立法當局的立場。在過往十年，越來越多的決判斷定於「司法遵從」的程度。儘管如此，香港一直缺乏有關司法遵從的概念的研究。本項目是首個全面和有系統地分析回歸後司法遵從的做法的研究，旨在探討法院在處理人權案件時，遵從政府決定的程度及影響其取態的因素。本研究亦會評估現時法院的態度能否息除大眾對於法院欠缺知識及認受性的擔憂。本研究會就香港的特殊憲制情況和制度環境，建議香港法院實行司法遵從時應考慮的原則，從而建立適用於香港的司法遵從的理論體系。

759613.label: Realisation of objectives
759613.value: All three objectives have been fully realized. FIRST OBJECTIVE I conducted an empirical study of Hong Kong courts’ deferential behaviour in constitutional rights cases between 1997-2014. This is the first empirical study of deference in Hong Kong. The parameter of deference that I focused on is deference in the court’s reasoning process about the merits of a rights issue. The study covered 261 cases, with the regression analysis conducted on 131 of such cases (to be explained below). The study: 1) revealed how prevalent the issue of deference was in rights cases and offered explanations on the patterns observed; quantitative methodology was used for this part of the study. 2) showed what foreign jurisprudence shaped the courts’ approach to deference; quantitative methodology was used for this part; 3) revealed how courts usually exercised deference and what factors affected the courts’ degree of deference. This was ascertained using a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods (to be explained in the next two paragraphs). An original methodology was developed for measuring the degree of deference courts exercise in reasoning about rights issues. The methodology ranks common strategies of exercising deference, such as rights definition, standard of justification and cogency of arguments, along a triadic scale of not deferential, moderately deferential and highly deferential – an assessment that involves both qualitative and quantitative methods. The methodology for measuring deference was applied to those cases which contained enough information for the methodology to be used - 131 such cases were located. Hypotheses on the factors that affected the degree of deference were developed from a qualitative study of the cases and an examination of existing literature on deference, and the cases were coded accordingly. Regression analysis was then conducted to test those hypotheses. The findings confirmed certain hypotheses while refuting others. The methodology for measuring deference was published as “A Preliminary Framework for Measuring Deference in Rights Reasoning” (2016) 14(4) International Journal of Constitutional Law 851-882. Journal: peer-reviewed, ranked A, one of the most prestigious specialist journals in the world, published by Oxford University Press and New York University Law School. Peer reviewer: “proposes an interesting and innovative framework… explicitly demonstrates the originality of his/her article and framework, as well as its contribution to the field.” The findings of the empirical study will be published as “Rights, Proportionality and Deference: A Study of Post-Handover Judgments in Hong Kong” (2018) 48(1) Hong Kong Law Journal (forthcoming, 2018). Journal: peer-reviewed, ranked B and 1st among local law journals. Peer reviewer: “This is an excellent paper. It explores a topic that has not been addressed in the literature so far... The paper is carefully argued and expressed. It is also methodologically sound and impressive in the breadth of data it evaluates… I found the paper to be near flawless in its execution and should definitely be accepted.” SECOND OBJECTIVE I examined the findings from the above study as well as the major post-handover cases on deference in order to ascertain the approaches to deference that courts in Hong Kong adopted. I surveyed existing literature on judicial activism and deference and reflected on whether Hong Kong courts’ approaches were normatively justified. My analysis revealed whether Hong Kong courts’ approaches to deference were 1) internally logical, consistent and practicable; 3) suited to Hong Kong’s institutional environment; 3) in line with the courts’ constitutional role in Hong Kong On 1, it was found, inter alia, that Hong Kong courts borrowed their approaches from overseas and accordingly also imported the problems of those approaches. Courts have been incoherent in applying even those borrowed approaches as well as inconsistent in applying a strategy of deference – that of giving weight to the government’s judgments. Other problems with the courts’ approaches were also identified. On 2, it was found that courts made categorical assumptions about the government’s superior institutional and constitutional competence in certain subject areas. They did not test those assumptions, which is unjustified because the decision-maker may not necessarily have superior competence on all matters within a subject area. On 3, there are two limbs of constitutional legitimacy – mandate from the constitutional documents and democratic legitimacy. On constitutional mandate, flaws were identified with courts’ current approach, namely, relying on the fact that the Basic Law assigned a subject matter to a particular branch of the government as evidence that the courts are constitutionally mandated to be deferential in reviewing decisions on that subject matter by that branch. As for democratic legitimacy, the courts have deferred on democratic grounds in two ways, one of which is unsound in Hong Kong’s constitutional environment, and the other, while sound, is wrongly applied. This is the first comprehensive critical evaluation of Hong Kong courts’ approaches to deference. The findings on this objective (as well as the third objective) will be published as: “Problems with Wednesbury Unreasonableness in Contract Law: Lessons from Public Law”, Law Quarterly Review (with Ernest Lim) (forthcoming 2019). Journal: ranked A* and 3rd in the UK, generalist peer-reviewed journal, one of the most prestigious journals in the Anglo-common law world. “Judicial Deference: A Principled Approach for Hong Kong”, in a special volume on deference in Ius Comparatum – Global Studies in Comparative Law (Springer, forthcoming). THIRD OBJECTIVE I have formulated a general approach to deference which courts should adopt in jurisdictions where the government is expected to respect the fundamental values of its constitutional order and where the courts have a role to play in enforcing those values (Hong Kong included). This general approach is formulated based on reflection on the approaches to deference adopted in Hong Kong and other jurisdictions (especially the UK and European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), which the Hong Kong borrowed heavily from), academic critique of those approaches, and the problems of Hong Kong courts’ approaches distilled from the second part of the study. The suggested approach comprises eight principles. I then applied those principles to Hong Kong to illustrate how Hong Kong courts should apply them in light of the jurisdiction’s unique institutional and constitutional environment. To distill what principles of deference such unique environment called for, I studied the text of the Basic Law as well as its drafting records and the Sino-British Joint Declaration to ascertain how deferential courts were constitutionally mandated to be. I also assessed the democratic legitimacy and the rights-consciousness of the legislature and the executive to ascertain the strength of arguments on relative institutional and constitutional competence. In addition, I examined relevant case law to discern the level of experience courts have had in adjudicating particular issues that they claimed to lack expertise over. Application of the general approach to deference I proposed to these local contexts yielded principles to deference that Hong Kong courts should adopt. This is the first comprehensive attempt to formulate an approach to deference that Hong Kong courts should adopt. The findings on this part will (also) be published in the two articles listed at the end of the above section entitled “SECOND OBJECTIVE”.

759613.label: Major findings and research outcome
759613.value: FIRST OBJECTIVE UK and ECtHR jurisprudence shaped the courts’ approach to deference; courts were less deferential to policies than to primary legislation; certain judges had an anti-deference impact; courts were less deferential when moral controversy was involved and more so when a case was politically sensitive. The findings were/will be published in: “A Preliminary Framework for Measuring Deference in Rights Reasoning” (2016) 14(4) International Journal of Constitutional Law 851-882 (ITEM C8(1)). “Rights, Proportionality and Deference: A Study of Post-Handover Judgments in Hong Kong” (2018) 48(1) Hong Kong Law Journal (forthcoming) (ITEM C8(2)). SECOND OBJECTIVE Courts have imported the UK’s “spatial approach” and with it all its problems. According to this approach, courts carve out wholesale subject areas as warranting deference. This does not allow courts to be sensitive to the factors for and against deference in each case. On institutional capacity, courts make sweeping, untested assumptions about the government’s superior institutional competence. On constitutional mandate, courts’ current approach is flawed because constitutional provisions allocating a policy-making function to a branch of government does not indicate how rigorous courts ought to be in reviewing the exercise of that function. On democratic legitimacy, while it is justified for courts to defer on the ground that a democratically-returned body is more likely to be correct on a particular question, it was unjustified for them to make crude assumptions about the democratic credentials of decision-making bodies. The findings on objectives 2 and 3 will be published in: “Problems with Wednesbury Unreasonableness in Contract Law: Lessons from Public Law”, Law Quarterly Review (with Ernest Lim) (forthcoming 2019; see part III thereof) (ITEM C8(3)) “Judicial Deference: A Principled Approach for Hong Kong”, in Ius Comparatum – Global Studies in Comparative Law (Springer, forthcoming) (ITEM C8(4)). THIRD OBJECTIVE The general approach I proposed called for, inter alia, courts to determine the standard of review according to the importance of the interest at stake, give weight to the government’s judgment only if the court was uncertain of the legal answer, and to ground assumptions about the government’s superior competence in evidence. Applying these to Hong Kong, I suggested the standards of review that should be adopted and factors that courts should consider in determining how much weight to afford a governmental judgment. The findings on objective 3 will (also) be published in the two articles identified at the end of the above section entitled “SECOND OBJECTIVE”.

759613.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
759613.value: The empirical study covers up to the year 2014 only. A number of important election-related cases were handed down in the past three years – judgments that were perceived to be deferential. Changing trends of judicial behaviour may be observed if the empirical analysis is conducted again, this time incorporating post-2014 cases and factoring in certain periods of time. Also, a study covering the post-2014 period would be able to cover additional judges, such as Au, who was excluded from the current analysis owing to insufficient data points. For cases handed down after the Court of Final Appeal’s 2016 judgment in Hysan Development Co Ltd v Town Planning Board, a four- rather than three- limb proportionality test should be used as the backbone of the methodological framework. I propose that after a certain period of time – an appropriate date for bracketing the study would seem to be when Chief Justice Ma retires – that the empirical analysis be conducted again. The findings of the current study will make for comparisons with those conducted with post-2014 data and may expose constant or varying trends in judicial attitudes. (These points were made in section 5 of ITEM C(8)(2).)

759613.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
759613.value: Constitutional rights adjudication allows courts to scrutinize a wide range of government decisions. To ensure that they will not thereby become policymakers themselves, courts have used the technique of deference – deferring to governmental judgments in assessing rights issues. This study is the first comprehensive study of deference in Hong Kong. The empirical part of the study reveals what factors determined post-handover courts’ degree of deference in rights cases, enabling litigants and the government to better predict judicial behaviour. The original methodology developed for the empirical study has significance beyond Hong Kong: it can be applied to other common law jurisdictions that adopt similar principles of rights adjudication, e.g. the UK, Israel and Canada. The normative part of the project is the first comprehensive attempt to evaluate courts’ approach to deference and to propose an approach that courts should adopt given Hong Kong’s unique institutional and constitutional environment. It identifies problems with courts’ current approaches and suggests principles courts could apply to take better account of their institutional limitations in policy-making without compromising their constitutional role to check against governmental abuses of power. These proposals will pave the way for a more coherent, systematic and sound approach to rights adjudication.

760213.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
760213.value: While climate change impacts on biodiversity become increasingly apparent, especially in North America and Europe, significant uncertainty remains whether climate change will have greater or smaller relative impacts in the tropics - home to the world’s major concentrations of species and diversity. There are empirical gaps both in what is known of tropical ecology and species distributions as well as questions of theory central to our understanding of organism-climate relationships. Hong Kong (HK), which lies on the border of tropical and temperate latitudes, represents an ideal location for testing how vulnerable temperate and tropical species are to climate change. The Lepidoptera (butterflies and moths) of HK, for example, are largely tropical in origin but include many species of temperate origin. This diverse group, therefore, offers an excellent opportunity to explore how species evolutionary histories (tropical vs. temperate) might structure ecological patterns and climate change vulnerability. In this study we will utilize butterfly and moth data collected in HK over the past decade, combined with new and continued monitoring data, to better understand temperate and tropical butterfly species responses to environmental and climatic heterogeneity. We will focus sampling and analysis on elevation gradients and specifically test the hypothesis that because tropical species are adapted to a narrow range in temperature annually relative to temperate species then tropical species should be more physiologically restricted and affected by changes in elevation and temperature. This hypothesis, developed in the mid-20th century, has been central to our projections of tropical climate change impacts and implies high vulnerability to warming for the tropics. In this case, the hypothesis suggests that tropical species (HK Lepidoptera of tropical origin) should be more physiologically limited by elevation than temperate species (HK Lepidoptera of temperate origin). To test whether tropical species are more constrained by elevation than their temperate counterparts we will quantify and compare the distributions of Lepidoptera at three elevational transects spanning ≥ 500 meters throughout Hong Kong. We will also model Lepidoptera distributions throughout Hong Kong and analyze projections of those distributions under a range of climate change scenarios. Such models will highlight differences or similarities in distribution changes between tropical and temperate HK Lepidoptera. This research will thus help to resolve recent and compelling questions about tropical species’ vulnerability to global change and aid in the development of effective conservation strategy and planning. 儘管氣候變化對生物多樣性的影響越來越顯著，尤其是在北美和歐洲地區，但是作為世界主要物種和生物多樣性集中地的熱帶地區，關於氣候變化是否會對其產生相對更大或者更小的影響方面，仍然存在大量的未知。在熱帶生態、物種分佈以及對物種與氣候變化關係的核心理論的理解領域方面存在研究空缺。香港位於熱帶和溫帶的邊界線，是一個研究熱帶和溫度物種受到氣候變化影響程度的理想地點。比如香港的鱗翅目動物（包括蝶類和蛾類）中，暨存在大量的熱帶種類，也存在很多溫帶種類。這個多樣化的類群為探索物種的進化史如何促成（熱帶與溫帶）其生態模式和對氣候變化的易感度提供了良好的機會。本研究中，我們利用過去十年間香港蝶類與蛾類的數據以及持續收集中的新的監測數據來更好的瞭解溫帶和熱帶的蝴蝶種類對環境以及氣候異質性的適應情況。我們將根據不同的海拔梯度來對數據進行抽樣和分析，來特別的驗證這樣一個假設：由於相對於溫帶物種，熱帶物種適應于一個更狹窄的全年溫度範圍，所以熱帶物種應該在生理上受到海拔及溫度的限制和影響更大。這個假設形成于20世紀中葉，對關於氣候變化對熱帶地區產生影響的推測并揭示熱帶地區對全球暖化的高度脆弱性起到了非常重要的作用。在本研究中，這個假設即表明熱帶物種（香港鱗翅目中的熱帶種類）相對于溫帶物種（香港鱗翅目中的溫帶種類）應該在生理上更受到海拔的限制。爲了研究是否熱帶物種相對溫帶物種受到海拔的限制更大，我們將對香港境內三條海拔的跨度大於500米的樣線上的鱗翅目分佈進行量化和比較。我們將對香港境內的鱗翅目分佈建模，并對氣候變化情景範圍內這些分佈的預測進行分析。這樣的模型將會揭示香港的鱗翅目中熱帶種類和溫帶種類分佈變化的差異性或相似性。因此此研究將幫助解決近期引人注目的關於熱帶物種更易受到全球變化影響的問題并有助於有效保護措施及計劃的發展。
